I know alot of people will want to rage quit the second they die and their empire falls apart because they didnt set up heirs properly, or when they lose a duel they should of won easily, but alot of that is the charm of the game just at its worst. Worth buying if your patient enough to learn to love it.

After playing this game on and off since 2012 (and not using the steam launcher as much as I could cos it chugged the game for me for soem reason) I have to say teh game is dieing.
The gameplay itself is a blast and you will have fun for the first 15-20 levels, I can promise you that. The graphics are good,, though not amazing, the crafting system is one of teh best I've seen in an MMO that is not Eve Online, it does the whole real time crafting thing real well. The community has always been pretty toxic when you step into the PvP aspects oft eh game but that is to be expected as some people have grudges with others that span years now or they simply hate a faction regardless of who is on it (there are 6 total factions though now a days they do not matter due to low player count in game and removal of faction based bonuses, the only advantage now is the armor cosmetics and which faction chat your can talk in). The PvE community however is prettygood and open to help people.
Now the bad. G1G (the company that bought FE from Icarus Studios) have been doing the minimal to keep the game ticking over and making money. The game was meant to be spread over 9 total zones and having an in depth and intriguing plot and story line. When G1G bought the game I belive 4 of the zones where done (don't get me wrong the zones in this game are HUGE and pretty well detailed). Now since 2012 to now, only 1 of the new zones has been added and it's one totally thought up by G1G and has practically zero addition to game play. It is effectively a mix of 2 zones or 2 parts of 2 zones I should say, saying that it does look good, it just has no body or soul, it's just that, looks and some newarea to grind in to get a new tier of gear. It's nice however it took over a year to finish and just looks like a rehash.
Now another thing that is a MAJOR killer in this game is MASSIVE CONSTANT LAG. I'm not kidding when I say if your playing early morning in the US or late at night in the US, you will have in game lag whenever you go to loot a body (1-10 seconds to loot where normally it's instant) or if you gather a resource node. It also happens in the chat with 1-5 second lag between hitting enter and the post appearing, if it appears at all (I've had messages just go into the ether and no, not muted or anything, just parts of a convo just never get delivered). These problems result in G1G having to restart the servers at least once a day where they have to take them down for up to 90 minutes, sometimes longer, just so the game doesnt crash.
Now saying all that I must say give the game a shot, it is a good game and the latency issues are newish...well month or two of it happening every day, butif you love post apoc games and just want to drive around mad max style in a car or beaten up dune buggy with a 50 cal on the roof, this is the game for you. It just sucks how most people don't give it a good run past level 20 as at 40+ (level 55 is max level currently) is where it starts to open up and give you freedom to do whateer you want.

I've got a few things to point out, the main one being the fact that I gracefully recomment this wonderful game for all platformer-games enthusiasts out there! Not only does it bring back the ideas and art development of old-school platformer games, the best games of some people's childhood or simply pleasure and destressing times for any person (which are all, of course, pleasant memories for every gamer), but it also has an individual way of becoming remarcable, intriguing the gamers to give it a try.
The story is not too complicated, it's rebellious against reality - which, after all, is the best thing about old school games...they take you to a new world, apart from reality. This game's world is very colourful, exciting and can be quite challenging sometimes.
I also have a strong point to send across the people who gave negative feedback, making complains that don't really follow accross to be agreeable on. For example, I noticed many complain about the camera mode not being able to control. Well, think about it please, if the base idea of the game is to keep it simple and to the point, why would you want the "easy" tasks to be extremely easy too? I say the camera mode, along with other tricky details, are what really make the challenge of the gameplay be actually challenging. The opposition of these details are what really give the game the perfect ballance - it's not too easy, but nor too hard. That ballance is what makes the game fun.
I respect each gamer's opinion, positive or negative, but if you don't like these game genres or simply don't have the patience to take on the challenge of the game, why do you play? It's a shame to insult someone's work for no real valid reason.
As all's been said, once again, I think if you're looking for a relaxing fun game and enjoy adventures, this is a great game for you!

Gelu is a short but fun platformer that reminds me of old flash games. The main gimmick in this game is that you can freeze your character, respawn, and then use the ice block as a platform. You can also click to destroy the ice blocks, but I only really used this on levels with ice blocks at the start of the level.
There are 40 single screen rooms to clear and in each level you need a crowbar to open the exit. A lot of the obstacles and mechanics are introduced at the start and are reused in interesting ways throughout the game. There is a minor thing that annoys me with the gameplay and that is that you can't create a platform at the spawn location. I get why this happens, but in some levels it can be difficult to get around.
Honestly? My biggest complaint with the game is that it's too short - I would love to see a sequel that lasts longer and has more mechanics! (also, a level editor would be pretty nice) The presentation is simple but it works well enough. I got this for free but I would say it's worth the low asking price if you're looking for a short but neat puzzle platformer.

Gelu is a decent puzzle platformer but nothing particularly stands out - music, visuals, and gameplay are all fairly OK.
- Simple game mechanic and responsive controls.
- Great game for beginners: the levels are fairly simplistic, deaths are not very punshing, and you get more than enough freezes per level (for the most part).
- The hitboxes aren't very clear.
- No story, not even a simple one. You just go from crowbar to door and repeat.
- No real sense of progression. No additional skills, game mechanics, or items. Also the puzzle difficulty doesn't increase gradually; sometimes difficult levels are followed by easier levels. I feel like the developer could have simply changed the level order to improve the difficulty progression.
- I found it very unnecessary to award the player an achievement for each completed level. Not much effort was put into the achievements. You basically get one achievement per level and one when you finish the game.
I'm glad that it only took me only 30 minutes to finish the game. Gelu is a decent game but does not bring anything new to the table. I was neither impressed nor disappointed, it was just OK. Even for the low price of 0.99$ I do not feel like this game is worth your money. There are better free platformers out there such as

A return to what games are supposed to be, addictive and just fun.
Speedrunners is a wonderful return to the fun platforming days of the NES. This is a quick to learn, yet difficult to master game that is simply just fun to play, and can be enjoyed in just a few minutes.
Essentially, the crux of the game is to just run and beat your competitors by being the last one still running. However, there is much the game and other players can throw at you to insure that is not always as simple as it sounds.
Gameplay is a wonderful mash-up of old-school NES platformers. Gameplay can best be described as a mix of Super Metroid, Bionic Commando and Mario Kart all rolled into one. You and three other racers (bots, online or even local games) charge through dozens of different levels jumping, ducking, sliding, avoiding boxes, swinging on grappling hooks, and shooting different weapons at other racers. In addition, the screen itself starts to slowly get smaller and you must maximize your speed and minimize mistakes. Game winners are determined by whoever wins three rounds first, and rounds themselves are over quickly, this is a great game to play if you can only dedicate a little time to gaming.
This is a fantastic game that I recommend to all.

I can only recommend this as a single player game, since I'm not interested in playing on the online servers. So far, I have only played on a local server, and occasionally with a friend. I've heard the online servers are ruled by hackers and griefers, so bear that in mind if you want to play online.
I recommend Conan Exiles, but with a few words of caution. I think Steam would benefit from a more precise user scoring system because sometimes a simple yes or no isn't good enough.
IMO the game is best played as co-op, but there are some major issues. In co-op, the client is bound to the server host by a very short "tether" which cannot be disabled. This forces players to stay close, which can be annoying when you want to split up to farm or explore. The early levels are VERY grind heavy. If you don't mind cheating, then hosting your own server and using admin controls can take the edge off. Otherwise, get a friend to play with you and stick together. Make a home base on the bank of the river, so it's easy to find it again. There are no waypoints or quest markers in this game.
My co-op partner and I have noticed some pretty bad bugs so far, and they only get worse when latency is high. Tools and weapons go missing when you try to swap them. Sometimes the game won't let me unsheathe my weapons or interact with any of the crafting benches. Tools and weapons breaking affect the other player and sometimes cause disappearances. The game is prone to crashing and server errors. However, these are bugs which I expect to be resolved before the final release. I would suggest turning off "Loot Drop on Death" because there's nothing more frustrating than losing all your hard-earned gear to a bug.
(04/05: As of the latest patch, I've been experiencing a particularly strange bug that teleportsme  into the cursed wall when I jump out of the river. WTF?)
Despite the lack of polish in the current build I've been enjoying the game greatly. It's fun to farm, explore and build. The combat is nothing special and the AI can be spectacularly r*tarded, but since this is essentially Minecraft in the Conan universe I don't count it as a negative. And who knows what later builds will bring us?
I can't finish a review of this game without mentioning the nudity. It's great. If you can't figure out how to get the nude bodies to show, make sure you enable Full Nudity in game settings and admin settings, if you're the host. Here's hoping Australia doesn't censor this one.
Recommended. It may be best to get the game while it's relatively cheap, since the price will likely go up the closer it gets to official release.

Single Player:  In single player mode, Woodle is a very basic game in concept and execution. For a low enough price, it's an OK one player game. It would appear as though it's made for children, but some of the gaps are unforgiving, and often if you fall, you'll have to start back at the beginning of a level. What makes the game hard (and hard to recommend) is the frequent camera problems...it's the games weak point. The camera shifts are often unclear and leave much to be desired. It kills the enjoyment of a simplistic "kids" game, but it's not a bad game. The camera gets crazy sometimes in single player, but if you are thinking that the multiplayer is of interest to you, do not get this game...
Multiplayer: Of course the co-op is a new feature which was added later, but the camera works just like a 1 player game. Focus on the first player. Player two will find him/herself lost, off the screen trying to get back. (With the XBox controller, you can press "Start" and respawn relatively near the first player...but you might get stuck in a "cliff loop" where you just keep falling and falling until player one moves far away from an edge.
Overall: The game is a pass for everyone...unless you have a child that you DO NOT like and want to give the game to in order to anger them with terrible camera work, and unforgiving respawns.

There are some good things about Overgrowth, like it's exceptional combat system and the brutal feeling of how quickly the fights end.
However, I can't recommend a game that, after this long of a development time, is still very unfinished. There are many flaws in the game that have been in the game for a long time, yet have not been fixed. For example, each fight lasts a few seconds. This wouldn't be a problem, but after you die you have to sit through an animation that brings up the "try again" button, click it with a cursor that is a purple missing texture symbol, run all the way back to the fight and die after two seconds and do it all over again. It may sound like I'm nit-picking, but this becomes frustrating after a very short period of time.
Let's look at the other part of the game, the arena. Here there is the exact opposite problem, where there is not enough of a waiting time between matches. Multiple times I have been killed before I even knew the next match was happening. Sometimes it is literally impossible to get off the ground before the next match starts and your opponent kicks you in the head so hard you die. Plus, half the maps in the arena mode are bad, and there are only four map. That means you effectively have two maps in the arena mode to play with which, as you can see from my playtime, gets old really fast.
And the cherry on top is that, almost all of the complaints I have in the game have gone almost unchanged for years. The arena being too quick was added some time ago, and there are now two usable maps in arena mode, but after all this time that is not acceptable. My main problem with the game is, like many other reviews, the lack of meaningful updates from the devs. Look at Prison Architect, that game had a new feature, bug fixes, and polish added every month. Look at RimWorld, there are frequent, game changing updates from the devs. And now look at Overgrowth, where the only really meaningful things that have been added are a few new weapons and some maps for the arena. I doubt these issues will be fixed for months, and I am honestly doubting if the game will ever be finished, or if the devs will just release it in an unfinished state.

With minimalist approach to, well, kinda everything Tengami makes it tricky to talk about individual segments on their own.
What we have on our hands is a point & click adventure, but don't expect many brain teasers in this one because every single element is subservient to visually stunning pop-out book art style and presentation it employs. You should also forego story. As in plot and characters, because the only narrative outside of game's visuals that you'll experience will be haiku poems, which also double as your reward for a job well done. Tengami presents, in my opinion at least, a zen-like quest as you go through different areas solving few puzzles and just observing as beautiful visuals immerse you as part of an experience.
Now, all of this could possibly mean very little to you when you consider how short the game is – it took me just a little over an hour to complete, and you should keep in mind certain chunk of that was me being dumbfounded by my own inability to count properly as one puzzle relies on your observational skills and basic algebra. I have no excuse. I hear the WiiU version supposedly has some additional collectibles to find, but that was obviously not the version I played.
Should you get Tengami? If you can find it really cheap and look past its limited straight-from-mobile format – yes. I wish I could go into detail further, but that's kinda it. It's a ride you have to take for yourself to enjoy properly.

Normally I would probably give this game somewhere in between just a YES and NO, but since I can only choose between the two I will have to stick with a NO (details below).
+ Platforming is really fun: The Prince can do a lot of different moves and (for the most part) is easy to control, making   leaping and running around a lot of fun. Plus the difficulty for the obstacles was pretty good.
+ It looks pretty (nothing really to add here)
- Really meh story: Dumb brother releases evil thing, brother gets possessed, go kill brother. There, now you can save some time and not watch the boring cutscenes.
- Comabt: It happens way too frequently and it almost always boils down to "Mash X until everything is dead". Sometimes there are some super big guys that charge you, but even then you just need to dodge and then mash X. There are some power-ups you can get once you get enough XP from enemies, but honestly I just found mashing X was way easier and quicker then using the powers.
- Screen tearing: There's no VSync option so you're going to have to live with it! It mostly happens during cutscenes but it's still really annoying. (especially one paticular cutscene had nearly the entire screen screen tearing yuck)
- GLITCHES: Definitely the most annoying thing about this game! A few times I've had poles disapear while I was on them and other poles wouldn't let me grab onto them for some reason, but those didn't happen that often. The most annoying and frequent glitch, however, was sometimes if you got hit by a big baddy or a trap you would fall down and be unable to get back up for a few seconds. Luckily you usually didn't take damage while you were like this, but it happened way too frequently for me to just me a minor nuisance.
- Crashes: I had the game crash 4 times while I played, 3 of those was in one paticular area that I did eventually get past (there were a lot of enemies that wouldn't give XP which I tried to skip, but once I killed most of them I got past it) and once when the credits were nearly finished. Maybe I was just unlucky and they might not happen to you, but I thought I should still point this out.
- Uplay: You better have a stable connection to play this! (plus any other negatives associated w/ Uplay) I didn't have any Uplay problems while playing but I thought I should point it out anyway.
So while there are a lot of negatives, I did enjoy the platforming enough where I normally would say "Maybe?". So if you think you can get though the comabt and annoying glitches, then maybe get it when it's on sale? Otherwise, I wouldn't blame you for skipping this.

I would have to say that I'm a very average player when it comes to actually playing games. I own more than I take the time to play. Of course I would recommend this game, since why not. However, if this game is for you -- well, I hope you will find out through this along with many other reviews that have been written about Tengami.
I wouldn't say this game has no story. It is impossible to build anything without a simple plot line/purpose (that is my belief that is). Although, it isn't the typical of what one expects as a story. There are no words, but simple images and a few lines of poetry. The game starts with a man under a cherry tree (sakura tree, if you prefer it), and the tree basically dies. That is when the man is awaken and set out on a journey to collect cherry flowers (sakura flowers) to bring back to the tree and, in a sense, revive it.
It is a very short puzzle game that shouldn't take any longer than two hours on average. It is a game I would consider as "to relax to" like sudoku, crossword puzzles, word searches. It has almost a meditative music, and the sounds of nature, supported with great art work. A game you might only play once, or again to see if you can solve the puzzle faster, or look back at things you might have missed, or even to play in the background for its soundtrack and admiring the art.
If it is something more challenging, quest like, thrilling, etc., this game isn't for you, but if it is something to relax and slow your day down with, I suggest to give it a try. Not all of life should be fast pace filled with action. It might be surprising what one learns when taken the time to slow down a bit.

Jet Set Radio is a very eccentric 90's themed game. Essentially, you play as a roller skater who skates around Tokyo-to spraying grafitti everywhere. Along the way you encounter rival gangs, people who you can compete with to join your gang, and the police. The latter plays the stereotype of extreme police brutality even just to catch some punks, using everything in their arsenal from helicopters to flamethrowers. The soundtrack has clear inspirations from 90s genres like Nu Metal, hip hop, and synthpop, among many others (my personal favorites are Miller Ball Breakers and Bout the City). The music just turns me on ;)
JSR certainly isn't lacking in originality. It's music is very diverse (as stated earlier), and it goes against the grain from many of the trends in gaming. The story in this game isn't anything to write home about, and the graphics can look really sloppy at times, but SEGA made up for it in the gameplay. The skating mechanics are very polished, and although it's easy to learn it's a
difficult game to master. It's certainly not easy, but it's not rage-inducingly hard becuase the game isn't unfair, and once you get enough practice, you can really get the hang of it. However, the gameplay was designed around using the analog stick. If you want the maximum enjoyment out of this game,
use a controller. Trying to input the motions for spraying graffiti is really clunky with the WASD keys, it takes a ton of getting used to, and it gets really uncomfortable after a while. It's certainly not impossible though, and you can still have fun playing it regardless (I know I did).
The amount of time it takes to finish the story line is somewhat on the short side (I play through games slowly and beat it in 10 hours). However, if you want to 100% this game and/or you want to challenge yourself to get Jet ranking on every level, I wouldn't be suprised if it was more like 100 hours because, again, it's a hard game to master. If you want replayability out of a game, I'm not very qualified to tell you, since I hardly like replaying antything.
In short, if you hate 90s culture, you'll most likely hate everything about this game. If you tend to prefer story-based games, JSR might be very forgettable. But if your preference is for gameplay, then JSR can be a really fun experience that I think you should try out.

I wish I had something good to say about Woodle Tree Adventures. It's colorful art style brings back fond memories of classic 3D platformers, which much to my dismay have all but disappeared from gaming in recent years. As much as I wanted to love Woodle, as a game it's among the worst designed, most disappointing experiences I've had in a very long time. It took only an hour of my time to complete, but it felt like so much more with how depressing those sixty minutes were.
Woodle Tree is a very traditional collectathon platformer on paper; traverse levels picking up inane objects to bring back a spirit tree that's grown sad over the disappearing water of the world. Upon actually playing the game, everything instantly loses its enticing charm, reduced to a lesson in how to completely ruin a genre that I hold especially close to my heart.
At the forefront of all these problems is the games camera, which for reasons I cannot understand was chosen to be fixed in place, presumably moving with you and positioning itself as to best allow you to get through levels. This is a bad idea for more reasons than I care to list, the biggest being that it makes judging the distance for jumps incredibly difficult, not to mention caused me an extreme amount of motion sickness (something I've never experience in a game). Levels are designed with a noticeable lack in direction, full of pointless dead ends, oddly position platforms, and invisible checkpoints that neither tell you when you reach them or work as intended much of the time.
The sound design is just sad to have to listen to, with awful sound effects and a soundtrack that is chaotic, perhaps even musically offensive. The cute art design is the only thing I can give scant amounts of praise to, but even that loses its charm when it jumps radically between styles, none of which are particularly interesting to look at or even reflect the lighthearted feel the game seems to be going for.
I'd like to say Woodle Tree Adventures isn't one of the most dismal games I've played recently, but there is nothing I can even partially recommend it for, and wish I'd headed the words of others and passed on it myself. It left me feeling hollow, and sad for the developer who almost seemed to have something at a point before it slipped through his fingers.
It's really no wonder the spirit tree is crying. I would too if I was stuck in this game any longer than I was.

BG2EE is a fine re-release of one of the greatest games of all time. BG2 stands at the top of the ranking at the classic RPG site GameBanshee - and deservedly so. Beamdog's Enhanced Edition brings the game to modern HD displays, and Steam - so that you never have to look for your CDs again.
There are many things that make BG2 great, and in their sum, they can be described as a spirit of complete and total confidence. It takes self-assurance to drop the player straight into the big hub of the game, bury him in quests, and let him figure things out. It takes conviction to fill a game to the brim with utterly broken enemies, spells, and abilities, and yet achieve a sort of a balance. It takes grand vision to hand-draw the phenomenal backgrounds of BG2, and compose a soundtrack fitting for a 3 hour epic Holywood production. It takes genius to emphasize the hero's companions to such an unprecedented degree.
And the results are magnificent. In BG2, you can one-shot majestic dragons, and be one-shot by nasty mind-flayers. You can yield insanely broken weapons such as Crom Fayr, and still enjoy finding a decent offhand in the Underdark. You can build your entire strategy around brutal backstabs, or never hide in shadows the entire game. You can power-game and try to beat the game with a solo Paladin, or pick an off-kilter class such as the Bard Skald, accept the roll the game gives you, and dive into adventure with your trusty comrade Minsc. You can exploit every mechanic to become a true demigod, or play it hardcore and delete your character if he dies.
And though the purely combat-oriented RPG in BG2 is good, it is the characters that really make the game (as is the case with other memorable titles such as Planescape Torment and Mass Effect 2). Video games seem to be a poor medium when it comes to conveying strong stories and plots; but they are perfect vehicles for character development. And fundamentally, as has been the canon in the West ever since the times of Plato and beyond, character development translates to a character's confrontation of his or her weaknesses, a journey through the darker corners of the soul, a quest for self-understanding.
It is in this aspect of its monumental edifice that BG2 succeeds, while perhaps not totally, at least to such a degree as to leave a lasting impression. Who can forget the trials of dark Viconia, her anguish at facing the cruelty of her kin imprinted upon her own soul, her doubts, her fears, and her eventual ascent to tranquility? Who can forget Minsc who finds himself a new witch in the little waif Aerie? What of Anomen, who visibly grows from a boy to a man before the player's eyes, and with the player's help? Is it not fitting that Sarevok, now humbled and desperate, should ultimately join his brother? Who can forget the player's sibling, the fiery little tortured Imoen?
And what of the protagonist's foes? The nasty little sister Bodhi, and the mighty - yet so tragic - Jon Irenicus? Surely the voicework on Irenicus is among the best ever done in a computer game.
Finally, there is the protagonist himself - forced to face his fears, his demons, his destiny, and his nature. Will he choose to become a God and wreak havoc upon mortals and divines alike? Will he ascend his throne and try to change the essense of his heritage? Or will he willingly forsake immortality, and tread the roads of Faerun along with his trusty friends? It is up to you...
And though one can distinctly see Bioware run out of steam by the time of Throne of Bhaal, the final episode of the saga still manages to include some of the finest fights of the entire series; and loot galore beyond imagination.
Before concluding this review, let me say a few words about Beamdog's new content. I did Rasaad's missions, and though he had been a pathetic weakling for most of BG1EE and some of BG2EE, after about the midgame, Rasaad became a monster. Toward the end he was as powerful as my main (a Blade) and Minsc. His quests, unfortunately, were horribly broken and buggy throughout the entire saga. When the quests worked, they were great. But most of the time they did not work. The final fight in Rasaad's sequence, in particular, is heroically buggy, and took me an hour of replays to win - because I had to figure out how to activate the correct triggers in the right order.
But, by and large, the new NPC's are solid, and fit the game reasonably well. They are nothing to shout about, but they work.
BG1EE took me 30 hours for a fairly complete playthrough; and BG2EE another 60. If you have never played the game, you should. And if you have, like me, last played it maybe a decade ago - well, with this rerelase, maybe it's time you refreshed your memories. Good movies and good books never get old. And neither will BG2.

This game is amazing.  I can't stop playing it.
Let's start out with the first thing you do in the game; character customization.  You have 4 races to choose from, each with their own unique traits, backstory, and affect how everyone treats you.  Lizards can dig without a shovel, Dwarves can crawl into small spaces nobody else can, Elves can eat body parts to learn the memories of the fallen (sometimes gaining skills in the process), and so forth.
You've got a lot of choices for playstyles as well, and it's not set in stone.  You could start off the game as a wizard, then transition into a battlemage who charges into the fray, then unleashes spells that require proximity.
Then, you've got the Tags.  Basically, they let you set up your own backstory, as well as giving additional dialogue options when the time is right.  Mystics can sometimes talk to the gods, whilst Barbarians want a *simple* solution to many problems.  But the best is yet to come...  and it's something that I'm a bit of a sucker for.  Music.  You can set the lead instrument on the soundtrack.  It's only four instruments, and the one you choose will be, well, the prominent instrument throughout the soundtrack.
Not a fan of character customization?  That's fine, you can select an Origin character.  These guys normally would be optional party members if you were to create your own character, but you can also play as them for your main character.  The choices are really interesting too; a lizard who cavorted with demons and got exiled, wanting to reclaim his empire; or a human who is a host of all kinds of spirits while a demon is trying to wrest control of her body.  They all have pre-set tags, but you can choose the class they start with.
Now for the gameplay.
Out of battle, stuff is simple; everything is performed from your clicking (duh).  However, even outside of combat your skills are still tested.  Persuasion can be a way to get out of a fight, or get more information out of someone, bartering lowers prices for you.  You can also steal stuff too, but be warned if you played the first game; the stealing has been revamped by quite a lot.  You can no longer just walk into someone's house, close the door and sneak about, stealing everything that isn't bolted down.  The moment you take something, no matter if you're sneaking or not, the townsfolk will become suspicious and try to search you.  Of course, there's ways to make sure they don't succeed, but I'll leave that since a lot of this game is about finding your own playstyle.
The combat is not really changed by much from the first game, but many more complexities have been added.  Surfaces play a crucial role to a mage just like before, however they have many more options due to the magic trees.  Water can be frozen, electrified, or turned into steam which can also be electrified.  Bless can actually turn surfaces, well, blessed, healing characters who travel through it.  (That includes everyone, so make sure blessed surfaces can't be accessed by the enemy.)  However, there is also Cursed surfaces, which carry extra effects to them.  Necrofire can't be put out by normal water, Cursed Oil can go off on MOVEMENT, and so forth.
Armor is no longer a stat that simply decreases damage received, it is instead its own bar.  This bar is crucial to manage, as it stops status effects.  Think of it as a shield; as long as you have a shield up, you can't be affected by the status of a surface your character may be standing on, with certain exceptions as Oil that slows you down.
As a general rule of thumb however, the game's combat is very challenging.  There really isn't many fights that have "cannon fodder" enemies; everyone is dangerous and they all know how to take advantage of the same things you do.  Be careful about that water you're standing on, for that mage on higher ground likely might have an electric spell he could cast, if your magic armor is down, and stun you.
My recommendation?  This game deserves all the praise that it's got and more.  The only real complaint I have is with the camera control, but that's mainly due to my mouse having issues with some games not registering the middle mouse click.  Plus, in battle you can get a top-down view if there's too many obstacles.

the development isn't dead, the devs even have a "show" on their website where they talk about the progress of the game, just because updates don't come out often and the game has been in development for a few years doesnt mean it's in development hell, because it still gets updates and as far as i'm aware they add quite a bit when they do come out. I should probably talk about the actual game now, since this is an edit and the original review was written before the game entered beta (which really proves what i wrote before now). Overgrowth is a brutal combat game based off of a skeletal structure instead of a health bar, the combat is insanely quick and challenging and requires a hell of a lot of concentration to get right, but it is a very simplistic system, right click to block and left click to attack. But behind the brutal combat there is a lovely parkour system which is just as refined as the combat and if you like both those things or one then this is quite frankly the perfect game for you.
THE WEAPONS:
Knives: quick and brutal but you can take a few strikes (slightly unrealistic in how they attack with slashes)
Spears: Long range stabbing and good for throwing
Short swords: one handed sword which can kill in one strike if the right attack is used but may take 2 hits
Long/Great swords: two handed slightly slower alway a one hit kill and really difficult to fight against.
GAME MODES:
right now there are a few game modes, the two main ones being Lugaru (which is the levels from the predecessor to the game named "Lugaru" ) and Arena which is a selection of levels in which you partake in gladiatorial combat against enemies, there are many variations on the match conditions and you will get most of your gameplay from this (the Lugaru campaigns levels are very short), but there are also other game modes like individual levels which are short little parkour and combat levels or sometimes just parkour but there is a large selection of them as well as user made levels. Finally there is the versus in which you and a friend fight using the games glorious combat system which is probably great fun but i dont have anyone to play with.
CONCLUSION:
Get the game if you want an insanely precise and deadly combat sytem and a beatifully smooth parkour system.
By the way you can break your neck if you land on it too hard (same case with your spine).

The greatest RPG of all time getting even better! I simply can't get enough of this drug of a game. And it's incredible how 15 years since I played it for the 1st time I find myself playing it and enjoying it just the same as I did in those days. This enhanced edition is truly beautiful and well polished, it runs like a dream, and everything is in place. The new companions are awesome, the refined gameplay works, and if you never played BG2 before then you should definitely grab this because otherwise you'll be missing out on a seriously epic RPG.
Now lets also note a few things. This is a very old game that has been reworked in a minimal fashion to make it compatible with Steam. As of this current patch gen, the game features an improved interface, new difficulties added, and the correction of many bugs. This doesn't change the fact the game is old! If you are not into vintage games, this title may not be for you, as playing this game is like getting on a time machine back to the early 2000s, which was the golden era of RPGs. My #1 favorite RPG of all time. Baldur's Gate 2 is a CRPG from 2000-2001, which uses the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd Edition (2.5E really since they introduce kits & high level "feats") ruleset, with a real-time twist. The game plays in real-time but can be paused at any point to assign orders, cast spells, or use items, which execute upon unpausing and complete during a combat round.
Huge amount of character customization, over 200+ spells, high levels of character advancement, and a ton of items, all with interesting background and stories behind them to really appease the min-maxing crowd.
The biggest selling points however, are the characters and storyline. You'll find some of the most unique, interesting, and downright fun NPCs in any game ever. The storyline, which may seem cliched now, makes the struggle with your divinity, much more real, when your divine essence is taken from you by force. Quests are far from straight-forward, with many of them introducing some interesting moral dilemmas. Not to mention the replayability introduced as your party members will chime in with their own thoughts, inter-party banter, and even party member conflicts which will require multiple playthroughs to experience.
Finally, there's a modding community working hard to adapt many of the old mods for the new enhanced edition. Thankfully, most of the hardcode in the EE version is the same, and most mods should work fine. Mods can add another 50-100+ hours to this already content-packed game.
I can't recommend this game enough. To players who haven't played CRPGs from the 80s-90s, be warned that there is a steep learning curve. But once you overcome it, you'll have one of the most defining experiences in gaming ever.
Big learning curve, but it's worth the time.

Bientôt l'été ("Nearly summer") takes me back to University and film appreciation courses. This is as existential as a game could possibly be. It makes "Dinner Date" look like Minecraft.
This is a walk on the beach simulator, diddling with a chess board simulator, yearning conversation with a ghost simulator. I think there were cigarettes and wine to be had, too.
While I'm generally down with the whole "this-is-not-a-game" concept, I would have enjoyed Bientôt l'été more if it didn't take an age to walk anywhere, and if it adhered to standard norms for controlling your in-game avatar. You have to close your eyes before you can open a door? What is that all about? I spent a lot more time looking at the control scheme than I should have needed to.
Also, the game apparently needs other people playing at the same time so you can be paired up male/female for weepy, maudlin conversation where you take turns selecting phrases from a list of approved phrases. Presumably you are holiday-fling soulmate lovers, by the tone of the conversation. If nobody else is present, you get to have this conversation with a ghost, but the ghost just chooses random phrases, which isn't very satisfying. My point is, it's essentially a multiplayer game, but multiplayer doesn't work because nobody is "playing" this "game."
Having said that, I still give Bientôt l'été a thumbs-up. Because, you know, well, ...boobs.

Forest Warrior took me completely by surprise. I looked at no reviews, videos or screenshots before I played the game, and I thought it was simply just a platforming 8-bit game. Forest Warrior is a 2D action-survival game. You fend off zombies, birds, and wolves that are attacking you in the forest. The game has great visuals and animations, wonderful and relaxing music, and interesting gameplay.
Gameplay –
You start off on the first night with just your hatchet, and many zombies attempting to kill you. You have to fight to survive and each wave has increasing difficulty. As you progress through the game you get more weaponry to fight off the enemies. The game is challenging, as you only have 3 hearts, but the game is still enjoyable. The only issue I had with the gameplay is that the range on the axe is very long, and seems to be a bit buggy, as the animation plays and the hit registers after the animation is completed. The birds are a huge pain, as they move extremely fast and you can’t seem to roll out of the way of them. You have special abilities that charge up by getting kills, which you can then activate to provide a huge advantage against the enemies. If you charge up all 4 bars, you unlock your rampage ability, which lets you spin around with your axe and destroy every enemy in your path for 20 seconds. I was unable to make it past Wave 4, but there are bosses in the game, as well as other weapons like grenades. It is very challenging, but I had lots of fun playing it.
8/10
Graphics –
I always gush over 8-bit or pixellated games, as it reminds me very much of many classics I love. The visuals are pretty and detailed, with the puffy clouds drifting by in the background as you slaughter zombies. I was very surprised by the animations however, as they are quite spectacular. The pause menu is very beautiful; it zooms out and has a lovely blue shimmer around the screen. When you swing your axe you feel the power in the swing, as the screen pulses and the enemy reacts very well to the axe hitting them. During the swinging animation there is a trail of blood falling behind the axe from the enemies you have killed. You can see the kickback when you fire the gun and it has a big flare from the bullet exiting the barrel. There is a blood splatter animation when you hit an enemy and when you kill them they shatter and pieces of them get blown away in the wind. Overall the game is very beautifully crafted with wonderful animations.
9/10
Audio –
The music in Forest Warrior is spectacular. It is very relaxing and enjoyable. For example, I have been listening to the menu screen music for the entirety of the time I wrote this review. The enemy sound effects, like the caws of the birds and the growls of the zombie are wonderful and sound very nice. The sound of your axe hitting the enemy is very satisfying, as you can hear the axe embedding into the enemy, and the splatter as well. The gun sounds very similar to a real gun and the sound of the bullet hitting is also satisfying. The soundtrack in Forest Warrior is amazing, and the sound effects are great.
8/10
Conclusion –
Forest Warrior is a beautifully crafted 8-bit indie game, and I highly recommend it. It is difficult at times but is very enjoyable. There is no real story to the game, but that is usually common in survival games like this, and a story in a game like this might not appeal to some people who just want to kill some monsters. It is a great game to play when waiting for time to pass or you just want to hop in and slaughter some zombies. However, I don’t believe the game is worth the whole $3.99, as there isn’t much gameplay, even though there are many waves to conquer. Nonetheless, it is still a great game and if you manage to catch it on sale I highly recommend that you snag it and have some fun killing monsters!
Overall – 8/10

tl;dr
This game is about treasure hunting! Search for wanted treasure that you can either choose to keep or sell for profit. Find artifacts in anomalies, or find a stash of weapons and ammo hidden under a log!
This game was incredibly imersive, which was awesome! I love this game. Easily ranks one of the best games I have ever played. Sniper game play was best gun play ever! (I stalked around always sneaking, and modified my guns for accuracy, arcing, and velocity.) Master difficulty was a great challenge!  (end of tl;dr)
Attempt to take out an entire building of sentient enemies with stealth attacks. The more silent you are, the more deadly you become. Enemies see only whats in their vision, but hear whats in their hearing range. Crouch for an aim boost with near silent movement. Turn on night vision and pull out your silenced weapon to become the ultimate STALKER! (easy, but still fun!)
Each NPC has a unique name, and they will remember if they like you. They can die from enemies too, though. The killed NPCs are replaced with a tenth as many fresh new NPCs, which makes you feel like you put a dent in the zone. If you shoot your friend once, they will forgive you. If you shoot them twice, then its war... Plus their faction will also like you less.
There are different groups/factions. Zombies, Bandits, Loners, Stalkers, Duty, Freedom, Military, and most feared of all Monolith. Bandits rob Stalkers, and Stalkers collect artifacts. You can save anytime you want. I suggest keeping 4 rotating saves. Which makes winning a serious battle, actually possible. Making you the most badass in the zone! Although, no one truly knows how cool you are due to saves! ;D (I wish there was a video replay, where it played back your battle. It would be sweet to see how elite your character is, minus the reloads of saves.)
Mutated animals run around constantly. The types of mutated creatures become really sneaky and different than you can imagine. They will often attack other mutants types, and even patrolling squads. Sometimes wiping them out. You will have to make decisions on helping NPC communities survive, which plays out as a different game with different endings.
Better equipment comes much faster from purchasing from a specific NPC for costly prices. But you will gain access to similar guns later, from fallen enemies, except armor never drops from enemies. You can watch a bullet fall with gravity as it speeds towards a distant target. If you choose to use a sniper weapon, you will have to adjust your manual aim to compensate for this new thing called gravity. Also, the distance between you and your target feels real!
You can also upgrade your favorite weapons and armor from certain characters. You scratch my back, I'll scratch yours. My favorite weapon is the silent sniper's Vintar BC named Tide. And the upgraded exoskeleton with servomotors.
Now for the meat of the game! There are artifacts which you treasure hunt for!! They are expensive, and fetch a very pretty penny when sold. But they also have bonuses which will help you defeat certain mutants and especially more anomalies. Artifacts are hidden, invisible from sight, but spring out when located in anomalies, which are dangerous ghost like traps. If you hear your radiation meter going off, throw a metal bolt by pressing 6, to see if you are about to get zapped by stepping on a trap. Also, if you hear radiation, you are probably getting pummeled with radiation poisoning. Might want to step back. Find better artifacts to get less exposure! But nothing* will save you from a storm, so if they say to take cover, then get inside where its safe.
Lastly, the atmosphere is really in depth. Everyone speaks with a Russian accent, and when the wind blows the bushes wave. Day/Night cycles and eating let you feel like you are really camping in the zone. Its cold and a loner's friend.
Press N for Nightvision
Press P for MAP, stats, and current chat logs
Press 6 for bolts
Press Y to change your ammo type
Press 9/0 for automatic fire or single shot fire
Press O to pull out your radiometer/geiger counter
I switched my shift to sprint, ctrl to regular crouch, z for low crouch, c for flashlight.
Press F to take stuff or talk to people
Press Q/R to lean around corners for less risky exposure to shots fired.

Along your journey you'll encounter many interesting characters who you'll enjoy interacting with, each with their own in depth back stories. The story itself is very well paced and manages to constantly keep you engaged, even if the quest journal is currently a bit difficult to follow. Nonetheless you'll enjoy reading through it to work out what to do next because you enjoy the story and what's going on in the game world, which if anything is a lot better than mindlessly following quest markers. On top of this the combat is very well thought out and original, think a fantasy take on Xcom but more fluid, and with more opportunity to experiment and be creative with your strategies. Whether it's quests, character development, or combat, you always get the feeling that there's near endless different solutions, and you feel satisfied when your choices play out the way you like.
Replay value - 10
Because of the amount of choices you're going to make in just one playthrough, when you start a new game it can feel like a completely different journey entirely, with a whole cast of different characters if you like, distribute them with different roles than last time, learn different skills that you never tried before and experiment with them in new ways. Solve quests in different ways to last time (I've found even that there's at times more than 2 solutions to a quest!), or find yourself doing new quests that you never came across during your first playthrough. Save an NPC from dying and find out if that leads to any new content you otherwise missed, or outright kill whoever you want and deal with the consequences, or rewards..... Also there's Tactician difficulty which is a great challenge for your next playthrough, and not only is it more difficult, but enemies will surprise you with new threats. On top of this there's co-op to enjoy with a friend which makes the game always worth coming back to.
Conclusion
It's a rare occasion to be presented with an RPG with so much attention to story and characters, yet at the same time have so much depth in the gameplay that you can become hooked. It's a true RPG which harkens back to the likes of Balders gate, yet much easier to pick up and play. Things like fully voice acted dialogue and a streamlined combat system make the game a very fluid and enjoyable experience. If you are already a fan of classic CRPG's, or a fan of RPG's in general then you absolutely owe it to yourself as a gamer to pick this game up, you will not be disappointed. If however your idea of an RPG is more something like Fallout4 or Skyrim then I'd say this, Divinity II can be a bit slow paced for console gamers to adjust to, but I promise you if you give it a chance, you'll not only enjoy a far better and truer RPG experience, but one of the best RPG's ever created.
Overall score 10/10 - must buy

I really really like this game but it is not for everyone.  I have been looking for a game with type of intense and deep strategy and diplomacy for a long time.  Where most games rely on hack/slash and army building/conquering through superior fire power, CK2 is centered on deep political manipulation.  Not since the first incarnation of Romance of the Three Kingdoms (dating myself) have I been able to find a game that does this well.
There are ton of game mechanics that I dont want to go into because someone more worthy than I can probably explain them better.  CK2 requires patience and researching game elements and NPC characters.  You really begin to understand the life of an anchient monarch who imprisoned his baren wife or planned the murder of his oldest, slothful drunkard son before he can take the throne.  In CK2, you do not simply play one patriarchal/matriarchal ruler, you play generations.  Thus, when you die, you assume the role of the next in line.  Each turn is a game year and this is an era of wars, plagues, and conspiracies to murder or dethrone you.  Building your legacy often requires establishing alliances via arranged marriages, or placing a son into the church with sites on becoming the pope.  CK2 is not a light hearted game.  Surrounding yourself with good, trustworthy people are key.  There are times when you need to build (rather buy) armies and conquor lands but most often, the road to victory is paved before battlefield is established.  You will find yourself digging and investigating the traits of everyone around you in order to find the best candidates to polulate your court or tutor your children.  Once accomplshed, you will then find yourself doing what you can to keep them happy.  For some, this means assinging courtly titles to them, for others it may mean finding them a spouse.  In short, 'Its not easy being King', or Duke, or whatever role.
Also, you dont necessarily start, or want to start as a king.  You will certainly have land holdings but aquiring more land and conquoring territiories will elevate you through the status pool.  Of course, this will also earn you numorous enemies along the way whose death wont always end your problems.  PS, keep the church on your good side.

Although this game can have some problems. Mainly with Hack-Shield. Once you get it working, have fun with your addiction. This game is pure fun. I can't get enough.
The developers goal was to basically combine console level Hack'n'Slash gameplay with traditional MMORPG features. And it worked. It worked so well. The character customization is a bit lacking, but it is still there. The game is not a money sucker by any means. When they same Free-to-play, they mean free to play.
The graphics overall are not the greatest, even on max settings. But as long as you are not a graphics Wh*** you should be fine. But overall, the graphic style is very nice. It's bright-ish Anime inspired graphics are not exactly new to the MMO genre, but overall are nice.
I haven't even gotten to the Combat. Oh my, I can not get enough of this gameplay. The combat is absolutely gorgeous. It has your basic left-click attack. Your right click is your special. And then you have your skills, the skills are respectivly on the number keys, which does take a little while to get use to at first. But after awhile it won't be so irritating.
The music in this game is also quite beautiful, and works perfectly in the background to build tension. It is no Kingdom Hearts or Elder Scrolls, but it is still quite nice. The composers did a nice job.

A great game that follows the styles of combat, obstacles and most things from the original trilogy of Prince Of Persia (The Sands of Time, Warrior Within and The Two Thrones).
Been a fan of this series for a huge long time, I used to think the game didn't have that kind of charm and fun in adventure and platforming like the original trilogy, after the spin-off game Prince Of Persia was released back in 2008. (which in my opinion was a good game that has nice story with good characters, though it was a strange spin-off) but I'm really glad I was so wrong
Obstacles and platforming:
- One of the two special charms of the whole series, hard to dispute this game can pull off without these beautifully made mechanism of traps, and the design of the way to guide the player through them.
- Some of the obstacles are back from the Original Trilogy (the Spikes, the straight-up high walls, the swinging axes, the running saw wheel..) and some even from the 2008 spin-off game (sliding slope..)
- Newer, bigger and much harder obstacles in the game (one of which is the multiple layers of water wall, which in my opinion is the hardest of all obstacles I have ever seen in the whole series, and also the swinging huge thorn tree log)
- The platforming has been upgraded to a higher new level, this means whoever still got the mind back when playing the original trilogy, now can rest assured that their style of platforming will be upgraded to a higher new level. Since it requires 1 or 2 more steps to pass the ostacles.
- The Saving Checkpoints were arranged nicely , typical of the whole series itself
Combat:
- No longer a young prince, this guy now can make a lot of nicer attacks, combos and smoother acrobatic movements. However, The Forgotten Sands does not have the old mechanism of using 2 swords + combos (which were in the original Trilogy) , or stealth kill (The Two Thrones)
- One thing has returned from The Sands of Time: You got a fight with a huge platoon of enemies by yourself! But that doesn't mean you can't take them all out.
- In fact, the enemies in this game are pretty not that hard to face, which doesn't seem to be much of a concentration in this game, since the design, scenery, platforming element and story of the game are the main focus.
- The new system of using 4 natural elements in this game are pretty nice to help you with all the combat, though after a while, you'll recognize that they are only useful in facing some types of enemies.
- A whole new system of upgrading (which was only from the spin-off game, not the original trilogy) will help you get so much better. And I agree with this decision of Ubisoft Montreal. No more running around trying to find the upgrades and water sink to recover the health (Warrior Within), you can get Health, Energy and XP from the enemies and vases (which is an old point of the original trilogy)
Design and graphic:
- The design of the obstacles, the platforming in The Forgotten Sands are smooth
- The color when using the elements are really nice, especially when you freeze the time flow of the water, each drop of the water wall is so clear to see and beautifully made.
- However,... once again, it seems the enemies are not really the main focus of the game, so they are quite not that well designed, but it doesn't matter, what matters is what they can do to you though.
I believe most people who used to play the original trilogy should check this game out and get immersed in the World of the Prince of Persia once more. Even if you haven't played the Trilogy, this game still won't make you feel disappoint at all. In fact, it may even bring you back to play the original trilogy itself!
Rating: 9/10 by me. -0.5 because the Djin temple quite lacked the design and change in the 2 pictures (you'll see, they should have recorded the moments of the game) , -0.5 because the challenge mode lacks too much effort invested by Ubisoft.
Have fun!
P.S: Ezio is also spotted in the game, though in different shape. But who knows, maybe someday AC and POP can be brought together.
- Of course, since it was released back in 2010, try to buy the game when it's on sale.

This game is a mix of TD and Arcade genres. From Tower Defense games it got point A, where enemies come from, and a target B, which they are trying to destroy. This game also contains "towers", which are not towers, but units, which follow your "Bard".
So the goal of the game is eliminate 20 waves of enemies moving your hero as a locomotive, while your units are killing enemies without your manual control. Despite moving and hiring new units you can also collect droppable items, like gold or notes (in game currency) and use powerups. I think.. that's all, what you can do in the battle... and, actually, it's enough to be satisfied..... enough until you die.
After the death, you appear in the loddy room, where you can upgrade your hero, troops and base using gold, which was dropped from the killed enemies in the battle. Each unit has 7 upgrades, there 20+ units. But only a few available at the start. Also, there are 10 upgrades for your hero with 2-5 levels and 6 upgrades with 2-5 levels for the base. In my opinion, it's a good addition to the game.
When you finished with upgrades you start the game and.... you appear at the level 1... again. Even if you passed Level 4 in the last session... you start from Level 1.... And that's the great problem with this game. It's incredible repetitive game.
So, actually I wanted to play further, but I didn't want to play the same levels again and again for just getting gold and I had not enough unit power to beat the next level.So... sorry, but I appreciate my time.
There are also two mine-games. First mode is endless run, classic arcade, you run until you die :D
The second is similar to main gameplay. The main difference you protect nothing except you. You will get new new unit every 20-30s. So, just run and survive.
Both modes weren't interesting for me.
- Interesting idea of the gameplay
- Nice sound design
- No bugs were found
- Cheap game
- Every session starts from the beginning of the stage. There are 4 stages with 5 levels in each one. So even if you passed 4 levels and get killed by the boss in the 5th level, you are forced to play about 15 minutes in the first 4 levels before you can give him a revanche.
- It's impossible to complete the game from the first try, because your squade is weak. So you need to replay the game again and again before you will be strong enough to kill the boss on the 20th level.
- The game looks the same during all 20 waves
- Annoying delay when Bard performs 5s guitar solo after each unit summoning or using ability
- Unbalanced difficulty curve. 1-4 levels are extremely easy ( and boring because of it), but when boss comes and wipes you out in a couple of seconds....
A nice idea for the game which was spoiled with insanely grind system and repetitive gameplay. I can't recommend it.

When building a new game in saturated genres, indie developers reach pretty far to find some impressive concepts to implement that make their game stand out.  With Bardbarian it seems like the most interesting part of the game, the idea that this warrior is using music as his weapon, is left behind – making the title itself less descriptive of the game than the generic genres it crosses over.
The title “Bardbarian” had me thinking I was going to see something heavily related to music, maybe even a rhythm game.  After watching the trailer I saw that it was a good bit different from that, but I figured it would at least involve a little more player involvement than I ultimately discovered.  The primary goal of the game is the defense of a crystal, so the premise is essentially a tower defense game.  You play the role of the Bardbarian who takes up this defensive goal, except you as a character have virtually no direct influence on the invading enemies that seek to destroy the town's crystal.  You instead play guitar riffs (which consume the resource you build over time playing your guitar) that recruit people that do the fighting.  Then your task is to drag these people around letting them attack the enemy for you as they gain their own levels and lose their own health.
The progress thread of the game is formatted in waves like any tower defense game.  Gold is dropped by your enemies to upgrade your fighters, unlock new fighters, upgrade your character's stats, and add features to the town and level.  You must make it to checkpoints to be able to start from them, which will prevent you from having to start the game from the very beginning for each run, similar to the way some roguelites work.  This design is where the game really hits its biggest problem.  It's set up in a way where you could, if it was at all possible, go through the entire game from the start, however you're easily beaten even before the first checkpoint in order to arbitrarily get the player to do upgrades.  This means that you're relegated to the same content repeatedly, not just to be able to get to a checkpoint, but to be able to gain enough gold to upgrade and move forward from that first it.  The game loses a lot of momentum very quickly with repetition, and upgrades rarely change the gameplay in any significant way.  I found myself burnt out on nearly every aspect within the first half hour.  What's worse is that they double down on that by featuring looped music and a lack of creativity in enemy design.  You end up living and dying by the upgrade system rather than player skill and that is a surefire way to make a game that slams the player with boredom.
I'm still going to be on the look out for developers that build good or even just average games on unique and fun concepts.  Bardbarian just isn't one of those.  Getting this game, regardless of it's low cost, isn't something I would recommend.  There are better games that cross over the tower defense and RPG genre out there, both new and old.

The first and most damaging is the fact that you cannot control the camera.  In a 3D platformer where it's very easy to mis-time your jumps, that's a quick road to frustration.  Even worse, sometimes the game will change your camera angle for you, making it hard to see a jump that a moment before was perfectly visible.  Add in the fact that if the character's pack is full it enlarges so much sometimes that you have trouble seeing past it and you can see that earlier potential just start to bleed away in a flurry of missed jumps.
The second flaw doesn't directly affect gameplay, but it affects immersion a lot.  That is, the character animation.  For the most part this is fine, and I really do like little touches like being able to jump until Woodle is upside-down.  Charming.  But when walking about the world, I noticed very quick that the walk animation doesn't interact at all with the ground.  The speed at which you move seems independant of the motion of the legs, giving a feel of sliding about which may not seem like a lot but since you have to look at this for the entire game, it gets a bit bothersome.  And to a degree, since you can't really tell speed from watching the character, sometimes it's hard to judge jumps and you're down into the abyss again.
The third is the general lack of explanation of anything.  I've played up to where I was able to buy a second leaf mainly by accident.  I had no idea why I was supposed to gather fruits until I pretty much randomly wandered outside the house for a bit.  I'm not really sure what it does yet, since there's no explanation when you get it, so I guess trial and error?  In any case, the game doesn't really give you anything to tell you that upgrading your leaf is significant, so it almost feels like the game doesn't care.  Even a little fanfare would be nice.
Overall, I'd say maybe a 6.5/10.  Barely recommend, mainly based on the remaining charm and the knowledge that updates seem to be planned.  Hopefully they'll fix some of these issues.

A cheap, low-effort, unpolished platformer.  Includes six levels for you to platform around, with the main goal being to collect three tears in a level before you can exit and progress to the next level.  Other collectibles include berries, which have only two uses: unlocking achievements and buying optional weapon upgrades.  The former are useless, the latter are only debatably useful, as many enemies are easily avoidable, and in a worse case easy to dispatch with your default weapon.  To make matters worse, there are three tiers of weapon upgrades you can get.  The first one lets your leaf fire a projectile (to make dispatching the already easily avoidable enemies trivial).  The second and third?  A simple color change, and a different particle effect for the projectile you shoot.  Not worth the effort to farm the berries for them.  Because of this, the game doesn't give you much motivation to actually collect any of the (non-required) collectibles.
From a gameplay perspective, the platforming isn't very tight.  Controls are often loose and slippery, which can lead to many frustrating deaths.  These deaths are made all the more frustrating with an inconsistent "checkpoint" system implemented in the game that randomly decides to respawn you in a fair location close to where you died, or at the start of the level.  However, once you get adjusted to this, the platforming just tends to be easy and...boring.  Even the enemies in the game present no challenge, often standing still and waiting for you to kill them.  There are maybe a half dozen enemies in the game total that provide a greater challenge of...moving in a line.  Literally one enemy in the game fires projectiles.  None of which are hard to deal with (except for the last one, which is elaborated on below).  The game does include a local co-op mode, but I fail to see a point to it, as (at least in the hub world) the second player is almost exclusively tied to the first player as the camera is locked on that player, leaving no extra incentives bring a second player as that player can't even help you explore and complete the level more quickly.
From a presentation perspective, the game looks cheap: almost every object is a simple mashup of a basic 3D construct, a cube, a cylinder, or a cone, scaled to give the illusion of a more complex object.  Animations, where they exist, are usually basic looping idle, or walking animations where the models in question simply waggle their arms or legs about.  Enemies, when dispatched, often simply fall over and just...vanish.  Sometimes with a poof of (barely recognizable) smoke, and sometimes with an extra sound effect.  Textures are simplistic, often including no detail.  One shining example of this lack of detail are the levels that include a snow effect, where the snow is represented by...an extra white, untextured cube stacked on top of other level geometry.  Finally, there are some very strange camera positioning choices in the game, and since the game doesn't let you adjust your camera angle or position, can make some sections more difficult than they need to be.  Finally, the music and sound effects in the game are completely unremarkable, with the end-of-level jingle being a recording of someone mashing an out-of-tune piano.
The game is also buggy.  Bugs encountered during my playthrough include: being pushed through the level geometry to my death by a moving platform, enemies that fire projectiles continuing to fire projectiles even after being killed, jumping up against the corner of certain geometry in the level causing the player character to flip upside down and become stuck, random white square appearing on the screen in the hub world (I assume these are meant to be dialog boxes of some kind, but don't display properly), camera angles often not correcting themselves when moving through a level, or after a death, and on rare occasions sticking in the pre-level cutscene position when you enter a level, rendering it unbeatable (since you can't see where your character is).  The worst offender though: the number of fruit you collect from a level doesn't reset when you exit a level unless you reset the game.  This allows you to enter a level, collect a ton of fruit, exit the level (which adds it to the total necessary for unlocking the achievements and the unlockable weapons), then re-enter the level and immediately exit to add the same amount of fruit to your total again.  You can do this non-stop to unlock all of the collectibles in the game, without even going past the first level.
My final thoughts: I feel like this game was the end result of a single developer new to developing video games.  The credits back me up on this, as many of the roles listed were done by the same person, with one exception besides the special thanks section.  If I take that into account, I encourage that developer to keep writing new games, as they're moving in a step in the right direction.  But I encourage them, for future titles, to remember to make the gamplay engaging and rewarding, to make smarter game design choices in terms of controls and presentation, and to spend some extra time polishing the game and stomping out bugs.  I also recommend not trying to compare your games to, frankly superior games (such as Super Mario 64 and Banjo Kazooie, which this game was compared to), when the only similarities are you can jump and collect things.
Only buy Woodle Tree Adventures if you desperately want to waste 30-60 minutes of your life, and you have literally nothing better to spend $3 on.

A collect-a-thon game with a cute woodland theme? This must be just like Banjo Kazooie, right?
No, no not really.
Let me explain. The main problem, the single most important reason I did not enjoy this game is because the act of collecting was not fun. Banjo Kazooie nails this down perfectly with a wide variety of things to do and collect, with different missions you need to complete in each level that utilize characters and the environment to keep things interesting. Woodle Tree Adventures doesn't have any of this. There are lots of little problems (which I'll go into in a moment), but this fundamental flaw is what keeps this game from being a must-play.
To put it kindly...this feels like it would be an amazing game on the Ouya, both in scope of gameplay and graphical quality. The sound assets are boring and repetitive, UI is amateurish, the textures are rough, enemy design feels poor...speaking of those enemies, depth perception is a major problem for me in this game. It often throws off jumps, but more annoyingly, makes it difficult to figure out where an enemy is in relation to myself, meaning I often found myself running into them trying to hit them with the leaf and got sent back to the start of the level. This is also exacerbated by the fact that there is no camera control, often with some very poorly chosen stock angles.
Is there a checkpoint system? There's certainly no visual cue for such, though near the end there's a series of jumps made difficult by the depth perception problem, and falling off that a few times I got sent only back to the middle of the stage, not the beginning. No idea if only falling checkpoints you or dying to enemies at that point would have worked, but I certainly never saw anything that looked like a checkpoint.
There's also the matter of abilities. Games like Banjo Kazooie or Mario 64 have lots of things you can do with different combinations of inputs, as well as power-ups. This game has jump, run, and hit, and the animations for all of these are pretty boring. The rucksack, which seems like a really cool idea, quickly wears out its welcome with the sheer size it grows to.
All in all, this feel like someone's first game project where they said "I want to make a new Banjo Kazooie," but didn't understand what makes that game great in the first place. If you've read everything I've said and think to yourself "yeah, I could put up with all that," it's currently 30% off for a total price of $2.09. If you don't mind the poor design and just want your collecting fix on PC, there are worse ways to spend your money. I would recommend it...with some
heavy caveats.

"STALKER: Call of Pripyat" is a great ending to an exciting trilogy. Where "Shadows of Chernobyl" felt rushed and unfinished and where "Clear Sky" was a bit jarring in it's UX overhaul, "Call of Pripyat" seems to have taken the best gameplay aspects from both titles to provide a wholesome experience.
Strelok was a Stalker. Scar was a mercenary. And now we get a chance to see the military's perspective on the Zone. Maj. Degtyarev is a skilled officer of the USS making his return to the Zone, now working undercover as a Stalker to uncover the circumstances surrounding a failed military operation to retake the Chernobyl NPP.
It's a refreshing change of pace playing as a character whose mission is clear and whose approach is both measured and unassuming. For the first time in the series, I felt less stringed along by fate and more in control of the story. The characters you meet are more memorable, largely because the dialogue is far more polished than in the previous titles. The upgrade system for weapons and armor and far less cumbersome to "unlock" than it was in "Clear Sky".
Areas feel more persistent in the right ways: clearing an area of zombies doesn't mean that they won't come back, but there probably won't be an army of them there next time. As you spend more time in the Zone (and, hopefully, acquire better gear), the more powerful monsters (notably, controllers and chimeras) will begin to appear more frequently. There are only 3 open areas (SoC and CS both had something like 9 or 10) but they are fairly expansive and well-mapped; each adds its own flavor to the game (Pripyat is finally the creepy ghost town we've always wanted), and each is worth exploring in depth. The anomalies are unique and well-defined; when you upgrade your scanner you will find them easily navigable, and farming artifacts becomes a game in itself.
The Zone finally feels alive. Emissions occur randomly, and you must prepare. This has the effects of making you drop your loot so you can run faster and leading you to seek refuge in unexplored ruins... where you're not likely to be welcomed. They also generate new artifacts, zombify some unfortunate Stalkers left in the open, and change the weather. All of this is beautifly implemented.
This last expedition into the Zone could easily be your most memorable. It's certainly been my most revisited.

It is now 22 November and I originally reviewed the game on 16 April.
Since then I have seen the game come a long way towards a finished product. Please do not get me wrong, There is still a long way to go.
Cons:
1. All of the major exploits have been fixed that have been found so far in the game. There are still a lot of minor issues to be addressed. The developers are presently taking time from adding content to fix the bugs and do some more optimizations to the game.
2.The optimization they have doen so far has improved my frame rate. My machine is presently still at the low end for a graphics card so I do see frame rate issues very quickly. The game has gone from a stutter step to where I can actually run with out the stutter. The only time I have seen this happen is when I am playing in the single player game. The server game has always been smooth, with a low frame rate back in April. Today, I am happy to say when I do check a server, I get a moderate frame rate.
Pros:
Not much has changed here. They did change the patch cycle opting for quality over quantity. This has resulted in larger patches and longer wait times between the patches. This has resulted in fewer hot fixes with the higher quality patches for the game.
