This game is amazing.  I can't stop playing it.
Let's start out with the first thing you do in the game; character customization.  You have 4 races to choose from, each with their own unique traits, backstory, and affect how everyone treats you.  Lizards can dig without a shovel, Dwarves can crawl into small spaces nobody else can, Elves can eat body parts to learn the memories of the fallen (sometimes gaining skills in the process), and so forth.
You've got a lot of choices for playstyles as well, and it's not set in stone.  You could start off the game as a wizard, then transition into a battlemage who charges into the fray, then unleashes spells that require proximity.
Then, you've got the Tags.  Basically, they let you set up your own backstory, as well as giving additional dialogue options when the time is right.  Mystics can sometimes talk to the gods, whilst Barbarians want a *simple* solution to many problems.  But the best is yet to come...  and it's something that I'm a bit of a sucker for.  Music.  You can set the lead instrument on the soundtrack.  It's only four instruments, and the one you choose will be, well, the prominent instrument throughout the soundtrack.
Not a fan of character customization?  That's fine, you can select an Origin character.  These guys normally would be optional party members if you were to create your own character, but you can also play as them for your main character.  The choices are really interesting too; a lizard who cavorted with demons and got exiled, wanting to reclaim his empire; or a human who is a host of all kinds of spirits while a demon is trying to wrest control of her body.  They all have pre-set tags, but you can choose the class they start with.
Now for the gameplay.
Out of battle, stuff is simple; everything is performed from your clicking (duh).  However, even outside of combat your skills are still tested.  Persuasion can be a way to get out of a fight, or get more information out of someone, bartering lowers prices for you.  You can also steal stuff too, but be warned if you played the first game; the stealing has been revamped by quite a lot.  You can no longer just walk into someone's house, close the door and sneak about, stealing everything that isn't bolted down.  The moment you take something, no matter if you're sneaking or not, the townsfolk will become suspicious and try to search you.  Of course, there's ways to make sure they don't succeed, but I'll leave that since a lot of this game is about finding your own playstyle.
The combat is not really changed by much from the first game, but many more complexities have been added.  Surfaces play a crucial role to a mage just like before, however they have many more options due to the magic trees.  Water can be frozen, electrified, or turned into steam which can also be electrified.  Bless can actually turn surfaces, well, blessed, healing characters who travel through it.  (That includes everyone, so make sure blessed surfaces can't be accessed by the enemy.)  However, there is also Cursed surfaces, which carry extra effects to them.  Necrofire can't be put out by normal water, Cursed Oil can go off on MOVEMENT, and so forth.
Armor is no longer a stat that simply decreases damage received, it is instead its own bar.  This bar is crucial to manage, as it stops status effects.  Think of it as a shield; as long as you have a shield up, you can't be affected by the status of a surface your character may be standing on, with certain exceptions as Oil that slows you down.
As a general rule of thumb however, the game's combat is very challenging.  There really isn't many fights that have "cannon fodder" enemies; everyone is dangerous and they all know how to take advantage of the same things you do.  Be careful about that water you're standing on, for that mage on higher ground likely might have an electric spell he could cast, if your magic armor is down, and stun you.
My recommendation?  This game deserves all the praise that it's got and more.  The only real complaint I have is with the camera control, but that's mainly due to my mouse having issues with some games not registering the middle mouse click.  Plus, in battle you can get a top-down view if there's too many obstacles.

Firstly I'll say that I absolutely love Baldur's Gate 1 and 2, however I can't recommend the game in the Enhanced Edition format.
The enhanced edition brings nothing new to the game that hasn't already been introduced in mods for the original. The updated graphics existed in the widescreen mod (albeit without the ability to zoom in to see an extremely blocky close up of characters). The new characters and quests are poorly written (dialogue choices are obvious and over the top - good, evil and sarcastic). Many of the quests seem to be attempts at comedy that both fall flat and break immersion in the game.
This edition seems to have done very little to fix what bugs, exploits and even spelling errors existed in the original game, despite these problems being well known in the community and frequently already corrected in the various tweak packs. To make matters worse I've suffered several crash to desktops, which I've never experienced with the original game (I have the GOG version of the original installed on the same machine with mods).
In my opinion the only two reasons to buy this version are for the (admittedly very fun!) Black Pits 2 or if you don't feel capable of modding the game yourself (perfectly understandable, but be reassured that the modding community is largely very helpful and supportive).

Don\'t get me wrong, this is a charming little game, I loved the concept.
However it felt like a game of missed opportunity for me. The concept of a pop up book was really good, the puzzles(whilst not challenging) never hit a level of frustrating or too easy. However its over before its really had a chance to discover the concept. Look at my playtime, that\'s it, 100% with nothing left to do. No extra\'s, no replay value, no collectibles, nothing. It\'s SUCH a shame because I want to say this game is excellent because the style and feel of it ARE excellent but I can\'t justify telling someone to play a game that is just over an hour long.
Maybe I would justify it if it didn\'t have artificially lengthy parts making the game actually even shorter than an hour. For example there is a lack of guidance(which is good for the discovery of the game) which makes it annoying when you KNOW what to do you just haven\'t clicked in the right place for the game to decide you can do it. Whilst this makes for an interesting discover mechanic in the puzzles, its a strange design choice in the non-puzzling elements which lead to a few times where I was left clicking closer and closer to what I wanted to do before hitting the develops mark. This is made even stranger as there is a distinct lack of continuity in how this mechanic works, most of the time there is a white glow you can click on indicating \"THIS\" is where you should stand. So to randomly remove that mechanic was confusing.
Overall, i\'d recommend this game if you want an easy 100% game added to your stats, its been bundled a few times too so if you can get it cheap or through a giveaway then its certainly worth a look.
TL;DR - Great concept, length lets it down.

For me, Tengami clocked in at exactly 100 minutes.
I would recommend Tengami, but not at $9.99. I think the developers should lower the price to around $2.99, a lot more people would play the game.
It was a fun, short and sometimes tedious adventure.
PROS:
The animation is wonderful.
The attention to detail is outstanding, especially the caves in the third level. I also liked how the developers tried to make the character's feet walk perfectly up and down the stairs.
The sound effects were spot on.
The music was insanely relaxing and gave the game a great overall feel.
Some of the puzzles were pretty fun.
Riding in a boat was pretty cool.
The poems were nice.
The ending was short and sweet.
The wolves in level one.
CONS:
The character's walking speed will be a BIG problem for those who don't have patience. With that being said though, I didn\'t mind how slow he walked, because you are supposed to enjoy the surroundings.
There are only THREE levels.
The second level was quite tedious. It makes you walk back and forth, back and forth, left and right, over and over.
Some of the puzzles in the second level were reused in the third level. I would have liked to have seen new puzzles in the third level.
There wasn\'t really any story.
The wolves were great in level one, but you never saw anything like it in level two and three. They seemed more "empty".
Overall, it was a decently fun game that relaxed me a lot.
I wouldn't mind seeing a second Tengami, only this time, make it cheaper, longer and don't repeat puzzles.

Given its cartoony nature, at first glance many are quick to label Awesomenauts as inferior, childish, or, “Not a real MOBA”. However, after over thirty-five hours, I can safely tell you these views are incorrect. Does Awesomenauts have all the intricate details and mechanics that another game in the genre (for example, Dota 2) might have? No, but that certainly does not invalidate it from the club. In fact its ability to streamline more confusing aspects of the genre sets this game apart. The cartoony art-style and platforming gameplay make Awesomenauts visually easy to understand, and allows the player to quickly begin enjoying the game.
After Awesomenauts drops you into its seemingly simplistic world, you slowly begin to see the more complex mechanics that make up the game, allowing you to enhance your play-style and ability the more you play, allowing for a high skill ceiling. The ability to unlock upgrades that can be equipped to customize your load out works well, guaranteeing that you won’t be overwhelmed at start. Although it may seem to be a simple-looking game, Awesomenauts quickly proves to be a fully fledged, feature rich member of the MOBA genre which is extremely fun, and I recommend it to anyone interested.

Baldur's Gate II:EE is the combined pack of Shadows of Amn+Throne of Bhaal which continue and conclude the story of Gorion's ward and their ascension into Godhood. BGII is arguably one of the best roleplaying games of all time with an incredibly deep, intricately woven and dark story that plays host to one of the best game villains and a plethora of tangential side missions, stories and npcs that make the world of Faerun come to life.
Shadows of Amn's story begins shortly after the events of the original Baldur's Gate, the opening cinematic and cutscene opens with your character being the unwilling constituent in the antagonist's demented BDSM fantasies. Little is revealed initially other than his name,
and he has shown some interest in you, or more specifically your heritage. His experiments are quickly interrupted by a besieging rival guild and in the ensuing chaos you are able to escape and you begin your journey in pursuit of Irenicus and his ilk to seek out your revenge.
Your adventure will see you travel the city of coin,
and the surrounding countryside of Amn as you pursue Irenicus down the Sword Coast. Throughout your travels you'll slowly learn the motivations and misdeeds that drive Irenicus and your interactions with him reveal the true nature of your lineage. Irenicus is a solid and well written antagonist although he isn't as insidious or devious as Sarevok.
Defeating Irenicus will throw you into Throne of Bhaal which is the culmination of the Bhaalspawn saga which pits you against the other most powerful Bhaalspawn in a
-esque showdown to become the reincarnation of Bhaal himself.
The gameplay is essentially unchanged from the first Baldur's Gate, at least at its core, it's still very tactical realtime combat with the ability to pause. Overall though the 'meta' is very different with [arcane] spellcasters being
strong in BGII due to the increased level cap and access to higher level spells and the abundance of powerful items, where as BGI was much easier as a warrior. Generally though the combat feels more enjoyable with a wider array of tools at your disposal and a greater array of vastly differing enemies to fight makes many battles feel varied and memorable. The further you push through the story of SoA and into ToB the more action oriented the game and combat will become as enemies get tougher and your character grows stronger. The increase in action will help accomodate for the weaker story in ToB. Overall though the combat is still very slow comparatively with any Arpg as it is designed to take some level of strategy and meticulous planning to succeed in BGII.
Graphically the Baldur's Gate series is timelessly beautiful because of the development decision to use painted 2d backdrops. The spell effects still look amazing and vary greatly between spells. The character models on the otherhand have not aged well and look very bland, pixelated and blurry but is a minor grievance in the grand scheme of things.
Having completed this game several times now, both playing with a full player created party, solo and then picking up npcs along the way the game offers a lot of replayability whether it be from the particular challenges and different strategies required of each class during fights with certain enemies and bosses or from the story arcs and commentary provided by the npcs you choose. This is a thinking man's game so if you're looking for a game with which to turn your brain off and have some mindless fun you may wish to reconsider. Those looking for a challenge and a riveting story this is the game for you. On a personal note, this is one of my favourite games of all time and I recommend it wholeheartedly, especially to those that enjoy a good rpg.

Baldur's Gate 2 is one of the greatest games of all time, surpassing the original in many ways. It was Bioware's Magnum Opus, their "Dark Side of the Moon", if you will. The Enhanced Edition is the same game, but there are some improvements that I feel make it a better experience. The improvements in BG2:EE are actually more helpful in BG2:EE than they were in BG:EE. BG2 severely lacked Evil aligned party members, most notably a thief. This has been rectified in the Enhanced edition, and you can now play a fully Evil aligned party. Dorn, Neera, and Rasaad return from BG:EE, each with their own extensive questlines, as well as a new companion, Hexxat the neutral evil Thief. The companion questlines span the length of the game, with additional quests every few chapters, concluding in Throne of Bhaal. Of course, these companions are totally optional, but I do feel they are a very welcome improvement if you happen to play an Evil party. Of course, the other Enhanced edition improvements are also here, like the name, object, and contaniner highlighting when pressing tab, as well as the adjustable zoom. They are very helpful, and make the experience much more enjoyable for a modern audience. Another cool thing is that a few new items will be  imported into Irenicus's dungeon if you happened import from the original BG:EE. They are nothing special, and they are mostly just items that you would find semi-early in the game anyway, but it's a helpful addition. On the subject of bugs, this game is significantly better than it was on release, but I did notice a few bugs along the way. Granted they were bugs present in the original game, but they were there. They were easily rectified by use of the developer console, and were very rare throughout my 220 hour playthrough, but just be aware you may or may not have to deal with that. Over all, I think BG2:EE is a fantastic game, just like the original. If you love Baldur's gate 2 and are itching for another playthrough, it is definitely worth it. If you haven't played Baldur's Gate 2, it is even more worth it, as this is the definitive version of one of the finest games ever crafted. Even at full price, you will get your moneys worth, as this game is around 200+ hours long.
If you are going to play BG2:EE I highly recommend you try out BG:EE first, as you will be more familiar with the new companions, as well as be able to import your character. Check out my highly rated review of that if you are on the fence.

I don't even know where to start...
1. Uplay
After launching the game from Steam, you will be redirected to Uplay. You will create your account, the launcher will install and patch for 30 minutes, to finally crash when login. The solution is to uninstall it and download it from the website. Once you loged in, you will have to avoid the agressive ads from Far Cry 4 and every freaking AC game to click on the play button.
2. The Story
The story is by far the worst in the game. Ubisoft, if you bring back the prince from the sands trilogy, why don't you make a story related to it? Ha, you wanted to play with the feelings of the fans of the saga to make some quick cash. "Hey look, we are going to bring back the sands saga" BULL SHEIT. Not only you make a standalone story with no conexion with other games, but you change completely the background of the saga. C'mon, who the hell is that brother who came out of nowhere? And what about the sands? Now they were created by a woman who lives in the clouds?
Ok, I get it. You created a new story, I could deal with it if it made sense by itself. But it's a horrible story, predictable, full of cliches, like a story for kids. The only original part is when a woman turns herself into a sword that can speak. It's original, but pathetic.
3. Music/Sounds
Let's move on to the music. In the original trilogy, the soundtrack was outstanding. From charming arab melodies, to agressive rock, there was always an amazing song playing while you were fighting enemies, or exploring, or making puzzles. But here we will find nothing. Some horrible melodies in the main menu and some other noise while you fight. Period.
The sounds effects are ok, but recycled from other games. Anyway there aren't so many sounds, only the sound of water, the sound of the wind, and the sound of the swords.
Ah, and acting voice (in spanish) is really, really awful. The actors play like they have no soul, or like they want to finish their job soon, get paid and go home. I don't think english voices are better.
4. Characters.
The main character is our beloved prince from the sands of time trilogy, but he seems to not remember anything from the first game. He is so amused whe he sees a f***ing sand of time. C'mon man, you look so ret*ard in this one.
The other character is the brother of the prince, who came out of nowhere with a entire realm for himself. I can't stand this character, thanks god that appears only for 10 minutes in the story.
Then we have a woman who lives in the clouds that turns herself into a sword.  I don't even have words for this.
Enemies are repetitive and easy as hell. The will stare at you until you kill'em.
5. Combat
From the nearly 20 combos and different attacks in the first game, to the almost infinite combos of the last 2 games... to the 3 attacks in this one. You can't even block...
Time powers are awful as well. The only decent is the rewind power, which appears in the other games. Other awesome powers disappeared in this one. Well, you can use an ability to turn your skin into stone, to make yourself invulnerable, making the game easier.
6. Gameplay
It feels like a point and click game. You kill enemies clicking on the mouse. Then you have the platforms, where you only have to push the space bar. You don't need to think, just presh the god*damn buttons. You have ONE puzzle, that can be made in less than 3 minutes if you are not so ret*ard as the people who made this game are.
The game is so easy I have died only because of bugs, making it a fast-pace game, which is good, because when I played it, I just wanted to finish it as soon as possible, uninstall it, write the review, and go back to the original trilogy to forget this piece of sheit.
7. Bugs
Oh man, I could write a trilogy of books and maybe make a movie out of the bugs in this game. You will experience a lot of lag, fallings through the world, and many situations where the prince is dead, but he is alive. I mean, after being hitted, 90% of the times he falls to the ground and is not able to get up, like he was dead, but you see the health bar almost full, and the only thing you can do is rewind or restart the game.
In the final boss you will face, not that passive demon who will wait until you kill him, but the boss o bugs. The prince is likely to stop moving, to stick in the ground, while he is still alive. In that moment, you are invulnerable, which it means that the boss or the ads will not hurt you. You can't even rewind on time, so you see yourself forced to restar the game.
8. Graphics
The only part of the game that doesn't suck. The graphics, overall, are amazing, even 4 years after. Solid and highly detailed. But the scenarios are empty, really repetitive, and the lack that charisma that all the scenarios from the other games has.
9. Controls
You will use only the space bar, WASD, and the left button of the mouse, son the controls don't mess up so much, just a bit lag while platforming (the prince jumps like 2 seconds after hitting the jump button, most of times). Camera is bad, but compared to other aspects of the game, is pretty decent.
10. Other stuff
There are more crappy things in the game, like that useless ability tree, but it doesn't matter anymore since the game is broken since the first second.
Conclusion
Do never buy or play this game, even if you are a die-hard PoP fan. Specially if you are a PoP fan. This game just destroys the entire saga. Disrepectful game.

If you want to chill out and look at space while floating in space, or chill out watching space on an oceanside bench, or induce a sense of isolation and peacefulness in yourself, spending a little time exploring this game is a nice way to do that. I didn't bother with the collecting of things that you can do in the game, I just wandered around the beach and unwound for a while.
It reminded me of how when I first played Ocarina of Time, I just spent thirty minutes watching the sun rise and fall, and the specks of light travel around the Kokiri village. Or when I'd play the first Mass Effect game and just stop driving the Mako for a moment and just sit still, staring at the planet hanging overhead with the great big chunk taken out of it. This is a game to just indulge in a beautiful wide vista and the feelings that inspires.
One crticique I do have is that the controls were a bit clumsier than I'd like. Sometimes I'd get thrown out of appreciating the environment because I'd get stuck or have trouble turning around.
Personally, I'd happily pay for something like this again but with smoother controls and a variety of environments to explore. Wow, if I could just wander the settings of Xenoblade Chronicles for example, without getting stabbed in the face by a Mechon, that would be lovely. I'd love an exploration game just about travelling around an amazing world like that.
Sometimes you want to save the world. Sometimes you just want to feel something and look out into the vastness of space.

You select a male or female character stored inside tubes. "It's nearly summer" you are told. You appear with your character on a simulated/virtual beach shore and walk it. Random phrases will appear drawn onto the ground. You "collect" ("remember) some of them by closing your eyes, you also hear them voiced  in French then (they are always subtitled in the language of your choice). You collect some object "hidden" beneath some worldly, "holographic" thing (a tree, a bush, a crane, ...) that disappears to reveal this object (chess pieces mostly, and one more unique and confusing one which leaves room for interpretation). You enter a house, meet with a virtual partner of the opposite gender in some sort of bar, put your objects in turns on a chessboard (freely, you don't actually play chess - some spots trigger the words/phrases you previously collected to appear on the screen and be voiced), take a smoke, drink some whine or select some pre-set of music tracks to play music-box like in the background. The lines you collect and make appear are circling around the two characters and their relationship, who are or used to be lovers  After that you leave the house, walk along the shore again, collect more phrases and another object and enter the house again. This you repeat as many times as you wish, at some point the simulation starts over again with you collecting about the same pieces again (the game however seems to remember all pieces you once collected - I've just started up the game again and could place all the objects I once picked up many months back when I first played this game).
The partner in the house is either A.I.-controlled or an actual human who is playing the game at the same time as you do. You don't see his/her name, he/she is a stranger, there is no text or voice chat to use, you only communicate with the words and through symbolism you can do with the chessboard and the objects, and the only indication whether there is someone else playing/waiting in the house is - from what I've been told and noticed - a window you see from the outside that has lights on. I haven't been able to meet up with a real human yet, because either the mechanics to match you up with one are not working too well or this game was never played by too many people to begin with. There is a Steam group one can join, and sometimes people try to group up through it. However this is a bit of a misleading way of playing this game, since it was obviously intended to meet strangers, an idea Tale of Tales originally came up with in "The Endless Forest", but which isn't executed too well in this game. A game that did this better was the PSN game "Journey". But I guess one must probably consider that "Journey" was a larger success than any of Tale of Tales' games ever were - the more players play these games the higher/better the chances to meet up with them. At some point no one will play these anymore, I guess, not even "Journey".
The control scheme isn't entirely bad but not exactly too enjoyable. This is a problem I keep seeing in the games made by Tale of Tales. You look around by moving the mouse to either side of the screen, you walk by holding down the left mouse button, you close your eyes with the right mouse button and run with spacebar. It feels odd/awkward and not very comforting. They could adapt to the more classic control schemes that games with a first- and third-person view give you, the usual WASD and mouse-look thing. I don't see any good reason in doing things differently there. Has it to do with being different for the sake of being different? Or are they inept and don't play their own games? I don't know, and I don't like being harsher to them than they deserve. You can play with a gamepad too, maybe I should try that and will feel better then.

I really really like this game but it is not for everyone.  I have been looking for a game with type of intense and deep strategy and diplomacy for a long time.  Where most games rely on hack/slash and army building/conquering through superior fire power, CK2 is centered on deep political manipulation.  Not since the first incarnation of Romance of the Three Kingdoms (dating myself) have I been able to find a game that does this well.
There are ton of game mechanics that I dont want to go into because someone more worthy than I can probably explain them better.  CK2 requires patience and researching game elements and NPC characters.  You really begin to understand the life of an anchient monarch who imprisoned his baren wife or planned the murder of his oldest, slothful drunkard son before he can take the throne.  In CK2, you do not simply play one patriarchal/matriarchal ruler, you play generations.  Thus, when you die, you assume the role of the next in line.  Each turn is a game year and this is an era of wars, plagues, and conspiracies to murder or dethrone you.  Building your legacy often requires establishing alliances via arranged marriages, or placing a son into the church with sites on becoming the pope.  CK2 is not a light hearted game.  Surrounding yourself with good, trustworthy people are key.  There are times when you need to build (rather buy) armies and conquor lands but most often, the road to victory is paved before battlefield is established.  You will find yourself digging and investigating the traits of everyone around you in order to find the best candidates to polulate your court or tutor your children.  Once accomplshed, you will then find yourself doing what you can to keep them happy.  For some, this means assinging courtly titles to them, for others it may mean finding them a spouse.  In short, 'Its not easy being King', or Duke, or whatever role.
Also, you dont necessarily start, or want to start as a king.  You will certainly have land holdings but aquiring more land and conquoring territiories will elevate you through the status pool.  Of course, this will also earn you numorous enemies along the way whose death wont always end your problems.  PS, keep the church on your good side.

tl;dr I find this game not great but still decent, and actually with quite a high skill ceiling that other reviewers calling this a boring grindfest might not have discovered.
Longer version:
Having read other reviews, I started playing this game with the expectation of mucking around casually for awhile and then stopping when it gets too grindy.
However, what I found was a rather fun and challenging game with an unexpected amount of strategical and tactical depth. Take, for instance, a common complaint that the party's hitbox is too large to apply common bullet hell techniques. However, notice that whenever you about-face the Bardbarian, his entire party maintains formation by going *through* him. When that happens, the party's hitbox shrinks significantly. It's still not a single point like in other bullet hell games, but by using this technique appropriately, you can actually dodge a *lot* of stuff.
Applying this and other techniques, and abusing various enemy behaviours and unit compositions, I did not have to grind much to beat the vanilla game, though I did have to grind what I felt was an acceptable amount. And whenever I died, I did not feel like it was due to not having grinded enough, but that it was due to a lack of skill or moment of carelessness which I then wanted to immediately improve upon.
That being said, I do feel that the movement is still rather clunky, the enemies and units are not wholly satisfying, and the game on the whole is a little lackluster, which is why I think that this is merely a decent game.

Pretty fun tower defense game with RPG elements. Took me over 11 hours to get all achievements as I played both normal and insane modes -- I suggest just doing insane mode as soon as you can since two of the achievements require you to complete it. The enemies are a little more difficult in insane mode, but you get gold much faster, allowing you to upgrade faster, so it balances out.
The good:
++ Wide range of units and enemy types give different ways to play and cause you to come up with different strategies.
++ The upgrade system for your units, the town, and perks for your hero are interesting and give some customization (until you just upgrade everything to max).
++ The artwork and unit designs are visually appealing.
++ A couple perks help you speed up how quickly you gain gold in story mode, which is helpful.
++ The music is good but gets repetitive after a while.
++ Full controller support.
The bad:
-- Becomes monotonous after a while. It really turns into a grind to get more gold to upgrade perks and units. To get the most gold, you have to beat the bosses, meaning you have to just replay from the beginning over and over. By the time you have a bunch of upgrades, this grind becomes ridiculously easy at the beginning levels and just a bullet hell at the end. Repeat until you get all achievements.
-- Survival and Escape game modes give different ways of playing the game but are pretty much only used to get an achievement for each as they're not an efficient way to earn gold. Plus, they're endless, so the only goal is to beat your best score or get on the leaderboard -- not a real reason to keep playing them.
If you play this game more casually, playing just a little at a time to seemingly reduce the grind, you'd probably get more out of it. Overall, I'd rate it 6/10, OK. Might want to wait for it to go on sale before you buy it.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R Call of Pripyat is the third, and with GSC Game World closing down, most likely the last game in the stalker series. The stalker games were a surprise hit right from the start and it's a shame to see the series end, especially with this game where everything seems to turning in the right direction once again.
Call of Pripyat, like the other stalker games, is an open world first person shooter with some minor RPG elements thrown in for good measure. You roam the radioactive wasteland surrounded Chernobyl, searching for "artifacts", valuable and rare commodities created by the various spacial anomalies created by the nuclear meltdown so many years ago. To keep things interesting you will have to contend with other stalkers wanting the artifacts for themselves, shadowy organizations with their own secret agendas, the Ukrainian military and of course, horribly mutated monsters.
One thing that Call of Pripyat does notably different from it's predecessors is slowing things down quite a bit. Instead of every map being a battlefield of constant and relentless attacks by seemingly unending forces from the various factions populating the zone combat is now much rarer. This has the very welcoming effect of making the game world feel like the radioactive wasteland it's supposed to be, every encounter is more intense because of it and it feels a little special when you encounter a group of stalkers who promptly tell you to holster your weapons or get lost rather than simply open fire on sight.
The faction system that was present in Clear Sky has all but been removed and this also helps push the pace of the game more towards Survival Horror than Mindless Shooter. While the factions still exists, still do battle with one another and still treat you differently depending on your actions there is no constant defend and attack missions and broken faction relations and this goes a long way towards making you feel like you're playing your own game, rather than just being another soldier in a never ending war.
Despite all the good there is still plenty of bad however. The game is much smaller than both it's predecessors and the great storyline and mysteries from Shadow of Chernobyl is nowhere to be found. Also the difficulty has been toned down considerably which will elate some and irate others.
The engine is still pretty bad, the animations have been cleaned up a little but are still very clunky and despite the graphical enchantments that the series has been undergoing since Clear Sky this game still has that "raw" feeling of Shadow of Chernobyl. That feel like you're playing something half-done. Something that could have used another year of polishing. While this might normally be enough to make you quit the game Call of Pripyat manages to accomplish the same fear as the original. It makes you enjoy it despite it's many flaws. Sure you will probably grab the first graphical enhancement mod you come across but that's not because you can't play the game without it, it's because you have to play the game regardless and just want to spare your eyes a little.
Call of Pripyat is a good way to end the stalker series I suppose. It's a good game and has many improvements over it's predecessors. But completing I still feel like something is lacking. A true "S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2" might not be something we will ever see but it sure is something we can hope for.

I'm 50 hours in and so far this is the best RPG I've played. It's clever, it's funny, it's sad and it makes you experience a lot of the lore through action (like taking part in an elven ritual) rather than reading books - of which there are still a lot. This game is beautiful and the detail might even overwhelm you at the start. One of the biggest criticisms of the first Original Sin was the steep learning curve and lack of purpose to your actions at the start of the game (a murder noone cares about). Larian Studios solved this problem beautifuly by letting the player first roam a smaller area and giving you a primary objective. The overarching story and your part in it are introduced in the first area (which alone took me 30 hours to finish).
The combat feels satisfying. The new elements introduced (armor and high ground) feel fresh and allow for different approaches to any fight. The fighting locations are carefully crafted and reward planing ahead and execution of the fight.
All in all this is an outstanding game. I feel the same excitement I felt when I played Baldurs Gate 2 for the first time as a kid. On a visceral level this is the biggest compliment I can give Divinity 2. Like Baldurs gate in it's time this game will set the bar all future RPGs have to judged against. This is a once in a decade game.

(Quick and short) I do urge to at least read (My experience playing) and (No Pay-2-Win...) section
PROS:
+Great community, mostly helpful
+Constant Updating
+Steam Workshop
+No Pay-2-Win, just Pay-2-Skip (Will describe later)
+Can trade/sell rare stuff for in-game currency, can even get an in-game currency discount at login

CONS:
-Repetitive gameplay
-Farming simulator
-When you think you farmed all the resources to where you don't have to worry about resources, Devs add new resources.
-Devs have said in the past that the game will not be a grind, but honestly does become a grind.
LOOOOOONG story, that is kind of long
(My experience playing) I began playing this game in March 2013, have consistently played for long time, but have taken a month or 2 hiatus here and there. Initially I enjoyed the game a lot but as I continued I started to get burned out due to the grind. I soon began to crave the grind as I began playing again, and then for some reason I began to enjoy the grind. Especially when I got a few friends to join me in the game. The three of us farmed together, laughed together, but soon both of them left and moved on. Since the beginning of playing, this game provided me some weird experience that reminded me of Star Wars Jedi Knight Jedi Academy (the first game I played consistently for 6+ years). Both games had fun parkour mechanics, the quick-and-easy melee to gun switch that flowed flawlessly during combat, power abilities that grew stronger with each level that also drained "energy" with each use, had the shield and health combo, and fluid melee attacks and combos.
(Why I put Repetitive Gameplay as a PRO and CON) No doubt at some point this game will indeed get to you and you will get worn out. This game does have you to farm resources and experience to level up all your gear, this can sometimes be a PRO because what you are leveling and farming could provide fun experience of dominating enemies with a push of a button. Other times it is a CON because what you are farming only occurs as a reward that appears on a certain interval that could be the end of round 15 or at 15 minute mark of an endless mission and you might not get it (However you might be able to buy it in trade chat). Overall Gameplay is fun, but will at some point get to you. I am currently on a hiatus from the game, got burnt out back in July of this year, and only popped in for an hour to see new content lately. I recently saw all the new farming items this update brought, and I still do not feel ready to come back to the game.
(No Pay-2-Win, just Pay-2-Skip) This system is great because every weapon and warframe can be obtained through blueprints. Don't want to farm for the parts, spend money to buy the weapon. Don't want to spend actual money, sell some stuff for in-game currenct in trade chat and then buy what you want in market. Want a Primed Warframe or weapon and don't want to spend real money? Look in trade chat for the parts (But you will need to farm resources to craft) and get them with the in-game currency you got from trading, or actually trade parts (if you get lucky and find someone who wants something you have). So the Pay-2-Skip aspect is really pay money to skip some grinding.
(The Community) The community is welcoming, helpful, and responsive. Most of my encounters with the community have been the combination of all 3. I welcome new players that join my public match and afterwards I usually ask if the would like help or if there is something they want to farm, and sometimes I even offer free items that they could use. I encounter other players like myself and we sometimes just give eachother prime parts or gear that one of us needs and never ask of anything in return. However, you will rarely run into players who actually argue with eachother in a public mission. Usually it is someone demanding a revive because they got downed and the rest of team are across the map (and they get upset because no one helped), a player calling out someone who keeps getting downed (and arguement begins), or bad communication in endless missions on when to extract (mainly occurs in public matching and not party). Overall great community.
(Devs saying not going to be a grind...) I am not sure how many others have heard them say this in one of their early Dev streams, but this was indeed said. When comparing to what they said to what you see how the game has evolved, the grind is real and growing. Initially we had 13 resources for everything in the game with differing rarites (4 common, 4 uncommon, and 5 rare). They have added I think 11 more? Some requiring you to play a certain mission and you receive it as a reward at the end, others are pick-up in certain missions, and others only drop from certain enemies that appear in certain missions. The RNG in this game is all over the place. Some people will never get a certain rare item for 50+ attempts, and some will not stop getting that same rare item. As the game continues to grow and progress, the Devs add new content but also ends up adding more content to grind. The Devs hardly release new content that is just purely "Fun" with no grind attached to it.
(Ending note) Sorry if the review has holes in it, I believe this is one of my first reviews. The last section about grinding is a reason why I have taken a break, the reason why I still play it, the reason why I can now play any game that is defined as a farming simulator, and a weird reason why I want to recommend this game. The grind is apparent, definitely growing, but sometimes actually a fun experience. No matter what I personally feel about the game and the grind you should at least try the game, possibily bring along a couple of friends who don't play it (or even finally try it because a friend asked you to join in), and possibly you might get hooked into this game like I did.

Lets be honest here. The developers are slow. This game has been an alpha since, like 2009 I think. However: The developers know what they're doing. The 'game' (if you could call it that) has come a long way since 2009. Graphical overhauls, new lighting (like every other update), Ai coding, etc.
The good:
-Fun time-killer (while it runs)
-One of the best hand-to-hand combat systems I have ever played
-Blood physics are incredible
-Parkour, combat, and more parkour
-Level editor enabled for every level
-The new(ish) arena modes give players something to do when they get bored of said editor
-If you have a thing against furries, for whatever reason, go ahead and expel that agression here...
The bad:
-No workshop support. I would like to play some user-created levels.
-Each new update (every few weeks or so) fixes multiple previous issues while creating 19 more.
-Dogs can't really jump. Don't play as a dog.
-Been in alpha for about 7 years
-I can't really see where they are taking the game, whether it be an actual RPG or more Arena combat
-The water is still fake
-No decapitations or amputations, even when you take a sword slash to the ears or tail.
The ugly:
-$30
-Crashes harder than Tiger Woods
Overall, the game works well in some places, but not so much in other places, if that makes sense. I find fun in whatever I do, but I have never once closed the game after 23 hours of gameplay.
It closes for me.
Update 2017: Definitely should earn "The Labor of Love" award.

At this point it would be wrong of me not to suggest this game.
PROS
It's a grand strategy that focuses on managing your family, your friends, your acquaintances, your court, and then once you have all that in order you begin expanding your horizons to snooping into the business of your friends, family, enemies, and total strangers whose land you desire.
The graphics are more than what you usually see in games like this.
The sounds have that nice quality where they're not repetitive or annoying, but rather invoke response cues as to what's happening. When a character is born or dies you immediately know before the text telling you. If you'd like something else there are nice workshop mods for it, but base is satisfactory.
The music is pleasing and I would go so far as to describe it as relaxing. It always seems to be the right tempo.
The mechanics of managing the strength of your genepool and family traits are what is so addictive for me personally. I really get a feel for my characters and it allows me to roleplay them more than what I had expected from the genre. It's what will continue adding another couple hundred hours likely for a long time to come.
CONS
The multiplayer is incredibly fussy and most games result in crashing due to networking issues or come out unresolved in my experience, but I still play multiplayer because it's usually a few hours in and we start a new story the next time we play. Saving and reloading that save to continue is feesible, but sometimes too much of a hassle for my lot of friends.
The price tag. It repulses many because they feel as though they may miss out without the DLC and I understand, but here's a real kicker: If your friend has any DLC and hosts a game then you get to experience the DLC without purchasing.
As for the singleplayer aspect of needing DLC I suggest getting it on sale and knowing which DLCS you need to buy to get the most out of the game.
Recommended for gameplay/mechanics:
Sword of Islam - $10 - Adds Muslims as a playable religion.
Legacy of Rome -$5 - Adds many features that I take for granted now.
Old Gods - $15 Improves revolts. Older starting date. Pagans, Zoroastrians, and some nice events.
Sons of Abraham - $10 - Adds Jews. Adds on to Muslims and Christian religions as well.
Charlemagne - $15 - Family chronicle (A history of your gameplay that's really nice.), earlier starting date, adds Zunists, and the ability to create a custom kingdom.
Way of Life - $8 -(Loosely recommended. Changes gameplay a fair bit. Best experienced without first. Adds more roleplay depth and ability to define your character and their actions, but the NPCs use the mechanics as well so it changes the feel of base game, but I like it.)
Total cost including base game: $93.00
Your initial reaction is probably "Ninety-three dollars!?" and I know. It seems outrageous, but I have five hundred hours and let me break down my rationalization of that.
The average price of a movie ticket is like $8.50 for about one and a half to two hours of entertainment.
The average price of a game of bowling is $10.00 per person roundabout. (It's been a while, so bare with me.)
In comparison I have a very high expectation of how much entertainment I should get from a videogame and I roughly put it at an hour per dollar spent. If I buy a new console or platform game and it is sixty bucks I expect sixty hours of gameplay from the title. The true gems are those that shatter that expectation to pieces.
CKII has given me five times my expectation and investment and continues to rack up more time. My initial one hundred and fifty hours were off the base game alone.
All things considered I owe it to Paradox and to my fellow gamers to strongly recommend this game.

I wanted to like Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands. I love the (admittedly westernized) genre of strong princes and fair princesses set against a backdrop of rocky mountains, roiling sand and Moorish castles. I was hoping to get some of that with some good graphics, music, story, and some climbing thrown in.
Well, forget the story. There is one, but not so you'd notice. The game is a series of climbing puzzles / challenges, with some hack 'n slash combat every so often. The combat is fairly easy, and the puzzles, with two exceptions, are not that hard to solve. Actually
the puzzles through, though, is intensely frustrating (I play exclusively with a keyboard + mouse). Lag is extraordinarily high. The game is sometimes not sensitive enough to input, and at other times too sensitive. Some skills and abilities are on a timer (freeze water for X number of seconds), so what seems a minor annoyance at the beginning of the game magnifies into greater and greater significance later on (expect The Aqueducts level to really give you trouble). I can put up with all that, though. The killer blow for me is the same thing I hated in Ubisoft's sister platformer, Assassin's Creed. Get into a place with one path forward, and the camera view locks up: you can't turn and look to see where you need to go without just blindly following the path indicated by the camera lock-up. I absolutely HATE this; I hated it in Assassin's Creed, and I hate it here. In this case, without the ability to look around, you'll die multiple times until you realize, oh, I need to go in X direction, so I need to do the upwards back-and-forth-between-walls climb three times to reach my objective ledge. Incredibly frustrating, and for me a game-breaker.
As  I said, the story is near non-existent. An invading army is attacking the castle, so the Prince's brother Malik unleashes King Solomon's army - of sand soldiers. The Prince has to figure out a way to corral the army - and stop his brother, who seems to be accumulating the power of the sand-soldiers with each one he kills. Whatever. I never really felt a connection to any of the characters. They're just there as an excuse for some platforming. The graphics are good, even by 2010 standards - fire looks very realistic - but the water is strangely low-res. And there is a lot of water in this game. The music is suitably evocative, but after capturing the initial mood, is repetitive and unexciting (thought the orchestration uses a number of different instruments and it sounds well-played).
Incredibly disappointed in The Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands. Not because it is bad per se, but because frustrating gameplay mechanics mean I'll be moving on to something else.

This game was hugely disappointing. It's the camera angles. In a game where you live or die by your ability to control the prince, the game dies, because even when you can control him it's painful to do so, and he ends up doing things which look stupid, like jumping at a forty five degree angle instead of directly toward a horizontal pole when missing means death, so it just feels stupid. The rest of the ingredients are all there and if there wasn't the one fundamental flaw which makes all the great features moot it would be one of the best (if not the best) of a good series, but instead it is the worst by a fair margin. If they'd just stuck the camera behind you (or given you that option) with commensurate controls, so you could run toward a pole and jump to the pole rather than having to guess whether you should be jumping "West" or "Northwest"...
Seriously this is a three dimensional game, so why should I only be able to move in precisely 8 directions, and those dictated by and gimped by the camera position? So close to a great game and yet so far.

Bardbarian is a flash based twin (actually single) stick shooter game, where the player doesn't have to shoot (because our party members do that automatically), just avoid the projectiles of the enemies and protect a crystal at the centre of the town. The game deploys various units we can use to kill the attackers and we can also use diverse upgrades to increase our chances for success. There's a main storyline and 2 alternative game modes.
One day, Brad, a retired barbarian decides to change profession and modifies his waraxe into a lute, therefore he becomes the Bardbarian. Of course the town he lives in happens to be in danger, so he must put his new skills into good use, by playing all kinds of tunes to summon allies and boost their abilities. Quite strange, huh? It reflects the general mood of the whole game and it does manage to be amusing.
The gameplay is simple, but enjoyable nevertheless: we have to kill increasing waves of monsters who swarm towards us from right to left and defend the crystal in the heart of our town from them. Since Brad is completetly defenseless (maybe turning his waraxe into a lute wasn't exactly the brightest idea),  we have to summon a group of units, who will be following us and let them do the killing. This will cost us music notes (displayed with blue numbers in the top-right corner of the screen) which is automatically generated as Brad plays his lute (it regenerates faster if we stand still). This will be our most important factor as it allows us to summon units and to play special boosting songs, that can increase our team's damage, defence, speed and a special one as well (which requires 5 kills to fill up), that can stun our enemies for a short while while also destroying their projectiles.
Just left to our music notes lies a yellow number showing the amount of gold we have, which we can pick up after killing enemies. With gold we can't do anything during the gameplay, but after restarting, we can purchase several important upgrades, that will be the key to our victory. Most importantly we can unlock new, more powerful units, increase the maximum number of our followers and their permanent level (they can also gain levels during gameplay, but they'll lose it once they die) and we can also get more hit points for Brad, increase speed, music note regeneration, moreover the defense of the town can be improved by purchasing guard towers, reinforce the crystal and so on. The first thing we should buy however is an upgrade that doubles the amount of all the gold we find :)
My favourite was a guy only labeled as the Town Drunk, who runs vertically between the inn and the bottom of the screen with a mug of beer in his hand, puking occasionly, creating puddles of green goo which can slow down and weaken enemies that step into them...
There's a wide variety of units at our disposal, but we can have only 3 types of them at a time in our party (we can summon multiple ones from the same type) and it would be logical to pick the most expensive ones. That's not the case however and I found some of them much more effective than the others, but of course this depends on one's playstyle too. The best combination in my opinion is a party composed of ninjas (excellent firing speed and damage), wizards (not the black, but the blue ones with lightning bolts that can pass through enemies and have knockback effect) and a shaman (whose spear can curse, slow down and summon totems on the corpses of fallen enemies). These guys all have great firing range as well, which is very important as we want to keep the distance from our foes, since going closer to them increases the chance of getting hit and relatively good damage too. It should also be noted that they can be unlocked quite early (except for maybe the shaman). The extra units (imported from other games) like Octodad, may seem funny, but their usefulness is minimal.
Enemy units are all a bit similar (they have different velocity shots) but that's OK, they provide a fair challenge (or can be almost impossible to overcome if you have a wrong set of party members) and they are determined to kill either Brad or the town crystal. There are four bosses, one at the end of each episode who are naturally harder to kill.
The other 2 game modes are 'survival', in which the longer we stay alive against the endlessly spawning foes the more scores we get and 'escape', where we must run from a horde of enemies and dodge obstacles. These game modes provide easy way to get money for the main story, but there are also achievements related to them. I found the escape mode more effective to collect large amounts of money, but it's only true after having reached a certain length, because the amount of gold piles increase drastically as we progress after that.
Having said that most people who criticize the game have problems with acquiring gold and the fact that grinding is required. By purchasing only the necessary upgrades (the gold doubling upgrade, the gold collecting raccoon, the 3 types of units I mentioned) it can be reduced to a minimal amount and the main story can still be finished even on insane difficulty.
Controls are fine, but the use of a controller is heavily advised. This is one of those games which are quite a bit easier using a controller, so do yourself a favour by playing it with one.
The graphics is what one could expect from a flash based game: very simple and cartoonish looking (which I don't like), but the animations are funny and it doesn't really need more. The music changes as Brad plays his different songs but still way too simplistic and can get on one's nerves, the same goes for the sound effects.
Bardbarian is an absolutely fun little casual game that can be entertaining for anyone (provided they have a controller) longing for a few hours of fun and monster killing with alternative game modes.

+ simple yet entertaining gameplay
+ plenty of units and upgrades to choose from
+ 2 alternative game modes beside the main story
CONS
- a bit of a grinding is required to unlock the desired upgrades
- music is annoying

It helps for a game to have a clever hook, but it needs more than just that. Doing something outside the norm is great as long as that's expanded into a full game and not left to prop the whole thing up. Bardbarian has a cute premise but really doesn't go much further than that, seemingly expecting the one joke it's built around and a few cameos from other indie games to carry its terribly thin gameplay. That works for an hour or so, and then it just becomes a grinding slog without a punchline.
Bardbarian is the tale of Brad, mighty barbarian and defender of some dinky village with a giant, important, and otherwise unprotected crystal at its center. On this particular day Brad doesn't feel like vanquishing evil, instead opting to fashion a guitar out of an old battleaxe and jam out. Luckily for him, the villagers, and you, this inspires all manner of mercenaries to come to his aid, shredding monsters as he shreds and drawing power from his power chords.
In other words, you control Brad but you never attack on your own. You can call in one of three chosen units when you have enough chords (generated passively) which will follow you around and attack things within their range. At first you can only call three helpers at a time but through the game's gold-powered upgrade system you can raise that limit, as well as upgrade each mercenary. Brad can also spend chords to buff his team in various ways, and stun enemies when he reaches certain killstreaks.
Monsters come from three lanes on the right and trundle towards your crystal on the left, and if either that or Brad is destroyed, game over. Your minions also have health, so you'll need to weave your whole formation through the lazy projectiles your foes will lob. The game is broken into four chapters of five lengthy waves each, with a boss on the fifth wave. Everything drops gold for you to buy upgrades with between runs; once you start playing you're locked into what you have until you win or die.
This is where the game starts to wear thin, because death is going to be stopping you pretty regularly. There's a significant jump in difficulty between chapters, mainly because of enemies getting huge health and damage boosts. Little critters you could kill in 3 arrows suddenly take 12. It feels like the power curve of a mobile game, forcing you to grind on your current level before unlocking enough upgrades to stand a chance at the next. That's exactly what I did, too, playing chapter 1 until I had the archer units fully upgraded, along with a larger squad size and higher base levels and other stuff. Chapter 2 was still a challenge but I pulled it off, and then Chapter 3 immediately kicked me in the balls until I died.
Ultimately the upgrade system is going to be your main focus, and it isn't even that interesting to begin with. Unit upgrades just make them generally beefier but the early units don't hold a candle to the later ones you unlock, so you can waste gold on guys that can't carry you to the finish line. There's a 2x drops unlock that's basically mandatory but terribly expensive, and the squad size upgrade is obviously the most important but scales ludicrously in cost. It's going to take a lot of grinding the same waves over and over, which will exacerbate how slow and long they tend to be, and how little you actually need to do besides dodging bullets.
Even the actual combat is underwhelming, with slow projectiles and weak sound effects for all of them. You get virtually no feedback on damage, either, with a hit doing a sliver of health and a hit one-shotting you looking and sounding exactly the same. There's very little variety in enemy behavior as well, and that extends even to the bosses. And forget about the survival and escape modes, because they dumb down the gameplay even further. Like I said, it's a cute concept to hang a game on but Bardbarian is paper-thin, offering little in the way of content or challenge to keep you rocking along.

All I have to say is that this is a superb game. I have played a good amount of Robocraft back in 2014, but Gear up pretty much gives Robocraft a run for their money.
Where Robocraft has only a large number of blocks, only three weapon types, and some gadgets. While Gear up has large variety of weapons, sub weapons for additional fire power, or different parts that make your tank move differently, make it stronger or faster, or give it an extra turret for even more fire power!
Once you start out you get a basic tank loadout and you will die a couple of times (by a couple I mean a lot). So I recommend you starting out in a server averaging with Rank 1 players. But as soon as you start buying and experimenting with different parts, you will become a force to be reckoned with.
So far there are only three gamemodes: Conquest, Team Deathmatch, Deathmatch.
Course by the time I write this review (2/1/2015) This game had only recently came out. So there might not be a lot of people populating the servers, but hey it just came out.
Since the game is Free to Play the game there are some limitations. When you start the game you only get one Tank loadout and a limited amount of parts you can store, but you can get an extra storage slot every time you level up and if you join the official Gear Up community group. In order to get more storage for parts and tanks you have to pay for either Basic or Premium membership.
Basic gives unlimited part storage as well as three slots for different tank loadouts, as well as a 2 G coin participation bonus.
Premium gives you everything Basic offers but gives you every part in the game, and a... single player mode? Why this isn't free I don't know.
If you really enjoy the game I would recommend paying for the Basic membership. Premium kind of breaks the point of the game where you pretty much have every part in your disposal and now asking yourself: Now what? If you ask me the fun part is working for those parts, and I wouldn't have built my winning tank without all that hard work.
Overall this game is fantastic arcade shooter that is easy to learn and hard to master, with plenty of gunfire and explosions to keep you coming back, as well as the large variety of parts to customize your tank to become the ultimate weapon.
Final Rating: What are you waiting for?

This game is amazing.  I can't stop playing it.
Let's start out with the first thing you do in the game; character customization.  You have 4 races to choose from, each with their own unique traits, backstory, and affect how everyone treats you.  Lizards can dig without a shovel, Dwarves can crawl into small spaces nobody else can, Elves can eat body parts to learn the memories of the fallen (sometimes gaining skills in the process), and so forth.
You've got a lot of choices for playstyles as well, and it's not set in stone.  You could start off the game as a wizard, then transition into a battlemage who charges into the fray, then unleashes spells that require proximity.
Then, you've got the Tags.  Basically, they let you set up your own backstory, as well as giving additional dialogue options when the time is right.  Mystics can sometimes talk to the gods, whilst Barbarians want a *simple* solution to many problems.  But the best is yet to come...  and it's something that I'm a bit of a sucker for.  Music.  You can set the lead instrument on the soundtrack.  It's only four instruments, and the one you choose will be, well, the prominent instrument throughout the soundtrack.
Not a fan of character customization?  That's fine, you can select an Origin character.  These guys normally would be optional party members if you were to create your own character, but you can also play as them for your main character.  The choices are really interesting too; a lizard who cavorted with demons and got exiled, wanting to reclaim his empire; or a human who is a host of all kinds of spirits while a demon is trying to wrest control of her body.  They all have pre-set tags, but you can choose the class they start with.
Now for the gameplay.
Out of battle, stuff is simple; everything is performed from your clicking (duh).  However, even outside of combat your skills are still tested.  Persuasion can be a way to get out of a fight, or get more information out of someone, bartering lowers prices for you.  You can also steal stuff too, but be warned if you played the first game; the stealing has been revamped by quite a lot.  You can no longer just walk into someone's house, close the door and sneak about, stealing everything that isn't bolted down.  The moment you take something, no matter if you're sneaking or not, the townsfolk will become suspicious and try to search you.  Of course, there's ways to make sure they don't succeed, but I'll leave that since a lot of this game is about finding your own playstyle.
The combat is not really changed by much from the first game, but many more complexities have been added.  Surfaces play a crucial role to a mage just like before, however they have many more options due to the magic trees.  Water can be frozen, electrified, or turned into steam which can also be electrified.  Bless can actually turn surfaces, well, blessed, healing characters who travel through it.  (That includes everyone, so make sure blessed surfaces can't be accessed by the enemy.)  However, there is also Cursed surfaces, which carry extra effects to them.  Necrofire can't be put out by normal water, Cursed Oil can go off on MOVEMENT, and so forth.
Armor is no longer a stat that simply decreases damage received, it is instead its own bar.  This bar is crucial to manage, as it stops status effects.  Think of it as a shield; as long as you have a shield up, you can't be affected by the status of a surface your character may be standing on, with certain exceptions as Oil that slows you down.
As a general rule of thumb however, the game's combat is very challenging.  There really isn't many fights that have "cannon fodder" enemies; everyone is dangerous and they all know how to take advantage of the same things you do.  Be careful about that water you're standing on, for that mage on higher ground likely might have an electric spell he could cast, if your magic armor is down, and stun you.
My recommendation?  This game deserves all the praise that it's got and more.  The only real complaint I have is with the camera control, but that's mainly due to my mouse having issues with some games not registering the middle mouse click.  Plus, in battle you can get a top-down view if there's too many obstacles.

Baldur's Gate 2. So many memories, so much enjoyment, so very very dated graphically.
I'll split this review into two part. The first part will be for people who haven't spent their fair share of time in
, the second will be for those like me, for whom the continent is like a second home.
Part one:
Baldur's Gatewas in many ways the defining roleplaying experience of the 90's. Not because the roleplay mechanics themselves were the focal point of the game. But instead because of the environment, built around that most epic of stories. I've you dear reader have had the pleasure of playing one of the later Bioware RPGs, you'll surely find familiar elements in the BG storyline (Dear EA/Bioware, when can I get to explore the daily trials of a humble grunt soldier / farmer's son in one of your otherwise wellwritten universes?). The NPCs are engaging, their party banter good for many a giggle, and their individual storyarcs satisfactory. The Forgotten Realms (DnD) setting well interpreted / used. One thing to note, however is, that some of the more obscure "classic" DnD mechanics such as Thac0 is used, it's silly in a computer game, and once you understand "which way" the number is supposed to go, you will quite likely happily ignore it again.
Gameplay-wise the game centers around 6-man party combat. Unlike another classic CRPG series, Fallout, you can't talk or sneak your way through the game. So combat is definetely the name of the game here. Unfortunately combat is not one of the stronger suits of the experience - and is in general something I would say Bioware isn't particularly good at designing. Practically it plays out as realtime 'with pause', which on normal to "harder" is required in pretty much all boss battles. It however lacks any of the
realtime satisfaction of hack'n'slash games, and at the same time is utterly hamstring in it's tactical possibilties while paused. So it's more of a half-baked measure of realtime/turnbased than best of both worlds, which is a shame. The spell system of the different caster classes is however rich in variance, and as has always been true, throwing fireballs into the face of your enemy has eternally been 'great fun'.
The one thing that may be a dealbreaker for many a younger / new gamer is the graphics. They're not horrible, but they are very dated. And if you are a
graphics enthusiast it is rather unlikely you'll find much enjoyment in this game.
Part two:
For the non-kids / teens / oldfarts like myself, how've already spent way too much time melting faces as the prodigal son of Bhaal: It's the BG2 you already know (and I assume) love. Not much has changed. It works on modern systems, without issues.
The extras haven't been noticeable enough to not seem entirely forgetable. Depending on your "internal rate of nostalgia", beware that Beamdog has redone the cinematics / cutscenes.
In my opinion the "it's on steam!" and multiplayer are really the most valuable features of this
edition.
As a small conclusion: Would I recommend this game to both the new 'uns and oldies? Wholeheartedly yes! Although I don't feel that the enhanced edition adds much, it's still one of the very best RPGs ever made, and will most likely retain that title for a very long time. Buy it!

The gameplay is pretty much like the older Prince of Persia games (except the combos, which are not present in this game), but the level design can often scare the hell out of you! It's recommended to buy the deluxe edition of this game during a sale (the price drops to $9.99) as you'll get two exclusive skins, one exclusive map, the soundtrack of the game and a free digital copy of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time too!

Awesomenauts is one of my most played games in 2013 and I believe it will continue to be one of my most played games in 2014. Why?
Just by the looks you can tell the amount of work and love that's been put into the game. It's pretty obvious that Awesomenauts is a game that its developers care about and not just some money chest that gets opened one time and then will be burried. Updates are rolling in regularly and the first Kickstarter-powered expansion pack is on its way as well.
What really makes this game so good though is its core gameplay. It takes the MOBA concept, takes away every unnecessary complex addition and adds some action driven 2D arcade gameplay. The resulting game is addictive but also works well in short bursts. Games rarely last longer than 15-20 minutes and the game introduces new characters carefully so you will get to learn their strenghts and weaknesses.
Just be warned that Awesomenauts' fun factor increases exponentially to the friends you're playing this game with. It can be rather frustrating if you're on your own and at mercy of inexperienced or downright dumb people. But setting up a team with two friends and communicating via Skype or Teamspeak will result in one of the best multiplayer experiences on Steam.
This game is worth every penny they're asking for and if you've got the chance to get this cheaper from a Steam Sale or Humble Bundle then give it a shot.

This game is like that family member you love but sometimes wonder if they are really related to you.  In many aspects it really does feel like a refreshed portion of the trilogy while bringing in fresh new elements, other portions however veer off from what I expected from the game going in. Playing the game when it came out honestly I hated it for stupid reasons but recently replaying it I found it an excellent game and I actually look forward to playing it again sometime.
Let me start by saying that this game is in NO way connected to the movie.  This installment is almost completely unconnected to the Sands of Time trilogy, in fact the only character featured in this who was in the trilogy is the Prince.  When I first played the game I really hated this, looking back however I feel a lot of care went into giving the feel of playing the trilogy while still leaving the original story alone.
Parkour is where in my oppinion this game shines, it feels like the trilogy on roids in this aspect. Everything just runs so fluid and the Prince is more agile than ever.  As the game progressed you obtain powers that allow you to control the environment which just adds to the amazing vibe the parkour gives off. What else can I say aside from I feel satisfied when I run up walls?
Combat is almost completely different from the trilogy, you cannot duel wield in this game which honestly is a little dissapointing from the start for me. The combat in this game seems to focus on taking down numerous enemies at a time. I would be a liar if I said that I didn't enjoy the combat in this game but it could have been greatly improved. With the trilogy it was awesome to use the environment to your advantage, this game however is parkour and combat are hardly ever connected. It's a crying shame actually as I think the abilities you unlock could have had some interesting uses in battle.
All in all for me this is a welcome addition to the franchise. If you are a fan of the trilogy I definitely reccomend giving this game a shot as more than likely you will like it. Just remember this has nothing to really do with the trilogy and although that may be a disappointment to some I for one am happy that the trilogy was not tampered with.

This game... Has not aged well.
Hearing about this game for years, I went into it excited for a great atmosphere and skating gameplay. Sadly, the game only delivers partially on either of those counts.
The gameplay is fairly frustrating. I played with a controller and I can't even imagine how poorly this game would play with a keyboard/mouse. The controls almost feel too stiff.. It's difficult to describe, but if you've ever played the Tony Hawk's games, you'll feel the difference. Things like jumps feel like they don't have any "air" to them and grinding is far more of a crapshoot than it should be. The whole goal is to rack up points by stringing combos and the cotrols make this more frustrating than fun.
As for the atmosphere. It tries, almost too hard, to capture a slightly futuristic inner-city Japanese feel. The levels look great and definitely capture that vibe well. They're bright, colorful and extremely charming. The characters, on the other hand, fall distinctly into the "trying too hard" category. They try so hard to be cool and current (at least for 2000) that it's aged poorly. It feels like one of those things I would have eaten up back in the early 2000s, but now I just look at it and cringe. Each character is an almost over-the-top stereotype that seems like the sort of thing that was more likely thought up by corporate suits trying to market to kids than anyone who actually has any experience in the skating subculture.
I just couldn't enjoy this. Maybe growing up with the Tony Hawk's games has colored my perception a little bit but if you want skating action, those games do it right. My experience managed to be more frustrating than fun, and unless you have some nostalgic tie to JSR, I can't recommend it.

Just terrible, artsy fartsy crap that only some fedora neckbeard would think is deep and meaningful.
You play as one of two people who wander around a boring landscape, thinking random wistful lovey dovey things that don't evoke any emotion whatsoever from the player except groans. Then the game suddenly decides to take you and your "lover" inside some building, where you sit and click on items at each other, and each item activates a sentence in a nonsensical conversation that's supposed to be "deep", but instead reads like laughable emo poetry. I didn't keep playing much after that.
Where is the love story that's supposed to make the player imprint on the characters? I thought the entire premise of this art game was to draw a beautiful allegory for magnetism across distance. Absolutely none of it comes through in the final product and I found myself laughing at the tryhard writing almost every other sentence.
The whole thing reeks of a 2deep4me college freshman who just finished a game design degree at Full Sail University and celebrated by taking a nerdy girl into his room to watch Fight Club and not drink alcohol because alcohol is for jocks, and then she friendzoned him, and then he created THIS masterpiece to express his feelings about The One still being out there pining for him. So if that's you I guess this game is perfect.
