I have to say, I had a blast with this game.  It’s essentially a type of DOTA/tower defense game.  Your role is to summon and buff an NPC party that follows you automatically performs its roll.  Attackers target and attack enemies in range, healers heal when you stop walking, defenders deflect ranged enemy attacks when they are struck and so on.  You earn gold as you play which you spend after you die to improve the town, units, buffs and other aspects of the game.  The music is pretty great too, it was stuck in my head for days.  There are 3 gameplay modes, which lets you switch things up a bit, as well as a harder dificulty to select when you create a new game file.
My list of complaints is pretty short.  Some of the units felt pretty underwhelming, and if you pick a good group you are essentially unbeatable, which can hurt replayability.  Since you only get one town and never go anywhere else there isn’t much opportunity for the game to present situations where using specific units or combinations is very impactful.  There isn’t much variety of enemies, which isn’t a big deal, but I think is worth noting.
I would love to see more locations added in an update, but as is it is still a great little game I would recommend picking up.

A part of me wants to recommend the game, and the other part cannot in good faith.
On the one hand, the game is graphically beautiful, with an amazing OST. The work on these two aspects alone is almost worth recommending the game. It's the meat of the game, however, the exploration and the puzzles that cannot be recommended. Much of the exploration is boring, and the puzzles can be unclear, but in their execution, are not very difficult. If you understand the puzzle being putforth, they are easy. However, some require exploration, that when unclear as to the actions needed to solve it, require tedious busywork exploring the areas surrounding the puzzle to see whatever symbol is needed to match up in solving it. It basically comes down to that. You find the symbols needed to match up with whatever order they are supposed to be displayed on whatever puzzle, to unlock an item needed to progress, or to open a certain doorway.
The puzzles are not fun, and if not something that can be solved on the screen that the puzzle is found, then requiring backtracking to other rooms. A few puzzles I actually looked up in guides to simply save me time in backtracking, or playing by whatever tedious rules the game required. That isn't fun, and takes away from the experience Tengami would otherwise provide.
It's more engaging than a pretty but boring "walking simulator" like Dead Esther, but what gives it more substance isn't enough to warrant a recommendation. If it's cheap enough, and especially if it offers the OST, the game can potentially be recommended, just to see and hear what is offered, but don't buy it for the puzzles.

When looking to purchase this game, there is a simple test you should perform before hand.
Firstly, do you like modern art? Because that's what this game is, a fanciful and supposedly symbolic experience in which you will reflect on whatever you can imagine to be the depth of the 'piece'.
Secondly, are you seeking an actually meaningful or deep experience that doesn't require DIY symbolism, perhaps with a strong but non-violent narrative? If you are, then turn away immediately, the game simply isnt worth your time.
And thirdly, do you mind performing repetitive actions with very little benefit? If you do, then perhaps you should try something else, like the Stanley Parable or something.
My personal opinion of the game is that if I have paid good currency on a piece of content, then there should actually be content and that content should be legible and self constructing. I should not receive a random set of letters and have to conjure up some sentence. The sentence should come at least partially pre-made to give the thought some sort of legitimacy. If I have to make it up without any kind of confidence that that is what the media was saying, then the thought won't only be short lived, it'll probably be too weak to have any kind of effect when it is in my mind. Deus Ex Human Revolution creates a moral dilemma out of a slowly constructed jigsaw that you see pieced together before you, the Stanley Parable hints at the deeper meanings of it's gags but only so much as to force you to complete the meaning yourself. Both games have made me seriously think about the messages they were pushing. This did nothing.

Whilst not as scary or immersive as the first game. This is probably one of the best roaming survival shooter games you can buy today on the market.
The game comes with a very flexible moddable (at times... buggy) engine with a semi-realistic ballistics system even down to somewhat realistic ranges on weapons (There are a few exceptions). Whilst this is not Arma II and rarely requires any sort of tactical planning, this game is still fairly authentic feeling for the most part. The only downside is enemies tend to lean towards taking a full clip to the torso to die on higher difficulties and the game forces you to rely on headshots in order to progress, but keeping it on normal keeps it from being too silly.
This game has very light RPG elements, such as quests and tasks to do, as well as a currency and the ability to change your loadout in your inventory.
Additionally Stalker CoP is very open ended, allowing for quite a lot of freedom and gameplay/storyline decisions, unlike previous games however the story is somewhat better put together and the game doesn't require you to be as invested in the atmosphere to enjoy it. If you prefer a on rails shooter and don't like games like Fallout: New Vegas, you probably won't like this game. IF you love exploring every nook and cranny... You will love this game as it generally rewards inquisitive gameplay.
Just be prepared to have a bit of patience with this game, as it takes some modding to fix bugs and issues, but nowhere near as much as Clear Sky or Shadow of Chernobyl. If you're keen to do a bit of research, there are tons of mods out there.
While I recommend this game, I also highly recommend you check youtube for gameplay videos, as it's not for everyone.

You know what the uncanny valley is? Where you look at something that looks like something else and it's kinda disturbing because it almost looks like the thing it's imitating, but not quite? That's A Walk in the Dark in a nutshell. It abashedly borrows from Limbo, VVVVV, and especially Super Meat Boy, but it seems like the creators didn't fully understand what made those games so great.
Like SMB, A Walk in the Dark is a reflexes based platformer that challenges you to get through the levels quickly. Each level is under a minute, usually under thirty seconds, and there is no punishment for death. But with SMB, the controls felt perfectly calibrated. With A Walk in the Dark, the controls are perfectly functional, but they feel a bit off. You don't stick to the walls, which seems strange for a cat. Momentum feels strange, like gravity decided to phone it in for the day. When landing on a platform, it's relatively common to get stuck on the corner of the platform. When playing as the girl, who controls gravity in a way reminiscent of VVVVV, the controls feel almost too responsive. None of these are game killers, but they all make the controls feel slightly off. If you look beneath, you'll see just as many people praising the controls as damning them, and my guess is that the people upset with the controls are the people who have enough experience with really good platformers to instinctively know what great controls feel like.
The art will probably grab your attention fairly quickly, but if you're anything like me, after a while, it will also start to feel a bit strange. Animations are just a frame or two too short. SMB's buzzsaws and spikes have been imported wholesale, but where they fit well with SMB's aesthetic, they feel out of place here. Many of the collectibles blend almost seamlessly into the background, especially in the levels where you play as the girl. And while the art style is frequently gorgeous, the blending of VVVVV's basic spikes, SMB's cartoonish buzzsaws, and Limbo's more realistic looking gears and creatures don't quite fit together into a harmonious whole. Look at the second-to-last screenshot up above (the one with 07.04 in the corner) to really see what I mean. Again, none of it really destroys the aesthetic, but all of that keeps it from being something really special.
A Walk in the Dark is never a bad game, but it's easy to look at the game and see how it could have been great instead of just being kinda decent. If you have cash to burn, there are worse games to buy, but there are also far better ones, too.

So, have you ever played Dungeons and Dragons? If you have, BAM, that's this game (Advanced D&D, but same thing), if you haven't though, then you're in for a treat. So this is probably the BEST adventure game ever. This is the second game in a two off series. Created by a Triple Entente of awesome consisting of Wizards of the Coast, Black Isle Studios, and the illustious Bioware. This is a great standalone game, but some references to the first game are always in need of some background.
The story begins right where the original game left off, after creating your character, you are thrust into the world of magic, adventure, dungeons, and amazing storytelling. Everything about this game is absolutely amazing, it is a great part of my childhood, and will more than be able to keep you and your friends happy in your own little fantasy world. You can go from fighting vampires in a graveyard, ogres in the countryside, defend against ancient evil spirits in dark ruins, fight off cults, answer genie riddles, and slay dragons.
That being said, one of the only downfalls to this game is that it's worldbuilding ability is far from stellar, in fact, aside from the multiplayer story mode, this game has no real replay value, and the only redeeming feature is that it is an epic game that sprawls through every facet of the Dungeon and Dragons game. The game at points can be insanely hard if you aren't a specific class or have a specific party make up (oh, and have fun being evil, Bioware made this before learning the joy of selecting your own path to victory, so it'll be almost impossible to play as evil).
All-In-All: This game is simply amazing, epic storytelling, beautiful visuals (even for their times), great character development, and absolutely awesome gameplay. A must play for fans of Dragon Age.

I have never been to Soho or Brighton, but I have always loved pinball.  I grew up during the golden age of pinball.  I played some really good tables, good themes, talking tables, etc.  The best tables always had great gameplay with smooth flipper action.  The theme was almost always fun, but good gameplay always wins out over theme.   I've played many a table where the hotspot on the flippers would klunk off an corner.  As the tables aged, the flippers would give the ball less momentum and the ball didn't roll as well ... leading to weak action (balls just going up to the target and .... falling well short to roll back down again without hitting anything).
Video pinball never ages or succumbs to weak action, burned out lights, poor ball rolling, etc.  There are many pinball games that capture this table realism and maintain the pinball feel like an actual table, but Zombie Pinball is not one of these.  Zombie Pinball offers an interesting approach to pinball, doing some really cool things that a real table never could.  And it does these things quite well.  The flipper action is smooth - no klunking off corners.  The flipper hotspots have a real smooth and satisfying result - usually to the top and down a winding side tunnel or pegging a target.  Very nice.
Floating video animations can be unlocked that are vaporized with the ball.  Multiball can be unlocked (two ball), and several other multiball scenarios can be unlocked with what appears to be a dozen or so balls.  Sometimes they are on fire.  It has a thoughtful "Ball Saved" mechanism, so that when multiball happens, drained balls are automatically shot back out onto the top (for a certain amout of time).  This way, you get a reasonable amount of gameplay with the multiball scenario that you spent the time unlocking (a super nice feature).  I've played a real world table that shot the multiballs at high speed right at the flippers.  If you weren't expecting it, they went straight down the drain - and there went your multiball.  Thanks for that!
Other tables can be unlocked by accruing Bloody Stars (basically points for scoring while playing a table).  It's fun to spend some effort learning to do something well with a reward at the end!  I haven't played all of the tables, but the main table is fun enough for the price of admission.  The unlockables are just a bonus.  I am having fun just playing the main table so far...
The configuration options for the game are very limited.  The devs just added using the SHIFT keys for the flippers, so that was really the big concern.  The keys can't be configured, but they are pretty standard.  Some people report issues with certain resolutions, but the Devs are on it.
The devs are active on the forums, and they have already implemented several suggestions.  Please feel free to add some constructive ideas!
Bottom line.  If you want realism, look elsewhere.  If you want something fun and interesting with smooth action and some unlockable rewards, right here.

Before beginning to write this review of Zombie Pinball, the reviewer carefully read ZP's Store Page. Actually, it says very little, and claims little more, except the possibly questionable “A super addictive gameplay”. In fact, Zombie Pinball is all it claims to be (with the one possible exception.) It is fun, it does (one presumes) have seven tables. Thus, this reviewer will give a positive review of a game that presents itself honestly, but will also attempt to include enough information to allow each gamer to make a personal choice.
Yes, Zombie Pinball does involve hitting BALLS with FLIPPERS, and by doing so, scoring POINTS. It has lots of SOUNDS, and LIGHTS, and does it ever have POINTS! And it looks GREAT! So it certainly does fulfill every component of the definition of “pinball”. But it is by no means “traditional” pinball.....
Zombie Pinball has seven tables, but at this point only three of them (very similar in most ways) are part of this review to any degree. The reason? Tables beyond the first one need to be unlocked by the acquisition of “Bloody Stars” in order to play. And while it’s not an overwhelming number of stars, for some beginning players it might take many hours of play to access each next table. (This player managed to get over half the required stars for the next table from a single, 1.3 billion-point game (since, vanished from history. "News at 11:00".)
As for scoring, Zombie Pinball offers an achievement when a player manages to “Obtain more than 100.000.000 points on any table” (table or game?), so clearly this game is geared toward the less experienced pinballer. And this reviewer doesn’t doubt for a moment that for these players the game will be a real blast, providing many hours of fun and considerable challenge. But for a more advanced player (with this player falling somewhat in-between), this game may not be more than marginally suitable or enjoyable. One can see endless games; literally games without end. Or at least, games lasting hours and hours, since most of the time there is more than a single active ball. As such, it’s unlikely that there will ever be a time without the opportunity to assure a "next" ball in play, with the relatively easy opportunity for extra balls. There does seem to be some indication of table difficulty increasing (far too gradually) as new tables are unlocked, so this review may be wrong, and need correcting later.
No doubt, for a less experienced player it will be exciting to have in excess of ten balls in play at once during a Zombie Pinball game. But for the experienced player this multi-ball play might easily account for up to a third (or more) of game time, with the flippers constantly “tattooing’ (or, pressing of the keys in a rapid, staccato fashion.) This "rapidly" (Har!) grows tiring, and more than just a bit boring. But, WOW!, does it build the points quickly! And did this reviewer forgot to mention: 5-ball games? (Great when quarters are at stake, but perhaps unnecessary in computer pinball.) A player may also invoke the previously mentioned “tattoo tactic” when the common “fire mode” is achieved, as it’s very difficult to see exactly what is, or isn’t, a ball. That’s also the case in some of the more flashy modes. Red balls have become the 21st century's version of "DIP", or "Darned Invisible Pinballs" ( at the best of times.) So clearly, the fingers will get a workout, two at the time.
Zombie Pinball includes some game-accessible modes which are interesting, but of minimal challenge to many players. In some of them creatures or items float across the screen, offering additional balls as they are hit. It also offers Challenges that might act to liven the game up a bit for more advanced players, 70 Challenges total. Each must be completed to continue to the next.  The first one simply reads “Validate 10 ramps”, but not a clue as to how that’s done, or quite what it means. And after scoring numerous billions of points, it hasn’t happened on its own for this player, so perhaps only the best players can achieve these 70 goals (or it’s really far simpler, and being overthought.) However, Challenges do offer additional, no doubt well deserved “Bloody Stars” for those figuring it out.

There’s a total of eleven Zombie Pinball achievements, most involving “Completing” individual tables. Apparently a table is “Completed” by invoking four specific modes. However, having received as many as thirteen times the “achievement” high score, and had the words “Completed” flashed on the screen repeated times…the reviewer has yet to receive this achievement. Not even on the original table. Who knows, at this point, what’s missing or done incorrectly? The “Rules” are very brief with terms that may be familiar to the DEVs, but are not expressed clearly enough, or sometimes grammatically proper enough to be helpful to this player. (Achievement statistics indicate that while nearly half of players have the high-score achievement, no one has any of the others.)
Currently Zombie Pinball has a number of bugs, apparently mostly under consideration. One causes the game to crash upon every exit. This reviewer encountered one on a three occasions where balls simply ceased being issued mid-game, and experienced the disappearance of the mentioned 1.3 billion-point game from the high score listing (though without the documentation necessary to substantiate.) Perhaps some of the other concerns or questions expressed in this review are actually not intended to be a part of the game. Perhaps we'll know soon.
This player hasn’t attempted to play Zombie Pinball with a controller, and it seems perhaps to be designed exclusively for keyboard play. The menu system is very poorly designed, but game play should be the deciding factor.
Who should buy Zombie Pinball? Completionists, of course. Beginning pinballers. Better pinballers who don’t mind throwing the last balls of a game away in order to leave the house. (Seriously.) Those who want to have fun without taking the experience too seriously. Those who want a pinball experience to cool down after or warm up before serious pinball. And certainly, those who enjoy zombies, which I suspect is the intent of this fun, but (so far) non-challenging game. For its moderate and fair price perhaps no one should ultimately be discouraged from this purchase.

Forgotten Sands is a solid game with a decent story. The problem is, fitting it between two parts of an existing trilogy means that by necessity, the game can't tell a story that both ties into the plot of the trilogy and is important to the trilogy's plot. As a result, Forgotten Sands is a standalone adventure which has absolutely no relevance to the overarching plot. It's also very similar mechanically and structurally to Sands of Time, but with a few new elements and small tweaks, and without the awesome framing device of the Prince telling his story (that's referenced at the beginning but is quickly abandoned). If you're a fan of the series it's worth playing, but it's not a good place to start your Prince of Persia adventures - Sands of Time is still my favourite and the best jumping-on point.

I thought I might give this game a review to help it along. The only reason I knew about it is because I have actually gone through every single title in my Steam queue. That's right. All 20,702 at the time of this writing. I feel like this title could use a little more attention.
I absolutely love coin-operated machines of all kinds, and I even have a bulk candy vending machine in my office for the use of students and visitors that come by. The opportunity of playing a game that simulated some of these games sounded appealing to me, so I put this on my wishlist. I was delighted when it game out for less than two bucks for early access. Two bucks! I grabbed it up and have enjoyed it so far. For a game of its price point, it does quite well. You won't find a whole lot of bells and whistles here, but what you will find is a game that re-creates many of the ticket redemption games found in arcades very faithfully.
At this point in time, there are 5 games, one of which is in testing. There's an electronic stacker game, a ball drop game, one of those where you push a robotic arm through a slot to claim a prize, a coin pusher, and a foosball table. They all run quite smoothly, although they are significantly easier than their real-life counterparts. This is NOT a bad thing, as the real-life counterparts are designed to eat your money, whereas this has no such goal in mind.
Moving forward, the developer intends to add at least three more machines, judging by the blank spaces on the menu, but I hope there will be more as time goes on. Each machine is unlocked by reaching a certain level of performance (unlocking stars) on previous machines. This helps to guide you through playing each of the machines, so you wind up getting to experience some that you may not have picked as your first choide. It also provides you with a reason to play each machine, in the hopes of unlocking others. The progression is currently linear, though, which means that it may take a while to get to machines you really want to play when more are added. They might benefit from changing it to allow players to pick what machines they want to unlock with their earned stars. The stars are not terribly hard to earn, and the game itself is not particularly deep at the moment, but the quality of simulation makes the $2 or less pricetag very worthwhile. I would definitely recommend this for some simple fun, especially considering how you can easily spend more than this at an arcade just playing some of these 2-3 times.

Let's get this out of the way, this doesn't appear to be a game where you play a machine of your choosing and earn rewards. Each machine has a win state in which you get up to 2 stars. The more stars you have the more machines are available. Once you complete a machine there is little point to go back to it. You can, however, if you so desire.
Graphically the game is passable. Although, there are no settings. None. Zilch. Hope you like fullscreen and stretched (I have a 21:9 monitor and some settings... at least fullscreen/windowed would have been nice). The audio varies by machine. I'm not sure if this is by design or if it's because some are unfinished.
Now, let's go machine by machine.
The first machine isn't one of my favorites. It's one of those where you have to press a button to drop digital blocks (on a screen... on your screen... so meta-blocks) on top of one another to reach a certain height. This one is quick to pass and not very enjoyable. The background audio is pretty good here, though. Nice ambience of an arcade area.
This machine has a spinning plate with holes, each with a different point value assigned. The object is to get the dropped bouncy ball to go into holes with high enough point values to total the amount needed to get 2 stars. I don't think I've ever seen one of these machines in person.
First of all, I HATE these machines. I have never found much enjoyment out of them as the win-to-lose ratio is far too low. The prizes in real life are usually pretty fantastic, though, because of this reason. But, I still hate them. And, it's a game where stereoscopic vision is pretty important, and it doesn't translate well to a 2D game. (I know it's a "3D game" but it's on a 2D screen) This one may be the game that frustrates people. But, the object is to get enough points to get 2 stars to get to the next machine. Each hole which the pusher can enter has a block behind it with an assigned number of points.
Finally! The meat of the game I was looking for! I love coin pushers. I once filled 2 giant trash bags full of won stuffed animals from our county fair. I probably spent close to $75... but still. There are no points you need to achieve to get stars here. Instead, the stars are laying on top of the coins and you just need to push them off. I want to see more of this style of gameplay added. The physics are decent at best, though. The pusher moves at full speed, but the coins fall and bounce in slooooooow motion. It's not a frames issue, they just react like it's quarter gravity. Even then this is still the most enjoyable machine, for myself anyways. It would have been better if there were other collectable objects that appear randomly each time you go to the machine to make the replay value high enough. But, it's still fun to try and get the 2 stars again on this one.
This one was in test mode when I played, and couldn't get stars. The table looks nice and the physics felt okay. But not much to say here yet, it's foosball.
Overall, it's a hard call whether to recommend this. I will say it's not for everybody. The game is clearly in it's early stages and more will come. But if you enjoy arcade games it's one to watch. However, given its current price of under $2, I say give it a go if you enjoy arcade style games and want to encourage further development. I know I do.

Tengami is just amazing.
The concept of leading your player character through a pop-up book is unique, and the visuals are, in my opinion, perfect fo the atmosphere.  The puzzles go along with the pop-up book theory, and are generally pretty simple to complete without being total pushovers.
The music is incredibly well-done, and I could easily sit and listen to it without even the benefit of the game.
Overall, it's a relaxing, peaceful game that takes about an hour and a half to complete (more or less depending on if you're rushing or dawdling).  It's not an action game and some might consider it boring, but if you like a peaceful puzzle experience you'll probably enjoy it.
To be fair, there are some minor downsides (load screens are long and your player character is a little slow), but nothing that ruined the experience for me.
So in summary, this is totally worth a play.  Wait for a sale if the $9,99 seems too steep for a two-hour game; I would personally pay full price for it in hindsight due to the beautifully crafted scenes and hauntingly gorgeous music alone.

Game developers should be encouraged to challenge the status quo with narrative and mechanics, but I feel that there are certain best practices for game design that Tale of Tales often overlooks for no visible reason or benefit to the game. While Bientôt l'été has the most conventional controls and straightforward instructions of their games to date, it still suffers from the same problem: some strange design decisions have little to nothing to do with the concept, and may even hinder it.
Imagine the PS3 game Journey: two players meet at random in a surreal world to make a connection. Except in Bientôt l'été, both players are chat robots stating phrases at random while smoking cigarettes, drinking wine, and playing chess (with a catch: you have to find the pieces first, but one at a time). The highlight of the game should be the multiplayer, but unfortunately it doesn't seem to be very populated (a symptom of its avant garde concept, I guess), and the interactions are severely limited.
What should be a virtual date with a stranger in a surreal world becomes tedius, with no real interaction or connection with said stranger. Unlike Journey, which limits your characters' intractability to serve the purpose of the mechanics and design, Bientôt l'été's design stands at odds with its concept, preventing players from creating any kind of meaningful connections.

After more than 1000 hours of playtime, I think I can properly talk about this game:
First of all, Warframe is a third person shooter/mmo fusion with very deep gameplay customization and character progression, lots of different activites to do (from defenses to spy missions, along fishing or space combat, as I say, IT'S HUGE), and constant rewards/things to collect.
You can play solo or coop, there are AMAZING story missions as well as daily and weekly challenges and special missions to make sure you never get bored.
The community is great, with lots and lots of people willing to cooperate and help others (it`s not always the case, but most of the time for sure, at least in my experience), and the dev's are some of the best in the business, with constant feedback and updates in favor of the players, from small things like armor and weapons coming almost twice a month and big events and content drops that feel like expansions coming every once in a while, but never for too long for you to want to abandon the game.
Oh, and if you haven´t noticed, it's free to play, but not in some kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t way, you can PLAY EVERYTHING FOR FREE, and never feel forced to pay for anything (to be honest, up until this point I have only spent 30€ on this game and I did out of my own will to help the studio, haven´t gotten any kind of gameplay advantage out of it, mostly cosmetic stuff).
All in all, I can only recommend for you to play Warframe, it's great and has content to play for a loooong time, and if you don't like it, you don't have to spend a single cent on it.

3000 hours in over 4 years, and still coming back to it. This game has to be doing something right
I love this game despite its missteps. I love the weapons, I love the player characters, I love the variety, I love the worldbuilding, I like the story (used to love it), I love the NPCs, I love the balance of grinding and monetization so that free-to-players still get their sense of accomplishment. I love how even during a timegate you can still go in and run missions to shoot enemies. I love being a space ninja commando, with superpowers, fighting in the distant space fantasy future against multiple factions with interesting and unique enemies.
But above all I love the developers, and the passion they still put in even after years of crunch time on major updates
The only problems can't bring it down for me. Older features are left without polish sometimes, because the devs would rather make new stuff. The power creep can get ridiculous, especially regarding primed weapons. Stealth is clunky outside of designated Spy or Rescue missions due to not meshing with procedural generation.
But even all this is not stopping me from playing at least one mission every day. This is not a game to 100% over a week, but if you're in for an action MMO, Warframe is worth a try

When it comes to nostalgia and gaming, there's generally three tiers of quality:
-Aged like a banana.
-Aged like imported cheese.
-Aged like fine wine.
Jet Set Radio is the latter. Everything from the stylized graphics, pumping soundtrack, and frustrating yet rewarding gameplay all hold up. The only thing that probably doesn't hold up is the controls. Not all of them, but having a button that controls the camera mapped to the same one that controls tagging can produce a lot of issues in missions that require near surgical precision to complete.
Does this make Jet Set Radio a bad game? Hell no! When you're grinding rails, running from the cops, and chasing down rival taggers, you can easily forget this one minor issue. But because of it, consider the game to have aged like a fine wine with a flawed cork.
9/10

I wanted to like this game so bad, but it has a lot of problems.
First off the AI, it's non-existent. When it comes to these survival games this is a huge problem, the AI is non-responsive so you can usually get in a few whacks until it finally reacts to you. Makes combat a complete joke at lower levels. You can get NPCs to guard your base, but the AI is so bad, you're better off not even having any.
Speaking of combat, it's just not fun. In pvp, everyone uses warhammers since they have the ability to stunlock. Yep, that's pvp combat for you, being knocked to the ground from 100-0 and unable to react. Archery is a complete joke, it's like shooting spitballs at someone (even NPCS), plus it's impossible to tell where your arrows are landing most of the time due to the way the arrow flies. Dunno if it's netcode or what.
So, let's talk about Servers. There are 1000s of servers. People only play on about 5 of them. The most active server is a non-official pvp server because it's heavily populated and heavily moderated. The official servers are overrun by hackers I've heard. You're really not given a huge choice in servers because 99.9% of them are always empty, so if you want active people you'll have to go to a pvp server which we'll get into in a minute.
Before that, I want to go over resource collection. It's the slowest thing in the world. I don't know how it's possible to play this game at a 1x multiplier on resources, cause most servers run a 3x and it's still slow as balls. When you have one of the first forges requiring 560 stone, that'd take forever to get on a 1x server. Plus there's a MASSIVE time gap between the tier 1 gathering tools (stone) and your tier 2 (iron). Even on a 3x server you're gonna spend hours getting the resources to even build your tier 2, and if you die and especially if your base gets raided on a pvp server, you're back to nothing. Not to mention that the resource distributions on the map are downright awful. All the iron is in the northern part of the map which is required to advance and protect your base. You can't even settle the southern part of the map because of this.
So, let's talk about base-building now that we've covered that. So, you're stuck playing on a pvp server cause everything else is dead, died a million times due to griefing, so let's say you build a base just like the ones in the promo videos. We'll if it's tier 1 you're gonna have a higher level player go in and either
1)Destroy the whole thing since they'll have tier 3 weapons which can damage tier 1 buildings.
2)Destroy 1 wall or however many is standing in their way and destroy all your smithing structures, which undoes all the work you've done and you're back to tier 1 tools.
They aren't doing it for your 1337 newbie resources, they're doing it to grief.
So, let's say you invest the hours into upgrading your buildings to tier 2 or 3 so that only explosives can damage it. Well, it's gonna be the 2nd scenario where they destroy 1 wall and any other standing in their way and set you back even harder. Btw Tier 2 buildings are insanely expensive and time consuming, I can't even imagine doing this on a 1x server. And remember, if you were lucky enough to invest the time into getting guards (Almost a tier 2.5 sort of thing), they're completely worthless!
Now, let's say you've teamed up with a bunch of people and you're able to protect your base 24/7, and you actually get a huge base like in the videos. You know those clips of the giant monsters stomping the buildings and the snake weaving in the destroying the buildings? That's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ player. The endgame literally revolves around religion where you can become these giant avatars and have free rein to destroy any base you want. Welp, so long the weeks you poured into building that super sweet city.
In conclusion, this is early access, will it be fixed? Maybe, but they really need to fix combat and make it so losing your base isn't as easy for your enemy and devastating for yourself, or else this game will be dead soon enough.

Nice little puzzle game. I don't normally care for such games, but the pop-up book nature of this attracted me, and made for a nice spot of gaming on a Sunday morning. It's such a simple thing, but it's done very well, and feels quite special.
Most of the puzzles are pretty straight-forward and simple, though the hints aren't often much help (it's worth noting that the devs have published a walkthrough on their site, so it seems clear to me that they want people to enjoy the atmosphere and mood of the game, rather than be frustrated by puzzles if you do get stuck).
It's a pretty easy 100% achievement game, if you care about that; just finish the game to unlock them all.
The main thing I'd complain about is the price; it is a very short game, with little obvious replay value, so if I'd paid full price for this, I'd feel quite disappointed (I got my copy as part of a bundle). But, if you can pick it up at a heavily discounted price or as part of a bundle, then it's worth your time.

EDIT9/2016::
So I made a review about this game in March of last year ... And frankly, not much has changed except maybe a graphical upgrade. There is now health-draining weather elements to constrain you to your shelter from time to time, some new enemies with extreme aggro, two crafting stations, one of which is used to break down junk and excessive equipment and the other to create some metal objects, including swords and crafting materials, and farming, which seems redundant with how easily you can find food anyway.
...Y'know, I hate to say it, but this game still seems like a poor investment on my part. The added features does give the game some additional depth, but it still suffers from a lack of challenge. The new enemies do admittedly make for some excitement considering their fast speed and tendancy to attack in groups, but they're not nearly enough to elevate this game above mediocrity. And as soon as you get a ranged weapon even they don't pose much of a threat.
There are plenty of games out there with survival elements to them; some of which focus on hardcore/realistic survival like Project Zomboid and The Long Dark, others which focus on base-building and defence like 7 Days To Die, and others which are just an elaborate excuse to slay enemies with the goal of gathering supplies like State of Decay or Subterrain; but all of the mentioned are good games because they focus on being whatever they are and manage to work in their level of survival to push the player into working hard to either win or just to survive as long as possible. They're fun either because they are challenging or they provide a lot of features and content to make your experience unique. But this game doesn't do anything right. It doesn't provide anything close to the features of 7 Days To Die or Subterrain, it doesn't have the content of Project Zomboid or State of Decay, nor does it test the player like The Long Dark... It's just a plain survival game that has little to offer other than the very basics.
Granted, for a two dollar game, this is okay. And the preview of the 0.3 version does show another graphical overhaul on the horizon. But frankly that's just sugar-coating to a very bland pastry. I guess I shouldn't expect too much given that this game only has one coder, but I feel like this guy is in over his head. A survival game needs a lot of attention to detail and knowhow to be accurate, fun or preferably both; something which I feel is beyond that of a single guy and his pet project. But given the opinions of the people who voted on my review, perhaps I'm wrong. Perhaps this game will become better with time... Or maybe it's just two dollars of disappointment.
Well, the developer has promised more content on the horizon, so we'll just have to see what happens.
EDIT9/2016::
First of, I'd like to point out that this is a preliminary review. As in, a comment on how the game stands right now. My attitude towards it will most likely change as it develops.
So, let's start off...
Right now this game contains about as much content as an average flash game on Newgrounds or Kongregate. It's extremely simple, and once you figure out how to move adequately you can easily fend off attacks by the wildlife (wolves and bears), whose only real difference is their speed. And if the developer reads this: You might want to change that.
Your main tools for harvesting the lands are rocks (as in common rocks you find lying on the ground) and axes; both can harvest any kind of harvestable resource (trees and boulders) or kill wildlife. There are also hammers and shovels, though their uses are limited to construction or reshaping the ground respectively, and they can't be used as weapons. Tools used exclusively as weapons include bows and handguns, which can be crafted relatively easily. Their advantage is not only in range, but they also slow your opponents drastically for about two or three seconds, making it far too easy to get in consequtive hits, assuming you have enough ammo. (And it would surprise me if you didn't, since that is also extremely easy to craft.)
You can also build your own house! Flooring, walls, doorways and roofs. Out of wood... J-Just wood... Oh, and different kinds of flooring with rocks, and wood... This will obviously be expanded on in the future updates, but right now it's just a bit boring building your own shelter, not to mention unnecessary since the map is littered with abandonned buildings. The only disadvantage to these is that you can't make doors for them, but meh...
All in all, I'm sensing the usual potential with early access games here. And if Scott Cawthon has proved anything, it's that single developers can produce good games. But right now, the game is far too limited, and much too easy. And it suffers from the same sort of problem that most survival games has: Hoarding! The game didn't do its description justice... Because as it stands right now, it's just another minimalistic survival game, with the same core ideas and the same problems. So sorry people, but I just can't bring myself to recommend this. And I'm usually a bit TOO NICE in my reviews...! You'd be better off playing Project Zomboid or something. At least that game has some challenge in its early stages...
But once again, this is only preliminary. I've put my money on this thing, so I better not be disappointed in the future as well. But I'm an optimist! So I assume that I won't be. :)

TL;DR: Early Access, 90 updates in 10 months, devloper is open to criticism and suggestions, $5 base price can't go wrong, even better if you catch it on sale.
Project Explore at first, sounds and looks like an exploration/walking simulator, but it's basically a top-down survival game similar to Don't Starve; there's a hunger/thirst meter, health and sanity which you have to maintain through items such as food and water, first-aid and entertainment (mainly from books). Crafting is very straightforward with an in-game recipe, which may make the survival aspect less challenging. The game is heavy on exploring and that's where Sanity comes to play because in order to continue exploring you need to stay sane. While other survival games use Stamina or Temperature as means of survival, Project Explore uses Sanity, which I find interesting and hope to see more depth coming from it as it develops.
--- 07 January, 2016 ---
There's been massive updates and the game is slowly getting better, my first impression was a top-down Minecraft, but visually and technically it's turning into Don't Starve. There's also major visual/graphical changes around the corner so it's worth looking at the announcements. I would still recommend the game at this point, rate of progression and price, it's definitely worth following if anyone is curious about trying the game out.
---- 23 March, 2015 ----
It's not a clone, but it's basically a top-down version of Minecraft; you cut down trees, you build, you hunt, you eat, and you die. You also collect dirty magazines and read them to stay... sensible.
The alpha version of Project Explore was only released two days ago, so there's a lot of content missing, many items still have no function, the survival aspect is really light (no thirst meter (yet?), being able to eat everything raw, nothing despawns/respawns, no durability), but there's so much potential for this game.

This game is beautiful and the detail might even overwhelm you at the start. One of the biggest criticisms of the first Original Sin was the steep learning curve and lack of purpose to your actions at the start of the game (a murder noone cares about). Larian Studios solved this problem beautifuly by letting the player first roam a smaller area and giving you a primary objective. The overarching story and your part in it are introduced in the first area (which alone took me 30 hours to finish).
The combat feels satisfying. The new elements introduced (armor and high ground) feel fresh and allow for different approaches to any fight. The fighting locations are carefully crafted and reward planing ahead and execution of the fight.
All in all this is an outstanding game. I feel the same excitement I felt when I played Baldurs Gate 2 for the first time as a kid. On a visceral level this is the biggest compliment I can give Divinity 2. Like Baldurs gate in it's time this game will set the bar all future RPGs have to judged against. This is a once in a decade game.

UPDATE: I can't even connect to a server let alone play single player/co-op. I literally have a game now sitting in my library that I cannot play. Will someone, ANYONE fix this game?
I will revisit my review when the game is officially complete.
Issues
#1 Pure online.
Despite being able to play by yourself, you still need to connect to a server. This makes it difficult to play if your internet isn't great.
#2 You NEED a beefy machine (even though, they have a setting for low end laptops)
If single player could be done offline, this might not be such an issue. However, my gameplay consisted primarily of playing for 1-2 minutes, then waiting 3-5 minutes for the lag to stop. I don't mean just slow down. I mean pure freeze frame. This occuring while playing on official server by myself. I can run most new games fine on this laptop so I know it isn't my computer.
#3 Constantly in combat
The NPC's in this game spawan around 5 minutes after being killed. They also notice you from a rediculous distance, making it impossible to work on anything for more than 5 minutes. I was pretty much in combat every 30-50 seconds of gameplay, which I am very surprised I managed to build a house being that after every piece I built I had to kill 3-4 enemies.
#4 Save point/bed
You really only made the bed last for one life? It should be a permanent point until the bed is broken. Ironically, I broke the beds and bonfire of enemies near my house, and they still spawn every 5 minutes.
Overall the primaary issues, in my opinion, are the lag. I could care less about the combat issues, I think it adds to the terror of living in a world like that, but with the lag it really makes getting into combat unbareable. I think if they were to make solo/co-op play offline I think that would help with most of the lag issues. I know like everyone else that this is early access, and I hope the lag gets better, but until then, the game really is unplayable for me and others with machines like mine. I suggest making single/co-op offline until the game is finished and there are less issues. I probably won't even after the game is finished play on a public server, so I won't say anything on that. I do like the look of this game though. The crafting mechanic is perfectly complex yet simple for anyone new to crafting systems. The combat is slightly realistic in a sense that if you are using a bladed weapon, body parts will get cut off. Character design needs a little more diversity and  better controls. I know that the sliders are pretty standard to every game with character creation, but these modifier's are difficult to harness without having the delicate touch of a surgen. The game also looks very beautiful. When I say beautiful I am comparing the graphics to skyrim when heavily modded. The games graphics are great, seriously! The last thing I want to touch on is the launcher and server options. When you launch the game, you have 4 options to choose from, and unless you know exactly what each option is without any description, you're only going to be launching the game. I don't know what these other options are for. The last thing is the server options. I needed to select on 2 different times to set full nudity. I am an immersion player, and when you lose your clothes you do not have a loin cloth growing out of your body if you're a man, and you definitely don't have a top and bottom growing out of your body if you are a female. I feel like the server setup process could be streamlined to one set of options for efficiency rather than having to find these options a couple of times to make sure things are operating as they should be. I like this game, and I am excited for the finished product, unfortunately until then, I can't play it. When it's finished I'll try again, and revise my review based on my experience then.

The longer I play this game, the more frustrated I get. Chivalry is extremely slow paced that I feel like I’m in the matrix. For example, all weapon swings are so overly slow that I usually block too early causing me to get hit, making me be punished for having a fast reaction when it should be the complete opposite. Additionally, when using a ranged weapon, the projectile velocity is so slow that it punishes you for being accurate, forces you to get much closer, and it causes plenty of accidental friendly-fire. Not only are these delay reactions annoying, but they’re also unrealistic.
Furthermore, there is a lot of issues with the combat’s responsiveness. For example, parries not blocking attacks, attacks not hitting the enemy, and so on. To summarize, this game is mindless fun, but definitely not competitive and strategic fun. For the most part you walk around in circles and try to hit each other in the back. The only time you’re having fun in this game is when you have a fair and non-exploitable fight, which rarely happens. The developers could do something about it, they just appear to not want to and instead move onto making a game that has an fantasy theme.
To conclude, this game is for people who enjoy mindless fun, but even then should only be bought during a sale. The joy in this game dies off when you get out of ranked servers. Advise you to keep an eye on Mount & Blade instead.

The game's been out for a bit now and I don't know if people need another review at this point but why not? Okay, so if you're looking into this game its because you're probably familiar with the concept, perhaps you've even played previous SCS truck driving games likes Euro Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2. This here is pretty much the same but set in south-west United States, in California, Arizona and Nevada. At the time of writing this New Mexico is in the works.
Visually the game engine does a good job with just about everything. Considering the size of the entire game world there's a lot of detail and a great variety of buildings and such. You never really feel like you're always driving in the same area. Trucks are very well detailed and come in different flavors of Kenworth and Peterbilt but many players feel that there should be more types of trucks. Textures are very good overall and the lighting is pretty convincing too, especially with sunsets and dawns.
The trucks have a great feels when you drive them on the road and you can opt for easy settings like auto transmission and such or more complicated that let you control everything in the truck. If you have accidents they'll affect your truck, indicated by a percentage. At 100% you're totalled and need to be towed. Just don't expect visual damage because there aren't any, not even a scratch.
To drive around you get help from the Route Advisor (GPS) which tells you exactly where to go. On the road and in cities you'll see regular trafic going about; cars, trucks, pickups and such, all obeying the law of the road; i.e.: stop signs, red lights and such. Police cars patrol and you'll get fined for any violation such as going over the speed limit, running stop signs or red lights. Sometimes however, the AI gets glitchy at intersections not governed by traffic lights and you can end up jammed up pretty good when the front car isn't moving though said intersection.
At the start of the game you have no cash so you make deliveries using trucks that belong to companies. When you get enough cash you can purchase you own garage and truck. As the cash slowly flows in you can then purchase additional garages, expend them, buy more trucks and hire drivers. The more you level and the more you'll get points to distribute in attributes such as bonuses for deliveries on time, fragile cargo, fuel aconomy and the like.
The game is pretty open about mods which means that you can easily find a plethora of stuff you can add or modify within the game like gas prices, trailers with real company logos on them, traffic density and such. Stability of the game can vary. Some mods can make the game crash and burn so if you have a lot you have to figure out which one is causing problems.
Of course, the biggest mod category being the trucks themselves and this can be a little minefield in itself. Many trucks are available of various websites and using them in game is as easy as downloading the mod file and dropping them in the mod folder. Activate them in-game and you're good to go. This is very good but there's a nasty backfire to it. SCS makes updates to the game and sometimes said updates can be bad news as functionalities dispear, mirrors go black, engines not producing sounds anymore or the truck not working at all. This can screw up your savegame pretty bad, especially if you have lots of modded trucks running. Another black spot to this is that some people have started making paid mods with prices easily being TWICE the price of the full game. The main problem being that if SCS updates the game and paid trucks aren't working you have no garantee that the modder(s) will continue updating his truck(s), again screwing your savegame file but modders also have your money. Unfortunately some of these paid mods manage to get leaked into websites and the distributors make no mention that it is a paid mod, leaving you unaware that this can cause problems in future game updates. Also, expect no help from SCS Software regarding this matter as they have remained perfectly silent on the matter of paid mods. Use at your own risk.

First off- the most important thing is: the most fun I have had in a game since I was about ~12 (I'm 27, and i'm talking about FF7). The action in this game is... amazing. Fast paced, intense, and above all it's just fun.
Also, character progression is great. Each class specs into 2 different tiers, and from there 2 more, etc. This, combined with the fact that you can spend your points on different abilities, means you can have 2 people from the class performing different roles and adds uniqueness (kinda) and flexibility. Each new ability you unlock can be dramatic, and the best part is you can pump points into any of them depending on how you want to play your character. I hate when games have the useful skills and the useless ones, and it's just a no brainer.
Unfortuantely (and this may have changed since i last played- let me know if it has) the in-game economy is set to nickel and dime you to death. I played up to level cap (when it was 50). Each new level they give you items to seal your good equip/items (thus allowing you to sell on the player2player market, otherwise your item is tied to your character). But as soon as you reach level cap, you get no more of these. This means, once you are out, as i was, you have to pay a ridiculous price for these seals. I can't remember what the price was, but it was ludicrous. There are free ones you collect in the game, but after playing for hours upon hours (i think my game time was arounf 172 hours?) i blew all of them and got maybe a few to work, if that. The rate of success on these free ones was so low, and the price of the paid ones so high, that it wasn't worth playing anymore because I essentially couldn't make a decent amount of money and i certainly didn't want to ditch my epic gear to an in game store for pennies. I sincerely hope that has changed since i stopped, but i doubt it has. Let me know though if it has, because i would LOVE to pick this game up again.
Also, i only dabbled in the PVP, but it was very good from what i played.
If this game had an option to buy it outright for a set price ($60? i would pay more even...) and just let you buy and sell freely in the market, maybe with some other options, it would be in my top 10 games ever, imho.
All in all, i would highly recommend playing this game- only with the foresight of knowing not to let yourself get addicted, only to have withdrawals when you force yourself off of it at level cap (when things get really interesting). Or maybe even play to level cap, and then start a new character.

It has some new interesting gameplay elements as well. The game is not too hard, but not super easy either. It does not become frustrating.
What is not so good?

It plays much better with a game pad, which is only a negative if you don't have one. There are a couple of frustrating moments in the game, where when you die, you get pushed back quite far from where you died, and you have to see the cutscene again. You can bypass it, but after the umpeenth atempt you get a litte tired. But this is not a problem in general.
A causal game?
Well, in the beginning I found the game does not offer much challenge, but it is still quite enjoyable as it teaches you the mechanics bit by bit. It also has good variety and pace so it never feels boring. I played through the entire game quite quickly compared to older titles, but I did not mind. Before noting that I said I do not recommend this, please understand that it's not bad.
With this confusing statement out of the way, let's get started. Bientôt l'été isn't a game. It's an artistic piece, and this needs to be understood. From what I could gather, the goal of it was to demonstrate how people can communicate, even if limited by language, actions, or possible phrases (as seen by the chess board in-game). However, this requires that someone somewhere is playing at the same time you are, unless you want to talk to an AI. It's a beautiful experience when it works well, but this is so rare I can't recommend a purchase at any time other than during a sale. Due to the game's artistic goal and nature, it was heavily slammed upon release, driving away potential players. Without a community waiting for another person to chat with, more people slammed the game for not having a community. This is Bientôt l'été's biggest problem, without players it simply cannot achieve the desired effect.
For this reason I suggest buying this when it's on sale. More players are likely to be experimenting with it at the same time as you, and you're more likely to see the beauty of limited conversation with a complete stranger.

Tengami is designed as a virtual pop-up book which gives the game a unique aesthetic. This is further enhanced by a beautiful original soundtrack that combines elements from traditional Japanese music with modern influences. The story is told through your interactions with the environment and includes several haiku poems. Though the minimalism is, perhaps, stylistically appropriate, I felt the story was disappointingly sparse. You advance through the game by solving simple puzzles in the environment such as folding the landscape to create bridges and passages, finding items and hidden symbols and entering combinations to open locks. The mechanics reminded me of games like Samorost, Botanicula and Machinarium.
Technical notes: The character's walking speed is tediously slow. Sometimes the music cuts out abruptly.

UPDATE: I can't even connect to a server let alone play single player/co-op. I literally have a game now sitting in my library that I cannot play. Will someone, ANYONE fix this game?
I will revisit my review when the game is officially complete.
Issues
#1 Pure online.
Despite being able to play by yourself, you still need to connect to a server. This makes it difficult to play if your internet isn't great.
#2 You NEED a beefy machine (even though, they have a setting for low end laptops)
If single player could be done offline, this might not be such an issue. However, my gameplay consisted primarily of playing for 1-2 minutes, then waiting 3-5 minutes for the lag to stop. I don't mean just slow down. I mean pure freeze frame. This occuring while playing on official server by myself. I can run most new games fine on this laptop so I know it isn't my computer.
#3 Constantly in combat
The NPC's in this game spawan around 5 minutes after being killed. They also notice you from a rediculous distance, making it impossible to work on anything for more than 5 minutes. I was pretty much in combat every 30-50 seconds of gameplay, which I am very surprised I managed to build a house being that after every piece I built I had to kill 3-4 enemies.
#4 Save point/bed
You really only made the bed last for one life? It should be a permanent point until the bed is broken. Ironically, I broke the beds and bonfire of enemies near my house, and they still spawn every 5 minutes.
Overall the primaary issues, in my opinion, are the lag. I could care less about the combat issues, I think it adds to the terror of living in a world like that, but with the lag it really makes getting into combat unbareable. I think if they were to make solo/co-op play offline I think that would help with most of the lag issues. I know like everyone else that this is early access, and I hope the lag gets better, but until then, the game really is unplayable for me and others with machines like mine. I suggest making single/co-op offline until the game is finished and there are less issues. I probably won't even after the game is finished play on a public server, so I won't say anything on that. I do like the look of this game though. The crafting mechanic is perfectly complex yet simple for anyone new to crafting systems. The combat is slightly realistic in a sense that if you are using a bladed weapon, body parts will get cut off. Character design needs a little more diversity and  better controls. I know that the sliders are pretty standard to every game with character creation, but these modifier's are difficult to harness without having the delicate touch of a surgen. The game also looks very beautiful. When I say beautiful I am comparing the graphics to skyrim when heavily modded. The games graphics are great, seriously! The last thing I want to touch on is the launcher and server options. When you launch the game, you have 4 options to choose from, and unless you know exactly what each option is without any description, you're only going to be launching the game. I don't know what these other options are for. The last thing is the server options. I needed to select on 2 different times to set full nudity. I am an immersion player, and when you lose your clothes you do not have a loin cloth growing out of your body if you're a man, and you definitely don't have a top and bottom growing out of your body if you are a female. I feel like the server setup process could be streamlined to one set of options for efficiency rather than having to find these options a couple of times to make sure things are operating as they should be. I like this game, and I am excited for the finished product, unfortunately until then, I can't play it. When it's finished I'll try again, and revise my review based on my experience then.

Do you like the mystery of entering an empty room and finding an item (or items) that you could craft with a couple clicks of punching a tree or a rock?  Then this is the game for you!
Seriously, a super early access game.  There's not much here, nor should there need to be at this point.  There's a world surrounded by water that you can't fish in, there's two types of animals and some bird shadows, a bunch of empty buildings with stuff that's easy to obtain if you don't mind clicking the "stick" button 30 times in the crafting menu, some sand areas that seem to spawn less animals, a night cycle, and some water areas that you can fish in.
The interesting stuff comes in when you go insane, which ironically doesn't happen if you kill enough animals (and bury them).  But yah, there's no point in hiding that there isn't a lot going on in this game yet.  And that's A-OK.  It has a great atomsphere with some effective mechanics, and even if you know you've got nothing else to do it still sucks you in.  That's probably the greatest victory of Project Explore.  There really isn't a lot to explore (yet), but it still makes you want to keep exploring it.

I disliked BG1 yet I loved BG2.
This is a BG2 EE review and while im sitting here writing it, i cant help but reference the start of an epic story which is BG1.
There are many people who will write that BG , as a series, is complete story of your character as they follow the path from start, middle and end of their own destiny.
I cannot argue with this valid point.
Yet I found that BG1 was clearly made from a company (Pre- EA Bioware) that had grand ambition , scope and excellent writing but didnt know how to implement this all into a single game.
What came from the end of BG1 was the experience , scope and confidence to make a vastly superior game in BG2.
When starting a new character in BG2 , all the back story that exsisted in BG1 is told to you in the opening trailer of the game. Who you are and what you have done have been generalised in a way that starting off in BG2 verses playing the first title of the series doesnt leave you lost.
Infact, anything you may have lost in terms of playing BG1 is redoubled in the amazing expansion called Throne of Bhaal, which takes the story of your past , present and potential future to levels that werent even touched on in the first title.
This expansion is included in BG2 EE so if you choose to buy this remaster , you will miss very little in terms of story.
If your old enough to remember Terminator and then watch Terminator 2 year later will understand this completely because they share a common trait.  The second incarnation is so vastly superior to the first that there is no need to experience/watch the first.
Im not going to beat a dead horse on the actual review of BG2:EE.
There are so many amazing reviews online that illustrate , far better than i could , all of the brillant traits that make this game one of the BEST RPG's of all time.
What stands out for me is the writing and PACE of the game.
Bioware crafted BG2 in a way , in the quest structure, that you never feel very far off the beaten path towards the end. All the side quests are meant to compliment the main story in some way or another.
And the side quests are easily the BEST of any RPG ive ever played.
That is not to undermind the main story at all, but only reiterate the strength of how impactful the side quests are.
I mentioned the pace of the game and I wish there was a virtual table I could bang to get this point across.
There are so many past and present RPG's I play where I get so wrapped up in the vast open nature of a game that the main quest or objective becomes a second priority.
This isnt the case in BG2.
BioWare cleverly crafted a way to keep the story in focus but give the player all the time they needed to explore and experiment. When you were ready, the story took main focus and ran forward at amazing speeds.
By the end of BG2 you feel satisfied. It truely is a complete story.
Yet if you feel is there more to the backstory that hasnt been complete, the expansion Throne of Bhaal answers them.
This expansion was made before the invention of DLC. Its a TRUE expansion with 20-30+ hours of content and RICH , character driven story. It could possibly be the best expansion ive played in my life.
It ends the story of a character you started from BG1 and ends it in excellent fashion.
This review was writtten for a very esoteric perspective. Made for a RPG fan who doesnt mind the learning curve of a good game and appreicates a epic story.  If there are gamers out there of this nature who havent played this game, I hope this review helps.
In the end, BG2 stand alone as one the best games ive ever played. It is a reminder that story, characters and solid gameplay trump impressive graphics and superfical gameplay.

The game's been out for a bit now and I don't know if people need another review at this point but why not? Okay, so if you're looking into this game its because you're probably familiar with the concept, perhaps you've even played previous SCS truck driving games likes Euro Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2. This here is pretty much the same but set in south-west United States, in California, Arizona and Nevada. At the time of writing this New Mexico is in the works.
Visually the game engine does a good job with just about everything. Considering the size of the entire game world there's a lot of detail and a great variety of buildings and such. You never really feel like you're always driving in the same area. Trucks are very well detailed and come in different flavors of Kenworth and Peterbilt but many players feel that there should be more types of trucks. Textures are very good overall and the lighting is pretty convincing too, especially with sunsets and dawns.
The trucks have a great feels when you drive them on the road and you can opt for easy settings like auto transmission and such or more complicated that let you control everything in the truck. If you have accidents they'll affect your truck, indicated by a percentage. At 100% you're totalled and need to be towed. Just don't expect visual damage because there aren't any, not even a scratch.
To drive around you get help from the Route Advisor (GPS) which tells you exactly where to go. On the road and in cities you'll see regular trafic going about; cars, trucks, pickups and such, all obeying the law of the road; i.e.: stop signs, red lights and such. Police cars patrol and you'll get fined for any violation such as going over the speed limit, running stop signs or red lights. Sometimes however, the AI gets glitchy at intersections not governed by traffic lights and you can end up jammed up pretty good when the front car isn't moving though said intersection.
At the start of the game you have no cash so you make deliveries using trucks that belong to companies. When you get enough cash you can purchase you own garage and truck. As the cash slowly flows in you can then purchase additional garages, expend them, buy more trucks and hire drivers. The more you level and the more you'll get points to distribute in attributes such as bonuses for deliveries on time, fragile cargo, fuel aconomy and the like.
The game is pretty open about mods which means that you can easily find a plethora of stuff you can add or modify within the game like gas prices, trailers with real company logos on them, traffic density and such. Stability of the game can vary. Some mods can make the game crash and burn so if you have a lot you have to figure out which one is causing problems.
Of course, the biggest mod category being the trucks themselves and this can be a little minefield in itself. Many trucks are available of various websites and using them in game is as easy as downloading the mod file and dropping them in the mod folder. Activate them in-game and you're good to go. This is very good but there's a nasty backfire to it. SCS makes updates to the game and sometimes said updates can be bad news as functionalities dispear, mirrors go black, engines not producing sounds anymore or the truck not working at all. This can screw up your savegame pretty bad, especially if you have lots of modded trucks running. Another black spot to this is that some people have started making paid mods with prices easily being TWICE the price of the full game. The main problem being that if SCS updates the game and paid trucks aren't working you have no garantee that the modder(s) will continue updating his truck(s), again screwing your savegame file but modders also have your money. Unfortunately some of these paid mods manage to get leaked into websites and the distributors make no mention that it is a paid mod, leaving you unaware that this can cause problems in future game updates. Also, expect no help from SCS Software regarding this matter as they have remained perfectly silent on the matter of paid mods. Use at your own risk.

I was a big fan of Sands of Time when it came out but never really bothered with the series except for trying out the reboot "Prince of Persia". This is the first one I have bought since SoT and I'm definitely glad I did.
I'll admit I was fairly sceptical about buying this game and it would never have come to my attention if it wasn't on offer but I own it now and I don't regret it. The game has an alright story, its nothing special but the characters never acted unreasonable or stupid which I had expected.
The graphics aren't too bad considering it came out in 2010, definitely nothing special although the facial animations were pretty good, at least for the Prince anyway. The voice acting was also pretty decent, the characters were convincing except for the occasional interruption of a puzzle by the Prince inner monologuing about how to solve it.
The parkour was up to the usual PoP level and with a few very welcome additions. The abilities to freeze water and teleport makes for some really interesting gameplay and adds a time element to the levels. However even though I could never place my finger on why, the sense of scale and feeling of progress wasn't as strong as in SoT. I regularly lost track of why I was going the way I was and the heights weren't brought to my attention very much. Luckily this didn't really take much away from gameplay.
The combat conjured some very mixed feelings. It started out being very boring, just chopping at enemies and moving on. I was really dissapointed to see my favourite elements removed since SoT. No longer did I feel like I was taking down bulky enemies through agility and manuevering, now I was the bulky one and I could chop them down in a few swings. But as the game went on and I experimented more and more I found it was decently varied and not as bad as I first thought. However late into the game you are given a powered-up sword and for the first five minutes I got a kick out of killing enemies in one hit. But then I realised any and all strategy it once had was gone.
The game started out as expected but entertained me throughout until the final boss, a clunky giant with lumbering swings and poor reactions, pretty standard and very boring but forgivable.
Overall I really liked this game, if you have never played Prince of Persia don't go for this one, start with sands of time. If you are a fan then buy this one, it's actually pretty good.

I am fascinated by this game, and yet I fear I will never get to play it to its full potential.   In this game you walk around a strange, silent world and can interact with objects to gain chess pieces.  You can then use the chess pieces to have a virtual conversation with a stranger.  The more chess pieces you have the more options you have as far as things to say.  The interesting thing is that you each play the role of lovers and so the conversation has a strange intimacy even though the participants themselves are strangers. The possibility is that you might share a moment of connection with a stranger over these bits and pieces of dialogue and action.  However, I have played this game three or four times and have never been paired with a living person.  The other choice is to participate in the conversation with a simulation.  And in this case, interaction with a simulation is hollow and completely misses the point because there is no chance for that spark of human connection.

You solve cool but not too hard puzzles by turning the pages, sliding and popping up parts of the world. Aesthetically, the game is very pleasing, albeit there's little to no interaction with the pretty world most of the times. The music is soothing, although it does sometimes cut off strangely.

The cons: slow and repetitive, very short, very little actual player interaction, the price.
The conclusion: get it in a bundle only.

Early Access, a re-review 5/16
Game has definitely polished up since it came out. When you first start a map, you're able to customize your character (even from above, you can see different hair styles and clothing color). Different biomes have been added, with temperature that goes with each environment, that does affect your survivability (too hot, you get thirsty; too cold, your hunger drops; too dark, you go insane), like your average survival game.
What makes it different is the dedication that the developer is putting into his game. Yes, I am actually the other half of the studio, but I am not a part of the game except for the occasional input and celebratory things. I was encouraged to revisit the game, and I am glad that SeaBass was able to take input from the community and put it in the game, because it made quite an improvement. Also, your occasional references to pop culture, or a glimpse of the developer's back story, is reflected in the 50 and counting items that are being added into the game. What I really liked is the nice amount of wildlife on the map (or at least a realistic amount) and the ability to refill water bottles (California should really take that advice to heart).
What I want to add as constructive feedback would be an easier way to control the game. Example, using a key, or left clicking on an item for it to move to the shortcuts or the crates (when applicable). It's more of a burden dragging everything around, and it's not efficient.
I also found way too many skeletons, torches, and rock (item) spawns on the map. I don't know, there just seemed to be a lot of stuff, and without a place with crates/a backpack on hand, it can get out of control.
Having died only on the fifth day to a dirty gang of creepy, blade-as-hands, no-goods, only makes me want to survive even longer. A game worth supporting and praising. Splendid job, SeaBass.

Flamethrower can dish out highest damage out there? Check. Two pairs of jet engines can provide controls in mid-air + has decent max speed? Check.
