To be a good craftsman, you have to wisely choose what part will fit to your purpose. Assembling only heaviest parts and make'em hover with tiny jet engines is possible. However, the mass is so excessive to jet engines work properly. Do you wanna build front-line heavy gatling tank? Get the most armored hull and turret, select powerful traction called Power Tracks, equip 3 gatling on main weapon slot and two support slot and you're good to go! Wanna build artillery? Long answer, yes but be ready for a bit of frustration. The game has a lot of mechanics that work well with each other. Taking VVVVVV's & Super Meat Boy's  gameplay with a Limbo asetic. It's beutiful presentated the game itself is very instersting with lots of good ideas stuffed in. However, the game has two glaring problems. Cave levels and physics.
Cave levels, or rather the time-your-reaction-down-to-the-excately-one-frame-to-not-die levels. They are instesting the first few times you run into them but after that you'll be thowing your keyboard, or controller, to the floor and hairpulling frustration. These levels require a pintpoint accuracy and even missing it but one frame could mean: ramming into the spike or ramming into the spike on the other side. With not checkpoints makes these infruatinling diffcult.
Now for the physics engie, it works alright but it seems like they couldn't get aerial momentum to work or walljumps. When you jump in this game, you either start at a standstill or at the speed you were just running. Then right after that if you so much as press a direction for even a second, you go flying in that direction. It's hard to make preciese jumps when  the platforms are almost as big as the cat. As for the wall jumping, sometimes it doesn't seem to register that you connected to a wall. Leveling you to fall of an edge or hit a spike below and have to start over the whole level.
Now that said, I still would say the game is worth the $6.99 price tag. You'll probably beat it in one sitting but try to come in knowing that the physics/cave levles will work against you.

I am not a platformer gamer.  At.  All.  Give me a FPS or a 1st-/3rd-person perspective exploration game any day -- I'm just one of those people who lacks the type of quick reflexes necessary for this genre.  I'm SUPER clumsy at these types of games.  So I wanted to offer my thoughts about A Walk in the Dark to anyone else who has similar game preferences:  don't be deterred!
If Bast or the girl dies, the reset at the start of the level is absolutely painless -- a puff of smoke and the clock is immediately restarted.  No big deal (though you'll miss out on a First Pass award for those levels that autoscroll).  The focus is on getting you started again right away.  I'm playing on a keyboard, and (as a non platformer gamer) I find that the response is quite good.  As others have noted, beware the non-blocky environment design which makes finding your jump/land points tricky:  the landcape edges that can kill Bast or the girl will feel extremely sensitive.  The levels are nicely scaled in difficulty, with early ones gradually training the player on tougher play patterns coming up later.
I find the soft monochromatic colorscheme and clean graphic design paired with the piano soundtrack very soothing.  A Walk in the Dark has become my in-between game:  if I'm stumped on a puzzle in a point-and-click or struggling with a boss in a FPS, I switch to this game for a break, clearing levels until I hit a plateau.  Check out the achievement list to see that yes, this is a tough platformer.  But the ability to replay any level individually (i.e., focus on what you can currently do and try as many times as you'd like to get the shinies, destroy dandelions, or get better and better times) can let you approach the game in a more casual way.

So far, I've surprised myself -- I actually hit the 37th level today, on my second play session.  Yes, I only rarely get the Shinies, FIrst Pass, or Par awards, and I'm on target to get the "You monster!" achievement for killing poor Bast 1000 times WELL before the end of the game.  It takes me exponentially more tries to clear a level than I expect it does for most gamers.  In all likelihood, I'll never see the levels past 50.  My stats are laughably awful, but I am having so much fun playing that I don't mind!

I absolutely recommend A Walk in the Dark.  It showed me that I can find real gems by occasionally stepping outside my comfort zone.  :)

This game was on track to be 5 stars all the way, but I ran into some issues.
I'll start with the good. Beautiful dialogue, animation, scenery, the whole deal. Combat feels nice, the variety of abilities and classes/races is really nice, too. An RPG for sure, as it allows for various choices when talking with people, and special interactions when you have points in certain areas, or are playing certain characters. Backstory is nice, well thought out, and there is plenty to do.
The bad. Combat can be extremely frustrating. I'm on classic mode, which I thought was easy mode enoguh, but beware, it's not. I've recently ran into my 5th encounter that I was unable to do without having to previously manipulate the fight. When I ask one of my friends, or forums, for advice, its typically met with "you have to cheese the fight" or something of the sort. I fear that if I go to Explorer mode, it will feel to easy, and will just become a game filled with talking to people, and running around. Auto-save once locked me into an encounter that I had to manipulate myself out of, which took a half hour, and then when I started manually saving, it was hard to remember to save so often, since encounters can happen so suddenly, following important thing you should've saved after.
Overall. I enjoy it, and I would a lot more, but the combat, and trying to find that mid-ground of challenging, but not too much, is hard. You feel excited to have some free time to play it, but you could potentially feel discouraged when you come across forced encounters that wipe your team. They put a lot of effort into this game, and it's one of the nicer games I've played in a long time. I'll personally need to find a way to enjoy this more without having the combat sour the mood. I can't live off the storyline and dialouge alone, and going into town and talking to people can often bore me very quickly.

Overgrowth is a follow up game to Lugaru, which was AWESOME! I'm happy to see how Overgrowth has evolved since the devs first started with this new game. I originally preordered it when it first went on preorder on Wolfire's website -- long before it came on Steam, and played the early alpha releases.
Everyone should keep in mind that the dev team is small, and are not able to roll out new content as quickly as a AAA sized company that can contract work out to other companies. The quality of what has been produced so far by the crew is impressive. The attention to detail, the variety in gameplay, depth of the combat experience, the animations ... it's all great. There just isn't any other game that relates to the kind of experience that you get with Overgrowth; it's a unique game.
Also, the devs are probably among the best for keeping their customers informed about their progress. People can complain all they want about how quickly the development is going, but they cannot say they are not doing anything. If you watch the update videos and keep up to date with what they are doing, you will see that they are not just sitting around doing nothing. They are rolling out high quality content without rushing it to release a final, poorly polished game.
Lastly, the framework that the devs have developed for editing worlds is a great component to Overgrowth. It allows you to essentially create your own scenarios and experience. It is not guided like a story mode, but it is enough of a sandbox experience that should appeal to a massive group of gamers. When I first saw the editor in the early alphas, I was blown away, almost overwhelmed, by the level of customization that is possible. Simply amazing.

I love European Truck Simulator 2, no doubt - smooth playing, no major glitches, wonderful way to spend time. Still, ATS didn't feel the same as ETS2, just located in USA, which I was expecting at first. Tried the demo earlier, which didn't feel that much different, but the actual game was a refund case on my account - even when bought from sale. There are probably some issues with the Xbox360 controller drivers as I coudln't get it work right out of the box the same as ETS2 and there could be some other details of programming of the game play that differ, something that tells ATS that little different from ETS2 to spoil the first impression. And I'm very sorry to have to say this..
About the looks of the game, the American style trucks are rather heavy on  visual details, thus the graphics might need more oomph on the GPU to look real good. More minimalistic European trucks are easier to render and look more "natural" and eye pleasing with less GPU power - which is an important point to consider. Also the cabins of the US trucks are a bit problematic because of their design, don't quite fit on a single HD monitor, thus side mirrors stay out of picture unless you zoom the cabin view to near max, causing the front window to narrow down quite a bit.
I will wait if there will  be a major update with some of these issues smoothed out, especially the gamepad compatibility to have another look at ATS, until then will stick with ETS2 and its DLCs, and maybe some independent mods too on top of that.
I can still recommend ATS with the above reservations taken into account and if you're not already familiar with ETS2 - or if you for some reason just don't like Europe particularly, or just prefer "America first" in general (joke) - otherwise, think of ETS2 as the game to go to first.

Beamdog has done what I could not have forseen, with their ridiculous Siege of Dragonspear expansion they have managed to turn the original Baldur's Gate Games into a blurry mess of Arcanum-style character sprites and failed UI-"upgrades". I will never understand the haters of this excellent remake. I also bought BG1+2 as original 6/4-CD versions when they came out. First in german, than a few years later as english DVDs, then at GoG again when they came on sale and I still bought the EE's of both games.
And you know what? They've done everything right!
1) The small tweaks go over extremly well, like 80 arrows per quiver slot.
2) The engine works flawlessly and the little UI enhancements alone were worth the money to me.
3) The new NPCs are mostly great. I especially adore Neera, who is so very different from the rest, maybe with the exception of Tiax. I also like Dorn, because both BGs generally lacked evil party NPCs that weren't overacting or plain insane.
4) Both EE's are easy to mod. Most Gibberling's & Co mods work, but you need far less of them. The 12-hour-installation of the Big World Project was a pain in the rear, and it usually took me several tries.
To sum it up, Beamdog delivered a pure Baldur's Gate experience with excellent new content in a very polished package.

I really enjoyed Dear Esther. I also enjoy Tale of Tales other games, like The Path. I simply do not understand nor enjoy this game at all. I went into it with low expectations and an open mind, I left questioning exactly what should be considered "art" in gaming.
Bientôt l'été is the most pretentious of pretentious indie art games. One that is "too deep for you" to even understand whatever trivial message it's trying to put across. Let me just say right now that when a developer needs to address their entire userbase in a forum post, revealing what their inspiration for the game was in order for you to understand its purpose, then the developer has completely failed to convey any sort of rational thought with their game. Still, no one slightly understands the purpose of Bientôt l'été and those who do are obviously elitist intellectuals whose thoughts and opinions on the matter are also "too deep for you" to understand yet again. It's hard not to call Poe's Law into play.
This game has a mechanical crutch which becomes limited by its users. The main attraction of Bientôt l'été is being able to connect with other players in a cafe of sorts, decked out with a chess board, a glass of wine, cigarettes, and the ability to communicate intricately with one another. Except this all falls apart when you realise you're the sole person in existence to be playing this game at this point in time, forcing you to instead substitute a human presence with artificial intelligence. This severely impacts the game as a whole.
I never found a partner to play with so I had to resort to A.I., and after collecting all of the chess pieces I managed to find a gun... although my character holds it backwards. Does this gun do anything more than intimidate the opposing player? If not, then there is no point to this game since there aren't enough people playing this game at any one time; you can't really surprise artificial intelligence.
The entire process of Bientôt l'été took me little over 80 minutes to achieve. After collecting the gun and positioning all the chess pieces in their correct order, hoping for something to "unlock" or tell me I've done something right, only to find out nothing much happens. I decided to go back out and collect more items, coming to a stinging realisation that the cycle has restarted and I'm collecting the very first chess pieces again.
This game is insulting.

The most recent release in the Prince of Persia franchise, The Forgotten Sands is an action adventure platformer that bridges the gap between The Sands of Time and Warrior Within. I got this game along with The Sands of Time which, in my opinion, isn't as good as The Forgotten Sands. BE WARNED: you have to create/log in with a Uplay account in order to play this game.
I haven't gotten too far into the story, but it's not awful. It's not that great either, but it's good enough that you're at the very least slightly interested. Basically, it starts out with you going to visit your brother, only to find out your brother's palace/castle being attacked. You fight some enemies and get familiar with the platforming. Once you meet up with your brother, he tries to unleashe Solomon's Army, the only hope for not losing the battle. This doesn't go as planned since you are then told that army is evil. That's about all that happens at the very beginning.
The gameplay is pretty fun. The swordfighting is enjoyable and well animated. You basically have three attacks: normal attack, strong attack, and aerial attack. Also, you can't block, just dive-roll. The platforming is very fun as well. Although it's really no different from the platforming in The Sands of Time, it seems more exciting in this game for some reason to me.
The game looks great. Like I said, the animations are pretty good and the characters look awesome. As far as I've gotten into the game (which is only a few hours) there isn't much variation in the locations. However, this is probably because you're in the same place.
The music is good too. Not the best soundtrack for a game I've ever heard, but it goes along nicely with the game.
There are also a few extra things in this game: challenge maps and extra skins/costumes. You get one challenge map and costume by entering the CD key in the Extras menu. You can also get Ezio's costume from Assassin's Creed by buying it with points through Uplay.
Overall, Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands is a pretty enjoyable experience. Fun combat and platforming and a relatively interesting story make this a good buy. The main things I don't like are the inability to block during combat and how a Uplay account is required to play, although this doesn't bother me a whole lot.
I give this game an 8.5/10.

First off, this is as much of a game as you'd call something like Dear Esther a game.
The "gameplay" consists of walking along a beach and finding out of place objects like a pile of coal or a field of wheat placed on the beach. After finding each of these objects, you get a chess piece to use in the cafe that's present across from the water.
When you enter the cafe, you sit down at a chessboard and wait for someone to connect (or use their extremely awkward in-game partner connect to actually play with a friend). After waiting at least 10 minutes to connect to an actual player, the view changes to a top-down of the chessboard and you both take turns placing your own chess pieces on the board. Some spaces make your character say a line of conversation (which can be found by walking across the beach).
Icy and I played this for an hour and a half and we could not discover any sort of progression. After you collect all your chess pieces you come across some sort of pistol. This pistol can also be placed on the chessboard, but does nothing else once on it.
The story seems to be a very weak and very cliche talk of romance between artists gone sour. I'm sure the developers have an idea of what it /actually/ means and expect some users to gain a lot from the shallow symbolism, but in all honesty this would have been better as a 15 minute independant film.
I would recommend against buying this. It doesn't belong on Steam.

As a huge fan of the Robert E. Howard books, I was overjoyed to know there was a Conan game coming out. Funcom? Who's that? They did what? Oh, okay. Skip forward to release of Age of Conan. Combat mechanics a bit wonky, but still innovative. Decent system. Graphics were lacking, and it seemed that every character face was just a slight variation of the one before it...which made the females resemble the males. Just....with mammary glands. Game turned out mediocre at best. Still going, but not sure how populated it is. Personally, I think Funcom fumbled the ball with that attempt at Conan the MMO.
Fast forward. I'm 50 now, and Funcom announces they're putting out another Conan game. I cringe inside, knowing the shambles they made of the previous attempt. Futilely I try to warn people, but nobody listens. I buy the game to see if I'm right, or if I'm way off base.
Turns out it's a little from column A, and a little from column B. It's fun and engaging game PLAY, but the story and actual mechanics of game play are utter tripe. One kind of attack, a dual slash for swords. Ditto blunt weapons. Different attack animation for two handers, but it's not really variation. I get it's early access, and there's room for improvement...but it's Funcom. Let's be real.
They used recycled graphic recources from their 2008 attempt at a Conan game to make character models that just....well, suck. Faces are just like before, blending into one another. No animation to them at all. Hell, other games with voip have facial animation when talking to add to realism. How much you wanna bet Funcom never updates the graphics and tries to shove an unfinished, buggy "release" down the throats of consumers with very little actual work done to the game itself.

I had fun playing the game for a bit, the puzzles were fun to figure out at first and the "pop up" sliders certainly gives the game a unique quality to it, however a little further into the game, things became more tedious. On a couple of occasions I had no idea what I was supposed to do next, so I checked with the handy "hint" option. Even then, you still might not be 100% sure if what you are doing is correct.
I can certainly appreciate the game and can see why some people would adore it, but sadly for me, the puzzles became more of a chore than a joy to solve.

In my previous review of the game from last year, I highlighted how the game feels like a disappointing, overpriced tech demo, and that I would update my review if the game ever left early access. The game left early access on October 16th, so here is my updated review.
I still can not reccomend Overgrowth. For something that took almost 10 years of development to make, I can't help but wonder where development time and money from early access sales even went. The UI looks unpolished and rushed, like Wolfire Games decided they needed to get Overgrowth released on a deadline even though most people who have owned Overgrowth for years would be fine with waiting another month or two to for them to polish the game. The two campaigns included in Overgrowth are both disappointing. The Lugaru campaign has a few very small levels, and that's it. The main campaign is slightly better than the Lugaru campaign but still has very small levels. Because the levels are so small, you will get to a level change relatively quickly. You can expect to wait on the loading screen between level changes for 30-45 seconds before being thrown into the next level.
Overgrowth is not currently, and has never been worth the $30 price. Overgrowth looks dated and rushed, is unoptimized, and has repetitive and unexciting campaigns.

Very cute game, the art is really visually appealing, not too much going on at once on the screen which is great. I'm not a huge fan of platformers, let alone TIMED platformers, but this is still a fun game to pass the time with, albeit really frustrating (for me) for a few reasons.
The controls seem really unresponsive/wonky at times. I don't know if that's because I'm using a controller, but given that this has full controller support, I would've imagined it wouldn't have been a problem. The buttons either don't respond, or respond too little. I could depress the jump button as hard as possible one moment for a long jump, and get a measly weak jump that'll kill me and restart the level, or the exact opposite issue with the same outcome. It also doesn't exactly feel like being as smooth as a cat; in fact, in some areas, I've seen my own three-legged cat jump more gracefully than Bast, which is just depressing. Bast just doesn't seem to respond to the controller in a typical cat fashion, and won't act like a cat when it really counts, especially around wall-climbing/jumping segments. Not to mention that the movements are really picky, but I feel like that's more a margin of error issue.
With that being said, the margin of error is so ridiculously small that it gets on my nerves, because of the movement issues. I could be completely in the clear of a patch of spikes, and still get killed by the very last one, despite being far above it. Or, in the case of the little girl, the movement is so incredibly sensitive when gravity's being inverted and you're having to constantly flip up or down to avoid spikes and move through the level, that you could so much as look at the screen wrong and be shoved into the wall of spikes without having even touched the D-pad/thumbstick, whichever you prefer to use on a controller.
My last small issue, and it's probably a very minor one, is the lack of checkpoints, which I wholly believed were what the dandelions were for. Instead, I discovered they're just for a ridiculous achievement. Imagine my irritability when I've gotten 3/4s of the way through a tough level with all of the above issues working against me, find a dandelion thinking it's a checkpoint, only to die and have to start the headache ALL OVER.
I do like this game, don't get me wrong. I just think there are a few issues that are a serious turn-off in terms of no one's gonna want to sit here and play this game for more than half an hour at most before leaving it alone for weeks on end, because looking at it only reminds one of the frustration endured. Do I think this game is worth seven bucks? Not particularly, but I didn't pay that much, so I don't really have to worry about it.

I will never understand the haters of this excellent remake. I also bought BG1+2 as original 6/4-CD versions when they came out. First in german, than a few years later as english DVDs, then at GoG again when they came on sale and I still bought the EE's of both games.
And you know what? They've done everything right!
1) The small tweaks go over extremly well, like 80 arrows per quiver slot.
2) The engine works flawlessly and the little UI enhancements alone were worth the money to me.
3) The new NPCs are mostly great. I especially adore Neera, who is so very different from the rest, maybe with the exception of Tiax. I also like Dorn, because both BGs generally lacked evil party NPCs that weren't overacting or plain insane.
4) Both EE's are easy to mod. Most Gibberling's & Co mods work, but you need far less of them. The 12-hour-installation of the Big World Project was a pain in the rear, and it usually took me several tries.
To sum it up, Beamdog delivered a pure Baldur's Gate experience with excellent new content in a very polished package.

Synopsis: Overgrowth is a visceral, satisfying, bloody (oh yeah) melee fighting game which serves as a great base for less than satisfying official content. Overgrowth is, officially, a game about the adventures of Turner, this sort of paper thin anti hero rabbit who lives in a world where animals have become anthropomorphic and have developed interesting, diverse cultures that are worth exploring in the story as well as in the comics published by Wolfire. However, Turner does not fit into that world. Turner, simply put, has unclear motives or is simply ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ given that the story revolves around Turner trying to save rabbits from the clutches of slavery while mumbling dreary dialogue about how he doesn't want to kill other creatures. Anyways, I think this is better presented in Pro-Con form.
Pros:
+ Combat is ridiculously good. Rather than an HP system like most other games, this game relies on a skeletal system judged by physics. This means that, say, getting wedged between a wall and a roundhouse kick closing in on the wall would result in having your head getting compressed, guaranteeing an instant death if not severe head damage which would make the next blow fatal. It would also mean that potentially landing 3 good punches might not be nearly as effective as one sweeping kick to the feet and one single kick to the head. Also, the weapons add an interesting dynamic to the game. For example, the dog broadsword is the strongest weapon in the game. However, an experienced player might be able to do better with nothing but their hands and feet. Another is how weapons apply to species. Take rats, useless midgets that crumple like paper until they get knives, an item which makes them forces of destruction as their high attack rate will butcher you.
+ Visuals are great. Game looks beautiful for something started in 2007/2008/2009 and gore is some of the best I've seen. Gore is completely determined by angles of strikes / where you get hit / the weapon. For example, your hands and feet can't do much gore damage unless you hit the enemy in the head, causing them to fall and hit their skull on rock. However, a knife will put lots of slashes into you, causing blood to drip from your wounds. However, this is nothing to say of the dog broadsword, which will, in one strike, cake the ground and your opponent in red. Brilliant stuff.
+ Simple to learn, tough to master. Also in a fair way. It solely depends on how skilled you are. Every attack can be dodged, every combo can be achieved. It's simply a question of one's ability to assess a situation on their feet. Particular situations though still need to be discussed as cons, so not quite.
+ Kickass level editor. Professional grade. Not the copy paste BS so many other games employ. If you have the will you could make a better campaign than what came packaged. Please do.
+Music is actually amazing.
Cons:
- Campaign is weak. It gives you official fighting scenarios which are worth the time, but the story is garbage. Synopsis: Turner is an anti-hero rabbit who, after the events of the lugaru campaign (not the official campaign but worth checking out because it doesn't try to be over the top) comes to some other island where different breeds of animals are locked in this sort of cartel that specializes in rabbit trafficking. Not a bad concept but Turner doesn't fit in due to his dialogue. Turner is comparable to a bad anime character and has one liners that are even worse. If Turner acted like every other character rather than making these quips about how he hates killing other animals (point of the game) and focused on actually saying something which mattered and gets a reaction the game could've been much more fun. The universe is great though. Read the Wolfire comics, that's what the story shoulds've been based on. Actually, the comics are great. Read them.
- Some weird bugs. Mouse twitching, weapons not picking up, navmesh errors, etc. Nothing that'll totally ruin the experience but still pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥
- Cats are absolutely BS. Cats are the only species which come equipped with these things called "guaches", which they throw at an impossible to react to speed. They get stuck in you, you fall over, you're screwed. Actually unfair.
Comments:
*This game had an absolutely awful development cycle which was objectively bad but in a way good, it shows that this game is a labor of love made by people that gave a damn rather than abandonware.
*This game's leg cannon move is overpowered. Neither good nor bad because you can complete the game mostly without it, but can be used as a crutch too easily.
Score: 8/10. Turner, everyone's least favorite anime hero, gets tossed into a world where nobody understands him.

This is, by far, the best cigarette smoking simulator on the market. At first, it seemed confusing with the long walks on the beach and random phrases popping up on screen, but only once I entered the café did I realize the actual draw of this title. As I sat at the chess board and waited five minutes for a partner to join, I then realized something else; I was the only person to buy this game. Thank god they included a computer controlled character to interact with or I may have missed the hidden gem in this pile of coal.
We moved our chess pieces across the board and spoke sweet nothings to each other until only silence hung in the air. And then I saw it. Near the bottom of the screen was a classic lighter and a half full soft pack of smokes. Move over wine glass! The true beauty and meaning of game play was at hand. Once clicked, the screen goes black and you can actually hear your character click the flint, light up, and take a long, smooth drag. You can almost taste the tobacco. A puff of smoke fills the screen upon return to the scene. The cigarette is then seen majestically smoldering in the ashtray on the table. If clicked again, another drag is taken until there is nothing but a snuffed out filter left.
Oh, but that's just the beginning. It seems there is no limit to the amount of cigarettes you can smoke! My only complaint would be that there aren't enough ways to put out your coffin nail. The choice to put it out on your lover's hand or leave it floating in their wine glass should be included in a future patch for the sole reason that some of the predestined lines are mad creepy. 8 out of 10 because I can't tell if they're menthol or not.

The only Prince of Persia game I have played more than 5-7 times. I know it doesn't seem that way, but that's because I first owned it on XBOX 360 before selling it a long time ago and purchasing it on sale on here about a year later.
The Prince of Persia is back, and he's smoother than ever. With a new engine for the series, new visuals, new gameplay, you'll be hooked. I think besides having one of my favorite characters ever lead the way again, the other part that got me hooked was the upgrades and the upgrading system itself. I really like games that have this, even if it's minimal. I don't like being stuck with the same set of skills and powers for the entirety of a video game.
The Prince is sent to study alongside his brother, Malik, in order to become a great leader. On arrival, he notices his brother's kingdom under attack again, only this time it's much worse. He is forced to rely on a mythical army to stop the invaders of his kingdom. He releases the army, and not only are the invaders turned to sand, but so too are his soldiers. The only thing that's stopping The Prince & Malik from turning are the amulets they acquire from when Malik released the army. Find out more by playing this amazing game.
I really like the smoothness of everything, from the combat to the parkour we all know and love. The Prince is also able to upgrade powers he later acquire and uses, his health, energy, attack power, and more! If you're like me, and you want to stay protected during a fight, so you don't have to scavenge too much for health and energy, then upgrade the power that armors you.
I recommend playing this game with a controller. Logitech gamepad's work easily with this.
The developers were able to combine SoT & WW into one fantastic game, and I couldn't have kinder words about it. I only wish there was some kind of epilogue DLC, where The Prince runs into something he has to deal with on the journey back home to his father. That would've made the game even more epic.
I look forward to more Prince of Persia games.
Overall: 10/10
PS. This was NOT a tie-in to the film, so don't expect anything to connect the two. Also, this took place BETWEEN Sands of Time and Warrior Within. A lot of people are forgetting that. I hope the next game will offer some kind of combo system, but I don't expect to see more than what I saw in Warrior Within, unless the next game is set after the trilogy.

Fallen earth really was a surprise for me. Ive been playing for around a year now on the standard client and I can't say enough about this game. Switching over to steam client version was perfect for sharing moments with friends. I am really having a blast playing it right now. Steep learning curve keeps a lot of the 'usual' mmo crowd out. This I like! Huge open sandbox world. Think I read over 5,500 quests and 11,000 square miles of area? MASSIVE!
The game has some amazing developers under its wing too. They are trying to improve the game daily with small updates, bug fixes and is one of the minor few games which takes community thoughts and feelings into persepctive.
Great community and if you get stuck or need a friend to help there are help chats, auctions, private chats & town chats (In-game!)
Class-less characters to play as you wish and 6 factions and the factions are not all against each other but have their enemies, arch enemy, and allies among those 6. The character design feature is superb also! Very open and user friendly.
The graphics and model designs are not the best in quality terms but its not about the graphics on Fallen earth. The quests and community is the main focus in my opnion; which is great! Got a nice mix of PvE and PvP. PvP in certain areas as well as conflict towns in the higher zones.
Concluding, Fallen Earth is a great game if you have a varied lifestyle with a couple of hours every week to login and play. System specs are a little high but this keeps the younger generations away, A more adult style game.
Worth a try! (4 Stars)

At every turn I found myself subjected to a dialog that was profoundly disturbing, of which if I am to understand Lacanian psychoanalysis properly, came to enjoy as a manner and extension of the game.

The only Prince of Persia game I have ever played (beside the classic side scrollers in the early '90s). From what I understand there is a trilogy of PoP games and Forgotten Sands is what one should call an interquel, an episode that portrays the events in between those that were explained in two other PoP games.
The story follows the prince who tries to help his brother, Malik. Malik was a bad boy and unleashed an army of sand creatures so it is now up to the prince to save the world from Solomon's Army. Story-wise, it offers nothing special, but I liked the struggle between the two brothers - there is a certain tension there that makes you want to proceed and find out how it'll end.
When this game came out, Ubisoft was in deep development of the 2nd or 3rd Assassins Creed game. You can only imagine how fluid the climbing in this game, right? Some of these climbing sequences are actually a bit over the top - the prince can later on solidify water to use them as columns or can rebuild the environment if it's in ruins (only for a short period of time, though). Some powers can be used against the enemies, as well, and while fighting you gain experience points and eventually, you level up. This is just a minor RPG component here as PoP is essentially an action-adventure game far from true RPGs.
Forgotten Sands has a very high production value that all Ubisoft games can be associated with. It's a relatively long adventure that all gamers should participate in. If you have never heard of the Prince of Persia franchise, you might pick this one up for starters.

Awesomenauts is a 2D MOBA (like League of Legends or DOTA 2, where you have to destroy turrets and a base) that focuses heavily on platforming (for escaping and attacking). There's a wide range of characters (with more being added) and each character has the choice of upgrades they can buy in-game, opening up plenty of builds to try out. And unlike other MOBAs, there's little to no learning curve. As you play more, you level up, unlocking more characters and upgrades. Even though only being able to start with three characters seems limiting, it makes it easy to jump in without having to do character/mechanic research (the short tutorial is enough) or be intimidated by choices. I'd say the only bad thing about this game is the fact that there are limited maps (four at the moment), but they're varied enough that I often don't think about it.
Overall, it's a MOBA that isn't too complicated but still fun to play, appealing to both casual and hardcore gamers of the genre alike. I'd buy it if you're interested in the genre but too afraid to devote yourself to learning it. And if you're a familiar, you'll feel right at home while still having different characters and mechanics to learn.

You start off playing as a cat in this silhouette-style platformer. The game feel is very nice; the animations on some of the jumping/wall climbing could use a little polish. The levels are short with few to no enemies, and your main goal seems to be reach the end within a time limit and/or grab a shiny thing along the way. The platforming and controls are simple here, you jump or crouch.
After a few stages you play as a girl and the main idea is to flip the gravity. Not exactly novel and there's a bit too much inertia + sensitivty it feels like at times, but nothing that ruins the game. Eventually you'll play as the cat with the same gravity-switch gimmick.
There's not much new or wowing here, but the game isn't bad. If the style or genre is something that typically interests you, you should probably take a look. If platformers aren't your thing, then this is definitely a skip as it brings nothing new to the table that will change your opinion of the genre.

Just to note, Baldur's Gate is my favorite video game. However, I can't recommend this "enhanced" edition.
I spent quite some time debating whether or not to recommend this game. It boils down to this: The original content is great. Still is, still always will be. It's an epic adventure with great characters, good plot development and fantastic modified-2nd edition gameplay. The graphics show their age, of course, but there are still some great backdrops and whatnot. The dialogue in this game is probably the best of any game ever made -- epic when it needs to be, and hilarious otherwise.
Why I don't recommend this game is the new content, which is poorly written and boring. The new characters are written by people who clearly don't comprehend the wit of the original game, but think they do. It's painful.
Seriously, go find the original version on the internet somewhere for a much cheaper price, and enjoy. If you can't find it or just want a Steam version (which is what I did), then go for it! You will still have a great time with this version!

Since I was about 5 or 6, I loved to watch my dad play fantasy games like EverQuest, Oblivion and Baldur's Gate II. When I was 7, my dad gave me my very own copy to play. Now I'm 14, it's been seven years, and I still think of BGII as the best game someone could possibly buy. It has shaped my entire life, gotten me interested in the fantasy genre - not just of games, but of writing - and, best of all, gotten me interested in D&D. Soon, I'll start a session of Pathfinder as a min-maxed munchkin half-drow shadowdancer, and I expect it to be the best game I've played yet.
BGII is tough. Really tough. I never actually beat Shadows of Amn legitimately until a few months ago, and even then I can't get past ToB's final battle with Amelyssan. But the game is huge, deep, rich, and complex, and I'd reccomend it to anyone with even a passing interest in fantasy.

Beautiful little puzzle game with a Japanese pop-up book aesthetic. Average completion time seems to be around 1-1.5 hours so it's the sort of game you boot up and finish in one sitting. Mechanically the game isn't particularly deep, combining rudimentary logic puzzles with counting and memorisation so the brevity made sure the game never outstayed its welcome. The story appears at first to be deliberately vague but the final credits shed a little bit of light on the overall purpose and meaning of the game so it's worth finishing to experience that. I found the art style and scene transitions charming and the music delightfully tranquil, it's a soothing, reflective experience and by calling it an 'experience' you'll almost certainly know if this sort of game is for you.

Baldur's Gate 2 is my favourite game of all time, so with that being said, the only question is: is it worth buying the enhanced edition over the regular, far cheaper version (from GOG, say)
New Content (without spoilers): BG2EE adds a handful of new companions with personal quests, including a single class thief, a wild mage, a monk and an evil paladin. With the possible exception of the evil paladin none of these are going to make your party on merit, and the writing isn't good enough to make you want to use them for role playing reasons. All in all, nothing that hasn't been done better by the mod community. There's a gay romance for a female player character which I would usually praise, but it's so tepid I couldn't decide whether I'd misheard and it wasn't really supposed to be a romance at all.
Speaking of mods, not every one has been updated to support EE yet (Item revisions/spell revisions are the ones I'm missing most at the time of writing) so check before buying if you've got favourites.
BG2EE comes with widescreen support out of the box as well as a trick that you can't replicate with the basic game and the widescreen mod - customisable font sizes and interface scaling. Having properly sized sidebars is a good thing on a high resolution monitor.
No reason to buy this over the standard version other than better widescreen support? That would be true except for one small detail - the standard version doesn't run properly on my laptop. This does. Enough reason for me to buy it - but I still waited for a heavy sale (elsewhere) before buying.
As for the bugs other reviewers have mentioned: haven't noticed any myself, but I'm mostly holding off playing more than a quick run through the campaign while I wait for more mods to become compatible.

UPDATED REVIEW  MARCH 11, 2017
Here's my review of American Truck Simulator. After 200 hours of game time play in the last 6 weeks since the first time I purchased it I am more excited than I was on day one. Why because of all the modifications out there especially when it comes to different trucks to drive. Check ou my profile I customized a new Peterbilt 389 rig, added Chrome LED Lights, Peterbilt illuminated LOGO, Bullhorns, Grill Bar, and a two spoke steering wheel and it only costed me about $65K (one of the cheaper modded trucks). Drives more smoothly, and the sound is AAHHHmazing!!!
Do I recommend the game?  Yes I do recommend buying this game at the price point of $20. Its no longer on sale for $10 but the sale comes and goes with the times. You will be buying it just in time for the update to ATS version 1.6 (currently in Public Alpha Beta testing.)
Thats where a couple of concerns come into play at. One being that when you first start playing you have plenty to do to occupy your time. However if you are a hardcore player such as myself that easily plays 4-6 hours a day driving up to 1,500 miles a day (78,000 XP, 48,000 miles approx. total) then you'll run out of things to do and will find yourself driving the same route over and over. At this point I have 75% of the roads covered in the game.
My second concern, and you should take notice to this as well is the modifications. Modifications are good, especially if you are trying to add an element or realism and spontaneous situations to the game. You can do almost every thing under the sun with the right mod. HOWEVER, with most mods being compatible to the current version of ATS 1.5.3 , once ATS 1.6 rolls out almost ALL OF YOUR MODS will cancel out and youll have to refresh and download NEW. That kind of bums me because I have the right mods for my game including my new Peterbilt 389 which im certain to lose (BUMMER)
However, if you want variety of places to go to and want to stay occupied look into Euro Truck Simulator for 19.99. You'll have plenty to do. If you still want to drive in America then get this game and go to the various different mod websites such as atsmods, modland (my favorite), sharemods etc where you can find different variety of maps, trucks, sound mods, whatever you can think of. Also same mods can be found directly in the Steam Workshop.(HOWEVER THIS GAME IS VERY CLOSE TO BEING UPDATED SO MOD CAREFULLY)
The upsides to this game is just that. There are so many options out there to customize the gameplay to the way you see fit. Remember it's only 3 states you have to drive in so customize it based on that if you want to continue to play this game days and weeks and even months down the line just be prepared to wipe your mod list clean if you choose to mod before the update.

Repetition in video games can be draining sometimes. There's only so many times you can jump on things, slash them, shoot them, right? And if that's the case for you the player, what must it be like for the characters actually doing the work? Bardbarian's a game that explores that a bit.
You play as Brad, a barbarian mercenary working to defend a nameless town and its giant magic crystal, which does...probably something important, since every monster in the area wants it smashed, although they never get around to saying what. Trouble is, Brad is having a bit of a mid-life crisis: surely there must be more to life than constant killing? The answer to that he finds is embracing his artistic side in the form of music, and helping other people kill things!
Bardbarian takes place in the town for the whole of the game, as twenty waves assault the crystal over the course of a single day. These make up four sections, with five levels each and a boss at the end. To combat them, Brad has to jam on his guitar and summon allies from out of the local barracks and wizard college; they move in to close formation around him, not unlike Tiny Guardians. This game is action-based, however, and you'll be moving back and forth to let your allies shoot down monsters with either the arrow keys, WADS, the mouse or a controller. You start off with a simple archer-wizard-fighter combo, but as you unlock units by passing waves you'll find more interesting ones, like a necromancer who curses enemies, and resurrects them as a zombie minion if they're killed under the effects of it. There are also some indie cameos from Octodad, a Super Meat Boy/Isaac tag team, and Shellrazer, who's from a mobile tower defense that isn't on Steam.
If twenty waves sounds a bit short to you, well, it kind of is. The length mostly comes from you kind of having to go back and upgrade your allies, Brad himself, and the town with the gold you get from killing enemies; even if you're very good at dodging they'll simply get too spongey. After every boss you'll have the option of starting at the next area whenever you do, so you won't have to start at the beginning every time. There are also upgrades to make gathering gold easier, such as the Pet, who will grab it from dead enemies so you don't have to.
Even with upgrades, though, the game can be quite tricky, and I wouldn't necessarily recommend it to people without experience in shooters. Most enemies have some sort of projectile attack, and it isn't long before it a minor bullet hell, with you weaving in and out to protect your squishier allies and Brad himself. You'll need to be proactive when dealing with enemies, too, as letting even a couple goblins get up to the crystal can lead to quite a bit of damage. Naturally, it's also a game over if you die yourself. And if you really want a challenge, there's an even harder difficulty you can pick right from the start.
It took me about nine hours to beat the game, although it might take a bit longer for someone not as good at action games. There are two optional modes in addition to it; a challenge mode where you try to survive against an endless horde of enemies, and a sort of runner minigame where you try to avoid obstacles. They can both give gold, but it still felt like the main campaign was the most efficient method of doing that, and it doesn't feel like they'd extend the playtime very much.
Bardbarian is definitely a good game if you can put up with some grinding, although I'm not certain I would buy it at full price. It's been on sale a bunch though, and can be found in one of the permanent bundles on BundleStars. It's a decent game with some charm for in-between larger ones, I'd say.

A fun little tower defense game with an interesting premise but not worth the $8 asking price. Buy it when it's on sale for 75% off like I did and you won't feel bad at all. I mean, it's pretty much a slightly more polished Kongregate game and honestly, there are free Kongregate games that are actually more in-depth and flat out more fun to play. I can't write the game off completely because I did get 5 hours worth of play out of it. But honestly it was more because I truly wanted to like the game more than I did because it is sort of an interesting take on tower defense style games and it is fun for a while as you progress and unlock new characters and perks.
My biggest gripe with the game is the fact that it's called Bardbarian and the entire premise is based around you controlling the Bard (essentially a pied-piper type character) and everything about the game revolves around music and, well, being a bard. However, the soundtrack is so depressingly lacking, it basically becomes little more than background hum if you play it for any real length of time. Sadly, the ONE song that is the entire soundtrack is actually quite decent. But it's one freaking song. And not even really a complete song but a riff on a loop. I honestly feel that if they were more inventive with the soundtrack and how it played into the game, the $8 asking price would not only have been reasonable, but it would have been a deal. IMO, games like this live and die by their soundtrack and sadly this game died with it's.
The overall gameplay is extremely satisfactory for a casual tower defense, the key word here being casual. I mean, you don't aim, you don't shoot anything, there is no placement of towers, you basically weave your band of hand-chosen characters, each with their pros and cons, through waves of increasingly difficult levels. That is, once you start progressing and unlocking more characters with increasingly different character traits. This may sound like an extreme bore but it really is balanced when it comes to difficulty and satisfaction as you unlock new characters and/or perks. Sure, you're only essentially bobbing and weaving and leading your charges into battle but, it's really not as easy as it sounds and there is a real emphasis on choosing your characters and perks wisely.
I'm giving this a recommend overall but at a warning that I honestly don't think it's worth the retail price. Put it on your wishlist and catch it on sale. I paid $1.99 during the Summer Sale and feel like I certainly got my money's worth for that price. I certainly don't mind supporting indie devs, especially when they release truly enjoyable content, but at some point, I have to ask myself if the price is worth the product when there are so many similar titles out there that you can play 100% free.

The first level of three introduces you very quickly to the main mechanic of the game: boredom.
I adore the aesthetics of this game and they nail the execution perfectly, but what it has in style it lacks in mechanics. The majority of your playtime will be dedicated to repeatedly clicking the ground to move, which your character does extremely slowly considering the sheer amount of Point A > B > A puzzles require, which could be easily fixed with a double-click run.
Puzzles are a great way to show off the game's style, but never take fun into consideration. Level 1 bores you with 'click/drag in the right order' while Level 2 punishes you with unintuitive/unexplained mechanics. Level 3 was great and got creative with the 'folding', though suffered from far too much travelling. And speaking of the levels, they last 20 minutes-ish each (for 1 hour total), yet take a minute to load despite being entirely planar-based.
The game is aesthetically stellar and I'm a fan of artsy puzzle games, but this simply doesn't offer me anything but tedium and regret for not liking it more. If you're willing to accept and enjoy the game on looks alone, then I highly recommend this, but as an total package or on gameplay alone, then sadly no.

Combat in this game is done with two buttons. Left-Click and Right-Click. Left is offensive, and Right is defensive or grab. The problem is that both buttons are context sensitive. You only punch or kick when ur near an enemy and only block when the enemy attacks. Sometimes you'll block, sometimes you'll a reversal. Making a fighting game context sensitive is the equivilent of having a platformer doing a jump automatically to the next platform. The next issue the game has is that The parkour system is kinda too simplictic. You can run up a wall, run along side a wall, and jump off the wall.That's it. The level design in the game doesnt really let you chain any of the parkour moves cause things seem to be spaced out to far to get any enjoyment out of it. Which brings me to the last issue. The game is bugged. I know its an Alpha and all, but when you can't load the first level in the Main Campaign, I think you shouldnt release it just yet. The level Editor is ok, but its kinda hard to enjoy when it decides to crash at random points for no reason. The bugs might be for MAC users, but its still a issue. Id recommend you dont buy this game until they can fix alot of the issues I mentioned. For an early access game, It has alot a potential, but needs alot of work. Id give it a 70/100.

I'm not a big review writer, but after finishing this game I feel like the people must know.
To begin, I'd like to say this game's lore and concept are fantastic, I would recommend it fully for those things.
There are, however, a ton of gameplay mechanics that are eh and make fights tedious and unfun, but those can easily be overlooked if you really play for the story. No, those aren't the issue.
The bugs are the problem. Countless, mindblowing, ridiculous bugs. I feel like I paid for an early access game, but it's not in early access anymore, and I bought it full ♥♥♥♥ing price. You have no idea how many odd things I've had happen. I'm not talking about bugs that you notice right away and just reload 5 minutes ago to fix-kinda thing, not wall clipping sillyness (Though there's some of that as well).
I'm talking:
-"Oh look that npc never prompted me for his quest so now I'm locked from one of the things that had me most curious and to fix that I'd have to reload 20-30 hours of gameplay ago",
-"Oh look I somehow have a 5th party member when the limit is meant to be 4, but that 5th npc can't really act and is attacked by all allied npcs, and there's no way to get rid of it".
-"Oh look because I used another one of the game's many options of approach (which is a really cool thing in theory) the story's all ♥♥♥♥ing backwards"
-"Oh look I killed the boss before he could transform into his "true" form, removing the discussion prompt that I'm supposed to get from finishing that, guess I ain't finding out what happens next with that..."
Last but not least: I just finished the final fight, but my main character died right before and I didn't get to resurect him, so the other characters get the final choices in the game...okay that's fine I guess...
BUT WAIT! Then, after the cinematic regarding that choice, there's only my main character left and I guess there's a bit of game left to play (new game+ kinda thing, perhaps?) but since he died in the last fight and all the other party members are gone, I get a game over prompt, allowing me to either load a previous save (before the final fight) OR just go to main menu.
TL;DR: Game's story's pretty good. Mechanics are nothing revolutionary, sometimes annoying but mostly bearable, bugs completely ruin immersion and make me not recommend the game in it's current state.

This game is basically a flash game, but a good one. You destroy waves of incoming enemies before they reach the town crystal (deliberate silliness). You cannot attack monsters directly, though: you have to chant out a small band of warriors which will follow you closely. The goal is to dodge projectiles, while coming close enough the enemies so that your soldiers can kill them. Which means: you basically only have to move. Simplistic, but it proves efficiently entertaining.
Of course, as it has a flash game mechanics, you won't be able to go very far on your first run, but you win money with which you can upgrade yourself and your followers (as well as diverse features). Everything is quite basic, so do not expect much. It is fun, though, even if you have to repeat endlessly the same few waves. There is some diversity among the monsters, and a good choice of different followers. Developers have surely been imaginative on that side.
It gets boring after a few hours of gameplay, alas. Plus, the additional modes (survival and run) are most boring. In the survival mode, you can not do anything but dodge every foes for entire long minutes. Running is slow and devoid of any interest. Only the main game mode is worth playing; the other two are for achievements only.
Do not spend more than 3 euros/dollars in it.

В глаза сразу бросается наконец современная графика, которой не было со времён четвёртой части. Хорошая анимация, сильный графический "движок", внимание к мелочам, например монетки вылетающие из под ног или то как принц следит за искорками из порталов. Боевая система упрощена сверх меры, оно бы было не так плохо, если при этом и акробатика не пострадала. Очень слабая планировка уровней, остановка воды многообещающая идея, так и рисующая прогулку по солёным застывшим волнам с зависшими в воздухе каплями, в исполнении обернувшаяся пресными трубами. Вода вытекает из труб и исчезает в воздухе, при остановке даже анимация продолжает играть, а все брызги исчезают и заменяются на стандартную модель. Так же остановка воды не влияется на не заскриптованную воду, например на лужи. Разработчики даже не добавили прогулок по коронам бьющих из под земли фонтанов. Да и всё использование почти не отличается от "нажми кнопку получи упор для прохождения", мало того убрали "розетки" и настенные трамплины, убрали рычаги, возможность вернуться назад и многое другое. Зато добавили прыжки по врагам в сеть акробатики. Мало того что оно совсем не реалистично, так ещё видимо не учли что видя врага начинаешь искать способ его убить и вернуться в режим акробатики, поэтому часто в упор не видишь способа продвинуться дальше. Говорящим мечом конечно никого не удивишь, но меч бубнящий заклинания при каждом взмахе - интересная идея.
Больше всего это похоже на то что Darksiders смешали с Spiderman: Shattered Dimensions и декорациями из четвёртой-шестой частей.

Well, what to say about this one? On many RPG-game community-sites, Baldur's Gate still ranks in Top 10 (just like the first part, Planescape: Torment and some other RPG games of Black Isles) although it is quite old and there is a reason for it.
Baldur's Gate II is a party based isometric strategical aD&D RPG game with a deep storyline, moral choices, real interaction between your NSCs, lore to almost no end... Almost anything a real good RPG needs.
ICompared to the first part of the series, there are some differences. The story is more linear. You have less open-world exploration but are driven either to your next main quest or to one of many subquests. This reduces the risk of newcomers getting lost in endless exploration without knowing what they have to do next, but I realy liked the true open-worldness of the first part, so this is a little downside in my opinion.
Everything else is still the same old-school RPG-style like the first part. So it is realy some kind of must-have for hardcore RPG gamers. Oh, and you can import your character from the first part which is a big pro for this game. There are only very few series which allow really carrying over your char.
This edition is shipped with the "Throne of Bhaal"-AddOn which was not the best Add-On Black Isles ever made. The story and the enemys truely seem overloaded and a lot exxagerated most of the time and so are the items and the  "epic" skills your characters will achieve to beat the game (which is not very hard, even on increased difficulty levels). Buit still it concludes the "Bhaalspawn"-storyline of the series.
The Enhanced Edition comes with another campaign "The Black Pits II" continuing the arena-fighting campaign from the enhanced edition of the first part with even more arena fighting, but also with a deeper story and more tactical options and more roleplaying between the fights.
It also has enhanced graphics compared to the original game and some new NSCs with their own subquests and interactions. Some of them you might know from the Enhanced Edition of the first part.
The enhanced edition also has some new character classes, skills and spells, but those are only bonusses. If you already own the original game, have some great mods installed and don't like arena-fighting, this enhanced edition might not be worth buying, but for all the others it is clearly a recommendation.

The gratuitous brutality of knightly melee combat teeters between comedic and cathartic in Chivalry: Medieval Warfare's gory encounters. Well-placed killing blows send limbs and heads flying, accompanied by fountains of blood spewing from drippy stumps that call to mind the iconic Black Knight duel in Monty Python and the Holy Grail. It's hilarious at times and excessively gruesome. Gutting foes has a lot more weight to it here than in other recent entries in the Medieval combat genre like War of the Roses or Mount and Blade: Warband. That alone doesn't make Chivalry the best in its class, but it does incite a certain bloodlust that'll keep you charging into the chaos.
Before heading into the crazed multiplayer matches that are Chivalry's lifeblood, the cleverly designed single-player tutorial is a fun little diversion that serves as an introduction to the conflict between the underhanded Mason Order and the virtuous Agathian Knights. Roaming different regions of the coastal settlement, you tackle training for basic and advanced combat, test out siege weapons, and take each of the four core warrior classes for a spin. Then it's off to war.
Hack and slash.
The quartet of unique class types is more versatile than it first appears. On one end of the spectrum you have heavily armored Knights -- powerful and capable of absorbing lots of damage at the cost of speed. Vanguard look similar but are more moderately armored, can charge short distances, and are adept at wielding heavy spears and polearms. Sacrificing armor for speed, Men-At-Arms are zippy warriors who can quick-dodge. While these three melee-oriented classes each let you make substantive contributions in battle, Archers are the weakest link.
Using a bow in Chivalry is sluggish, imprecise, and far more of a hassle than it's worth.** Other classes also have access to secondary short-range missile weapons too. Admittedly, I love the Archer's arrow cam, which is a cool feature, but long-range combat is nowhere near as fun as it should be -- it feels unnecessarily punitive.
When you get down to it, the broad range of weapons is what really set each warrior type apart in function and helps complement their inherent strengths. Each class' basic loadout can be expanded by hitting certain kill quotas with a given weapon, unlocking the next one in line. There's a lot of different gear to open up for each character. You can carry a heavy primary weapon, a lighter secondary weapon, and an unlockable special item into battle, which leaves ample room for tinkering until you find the sweet spot loadout-wise.
Playing as an archer isnt very much fun.
Part of what makes the melee combat so satisfying is its speed and simplicity. Unlike War of the Roses, where there's so much depth and variation among attacking and blocking that it can get unwieldy, Chivalry takes a more user-friendly approach. Basic swings, jabs and overhand attacks are handled with the left mouse button and the mouse wheel, while blocking only takes a single click of the right mouse button. Combos are simple to pull off and other moves like feints or special class-specific attacks utilize accessible keyboard commands. In contrast, it may not feel as deep of a system as other games, but it's easier to parse when you're in the midst of a crowd with weapons swinging every which way. That's a good thing, because combat is fast-paced, bloody, and in-your-face. I also appreciate the option to switch instantly between a first and third person perspective, which makes battles more dynamic depending on your mood.
Free-for-all and Team Deathmatches are rowdy killing sprees that play out on smaller portions of the map, while the bigger Team Objective matches open up the entire stage and sport multi-tiered objectives specific to each map. These massive battles have you doing everything from defending a royal family and keeping a village from being torched to preventing catapults from being destroyed or defending a signal fire. Your choice of faction will determine whether you're on the attacking or defending side, and the flow of these large-scale encounters progresses through several levels of mission objectives before a victor is decided. While there are only six maps available at present, they're all very well designed, huge, and visually striking. Dark forests, sunny desert cities, castle ramparts, and rocky beachside cliffs are just some of the beautiful settings you'll carve up opponents in.
My verdict
Lopping off appendages in gory displays of warrior aggression makes Chivalry: Medieval Warfare's up-close and personal melee combat a gritty and fulfilling on a primal level. Though the lack of complexity sometimes works both for and against it, getting caught up in the flow of battle yields many hours of man-stabbing amusement. Like its competition, Chivalry hasn't quite perfected the formula for medieval warfare, but it's a violent, fun time nonetheless.

An Indian family fleeing from oppression in their home province found asylum in my Kingdom of Norway. Why not, I thought. The father of the family was a decent warrior, so I allowed him to command troops in battle. He distinguished himself in many wars over the years and was awarded one of the recently conquered counties in Northern Germany. He continued to serve me loyally and has even converted to Norse religion. For his service I gave him a duchy to rule. Generation after generation his descendants continued to marry local nobles.
Now, nearly two centuries later, Germany is ruled by white dudes in turbans who think they're Indian, worship Norse gods and train War Elephants. Breaking history has never been so much fun!
I started playing CK2 during a free weekend. It looked like something I might like, so I gave it a try. I bought the game the next day along with several DLCs and never stopped playing. CK2 has now climbed to number 1 of my most played Steam games, in spite of being in my library for less than a year. I don't recall another "game addiction" that lasted this long for me. And there is the fact that nearly 400 hours into the game I've only played as one of the many game religions, one of the numerous cultures (disregarding the training scenario). Playing as a different religion, culture, starting location, starting rank changes the way you play the game. You could even start your second play through in the exact same character as last time and the way things will go will be entirely different.
This game is more complex than any other strategy I've played before. It takes a while to take it all in. Luckily there are in-game hints to what every screen means and what every button does (you can switch these off later, but I found myself checking every now and then). There is also a tutorial campaign that will teach you how to play.
What adds to the fun greatly is the fact that you play as a specific character. Their traits and abilities make them more appropriate for certain roles within the Kingdom than others. The current King might make a better priest than military commander, but you don't say that out loud in front of your liege (or their spymaster). Once your character dies, you play as the heir to their titles, this being usually one of their children, depending on the hereditary laws of your realm.
Feel like expanding your Empire? You don't necessarily need to wage war to achieve that. Why don't you marry your eldest son to that second daughter of the neighboring empire and then make sure the first-born daughter (already married) has a little accident
she has children?
However as I am not the patient type I prefer marching my armies into enemy territory and be done with it. What I love about the battles is that the smallest thing can change the outcome of the battle (much like in history). The commander of your strongest flank was killed shortly after the skirmish began and his confused troops now run around the battlefield like headless chickens? Well, s**t happens.
There is always a chance, however small, that things will go wrong. It's up to you to play the odds (don't put your only heir in battle, especially while he's sick) and have a backup plan in case things don't go your way or you might end up losing your realm, or the entire game. Once I lost a major battle and most of my personal army. One of my vassals decided now was the good time to revolt, my stronger neighbor saw it as an opportunity to invade and on top of that a peasant uprising started in one of my counties. Bottom line - I lost it all and had to make tribal huts in Norway my capital, which was a bummer after living in a mighty castle in Western France for two generations.
The good news is you can appoint commanders as you see fit, provided your authority within the realm is strong enough to do so. Each of the several types of troops (and culture specific special units) has a different attack and defend stats and these evolve as you research technologies and construct special buildings. Your commanders can employ various tactics during battle, some of which depend on their personal traits and/or martial capability.
There are many situations you will find yourself in - often thanks to random events, most of which require very specific conditions to be met first. Many events are bound to a specific time and realms that existed at that point. I will not spoil these for you because I found it to be a lot of fun to face some of them followed by a palm on the forehead and an exclamation: “Of course, I (sort of) remember this from history lessons!”
I’ve always been interested in history and considered my knowledge of geography very decent and yet I’ve learned a lot of new facts by playing CK2. My natural curiosity took over and I've since researched many medieval realms and rulers online.
If you’re feeling competitive then know that achievements are only awarded if you play on Ironman mode. So please make sure that if you come across a player with some of the most difficult of achievements you salute and/or bow as appropriate.
At some point you might find yourself lying on your death-bed. Your son and heir might be an imbecile, your younger brother has possibly convinced half of your court he'd make a better King than you and yet you’ll enjoy every minute of it. This game has my full recommendation.
If this looks like something you might like then give it a try. But be warned - You might be buying the new number 1 in your library and may thus face the "Should I do something meaningful with my day or should I finally become the King of England?" decision. And we both know it can only go one way from there.

This is a great idea for a game! It looks great even now, has a (mostly) great soundtrack, good level and character design, and it's fun when it works. The problem is that its controls are best described as "drunken cow driving a bus on ice." I started to enjoy this game several times, and every one of those times the very next level ripped that away with an infuriating refusal to do what I asked. What ultimately did it in was the second race level, because these combine bad controls with a seemingly deliberately confusing path, ridiculously little room for error, and, in the second event, an AI opponent who veers all over a narrow pipe and smashes you in a random direction on contact. It isn't helped by the fact that the most reliable way of getting ahead of him is dash-jumping, which makes the controls even less usable.
I absolutely see why this game has so many fans, but I can't possibly recommend something that's so often this infuriating to play.

At first glance, this game may appear to be a visual masterpiece with a beautiful atmosphere that is engaging and fun to explore. However, I do not recommend wasting your time with this game.
Along with the repetitive, melodramatic piano tunes, this game lacks a lot of depth. The rather forgettable story unfolds as you progress through the game, relayed as a series of images depicting some history behind the game's characters. You are required to explore the land and scale massive buildings looking for supplies to help save your sick/dying brother.  Miku (the girl you play as) moves painstakingly slow. There is no option to "run," and often when climbing certain handholds, your character will "slip" for a moment and take a few extra seconds to actually make it up. In addition to the main story "supplies," there are 60 "secrets" to uncover in this world, which, given the slow pace of exploration, will just become agonizingly boring to find.
I bought this game for $1.99, which was a great price, but not worth the hassle for this game. If you are an achievement hunter, it will take between 3~5 hours to 100%, but even so, save your money.

Submerged is a short little game mostly focused on climbing and boating around a post-apocalyptic world.
About the game itself:
You play as a little girl who arrives in a city, or at least what is left of it, almost completely under water, with only tall structures stretching above the surface. It is up to you to pilot your boat around the buildings, vines and animals and to climb the skyscrapers in order to find medicine for your sick brother and upgrades to speed up your boat, as well as chronicles of the world past and what happened to end it. There is practically no dialogue in this game, and while the very basics of the story (sister tries to save brother) is explained, everything else is for you to extrapolate from the hints given or fill in for yourself.
Pros:
-Post-apocalyptic visuals are pretty if that is your type of thing (overgrown, flooded and deteriorated cities)
-The atmosphere is probably this games biggest strength
Cons:
-Somewhat short, took me about 4 hours to 100% this game
-Gameplay consists just of exploring the city with your boat and climbing the architecture
Personal Opinion:
There really isn't that much to say about Submerged, it is quite simple and the story is more hinted at than actually present. The name is poetically fitting though, seeing how if you enjoy submersing yourself in atmosphere and taking in the landscape, this can be quite fun to you. I really felt like a little girl, surrounded by an endless body of water and alone (or maybe not?). No grand epic, no complex story, no great action, just a little window into a world which you either enjoy or don't. So if these kind of games aren't your beer, this won't change that. But if you're looking for a short and atmospheric experience, wait until it is on sale, as I definitely think the full price is to much, and I'd say from 10€ downwards I recommend diving in.
