Pros:
+Excellent gameplay for both new and old players
+Tons of part variety and synergy
+You can climb on walls
+Reminiscent of Mechwarrior in that tactics and terrain actually matter. Turrets can only aim ~30° above horizontal, so a height advantage really is an advantage.
+The business model doesn't suck♥♥♥♥♥ you can buy multiple new parts after 1-4 games
+You can climb on walls
+Unique weapons such as a sawblade that flies along the ground, cannons with bouncing shots, and harpoon launchers
+Unique parts, such as a pair of fans that pretty much turn your tank into a helicopter, or the dual-turret hull that turns your tank into a battleship
+There is no "uber build," pretty much every weapon combination works, no matter how haphazard
+You can climb on walls
+Despite coming off as "casual," can be very fun for both relaxed and focused players
+The default gear also doesn't suck♥♥♥♥♥ I got a decakill in my second game using all Basic gear and some serious flanking.
Cons:
-Stability is pants. The game crashes, for me, 6-8 times a day, and hangs at least 3 times every game. Framerate is a solid 60 FPS, so this must be some issue with the engine. If you can't deal with this, good luck.
-Balance isn't perfect. The heavier sniper rifle can instakill any tank under 75 health, which is most light/medium tanks. Harpoon launchers and spears are more or less godmode if you can lead your shots.
-This is a team-centric game, but the chatbox is practically invisible.
-Netcode is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Like, Space Marine♥♥♥♥♥♥ Unless you have sub-80ms ping (which, to be fair, isn't hard if you're playing with people in the same country), you'll see stuff like other players sliding through the ground and end up being blown up by your own mines, despite being 50m away from them.
Overall, a good game, though probably not ready to be out of early release quite yet. The devs need to put some serious work into engine stability. But don't take my word for it, take it for a spin! It's free!

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is GSC Game World's magnum opus. They went out with a bang by making not only the best game in the series but their best game ever.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is a First-Person Shooter / Role-Playing / Survival Horror game. It's what happens when you take the best elements of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, stick them together and add open-world exploration into the mix.
After the slight misstep that was Clear Sky, GSC Game World listened to the fans, did a complete turn in the other direction and went back to what made Shadow of Chernobyl such fun to play.
Call of Pripyat is set after Shadow of Chernobyl. You play as an undercover military agent, Alex Degtyarev. You are sent into the Zone to find out why a party of helicopters, that were advancing into the Zone after the events in Shadow of Chernobyl took place, crashed.
This is without a doubt the most polished game of the series. The game gives you three incredibly huge open areas for you to explore however you want, with lots of side missions to do and things to find. Exploration has a heavier focus now than it did over the last two games.
The "A-Life" system, artificial life designed to react worldwide to what happens in the Zone, is now better then ever, monsters will move into places that might have been previously been occupied by humans or other mutants. This makes locations around the Zone a constantly unsafe place to live, especially at night.
GSC Game World also brought back the visual and sound indicators as well as the need to eat and drink. You can now also sleep if you want but be sure to eat something before you sleep.
The story is also mush improved over S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky and whilst this game keeps the horror parts pretty short, the mutants are just as terrifying as always.
Nothing more really needs to be said, excellent story, excellent combat as always, an experience you will not forget for a long time. If you enjoyed the previous games, Shadow of Chernobyl in particular, then get this game. You will not regret it!
P.S. Grab the "CALL OF PRIPYAT COMPLETE" modification to enhance the textures, fix any remaining bugs and small translation issues.

Submerged is overall a decently good game. It's really a calming with its music and allows the player to have the freedom of roaming the flooded city.
Story-wise, it's really beautiful and tragic. It shows the story of the two characters of the game, which is delivered amazingly. It's quite rare to see games showing the characters' backstory instead of telling it. It also gets more suspenceful everytime the story progresses after collecting a kit per day. There is also 60 collectibles scattered across the city where it shows how the city is before and how it is now.
The atmosphere in the game is calming and mysterious. The music is what makes roaming the flooded city relaxing and peaceful without an end. Not only that, but within ceratin areas, you will get to see a whale or a shark and dolphins swim with you side-by-side. The mysterious part is when climbing to reach certain areas, non-hostile "zombies" can be seen before vanishing after to are close to them.
Gameplay isn't the best. Although the main character's movement seem decent but slow, driving the boat is a bit troublesome since it feels cluncky. Climbing up and down get repetitive since it's the only way to method to reach one point to another to either get a kit or to get a collectible which shows the story of the city.
Overall, I recommend this game if you want to enjoy a good short story while relaxing at the same time.

Visually, this game is stunning. It looks amazing, mysterious and the overall art style is fantastic. The music is, even if very repetetive at times, really nice as well.
But there's where the good things end.
To me, a platformer should be about having total control over your character and being able to use your skill to be able to progress. As the game goes on, the levels get harder and you're supposed to use your experience from earlier levels to clear the later ones.
This is made impossible by the controls of this game, which might be the wonkiest I've ever seen in any game. It's extremly hard to be precise when playing through this game and yet, the game requires extreme precision to get the shinies, clear the challenges or, heck, even clear the normal stages! If you create a game and want to creat challenging platforming you create difficult levels and use intricate level design, not controls that work against the player.
And this is why the music is annoying, even if it's good - listening to the same music over, and over, and over again as you try to battle against the controls make it so you'll lose any good memories with that music, thus not liking it.
I really want to recommend this game due to it's visual style, but I can't because this games fails so greatly at what makes a platformer a platformer.

Controls:  On the ground changing directions happens instantly, no delay super nice.  In the air however you float around sceaming and the computer BACK UP BACK UP!  But noooo!  It wont, it can't.  The girl is so fricken big the levels with her were a pain, and since I have such a hard time with the air controls I found the cave levels to be the most fun, as all you have to do is time your jump right.
That is... until I almost won the game.  It occured to me that it is a really good thing that this game is not multiplayer as a few platformers I've played have been, because with a 5ms delay it would be impossible, the window to actually make your jump on the end cave levels is like 0.4 seconds long, and 0.4 might be a little generous.
The levels are at most around 20-25 seconds long, most can be completed in about 12-15 seconds.
Now you may have recommended this game, and that my review seems negative... here's why.  I was thinking about it and I want my friends to suffer at least as much as I did with this game.  I've decided, if one of them can win the game which is all 100 levels, and get at least 75 Shinies before they accumulate the 1000 deaths achievement, I will give them 20$.   I want my friends rediscovering all of their swears and all of the colorful ways to use them, and then I want to laugh in their faces as they get so close and fail miserably right at the end!  That being said... I have a feeling at least one of them will breeze through this almost impossible game pretty much flawlessly and be like, meh... that wasn't too hard...
That said, for that reason, I say yes, I would recommend this game, because well... In an odd way, I'm doing just that to my friends. :P   However, if you are thinking about playing the game, and you don't mind achieving the far too easy to get 1000 deaths achievement, then yes, go ahead and get it, you might like it.  I personally will likely NEVER TOUCH THIS GAME AGAIN!   And I mean that with all the seathing hatred I can muster... Aaah, my rant is over... now I can feel better.  (°-°)

Recommended, but with reservations.
Warframe absolutely meets the model of a fun, free-to-play game. Having played it for nearly 1000 hours now, I've experienced most of what the game has to offer, and al though I'm reaching endgame, I still play it quite a bit daily. That being said, Warframe still has a lot of minor and major issues that tarnish the quality of play and makes the game feel rather unpolished at times.
It's hard to describe what kind of game Warframe exactly is. My best description would be that it's a coop third person shooter with parkour elements, although that barely scratches the surface of it. It's like if you added guns into Assassin's creed and made it multiplayer! It's absolutely a lot of fun, and when I first started playing it, I was absolutely addicted and could not get enough of it. The initial mystique of the game is alluring and everybody should at least try this game.
I'm also a big fan of the premium model, where it doesn't feel pay-to-win at all and is based entirely around convenience (e.g. speeding up build times) and cosmetics. Although I don't normally spend money on these games, I have no problems supporting Digital Extremes and buying a bit of platinum, especially when they offer deals on it. It's also very possible to get everything without spending money at all, as it's rather easy to trade for play with in game items.
However, like I said, Warframe does have quite a few issues that range from minor inconveniences to game-breaking. The first would be how players are introduced to the lore and concepts of the game. The tutorial for beginners is absolutely terrible, and I honestly had no idea what I was doing or what anything was for my first few weeks or so of playing. There's very little accessible in-game that explains how concepts such as mastery rank and weapon levels work, and how to progress in the game. The wiki does offer a lot of useful resources in learning the game, but I feel that players shouldn't have to refer to third party sources to learn to play. The lore is a similar issue- although the story gets extremely captivating later on (no spoilers), so many of the characters were introduced in limited time events very early on in the game's development, before I and many others started playing. As a result, we really feel no personal connection to many of them and don't even know their backstory when they come up in the plot, which makes for a rather slow and lackluster story initially.
There's also other issues that make the game feel plain unpolished. These range from UI issues such as hack-lag (a one second delay between finishing a hack and the hack actually being counted as completed) that can ruin some close hacks and make the game very frustrating, to community issues such as a pretty terrible system of in-game trading. The latter issue isn't as big a problem now with community websites such as Warframe Trader, but again- this isn't something it should be up to the community to do. Some other issues also include a nonstatic menu (try opening up the esc menu when bullet jumping) and the lack of descriptions of buffs, which can make it pretty confusing when there are a lot of support warframes in your squad.
Although my opinion of DE is generally positive, there have also been headscratchers where you just can't understand their game design and priorities. A "controversial" issue is universal vacuum, which DE refuses to add in but most of the community seems to be in support of. There have also been instances where major game-breaking bugs (e.g. invincible Lephantis, a boss) have gone unfixed for months while minor, fun bugs such as flying fish were patched within the same day. S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is GSC Game World's magnum opus. They went out with a bang by making not only the best game in the series but their best game ever.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is a First-Person Shooter / Role-Playing / Survival Horror game. It's what happens when you take the best elements of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, stick them together and add open-world exploration into the mix.
After the slight misstep that was Clear Sky, GSC Game World listened to the fans, did a complete turn in the other direction and went back to what made Shadow of Chernobyl such fun to play.
Call of Pripyat is set after Shadow of Chernobyl. You play as an undercover military agent, Alex Degtyarev. You are sent into the Zone to find out why a party of helicopters, that were advancing into the Zone after the events in Shadow of Chernobyl took place, crashed.
This is without a doubt the most polished game of the series. The game gives you three incredibly huge open areas for you to explore however you want, with lots of side missions to do and things to find. Exploration has a heavier focus now than it did over the last two games.
The "A-Life" system, artificial life designed to react worldwide to what happens in the Zone, is now better then ever, monsters will move into places that might have been previously been occupied by humans or other mutants. This makes locations around the Zone a constantly unsafe place to live, especially at night.
GSC Game World also brought back the visual and sound indicators as well as the need to eat and drink. You can now also sleep if you want but be sure to eat something before you sleep.
The story is also mush improved over S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky and whilst this game keeps the horror parts pretty short, the mutants are just as terrifying as always.
Nothing more really needs to be said, excellent story, excellent combat as always, an experience you will not forget for a long time. If you enjoyed the previous games, Shadow of Chernobyl in particular, then get this game. You will not regret it!
P.S. Grab the "CALL OF PRIPYAT COMPLETE" modification to enhance the textures, fix any remaining bugs and small translation issues.

*TL;DR*: A dated game rushed to completion, with the result being shallow, unpolished and short. 4/10
Rock Paper Shotgun's review of the game perfectly summates everything wrong with Overgrowth. Nevertheless, I feel obligated to explain how I feel about the game, especially considering it's no longer early access.
Graphically speaking, it looks like a remastered version of a ten year old game. The lighting and assets are very dated looking even at high resolution at maximum settings, and some new effects like motion blur and bloom and very vibrant skyboxes still can't make the game look good. This wouldn't be so much of an issue if the game ran well, which it doesn't. Performance isn't truly atrocious but it really leave something to be desired, chugging in vegetation-rich levels even on recent high-end graphics cards like my GTX 1070.
Gameplay wise, it's a strange mix of extremely polished features and incredibly unpolished features. This probably stems from its almost decade-long development time. But overall, gameplay is limited to platforming and killing. Platforming is pretty bad, as the movement system is neither direct enough to have precision nor helpful enough to prevent mistakes on the game's part. You never know if you're going to be wallrunning or rebounding off a wall because the control is the same, but the outcomes are quite different (one kills you). For this reason, the parkour is more a chore than any fun.
The combat is the other part of the gameplay. When I played the alpha, the combat was actually genuinely fun: one-on-one or one-on-two duels with other rabbits means you have to have both mechanical skill to react quickly and appropriately, as well as strategic skill to decide when and how to attack your foes. This is what you see in most gameplay videos; a quick and skillful, punch-and-parry martial arts faceoff.
Unfortunately, in the release campaign, the developers have made your character often fight against several non-rabbit characters at a time, which leads to an asymmetric fighting situtation, instantly breaking down the combat. It's typically possible to fight other species using the combat gameplay designed for other rabbits; either you're against dogs or wolves, both of which are too big to counter/block, or you're against rats, which you have no need to counter. The result? All that fun combat that the alpha had is thrown out the window in favour of goomba stomping everything or just spamming kicks. Similarly, the fighting system isn't designed for three or more enemies, as they will all attack at the same time which removes the possibility of blocking them or beating them back: your only option is taking flight and goomba stomping each of them individually. Weapons are really poorly balanced, with knifes being largely a hinderance, but a broadsword being a f*cking cruise missile against your opponents when thrown- and it's the other way around for the AI; they hack-and-slash your gut in an instant with a knife but seem to struggle with the concept of wielding the broadsword, often doing leg sweeps while holding the unstoppable blade.
It gets worse. Although the game engine supports a basically limitless scripting system wherein escort-, delivery-, defense- and whatever-missions are possible, the developers have made all levels in the campaign either: 1. kill everything, or 2. reach a location through platforming. For this reason there is no complexity to the game, not to mention its linear campaign. You're given a knife for most missions, there's a bit of dialogue explaining that you need to kill the baddies to save the rebels, and then you slaughter everything that moves. Maybe, if you could choose a weapon other than the provided knife, or sneak past the baddies to pass a mission, or use environmental kills, or call for allies to help, or anything, it would be better, but no.
I mentioned linear campaign, and I think i need to expand on exactly how linear it is. Ever level starts with dialogue, then you walk to a place, talk to a person or yourself, then either platform or kill everything. Nothing you do matters, no decisions are possible, there's nothing to explore, nothing to collect, no alternate means of completing the level. Actually, don't even try exploring, you'll probably just stumble upon something unfinished or out of bounds or get lost.
Okay, story time. I had high hopes for the story after reading the Overgrowth comics, since it was clear there was a considerable amount of lore to be told. Well, that didn't pan out. I don't want to spoil the story, but it's really basic and devoid of any depth. The dialogue is awkward, there's no character development, and there's these really cheesy lines that make me cringe. Above everything, there's just absolutely no emotion.
It honestly seems they almost forgot to add the lore, as the only lore present in the game is text on the loading screens. Skyrim proved that loading-screen lore isn't a bad idea, but Skyrim has hundreds and hundreds of lore snippets across its hundred-hour plot. In comparison, Overgrowth's Lugaru port AND main campaign can be completely in under two hours, so you'll see around 30 quotes of lore total.
On a positive note, modding support is excellent. Apparently a mod called Therium-2 has a massive campaign that is longer, deeper, and allows decisions and other richer gameplay compared to the developer-made campaign. That's probably worth checking out
Honestly I'm just really disappointed, and I think the developers probably are too. I am glad that it's no longer in development hell, but it seems that they rushed it to completion because there was no passion in the game anymore. If you pick through the game files, you'll see all the assets that aren't used, all the gamemodes that were started then axed, and so on. It's clear that this game had wide ambitions but after so many years they decided to make a simple campaign and release it as-is just to close the book on this game.

In this challenging platformer you get to be a cat named Bast. Your best friend (owner?), a girl, is whisked away by a creature akin to grim reaper and you have find her. To do this you have to run, jump and crawl through 100 levels of increasing difficulty, all with high contrast graphics similar to Limbo.
There are actually three different kinds of levels. In all of them you have to reach the light at the end of the obstacle course of a level. Cat levels are the most numerous of the bunch. They are the basic platforming levels where you, the cat, can run, jump and wall-jump through the dungeons filled with lethal spikes, playful porcupines, levitating spike balls and moving saw blades and spear traps. Later on there are crumbling, disappearing and reappearing, occasionally sharp-edged platforms to watch out for and also happy swinging giant spiders and cannons with both regular and homing bullets to dodge. Spiky death is pretty much guaranteed.
Second kinds of levels are the girl levels. Girl is trapped in a spirit world, filled with (surprise!) spikes and saw blades and other lethal things I already mentioned. However, for an unknown reason she can jump to the ceiling and back at will. This being the only thing she can do the game pumps a lot of levels out of the simple movement mechanics and both stationary and moving traps.
The third and the most frustrating level type (for me) are the cave levels. In these the cat moves with the same jump-up-and-down mechanics as the girl but running constantly. Precision jumps are easy enough in the early levels but later on they have to be made within a tiny fraction of a second, quickly accumulating tiring deaths. Sometimes you also have to crawl under deathly spikes, bullets or those sneaky, swigging spiders. Frankly, I disliked the cave levels a lot because the speed makes the imperfect hitboxes significant. Also, why must Bast suddenly run when s/he was fine with careful jumps before? Fortunately, there are only some 20 cave levels, so they are in the minority.
Most levels are quite short, lasting just some 10-20 seconds. You get an achievement for par-timing all levels, which is fairly difficult but gets easier as you learn to control both characters. There's also a shiny collectable in each level. Cave running levels don't have par-times, instead requiring you to beat them on the first go. That sounds evil but it's a bluff because you can just try the level again from the level selection screen after each failure to try again.
After beating the game there are ten more challenge (cat platforming) levels to beat that are even more difficult than the story levels. Fortunately they are not required for the acquirement of the ultimate achievement: Ninja Cat. To get that you have to beat the game without dying more than 10 times. It's a very difficult and frustrating achievement despite that you can beat the game in around half an hour.
Unfortunately, the last few of the cave running levels have speed sections that lag the game to a halt, making it jerky with a framerate less than 10. This makes those very precision-heavy levels virtually unplayable. I know this is a problem with my system but I have tried the game on three different computers, a laptop and two desktops, all of which have this same problem (and AMD Radeon type cards that are probably to blame). It makes the Ninja Cat tries a true pain. For some reason the levels work alright when I first start the game but not if I play through all the levels.
All in all, A Walk in the Dark is a very challenging platformer. Granted, sometimes the deaths become really annoying as the hitboxes don't exactly match the graphics, but it's worth its present price (6 €) and can often be grabbed for half that on a sale.

Let's start with the positive aspects of this game:
+ It looks fantastic. I really like the art style.
+ Music is okay
But it all fails at one really important thing. The control. There's a delay between pressing a button and the reaction in the game. I found out at a later point, that you can reduce the delay by playing in window mode but that might just apply to myself.
I guess the developers knew they ♥♥♥♥ed up the controls, because one of their achievements is to die 10k times. Which you will probably obtain at the middle of the game.
The game itself reminds me of a mixture between Limbo (art style), Super Meat Boy (difficulty) and VVVVVV (gravity changes), which is nice but the level design starts to get okay to good after the first third of the game, which is sad.
There are 3 gameplay types basicly.
Normal platforming (reminds me most of super meat boy)
The girl: platformer like VVVVVV (really frustrating with a delay up to 0.5 seconds for me)
The cave: scrolling levels with VVVVVV change gravity aspect (really really frustrating, because some levels require pixel perfect "jumps" almost, and I really recommend not trying to achieve the "first try" badges.
Each level requires for 100%ing that you beat the time and collect a shiny object in every level (except the cave once, where there is no time to beat but "first try" it). You don't need to do both extra objectives at the same time.
You also don't need to play the levels in order, you can skip some if you can't beat them.
For collecting 10 shiny objects you unlock a challenge level. If you got used to the controls they are really nice actually.
This game is a nightmare for all completionists. In order to 100% the game you need to pass all cave levels without dying once. That is really frustrating, because if you do you need to shut off the game and then restart it and then try it again once. That delay I wrote about makes this impossible for me.
There are also some weird aspects ... for example: The "cutscenes" in this game are weird. They are mostly like 1 second long and do nothing to present a story or whatever and the main menu looks really bad compared to the actual gameplay.
All in all I really want to like this game but the controls give me the feeling that most mistakes where not made by me but the game, which is something you don't experience in Super Meat Boy or VVVVVV.

This game was on track to be 5 stars all the way, but I ran into some issues.
I'll start with the good. Beautiful dialogue, animation, scenery, the whole deal. Combat feels nice, the variety of abilities and classes/races is really nice, too. An RPG for sure, as it allows for various choices when talking with people, and special interactions when you have points in certain areas, or are playing certain characters. Backstory is nice, well thought out, and there is plenty to do.
The bad. Combat can be extremely frustrating. I'm on classic mode, which I thought was easy mode enoguh, but beware, it's not. I've recently ran into my 5th encounter that I was unable to do without having to previously manipulate the fight. When I ask one of my friends, or forums, for advice, its typically met with "you have to cheese the fight" or something of the sort. I fear that if I go to Explorer mode, it will feel to easy, and will just become a game filled with talking to people, and running around. Auto-save once locked me into an encounter that I had to manipulate myself out of, which took a half hour, and then when I started manually saving, it was hard to remember to save so often, since encounters can happen so suddenly, following important thing you should've saved after.
Overall. I enjoy it, and I would a lot more, but the combat, and trying to find that mid-ground of challenging, but not too much, is hard. You feel excited to have some free time to play it, but you could potentially feel discouraged when you come across forced encounters that wipe your team. They put a lot of effort into this game, and it's one of the nicer games I've played in a long time. I'll personally need to find a way to enjoy this more without having the combat sour the mood. I can't live off the storyline and dialouge alone, and going into town and talking to people can often bore me very quickly.

Tengami is defined by its visuals, which is great (since they are stunningly executed in a unique genre and style) and not so great (since the game's content doesn't quite live up to its look).
In terms of gameplay, this is a short (1-1.5 hours) point-and-drag puzzle adventure with lots of walking between hotspots. Puzzles mostly consist of matching various fold-outs to create a path for your character or to find an object that will unlock a door. There isn't a lot of challenge here, as the puzzles are few and trial and error will work in most cases. If you're looking for a puzzle game to occupy your time, Tengami will disappoint you.
In terms of experience, however, this is a little gem. The game's slow pace (as you walk from place to place) and gentle puzzles allow/force you (depending on your personality) to appreciate a journey through a gorgeously crafted landscape, accompanied by an atmospheric soundtrack that fills out the sense of a mythical pop-up world. Timelessness and poetry—turns out they can be strengths in a video game.

The core concept of Tengami that puts you inside a 3D popup book is brilliant. And the environments are beautifully crafted. The pace of action is slow, slower than is required given the nature of the puzzles, but at least you get time to soak in the gorgeous papercraft visual style as your guy runs around.
About the slow running - I've seen several other comments about it. It took me a while to realize it but I found the slow movement to be a framerate issue. I first fired up the game in fullscreen, and although the refresh rate seemed ok, the guy moved slow and all the world effects like snow, leaves, magic effects, all were slow. I realized it when the guy started moving quickly at one point. I switched to 800x600 windowed mode and the game ran much faster. The game is probably capping the frame update time once it starts getting long frames, resulting in the slo-mo effect.
I found several of the puzzles to be not very intuitive. There was sometimes no real clue as to what was required. And in levels that required a lot of moving around to figure it out, the slow pace of movement didn't support that. However, I have no shame in opening up a walkthrough when I get stuck, and with a little help, I motored through this game under two hours.
It was well worth the $3.39 price I picked it up for in the Humble sale.

Great, unique game that any grand strategy enthusiast should purchase.
Crusader Kings II fills an excellent niche of strategy where the goal is to control and survive internal struggles as it is to survive the machinations of your neighbors. This is fantastic game for single or co-op play.  It takes a long time to learn and master, but once you've got it the game becomes very fun and satisfying.
My primary complaints lie in the underdeveloped economic side, underdeveloped religious system (especially for non-Catholics and non-Norse) slow casus-belli capture-one-county-at-a-time conquering system, and multiplayer instability.
Note: The developers have consistently released new content for the game, which is incredible.  A lot of the key additions are also given for free for vanilla users.  That said, there are some DLC expansions that add important new systems or create additional depth to existing ones, which therefore should be purchased with vanilla.  If on a tight budget, I would definitely pick up Old Gods.  All other DLC at your discretion.

Bardbarian is a casual RPG "tower defence" game. You play as Brad the Bardbarian and your aim is to protect the town crystal, which is conveniently placed at the end of the town, with a huge field of open grass separating it from the forest. This game is different to other games in the RPG tower defense genre, however, because instead of the main protagonist, Brad, fighting, he summons troops using notes that he has played on his lute to fight for him. The troops can range from wizards and mages to knights to even mechanics, so you can make some pretty interesting crew combinations.
The main idea of the game is very similar to that of "Earn to die". You obtain money as you play and you can use it later to upgrade things in three different categories. Your troops, your town, or yourself. This can lead to some extremely repetitive grinds for gold, but other than that the gameplay is excellent. There are 2 different types of difficulties: Casual, and Insane. Casual would be for people who haven't played much of the genre before, but for me, insane was just the right amount of difficulty to make it fun. Having to dodge while still being in range to shoot makes this like no other tower defence.
All in all, I'd say that everyone should give this game at least a shot. It's very enjoyable and the price is pretty fair for the content you get.

I don't normally write reviews, and I sure wouldn't do so with so little time invested, but my standards are based on how many hours of entertainment I get per dollar spent(I like a 1:1, higher is obviously better). So here goes what little I've got.
Starting off, I only paid $2 for this game on sale. That sort of artificially inflates my value, but that's not a problem per se.
To put it plainly, this game is pretty, simplistic, and mildly entertaining. My recommendation comes heavily weighted on it being on sale, however that is not due to lack of quality, but rather lack of content. As other reviewers have expressed, there isn't much to do except explore and collect the same few things repeatedly. I caution on this however as the value of this game is in the beauty.
For such a simple game with little to offer in the way of activity, exploring alone can easily be worth an hour or two of your time from what I can tell. The game world is small but complex enough that you could spend a good amount of time riding the boat around just taking in the scenery. For $2 that was worth MY money already at half an hour in of pretty much just that. I may or may not even play the game more than that, still won't be disapointed.
Assuming the devs get enough people drawn in with this to turn a profit, they have an excellent starting point from which to make a new game with more/better content. I hope they do exactly that. Adding the quality of this game up though, it's worth money, how much is really going to vary per person, but for me it's a thumbs up.
TLDR; Buy it on sale, full price maybe not but still wouldn't be the worst mistake you ever made.

I just want to start off by saying that I cannot recommend this game due to one fatal flaw in the game itself. Some may not find it to be too bad or find it enjoyable, but it ruined the experience for me. But first, the positives of this game. The game hosts an awesome art direction that feels very immersive and unique, as the lighting feels like it is radiating out from the background in many of the levels, along with the foreground always being in a state of shadow. Along with the art, the soundtrack helps as well to create an experience that allows the player to further get enthralled into the game....
That is, if the clunky controls didn't have you swearing at the game every 30 seconds. I'm sorry, I understand that the game is suppose to be difficult, but in my opinion ramping up the difficulty via awful controls is probably one of the laziest ways to do it. Also, for the record I was using a gamepad (A PS3 controller to be exact). The physics of both the cat and the girl always feel... floaty for lack of a better word. And not the Super Meat Boy kind of floaty, it feels more like nothing will turn or move easily, slightly like the physics of the original Super Mario Bros., but much worse. Of course, floaty physics would not be too much of a problem if the levels were not so exact as to where you have to land and jump to. I like challenging games, as I love Super Meat Boy and Bit Trip Runner, but this game feels unecessarily difficult due to it's poor controls. Ultimately, it is kinesthetically unattractive and ruins the whole experience for me. I have to give this game a 5/10, and to only buy it if it is on an extreme sale, or if you think I'm just whining and the controls can't be
bad.

Followers getting stuck, side quests not completing, quest log being updated for no reason, endlessly respawning enemies in a certain fight, some fights starting with enemies being miles away from you, quest markers never updating, blinking toolbars ... these are the ones I can recall right now but there are many more.
Still, if you can get over the bugs, you also need to get over the flawed as hell gameplay with amazing features, listed below :
- Chose a wrong dialogue during a conversation, blocking yourself permanently from the possible rewards or quests ? Reload.
- Killed an essential character during a fight that you were supposed to talk to afterwards ? Reload.
- Accidentally tried to pick up one of the owned items scattered all over the place, reducing the attitude of every single character around towards you ? Reload.
- Got a great item for your character but forgot to save and died or made a wrong choice soon after ? Realoding won't help, that item will be replaced (randomized loots each time).
- Got an item but have no idea what it does ? Don't worry, developers have no idea either.
- Is there a feature in the game that isn't working at all ? It was probably left there from the alpha stage of the game (as if it isn't still is) and they never bothered to remove it.
Oh wait, there's more :
- If your enemies are higher level than you, they get a damage bonus, making the fight much harder than it's supposed to be. If you are the one with higher level, the fight becomes too easy and uninteresting.
- Worst armor system in any game of its kind, they just add more health. No physical resistance.
- Lackluster crafting system, I've never bothered to use it even once except for quest-related things. Same goes with combining things because you will never really use it other than to enhance runes.
- You can miss out on an entire quest just because you haven't seen that small switch, didn't have enough wits, didn't speak to that well-hidden character that you can only see with spirit vision or didn't eat that body part.
- There are so many things to pick up and 99% of them are useless. You will end up selling most of your things for gold but guess what ? Gold is nearly useless because merchants never really sell anything that exactly fits your character. Your character is a pyro + summoner hybrid ? Good luck finding a ring that gives you a plus in both of these.
But ... but doesn't it have any good sides ? It surely can't be that♥♥♥♥♥♥if you have played for that many hours you casul♥♥♥♥♥troll !
Well, lets see :
- Story is good, better than what they offer you in most other games.
- Graphics are great.
- Nice music, could be better though. I don't think I will ever be satisfied with any game's soundtrack after playing NieR : Automata but that's just me.
- Even though the fights can get really messy, they are fun at times.

In summary, you should think carefully before purchasing this reload simulator and don't listen to excited fanbois who are like "AMG BESSSST GAME EVUR TBH" or "GOTY 2020" etc.

A Walk in the Dark is a beautiful and atmospheric game with a few love-it or hate-it flaws.
On the plus side, the aesthetics are great, and as a platformer, it's challenging, but the levels are short enough that you can pull it up for a quick play without having to invest too much time in one sitting. The story is simple, but cute in a kind of LIMBO sort of way.
On the down side, the challenge comes from the lack of minute control over your character, and the fact that merely brushing something can kill you. In other words, the challenge comes from trying to operate the game's mechanics, rather than any real sort of puzzle or manipulation. Even early on, it may take several tries to finish a level, and you may feel like you passed or failed on luck.
Bottom Line:
I recommend the game for people who have a love for challenging platformers, and the feel of games like LIMBO. If, however, you get frustrated easily, or are looking for a casual play, this is probably not the game for you.

Let me first say that I am not a hothead nor a young man (I was born the year JFK was elected president).  I rarely buy EA games because generally the risk outweights the value of the game prior to release.  However, I was really interested in giving MyRPG Master a shot, since it appeared to solve many of the time crunch issues that I face as a developer.
However, let me warn anyone else who thinks this would be a reasonably good investment, DON'T BUY THIS SOFTWARE!
Here are the exact reasons why I make such a recommendation.
1.  MyRPG Master is really nothing more or nothing less than a commercial (alpha) add-on to Torque 3D, which is by the way completely free and uses the VERY liberal MIT open source licensing agreement.  A lot of the core tools in Torque 3D are similar to MyRPG Master.  The devs of this software have added some very useful RPG tools, but in doing so they made all of the code proprietary and non-open source.  Although this is completely legal in terms of the MIT OS license, it doesn't make many friends.  Furthermore, the devs of MyRPG Master actually blocked (or removed entirely) some very useful native Torque 3D features, such as being able to add animations to your imported DAE 3d models rather than having to buy or make these models with the animations built into the DAE file.  They also did another tricky modification to the original engine by setting the link color of a very important aspect of the engine to the same color as the edior's background, thus you cannot really use that functionality either.  The tool also is not compatible with Torque 3D's base engine from the testing I have been able to do given the way that the devs locked down so much of the scripting.
2. English documentation and tutorials is almost non-existent.  Other's have mentioned this as well so I won't belabor the point.  You have to figure out a great deal of things through trial and error as a result.  So instead of saving you time in your game development it actually can take much longer.  Since you cannot access their scripts there is no insider way to figure out how things work by examining the scripts and so forth.
3. This last problem is not a result of the way MyRPG Master has been implemented, but rather is a tiny rant on my part concerning the inadequacy of the Steam EA return policy.  Perhaps 2 hrs/2 weeks is sufficient for a relatively uncomplex EA game but for a development tool, two hours is just about enough time to open the tool and get somewhat familiar with the editor interface.  Come now Valve, the Steam community pours millions of dollars into your company, the least that you can do is make a reasonable return policy for those people who are willing to pay a company to do beta testing on their product (an odd concept to me anyway).
So as to be fully truthful about MyRPG Master I will say that so long as you are willing to pay for animated models in Collada (DAE) format or are proficient at making such models yourself and don't mind taking the time to do so then this is not a bad tool.  Though if you have that kind of time you probalby would still be better served by downloading the base Torque 3D engine and scripting the tools for your project as needed.
The bottom line: If you are a developer and a tool like this appeals to you, save your money and go download  the FREE Torque 3D engine instead.

Cradle is the closest thing I've ever played to true art.  The concept bethind the game is dense and immense, as well as complex and uplifting.  The exquisite graphics, novel art design, and truly soulful soundtrack all contribute to a masterclass assembly of arthouse video gaming.  The game is short, has limited replyability, lacking multiplayer or co-op.  Branching paths are non-existent.  The story is a parable of spiritual metaphysics and the impact of humanistic love hard-wiring our ability to manifest the destiny of our species and reality.  The game basically addresses concepts of parapsychological neurology, social empathy and quantum mechanics in a cohesive system that prognosticates a flexible, dynamic and hopeful future for humanity.  That about sums up all I can say about the game's plot without giving it away.
The game also challenges principles of empiricism in the determination of true, iconic beauty and requires careful investigation of surroundings to promote awareness.  Basically, don't play this game if you lack patience or don't want to be challenged intellectually.  Part of this game's charm is ruminating about the various conflicting concepts and attempting to generate a sensical synergy that is both reasonable and enjoyable.  The game, aside from an opaque plotline and limited content, also suffers from poor performance (due to their unigine choice), where the game often demonstrates lagged controls.  The game crashed to desktop for me.  The cube-based minigames can often grate on a player.  I also suffered a problem with my achievements not showing up.
However, as a whole, for 5-7 USD, Cradle is a thoughtful, beautiful and peaceful foray into what it means to be human and how our own humanity can impact reality in profound ways.
Recommended.

I have been a prince of persia fan for a long time and I've played every one of them, I would say it is one of my favorite game series of all time. I was one of the people who was disappointed with the  PoP game made in 2008, the cell shaded styled one . I enjoyed it for what it was but I felt it was a move in the wrong direction. I liked the beautiful art design but it really was just too easy.
As for this game, considering it was made in 2010 the graphics were very well done. The prince and his surroundings are very detailed and everywhere you look there has been a great attention to creating a beautiful world to enjoy. From the wisps of sand moving below a swinging trap, the great use of light peering through cracks or the fine details on clothing and armor. Everything looks great. Including the newly designed prince. PoP games have always had great graphics and this game continues that tradition.
As for the game play, I think it is great how the designers have added the control of elements, like water, into the great gameplay that we saw in the previous games. It really adds a welcome new twist to the action/puzzle solving style this game series has always done so well.
I see alot of people knocking the combat, well for me I love it. I like that I can charge my attacks, I like that I can kick enemies down and I really like the addition of finishing moves that are stylish and enjoyable to pull off. Quite simply this is the best combat engine ever use in a PoP game. As for it being easy, well I think it just makes you feel more powerful and I for one enjoy the fact that its not frustrating. It keeps the game moving along and that is something I prefer over games that have overly difficult combat (ex : Ninja Gaiden, Dark Souls) I think it was done purposely because the game was meant to be enjoyed by more than just hardcore gamers.
One thing that makes the combat seem easy is the addition of powers that you unlock with experience points. Like an RPG you can spend these points anyway you see fit to give you special abilities like stoneskin or allow you to knockdown all surrounding enemies with a wind based attack. Again I find these abilities a welcome addition to the game and I like the carrot being dangled knowing that I have more and more powerful ones to unlock as I progress through the game.
As for the sound I think this was well done, just like everything else in the game. From the voice acting to that music to the background sounds everything works well and never distracts for the experience. Which for me is what good sound design is.
I can't help but wonder what it is that gamers and reviewers who knock this game want from their games. This game is polished and fine tuned. It looks great and plays great. It has everything we loved about the past games while injecting some fresh new ideas into the mix. It gives you more of everything. More enemies, more abilities, more combat choice with finishers, new puzzles that use traps and timing as well as the new addition of elements like turning water solid. I think people look for the smallest imperfections when they should be enjoying what is so good in the game.
Sure the camera can occasionally be out of place, but what game like this has a perfect camera ? Actually I haven't experienced any real problem with it so far anyway. It has a snap behind button and rotation control, so whats the problem ?
Prince of Persia Forgotten Sands is an excellent game and in my opinion the best in the series. It has a great balance of action, combat and puzzle solving all set in a beautiful world and for me thats all I wanted and the team at ubisoft delivered in this latest PoP adventure.

Tengami is a gorgeous, 2.5D, point-and-click puzzle game set in a Japanese pop-up book. The most appealing aspect of this game is the art--unique and simplistically beautiful. The pop-up book allows for some interesting game mechanics. The poetry is a nice touch.
There's little variation in the sound effects, the music is kind of generic, and some puzzles are repeated, but I attribute these to the fact that it's a small game. The pace of the character's walking is a little too slow for a game that requires this much backtracking, but I suspect a faster walking pace would make Tengami even shorter than it already is. There are some awkward changes in the music where it would just stop abruptly and some minor clipping around the character's feet. This is kind of a personal problem, but the sailing made me motion-sick.
My biggest issue with Tengami is the lack of substance. It's aesthetically pleasing, but there's no real objective or storyline. However, if you're looking for a short and pretty game to entertain you for an hour, Tengami fits the bill.
Platforming had 2 abilities that made it interesting and at times tough; "The Final Climb" was awesome.  Otherwise just "ok."  Beware the Ubisoft UPlay PC client though - it WILL try to♥♥♥♥♥♥you.

Tengami is like a 3D pop-up book I never had, enhanced with serene music background & outstanding Japanese themed visuals. It really feels like a book - you can turn the pages, slide little pieces of "paper", flip the decorations to modify the scene, etc.
Gamewise it's an exploration/adventure with minor puzzle elements (although no puzzle is repeated, so it constantly feels fresh). There is quite a lot of walking (and backtracking if you wont figure out things right away), but due to its soothing soundtrack & beautiful art, I find Tengami to be contemplative in nature - meant to be played when one wants to slow down, tune out and relax. :)
Unfortunately it's very short. It took me a little under 90 mins to complete the game. Other than that, I enjoyed it. I may even replay it someday when I'm in a mood for this kind of experience :)

Visually, it takes the best of the preceding PoP games, some of the areas are truly magnificent and fun to explore. Platforming is largely the same as the previous games, but with a few new moves such as freezing water to create walls or climbable pillars. Sometimes it gets rather complex to do wallruns, freeze, reverse time, etc. which presents a certain level of challenge.
Combat is much improved in this game, and is much less boring than in the previous games. Mostly because of the upgrades available after collecting experience points. It makes you happy to fight hordes of enemies, knowing you'll be able to get the next upgrade. Those include adding to your health and energy bars, as well as powerups that can be used against enemies. The story is kinda meh and the game is surprisingly short, but other than that it's very enjoyable. More PoP fare for fans of the series, with a few new well-executed features. 7/10

The ending was as unsatisfying as imaginable. We're left with absolutely nothing except a story that just stops, for no clear reason. I wanted to love this game, but I'm just aggravated by it. It's a classic case of wasted potential. And what's more irritating is the way it plays its conclusion, as if it's some shattering reveal, when in fact it's meaningless.
I'm so glad I never bought it when it was more expensive, and ended up getting it as a gift, but I'm still annoyed. Avoid if you want a good story, or even one that makes sense.

This is a direct copy-paste of my review for Baldur's Gate - Enhanced Edition, as it pretty much covers everything I have to say about the sequel as well:
Personal rating: 10/10
Replayability: High
Budget: If you already own the original, buy on sale only.
Lenght: ... It took me years to finally complete it. I'd wager an experienced player can get it done in a week or more. No less.
Baldur's Gate is hands-down one of the best games I've ever played. While initially, porting D&D into a tactical real-time gameplay setting should set off some alarm-bells, this game is one of the most tactical games I've ever played, requiring precison, patience and understanding.
It's also a roleplaying game that allows you to explore the, now venerable Forgotten Realms setting that I grew up with (Fantasy books ect.). It features a soundtrack and memorable characters that you will NEVER forget. You'll find yourself hearing things in real life, that almost makes you burst out a quote from this old gem, that no one will get.
The biggest problem with Baldur's Gate, is that it's ancient by now... Which is where the enhanced edition comes in!
Upgrading the game to HD and even upgrading the game engine and interface to the same standard as the sequel is exactly the kind of boost the game needed to become playable, even to people who didn't grow up with it.
Enhanced edition also features some new content. While I appreciated this, I'll be honest and say that I didn't quite feel that this new content entirely fit with the mood of the original game. It was a bit too... Humorous and... Cute. I mean, considering the rather dark underlining theme of the game and the story, it just didn't feel quite right, but this is to be expected as the update was done by a third party.
Baldur's Gate, to me, is the predecessor to all modern RPG's.

A possitive review, with qualifications and reservations.  First, know what you're getting into.  This is an EARLY ACCESS, OPEN WORLD, SURVIVAL GAME.  Yes, they are notoriously buggy.  No matter who makes them.  This one is no exception.  You are GOING to experience issues.  Don't go into this thinking you are going to be lucky and be the one guy who doesn't.
That said, the devs at Funcom are better than most at addressing these bugs in a timely fashion.  Even and especially when they have created new ones (or reawaken old ones) with the patches they put out.  ;)
The next possitive thing that I have to say is that this game is obviously going places.  They are putting out content at a blistering pace.  There has been completely new, meaningful, content added to the game, almost on a weekly basis.  Major fixes and adjustments DO come out once a week like clockwork, sometimes more often.
Next, the devs DO listen to the community and what we want.  They have already made several meaningful adjustments to the game based solely on community feedback.
Now, arguably the most important part of the review: You have to ask yourself, what kind of gamer are you?  Are you a PvPer who wants to play with lots of other people on a semi-massive scale on dedicated official servers?  If the answer is yes, then honestly, you should probably wait awhile on your purchase of this game as they have had the most prevalent problems in exactly that area.
But, if you are one of the following: PvPer wanting to play on private dedicated servers or a PvEer wanting to play on private dedicated servers, co-op, or alone, then this is deffinately a game to jump in on ASAP.
One final word of warning, if you plan to play co-op, it is "tethered".  Meaning, you can only go so far away from the host.  But, as long as you work well as a team with whoever you are co-oping with, this really isn't an issue.
Hope this review helps you decide to give Conan Exiles a try, its worth it now, and is certain to deffinately be worth it later.

Dragon Nest is like your classic RPG. You do quests and level up, yada yada ya. However, unlike games such as Mabinogi or WoW, the combat system embraces fluidity of skills. It's not turn-based and moves can be used whenever they're available during dungeons. The skill point system can be tailored to one's playstyle. It's quite enjoyable to play with friends, but playing in public parties is tolerable. The currency is easily gained and lost through progression and you don't need to spend money to access moves or slots for moves *cough* Spiral Knights *cough*. The NX cash shop, or the Dragon Vault, presents a variety of items such as costumes, which you don't really need to succeed, or functional consumables which the game gives you for free. The game's content is ever-expanding in the storyline and a lot of effort is put into it (even if most of you probably click as fast as you can through quests without reading).
There aren't a multitude of downsides that can't be solved by the player themselves, but first and foremost: Dragon Nest is licensed (?) through Nexon. Their customer support is horrid. The couple of weeks before December had a lot of problems with connection, disconnection, and overall lag. However, the compensation for issues is usually worth it. Another problem is that single-player play can get monotonous because like many RPGs, the game is grindy, but that can either be remedied by playing in a party or y'know, taking a break. The community is riddled with individuals of almost all ages, ranging from the stereotypical whiny, slightly-illiterate "twelve-year old", to people who are married and have kids. One last drawback is that to run certain dungeons (nests), public parties usually require players to already be geared upon joining, however many guilds and other players are nice enough to help individuals who are new to levels and the game overall.

Zombie Vikings is a mix of Castle Crashers with the graphics style from Stick it to the Man (Ray is even a DLC character here).
There's not much to say. You have 4 characters (+ 3 DLC and 1 unlockable, which makes 8 in total) with which you hack and bash yourself through about 30 levels in total. These mainly consist of fighting, fighting and more fighting...and the occasional boss. Your characters have different attacks, charged attacks, aerial moves, special attacks (that can also be charged), etc. Every character is unique but follows the same principle. Choose whichever one you like best. The meat of the game is arguably in its multiplayer component...and 4 people can play locally on 1 screen...yaaaay for party games!
Just focussing on the story mode, which is quite funny and well written actually, and you'll be through in about 7 hours give or take. After each level (and each completed side quest) you will unlock new weapons and runes to use. Each character has access to some unique runes that enhance his gameplay and every weapon has different effects, some have life steal, some stun enemies while dashing through them, others shock them, others heal your friends while carrying them. Stuff like that. Unfortunately you still have to buy the weapons and runes with the ingame money you collect in the levels. One playthrough is definitely not enough to unlock everything...if you really want that.
DLC characters can be skipped imho, but when the game is on sale or when you have 1 to 3 friends to play with it's definitely worth the low price of admission. It has more content than some AAA games if I'm honest...

Jet Set Radio is an extremely interesting game that has recieved much attention over the years. It is a rather fun game, but at the same time the game suffers on many different levels.
The gameplay of Jet Set Radio is rather interesting. You play as part of a group of Punks that decide to graffiti areas of the town you are in. You do this by rollerblading across maps of varying length, depending on the stage and how late in the game you are.  Its a rather refreshing game, because it isn't seen too much in games. However, the game is mainly split into two different parts as a result of the two extremely different styles of gameplay. The graffiti painting is extremely shallow as a mechanic, because you just move the joystick in a certain direction as a quicktime event. However, the directions you move the joystick in is the same for every single piece of graffiti you paint. It becomes quite tiring because halfway through the game you will probably have the patterns down by muscle memory, and it becomes rather a pain to have to move the joystick in the same directions every time. The game would have benefitted from having you move the stick inn a different direction, or having different patterns. Otherwise the graffiti spraying just becomes you moving the stick as fast as you can while still being slow enough for the game to register you starting the pattern. However, the patterns you follow change depending on the character you pick, so you can choose a different character
In terms of the rollerblading, it requires you to be good at the game if you want to get far.  Whenever you start moving, you start out at a very slow pace. To be able to get to a decent speed (to where you can actually grind on rails), you neet to press a button. However, there is absolutely no reason to not be pressing this button every single time you are on the ground. It would have been much better if they had made you speed up by default when you are on the ground.
There are two main types of "special moves" you have in terms of rollerblading. Other than just moving and jumping you are able to grind on rails and jump off of walls. Jumping off of the walls actually is much easier than it seems at first, and poses no real challenge. However, the wall jumping is extremely situational, because there are not many gaps that actually require you to wall jump, and there are very few places where wall jumping can be beneficial, or even possible. Most of the time is is either to go through a small shortcut or to get to optional spaces to spray paint.
Grinding on rails on the other hand is an entirely different story. You NEED to learn how to grind on the rails if you want to be able to have a reasonable speed, or to get away from enemies. Not being able to land on the rails is disasterous. Without mastering rail grinding, entire sections of the maps are locked from you. Without grinding, the game is completely unbeatable. However, it can be quite finicky to get on a rail. You need to be absolutely set on where you are going to be before you start your jump, because you get very little control of your character while in the air. As such, you need to be able to determine where you will be as you are jumping. You also don't cling to rails, so you have to be completely precise.
The stages are usually pretty easy in the beginning, but halfway throughout the game the difficulty really goes up. After tagging different gangs' graffiti you have to tag the gang members as they run away from you. However, you have to be extremely close to them, and then spam the graffiti button. This is extremely tedious, because they follow the same path and loop around the map, and are just barely slower than you. Not only that, but the areas you have to go through can be extremely tight areas, preventing you from really gaining on them, because you need perfect inputs to keep your speed. These can be extremely tiresome, because there are three gang members for each of these stages, and you have to complete them. However then you have to face against certain enemies while trying to tag graffiti on the walls in other stages. In the earlier stages these enemies can be easy to avoid/get rid of because they are just people on foot, or they are helicopters you can take out by tagging. However, later on you face other enemies that have extremely long range attacks, or high manuverability. In one stage, the enemy has jetpacks, so you are not able to lose them. It also doesn't help that you have no way to fight back, other than tagging helicopters as mentioned earlier. All you can do is run.
The game is also extremely short, only taking me 5 hours to beat. However, I left the game idle for an hour in there, and I've played the game twice before, so about 4 hours. For someone's first time, 5-6 hours would be expected. There isn' much reason to replay the game afterwards, because it's just the same missions in the story mode again.
Luckily, you have many characters to choose from in the game, many of them having unique stats. These stats are Power, Technique, and Graffiti. These control your health, the speed and points you get from grinding, and the difficulty and points gained from tagging, respecitively. Therefore, power is more of a difficulty rating. The higher it is, the easier the game is, and the lower score/rank you get. However, one stat that should exist is the number of paint cans a character can carry, because each character has their own limit. However, this stat is never shown, and you pretty much have to look up how much each character can carry.
The music is pretty good, not only for some of the tracks (though there are a couple duds) but for the way the music switches between tracks. Instead of fading to nothing as a track ends and going to another one, they transition into each other natually as if there is a DJ changing the tracks. It took me a while to notice this, because I thought that the music was instead just a few really long tracks. It's quite impressive, because it doesn't take you out of the game, and fits with the style of the game.
The graphics, despite being from the early 2000's, are still presentable today because of the more stylized approach take by the designers. The cell-shaded graphics are still pleasing to see today, however, some of the textures (especially facial ones) could have been cleaned up. Either way, the game has definitely aged well graphically.
Overall, the game, while having its drawbacks, doesn't cease to be a fun experience as long as you are good at the game. If you figure out the mechanics, and can learn to hop from rail to rail easily, the game can be an absolute blast. Otherwise, the game can become quite a slog, as you slowly make your way to the tag locations. The game doesn't offer too much in terms of replay value, but is fun to pop in now and again. However, if you have an original Xbox, I would much rather reccomend Jet Set Radio Future, which made the gameplay less clunky overall. However, this game is still fun, and with various features like all of the characters and the customizable graffiti art, you can have tons of fun with it.

What made me interested in Submerged was first and foremost its awesome setting, which definitely didn't disappoint. You play in a surprisingly large city with lots of tall buildings and structures but has been submerged seemingly a very long time ago, so only the top parts of the buildings are visible. They're also dilapidated, missing chunks and covered in moss, ivy, bushes and trees. It looks like nature claimed it back through both water and vegetation. Your main mode of transport is by boat because the majority of the city's surface is water, but some buildings can be climbed on by ledges, pipes or thick patches of ivy and walked on top of. There is a dynamic day and night cycle and a lot of (mostly aquatic) wildlife in the city. At night, you and big animals leave trails of blue biolumescence in the water.
In many ways this game reminded me of Journey and ABZÛ, although not as brilliant, because it doesn't have traditional storytelling nor combat, is a short relaxing and exploration-heavy game, has a fantastic setting and looks beautiful. This is a more open-world experience as you can go anywhere from the very start and nothing gets locked off as you progress. There is no stress in this game: you can't die because there's no combat and you can't fall off of anything you're climbing.
I won't detail the plot to avoid spoilers. While it is conveyed rather minimalist in the form of cutscenes without dialogue and some background plot about the game's two characters and the city itself, it was interesting enough to make me want to find out how it continues and ends. There are some mysterious things lurking in the city, but that's all I'll say.
The game is very repetitive in nature, which seems to be the main complaint about this game, followed by its length. The main story is a lot of boating around, climbing buildings to get supplies and seeing very similar cutscenes ten times over, and looking for collectibles and upgrades is a lot more of the same boating and climbing. I personally didn't mind it a whole lot as I just loved the experience and the exploring of this world, though much more variety in the gameplay would have put this game on a higher level.
All in all, I'd say it's worth playing just to experience the setting and enjoy the scenery, but I feel like it definitely wouldn't offer enough for most people to justify its full price tag. However, at the moment it's got a whopping 90% discount, which isn't even the first time that's happened, and at that price it's just a steal.

The last chapter of the STALKER Trilogy, Call of Pripyat is a distillation of the franchise, taking the good from previous iterations and leaving out much of the bad. The quest-based story is more streamlined (and best of all, functional) than ever before and a revamped upgrade system for the weaponry ensures that you always have something to buy with your meager cash. Best of all, it exemplifies the strange events and landscape that made the first game stand head and shoulders above other first-person shooters. There are simply no words to describe the otherworldly beauty of the Zone and my best moments in this game were not blasting mutants, but drinking in a peaceful sunrise or watching the flashlight beams of a team of stalkers as they make their way through a forest at night.

This is a perfectly designed game, but a terribly programmed one. The level designs are clever and interesting, with what should be a steady difficulty curve, but movement--particularly jumping--feels drunken and ungainly.
* The forward momentum of a typical jump is about equivalent to Shovel Knight's forward momentum when he's jumping in the direction of a strong wind
*Hitboxes extend out so far, you can die by jumping straight up when there are spikes on a platform to the side of you.
*The wall jump tends to be more of a wall headbutt, followed by an immediate fall onto spikes.
Every level plays like the aerial equivalent of an ice level, and that's simply unworkable for what's clearly supposed to be a twitch platformer requiring precise control.
On the rare occasions this game works, it works beautifully. I don't think I've ever seen a game cry out this hard for a tool-assisted speedrun. But if you simply want a fun, challenging platformer, play . . . well, any of the games it rips off besides Limbo.

This game is very simple, which in a lot of games would work for it but in this case works against it.
Gameplay/ Mechanics
I'll reveal the gameplay without revealing any of the plot: You have a boat in a submerged city, you have to explore the city and find the locations of crates you need on top of towers. You park your boat, climb the tower, get the stuff, repeat. And by repeat, I mean REPEAT. You have to do that about 9 times to complete the game, and there's almost no variety. The climbing mechanic isn't very fun either. It feels very wooden. You can see every path that you can take easily (though it may not always be the right one) and there's no real thinking/ problem solving involved.
As far as the boat goes, it really isn't very fun to pilot. It has two speeds: fast, and boost. The only upgrades you can get for it (that I saw) were to increase the time of your boost. If you hit something, you bounce off like a ping pong ball.
Visuals
For an indie game the visuals are impressive. It's got a good mix of climb-able structures both tall, wide, ruined, overgrown, etc. and some landmarks scattered throughout the city. The city feels small at times, but the buildings make it feel like it used to be a real, thriving city. As far as the creatures go, they pretty much just took real animals and reskinned them to fit a toxic world, except for one (which I won't mention because it's the biggest 'oh no' moment of the game).
Audio
The soundtrack is nice, a piano and violin playing somewhat discordant but beautiful music. It's not always on, usually only during cutscenes, and it lends an ominous feeling to the game as a whole.
Story
Very subpar. I completed the story in 2 hours and SPOILER:
It's very flat and (as much as I hate to say it) uninspired. In the first few minutes of the game you find out
which is what drives you to do what you do. The only thing is,
So you go do that, but
At the end,
That last cutscene takes about a minute and it's a chore to get to it, and it's deeply unsatisfying.
Wrapping it up
The story isn't compelling enough to put up with the gameplay. It's a decently fun visual experience through a word that we don't see a lot of in media, and for the 2 dollar sale price it might be worth it if you're REALLY into exploring and simple platforming. But I can't recommend this game for anything close to its 20 dollar price tag. MAYBE if you have nothing else in your backlog, pick it up on sale.

Other than that, very interesting sci-fi concepts and ideas, a strange but really intriguing story and the art-style, I have to mention it again, as it was just amazing.

Okay, so what has to be said first is that this software is early access. There is limitations to what you can do with it at the moment. If you are willing to work with these limitations and are not expecting to make a full, working game just yet, this is a dream come true. Also, expect that making a game - even a small one - is a LOT of work. I've only scratched the surface with the couple of hours I've put into it so far.
But I can see the promise in this. The models and graphics etc. that come with the software are very decent. Some of them are absolutely beautiful, all of them are usable. Map-building is fun, challenging and easy enough to learn. Possibilities are endless.
The one big downside for me at the moment is the lack of good tutorials. There are some, but not nearly enough. Learning the software requires a lot of trial and error, experimentation and a bit of luck. So far I've not faced anything that I couldn't figure out if I tried enough, but this requires some patience. If you aren't willing to learn "the hard way" maybe you need to wait a bit for tutorials to emerge before you decide whether to buy MyRPG or not.
All in all, I do recommend this software and I'm very very excited about it! Can't wait to see how it develops and what will come of my own projects.

I can't reccomend this game. It has some going for it and it's ok for a Philip K♥♥♥♥♥♥type short story.
