I started playing this earlier today, and couldn't put it down until I beat it, an experience I haven't had since Limbo. (The similarities between the games are very, very slight, however--essentially limited to 'generally dark shadowy art style.') Where the game shines is in the controls: playing as the cat feels just as graceful as you might hope. Simply jumping around is fun--the same sort of feeling you'd expect only from a super mario game, where the fluidity of the jumping mechanics makes idling around the mushroom kingdom/delfino plaza highly satisfying. The cat's levels feel less like VVVVV and Super Meat Boy and more like The Impossible Game, if it were granted free motion and a graceful high-flying update. The little girl's levels--though outnumbered probably 5:1--are not as strong; she controls more awkwardly, and her broad figure makes it easier to accidentally hit spikes, blades, etc. But her levels, like I said, are infrequent; they act as a sort of breather from the main, catty game, and are not nearly as difficult as the cat's, so they're mostly unobtrusive--just somewhat unnecessary. Its other downfall is its slight story and beautiful but tragically brief and basic cutscenes. But these elements are really just a frame for the excellent precision platforming.

Great game with intricate strategy. Provides hundreds of hours of replayability and an infinite array of possibilities of gameplay, with an incredible freedom that is characteristic of Paradox games. It is of course not perfect historical-wise but it is really deep when it comes to that aspect with tons of historical events. There are also great mods and some really nice dlcs to add to that content, although the game is pretty complete by its own. For starters in this genre of strategy games or  in Paradox games in general, Crusader Kings 2 should prove the best choice. It is not so difficult to get into and has the hole high degree of personalization of the strategy with all the rpg aspects of the game that makes some players praise it as the best game of Paradox. It is in reality a very different game from the other Paradox games such as Europa Universalis or Victoria that provides an unique kind of fun as you control the rulers instead of the nations. I personally think that despite some flaws it encompasses very well the time spam of the Middle Ages and couldn´t recommend more for any player of strategy that is fond of that period of history and of the presence of rpg elements in games in general. Finally, don´t bother with the original Crusader Kings as this one is far superior - something that is not very common nowadays with all the awful sequels we are seeing.

I was initially intrigued by Cradle due to its art direction - an aesthetic mixing mongolian folk patterns and matrials with elements of cyberpunk - all wrapped in beautiful palettes and sharp textures, somewhat reminescent of 2008 Prince of Persia.
Unfortunately, while beautiful, the game world is extremely empty, with only two locations of note and a third "temporary" one appearing every now and then.
The gameplay does not help the matter - it is incredibly repetetive, bouncing the player between the starting location "A" where quests are given through lenghty exposition and location "B" where you'll end up playing the same tideous mini-game over and over in a series of quests that feel very copy-pasted.
The story is not very well developed, either - feeling like a work of rather inexperienced writer - attempting to create drama and suspense, but succeeding only at drowning the player in cheesy terminology and lore that feels, honestly, very immature.
Many of the challenges are quite obfuscated and somewhere half-way I decided to grab a walkthrough, completing the latter half of the game on auto-pilot. I was hoping the plot will redeem itself, but unfortunately I feel like I should have spent my time another way.
On the postive - the two locations that do exist, look gorgeous (especially the starting one) and the tramway is pretty cool too.

Ok, let me get this out of the way:
People cry about "Microtransactions" in the game, but you are never forced to buy anything nor will speanding money will give you an advantage buy-able items are PURELY cosmetic, i havent spent a dime on cosmetics and i still enjoy this game a lot
Now about the game let me begin in the major points of the game
Pros:
No hand-holding mechanics: Your camera wont be locked to always aim the enemy or pushing buttons in a certain order to do a combo, you MAKE the combo with the main 4 or 6 different attacks all weapons have
Skill matters: As ridiculous as this sound, it makes sense the way you´re looking will affect the time a swing will land, most people confuse this with broken mechanics, both effectively using this method and blocking requires different degrees of practice you can totally tell the difference when fighting a new player against a skilled player, it´ll be a one-way massacre wich leads me to my next point
Balance: You might think that in a game where enough skill can turn a fight into a one-side massacre will be unbalanced but devs do some classic things about this, they make new player-only servers to prevent this they might be full as of now because of the 90% off means a large influx of neophytes but it does help a lot, be aware tho it wont fully prepare you against real pros if you want to fight those it´ll take a fair bit of time but will reward in the satisfaction of beheading that golden-hatted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that used to kill you 0 - 10
Cons:
Performance: While the game should run well in all systems, its not very optimized and framedrops can turn that amazing
1v4 ez win into losing your head to a 2 meter sword before even noticing, expect some crashes here and there but never too annoying
Balance could use some tweaks: The vast majority of weapons are balanced to work very nice with damage/range/speed expect for 1 weapon: THE ♥♥♥♥1NG DAGGER! so far if a fairly-skilled person with it can counter most weapons on a high-level skill person, and personally i struggle an awful lot against this weapon
The game is unique in the genre and overall really good in the industry, combat slown down to facilitate the reading of swings and relying more on skill rather than real-life accuary but its still very accurate historically speaking, i would totally recomend this game and give it a nice 9/10 easily the best FPS meele combat game

This game, along with its companion, Euro Truck Simulator 2, is truly sublime. One of the best games I have ever played, ATS may lack action, and violence, and role-play, but it has something appealing to it that I just love.
First of all, the development company, SCS, is just amazing. Though a few DLCs and events are a little unnecessary, they listen to community advice, continue to work on the games, and continuously work to improve the games.
To address most negative feedback, I will start with the content. The map is not very big, only including three states. This is because SCS Does not have many employees working for them, and because it takes loads of time and money to recreate the terrain with detail. More states are going to be added as paid DLC, but the progress is extremely slow, and at this rate we probably will never get all of the US. The low amount of trucks is due to licensing, meaning that to legally use real brands in the game, SCS has to pay money to them. Which again, they say is happening, but there has not been any progress with new trucks for this game, even from the two manufacturers it has.
Now, to start with the pros. In the base game, you get four outstandingly detailed trucks, many trailers and cargoes, a competent AI system, and amazing graphics. The quality and attention to detail is amazing, and the sunsets are truly unreal. The game is also very relaxing, and is great to calm down after a bad day, or stressful experience.
In short, the pros are:
. Competent AI system, including suspension physics in the AI
. A large range of immersion-enhancing features, such as sleeping at rest stops, and going to weigh stations
. Sublime graphics
. Realistic yet forgiving physics system, I can't give a full opinion because I use an Xbox controller
. Realistic cargoes and cargo destinations
. Environment feels lived in, with pedestrians and lights and sounds
. Cities are amazingly detailed
. Trucks are amazingly detailed
Now for the downsides. The biggest one is how the next 46 states (assuming we don't get Hawaii) will be introduced through paid DLC. This means we will have to pay to play them. Although I disagree with this business move, all we can hope for is that the prices are low. The framerate of this game is also slightly lower than that of its companion.
Overall, the cons are:
. New states will be paid
. Slight performance issues on lower end systems
. Seems to have stability issues, I have experienced crashes
. AI can be strange
. Menu music, though good, seems a little stereotypical
In conclusion, I highly suggest for anyone to get this game, and hope this review has helped you to make a decision :)
Please note, although third party modifications, or mods, are available, the developers are in no way responsible for them or any problems they cause.

Tengami is an interesting, beautiful art project and a good showcase of visual design. But it can hardly be called a video game.
Tengami is an experimental art showcase where the game designers tried to imitate pop-up books in the style of classical Japanese origami. They created a unique, interesting experience.
An experience, but not a game. There is no story. There are no characters. It offers nothing but long walks and a set of puzzles of the same principle: rotate elements of the scenery until you find the correct combination.
Buying Tengami is like paying a group of artists for an hour-long showcase of their art. But if you wanted a puzzle game with its own individual graphic style… then navigate away from this store page.

There are puzzles and there are places to explore, but everything that is done in the game is part of that whole experience.
It took me a little over an hour to beat the entire game and see all it had to offer, so if you base value on time spent I couldn't say that this game should be picked up for full price ($9.99 now). I purchased it as part of a Humble Bundle and am extremely pleased with it, definitely a game I would suggest getting during a sale. The visuals are beautiful and run smoothly, the music is gorgeous, and while the story is minimal it leaves you feeling satisfied at the end. I would rather have a game that leaves me wishing I could have played more of it than dragging me on as it tries to stretch for time.
It isn't perfect, but for what it is Tengami is as close to perfection as you can get for an interactive narrative. You'll get some wonderful 'oh, so THAT'S how that works!' moments and while the puzzles are minimal they leave you feeling as if you achieved something. I do wish that there had been more tabs to pull, pieces to slide, etc... that were just there for environment's sake, this isn't a game you want to poke around and explore in, follow the path you're guided down for the best experience. I also wish that the character had a run animation although I am torn on that. Part of the game is the relaxing pace, but sometimes you do have to wander a bit to get from point A to point B and while it never left me frustrated it would have been nice if our character could have put on a light jog sometimes.
TL;DR Grab it on sale or in a bundle, a short but beautiful experience that will leave you smiling.

A Walk in the Dark is an artfully done little 2D precision platformer. It's good for a few hours of entertainment, and is recommended for its art style, including music, and enjoyable gameplay. On the downside it's too short and doesn't offer enough challenge to play for very long.
You usually control a black cat, named Bast, and less often the cat's owner, a little girl named Arielle, through 100 short but fairly tricky levels. There is no story to speak of - it appears that the cat and girl are separated and are trying to get back to each other, which is all the motive they really need. Your goals are to (1) not die as you make your way to the end of each level, (2) optionally complete the levels within a "par" time, collect a difficult-to-reach "shiney" in each level, and beat a few auto-scrolling levels without dying on your first attempt.
Without a plot, you might entertain yourself by identifying all the gaming elements that AWITD has borrowed (ahem, stolen) from other games. This is true both of its art direction and gameplay, although the game adds just enough of its own personality to make it feel like more than a knock-off.
Starting with the game art, the most obvious influence is Limbo, as the characters and landscape slide by in silhouette. But where Limbo was dark and violent, this game always stays light and fairy-taley, with your character's many deaths rendered with a rather artful puff of black smoke. The backgrounds come from any number of recent indie platformers, with bright contrasts and light blooms and generic "world" colorings. The game's music - tinkly piano - is unusually good, although after awhile the repeating themes start to wear thin.
If you've played Super Meat Boy, you'll instantly understand how most of the cat levels work: precise jumping, up to and including sticky wall sliding and avoiding spikes and spinning blades. If you've played any of the million games that incorporate an inversion mechanic, you'll recognize the girl's (only) trick, a gravity flip. If you played VVVVVV, you'll recognize similar tricky flipping challenges in later cat levels. If you played Bit.Trip Runner, you'll recognize the auto-scrolling levels. Unfortunately the game is too easy and too short to really stand up to any of these others - only the later levels were really interesting or challenging, and the game could have been more satisfying if it had more thoroughly explored its own interesting mechanics.
Overall this is an enjoyable, but light, little game.

I'm personally a big fan of tower defense style games, my absolute favorite beig Orcs Must Die! 2. Bardbarian, however, is a very close second.
With Bardbarian, you don't actually do any attack yourself, or set up towers that attack lanes of enemies. Instead, you move freely about the battlefield, commanding your troops who you bring in with "Sick Lute Licks," which in turn attack the enemies who come in from the right side of the screen. With a variety of attackers (Some long range, some short), a variety of enemy types, and a slew of upgrades to make your life easier, it's a fun game to play...if only for a few hours.
The main issue I personally have with the game is that there is litle longevity to it. Once you learn the enemy types and ugrade everythin to max, you could probably beat the game within 6-8 hours, even less if your quick about upgrading your stuff. Even the addition of an insane mde, which barely amps up the difficulty itself, isn't enough to satisfy me for very long. The game does however, have three main games modes.
The campaign is split up in to four sections with five levels each. At the end of each level is a boss. Beat the waves, beat the boss, move on. Simple enough. The other two modes aren't so standard. Survival has you in an enclosed area with enemies coming from all angles. Instead of summoning your troops like you do in hte campaign, you find them on the field. This is nice because the notes you generate to normally summon units can be diverted solely on powerups for them. It stinks because they don't spawn into the gamtoo quickly, and you are often times left defenseless, seeing as you are unable to attack on your own. The final mode is Escape, and its basically a run right as long as you can while a wall of death follows you. You collect gold along the way and avoid enemies, making it a good mode to make some quick gold if you need to.
All in all, the first few hours of the game were just plain fun for me. Unlocking new allies was always nice, and upgrading them, the town and myself added that extra touch. The other games modes were a lot of fun too. But as I stated befor,e once you get into the 6 hour mark, and have upgraded almost everything...it get sold fast. If the game has any future updates, I'm unaware, so as of right now, it's a good experience, but for a limited time.
If you want a game to kill a few hours with, I highly recommend it. If you want something that will keep you entertained for a long time...this will help ease the pain of waiting for Fallout 4 to download...

Ok, let me get this out of the way:
People cry about "Microtransactions" in the game, but you are never forced to buy anything nor will speanding money will give you an advantage buy-able items are PURELY cosmetic, i havent spent a dime on cosmetics and i still enjoy this game a lot
Now about the game let me begin in the major points of the game
Pros:
No hand-holding mechanics: Your camera wont be locked to always aim the enemy or pushing buttons in a certain order to do a combo, you MAKE the combo with the main 4 or 6 different attacks all weapons have
Skill matters: As ridiculous as this sound, it makes sense the way you´re looking will affect the time a swing will land, most people confuse this with broken mechanics, both effectively using this method and blocking requires different degrees of practice you can totally tell the difference when fighting a new player against a skilled player, it´ll be a one-way massacre wich leads me to my next point
Balance: You might think that in a game where enough skill can turn a fight into a one-side massacre will be unbalanced but devs do some classic things about this, they make new player-only servers to prevent this they might be full as of now because of the 90% off means a large influx of neophytes but it does help a lot, be aware tho it wont fully prepare you against real pros if you want to fight those it´ll take a fair bit of time but will reward in the satisfaction of beheading that golden-hatted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that used to kill you 0 - 10
Cons:
Performance: While the game should run well in all systems, its not very optimized and framedrops can turn that amazing
1v4 ez win into losing your head to a 2 meter sword before even noticing, expect some crashes here and there but never too annoying
Balance could use some tweaks: The vast majority of weapons are balanced to work very nice with damage/range/speed expect for 1 weapon: THE ♥♥♥♥1NG DAGGER! so far if a fairly-skilled person with it can counter most weapons on a high-level skill person, and personally i struggle an awful lot against this weapon
The game is unique in the genre and overall really good in the industry, combat slown down to facilitate the reading of swings and relying more on skill rather than real-life accuary but its still very accurate historically speaking, i would totally recomend this game and give it a nice 9/10 easily the best FPS meele combat game

I came in playing this under the impression of getting a variant of Evil Within; a kind of "Saw" meets a Walking-Simulator. On first look you do get that, but...oh SO MUCH MORE. That I didn't ask for.
This game is a complete clustermess of things, ideas, themes, gameplay-variants - and they don't fit together at all. First off, the whole story and its bait/switch twists and fragmented turns felt like total self-indulgence. It has themes of sabotage, parenthood, violence, betrayal - but they are superficial and don't really get together to make a point.
As jiggsawed as the story is, the gameplay follows - we begin with a puzzly-like game, but in the end the whole game has like 5 puzzles. The complete theme of the walking-simulator in the horror-asylum is abandoned as a one-trick pony. Then we get swamped with too many action scenes. The game offers an action approach and a stealth approach, and both fail miserable - the shooting is bad, that strange CornerGun is the most awkward idea of it all. The stealth doesn't really work either, as enemy placement is pretty much enforcing combat gameplay, and it's not really clear how/when enemys spot you. Also, they shoot you from like 50 meters away straight in the face.
You can see that this game is full of indie ambition, and certain key elements would be nice. But it tries too hard at being all artsy and diverse, that it forgets to make any point at all.
I really needed to get this off my chest, because those 9 hours really made me angry at the wasted opportunity, and the whole "female betrayal" subplot I find actually offending and sexist.

This is a game that raises far more questions than it answers, both in terms of its story as well as its design. Why is the map so vast yet all of the play area relatively constricted? Why does the ending come long before you understand what's happening? Why does the game tantalize you with the suggestion of a vast, intricate world, but never show it to you? Why are the block minigames so awful? The only explanation is that this was a game made on a budget, and that the creators cut all the corners they could to produce a barely viable product.
Ultimately, Cradle is a game of wasted potential. I recommend it only to novelty seekers because it had vision, not because it is a good game. Everyone else will lose nothing by passing it up.

The Baldur's Gate series is without question the apex of Bioware development and a masterpiece CRPG. I'm not going to comment on whether or not the series is good or bad since it goes without saying that any rpg fan needs to at least give it a spin. What's important and what I struggled with since the enhanced editions launched was whether or not these new editions were worth it, or whether or not I should just dust off my CD copies from the days of yore.
It's true that there isn't anything in the enhanced editions that can't already be done with mods. The last time I tried installing the CD versions and modding it all up was a tedious experience though. It's also true that the added content is forgettable; the Black Pits is something that I'll never touch and the new NPCs range from tolerable (Neera, for example) to poor (Hexxat, for example).
But I couldn't care less about the above. For me it boiled down to two things: One, was this version easier to set up and two, was this version buggier than the originals. The enhanced editions are no doubt easier to jump into on a modern computer due to many of the enhancements mirroring typical mods that you'd want to install (porting BG1 to the ToB engine, for example). Many of the community's mods have been updated for the Enhanced editions as well, so you can still cry in a fetal position as Swords Coast Stratagems mages rip you to shreds if that's your thing.
Now, bugginess is obviously dependent on many variables and I can only experience my own playthrough of the series, but apart from one crash to desktop in the opening dungeon of BG2 my playthrough from BG1 to ToB was smooth and clean. The official forums would make you think that the game is a bug ridden mess and it kept me away from purchasing for months, but I do not regret purchasing it in its current state. I won't be touching my CD copy of the series again.

The Good:
-The best combat system of any RPG I've ever played. The system involves having an abundance of awesome skills at your disposal and several fighting game mechanics. The system is perfect for creating a ton of different combos that flow together very nicely.
-Leveling up is always rewarding. Not only will you see very noticable differences in your performance with new gear, new skills are unlocked frequently.
-While the class selection may appear small at first, each class branches out into 2 paths twice. So with the current 6 classes available, that's really like having 24 classes.
-Each class feels unique. This includes the classes that are made from branching out. Lunar Knights and Gladiators may both be Swordsmen, but the only similarity between the two will be a couple of basic skills and their character model.
-PVP has a great amount of variety. You can join a 1 on 1 lobby to fully experience the fighting game mechanics, you can participate in hectic 16-player team deathmatches, free-for-alls, and "kill the other team's leader" matches, or you can play the ghouls mode, which is a standard zombie mode that functions well as a completely level-free form of PVP.
-Higher-level PVE and PVP demand a high amount of skill from players.
-Leveling up is mostly painless. There will be patches of grinding you'll do here and there, but the grinding in this game is much less repetitive than in other RPGs.
-Every skill you are given has a purpose. There are very few skills that become obsolete.
-Tons of stat builds to choose from.
-The voice-acting is full of personality when it's there. Voice-acting is most prevalent during combat, with many skills making the character using them say something. Important NPCs also have voice-acted greeting and farewell lines.
-The main story is solid and easy to follow, even if you're like me and skip through most of the dialogue. It will also provide cinematics to spice things up from time-to-time.
-If you put in the time to read it, the dialogue for main and side quests is well-written and genuinely funny.
-Locations are very diverse and well-designed.
-A unique art direction that combines cute with badass perfectly.
-It's easy to find parties at peak player activity times.
-Tons of seasonal and update events with useful rewards.
-A solid guild system with features such as custom guild emblems, guild storage, and guild buffs.
The Bad:
-The format of the world. While it's perfectly functional, it's a huge shame that this game isn't an open world. The only time you'll ever feel like you're in a populated world is when you're in a main town. As soon as you leave one, the only players you'll have any physical contact with is whoever is in your party, which only includes up to 3 other players at a time. There will be a few NPCs out in the non-main town areas, but they don't help the feeling of loneliness very much.
-All PVE gameplay is instance-based, and the instances, while being highly detailed and just right in length, are usually a linear path. Sometimes quests will give you additional objectives besides getting to the end of an instance, but that only happens rarely.
-Minimal character customization to start out with.
-You'll have to ask around for info on the game's deeper mechanics such as paralyze, super armor, and knockdown.
-Skills are not always described nearly well enough. Skill descriptions never provide information like how many invincibility frames a skill has, how strong it's ability to break super armor is, etc.
-Armor sets that you don't buy with real money only have one appearence per rarity. For example, a common and a rare set of armor will look different, but a level 20 set of rare armor will look exactly the same as a level 50 set of rare armor. This happens in a few cases with weapons too, but not usually. Curiously, headgear is a part of all gear sets, but will never be visible on characters unless it's one of the epic-rarity headgears (which do actually have differing appearances compared to other epic headgears).
-Server instability can be an issue at times.
-The things that cost real money are terribly over-priced. A full set of cool-looking armor that gives some extra stat bonuses costs about $20, though you can reduce the price a bit if you're willing to "rent" the armor for a limited time instead. Having played Nexon games that use this format of over-priced microtransactions since 2005, I have never bought a single thing from these shops and have enjoyed the games anyway. As a side note, you can earn NX (the currency used for these microtransactions) for free, but the means of doing this often involve a LOT of personal information sharing to a LOT of shady websites. If you try to use fake personal information, you'll end up like me and get permanently banned from the service.
(Overall, the cons aren't very significant, so just give this game a try)

Zombie Vikings:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Odin, the All-Fathers of Nordic Gods, is sitting down at his table and relentlessly polishing his staff as he wants to have the most sparkling staff in all Valhalla! After reaching his goal, Odin looks with his good eye at his amazing achievement, when suddenly Loki (The Wizard of lies) bursts through the front door and manages to steal Odin’s good eye! Absolutely furious, he summons 4 Zombie Vikings and sends them on the quest to retrieve his good eye.
Zombie Vikings is a co-op action brawler (up to 4 players) with really good, fun artwork and with an abundance of  humour.  You will take control of one of four zombies (each has their own power moves) and battle your way through 30 fun levels in different worlds.  Some levels will have side quests, make sure to look everywhere to find them. Your aim is to eliminate all enemies and collect as many gold coins as possible. You will find coins in chests but also in barrels. However, barrels could have brains in them, which is one way to regenerate your health.
With the gold coins, you will be able to purchase new weapons or runes. Some of them you will get by achieving a side quest and the others by finishing the levels. In some levels, you will be able to purchase a new weapon or rune (if you have the coins of course) at the shop which usually appears half way through that level. You will not miss it, 2 kids will be next to the shop and will try to get your attention.
You will jump, parry attack, execute special moves, slash your enemies and even stick object (bombs, barrels, foe and more) at the end of your weapon and throw them to other enemies - Great fun!
Great and funny cut-scenes that will keep you entertained all the way through this great story. The soundtrack is good and the controls are good and responsive (gamepad).
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great Story and cut-scenes
-	Wonderful artwork
-	Good Humour
-	Plenty of weapons to unlock
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can’t share gold on multiplayer
-	A bit repetitive
Zombie Vikings is a good, fun brawler with wonderful artwork. A good addition to your game library.

This game, along with its companion, Euro Truck Simulator 2, is truly sublime. One of the best games I have ever played, ATS may lack action, and violence, and role-play, but it has something appealing to it that I just love.
First of all, the development company, SCS, is just amazing. Though a few DLCs and events are a little unnecessary, they listen to community advice, continue to work on the games, and continuously work to improve the games.
To address most negative feedback, I will start with the content. The map is not very big, only including three states. This is because SCS Does not have many employees working for them, and because it takes loads of time and money to recreate the terrain with detail. More states are going to be added as paid DLC, but the progress is extremely slow, and at this rate we probably will never get all of the US. The low amount of trucks is due to licensing, meaning that to legally use real brands in the game, SCS has to pay money to them. Which again, they say is happening, but there has not been any progress with new trucks for this game, even from the two manufacturers it has.
Now, to start with the pros. In the base game, you get four outstandingly detailed trucks, many trailers and cargoes, a competent AI system, and amazing graphics. The quality and attention to detail is amazing, and the sunsets are truly unreal. The game is also very relaxing, and is great to calm down after a bad day, or stressful experience.
In short, the pros are:
. Competent AI system, including suspension physics in the AI
. A large range of immersion-enhancing features, such as sleeping at rest stops, and going to weigh stations
. Sublime graphics
. Realistic yet forgiving physics system, I can't give a full opinion because I use an Xbox controller
. Realistic cargoes and cargo destinations
. Environment feels lived in, with pedestrians and lights and sounds
. Cities are amazingly detailed
. Trucks are amazingly detailed
Now for the downsides. The biggest one is how the next 46 states (assuming we don't get Hawaii) will be introduced through paid DLC. This means we will have to pay to play them. Although I disagree with this business move, all we can hope for is that the prices are low. The framerate of this game is also slightly lower than that of its companion.
Overall, the cons are:
. New states will be paid
. Slight performance issues on lower end systems
. Seems to have stability issues, I have experienced crashes
. AI can be strange
. Menu music, though good, seems a little stereotypical
In conclusion, I highly suggest for anyone to get this game, and hope this review has helped you to make a decision :)
Please note, although third party modifications, or mods, are available, the developers are in no way responsible for them or any problems they cause.

I do recommend the game to some degree:
- Starts easy but becomes extremely challenging or frustrating (pick your side) later on
- Story is nearly nonexistent and only there to give you a reason to do what you do. A "damsel-in-distress" outline: Girl is kidnapped by evil thing, cat trying to rescue her. I think the introduction cinematic giving you this outline is basically identical to Super Meat Boy (and that in turn is probably imitating Super Mario Bros)
- The gameplay follows in the wake of Super Meat Boy and VVVVVV: Run through the levels as quickly as possible and evade obstacles by jumping, wallrunning and switching the direction of gravity (walk the ground and ceiling). It's mostly about having quick reactions and understanding when to jump and how far to move the cat in either direction.
- Art looked good at first, but it's becoming repetitive quickly. You see the same backgrounds over and over just with different color sets. The settings sometimes switch, but there are only like 4-5 and they switch back and forth. The music isn't too bad and may have a few recognizeable tunes, but I haven't come to notice more than 3 or 4 tracks that ripple around a bit meaningless (bad mouths may say it's dull, simply).
- Even if the story, art and music were better: You wouldn't come to appreciate it too much. The later stages in this game become so difficult your thoughts will mostly circle around coordinating your jumps and moves pixel by pixel, and hitting your keys to the nearest millisecond for there is almost no room for error later on.
If you are looking for story, art and music that keep you drawn to the end don't buy it. If you are looking for a platforming game that refuses to hold your hands and that punishes every mistake you make you'll enjoy and at times probably curse this, as seems normal with these kinds of games.
Keep up the good work!

One of the least favored Elder Scrolls games, is my favorite. The game itself just offers a gigantic adventure that lets you make your own character and just do whatever you want, maybe not to the extent of Morrowind, but still pretty open. The enviroments look colorful and vibrant, like looking at a painting. The side quests are some of the best quests  I have ever played in a WRPG before, there are just so many to play through and to complete, it took me forever to get most of this game done. Also want to say, being that I played this mostly on console and then moving to PC, it just felt more right on PC instead of console, so that also boosts what I believe is replay value and give it more "points". However, there are many faults that one just cannot look over. First off, the gameplay. The combat is quite floaty and it feels like slicing air at times, and it also can feel somewhat unresponsive at time, on the PC and console versions mind you. Next, the modeling for NPC's is absolutely horrendous. They look quite ugly, and it really can be a turn off for some people, but I was able to get over it just because I really love the game. Next, I PERSONALLY find the magic system to be a tad off. I can see that they were experimenting, and I would give them a passing grade for it, but it just does not feel right. I will say though that it does feel right for restoration spells, it works quite well for them. Another thing is that the dialogue options are black and white, like most RPG's in general. I suppose this is a general complaint for all RPG's, but it can be pretty cookie cutter in this game. Also, the leveling system is quite garbage as well, as the enemies level up with you, so it offers little to no challenge for the player, unless it is a first run and you have absoultely no idea what your doing. With all these faults, you might say I really hate the game, but, the goods in this game REALLY stand out and that's why I love this game. The questing and exploring is done really well in this game, disregarding popular belief. I will give this game a solid 7/10, no questions asked, well earned score. Personally though, i find it a  8.5/10, but hey, I can't be to biased. I would HIGHLY recommend waiting for a sale and picking up the GOTY Deluxe edition when available for ANYONE who likes RPGs.

Did you make it through Super Meat Boy without throwing your controller through the screen? Have you played and enjoyed the gravity-reversing platformer VVVVVV? Are you a fan of auto-run levels in games like BIT.TRIP Runner? Did you like the dark aesthetics of Limbo? Are you a cat lover? If the answer to 2 or more of the above questions is "Yes", then you will probably like this game.
For the most part, the gameplay is very Meat Boy-esque, with short levels full of spikes, saws, and other nasty obstacles. You play as a cat whose goal is to make it to the end of each level in one piece, which is easier said than done. It's a very simple game, mechanically - your only abilities are jumping (including advanced wall-jumping techniques) and crouching. There are also two other types of level variations: "auto-run" and "gravity-swap". In the "auto-run" levels, you have no control over the cat except to jump or crouch as the level scrolls by automatically at high speed. The "gravity-swap" levels, in which you play as a little girl instead of the cat, feature gravity-swapping gameplay similar to VVVVVV. Aesthetically, the game is really nice looking, with dark silhouette foregrounds and backgrounds of varying colors and styles. It's sort of a mashup between Limbo and NightSky, and works well. I must also make a note of the soundtrack, which is pretty good. The music is fairly low-key and consists of nice piano arrangements, with a few additional variations in the later levels.
So how does it actually play? For the most part, it's good... but it's not perfect. Hard-core platformers like this really need to nail the mechanics perfectly - the controls and the character's interaction with the world need to be spot-on, so that when you die, you feel like it was your fault, and not the game's. Unfortunately that is not always the case here. An especially frustrating aspect of the game is the collision detection, which feels very inconsistent and "wrong" at times. You will die from spikes that you swear were nowhere you, and other such inconsistencies. Ultimately, you just have to learn (and make peace with) the quirks of the game and try to be super-aware of exactly how you are jumping in certain situations. The "auto-run" levels, in particular, can be a nightmare, requiring pixel-perfect timing of jumps to complete.
That said, for all of these rough edges and frustrations, I still think this is a pretty good game overall, considering its low-budget indie nature. It is very much worth checking out if you like hard-core 2D platformers like Super Meat Boy. This isn't nearly as complex or polished as that game, but for the amount of content you get (100+ levels) and the reasonable price, I think it's worth picking up. Again, that is assuming you are up to the challenge - despite the cute exterior, this is not a casual game. Some of the later levels can get pretty difficult. So if you don't have a lot of patience, you might want to hold off on a purchase. Additionally, as is the norm for 2D platformers that require precise input, I also recommend avoiding this game unless you have a controller.

Cradle, at its core, is a puzzle game. but it is so, so much more than that.the intracacy of each object, and the level of interaction and description is phenominal. nearly every object in this game is interactable, and has some kind of descriptive text as to the histoy, lore and background of each and every scrap of paper, stick and cube.
this game is ludacrously in depth to the point when i first started playing i had no clue what was going on, which i suppose can be a bit of a turnoff for some but me being the explorer i am, i felt right at home.
you play as enebish, a mongolian native who has lost his memory after awakening from a dream state visor in his family yurt. right off the bat, you are thrust into this world as if you were enebish himself. confused, scrambling for answers and figuring it out as you go. inside the yurt, you find a human like adroid woman with flowers coming from her legs. you later discover her name is ida after peicing together some of her parts. she soon becomes your friend, guiding voice and the center peice in the games story. off in the distance behind your yurt, you will see a massive structure which you soon learn to be called the
this place holds the clues as to the fate of humanity, and why all humans now reside in androids such as ida. This is also where the bassic puzzle games come into play called pavilions, and although they seem simple in nature, they are quite engaging and can be difficult.
Each pavilion comes with a reward part which you use in order to repair ida and her slowly declining state.
So, now onto the pros and cons. well start with cons.
Although this game is massive already, the map you play in is essentialy a large circle in the mongolian plains, so theres not much large scale exploring besides your back yard and the gebera garden.
EXTREME DEPTH COMES WITH EXTREME CONFUSION. you will often find yourself wondering where a certain part is with very minimal hints.
repeatative walking is very common in this game
alot.of.Reading. if you are offput by very long texts of reading, this is not your game. 75% of this games context is spent reading.
the interface for how you interact with this is very simplistic and can be a bit annoying at times.
the storyline can be very confusing if you dont know what text to read, or you arent following along.
Now, onto the pros!
OPEN WORLD!
the scenery, style and art of this game is PHENOMINAL.
the physics are extremely realistic and very well polished.
gameplay is more or less smooth, in that, your objectives are clear, but how you get there is part of the puzzle :)
BEAUTIFUL Soundtrack and Score.
Secrets, Secrets, Secrets!

i enthusiastically recommend both this game, as well as the enhanced edition of baldur's gate.  my understanding is that both products were unacceptably buggy upon release, but the current versions (july 2014) seem quite stable.  i haven't had any problems with either product, save one:  the throne of bhaal expansion keeps eating my shield of balduran!  i haven't reported it yet as beholders don't play a significant role in ToB.  *shrug*
if you are expecting a major graphics overhaul, you will be disappointed.  most of the original art assets are gone (gee whiz, bioware!), so a simple HD remaster is out of the question.  you will get some new NPC's, which i personally enjoyed quite a bit.  as this is a matter of taste, your mileage may very.  for me, it was a chance to play with a party i would never have chosen for myself:  monks & wild mages?  ew.  but it's been great, and for those that are patient enough to stick with rasaad, you will find that he is insanely powerful by the time the ToB expansion begins.
the interface, while seeming the same, strikes one as less clunky.  several small conveniences quickly seem impossible to live without.  & the load times.  oh. my. gawd.  honestly, if you plan to spend much time with the BG saga, you will be amazed at how quickly saves and areas load, in contrast to the original offerings.  this is something no mod can change in the original game (at least not that i've seen), and the idiot-proof install & play package will have tremendous appeal for those who lack either capability, inclination, or time to mess with modding the now-antiquated technology of the original release.

Cradle offers an important lesson on how video games operate.
It's not well-designed; any game that kindly allows you to skip its "look, we've got gameplay" sections is admitting to the fact that those sections are arbitrary at best (or, in Cradle's particular case, are gut-wrenching torture that I'm pretty sure has been outlawed by the Geneva convention). Even then, however, Cradle does an impressive pirouette of backwardness by only letting you skip those sections
you've lost once—which is in itself a tedious task. The rest of the game consists of mundane tasks that make you grab and throw cumbersome objects and go for long repetitive runs. Unfortunately, a couple of interesting and innovative puzzles that are there do little to change the overall impression.
The plot avoids the bane of "plot-driven" videogames, overexplanation. In fact, it's so good at not getting in one's face that by the end of the game I had zero idea as to what had transpired. Without the hidden notes (the very existence of which is only hinted at by the Steam achievements) the plot offers decent exposition, but little in the way of describing the actual events of the story. One of the characters the ending revolves around, Mark, is only mentioned two or three times.
And yet, despite its many flaws, I've given Cradle a thumbs up. Why?
Because I adored every single minute spent in it.
Yes, Cradle is badly-designed. However, it is also visually stunning and inventive (the mostly realistic 3D combined with an obviously painted skybox allow for incredible imagery). The music is gorgeous, the mood is thick, and the setting—the setting is insanely original, charming, unique, and intriguing.
Mongolian transhumanism.
Let that sink in. Mongolian. Transhumanism.
Have you ever thought that you may one day utter such a combination of words?
No. No you haven't. Which is exactly why Cradle deserves all the recognition in the world.
The setting and plot of Cradle revolve around an oxymoron, the vivid contrast of a hi-tech android against a mongolian yurt. It's never quite obvious where the complicated sci-fi story ends and a poetic parable begins. Even the scattered representation of the plot serves Cradle well: you may not understand everything that transpired, but you'll still get the general gist of the odd, beautiful, and (admittedly) slightly funny world you've visited.
And in the end, it trumps everything. Because video games are the art of creating
.
And that is the one thing that Cradle undoubtedly succeeds at.

Bandai took a real chance on this game.  A psychological mystery thriller with FPS elements where combat takes a backseat to investigation.  And there is a lot of investigation.
Get Even's strongest point is its story and this is made apparent very early on.  The english voice actors did a phenomenal job and deserve special note here as without them, the game would not be the enjoyable experience it is.  The story itself is told through unreliable narrators, as memories are themselves unreliable.  Turning this aspect of the mind into gameplay is a challenge and Farm 51 for the most part succeeds in doing so.  The only failures on there part are honestly ones I find insurmountable with video games as a medium.
The investigation aspect of gameplay is well done and reminds me of the Condemned series take on investigation, but Get Even has less hand holding and that makes it vastly more interesting.  The search for clues is fun, and wow are there are a lot of them.  Thankfully you will gain the ability to review all of your clues at an early stage in the game as well as the ability to go back to each area to look for any clues missed on your first pass.
Combat isn't anything to write home about.  Standard fair, although the CornerGun is fun to play with.  Unfortunately, you don't always have access to it.  Combat itself feels almost unavoidable at times.  Stealth mechanics are a weak point in Get Even, as vision cones seem inconsistent and will swing all over the place as the enemies twist their heads back and forth like they're having as seizure.  This fault is a serious one as there are actual story and gameplay consequences for managing to avoid conflict.
Graphically the game isn't particularly special.  They feel slightly dated but aren't ugly and the animation is good.  However I did mention the strongest aspect of Get Even is its story, which manages to keep you hooked and invested in the search for the truth.  Even if your reach the end of the game, which I did in eight hours, you will most likely not have found all the clues on each stage.  I don't know if that will unlock some kind of extra "True Ending", but I'm going to give it a go anyway.
Overall:
Story 9/10:  Strong acting, pacing and writing.
Gameplay 7/10: Investigating things is fun and the CornerGun is a neat gadget but combat is overall generic.
Graphics 7/10: They do an adequate job for the most part and the animation is solid, but much of it feels last gen.
Sound 8/10: While not bursting with variety, the music is pretty good and while the cute pop song is catchy, its used in some odd places in-game.  Audio is mixed well, voices are clear, Sfx's are clean and ambient noise is great.  Really helps the atmosphere.
Worth getting if you like your mysteries, if you like the movie "Inception", if you prefer strong story over gameplay.  Great job all around Farm 51.

I played ATS before ETS2 so I really had no comparison to start with.
ATS is a remarakble game. The graphics are top notch and the "task oriented" system of missions is pretty cool. Definitively the highlight is the scenic views everywhere; there is something wonderful passing by LAX and seeing al those planes go up or riding at 2 am in the middle of the Arizona desert and see 2 UFOS moving haphazardly in the middle of the night sky. Sunsets and dawns are magnificent and the ther eis a certain identity to driving a trailer truck: it is not the same driving the truck by itself, driving it with a trailer full of tires or if it hauling a container with gas, you can certainly feel the difference, and I am sure those who are using driving wheels for controllers will appreciate.
The game doesn't have soundtrack per se, instead it has a collection of internet radios, which is fantastic as you can tune in the type of music you feel will be better driving the long disctances. You can also configure to play your collection of MP3 files.
Controls are tight and it is not hard to get the hang of it, but it also has millions of different options to customize your experience. The same can be said with graphis, game play and some other stuff.
My only concern is that the area that encompass ATS feels small, compared to what I later discovered was the playing area of ETS2. You have California, Nevada, Arizona, which are huge, but can get repetitive you get to a certain high level. I hope we get to see new terrotory soon.
I also feel a little disappointer by the available brands of trucks. Right now, only a selection of Kenworth and Peterbilt trucks are available, and while they are nice and very customizable, it would be amazing to see more, akin to ETS2 which I Nlater discovered had 4 options for car brands.
I won't lie, if you are looking for the next action intense game, this is not it. ATS is more relaxing than anything else. Its scenic views are amazing, it doesn't matter if you are in the middle of nowhere in Nevada or travelling through the sprawling cities of LA and San Franciso. A couple of missions more an turn in a whole night of driving, which speaks a lot of the value of this game.
Highly recommended.

Zombie Vikings is a beat'm up similar to what you'll find in Castle Crashers. It features a fast paced combat with an interesting art style.
You have your choice of 4 (6 total with the DLCs) characters, and you can play upto 4 players at once locally. The characters play mostly the same, with their special attack being the aspect that separates them. You have your basic attack, when held it'll do a more powerful swing. The more you chain the more damage you'll do. You also have a block and a roll as defensive maneuvers, and of course you have your jump and jump attack as well. To help round things out, there is also a throw key, that allows you to carry and throw a variety of things, your allies, objects and enemies. The most interesting attack is the special key that each character's signature move. Like the regular attack, it has a quick press, and a hold variation. Each character's special varies quite a lot, from throwing groups of enemies, to a scorpion like arm harpoon that helps you continue your combo.
The game plays very similar to the likes of Castle Crashers. You and possibly a group of your local friends will head out, button mashing and comboing your way through any give map. Throughout you'll encounter a variety of different enemies and boss battles. Most of the combat plays out as you expect from any given beat'm ups. Zombie Viking's combat does feel smooth, responsive, and quick, but it don't really do anything to move the genre forward, but it at least feels good. Because of the variety in maneuvers available, the game does feature some depth in mechanics to learn, however it's also not the hardest beat'm up I've ever played.
The art style and overall presentation of Zombie Vikings is superb. It features an interesting digital paint look, that's whimsical as it is comedic. The sound track, voice acting, and story also reflect this. As far as presentations are concerned, I don't have much to complain about.
Overall Zombie Vikings doesn't do much in the way of moving the genre of beat'm ups forward, but what it does do it does competently, and is overall an enjoyable experience.
Pros:
- Great presentation
- Fast and responsive combat
- Interesting special moves
- Easy to get into
Cons:
- Can be repetitive
- Doesn't do any thing overly original
- No online

The style, art, and music have held up well but the gameplay has become a victim of Father Time.
This was a fun romp down memory lane for me as I grew up in a household that had a SEGA Dreamcast. But beyond former fans of the game I would have a hard time outright recommending this title. The very simple gameplay was unique for it's time but over the course of 15years has become a bit clunky and aged. The quicksand feel of freeskating and your limited abilities can be downright infuriating in the late levels. But I pushed on because I had beat it as a much younger human so gosh darn it I could beat it as an old boring dude!
The charm is all still there. The music, the early cel-shading, the unique setting, the era vibe, etc. It has all held up great and brought warm memories. Combine that with the low low lowww sale prices this game can be found for (down to the price of FREE). And I can still recommend this. Heavy warning for the younger crowd or people who never played it on SEGA Dreamcast though; That gameplay really hasn't held up and it'll be a departure from what you're used to.
Some final technical notes; I played with a 360 controller so I cannot vouch for the keyboard controls but I feel comfortable urging controller use. Can't imagine trying that with a keyboard... Also, this IS locked at 30 frames per second but like some other older games its performance is tied to the frame rate and cannot be changed. This is actually a time where a port gets a pass in this regard. You won't find (or need) any video settings beyond resolution. And finally the bonus content is appreciated (extra music, mini documentary).
Grind a rail for me.

Zombie Vikings is an action brawler game developed by Zoink Games. Loki has stolen Odin’s good eye and Odin tasks four Zombie Vikings with the job of retrieving the eye at all costs! Along the way you’ll find yourself faced with a fair few boss fights, some funny moments and bucket loads of loot!
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
Zombie Vikings appearance is, without a doubt, the best thing about it. It has a unique style which falls somewhere between hand drawn and cartoon-y and it looks great. Everything in the game is well designed too and the character models look good close up as well as zoomed out.
Zombie Vikings’ gameplay consists of moving through levels, killing enemies and collecting loot. It’s really rather simple and while simplistic gameplay can be good, I felt that the gameplay here had a real lack of depth, especially when considering the price of admission. As it’s a brawler game most of the gameplay comes from the combat but unfortunately the combat felt, to me, like it was just button smashing with the occasional break to pick something up and lob it at an enemy. You have three ways of attacking in Zombie Vikings: a regular attack, a signature attack and the ability to pick things up and throw them. Each of these can be charged which, when unleashed, performs a different attack. The signature moves for each character are pretty cool but for the most part I found them to be less effective than just mashing the regular attack button. So just to clarify, what I mean by lack of depth is that it’s basically just button mashing but there’s not really any change in combat from the start of the game to the end and there’s very little difference in difficulty.
As you can probably see, Zombie Vikings is 2.5D, and this works well for the most part. It makes the game more challenging as there’ll be enemies you need to move around to hit and enemies who throw bombs at you will be able to throw them at you even if they’re in front or behind you. The only issue I had with this was that you can’t move forwards or backwards when attacking but you can move left or right, most enemies move around while attacking you so I found it frustrating to not be able to attack them.
The map is effectively split into sections. Each section contains three or four normal levels as well as a boss fight. Since these areas are actually different parts of the in-game world they each have their own enemies as well as appearance etc. Even though they have their own enemies there’s very little variation between enemies with about three enemy types being present in each area, just re-skinned, and then a couple of unique ones per area. While this does allow you to get pretty good at beating those enemies I’m pretty sure that’s not a good thing, it just leads to a lack of variety which I found started to stop me wanting to play more.
The levels themselves are no more complex than my description of them at the start of this section. The only thing I didn’t mention is that most levels have optional side-quests that you can complete, the reward for completing these is a unique weapon. The weapons have their own stats but for the most part they’re all good so you can just choose whichever one you like using the most. As well as weapons you can also equip runes which give you some sort of bonus such as increasing your health or giving you health regeneration.
Zombie Vikings has a great soundtrack. While I didn’t really notice it while playing the game when you’re in a menu or on the map etc. you can really appreciate the good music. The voice acting is also incredibly good in Zombie Vikings. The story is pretty wacky as is the humour and so you really need full commitment from the voice actors and that’s definitely what we’ve got here.
Zombie Vikings is reasonably fun for a couple of hours, particularly if you like the kind of humour in the game but its weak gameplay and high price mean you should only consider it when it hits somewhere around the 75% mark.

The puzzles themselves are rather simple, with only one or two requiring much thought - in some cases, backtracking is necessary to notice that something has changed, but otherwise they're relatively straightforward.
The music is pleasant and relaxing, and serves to fit the gameplay.
Ultimately, it's quite short - about an hour. Recommended for those looking for a relaxing, not terribly difficult, adventure game. Just keep the length in mind when determining the appropriate price to look for.

This game is like a action rts.
Your main character does not attack but can summon or rally his troops.
He has a little racoon pet that can be upgraded to fetch things like gold or items from the town folk.
You pick 3 out of up to 15 classes to take into battle to summon them and help you fight.
Bard will slowly gain notes over time or they can be dropped from enemies.

The villagers and fort can also be upgraded so they give you items and add defenders to your fort.
In the main story you play through 4 sets of 5 levels with the 5th always being a boss (there is also a days 2).
In Survival enemies and friendly units will randomly spawn on the board and you try to see how long you can stay alive without any bard powers.
In escape mode you have no bard powers and try to see how far you can get wile avoiding poison pools, enemies, & there shots.
Overall its not a bad take on rts games and the units do vary and will change your play style depending on who you bring.

- There are flashes of great ideas here, especially for fans of detective or thrillers adventures, but they all feel half-baked, and the lack of an FOV slider also sucks (I really had to download the file editor for Bulletstorm to change the FOV from 60? Really?). Unfortunately, the presentation never rises above "impressive" mod for me, as the animations and polish feel extremely lacking, despite good voice acting and ambitious ideas. Just can't recommend.
It's hard for me to give this game a "Do not recommend", but ultimately, I felt frustrated and displeased after 2hrs of play. I didn't want to continue, as I felt that it was not only a chore to set up properly, but a chore to play.
To start, the game has no FOV options. You start with a 60-degree FOV that makes your eyes want to bleed. After searching the net and following a few red herrings as to where the dang config files were, I discovered that you could change the FOV there. Not a deal breaker, but not exactly ideal either. Took me about 30-45min, all in all, to find the file, make the edits, and then test out multiple FOVs to see what would work best for me. Fortunately, that was the only configuration issue I had. The graphics are fine otherwise, though I was disappointed that there was only one slider for "Master Volume" (why can't games separate their audio tracks in 2017?).
Unfortunately, what followed was a mix of interest followed by strong displeasure. The game starts out with zero context for what you're doing, but as you start wandering the opening level, you start to get an idea of what your goal is and it unravels bit by bit. The tutorial for learning what each of your gadgets do is actually implemented quite nicely for such a low-budget title, and it's all very clear as to what you can use each of your tools for. However, after the opening level and a few story points later, the game took a bit of a dive for me.
Ultimately, GET EVEN is sort of a detective/investigative adventure, but it's also a bit of a walking/horror game as well. But then it's also a stealth game, and definitely a shooter. The problem is that it doesn't do any one of these genres amazingly. It executes them all adequately, but leaves you feeling very disjointed. This is made evident when the game specifically tells you that killing people will lead to a bad ending, and that sneaking your way through areas is the best option. I don't mind this inherently. I think it works very well in games like Dishonored, when you have 20 options as to how to get through an area without being caught. However, GET EVEN has one method of sneaking: don't get caught. You literally crawl everywhere and just try not to be seen. You can't pick up items and throw them to distract enemies, you can't do ANYTHING to distract them, there's no real knowing how far the sound of your steps travel because many enemies trigger on proximity vs some measurable noise or distance. In addition, it takes about 3 bullets to be killed, and if you DO decide to kill anyone, the death animations are AWFUL for the enemies. They fall on the ground and seize up in that weird tiger pose from Michael Jackson's Thriller video.
So, we've established that killing people will lead to the worst ending, and that sneaking is not easy and really not even rewarded (there's one room where the game repeatedly says "Don't kill this guy! Don't take away his music" and other things that mean hey, don't kill this guy, and you can't sneak around him at all. He stands near a door and is FORCIBLY triggered if you even try to sneak around him to get to the door). Now you're left with essentially running from autosave to autosave, hoping that enemies might lose aggro on your way so that you don't have to kill them. Meanwhile, you're finding magazines of ammo for your gun every few areas because hey, you might need more bullets, BUT DON'T KILL ANYONE, KILLING PEOPLE WILL GIVE YOU A TERRIBLE ENDING. The game reminds you repeatedly that disrupting the status quo of your memories will screw things over for you.
In the end, I couldn't take anymore. The game looks alright, but the animations are terrible. Overall, it looks like someone made a Half-Life mod, gave it pretty good voice acting, took some interesting gameplay ideas and threw them all into a blender, and then spent about $100 on polish and shipped the game as is. It's a shame, because I think there's some good here. Clearly, the positive reviews have been able to get through all the crap I can't. My major beef is that the game gives me crazy weapons to kill people, and then tells me absolutely not to kill anyone if I want the good ending, yet sneaking around and stealthing is such a chore due to no REAL stealth mechanics. It feels worse than when games like Wolfenstein shoe-horn stealth in.
Overall, no recommend for me. It's a shame; I've been waiting to get this game for months, and I finally picked it up on the sale and was hugely disappointed. I don't want to discourage the devs; I think they have some dope ideas, but this one really should have been cooked a little bit longer, or received a little bit more feedback, before being released.

A Walk in the Dark is a straightforward game with what seems like a straightforward mission - 'Make it to the end of each level without dying'.  Well...it sounds easy enough, but when you throw in some obvious and not-so-obvious obstacles and threats, each level becomes a point of intrigue for the overly analytical person.  You'll find yourself picking apart the levels in an attempt to streamline your run through.  The game keeps you drawn in even when you find yourself repeating a level constantly out of the desire to get that 100% completion, where most games would infuriate the player by that point.  It's definitely worth the play-through, and worth coming back for more when you feel like zipping through previously completed stages.

You are a barbarian that is tired of pillaging and wants to be a bard instead.
So, Bardbarian. The entire backstory is there in the title.
Unfortunately this new devotion to music and abhorrence of inflicting violence could not be timed worse, since an invasion force of monsters is approaching the quiet town you live in.
Why? Nobody knows. There is no plot beyond the setting.
This leaves the town in a pickle though, without the barbarian they will need another way to protect their town.
Despite no longer fighting directly the Bardbarian has decided to help. The local adventurers' guild has plenty of warriors around and all they need to join the defence is some encouragement. Musical encouragement.
So the Bardbarian runs around the battlefield, playing (monotonous but fun) music to gather a resource called Notes. These notes can be spent to recruit warriors from the adventurers' guild who will start following you around the battlefield, attacking any enemies that come close.
This turns the game into a defence game, you navigate your group of adventurers around the battlefield to keep the monsters away from the town square where a magical crystal does... something important, apparently. Wave after wave, until you get a boss fight and move on to the next segment of the game and do it all over again.
After your almost inevitable failure you spend the gold you earned from the enemies the adventurers have vanquished to upgrade... quite a lot of different things. Upgrade your units, unlock new units, upgrade your own stats, research spells and facilities around the village that make your time just a bit easier.
A weird item that you can buy is the Golden Guitar, which doubles all future Gold income. It's a relic of the time where the game had a cash shop on mobile, but fortunately it can be bought with regular currency in this Steam version. You should do that as soon as possible.
All in all the game gets a bit repetitive as it goes on, and some of the later units are so much stronger than the other ones that you don't really feel like you're customizing so much as levelling that one unit until you get past the level you're stuck on.
However, it's a pretty game with a lot of content and a solid soundtrack.
Recommended if you're looking for a fun defence game.

GET EVEN is a mix of FPS, mystery, and psychological thriller. It involves grabbing pieces of evidence in fragmented memories to give insight on a bomb being tied to a girl and going off. The game definitely has many interesting concepts that individually do a phenomenal job of conveying the story. The soundtrack and story are some of the best I have ever experienced in a video game, and the visuals greatly represent the complex story beginning to end and their are few gaps in the story that cannot be argued with evidence in the game. However, where the game falls apart is the gameplay. First, the game encourages users to never kill anyone, but gives the gamer no non-lethal weapons, who are forced to hide behind cover and die many times. I also feel like the three genres didn't mix well and I had no idea what I was playing because different memeories can be drastically different and it is extremely difficult to piece these ideas together without doing a massive amount of reading pieces of evidence and many vague cutscenes that are also very difficult to piece together. All of this just makes the game extremely boring and makes me feel like I am reading a book with my mouse and keyboard. I also noticed quite a few bugs like stuttering every now and then and getting stuck in a wall. The game feels like a mish mash of ideas that show promise, but never feel complete together. I hope we see a GET EVEN 2 that revises some of these gameplay elements

Crusader Kings II is an amazingly fun game with the right people, although does have a few grudgingly annoying features.
The game has dozens of DLCs which is a bit irking considering most are features which should have been added in free updates. However, only one person needs to own the DLCs to play with them on multiplayer (he has to host the game). Thus, the usage of DLC in this game, like other Paradox Games, is fair, but the amount of DLC is a bit excessive if you ask me. If you plan to buy this game, you should all agree on one friend to buy the CKII DLC pack to enjoy many of the features I will discuss below.
The ruler designer/custom nation creator features are incredibly fun, and my friends and I will often spend over an hour designing the most outrageous nations and leaders. Many laughs will be had when one of your friends creates a completely broken overpowered character while another makes an inbred, hunchback moron control half of Western Europe.
The game features many fun mechanics allowing you to host events, engage in intrigue, or gain power within your religious faction. You can play anyone as small as a local mayor or Duke, or the King of the Holy Roman Empire. Using wit, you can grow your nation, or cause others to fall apart by supporting rebels. Many things are possible, and this game offers a level of depth that in my opinion, can't be matched by Civ V or many other strategy games. Relationships with important individuals are a major aspect of the game, and are affected by factors such as your traits, religion, and actions throughout your reign. You must balance relationships with your own family, councilmembers, vassel stakeholders, other nations, religious figures, noblepeople, and many more. You must also ensure the continued existence of your dynasty by getting down dirty and ensuring your own children don't kill each other (they do, unfortunately enough for power grabs). Overall, all these features, as I mentioned previously, give extreme depth to the game, and discussing the hilarious random events that occur to your friends playing with you will surely lead to some good memories.
A few things I don't like - sometimes, I feel that the relationship mechanisms and family systems are a bit too petty and require too much micromanaging when I am often more concerned about taking over Europe. Another Paradox game which is almost perfect in my eyes is Europa Universalis IV. This game is much more grand in scale and enables you to do much bigger things without as many petty game mechanics. If you can only buy one game, I would encourage you to get that instead of this, although CKII has its many charms. Secondly, war REQUIRES a Casus Beli and a lot of Prestige, which can make some conflicts take a frustratingly long time to set up before you can actually fight. EUIV also does a much better job with this. However, if you wish to play less aggresively, this shouldn't be a problem at all, you will only notice this if you are trying to grab lots of land, which the game doesn't seem to want you to do.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but would recommend Europa Universalis IV more. I would also only recommend playing this game with friends and I would recommend that one of the friends you play with (or you) get the DLCs as there isn't as much you can do with the base game. Get them a pizza or something better to make it up to them.

Cradle is a game of contradictions in its design. The developer has to be commended for creating such a detailed world infused with Myst-like levels of glorious attention to detail, both in plot and aesthetic designs. Unfortunately there's a more frustrating side to the game: The dreadful cube minigame which you need to go through a total of 4 times and each time is more infuriating than the last time. There is zero fun to be derived from these parts of the game and while the game does try to justify these strange rooms in the story, they still stick out like sore thumbs.
However, whenever the game actually becomes a true adventure game (where you explore your surroundings and make sense of the highly emotional and philosphical plot by interacting with several items and speaking to the few NPCs), it's a truly magical experience to behold indeed.
To be honest, Even though the cube minigames drove me mad to the brink of quitting the game, I still enjoyed the ~6 hours I spent with it. The plot is vague and amazing at the same time and the beautiful world they have come up with looks absolutely dazzling. An adventure game with a pacing that limps but well worth the asking price.

A short, pretty atmospheric, super casual laid back game well worth it's money (bought it for 1,99€ on a sale). The game is about curing your younger brother by finding nine emergency rations spread all over the mostly submerged world. After each of them you get a bit more background story of what's going on in the world and why your son was injured in the first place. The story is told mostly by symbols and primitive paintings.
The gameplay is 80% about climbing buildings, looking for those emergency rations. It's mostly very linear and straight forward and each climbable building got some extra secrets. Those are usually also very straight forward. 15% you spend in the boat, finding those buildings. The rest 5% is looking at short cutscreens and the symbol paintings/cards I mentioned earlier.
Other than that there are a bunch of collectables, cards about the world and some of it's animals. There are also boost/turbo updrades for the boat, which is mostly useless.
I finished the main story and collected some extras in about 1.9h according Steam. I recommend the game but don't think I ever will go back to find all collectables, the gameplay isn't interesting enough for that. This game should work for non gamers and kids too with the basic concept and simple to use controls. There is no difficulty to talk about.
