The story for
is a very interesting one. It has many elements of differents sci fi/artificial life stories i've read or played before but it creates something of its own.
You play a mysterious character, who wakes up in a mongolian hut in the middle of... some place. He doesn't remember exactly who he is. But soon he starts to find papers and pictures and stuff that  tells him who he might be. The story anyway begins to flow when he finds a neurochip and he's able to communicate with the conscience of someone called Ida.
Long time ago, humanity found a way to be able to transfer someone's conscience into a mechanical body. This was seen as a way to be able to save someone's life who might be suffering a terminal disease or just simply to extend life.
Soon, it was discovered that there were various side efects to this "transfer of conscience" some of them good and some of them bad. And a new type of energy was found, maybe as a result of these experiments with the mind and the body and what exists between, or just maybe because other reasons unknown, unseen.
The real problem was, that after sometime an accident occurred. An explosion who released a deadly toxin, wich attacked the central nervous system. All people died on earth. Too quickly. And only the ones who were transfered to a mechanical body survived. A few thousands of robots with the conscience of an ancient human being remained on earth.
And its like that that this story begins, wich after playing it, i have to say its pretty short, and its a shame, not because it is not long like other games, but because the back story is so amazing, and could be the source for such a great open world adventure (or just and adventure) that it feels a sort of wasted oportunity. There is in fact, much more to the story that what first is given. But almost everything is optional, you have to search through papers, and clippings, and screens the story of what happened (it is not mandatory to finish the game)
But at the end anyway..
. There is a hint of what happens, but it really ends in a big question mark about what happens. And there are many things wich are introduced but never explained, not in the least. During the game itself you have only two places to go, but they are very well done and utilised. So, it is limited in space and duration, but that is not to say its really short. The game can take several hours to complete depending on how much back story you search, and how much time you take for every thing you do. On this point, it should be said that this game is not a walking a simulator, there are in fact many actions and things to do. Allthough...
... its not impossible, but it could use some improvements. Sometimes it is difficult to handle objects...
, both the atmosphere tracks and the stories one. The game is relatively short and still manages to have 90 minutes of original soundtrack wich is amazing. It is safe to say that almost every important action you made during the game has a distinctive soundtrack moment, and all are very well done. Some of them have lyrics. The music reminds me a little of the Atlantis 3 soundtrack and electronic ambient music, something like the one from The girl with the dragon tattoo from Trent reznor and Atticus Ross.
So, the game is definitely flawed, but, it has also some really interesting parts, and excellent back story and some excellent music. Wich, ironically, are two things many games fail from time to time.
So, it is because of that maybe, that in the end, it is something of a letdown that not much happens.
There is in fact an end to this story, but with such a great back story (wich plays of course a part during the ending) it is a shame so much details are left.... just there. Undeveloped.
But still it was a very interesting experience to have and i recommend it (if you don't have other games to play) it is a short and somewhat sweet experience.

This game has a lot of potential and my opinion of it changes as more things are developed and added to the game.  It is definitely worth checking it out if you like survival/craft games, but I have to warn you that you need to be patient as the game continues to develop.  There is definite room for growth.
That being said, this is the 6th or 7th title in this genre that I have played over recent years and it is definitely different from the others.  The graphics and setting are stunning this early into development and I love the ability to raid NPC villages and claim NPC thralls that you can employ as slaves in your base to gain production benefits/perks.  As this continues to develop I am excited to see what perks each of the NPC types will bring.
The crafting system is a bit confusing at first and definitely takes some getting used to.  There is some good depth here and I anticipate many changes as the game progresses (hopefully a more intuitive system/better GUI).  There is a search feature that helps with finding the recipes I need quickly, but knowing what recipes to acquire takes time and focus.  Luckily there is an ingame mechanic to wipe your memory and pick your recipes all over again if you goof up or just want a change.
I like the ability to claim land and construct huge bases for my friends and I, but the raiding system needs a lot of attention.  Inventory space is too low for bigger raids, not having mounts or vehicles definitely puts a damper on game play when you have to ferry loot back and forth for an hour or more.  Also, you can build amazing cities/bases but that can feel futile when there is absolutely no protection from "god raids" - which essentially allow a single player to summon an avatar of a god and totally level your base in 45 seconds.
Another downside to the game is the lack of community/sheer number of servers out there atm so make sure you bring plenty of friends to make the gameplay exciting.  Without them the grind is very unforgiving and it could take a lifetime to get anywhere.  Religion plays a huge role in the game and that's completely uncovered at character creation.  Trying to figure out the system and how to unlock temples and such can be hard for new players.
I would avoid public servers right now because they are a complete mess due to the exploits and trolling that are all part of an alpha stage.  Try to find a server that matches your playing style and has an active admin or staff to assist.  One that consistently works to develop their community is essential so that you don't find yourself solo in this very unforgiving world.

Dragon Nest is an instance-based action RPG playing much like an arcade game with no targeting, a strict class tree, a less strict skill tree, and more or less no character customization whatsoever. For instance, all Tinkerers are time-travelers who somehow turned into adorable lolitas, and all Kalis are abundantly female spirit dancers with sweet, slightly shy temperaments and dead masters.
Masters in their tribal ninja teachings, not BDSM masters. Moving along.
Dragon Nest's English localization is -incredibly- well-done, with dialogue that is not only legible but actually full of character and humor. The voice acting is goofy, but in a way that lines up with the character in question. The child king is nasally and distinctly lacking a courtly presence, while the storage NPC constantly complains about the horrible things other people / you leave in storage. The marketplace NPC will insult you for being poor (regardless of how much money you are holding because he's so damn rich.)
Dungeons have multiple difficulty settings, and the baddest♥♥♥♥♥dungeons are the titular Nests (though not necessarily dragon nests.) Abyss is the fourth and highest difficulty of any other dungeon, but it is the first difficulty of a Nest, and most of them have a Hell or Hardcore one that's much much harder than that. Nests are effectively your chokepoints for progress through the game, and at any given time one or more Nests will be the "endgame" dungeon. The catch is, you can only /win/ one given Nest a limited number of times every week. You can fail as many times as you want, but the great majority of items from Nests are only acquired after a successful clear.
Sadly, despite its charms, some significant flaws mar Dragon Nest and detract largely from its otherwise polished gameplay:
- As said before, character customization barely exists and development is largely one-way-only - there isn't as freeform choice in character build as there would be in a standard MMO like WoW or Everquest II. It's basically an online arcade game.
- It is possible to miss content. This is usually something trivial such as a non-title achievement, but it will still drive completionists up the wall.
- The game is entirely instance dungeon-based with little to no open world. The exploration fields don't have any combat in them, nor any content other than NPC's to talk to and gates into instance dungeons (similarly to Sonic Adventure.) This can make the game feel very railroaded and monotonous.
- Costume items, which are largely cash-only and non-tradeable, also give you stats and perks. This means they're not costumes. They're cash-only equipment.
- Titles also give you stats, but the majority of those are acquired ordinarily ingame and you may use a display title different from your stat title.
- As with most if not all other free games that have equipment upgrades available, Dragon Nest's equipment upgrade rate is abysmal without paying cash to improve it and/or protect items from destruction. These items thankfully can be traded, but as cash items they will cost a small fortune.
- Holiday events, and events in general, almost never give anything permanent and unique. They give consumables and temporary costumes at best, or items that can be obtained in normal gameplay. They're generally quite underwhelming and unrewarding.
- The keyboard control scheme is VERY awkward and can't be remapped.
- If you like endowed girls at all you won't be able to play as Kali, because she's constant softcore pornography on the screen and very distracting. She's the only character with jiggle (Archer / Sorceress / Tinkerer are all B-cup or less whereas she's at least a D-cup with a huge butt) and her dance animations border on profane. This is especially jarring given her dialogue is written as though she is very sweet and innocent.
Despite these flaws, the game is colorful and fun with only a couple friends. You can form guilds, but only four-odd of you can run a dungeon at once anyway, so you don't need to bring a legion.
And Tinkerer is SUPER CUTE. Give it a shot and see if you like it.

Zombie Vikings is a side scrolling hack em’ up four player co-op with incredible story and a few unique and fun mechanics. The art is done in an incredibly thematic hand painted style and it’s really quite a beautiful game in terms of aesthetics. The game play is similar to Castle Crashers and other side scrolling hack and slash types of games. You are able to gain money and buy upgraded weapons or runes after you find them in the game world.
What I enjoyed:
Drawn together – The art and style in this game is fantastic and beautiful. There is a rare occasion when I will stop and admire every aspect of the art in a game and this is one of those. Every character is extremely detailed and has a magical whimsical feel. The backgrounds and environments are incredibly detailed and include tons of really wonderful scenes. I am really pleased that this level of painterly quality is displayed throughout the game.
Zombie speak – Generally speaking, zombies groan and moan, and are boring to talk with due to their lack of personality. These zombies are not lacking in wit or character, and their voices are just incredible. The voice acting in the game is really superb and the story shines due to amazing personas displayed by each individual character. The villains are also extremely witty and funny adding a deep sense of humor to the game and story.
Keeping it simple – I like that the combat and unique mechanics of using different pets or body parts for various purposes. The game really shines once you get used to this aspect. Throwing a talking head at your enemies has never been so fun. The control scheme is not overly complicated but I do suggest using a controller as it seems this game was designed to be extremely controller friendly. I found the controls to be crisp and responsive, which is important in this type of experience.
What I disliked:
Switcheroo – I really enjoy this game so it is hard to find many flaws. One suggestion I may have is that when you aren’t playing co-op you have the option to switch between the characters. The levels seem short enough and designed to be played multiple times so this really is not a necessity just a minor concern during the game. The game is very well done so it becomes difficult to find flaws vs suggested improvements.
Short story – The game itself is not short, but the description about who these zombie vikings are and why they are talking to Odin is brief at best. I quickly found myself invested in their quest, but initially I did wonder what in the world was going on, and why we were helping Odin get his eye back. The story itself is fantastic and fills in the gaps well, so this is again, a minor concern.
Zombie Vikings is fun with one player, and insanely fun with four. I suggest grabbing your friends, grabbing a weapon and a zombie, and heading out on this adventure. These silly zombies will have you chuckling, and their villain counterparts aren’t witless either. The level of humor and attention to artistic detail in both visuals and story is beyond that of many retail titles, this is a gem of a game and I would venture to guess mine won’t be the only highly appreciative and shining review of this super fun co-op game.
Score: Buy it now

With a gen-u-wine bonafide humourist in the shape of  Saturday Morning Breakfast Cereal author Zack Weinersmith penning the script, ZOMBIE VIKINGS is rammed and I mean forcefed to ♥♥♥♥ing breaking point with dialogue and cutscenes to the eventuality where the game feels more like a sketch show than anything else. You can barely move from one screen to the next without hearing some quip or comedy routine going on which, y'know, while you're playing the actual game is fine. In fact, it's downright admirable how much hard work, talent and creativity has gone into the script and voice acting; you'll be hard pressed to find another game this year with the sheer amount of writing per square inch that ZOMBIE VIKINGS throws at you. There are a metric Cthulian arseload of pre-level scenes, post-level scenes, inter-level scenes and if they're not your thing, that's fine, you're more than welcome to skip them but herein lies the problem. If you don't enjoy this game's story and humour, then what you're left with is a very routine slash-em-up. The combat mechanics, y'know, the hinge of the entire game, feel lazy, moreso when stretched over more than two dozen levels. There's no crunch, no satisfaction in defeating your opponents and I strongly suspect that the multiplayer aspect that ZOMBIE VIKINGS is selling itself on is, much like the cutscenes that easily take up over half of the game's actual playtime, a counterbalance for how banal most of it feels. Don't get me wrong, it's not punch-you-to-the-ground, f**k-you-in-the♥♥♥♥♥♥terrible. There's nothing WRONG with it but as a six hour experience, it drags hard and it feels like the gameplay has been tailored to fit the gargantuan script rather than the other way around.
I'd still advocate giving it a try if you're a fan of the genre. The cosmetics may do a lot more for you than they did for me and this'd probably sit a lot prettier if you went at it a bit at a time, rather than the start-to-finish marathon I subjected myself to. Maybe get some friends too. All mine are prejudiced against ancient Scandanavians so they refused to play this with me. I've really got to stop hanging out with the f**king Saxons.

Experience all the death and misery in the life of an average Russian from the comfort of your own home!

What is it?
While Zombie Vikings retains much of the look and some of the comedic style from Zoink's first game Stick it to the Man!, it is a very different game that can be essentially described as an arcade-style beat em' up.  Players can choose from one of four different characters which all have their own unique set of attacks and feel to them and then progress through a series of levels which are mostly straight-forward, but occasionally have hidden side quest objectives too.
Some may compare the gameplay to Castle Crashers, and they wouldn't be wrong for the most part, however Zombie Vikings does have less RPG elements with its lack of a leveling system.  While there is no character leveling progression, there still are quite a few weapons to find, purchase, and collect throughout the journey each which have their own stats and unique effects.  In addition there are also trinkets which provide passive benefits as well.
While the game is clearly designed with co-op in mind as can be seen in the ability to pick up and throw other players and through portions where all players are sewn together into one giant zombie viking, it can still be played solo.  When going solo players are accompanied by a unicorn pig which will fire a cannon when players hit it.
Story is a relatively strong element, which shouldn't be a surprise if you've played Zoink's first game.  Expect plenty of cutscenes and comedic dialogue between characters that makes the game feel like an interactive Saturday morning cartoon of sorts.  To set the story up without spoiling anything, Odin has resurrected four zombie vikings to send them on a quest to retrieve his eye which has been stolen.
While you won't see a lot of depth in the gameplay of Zombie Vikings, it's not something that should disappoint as often times the fun of the beat em' genre lies directly with its lack of it since you can sit on a couch and enjoy it with just about any type or skill of gamer.
What's Good?
- Each character truly felt unique with their basic and special attacks
- A decent amount of weapons and trinkets to collect each which have their own unqiue stats and effects
- Optional side quests during levels
- Designed with co-op in mind rather than just tacked on thanks to features like being able to pick eachother up and toss them around and form into one giant sewn up zombie viking
- Solid controls with support for both keyboard and controllers and remappable bindings
- Great art style from Stick it to the Man! returns
- Fun and zany soundtrack
What's Bad:
- During actual levels the framerate feels noticeably less smooth than the cutscenes which are smooth as butter.  I was a bit baffled because FRAPS reported it was running at 60 FPS meaning maybe this is just the way it is supposed to animate.
- For everyone but the host, the online co-op experience is not very good at the moment.  Expect weird animation lag which takes away from the fun of combat as well as gold pick ups not even appearing meaning the host can snag all your precious gold before you.
- I would have liked to see more lite RPG elements.  Even a simple leveling system would have made me feel more invested into a particular character making the experience better overall.
Neutral Thoughts
- The humor will really resonate with some and leave others possibly annoyed with its mix of childish and immature sometimes mature humor.  If you like beat em' ups however I wouldn't be too concerned whether the game will make you laugh or not.
Should You Buy It?: A BIG Maybe
It's very frustrating with this game, because I do love the art style and beat em' ups are one of my favorite types of games, however certain issues did kind of ruin the experience for me to an extent.  While I can't speak for the PlayStation 4 version which may function flawlessly, I can't recommend picking this game up if you were planning on playing it with friends online because of the lag issues.  If you want to play locally it is a different story as it is more enjoyable, however still kind of held back by the strange framerate issues which both myself and another friend experienced on our machines.  It's a good game simply held back by technical issues, so while I can't easily recommend buying it right this moment, it could switch to a yes with a simple patch that fixes these framerate animation and lag issues.  However, if you were planning on playing locally and aren't too picky about framerate, then by all means go ahead and buy as it should be a great experience for you.  I really dislike Steam's two option review system as this game is definintely not an outright no, but at the same time I can't just recommend it everyone, but for now I'll leave it with a Yes and hope people actually read reviews.

This game would be on my top ten games of all time list.
I believe this is the best STALKER out of the initial three (Shadow of Chernobyl, Clear Skies and Call of Pripyat). I say this because I feel it is the least buggy, and most open.
It has the STALKER usuals: It's scary, with pitch-black abandoned Soviet bunkers and genuinely creepy monsters. It has atmosphere in droves. The AI behaviour of the wasteland's inhabitants feels convincing and leads to interesting happenings. And hunting for artifacts is better than ever.
It's also the most open and least linear STALKER. You are given an overarching mission and left at that. The game does not spoon-feed you quests or information, so you work towards this overarching mission piece-by-piece, and are always on the look-out for more clues. So it's almost relaxing... when it isn't scary.

Not a very good game, simply said.
First the superficial stuf out of the way, not much to say about it anyway:
Graphics and sound are fine, but nothing special. The controls are in order and the gameplay isn't all that bad.
Now for some deeper information:
Game isn't P2W, but when a rank 2 newbie enters a match with a bot made up of the most expensive parts in the store you know he got the premium package. Now I don't blame the player, but the devs made a horrible decision there. Premium unlocks every part, meaning many people that get it will be those that purely want to ruin other peoples day, not those that have a genuine interest in the game.
Premium packages can completely ruin the matchmaking, a matchmaking which is terrible to begin with. Without a premium package, the F2P player is forced to a single bot and limited parts they can have in storage, severely limiting long term customization. With different maps that may require different setups or leave certain setups relatively useless, this is quite punishing for F2P players.
The reward system is a complete mess. You gain exp which ranks you up, which is purely used for matchmaking, (Which is a horrible way to deal with matchmaking) and it feels like gaining exp is actually punishing.
You gain points to purchase new parts with each match, with a minimum of 1 for participation. An extra 2 is awarded if your team wins. You get another point for every 10 kills or 5 captures in conquest mode. So you'll normally gain 1-5 points, which isn't all that bad. (5 can be pretty difficult.) But a win is heavily dependant on your team, no matter how well you perform, so you may often get out with just a single point. On the other hand, if you perform too well you won't reach the 5 captures / 10 kill quota for the extra points.
Store parts generally range from 4 to 12 points to purchase.
The whole system really is horrible proven by how many important actions do not influence point gains, such as healing teammates, assist kills and taking a single point off a capped flag to stop the point gain, an extremely important tactic in conquest. This flawed system has a heavy effect on the gameplay which should be a lot more dynamic but instead forces people into select roles in order to attempt to go for those extra points.
Relatively crappy server browser compared to the standards of today, no filtering and a clear rank indicator allowing high ranks to gank low rank servers.
Lag plays an annoyingly large part in this game. People with pings all over the place isn't uncommon, dying from someone lag teleporting around you is quite frustrating. The whole way the game seems to deal with the latency issues is just "Let everything keep going the way it was when the lag started" meaning the most annoying sudden direction changes occur when trying to target your enemies. As your screen registers the enemy as still going ahead, or going in a circle, while, for example, it's actually behind you.
The "Gear Up" part, or bot building part is extremely simple and unsatisfying. It's no different than equipping your character with different armor, weapons and support items.
I do not recommend this game, and there are much better similar games out there. But if in doubt just give it a try - It's free, after all.

A brawler with great humor and characters. Especially fun with friends!
This devs  behind this game made Stick it to the man. Both games have a super unique art style, and cool animation.
You can choose between 4 different resurrected characters, each have their own weapons, and unique attacks. They even have their own unique dialogue within a level, which gives you extra reason to maybe replay levels.
The writing really had me laughing out loud. It's funnily written, and the voices are very well done. The music is cool and upbeat. The game does also have a few pop culture references, and breaks the 4th wall by mentioning things like Instagram and Tumblr. Normally I don't like that kind of stuff, but I feel like it's done in a funny way here.
Now the gameplay, I found it pretty similar to Castle Crashers. Both games don't have an entirely in-depth system, but I personally still had fun with it. You have your basic attack, as well as a signature move that is very unique to each character. One enemy can fly into the air and come down crashing into a group of enemies, while another can drop skulls that are launchable by any player.
One of the most fun features is you can pick up different objects and other players. You can even stack them. I loved picking up my teammate while they held random enemies. It's hilarious fun.
Collecting coins is satisfying, as you can then use them to purchase new equipment.
My main problem with the game is  you don't share money, so you need to co-ordinate with your partner to equally divide your loot so you can both upgrade. There were also a few graphical glitches in some of the cutscenes, but not too severe. Just a few blurry areas which took you away from the moment for a bit.
Overall though, it's so much fun. I love the world, voice acting, characters and jokes.

Talk about simple madness and fun! I really like the game.
Filled with absolutely cringey and hilarious humour you are one of four zombie vikings sent on a quest to get Odin's eye.
The game is certainly made for multiplayer in similar fashion to that of Castle Crashers, but even alone it is still wonderful. Lots of voice acting, cut scenes and humor to blend it all together. Along with lots and lots of slaughter, which you clearly can't have without the accompanying laughter.
Hedgy is my favourite hero, half man half porcupine zombie; and a being of few words.
The art style is simply great, everything is 2D to the extreme and suits the game rather well. During combat or cutscenes you'll notice that when a character turns they are simply a thin line when looked on from the side. It's a little detail I really appreciate.
Combat mechanics are very simple. Once again every smash-em up like. Fast weak attacks, jump, block/roll and a special. Each character does play very differently. Everything from small and fast, to slow and very powerful.
Also if you play single player you get Piggy to help you on your journey. He can give you a boost into the air to do a devastating dive bomb attack; or he can carrying a cannon on his back.
He's also small enough to be used as a projectile himself. Simply pick him up and charge up a throw attack. This actually combos rather well with his cannon barrage. Slap him to start the cannon and then pick him up and run around blowing things up.
Story wise, the game is very witty. Although if you don't like american humor and mannerisms you won't like the game too much. Even so I think they do suit the game, and the detail and amount of voice acting really adds to the game. Even some simple enemies are voiced over, and can have a go at you during combat.
Some of it, well, a lot is also downright cringey. This is either a positive, or negative depending on who you are and what you like.
The game wouldn't be complete without some loot though. You are vikings after all; so while you smash everything in sight collect as many coins as you can. These can be used to buy new weapons you've unlocked and runes which add anything from extra health to movement speed.
Be warned though, the average weapon is rather expensive, so if you do get the chance try and do some side quests. I helped a certain fluffy monarch and got a cat on a stick as a weapon. It's a great weapon.
All in all, Zombie Vikings is simply a blast and I would heartily recommend it to any fans of the genre that like silly games and some cringey dialogue.

I got pretty annoyed at some points but I wasn't annoyed at the game, just annoyed at my inability to get past an obstacle.
On the downside, the default controls are horrendous. I had to re-map my controls multiple times while playing but there's really only 2 actions so it's not too hard to get used to.
This game is really good if you just want something entertaining to sit down and play for a few minutes or half an hour. It definitely isn't something you would want to sit down and play for hours at a time as the gameplay is pretty repetitive and you would probably end up wanting to rip your hair out by the time you were finished.
Overall it looks great, sounds nice, and plays smoothly, but the controls are a bit mediocre.
It's fun to play, but what's currently there is nowhere near being worth 30$

Get this game if you want something as a break from your routine, both from your usual gaming and no doubt from real life. Alright, let's get the positives out of the way first:
Graphics  -  The game looks very nice. While not the most amazing game I've ever laid eyes upon, it is by no means ugly. The art direction makes the world feel very natural with the way the submerged buildings are covered in piles of flora. The main character has a nice design as well (she isn't given a name, so I'll just refer to her as
from now on).
Sound  -   The music in the game is good. Music is a form of media that is heavily reliant on one's taste, so you may enjoy the score more than myself. That said, I didn't find it mind-blowing, but I didn't think it was bad either. Just like with the visuals, the game has left me with a very neutral perception on the music.
Now for the negatives:
Gameplay  -  Phari's abilities are very slim. She can't jump, run, crouch, use weapons of any kind (which makes sense, since the game lacks combat altogether), swim or even interact with anything beyond contextual button presses. Most of the gameplay is split up between exploring the city in your boat, and climbing up buildings Assassin's Creed / Prince of Persia style with Phari. However, unlike AC or POP, Phari can't jump or wall-run, so how do you climb? You walk towards an object (be it ledge, pipe, ladder or vines) and she'll just start climbing. That's it. The entire game could be played with one hand if you didn't need to manually control the camera. The collectables are by-and-large meaningless as well, outside of the "main" ones. Which leads me to the next section...
Story / Length  -  Even though the game feels like it revolves greatly around the story, it's largely unimportant. In fact, I dare say that this is the most pointless and anticlimactic story that I've ever experienced in a video game. I'm going to spoil the entire story here (not that there's much to spoil) so be warned.
It doesn't help that the game can be beaten in 2 - 2.5 hours. You can add some game-time if you go out of the way for the collectables, but even then that would only be another 30 minutes to 1.5 hours at max. You don't even get anything for collecting all of them, just achievements as far as I'm aware.
Conclusion: While the game looks and sounds nice, it's severely impacted by the lack of content, replay value, story and engaging gameplay to warrant a purchase at full price. For $20, you can get far better games and a hell of alot more mileage to boot. I myself got the game for $2, and for that price, I'd say it's decent enough as a way to kill 2 hours, but then again, there are plenty of activities that are a much more productive use of 2 hours that are also totally free. Like, say, writing a review that is way too ♥♥♥♥ing long for it's own good because you've never written a review for a game before and you go into excruciating and unnecessary detail as a result. Just, y'know, as an example.
If you actually read the entire review, then thank you, and I'm so, so sorry.

Not enough content to justify purchasing at $10, let alone full price.

A bit hard to classify this game closest would probably be bullet-hell, except without you firing back as your hired NPC henchmen do that for you, with a touch of RPG and Rogue to finish it off. The cocktail is surprisingly good.
You can get notes (resource) by killing some foes, a certain unlockable structure and by standing still (generally ill-advised). With this you can then hire your henchmen, stronger ones unlocked as you proceed through the day (read: levels) and of course the more powerful the more costly. Upon dying you can use the second resource (gold) to permanently upgrade yourself or your henchmen.
It also comes with 2 minigames (to help gather some gold, both also unlock a henchman), one a running (just prevent getting hit) which is the least fun one IMO and a 'survival' mode where you randomly get henchmen to you with increasingly difficult enemies, which is a little more fun. But the best fun is of course gotten from the main game.

Did you ever play Limbo, Super Meat Boy and VVVVVV and think "these are fun games, but what somebody really needs to do is combine them together?" No, I didn't either and if you are the type of person coming up with these ideas it might be time to take a step back from gaming for a while.
But once you come back again, A walk in the dark might be just the game for you.
Going in I had very different expectations for the title. The screens promised typical indie platforming with a nimble cat protagonist. I also expected some sort of dark and foreboding story through long levels that ultimately didn't go anywhere. In reality, there is a little bit of story there but the game didn't seem to think it was important so I won't dwell on it either. What does matter is how it plays and this is where I got something quite different.
You take the before mentioned artwork of Limbo, add in short Super Meat Boy type levels and just when you are getting used to the game it becomes VVVVVV before cycling back through once again. It is a strange sort of mashup given the heritage is so obvious, but strangely the game doesn't really offer anything new. If you have played those games you should know what to expect here and very little more. The levels are short, if you die it is back to the start and pretty much anything you touch will kill you. Rinse and repeat, perhaps trying to get a better time until you are done.
While that sounds simple, this isn't to say it is necessarily a bad thing. What it does mean is it is just an uninspired journey, as you navigate the cat Bast and little girl Arielle through the 100 or so short levels. Arielle in particular needs special mention. She is much slower than the cat and doesn't have the double jump or crouch run abilities. On the other hand she has the VVVVVV gravity mechanic allowing her to switch the polarity to run along the ground or the ceiling. While this makes sense from a variety perspective it doesn't change the fact that her levels are a lot less fun to play. Then the game actually gives the exact same ability to the cat for certain stretches, making her inclusion even more redundant.
To make up for the lack of ideas the rest of the package needs to be exemplary. A walk in the dark doesn't do the worst job in terms of presentation and the sound and music are as good as you might expect from a modern indie game. It is just that there isn't much else to see or do. The cat (only once again) has a light collecting mechanic as you speed through levels. But unless you are particularly obsessive there doesn't seem to be a lot of point in beating the arbitrary times or gathering all the shiny things.
If anything this sums up the whole experience for me. The game is simply "there". The titles the mechanics are based on are quality efforts, so those same things work well here and you do get them all in one game. The controls are fine, if not perfect and the graphics and music do the job.
Would I then recommend it? Maybe, but only at a very cheap price and you would still be better off with the base games. I could only think that this game could serve as a gateway to the more fleshed out titles perhaps for a younger audience (but those games do an excellent job of leading in new players too).
So overall, I would have to rate this as a game I have played.

An underrated, underplayed gem of a game that will move you, haunt you, and mess with your brain.
You take the role of an armed hero, going to save a damsel captured by terrorists. Except, as it turns out, it's nowhere near that simple.
A big disclaimer for this game is that's it's really more of a walking simulator than an action filled-FPS. I happen to be a big fan of both walking sims and FPSers, so I didn't really mind, but if you're wanting an action-packed experience, prepare to be dissapointed.
That being said, it still manages to be incredibly engrossing, featuring a compelling, mysterious story that both picks at your mind enough to be frustrating, and unfolds enough of itself that even a dummy like myself can pick up on what's happening. The characters are well fleshed out, and the voice acting is absolutely
. I mean, just flawless. Possibly some of the best I've ever heard in a video game. Everyone from the most central character to the most throwaway grunt gets a voice actor that blows many AAA game's away, no competition. Massive props to all actors involved, it brings so much weight to the game.
The soundtrack is brilliant, an inspired mixture of classical strings and piano mixed with electronic distortion that's not quite like anything I've ever heard before. It's definitely worth a buy all on its own.
Beyond the fantastic "main" songs, the soundtrack is also used interestingly and effectively to convey emotion in a way that's actually rather reminiscent of theatre, getting you inside a person's head, getting you feeling their feelings using sound and music. It will warp disconcertingly when experiencing disorientation, drop into a sinister growl when near a shady figure, and rise into a sharp crescendo upon experiencing a relevation. It's good.
Unfortunately, now we have to get to the gameplay. As I said before, this game is more of a walking simulator in my eyes, but there are wide swaths of "real" gameplay thrown in, too. And they're not very good.
At the very best, it's lukewarm, spectacularly generic stealth, with a few minor gimmicks sprinkled into to kind of set it apart a little.
At the very worst, it's Call of Duty with a $5 budget.
Around three-fourths of the way in, some new gameplay mechanics are added that freshen this up considerably, but frankly, until that point, it's rather painful.
Thankfully, these segements are usually rather brief, and are blended with the story well enough that you never get pulled out entirely by them. In my opinion, they could have been removed entirely and the game would have been better off for it.
Other than the gameplay, my other gripes are very minor.
Firstly, this game is a little rough around the edges when it comes to both graphics and controls. Nothing major, but a little jarring for me, especially since I've been playing through some huge ultra-polished titles like Wolfenstein II and SOMA.
Secondly, you revisit a lot of the same small, linear levels again and again throughout the course of the game. On paper, this seems like it should be a bigger deal, but in practice I really didn't mind at all. This is because it's handled very well, with logical reasons for returing and strong story beats making each trip through what's basically the same level just as engaging as the first time around. It's an impressive example of a samller-budget game taking full advantage of its assets in a smart and well-done way that doesn't detract from the experience at all.
In summary, GET EVEN is flawed, a little rough, and absolutely delightful. Try it if you're looking for a game with powerful, mature storytelling, an inspired soundtrack and sound design, and an emphasis on player choice and discovery.
I got 7 hours out of it, but it has enough replay value I could see someone getting at least 10, if they were so inclined.

Coming from games like the Total War series or the Civilization games, you might notice similarities to both at once. Think Medieval Total War played completely on the overview map but injected with a touch of Civs intrigue and a lot more provinces/factions.
But that is barely, if ever scratching the surface. If you are a fan of Game of Thrones court politics or a history buff interested in having his own alternate timeline sandbox to play in, you are right at home.
Want to be an English duke who sleeps with the king's wife and then assassinates said king to inherit his realm? You can do that.
Want to start as a Hindu Indian raja and expand all the way to the Mediterranean while crushing the Arab Empire? You can do that.
Want to be an ambitious Norse pagan in Scandinavia who amasses enough men to conquer Britain and impose the worship of Odin on all of Europe? You can do that too.
Want to be a Zoroastrian prince in the Asian steppes who marries the princess of another khan but also has a b:astard son he got with his own sister? Guess what? Fair game.
Before said description drives you to buy everything, be forewarned.
1.If this is your first grand strategy game, you have a bit of a steep learning curve in the beginning that, once surpassed, simply makes the game "click".  I absolutely recommend a must watch tutorial by Arumba on Youtube that does a far better job explaining stuff than the otherwise solid in game tutorial. You also might want to start as an Irish count in 1066 to get a hang of the game mechanics.
2. The base game has come a long way since launch and you can have a solid amount of fun with just it in your library. But the meat of the game and the huge range of choices is locked behind DLC. That wouldn't be too much of an issue if there weren't so many of them. I would absolutely not recommend paying full price for everything - sales are your friends as they usually group a bunch of DLC together for a fair price. You also don't need many of the flavour DLC.
If you do buy the base game and decide to get the DLC gradually and later, for the safety of your wallet and for the biggest wealth of content, two are a must and are not expensive in sales - Sword of Islam and the Old Gods. Both unlock previously unplayable factions (aside from India) and Old Gods gives you an earlier starting date in the 9th century which many consider the best one (I tend to agree as Charlemaigne, while starting even earlier, isn't well balanced or pretty to look at). The rest you will get will be mostly based on your interests as each expansion tends to target one group of factions and mechanics.
If you do have all or most of its content, you might agree with me that this is the most content packed and interesting role playing experience you have or will play in a long time. Simply for the amount of fun, investment and character immersion it is as of now my absolute favorite game of all time, faults and all. If the two points above don't scare you off, give it a chance and you will be heavily rewarded. What is more, the game is probably the best intro to grand strategy games you can find. Europa Universalis IV is another game from the same developer focusing on the Early Modern Era and it has an interesting feature where you can continue your CKII saves in a new time period, potentially making your game last for over 1000 in game years.
Join in and welcome to CKII! Deus Vult!

This game is a trip.
It's hard to really describe it without spoiling too much, but the game's story deliberately messes with you and makes you question what is actually going on.  I'll say this much: the central conceit of the game revolves around a device that allows the user to play back memories.  It starts with a hostage rescue scenario and goes from there.  The chronology of things is intentionally distorted to keep the story mysterious and thrilling.  The only complaint I have is that the ending is long-winded and hits near soap opera levels of melodrama.  But it ties everything together into a very satisfying conclusion.
It's a shame then that the gameplay doesn't always live up to the story.
For instance, the game has a morality system in place where if you kill too many people in the memories you play out (specifically during sections where stealth is an option from what I can tell), you'll lock yourself into the bad ending of the game.  So, to get the good ending, you'll have to be stealthy.
And oh GOD the stealth.
It's not the worst in the world...it's just so barebones.  For a game that encourages you to sneak past enemies without killing them, there aren't a lot of options for doing so.  Why couldn't I have a non-lethal takedown move or a tranquilizer gun or ANYTHING really?  It would make certain sections feel less tedious, especially when guards are placed right on top of the EVIDENCE YOU NEED TO PROGRESS.  There's one level in particular that does this, and my solution was pretty much to forgo stealth and run in, scan the evidence, then run out before I got shot to death.
That's another part of the game: scanning things with your phone to gather evidence along with reading notes and stuff.  The game feels like a combination of Condemned: Criminal Origins and F.E.A.R. along with Dishonored for the morality system.  And it works very well.  It makes you feel like a detective combing through the memories and slowly piecing together what happened and why.  And just when you think you know what's going on, the game pulls the rug out from under you with another plot twist.
But if you ever do decide to give in to combat, you'll find that it's kinda weak.  It just feels clunky and sluggish if you try to play the game as a straight-forward shooter, which is probably why they de-emphasized the combat so much.  Not to mention that collecting all the evidence in a memory and unlocking another weapon feels pointless if you're trying to go for the good ending.  It's like "yeah great I got this new gun...that I'm NEVER GOING TO USE".
Despite all that though, this game oozes style.  As I said, it deliberately messes with you, with the layouts of levels changing or warping as you go and things appearing or disappearing when you turn back around.  It's an effective, trippy experience that still remains on my mind even after finishing it.  It's one of those games that would never be made under a AAA company's banner.  It's unique, bold, and ambitious...even if all of its parts don't work as well as they could.
It's not a game for everyone.  In fact, I don't know if it's a game for a lot of people.  But if you can persist past its problems, you'll find a gem of a game.  A flawed gem yes...but a gem nonetheless.

Bladur's Gate II is an old paused based RPG based on 2nd edition Dungeons and Dragons.  The game does very little handholding and very little explaining what the rules mean, which are two of the major complaints I've heard about this game.  I personally love the lack of hand holding, but.. to each their own.
The game really and truly feels.. alive.  It does this by having interesting and enjoyable characters, locations, and quests.  Sometimes things don't make sense.  Sometimes people say a little something that helps you along, but that little something is not recorded anywhere.  Sometimes things happen for seemingly no reason.  The end result?  The game feels like it's real.  People have their own wishes and desires, and you need to balance each party members' goals with your own.  Combat is fun, and very challenging.  You can make a choice that impacts you in ways you won't even realize until you play through again, which is one of the more amazing things about this game.  Modern games give you 'choices', where you 'choose' good or bad.  Baldur's Gate II blurs the line.  There are multiple paths to nearly everything, and very few (if any) of them are marked as "good", or "bad".  Say the right thing or have the right person with you and you might avoid combat.  Do the wrong thing and you'll get attacked without ever realizing there was another possibility.

This game has great potential. But as it is now, I wouldn't recommend it for the following reasons.
The bad
1. The cheating. There seem to be so many exploits, and hackers. Whenever you set up, grind and build a half decent base. Even in a pretty well defended location. You wake up the next day, and it is all destroyed. A couple of times, fair enough, but time after time starting from scratch. It gets repetative.
2. The commity at least in Asia where I play, seems rather obnoxious. Partly for the above reasons. If you like competative play, then fair enough. But if you are more into the roleplaying aspect, as I am. Maybe try one of the E.U or American servers.
3. Bugs and glitches. Well, early access. But I am tired of companies expecting us to pay to test their products, especially when their products are so easily maniputated by hackers who ruin it for people who are genuinely trying to play the game as it was designed to be played.
The Good
1. I never played Minecraft or any other survival games, but i love the building. It is really great making your own towns etc. But if you are into the building side. Stick in PVE.
2. Great setting. If you like conan, or ancient Egypt, you will be interested in the lore of the game.
3. It has really good potential IF the problems continue to be ironed out, and if the official servers are better moderated. At the moment, i fear this game will go the same way many other similar games went with a hackers ruining it, and developers who stop bothering once they have met their sales targets.
In summary, come back and look at the comments and opinions on this game in 6 months or so. At the moment it is very frustrating. I want to like it, I really do. And if the dewvelopers continue to work on it, then it will be a great game.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Number one vote for one of the most precise and beautiful games I have ever played. A Walk in the Dark is an amalgam of puzzle, platformer and speedrun, rolled into a gorgeously crafted game. In A Walk in the Dark you play 2 roles, a girl who is enamoured by her cat, and a cat that's enamoured by said girl. The storyline is pretty brief, the girl and cat are separated, and the two partake in finding each other. It's actually kinda heart wrenching to me personally as a lover of animals and the bond between what could ultimately be your best friend is understood by both the game and the player, it shows, and it's executed very well.
So let's talk about the meat of the game. I do prefer the cat levels so we'll start with them, there are two modes of play for the cat, platforming and speedrunning. Speedrunning has you on an auto-scroll chase to the end of the level, whilst avoiding obstacles by jumping from floor to ceiling, almost like flipping the gravity, similar to the popular indie game VVVVVV. The platforming levels will have you navigating some perfectly designed levels with the tightest controls you will ever use. The cat can control his jump height, his speed and can wallkick.
The girls levels are platform based, and the mechanics involved are very very similar to VVVVVV, albeit with a bit more inertia to make things difficult. The girls levels have sort of a floaty charm to it, separating it from VVVVVV.
The hook here for me is the wonderful aesthetics. The art style is so good, almost boasting a Limbo-esque feel with some wonderfully scrolling backgrounds, coupled with an ambient vibe soundtrack with lashings of deep piano. A Walk in the Dark is not easy, I think I actually now hate cats, and girls that float. The engine is so well designed and so precise it will have you on your knees, begging for something easier.
I jumped into A Walk in the Dark expecting some kind of cinematic platformer, as the inspirations from Limbo are apparent, at least graphically. What I got was a well designed, precise and gorgeous little platformer/puzzle game that has taken the very best from games like Limbo and VVVVVV, turned into something a bit more thought provoking. A game for fans of the genre, a game for anyone who likes being dominated by difficulty, cat-lovers and indie gamers alike. A Walk in the Dark is awesome and brilliant, one of the best indie games I've played. Very much recommended.

I wish there was an 'uncertain' option for reccomendations, instead of just 'yes' or 'no', as that's how I feel.
When you start out, you have a freebie load with junk gear. You can buy any new items you want with wallet points that aren't that hard to earn (You get 1 for participation, 2 more for winning a round,  1  for capping 5 points in a round. items cost around 3-10 points, and the rounds are about 15 minutes). If you want enough items for more than 2 loads, you'll have to pay. No problem with the wallet system, it's most certainly not pay to win.
Now onto the tanks. I expected a bit more variety... Here's a list of the major parts categories:
1. Weapons. These attach to turrets or to the hull (On the 'hammer' hull. The hammer hull is a huge joke as the weapon cannot really be aimed, fires independently of the turret, and the hull itself is weak.)
You can get flamethrowers, machine guns, sniper rifles, lasers (That have a stupid velocity and travel about the same speed as machine gun bullets, which are also commicaly slow.), cannons, plasma guns, and several others. Note, you can only fire 1 weapon at any time, even if you have twin turrets, a weapon on your hull, or a turret with dual weapon slots.
2. Hulls. Your propulsion system and your turret(s) both attach to the hull of your tank. The hull provides armor, a larger hitbox, and (for some hulls) a place to attach a useless weapon or two supports.
3. Turrets. There are many turrets, with many different goals. All provide varying hitpoints, rotation speeds, weapon slots (Up to two, but they cannot be fired together), and support slots. Some do not have any supports.
4. Supports. Since you've been wondering what they heck I keeo saying 'supports' for, I'll explain.
Supports are guns, armor units, healers, weight reducers, etcetera. They do less damage or are less effective than any other items designed for their task, but can be fired with your weapon. Hence, you will always want a turret with a support on it, as they give you a significantly better DPS.
5. Propulsion. Tanks can be moved by treads, legs, fans, or even a... slime ball. Treads are generally better as all-rounders but cannot strafe. Fans can strafe and move across water, but are less powerful. Legs let you climb onto walls but are unpredictable, awkward, and generally slower. The slime ball is a strafing tread.
So how do the developers get their cash if this can all be earned, and quite easily, in a few days of playing? As a F2P you have limited item storage space, although you can store more parts as you level up. (Last I leveled, I could store 11 parts, which was enough for me anyhow.)
Now onto the technical details, where the tasting gets unpleasant. This game, put frankly, has the optimization of a marathon runner carrying dumbells and pushing a wheelbarrow. My PC does better handling Planetside 2, an extremely cpu intensive game, with 200 players in a battle, than it does this little low-poly tank game with 8 vs 8. Kinda ridiculous.
Controls are tanky, mouse sensitivity can be changed by a sliderbar with arbitrary numbers on it. There is no raw input option.
To wrap up, how's the balance? Are there ridiculously overpowered weapons that only jerks use? Yes and no. Sniper rifles do insane damage, but have stupidly powerful scopes (probably 6x zoom on small maps), bullets slower than real life arrows, and the tank itself jitters in a ridiculous manner. Flamethrowers will pawn anything within their grasp faster than you can say 'flammenwerfer', and don't have any true downsides on a fast tank.

There are few games in the world which managed to confuse me with plot twists and this is one of them. Does it mean that this is a bad game then? No, not at all!
Get Even is a wonderful game which tells the story of Cole Black; seemingly a man who has nothing special about him. He awakens in a room with a mobile phone. The game starts off by telling you to stay away from a handover site, as people have a girl kidnapped and there's nothing you can do to stop them.
Being the hero you are, you try to do your best to save the girl. But, as predictable as it may be, you fail at this.
A few moments later, you realise this is a flashback and that this has all happened in the past. You are then put to the test by a man called Red, who orders you to investigate what really happened before and during the kidnapping via reliving past memories.
You are then sucked into a plot with so many twists that you are like "but wait, I thought that... or was it... hang on, is Cole Black as innocent as he seems? Or is there more to it?"
The most interesting about this game is the soundtrack. From very suspenseful music during suspenseful moments, to very dramatic and very sad sounding themes, this game is a gem in that aspect.
A lesser gem is the voice-acting. The main character's voice acting feels a bit off, as if there's almost no emotion. This may be due to the fact that Cole Black has no recollection of the events that happened and therefore, doesn't know how to react to certain situations.
Another aspect of the game I found intriguing is the so-called Cornergun. It allows you to (how surprising!) shoot around corners.
The puzzles in this game aren't too hard, but what makes it great is that you can "revisit" missions in order to improve your 100% collection rate of documents and audio recordings. Doing this "rewards" you eventually ( I won't spoil, but it's worth it, trust me ;) )
All in all, I liked this game a lot. And it has a certain replayability to it. But once you finish the story, the replayability loses its interest, due to you knowing what really went down and who Cole Black is.
So be sure to check out this game on Youtube. If you like a complicated plot, with many twists, and a great OST; then this is the game for you!

I can't immediately think of any game I've ever played that has such an amazing story. If you've ever seen a movie that causes the audience to sit in contemplation for 5 minutes while the credits roll, this is the game that does the same.  It throws away the typical good guy/bad guy character models and sticks to a really interesting and almost scientific model of how we remember our lives and how we alter our own memories.
The sound design is perfect.  The score is incredible and fitting in every moment, and all the little details are there.  Their is 3d audio for headset users.  When you are sneaking near enemies or are about to be spotted, you can hear the main character's breathing intensify.
Everything feels very handcrafted, the details in each room, the clues that are scattered about, the little plot points hidden in conversation.   Initially it feels that the memories are randomly chosen, but as the story progresses you learn the logic of the environment.  To me, this is everything a story driven game should be.  I believe it is a perfect 10/10

Crusader Kings II is an amazingly fun game with the right people, although does have a few grudgingly annoying features.
The game has dozens of DLCs which is a bit irking considering most are features which should have been added in free updates. However, only one person needs to own the DLCs to play with them on multiplayer (he has to host the game). Thus, the usage of DLC in this game, like other Paradox Games, is fair, but the amount of DLC is a bit excessive if you ask me. If you plan to buy this game, you should all agree on one friend to buy the CKII DLC pack to enjoy many of the features I will discuss below.
The ruler designer/custom nation creator features are incredibly fun, and my friends and I will often spend over an hour designing the most outrageous nations and leaders. Many laughs will be had when one of your friends creates a completely broken overpowered character while another makes an inbred, hunchback moron control half of Western Europe.
The game features many fun mechanics allowing you to host events, engage in intrigue, or gain power within your religious faction. You can play anyone as small as a local mayor or Duke, or the King of the Holy Roman Empire. Using wit, you can grow your nation, or cause others to fall apart by supporting rebels. Many things are possible, and this game offers a level of depth that in my opinion, can't be matched by Civ V or many other strategy games. Relationships with important individuals are a major aspect of the game, and are affected by factors such as your traits, religion, and actions throughout your reign. You must balance relationships with your own family, councilmembers, vassel stakeholders, other nations, religious figures, noblepeople, and many more. You must also ensure the continued existence of your dynasty by getting down dirty and ensuring your own children don't kill each other (they do, unfortunately enough for power grabs). Overall, all these features, as I mentioned previously, give extreme depth to the game, and discussing the hilarious random events that occur to your friends playing with you will surely lead to some good memories.
A few things I don't like - sometimes, I feel that the relationship mechanisms and family systems are a bit too petty and require too much micromanaging when I am often more concerned about taking over Europe. Another Paradox game which is almost perfect in my eyes is Europa Universalis IV. This game is much more grand in scale and enables you to do much bigger things without as many petty game mechanics. If you can only buy one game, I would encourage you to get that instead of this, although CKII has its many charms. Secondly, war REQUIRES a Casus Beli and a lot of Prestige, which can make some conflicts take a frustratingly long time to set up before you can actually fight. EUIV also does a much better job with this. However, if you wish to play less aggresively, this shouldn't be a problem at all, you will only notice this if you are trying to grab lots of land, which the game doesn't seem to want you to do.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but would recommend Europa Universalis IV more. I would also only recommend playing this game with friends and I would recommend that one of the friends you play with (or you) get the DLCs as there isn't as much you can do with the base game. Get them a pizza or something better to make it up to them.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 - 2017 GEM.
Finding a game that mixes RPG, D&D, customizable class/ characters, good story telling, beautiful aesthetics, crafting system, tactical turn based battle, and option to play co-op? This game pretty much offers it all up on a silver plate.
I've played the first Divinity Original Sin, and my impression of that wasn't so strong, however I decided to give this a try, and it definitely floored me.
None too many games I've played have done a swell job in buffing lores, stories, and open ended quests for you to explore. You don't have to be a lore-lover or a rouge type gamer to enjoy this. There's a sweet spot for everyone.
I went looking for a plain old adventure-with-consequences game, and spent more time reading up short lores here and there instead of speeding through it.
I can't believe I've spent 80+ hours (solo play) and still haven't completed it yet. Actually for the first chapter, I managed to spend 8-9 hours (and this was just purely exploring and figuring out quests). Halfway through the game, it even conjured up my nostalgia for Dragon Age 1.
CONS/ AREAS FOR IMPROVEMENT:
-Sometimes there are NO warnings before huge consequences take place. And when it happens, it's too late to alter (unless you are bothered to load up a game save 1 hour ago+). This happened a few times for me, the most painful one for me being: I couldn't take my companions to the next chapter because I'd missed that one window to convince them. They were absolutely gone. I loaded a previous save, but ever since that happened, I ended up tracking quests on wikia instead in fear of a major slip up

Необычный квест. Необычный – это первое, что хочется о нем сказать (хотя он похож на Мисты и недоброй памяти Обдакшн). Понравилось графическое решение, интересно выглядят персонажи, красиво сочетается достаточно реалистичный вид вещей и такое странное небо. Интересная озвучка, она скорее понравилась, чем нет, хотя женскому персонажу хотелось добавить чуть-чуть больше живости, вот капельку бы. Хотя сам факт, что озвучка есть – уже огромный плюс для инди-квеста.
Понравилось, что практически все вещи можно брать в руки, бросать, и далеко не все из них пригодятся. Это интереснее, чем брать подсвеченные предметы и думать заранее, куда их придется всунуть. Как будто действительно очнулись в непонятной, полной хлама комнате и стали разбираться, где мы вообще. Но иногда бывают казусы – если игра такая реалистичная, почему ягоды с дерева можно сбить только одним предметом, а не кинуть что под руку попало? Ну, и когда выкинешь с глаз долой какой-нибудь надоедливый предмет, а он потом понадобится…
Категорически не понравилась часть с кубиками. Это даже не головоломка, там думать не надо. Это аркадная часть – надо быстро бегать и кидаться кубами нужного цвета, судорожно путаясь в кнопках, пока противодействующий кубический вирус все не сожрал. Это неинтересно, это неуместно в квесте, слава небесам, что можно эти части скипнуть, но чтобы скипнуть, надо проиграть. То есть 5-10 минут отстрадать на кубических галерах все равно будь добр.
Напрягал движок, у меня пару раз была ситуация, когда я намертво застревала в каких-нибудь кустах или заборах, приходилось загружаться. Движок просто не создан для динамичного прохождения, поэтому неприятно было столкнуться с необходимостью лазить по верхотурам с дырками в полу, как ассасин. Только ловкости и управляемости ассасина герой квеста, к сожалению, лишен.
Ну и к главному – сюжет. Он, безусловно, интересен и цепляет. Как так получилось, что герой очнулся непонятно где и ничего не помнит? Что за девушка-робот у него на столе? Что вообще случилось с этим миром? И распутывать загадки постепенно, находя вокруг какие-то газеты, бумажки, плакаты и прочую макулатуру, мне понравилось. Это еще один вариант постапокалипсиса, и весьма неплохой по завязке.
Испортила впечатление концовка. Она скомканная и абсолютно непонятная. Молния, бабах, два человека обедают, смска, титры, все. Я поняла смысл смски, поняла, что за девушка за столом, но когда это происходило, как связано с основными событиями игры, как это вообще возможно – не объяснили. Разобраться, как я поняла, все-таки можно, но если заранее облазить все локации по сантиметру и прочитать абсолютно все документы очень внимательно. Не должно так быть – здесь же открытый мир, пусть и маленький. Очень легко что-то не заметить и упустить. Концовка все-таки должна давать основные пояснения, а для самых внимательных можно прятать по кустам только детали, которые послужат вишенкой на торте, но не будут ключевыми для понимания сюжета.
И второе – сюжет все-таки не продуман до конца. Он четко вписывается в границы научной фантастики, но в нем очень много допущений и мало объяснений, чего жанр не приемлет. Как минимум ключевое событие развязки нужно было хоть как-то обосновывать.

Early disclaimer: this game is EA. That means there will be constant bugs, updates,  and hotfixes and the like. I've played several EA games and this is on the right track and is continuously improving. Do not buy this game yet if you expect a finished product.
That being said, the game is in a very playable state, and even after 90 hours I still find myself wanting to play as much as possible. The devs have stated their inspiration is a mix of Ark and Skyrim. With 300+ hours in Ark, I can tell you Conan is undoubtedly better already in terms of optimization and server lag. The graphics are great, and performance is as good as you could expect.
The biggest drawback right now: do NOT play on official servers. Officials are overrun with Chinese exploiters and griefers. Due to the gods system, which is not at all balanced yet, the chances of having an actual base for more than 3 days on an official server are very low. For the Chinese, the concept of victory in PVP survival games is centered around driving players off of servers. They grind like crazy, build up god tokens, and completely wipe the map in weekly or biweekly cycles. Duplication glitches, building inside rocks, glitch jumping--these are all completely fair game to Chinese players. I'm all for PVP, but why even have a building system when it only takes 3 hours of work to nuke the entire map? Official servers typically sit around 10-20 players after a wipe or balance update, but quickly drop down to 5 and then 0 once Chinese griefers take charge.
Right now, you are much better served playing on unofficial servers with active admins and balance friendly settings. Limited god timers, limited pvp windows,  and/or unofficial rulesets are what make this game playable right now. This allows for fair pvp by having to use the somewhat-balanced explosives system on high tier buildings. Without gods nuking the map every 3 days, you can actually build large bases or complexes that take a fair bit of work to raid effectively, which I am sure is exactly what the devs had in mind. The construction system has some bugs that need to be worked out, but even with the current, limited selection of pieces you can craft some truly excellent buildings and bases.
The top thing this game needs right now is a VPN and/or low ping ban, and the devs have said this is on their to do list. This will keep players on their geographically correct servers and substantially improve ping and quality of life on official servers. The devs have promised some form of god defense, which will greatly help to stabilize and balance the game as well.
Updates have been coming on a weekly basis like clockwork, and since launch the dye system and catapults have gone live, in addition to several bug fixes and some additional content such as weapons, armor, etc. Tameable animals and mounts are coming, as are new biomes, dungeons, and an NPC purge event. The devs have been responsive and open to feedback, even going as far as giving exploit hunters $100-$500 USD for uncovering serious glitches and exploits. They seem to truly care about the game, and also have a rough roadmap on how to make it great. I think this has the potential to grow into something big.
PVP and creative building aside, right now there is rougly 100 hours of content, although this number could very well triple in the coming months. Overall, the game is great fun, albeit a bit prone to instability due to constant tweaks and updates. I find myself wanting more, and can definitely recommend it even in its current state. Being honest, $30 is a very fair price for a game that will definitely be $60 when it releases in full next year.

Jet Set Radio was a game originally released for the SEGA Dreamcast back in 2000 before SEGA decided to pull the plug on making home consoles. The game received near wide critical acclaim and of course SEGA decided to port the game onto many other platforms, including that of the PC
Jet Set Radio takes place in Tokyo, Japan. Where rival gangs graffiti each others turfs to gain control and a DJ runs a pirate radio station simply known as Jet Set Radio. The Police, SWAT and an annoying detective try to stop you, who make part of the GG's, from graffiting walls nd ruining Tokyo
The graphics are of a type of Borderlands graphic style, which is shell shaded and very colorful, which is really nice. Music as well is really good and not for one second did I mute the music. The voice acting is okay, but not the best. The game got released in 2000 thus some gameplay elements may be a bit out dated or stiff but overall not bad gameplay. The only thing I will comment about is the jumping, it is awful, when you what your character to jump somewhere, he/she decides to jump to the other side. Another thing is when you try and outrun the police, SWAT or annoying detective, your stamina runs low so quickly! So you are in the fire line of dying!
I remember playing Jet Set Radio on my cousin's Playstation and it was a lot of fun to play, now I can say that I own the game personally on my PC, but, how does it fair as a port?
As a port I must say it is one of the worst ports I have seen. Performance wise it runs well on modern day systems and not once did I encounter a crash, but to play, it is near impossible on a keyboard. The controls are so confusing that I gave up after a few minutes of playing and started playing on my controller. This game was not designed for a keyboard in mind, the game's button prompts are all XBOX/XBOX 360 controls. So much so, I had a hell of a job trying to figure which button does what
I would only recommend this game to people who either have a controller or have played/love Jet Set Radio, otherwise, don't bother...
