A Walk in the Dark is an esoteric compilation of odd and ends ripped from some of the most memorable platformers of recent years. The influences of Super Meat Boy, VVVVV, Limbo, and others are easy to spot but this proves to be its biggest downfall, as while those games pushed the genre forward A Walk in the Dark stagnates it. By doing nothing unique it doesn't manage to distinguish itself, and simultaneously fails to live up to those that it so liberally borrows from.
Encompassing 100 levels, gameplay is split between three distinct styles of play. The majority consists of typical minimalistic platforming, which from the start establishes the extremely taxing difficulty that only gets harder. The other two portions are slower paced sections that swapped your jump for a gravity switch mechanic (ala VVVVV), and runner-esq cave levels that again task you with switching gravity to avoid the oncoming obstacles.
While the different parts are solid enough, I was never impressed by the level designs or use of the different mechanics. It's very "by-the-numbers" and I feel a wasted opportunity to do something original with the interesting setting and character. Controls while mostly tight lose a lot of their precision once you're in the air, and the inability to quickly turn on a dime lead to many unjustified deaths. More troublesome than that is the unpredictable wall jump which often doesn't work and repeatedly sent me into the row of spikes or endless pit almost always at the bottom.
The one thing the developer did get right was the soundtrack, which is a beautiful arrangement of instrumental pieces that somewhat makes up for the otherwise underwhelming package, and does a great job matching the tone of the environments. The artwork is also gorgeous to look at, but it felt directionless. A handful of short vignettes attempt to flesh out the meager shell of a narrative, but they completely fail in that regard and left the game feeling hollow and meaningless. Great stories and platformers might not often go together, but in this case the world the developer was trying to create is simply begging for something, anything to drive the experience forward.
That could have been the communal aspect of competing in speedruns, but again the developer flounders by placing what ought to be a central prominent part of the UI (leaderboards) behind far too many menus, requiring you to quit back to the map and then check times level by level. It's a clunky and dated design decision, and frankly feels as if it was included out of some sense of obligation, with little thought as to the actual implementation.
If you are a fan of challenging platformers you could certainly do worse than A Walk in the Dark, but on that same note you could easily do a lot better. Taken on its own merits I actually found it mostly enjoyable (if also frustrating), but with how oversaturated the platforming genre has become there are dozens of more interesting and fun options available. In the end it seems the developers were themselves walking in the dark, and never quite managed to find their own way for the game they created.

The problem with this game lies in the technical aspects. A fun game occurs after:
-You successfully are able to launch Awesomenauts
-You find enough players to make a game
-Aforementioned players are in the same country as you
-The game doesn't throw a tantrum and your ping remains stable (assuming the previous two criterion are fulfilled)
-VSync doesn't abandon you mid game and your screen doesn't tear like rice paper
-Your GPU that can run Far Cry 3 at 60 frames doesn't abandon you in game

And then...
-You join a full game, and not 20 minutes into a team that's getting stomped
-Matchmaking makes a game that all players are of relatively similar skill levels
-You do not join a game where the enemy team is a premade, and using Skype to wreck your team
Bit of a hurdle, huh?
This game shows tonnes of promise, and when you actually get into a good game, lots of fun is to be had. But when you consider that Dota 2 and League of Legends emulate a similar style of gameplay, without the problems or the pricetag, Awesomenauts falls flat.
The dwindling player base and plethora of new technical problems makes an otherwise stellar addition to your library merely mediocre, and I cannot recommend this.
tl;dr - fun game, infinite technical issues, don't buy.

GET EVEN is an amazing expiriance. A fantastic tale about memories and regrets.
The main thing that makes this game feel so great is probably the world of the game itself. The world of GET EVEN is incredibly creative and interesting from the unique way of storytelling to a great soundtrack that not only helps to tell the tale but also feels like It's the part of It. Exploring it gave me an incredible feeling, like I was looking at and analysing a beautifull painting.
THE STORY: You play as Cole Black. Your mission is to save the hostage, hovever it turnes out the hostage is attached to a bomb. Before you get the chance to save the girl, the bomb goes of. Suddenly you wake up in an unknown location. Now a mysterious perona called Red takes you on a journey to relive your lost memories to find out what really happened.
The story is quiet simple but the way it is told is interesting and memorable. It also asks some interesting questions about the memories that will keep you thinking. Fans of "Inception" will definately like it.
THE GAMEPLAY: Gameplay focuses on exploration and solving puzzles as well as either stealth or shootouts (which ever you prefer). The main devices that will help you in the game are phone with number of gadgets like uv light, scanner or heat sensor and The Corner Gun that will allow you to look around and shoot from a save place. These gadgets are really fun to use. The phone will help you solve a number of puzzles, find clues and avoid enemies. The Corner Gun is really satisfying to use when looking around while surrounded by enemies as well as finding creative ways to shoot them around the corners.
THE SOUNDTRACK: The score of GET EVEN by Olivier Deriviere is simply amazing. All the tracks have a deep connection to a place you are in as well as the whole story. The haunting sound of a clock you will hear through out the whole game, the sound of Black's heavy breathing turning into music when you engage in combat, The lunatics in the asylum rhythmically singing "The Party! The Party!" louder and louder as you progress. These are just some of the incredibly creative ideas you have to expiriance for yourself.
THE VOICE ACTING: The voice acting is good. You get a number of autentic sounding voices that really build the characters. Close to the end of the game voice actors give some amazing performances you need to expiriance for yourself.
THE GRAPHIC: The graphics are all right at first glance but when you look closer they aren't that impressive. Locations might also get repetetive. Probably the weakest part of the game.
THE CONCLUSION: GET EVEN, in My opinion is a must have. It is rough around the edges in some aspects but there is enough good that you can ignore the bad. It is an amazing expiriance you won't forget.

So many things to do, so many stories to act out... but there is a feeling that, once you've played one dynasty, you've played them all. The Hindu vs. Muslim vs. Christian vs. Nordic dynamic doesn't afford a variety of playstyles as much as it adds slightly different flavors to a single, overarching playstyle. You can spice it up yourself by role-playing, goal-setting, or imposing restrictions upon your character, but ultimately (and surprisingly), the game suffers from a lack of variety.
What makes the game worth it are the wacky, random stories that write themselves: that one time you had to murder all your uncles, or throw all your sons in prison; fighting (or fending off) a crusade, plus two other wars on the side; your one character that managed to kill the white lion; seducing all three of the royal concubines.
All in all, buy it (and the DLCs!) on a sale and give it some time. You'll be happy you did.

I don't know how I feel about this game.
It's fairly good for what it is but it's not what I expected at all. The trailers and pictures made it seem like it was going to be a psychological horror shooter and it kind of is, but that all takes a back seat to the narrative and hunting for clues and notes. The story (and game) starts out strong but it slowly starts becoming more and more stale. I love games with good stories but this hardly feels like you are actually in control of anything. This game seemed really promising and could of easily been a cult classic of sorts if it was actually done better.
The game is full of small choices you need to make in order to progress, which are all suprisingly well done and make you feel like they have weight. For example, if you decide to let a cultist out of his cell he will send the asylum into chaos and kill a few characters you would of otherwise met.
The entire time you play you are critized for not doing exactly what "Red", your guide/captor, tells you to do. If you even once decided to go against Red (this includes killing anyone you can stealth around) you are locked into the bad ending. You can go back into the memory and redo the levels (which I did after I got the bad end) but it was extremely tedious and boring.
The game is also full of unskippable cutscenes which hide themselves as being gameplay by locking the game in first person and giving the player control during them. The worst of these cutscenes are the "Fallout 4 Kellog's mind circus sideshows". (Title WIP) this is when they do the whole you are inside their mind/memories. Walk over here to this part of the memory while you can see synapses everywhere. These are a neat gimmick at first but you quickly realize how lazy and boring they are, especially when you've seen the gimmick for the 15th time in the last 2 hours. This game is the epitome of telling instead of showing.
This game is basically Dear Esther with very mediocre gunplay and bad stealth gameplay slapped over it. Walk down the corridor until the story progresses and sometimes shoot things or sneak past them. Oh and there are simplisitic puzzles on occasion.
It was a fairly enjoyable experience minus a few things that were infuriating, but if I had known I would feel the way I feel about it now before I bought it I would not have spent 15 dollars on Humble for it.

Nexon has developed a reputation for releasing games that, while great on a gameplay level, are filled with microtransactions and alterations to the game to force you to buy them. While Dragon Nest continues this legacy to a degree, it's not as bad as other games the company has put out. From a gameplay standpoint Dragon Nest is very fun with its combo-based combat. The six classes (as of this review) are all fun to play in their own ways, and the specializations they can take let them further define their styles in unique ways. While the early levels can be a bit of a slog, once you get to around level 30 the game really opens up in terms of the skills you get. And whether your fighting alone, with a friend, or against a friend the combat is always enjoyable.
It's unfortunate then that the rest of the game around it is a little shallow. Quests are your standard affair, either go here and kill this or go here and collect this. A few quests spice things up in interesting ways such as giving you an overpowered NPC helper or giving you a unique enemy to fight, but such quests are few and far between. Thankfully if fighting AI monsters gets boring you can always fight your fellow man in PvP. PvP is fairly balanced (with a few exceptions) with an emphasis on personal skill rather than your gear and stats.
This brings me to the much despised part of any Nexon game, the cash shop. While games like Mabinogi and Maplestory are pretty much pay-to-win when it comes to their cash shop, Dragon Nest really doesn't feel that way. Sure the costumes give nice stat boosts and there are items that protect your gear from breaking while enhancing them, but such things aren't necessary unless your absolutely serious about min-maxing. Even then you should be fine as long as you invest in a decent skill build and have practiced enough to use your skills to their fullest. You even get a special level up reward box that gives out certain cash shop items like storage and inventory space, meaning you don't have to spend a dime so long as your patient.
I have a feeling alot of people have/will blow this game off just because Nexon is publishing it, which is a shame. While it has its flaws Dragon Nest is a pretty decent action game if you put some time in it. It might not be the best game ever but it certainly is leagues above some of Nexon's other games. I advise you to give it a try and at least play up till level 30 or so before you pass your final judgement on the game.

- Play as an FPS, you use a mobile phone as your HUD , switch between apps for Map, Camera, thermal, Text messages etc, I personally really didn't like this as it felt clunky and more often than not was a pain to keep switching between map, and Thermal (your Right click to zoom with weapons is done via Thermal / Camera so you can't have map and this open at once.

Tengami is a beautiful game, with a lot of thought into its design, no doubt. The pop-up book style and the more traditional Japanese aesthetic are impressive, and the soundtrack adds a lot to the game's atmosphere. In that sense, it's great!
However, the overall "game" just falls short. As a game, it has nothing. Even as an "experience", it just feels empty.
It's clearly an iOS game, and not in a good way. Perhaps it's good to have on your phone and play 10-15 minutes before going to bed, but nothing else.
So, what are the problems?
First, the sound design in general isn't very well implemented. Half of the time, the tracks simply stop playing (and I'm not sure what triggers it, they simply stop) leading to silence... In the other half, the tracks stop, and another begins. It just feels unnatural and "breaks the immersion". What could have been a really nice experience will leave a bitter taste after that.
Then, there's the problem with the puzzles/story. The puzzles are meaningless. At least they seem to be, and the game never does anything to change that. There aren't really unique a well explored mechanics. 70% of them are simply trial and error -- although not the frustrating kind -- simply going up and down through the pop-up book's layers. They're ok, but are simply there to make time, I guess.
The other 30% require a bit more attention from the player: for example, spotting little characters more or less hidden in the pages, or counting the symbols hidden in structures.
But even these are meaningless. They have no real connection with the experience, other than being puzzles set in a pop-up book.
The story is presented through a couple of cutscenes, but there really isn't much of it, at all. At the end of each chapter, you're presented with a Haiku as well (I think that's what it is, anyway: a very short poem, composed with 3 phrases, aiming to capture a single moment). The problem with that is that you don't really have access to those poems after seeing them... if you didn't write them down, it's not really conducive to interpretation or whatever else...
Again, the puzzles are simple, but not elegant or meaningful. They're simply there.
It's a cool visual idea, but then they've done absolutely nothing with it, game-wise. A great example of an iOS game that actually uses every aspect to deliver a very interesting experience, despite being very clearly design for mobile phones and short playtime, is Year Walk. That game is brilliant. And every single puzzle and scene is meaningful in some way. And the game makes you replay it several times, each time giving you a bit more insight into its meaning.
If you're looking for that kind of experience, definitely get Year Walk.
It's unfortunate that Tengami is as empty as it is... It's a very beautiful game, but it's just that. Pretty to look at. Here's hoping that they do something more with their next games!

This game gets a thumbs up from me, but I would like to help other potential players calibrate their expectations, because I was at times frustrated by it.
In total you'll experience a humdrum and yet cleverly told story, with really excellent voice acting. But it does seem to drag too long, and does at times get overly dramatic. Nevertheless, it will still manage to keep you on your toes and surprise you.
But, the gameplay. The game often appears like many kinds of games--FPS, stealth FPS, adventure--but at its heart it is a walking simulator: a linear story made of levels which allow for varying degrees of interactivity but in the end your goal is really just to get from point A to point B. This confused me, because in some of the more open levels I thought I had a deeper goal that would require exploration and creative thinking and reward them. But, no, there wasn't anything else I needed to do. If there were obstacles, I had to kill them, sneak past them, or even run past them. But all that mattered was getting to point B.
And that's really fine, as long as you understand that. I often got lost in the tumbleweeds because it felt like I was a protagonist in an “adventure.” But exploration just rewards you with collectibles and achievements, nothing that's intrinsic to the game itself. If that sounds good to you, then you would probably like
...
...Except that there those obstacles at times can be quite challenging, and this is from someone who plays quite a bit of FPS-type games. When all I wanted to do was get deeper into the story, I found the lackluster and difficult combat scenes to be frustrating, especially when dying sent me way back to the beginning of the scene.
So, understand what this experience is about, play it on lowest difficulty, go with the flow of the story, and I think you'll have fun. I did despite the frustrations!
Oh, and I should add that I played this game on a 3D projector using Tridef and a user-contributed profile. Looked amazing!

Tengami is a beautiful game, no doubt.  But words that more accurately describe the game would be 'Different to anything else you'll ever play'.
In essence, Tengami is a point-and-click adventure game.  One with an original mechanic upon which the entire game world is built.  The game plays like paging through a pop-up book.
The genius of the game design comes in the fact that some of the puzzles are tightly integrated with this game mechanic and traversing the world is a joy.  Patience is needed though as you can't make your character run or move faster at all.  Those with little patience might have a hard time playing this game and get frustrated quickly.
The hero tying the game together is the excellent music and sounds.  Soothing melodies create a fantastic atmosphere and made me want to close my eyes and listen to the music on repeat.  Even though the music sometimes abruptly cut to silence (possibly some bugs), the surrounding environmental sounds filled up the silence and kept the atmosphere intact.
Great as this game is, the end comes fairly quickly (it took me about 90 minutes to play through) and left me wanting much more at the end.  Hopefully this is the first in a series and we'll see more of the same from Nyamyam.
Highly recommended.

A cryptic story presented with excellent voice acting, good writing and decent pacing.
The gameplay can arguably be a bit contradictory to itself, and parts of it not well fleshed out.
Visuals are for the most part good, except for some texture loading that can be a bit jarring.
It ran quite good on my rig, around 90-110fps @ 1440p and max settings with a GTX 1080 and overclocked i7-3770.
You are presented with two options on how to complete most of the levels.
or
The Corner Gun, a weapon that is available to you for most levels is an awesome concept, and well executed.
It's tempting to use the Corner Gun in order to just plow through the levels on a power trip, but the game urges you not to.
The concept is that if you go in guns blazing, the memory you are in will be corrupted.
I like the concept, it presents you with an easy and tempting method, at the cost of possible corruption in the level you are exploring, thus altering the story ever so slightly.
The problem comes when you try to do it non-lethal stealth, and after reading about it's implications, it was something I gave up on rather early on in the game.
The only stealth mechanic this game has to offer is "crouch" and "sneak". It lacks any depth, and it is terribly boring.
Having watched all endings too, I would argue that the "reward" does not justify the struggle.
And giving up on the stealth aspect of the game, was the best thing I could have done.
I just powered through the levels, utilizing the corner gun to it's full potential and had a pretty good time doing so.
It paid of..
They nailed the atmosphere, sound design, music and voice acting.
This is not an action game, not really. It's a narrative driven mystery, with certain action and puzzle elements to it.
I quickly settled in with that fact, and did as the game literally told me,
.
And it's not a secret, I think you have to enjoy that aspect of a game, wandering, discovering, reading and piecing together the story. Often the devil lies in the details, and this game does not hand you all the details on a silver platter.
It requires some thinking, and the ending is well executed.
For me it was fairly easy to forgive it's weaker aspects, mainly the action and stealth parts, for it's rich story and all around high quality in presentation.

You have to aim your own weapons (more on this in the PVP section) and there are a number of abilities you can activate during combat to give yourself an edge. This part of the game is done pretty well, combat is intuitive and if you pay attention to the tutorial, fairly easy to pick up.
The crafting system in this game is fantastic, almost every material needed to craft everything you could ever want can be salvaged from the world, harvested at player created farms, collected by player made harvesters in PVP zones, or purchaced off the Auction House.
This wasn't that big of a deal to me since I don't get hung up on graphics much, but this game was developed in 2009 and the graphics look pretty dated.
I don't get alot of the complaints about this as at no point were any of the sector hubs empty. As a crafter I had no trouble making money off the Auction House as there were plenty of buyers for most of my products (once I figured out how to price them properly). You probably won't be tripping over other players when you're out in the middle of nowhere on missions, but is that a bad thing?
FE is good about this aspect as well. There is a cash shop where you can buy boosts to things like experience and faction point award rates; but there's no explicit thing you can buy in the cash store that will give you any advantage against an equally skilled and leveled player whom has never bought anything from the cash shop. The items you pay real money for are largely cosmetic or purely for convinence.
This is by far the most mixed aspect of Fallen Earth. FE does reward pvp kills against different factions with a pvp currency, but in a move I haven't seen in any other MMO (except EVE), FE adds a reason to fight in PVP zones other than pvp currency, Harvesters. Harvesters are player created structures that generate crafting resources that hard to impossible to find outside PVP zones, and as you can guess can only be placed in PVP zones. When all goes well PVP is fun & rewarding, regardless if your faction holds the conflict town at the end of the day.
So what's wrong you ask? First off you're not likely to get a real taste of PVP untill you're close to level cap, granted if you hang around the level 20-45 conflict towns you might bump into an enemy faction; but if you do it's likely to be a clan blob of 5-10 people leveling their alts & steamrolling anyone in their path. The reason the lower level zones are so empty? The level debuff, which cripples anyone above a given conflict town's level range. The idea isn't a bad one: to keep tweaked out lvl 55s from curb stomping fledgling pvp players. But instead of bringing them on the level of people supposed to be in that zone it effectively renders the higher level player helpless; as a result nobody goes near conflict zones if there's even a chance they'll get hit with the level debuff.
But the absolute worst part is the proliferation of hackers (aimbotters and the like) in pvp. G1 does a pretty inconsistent job of keeping hackers in check; every once in a while they do a purge of hackers and PVP becomes fun again, but they always seem to come back. 90% percent of the challenge in pvp is consistently hitting your opponent, preferably with headshots which do considerably more damage, getting good at hitting and avoiding being hit is the core of PVP. So you can see how the fun gets quickly sucked out of this critical part of the game when you have ENTIRE CLANS able to sweep whole PVP zones simply by activating a 3rd party hack and racking up 100% accuracy while their opponents have no recourse what so ever. The fact G1 has been unable or unwilling to find a long term solution to this problem is by far FE's biggest problem.
Fallen Earth is f2p game that isn't pay to win; that alone makes it worth a try. But digging deeper this game has plenty to offer in terms of PVE, crafting, and (if the hacker population is culled at the time) end game PVP. It's really up to what you value in an MMO if FE is worth your time; it certianly is for me despite it's faults.

I find it difficult to review this game in a way that does it justice; it's not a particularily "good" game, but it's very-very far from being a "bad" game.
Cradle has a meticulously created, hauntingly beautiful and sometimes surreal game world... which, save for two locations where the vast majority of the game takes place, is completely empty.
It has a deep, meaningful and sometimes outright disturbing story about topics like over-exploiting technological advancements without first understanding the possible consequences, segregating people into "lower" and "higher" classes purely based on properties they have no control over, about what ends may justify what means under circumstances so dire that the survival of mankind itself is at stake, and about many other aspects of the human condition in general... which is then told in a rather incoherent way that may make it too hard for many to fully piece together, understand and appreciate it.
It's far more than a "walking simulator", but not nearly enough to be a proper adventure game. It tries to provide a small variety of gameplay elements and activities, but most of them are not particularily exciting or entertaining, and at some points infuriatingly difficult. Its relatively short playtime oscillates between intense sections with story exposition, and pretty much nothing but travelling back and forth between a few points of interest in between those times.
Why do I still recommend Cradle? Because in spite, and above of its flaws, it's still a memorable experience: thought provoking and shocking, touching and scary, telling a tale about good intentions turning into fatal mistakes, a tale about a future that was supposed to be grand, but ended up being worse than hell itself.

Point and click game in 3D with some platform elements and some hectic action-platform minigames thrown in for good...i mean bad measure.
The game is not open world, initially i considered that false advertising but i think that was a bit too harsh, because i doubt it was intentional, the developers are Mongolian/Russian and i guess what they were trying to say was that you can move freely around and go anywhere.
Highlight of the game for me, was the art, very good quality surrealistic style (in my non-expert opinion).
At its heart, Cradle is a point and click adventure game in 3D, which is uncommon.
Even more uncommon is the decision to throw in one instance where you need some platforming skills and four minigames of the action-platforming type that are mostly hectic and not very developed, reminding of bonus stages in old platform games.
Good thing they are not mandatory, if you fail one of these four action levels, you have the option to retry, or to skip with no penalty other than not getting the achievement for it.
The story is weird, just like the setting, it doesnt make much sense, but then again you dont go into a surrealistic science fiction story expecting it to make too much sense.
The thing about the story is that it sucks you in, something special about it that will keep you going, wanting to find out more, and it blends very well with the visual setting.
The game is very short, it took me 6 hrs, with one hr wasted without getting to a save point while i was trying to decide if i refund or not.
Also worth mentioning im horrible at point and click games, always missing stuff....i think this is the very first point and click i ever finished in my whole life, and thats only because it was short, visually impressive, and i really really wanted to see where the story goes...which was an odd ending but  it doesnt matter, the trip was fun and thats whats important.
Giving this game a thumbs up, because it definitely does not deserve a thumbs down, BUT...i definitely do NOT recommend buying it unless you know what you are buying: a very short, quite basic, visually impressive and unusual adventure game that relies heavily on atmosphere and visual impact.
A game that while not being polished or very well done, it does leave a lasting impression and thats something that might seem unimportant or useless, but for me it is what separates the wheat from the chaff.

This review is a recommendation with a 20-foot-tall BUT attached...  Absolutely gorgeous game, first of all.  The location is wonderfully realized and makes you feel like you really are in the middle of nowhere.  The area feels so big I never wanted to just go in one direction to see how big.  The whole world is scattered with tons of things to read.  It was cool that the main character was not a generic white guy, and the other main character was a lady.  The game very gently nudges you in a direction as to what your next objective is, so it never felt like it was hand-holding.
BUT, all of this comes at a price...  The objectives of the game are so vague, it can be really hard to even know what the hell is going on.  "Find a red thing to do something with".  WTF am I supposed to do with that??  The game is built on what feels like a very thought out world that is not explored in the slighest.  The only other character is a robot with a wacky nose.  It's never explained why...for either part.  The ending is super abrupt and is barely explained at all.  Lastly, the game is chocked full of this horrific box puzzle game that is both not fun and very uncharacteristic.  You can however skip these games after you lose for the first time.
P's & C's:
+ Beautiful
+ Streams wonderfully
+ Good writing
+ Lots of intractables
+ Doesn't hold your hand
+ Can skip the box portions
- Ending is abrupt and unsatisfying
- World not very well explored
- Doesn't hold your hand...barely even gestures in a direction
---- Box puzzle that really seemed tacked on and almost made me stop playing (until I found out you could skip it)
tl;dr: While I wouldn't recommend playing this game, it was competent enough to warrant not giving it a thumbs down.

As a professional truck driver of 17 years who lives in California, I am fairly impressed with this game.  The developers did a great job capturing the feel and geography of the Southwest and truck operations.  There were some little niggling graphical oversights (no Joshua trees in the Mojave desert? Biplanes patrolling Calfornia freeways?) but they are minor complaints.  I was able to recognize specific landmarks, and though the developers took some artistic license with the freeway systems, they remain close to their real life counterparts.  I would enjoy seeing more states added, I think the Western 11 states would be good.  The Central US would just be too boring to recreate (anyone up for a drive across Nebraska/Kansas/North & South Dakota?) but the East Coast could be a blast to drive!  Their could be more truck specific options added, like an interaxle differential switch, or an expert option where the player has to adjust the tandems and fifth wheel slide to make legal weight.  Or if you are a real nerd, the requirement to operate under the 11/14/70 hour rules.  I look forward to seeing more states and trucks added, and I highly recommend this game.

- 결론부터 말씀드리자면, 전 모두에게까지는 아니더라도 이 게임을 추천드리고 싶습니다.
' 플루토니움' 프리퀄은 게임 속 대사와 이야기들을 읽고 그들의 세계에 빠져드는 것을 좋아하는 사람들에게 추전하는 작품입니다.
전 '플루토니움'이 사람들에게 흥미를 끌고, 집중하게 만들고, 결론적으로 작중의 모든 것에 팬이 되실 만큼 크고 잘 만들어진 세계관에 기반을 두고 있다고 생각합니다.
게임의 스토리는 훌륭합니다. 대부분은 '플루토니움'이란 정확히 무엇인지, 또 이 게임이 앞으로 어떻게 전개될지에 대해 집중합니다. 게임 중간중간 들어가 있는 튜토리얼 격 이벤트들은 모두가 쉽게 할 수 있을 만큼 간단합니다.
연출도 뛰어납니다. 이 게임을 플레이해보시는 분들 중 대부분이 특히 극후반부 연출에서 감탄하실 거라고 생각합니다.
게임을 끝내시고 쿠키 이벤트까지 완료하신다면, 전 여러분이 게임 본편을 기다리게 되실 거라고 확신합니다. 지름을 준비하게 되실 거에요 +_+
하지만 제가 앞서 말씀드렸다시피, 게임의 80퍼센트 이상은 조작이 불가능한 비주얼 노블에 가깝습니다.
게임 내의 전투 시스템 튜토리얼 이벤트가 꽤나 인상깊지만, 그 파트를 플레이하시기 위해서는 최소한 3~40분은 스토리를 보시며 기다리셔야 합니다.
꽤 지루하다고 느끼실 수도 있습니다. 제 주변에서 해보신 분들 중 몇몇도 그렇게 말씀하셨고요. 게임의 개발진들이 게임 내에서 스킵이 일부 가능하도록 만들어 두었다고 해도 어쩔 수 없겠지요.
'플루토니움' 게임 자체에 비난받을 점은 없다고 생각합니다. 그저 플레이하시는 분들의 기호 차이가 이 게임에 호불호를 나눌 뿐이지요.
제게 있어서는, 전 이 게임이 굉장히 맘에 들었고 여러분께 꼭 추천드리고 싶다고 말할 수 있겠네요. 2,200원의 가치는 한다고 생각합니다.
다른 게임들이 이 게임에 비해 싸다고 해도, 제게는 이 정도 연출에서의 놀라움을 선사한 게임이 몇 없었거든요.
읽어 주셔서 감사드리고요. 도움이 되었기를 바랍니다.
그리고 어찌 되었건간에 전 게임 본편을 기다리겠습니다 :)

A Walk in the Dark is a great platformer with some great visuals, simple but great. The movement animations are great, the way the character runs or turns around in midair after a wall-jump. The death animation is great too.
The gameplay is tight and fast, greatly reminiscent of Super Meat Boy. Controls are just as responsive (though there's a more inertia to the character), death just as sudden, and getting back to play just as fast. Runs are timed putting the focus on speed and reflexes. In fact, the game feels so similar that I play it as SMB and find it difficult to get used to the more weighty movement.
I really can't recommend it enough. Everyone should play it, especially fans of skill-based platformers. For me a quick look turned into hours of play even though I can't use one arm - controls are just directions + 2 buttons, easily played with even one hand.

WARNING UP FRONT - The recommendation is qualified. If you're a person who needs a 90-100% stable game of this type to play, this game is not for you. This game is in an unfinished state and will be for quite some time as they refine the code and add features. There will be lag issues, and there will be exploits if you're brave enough for the public servers, and there will be glitches.
Now, to the review.
Being the fourth survival/crafting type game I've owned, and being radically different from the other three, I can't compare it to other games such as Rust and ARQ. I can say that it does evoke the setting quite well even in this early form. The addition of the ability to (let's not sugarcoat it here) raid NPC villages, kidnap NPC's, and eventually put them working in your base as slaves is an interesting twist. The crafting system seems deep for a game in Early Access, if a bit confusingly laid out as it stands right now. NPC combat interactions are pretty good, as they will actively attempt to flank shield using characters. Constructing buildings is it's own headache at times, with random wall facing and graphics issues. Graphically, the game is pretty, but for interests of stability only the highest end users will get to run it above Medium. Even at Medium, though, you'll enjoy the look.
Downsides? Make sure you bring plenty of friends - I can't imagine soloing or duoing this game, because the grind is real and very unforgiving. As it stands, religion in the game plays a large role, but that's completely unexplained at character creation and it's very hard for new players to figure out how to unlock structures they'd want or eventually need without a lot of wasted effort. Public servers right now are a complete mess, due to the inevitable exploits and trolling of an alpha game.  ALSO, THIS IS NOT A GAME FOR SMALL KIDS. This is not Minecraft. Slavery, nudity, and cannibalism are all parts of this game - if you don't think your kids can handle it or you don't want to deal with it, don't buy it.
Overall, it's worth it as long as you don't treat the largish Early Access cost as meaning it's a fully fleshed out game and you have folks with you. Even at 30 bucks for me, it was a good investment, and I'm eagerly awaiting what's coming. People with less patience might want to wait for a few months and take the hit of the price probably going up as it approaches final release.

The problem with this game lies in the technical aspects. A fun game occurs after:
-You successfully are able to launch Awesomenauts
-You find enough players to make a game
-Aforementioned players are in the same country as you
-The game doesn't throw a tantrum and your ping remains stable (assuming the previous two criterion are fulfilled)
-VSync doesn't abandon you mid game and your screen doesn't tear like rice paper
-Your GPU that can run Far Cry 3 at 60 frames doesn't abandon you in game

And then...
-You join a full game, and not 20 minutes into a team that's getting stomped
-Matchmaking makes a game that all players are of relatively similar skill levels
-You do not join a game where the enemy team is a premade, and using Skype to wreck your team
Bit of a hurdle, huh?
This game shows tonnes of promise, and when you actually get into a good game, lots of fun is to be had. But when you consider that Dota 2 and League of Legends emulate a similar style of gameplay, without the problems or the pricetag, Awesomenauts falls flat.
The dwindling player base and plethora of new technical problems makes an otherwise stellar addition to your library merely mediocre, and I cannot recommend this.
tl;dr - fun game, infinite technical issues, don't buy.

Many of the popular comments are negative on Overgrowth's slow development, but keep in mind they hired more devs recently and updates went from several month gaps to 1-2 weeks each. That's good for Overgrowth, which from the start was built from scratch, on their own engine, that simulates realistic physics, forces, impacts and flowing blood, all in real-time. It runs smoother than butter for me.
What it is currently is really a sandbox. There's a big selection of pre-made levels, mostly Arenas and landscapes, and you can spawn in many items (trees, buildings, NPCs, weaponry). There's a lot of potential to make your own stuff too, since you can resize and transform assets as you please, as well as plot paths for NPCs to move on. Personally I'm not too interested in all of that but it leaves huge room for mods, which you can download from the SUMLauncher on the Wolfire site.
But enough of brushing over the technical details, the gameplay is key. Combat is phenomenal in every way. You can throw your adversaries over your head, kick them to death, roundhouse kick their faces, disarm them, whatever you please - all of it can be done by the left and right mouse button. Incredibly easy to learn, incredibly hard to master. The game's got fluid animations and motion too, and it's very easy to do parkour and blend that into fighting. Wallrun, jump off and slam dunk a bunny. This game's got it all.
I personally love this game, though I understand it's not for everyone. Something something furry heaven, blah blah development hell etc. For what's in the game now I think it's well worth your money.

Great game
Pro's:
Fast and fun arcady action that is quick to learn. It is stress free and fun to play in small bursts, or in long grinds. Being a F2P game, there are no microtransactions that ruin the games balance or give people an unfair advantage. It is a very fair business model that I think more dev's should follow. You can only pay for more part slots in your storage, or to unlock all of the parts early. Even unlocking all of the parts early isnt an unfair advantage because it is possible to do well with the starter tank and the parts that you onlock early on. Parts dont scale to level, so it's not like some guns are more powerful than others. Guns just perform different tasks and accomodate different play styles. I get the feeling the devs want to earn you money instead of exploit you for it. Im thinking about paying for premium later just to make sure they get my support.
Con's:
There are some major bugs in this game.
- Random crashes to desktop
- Unable to change graphical settings without the game crashing and no changes being saved.
- Some textures didnt load in for me in the parts store which proceded to crash my game a few times.
- Unable to spawn on certain points on the map.
- Screen freezes and connection issues
- Possible invincibility bug
Also when you first start out, a lack of a good ranking system will frusturate new players. Someone who is just starting out with a starter tank will have to fight level 20 tanks who have more weopans and body styles unlocked, and will just have to deal with it until they unlock more tank parts. I dont know if it is something they can fix in the future, but every once in a while games will be one sided because of the discrpency between what players have unocked due to how long they have played. I however would blame not knowing how to play the game more than I would the parts because with some experience you can beat anyone with the starter tank pretty easily.
Grade: B -

To start with, I give this game a thumb down not because it's a bad one, but because there are a lot of better ones out there.
Essentially, it's a lacking copy of robo-craft with a bit of tablet-like menus. You ride around in a go-kart, supposedly called a tank, that has no weight to itself whatsoever. Even the heaviest ones are fast and "floaty".
The balance is alright, you can get anything quickly due to the pretty fair payment system. However, there is very little worth unlocking as many weapons are simply inferior to all the other ones.
Actual matches end up as idiot-shooters. The kind of shooters where the best players are best, only because they know how to walk with their character properly. You either go up to someone into the melee range and unload your gun on them, or hid somewhere with the sniper rifle.
There are four kinds of pick-ups in the game. Health, shield, ammo, that you will need frequently, and the unexplained red floating♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I think they are supposed to resemble a rocket or something and I have not found what is their use.
I can't call this game fast-paced nor slow-paced due to it's pretty lacking design. It feels fast and light-weight, but the limited ammo makes it feel more tactical, while all weapons make quiet sounds that lack any omph! in them, except for that one gatling that just made me go deaf after I played two quiet games and then got it unloaded on my face.
I say it's a fair and nice game, but there are better ones on steam itself. Try another one, like robocraft or something. It looks the prettiest of it's kind, but that's about it. It feels like a project lacking overall design but being full of small ideas put together.

Coming from games like the Total War series or the Civilization games, you might notice similarities to both at once. Think Medieval Total War played completely on the overview map but injected with a touch of Civs intrigue and a lot more provinces/factions.
But that is barely, if ever scratching the surface. If you are a fan of Game of Thrones court politics or a history buff interested in having his own alternate timeline sandbox to play in, you are right at home.
Want to be an English duke who sleeps with the king's wife and then assassinates said king to inherit his realm? You can do that.
Want to start as a Hindu Indian raja and expand all the way to the Mediterranean while crushing the Arab Empire? You can do that.
Want to be an ambitious Norse pagan in Scandinavia who amasses enough men to conquer Britain and impose the worship of Odin on all of Europe? You can do that too.
Want to be a Zoroastrian prince in the Asian steppes who marries the princess of another khan but also has a b:astard son he got with his own sister? Guess what? Fair game.
Before said description drives you to buy everything, be forewarned.
1.If this is your first grand strategy game, you have a bit of a steep learning curve in the beginning that, once surpassed, simply makes the game "click".  I absolutely recommend a must watch tutorial by Arumba on Youtube that does a far better job explaining stuff than the otherwise solid in game tutorial. You also might want to start as an Irish count in 1066 to get a hang of the game mechanics.
2. The base game has come a long way since launch and you can have a solid amount of fun with just it in your library. But the meat of the game and the huge range of choices is locked behind DLC. That wouldn't be too much of an issue if there weren't so many of them. I would absolutely not recommend paying full price for everything - sales are your friends as they usually group a bunch of DLC together for a fair price. You also don't need many of the flavour DLC.
If you do buy the base game and decide to get the DLC gradually and later, for the safety of your wallet and for the biggest wealth of content, two are a must and are not expensive in sales - Sword of Islam and the Old Gods. Both unlock previously unplayable factions (aside from India) and Old Gods gives you an earlier starting date in the 9th century which many consider the best one (I tend to agree as Charlemaigne, while starting even earlier, isn't well balanced or pretty to look at). The rest you will get will be mostly based on your interests as each expansion tends to target one group of factions and mechanics.
If you do have all or most of its content, you might agree with me that this is the most content packed and interesting role playing experience you have or will play in a long time. Simply for the amount of fun, investment and character immersion it is as of now my absolute favorite game of all time, faults and all. If the two points above don't scare you off, give it a chance and you will be heavily rewarded. What is more, the game is probably the best intro to grand strategy games you can find. Europa Universalis IV is another game from the same developer focusing on the Early Modern Era and it has an interesting feature where you can continue your CKII saves in a new time period, potentially making your game last for over 1000 in game years.

Here is a lot of good stuff, but almost everything is spoiled in some way.
There is a great and intriguing story, but meanwhile game shoves you tons of notes and documents, that sadly are utterly boring and mostly meaningless. Almost every level ends in a room with 6-8 new notes, and reading them breaks any flow and dynamic you had.
Suspense is constantly broken by ragged narrative and whole "it's a memory" setting.
Stealth is too simplistic to be satisfying, shooting is simply weak.
Visuals are pretty nice and atmospheric, but game does poor job of hiding texture loading, forcing you to look at muddy smudge of a game for some time after every restart.
And most of all, all of the game mechanics are completely and almost deliberately conflicting with each other.
Game gives you a CornerShot, which is awesome, slaps thermal vision on it and lets you kill targets behind corners, making for a great power fantasy fighting against a large number of enemies.
And then it tells you, that you shouldn't kill anybody, for story reasons and threat of bad ending.
Later if you'll encounter a "shooting section" and think, that maybe game plans to keep a balance between stealth and action sequances, but no-o-ope. Any aggression from that point is "bad" and game will remind you about it constantly.
Game EVEN gives you SMG and a sniper rifle, while keeping a dissapointing look, if you decide to use them.
But it's encouraging you to replay levels. Basically, you can un-do any killings to get a good ending. But it isn't obvious. What IS obvious is the fact, that you can find every note on a level to GET a new gun!
There are ~10 different weapons, that are locked this way, and none of them are for "stealth" gameplay.
Actually you don't have anything for stealth gameplay. No coin tossing, no light mannipulation, no sound masking - nothing. Only a minimap with all the enemies and simple crouching.
Last third of a game is action only. That's the place, where you can finally GET EVEN and CornerShoot your way through! Yeah!
Wrong again, kiddo. Game takes away it's most interesting gimmick and gives you some wierd warping to fixed positions and assimilating enemies.
It's a mess. Not a disgusting or unplayable mess, but still a mess. A lot of interesting stuff conflicting with each other and spoiling the fun of any of them.
And everytime you think that GET EVEN is finally on the right track, it CornerShots itself in the leg.

This was a fun little game that took me only an hour and a half to complete. That includes getting all four of the achievements. There were no secrets or collectables that I noticed so I assume that I saw all the game had to offer in 90 minutes, and that was with half an hour on the final two puzzles. Of note, the player walks a small figure across the pop-up book and this walking takes the majority of the time. If you recall playing old LucasArts or Sierra adventure games before they introduced the ability to quickly teleport to the edge of the screen you'll have an idea of what I am talking about. Remove the walking and this entire game takes no more than half an hour to beat. The content there is enjoyable enough if you like unique puzzles in your adventure games, but outside of a handful of haikus there is no story here to speak of, which is often one of the key components of adventure games. The music and art are lovely and the puzzles at the very least aren't frustrating and all but the final one I felt made a decent amount of sense. But as quantity goes down, quality has to go up to even out the value, and in this case, unless you are a huge sucker for this style of art, I can't recommend this game for $10. If you get it in a bundle or on a major sale for 75% off I would say it is worth playing, but for a game this short a complete lack of a story component and puzzles that are smart but not brilliant just make the whole package not worth the cost.
If you have the money to spare then I can say I enjoyed my 90 minutes playing this game. But if you have a limited amount of disposable income there are many better games that can be had for $10 that will also last you far longer.

This is the best game I've played this year by far. I'm calling it a masterpiece:  Having finished it just now, and being in stunned awe over the ending, that's the superlative that comes to mind.
Most every aspect of game design I can think of is at the highest professional level in Get Even.  Probably the weakest -- or shall we say the most superficially conventional -- is the FPS stealth/shooting mechanic, which combined with the simple 'detective' aspect of searching for clue items to pick up, along with the investigative tool cellphone/scanner, will have new players comparing it directly to Condemned: Criminal Origins.  But this is only the first layer of gameplay, and even this gets more interesting and involved later on, as stealth comes into play.
Visual design.  This game takes place inside the minds of the game's protagonists, and prolific use is made of effects, like blurring, shaking, warping (Quantum Break's swirling triangles, e.g., are put to good use here).  Artwork and environments are detailed, varied and interesting, many eliciting an emotional or aesthetic response, and increase immersion in the game world.  Yes, they are often borrowed from other titles:  QB's triangles, Condemned's mannikins; moving floors with isolated vignettes -- various games use these as a story-telling mechanic, to break up gameplay; Get Even's borrowing is not plagiaristic but flattering.
Another example of fine visual design I'm very impressed with is how attention from an enemy who has detected you is indicated and tracked onscreen, with a blurry sundog of differing colors on the screen's perimeter, along with a quickening of your character's heartbeat and breathing.  This is incredibly effective in ratcheting up tension and providing information at the same time, without being trite or obtrusive; damage is indicated by light blood spattering onscreen and grunting.  I was hardly aware of a UI display at all during the game, it was handled so deftly.
Writing and plot.  Masterfully done.  Plot morsels are carefully unpeeled for the player's delectation slowly over this many-course meal.  Resist any temptation to read plot summaries or reviews:  Go in blind.
Sound design and music.  This is the cherry on top, and it's so good in Get Even, that it sets my nerves on fire at some points and has me cheering and dancing in my seat at others.  Environmental sounds, haunting musical pieces, catchy pop tunes, ghostly voices whispering from all directions, superb voice-acting, all fill the aural landscape in this game.  Wear headphones while playing.  Good headphones.  I immediately looked for the Signal Bars song online, and bought it (details
)
Get Even gets my highest recommendation.  Get it, play it!

Bandai Namco isn't a publisher that is exactly known for releasing horror games, which makes Get Even their debut into the genre; unless you care to take into account the hit puzzle-platformer Little Nightmares. Released on Steam in late June of 2017, Get Even is a psychological horror/mystery title that mixes elements of first-person shooters, stealth, walking simulators, and detective games. In theory, the genre meshing sounds like it would make for an intriguing adventure, but how well does it work out when put to the test?
For the majority of the game, you take control of Cole Black; a contracted killer who also doubles as a security guard for a technology company. The only memory that Black has is trying to save a girl that he finds in a basement, who has a bomb strapped to her torso. Although he fails to save her, Black survives the blast and wakes up in an insane asylum with only one voice of guidance; a man simply known as Red. As Black progresses through the institution, he slowly uncovers more of his memories that surround the event and circumstances of the captured girl, all the while the mysterious voice of Red urges him to continue onward.
Bandai Namco's partnership with developer The Farm 51 should be the first indication that Get Even isn't going to be an out-of-this-world experience; their catalog of releases is medicre at best, consisting of the two part NecroVision series, Deadfall Adventures, and the more successful Painkiller: Hell & Damnation reboot. That being said, Get Even isn't a horrible game by any means, but rather it flounders around in the abyss of mediocrity; it occasionally rises up to meet expectations, but then it sinks back down again to par, and sometimes sub-par, standards. This is due largely in part of the mish-mashing of gameplay genres, a feat that can work out well if done correctly, and the storytelling that gives birth to a convoluted plot that eventually gets explained, but then continues on for far too long.
It should also be noted that the three provided trailers on the store page are vastly misleading in terms of what this title is actually about and how it really plays. You may have the first impression that Get Even is equipped with a heavy Condemned: Criminal Origins influence, and while that connection is undeniable in some areas of the game, it is not as prevelant as any official footage would lead one to believe. There's also an unmistakable presence of horror in the videos that isn't actually included in the game, the best that it gets are a couple of well placed jumpscares and the rest can be classified as 'psychological action thriller' in the vein of Murdered: Soul Suspect; though with more deteriorated environments.
In some areas of Get Even you will have a gun, but at all times the developer has intended for you to be stealthy so that you can get the "good ending" when you finally finish your 7-8 hour excursion. In other areas, you will be exploring  locations with your phone and using it to scan objects for evidence. At other times, you will simply be walking around, experiencing memories of events. Choosing to be as stealthy as possible, as well as finding all of the evidence in each chapter, will extend your gameplay time to around 13-15 hours. The playtime-to-price ratio is exceptionally generous, especially when considering that the game's optimization is top tier and the graphics are high grade; at fully maxed settings at 1080p resolution, I experienced nothing less than 144 FPS at all times on my GTX 1080/i7-6700k rig.
Bringing it back around to the plot of the game, Get Even tries too hard during its early stages to be needlessly mysterious. Though you are uncovering Black's broken, fragmented memories, the overwhelming amounts of "who are they talking about now?" "who the frig is this person?" and general inability to understand even the most simplistic version of what is actually going on will turn a lot of people off during the first few hours. Though everything is eventually explained in great detail, the title continues to explain the same things over, and over, and over, and over again to make sure that audiences understand; this leads to the entire experience dragging on for much too long.
In other words, Get Even really doesn't do anything to reinvent the horror wheel, or even contribute to its advancement. It's a mash-up of ideas that have already been executed well by Condemned: Criminal Origins, Murdered: Soul Suspect, Assassin's Creed, Stairs, and many other titles. Additionally, genre meshing doesn't make this game any more or less interesting, and the storytelling could use some work. Neither Black or Red are captivating characters by any means, nor are any of the eccentric psychos that you will meet around the insane asylum. While playtime versus price is exceptional, the rest of Get Even's charactaristics do not stand up to the expectations that it sets, which leads to disappointment in the end, and that ultimately leads to me telling you to grab this one half-off or lower.

i think in the end, i am going to recommend this game, but only with some caveats.
a) this game initially gave me some remarkable motion sickness. changing the FOV in the settings and being careful not to move the mouse/camera around too quickly seemed to solve my problem.
b) it is rather short. my play through clocked in at 10 hours, and i feel like that was a bit on the long side of the average - i have no sense of direction, and got lost several times while doing the outdoor puzzles.
c) the ending is ... not exactly rushed, but more like, abrupt? yeah. if you enjoy endings that require you to sit back and think about them, and perhaps puzzle them over with others on a forum somewhere, than you will like this ending. if you're someone (like myself, i admit) who prefers that the game put a bit of a tighter wrapping on the package for you, this ending might leave you disappointed. the answer is definitely there, and it is solvable, but you'll have to solve it yourself, the game's not going to spoon-feed you.
however, this game is beautiful, and the setting is extremely detailed and well thought out. there aren't but two "locations," with some gorgeous Mongolian Steppe and a few tram stops thrown in, but they are beautifully rendered, and detailed in a logical, real-world way, i.e. your first puzzle is recipe-based, and you'll find the kitchen knives and the spices in the kitchen. the weather is beautiful, the music is subtle by affecting. the main character's voice acting leaves a bit to be desired, although it's up for debate whether that might not be on purpose, but the whopping two other characters you meet are well-done and vibrant, if not excatly sensible at first.
overall, i feel like this is a game where the developers left so many Clues and gave so few Hints that it's going to take two or three play throughs to find everything they put in and get some closure. if you like thorough settings and you don't mind puzzling endings, you'll like Cradle.

I'm kinda conflicted on this game. It's big and expansive, and offers an immense level of freedom like the other elder scrolls games, but it also is an extremely vanilla, by-the-numbers fantasy fare. There isn't a whole lot here to differentiate it from other fantasy mediums, and could have easily taken place on Middle Earth, Shanarra, Faerun, or Azeroth with very little modification. Every region and town here is forgettable, and the uniqueness and inspiration found in the other elder scrolls games, just seems to be missing. There are a few surprises and spurts of flavour here and there such as the Lovecraft-inspired HackDirt, and the Dark Brotherhood questline, but that's all they are, just small bursts of flavour, in a giant bucket of vanilla.
So why does this with all it's lacklusterness still get a recommendation. Even though, it lacks the excitement of exploration, the game is still fun, and huge. It's easy to get into, and the elder scrolls signature freedom is still here. It follows the same character building mechanics of Morrowind, but with slight improvements to the skills and gameplay, that make getting to higher levels in any skill that much more rewarding and the game actually more fun.
This game also simultaneously showcased the best and worst dlc ever, but also has a mature modding community (not as in adult content, which I guess is also there, but more in the number and complexity of mods available, and the understanding of the modding tools by the community) that is still cranking out amazing expansions and improvement tweaks.
If you are interested, I would highly recommend the better cities and unique landscapes mods, which help alleviate the vanilla-ness of the game and help to differentiate the regions from each other and make it more fun to go exploring.

I found this game to be both an aesthetic, almost ethereal delight and a small wonder of a creative game mechanics, gorgeous artwork and enchanting soundtrack (both the music and the sound effects). No, the puzzles are not difficult, nor do they need to be for the game like this to be effective, satisfying and enjoyable. If your idea of what qualifies as a game is very narrowly defined by ideas of concrete challenges and tests, If you need games to fill some void left by your own lack of real life validation, then you will likely be impatient with this game. But a bit of wisdom will tell you that not all challenges can be boiled done to what you can score or beat. There is something to be said about a game that so superbly offers the player such enriching immersion in such a short span of time (indeed the game is appropriately short), and with such sparse use of words. The challenges of a game like this is to be present to it, to be able to set aside your expectations and be open to experience what it has to offer. "Mindfulness" as what trendy lifestyle gurus might call it, but it's a virtue that's long been valued by wiser folk. I dare say this rather mindless world could use more games like Tengami. Bravo, Nyamyam.

The visuals are great, some might say fantastic, but the game's length doesn't make it worth the normal $10 price. If anything, it's worth getting Tengami in a large sale or a Humble Bundle so you can have other interesting games to take up your time with. The puzzles are also another point that make me hold back on recommending this game because of their simplicity and lack of variety. Most of the tab pulling and folding mechanics are interesting, but there are some more mundane "memorize this" puzzles sprinkled in throughout the game.
Maybe if the game had more than three levels, or some secrets, I could recommend it. But at its current length and price, Tengami is something that you should wait till a large price drop for.

Tengami takes an interesting concept and does almost nothing with it.  It's an extremely short adventure/puzzle game with very trivial puzzles (except the very last one, which is quite annoying.)  I easily beat it in less than an hour.
There really is nothing interesting in the game past the artwork and the main game mechanic of altering the environment by flipping pop-up book pages.  It never really goes anywhere though and I can't help but think it's hugely wasted potential.  This style could be used to produce an interesting game akin to Paper Mario, but here all we have is some pretty artwork and simple puzzles.

It's interesting how lands far away from your own experience their own chances and changes. In one game, you may notice a king's untimely death. His kingdom, now under the rule of his too young son, fractures due to internal and external threats. In another game, after dealing with your own enemies, you might glance across the continent and realize that kingdom, which had imploded last time, has become a domineering empire.
I'm not going to go through Crusader Kings II's strengths; obviously I've enjoyed the game. It's well worth buying the game and particular add-ons when they're on sale.
Nevertheless, there are flaws to take into account:
1. There are too few unique events given how quick it is to write and program them in. You'll often spend game years between encountering any, and you'll keep seeing some of the same ones over and over.
2. The RPG aspect needs work. The characters aren't as deep as they should be. Generally, what you do to one person, you can do to another, and the "whys" behind actions aren't taken into account. Relationships are based off arithmetic, and it's difficult to genuinely feel close to a friend, child, spouse, etc.
3. Computer-controlled rulers aren't very proactive or difficult to defeat. Want to wage war against the Holy Roman Empire, which controls ten times as many troops as your tiny kingdom does? No problem: bring in effective commanders, take advantage of terrain, and crush the enemy armies while they're still small and trying to group up. It's common to get rid of ten or tens of troops for every one you lose. Other nations aren't likely to try to conquer your own land, even if you're much weaker, creating passive games.
4. The game gets boring after you become the region's powerhouse. There's no point taking over the world, because by the time you have a respectable kingdom, nevermind an empire, you have no competitors. It just becomes a matter of time until you slowly conquer Eurasia, and your only difficulty becomes keeping your nation intact. After you get to this point, you might decide to start a new game in a different part of the world.
5. The biggest pain is efficiently delegating conquered territory to vassals; unless you let your steward do it for you, which brings its own problems, you'll have spent more time painstakingly distributing your land than gaining it.
It's an excellent game, and I'd like to see improvements to the aforementioned issues in future expansions or versions to make it a phenomenal game. But that's not going to happen, so these flaws will remain.

The world in this game is immersive, atmospheric, and uncanny.  Exploring it was pure pleasure!  If that sounds appealing to you, then I think you'll find that this game is worth buying.  At the very least, you won't regret supporting the developers (I certainly don't regret it!), and it's not too expensive either!
That said, I honestly did not like this game.  Leaving aside the beautiful environment to explore, this game is one-half mystery novel and one-half interactive puzzle.  Therefore, the storyline and dialogue factor heavily into the overall experience.  Unfortunately, however, the developers' greatest achievements are to be found in the areas of graphic and level design... *not* the narrative aspects of the game.
I immmediately noticed how bad the voice acting was from the very beginning of the game, and I couldn't get over it!  It stuck out like a sore thumb for the full duration of the game.  Honestly, the developers probably would have had better results if they'd just hired the first people they could find at a random bus stop!  I mean, *come on!*
But perhaps even worse, the writing was so cringe-inducing!  Have you ever heard a teenager say something that he or she *thinks* is profound but, in reality, just sounds naive and idealistic?  The storyline and dialogue struck that chord with me over and over again throughout this game.  It vaguely reminded me of a bad anime series, somehow.  And the ending... man, I think that ending gave me diarrhea.
In summary, the writing and voice acting in this game are terrible, and while I can't recommend this game, I do think the atmosphere alone will satisfy some players.  As always, please consider compensating these developers for the work they do.  Video game developers *do* produce value, and they rarely charge players enough, in my opinion.

Ever wondered why so many games these days have for-pay cosmetics?  TF2 with its keys, Overwatch with its loot boxes, CSGO with its skins? Get Even feels simultaneously like a bad game and an absolute must-play. It's one of those things that just looks and feels like it tried to be too much and failed. Even so, it's just so engaging and visually stunning and atmospheric and all those buzzwords.
I played through once to the "bad end" and I may at some point go back and try to do a clean, stealthy run, but in my opinion there's little motivation to do so. Based on info I've already recieved I can probably guess how the good end will go. The game provides you with a couple of really great tools, one for puzzle-solving, and one for stealth-shooter-ing.
For puzzle solving, you're given your phone. This actually comes in handy when trying to avoid detection, as it lets you know where enemies are and which way they're looking. It also lets you rewrite your environment within memories, search for evidence and memory fragments, and review the story so far.
The great Stealth shooter element thrown into the game was a weapon mod called the Cornergun. pop a pistol or smg onto it, and you can shoot around corners. It even has heat vision on the monitor, so you can make out someone hiding in tall grass, no problem.
However, your "therapist," a man calling himself "Red," absolutely insists that you kill no one. Having the cornergun, the knowledge that you can take a LOT of bullets before the memory resets, and the fact that even following the enemy's movement pattern exactly can still get you caught, I felt no strong need to actually obey Red. In hindsight, the ability to bullet sponge would have been a great chance to just try booking it through enemy fire, but that didn't give me much time to investigate, and yes, they did put info behind people who would kill you.
For some people, the "pacifist run" perks  might add to the fun, but for me? I prefer using every tool at my disposal to get through a situation, and that means using the goddam Cornergun!
Anyway, little rant over and done with, I return to my claim that the game tried to be too much and failed. If they had taken out just one element of the game - be it story, stealth, clue-hunting, puzzle-solving, shooting... Remove ONE of those, and we  might have a 5-star game. As it is, we have a 3-star I really think you should check out anyway.

Ok, so let me start right off the bat that is is not a game for everyone. Its titled as an "action" game but that's the least of what it is. Its a game based on exploration and some deep storytelling. And our protagonist has to piece together all the puzzles to get the clear picture of what exactly happened. Its a sort of detective based creepy/horror game though not scary in a traditional sense. Anyone looking for jumpscares or monsters will be dissappointed.
1-Story- Those of you who are looking for an amazing story with rich and relatable characters will find it a great gem. The story is explored with great mystery and the way all the details connect in the end gave it a great Hitchcock/Fincher vibe. There are very few games out there who take the game's story on such an engaging and emotional level. This is one of those games. The developers took a great risk here by eliminating actions, explosions etc and focusing on the story and exploration. Some of the levels are basically walking from one part to another and uncovering things as you go along. No action. They did a good job with the story else the game would have been boring quick.
2-Combat-Combat sections are a little clunky in this game which led to a little frustation as the game basically motivates you not to engage or kill any enemies. Even when you do engage in a fight (as the game gives you a lot of weapons to try out) it feels a little unpolished. Also, the stealth section of the game is pretty hard and definitely requires patience and observance to get through. One weapon i have to say takes the cake in this game is the Cornergun..which if you play you will know how awesome it is :).  Also you get some achievments and the game's good ending if you proceed the game with stealth or minimal kills.
3-Graphics- I always prefer gameplay over graphics and therefore I found them to be good. I did encounter a few glitches where the main character would randomly get stuck while passing doors and I had to reload the whole checkpoint to get past it. On reading through the steam forums I found that some people experienced this problem. I had no issues while playing this game, however, the game's FPS tends to drop a lot in outdoor areas below 60 irrespective of the video card. Indoors the game works smooth. As the graphics were not that high tech I did not expect that to happen. Hope the developers release a patch soon which fixes this issue as most of the stealth and combat takes place in outside areas. In indoor areas its basically exploration and puzzle solving.
4- Sound and atmosphere- The sound and the music is truly exceptional. The music makes use of simple sounds like breathing etc and makes it into a looping playback. The other thing which is awesome in this game is the Cemetery level with the awesome song in the background (You have to play it to experience it :) ). The sound of the inmates coupled with the music makes it truly scary and warns of impending danger the more you move towards your objective. The music resonates and increases in intensity the more you move forward. The atmosphere and the way you use your cell phone to solve clues definitely reminded me of "Condemned:Criminal Origins" but apart from that its a fresh take in the FPS genre.
If you are looking for something new in the games genre and want a completely focused story based experience give this one a try you won't be dissapointed.

I'm kinda conflicted on this game. It's big and expansive, and offers an immense level of freedom like the other elder scrolls games, but it also is an extremely vanilla, by-the-numbers fantasy fare. There isn't a whole lot here to differentiate it from other fantasy mediums, and could have easily taken place on Middle Earth, Shanarra, Faerun, or Azeroth with very little modification. Every region and town here is forgettable, and the uniqueness and inspiration found in the other elder scrolls games, just seems to be missing. There are a few surprises and spurts of flavour here and there such as the Lovecraft-inspired HackDirt, and the Dark Brotherhood questline, but that's all they are, just small bursts of flavour, in a giant bucket of vanilla.
So why does this with all it's lacklusterness still get a recommendation. Even though, it lacks the excitement of exploration, the game is still fun, and huge. It's easy to get into, and the elder scrolls signature freedom is still here. It follows the same character building mechanics of Morrowind, but with slight improvements to the skills and gameplay, that make getting to higher levels in any skill that much more rewarding and the game actually more fun.
This game also simultaneously showcased the best and worst dlc ever, but also has a mature modding community (not as in adult content, which I guess is also there, but more in the number and complexity of mods available, and the understanding of the modding tools by the community) that is still cranking out amazing expansions and improvement tweaks.
If you are interested, I would highly recommend the better cities and unique landscapes mods, which help alleviate the vanilla-ness of the game and help to differentiate the regions from each other and make it more fun to go exploring.

Don't know that it's worth $30; but you can get it off a website that may include a G, a 2, and an A in the title for around $15. I had to remove the link/actual title because Steam isn't particularly fond of them.
It's definitely a lot of fun if you can run it and like the combat, but updates haven't come too often and it's likely you won't see much more progress than what's offered here in the final release. However, that isn't to say it hasn't definitely been updated. It seems they have kicked up their efforts recently, as well, but I can't say much for sure. There's a lot more to the game than there was when it started off, including the fact that it is MUCH easier to run now. If you own the game and didn't like the way it ran before, I heavily recommend revisiting it.
The game doesn't stretch very far past what you can see in the screenshots and trailer, but for a quick rundown, and things you should consider before buying:
- The game features relatively quick, primarily hand-to-hand and melee fighting, with a very intricate movement system. There are many maps dedicated entirely to parkour.
- The modding community is fairly sized, and extremely dedicated. If you own the game or plan on getting it, you should definitely download SUMLauncher for it as well. You can easily install and manage mods, as well as adjust advanced graphics settings, controls, etc. I consider it essential.
- There are no current plans for multiplayer, though there is a decent mod for it currently in development.
- The dev team is pretty small, and probably won't expand. As of the last few months, updates have come a bit more frequent, but just keep in mind that anything could happen to this game.
