Get Even suffers from identity crisis, it's trying to be a gripping narrative driven experience while also being an in depth FPS game. This means it features interesting mechanics like a gun that can shoot around corners and mobile phone version of the Arkham series' detective vision, but neither are allowed their full potential. It's blatantly obvious that using lethal or direct force will result in the worst ending in the story so you're discouraged from using your weapons, but then you have so little health that you're better off just avoiding combat all together if possible.
This isn't bad but it is clearly a game that needed more polish before launch but for what it is, it's an interesting and genuinely intriguing combination of first person shooter and walking simulator.

I'm kinda conflicted on this game. It's big and expansive, and offers an immense level of freedom like the other elder scrolls games, but it also is an extremely vanilla, by-the-numbers fantasy fare. There isn't a whole lot here to differentiate it from other fantasy mediums, and could have easily taken place on Middle Earth, Shanarra, Faerun, or Azeroth with very little modification. Every region and town here is forgettable, and the uniqueness and inspiration found in the other elder scrolls games, just seems to be missing. There are a few surprises and spurts of flavour here and there such as the Lovecraft-inspired HackDirt, and the Dark Brotherhood questline, but that's all they are, just small bursts of flavour, in a giant bucket of vanilla.
So why does this with all it's lacklusterness still get a recommendation. Even though, it lacks the excitement of exploration, the game is still fun, and huge. It's easy to get into, and the elder scrolls signature freedom is still here. It follows the same character building mechanics of Morrowind, but with slight improvements to the skills and gameplay, that make getting to higher levels in any skill that much more rewarding and the game actually more fun.
This game also simultaneously showcased the best and worst dlc ever, but also has a mature modding community (not as in adult content, which I guess is also there, but more in the number and complexity of mods available, and the understanding of the modding tools by the community) that is still cranking out amazing expansions and improvement tweaks.
If you are interested, I would highly recommend the better cities and unique landscapes mods, which help alleviate the vanilla-ness of the game and help to differentiate the regions from each other and make it more fun to go exploring.

Imagine if Christopher Nolan had invisioned Inception as a film noir detective story mixed with a dash of horror and you have the premise of Get Even. A game with some of the best writing in gaming period and a sense of style that reaks of technology fiction like the Matrix and Inception. Having beat the game I can say this is easily one of the best stories in all gaming and worth the price of admission for that alone.
However If you are in the market for gameplay the game plays somewhere between a detective story point and click and a first person stealth shooter. You will do alot of evidence collection and puzzle solving but until the mid point of the game you will not be shooting much of anything. I really don't want to delve into the story except to say it is exellent and the twitsts although predictable if you pay attention are still gut wrenching because the acting of the voice actors is so spot on you feel for every character.
There are a ton of collectible notes, tapes and side items that actually serve to flesh out the story in an original way as you will eventually find a place where you collect them all towards a 100% rating. This rating will then unlock a code that will give you even more story and ultimately allow you to gain the best ending to the game.
The games main flaw is that untill late into the game you really don't feel like you are doing anything that original gameplay wise and even then the complexity is so low that you never really feel as though you are having a great deal of fun using the games systems rather you are compelled because the games story is so good you need to know how it will all play out. I feel if you are a fan of telltale style games and want a little more control over your experience you will be in heaven with this game. However if you avoid games of this nature and need gameplay to be engaged you will likely not enjoy the experience because it feels subpar.
I need to split my rating for this reason as the story alone is the best I have experienced so far this year and is an easy 10 out of 10 however the gameplay is only at a 6 of 10 You have tools that are interesting but don't feel fun, and untill that second chapter in the game you feel as though you are not doing anything that original in the game world. Even when they do evolve the gameplay you will soon feel like you are just going through the motions in service to the story. If the developers had tightened up the gunplay and given you that powerful feeling the whole game this could have been a game of the year contender as it is it should be on everyones radar for a writing award for gaming as it sets the bar so high very few games to date can reach it's heights.

Although I have played enough of this game to offer a fair review, I will choose not to and instead offer one of my favorite recipies for my favorite dish, Boeuf Bourguignon Knopf.
First prepare the bacon: cut off the rind and reserve.
Cut the bacon into lardons about 1/4" thick and 1 1/2" long.
Simmer the rind and the lardons for ten minutes in 1 1/2 quarts of water.
Drain and dry the lardons and rind and reserve.
Pre-heat the oven to 450°F.
Put the tablespoon of olive oil in a large (9" - 10" wide, 3" deep) fireproof casserole and warm over moderate heat.
Saute the lardons for 2 to 3 minutes to brown lightly.
Remove to a side dish with a slotted spoon.
Dry off the pieces of beef and saute them, a few at a time in the hot oil/bacon fat until nicely browned on all sides.
Once browned, remove to the side plate with the bacon.
In the same oil/fat, saute the onion and the carrot until softened.
Pour off the fat and return the lardons and the beef to the casserole with the carrots and onion.
Toss the contents of the casserole with the salt and pepper and sprinkle with the flour.
Set the uncovered casserole in the oven for four minutes.
Toss the contents of the casserole again and return to the hot oven for 4 more minutes.
Now, lower the heat to 325°F and remove the casserole from the oven.
Add the wine and enough stock so that the meat is barely covered.
Add the tomato paste, garlic and herbs and the bacon rind.
Bring to a simmer on the top of the stove.
Cover and place in the oven, adjusting the heat so that the liquid simmers very slowly for three to four hours.
The meat is done when a fork pierces it easily.
While the meat is cooking, prepare the onions and mushrooms and set them aside till needed.
For the onion, if using frozen, make sure they are defrosted and drained.
Heat the butter and oil in a large skillet and add the onions to the skillet.
Saute over medium heat for about ten minutes, rolling the onions about so they brown as evenly as possible, without breaking apart.
Pour in the stock, season to taste, add the herbs, and cover.
Simmer over low heat for about 40 to 50 minutes until the onions are perfectly tender but retain their shape and the liquid has mostly evaporated.
Remove the herbs and set the onions aside.
For the mushrooms, heat the butter and oil over high heat in a large skillet.
As soon as the foam begins to subside add the mushrooms and toss and shake the pan for about five minutes.
As soon as they have browned lightly, remove from heat.
To Finish the Stew:.
When the meat is tender, remover the casserole from the oven and empty its contents into a sieve set over a saucepan.
Wash out the casserole and return the beef and bacon to it (discarding the bits of carrot and onion and herbs which remain in the sieve).
Distribute the mushrooms and onions over the meat.
Skim the fat off the sauce and simmer it for a minute or two, skimming off any additional fat which rises to the surface.
You should be left with about 2 1/2 cups of sauce thick enough to coat a spoon lightly.
If the sauce is too thick, add a few tablespoons of stock.
If the sauce is too thin, boil it down to reduce to the right consistency.
Taste for seasoning.
Pour the sauce over the meat and vegetables.
If you are serving immediately, place the covered casserole over medium low heat and simmer 2 to 3 minutes.
Serve in the casserole or on a warm platter surrounded by noodles, potatoes or rice and garnished with fresh parsley.
If serving later or the next day, allow the casserole to cool and place cold, covered casserole in the refrigerator.
20 minutes prior to serving, place over medium low heat and simmer very slowly for ten minutes, occasionally basting the meat and vegetables with the sauce.

There's no  way  a short review such as this   can do justice to a game like Oblivion, it's too massive and there' too much to experience, especially when you factor in the number of custom made modifications that are available for this game.  Almost approaching the same as Unreal Tournament and the early Battlefield games (BF1942, BFV and BF2); we're talking several hundred gigabytes of free content at least (I have around 500GB for Oblivion and over a Terabyte for Battlerfield 2).
The initial stage of the game where you have to escape the cobwebbed, dark and sometimes dank dungeon is   a little depressing, but still   a pleasure to experience the first few times around (it’s one of only   a few  linear parts of the game - another one is where you get transported into a painting), then you hit the outside, exiting the dungeon via a sewer drain.  On my first time it was a moonlit night and I was actually awed by the sight that I beheld.  I could see   the dark shapes of mountains and   the moonlight gave an eerie look to the small clouds slowly passing by.  The sky was full of glittering stars and I could see some distance ahead to a small broken down castle keep, all of which, even in the dark looked amazing.  I thought Morrowind was fantastic, but this was even better.
I waited utill sunrise and was even more impressed by the amazing vista before me, Mountains  clothed in forests, morning mist,   a sun rise that looked almost real and  amazing,  the lush grass waving in the breeze, and    a whole host of other things swamped my  visual cortex.  Every step of the way, I marvelled at how realistic the grass, rocks and other objects looked.  Buildings, the imperial city, villages and towns all had their own distinct feel and charm.  The transition from night to day and back to night  is a pleasure to see; with HDR lighting, bloom effects, specular highlights and  parallax mapping  giving the game    some of the best visuals I’ve seen to date (well, maybe not the last    couple of years of AAA  game releases).  The effects are amazing, even now seven years after its release it still looks brilliant.  You can get several mods that improve many of the textures (the largest of these is around 3GB in size).
The usual RPG elements are present; for example, levelling up, plus  resource collection for  crafting magical weapons and  potions as well as stocking  yourself with  better armour, weapons , arrows, spears, potions etc.    Combat is nothing special, but still satisfying when swapping between bow, sword spear and magic.  Despatching enemies isn’t too hard, especially once you’ve got a steady stream of healing potions.
If you still haven’t purchased this game, now is the time to get it.  It includes   the expansion The Shivering Isles and the mod package Knights of the Nine that contains several   new missions, etc.  You can see several videos

Cradle is an experiential adventure - that is, you play it simply to immerse yourself in its world for awhile. The story is coherent enough to form a narrative framework, but also very open-ended and vague. There's no beginning or end, no triumph or loss, just a small piece of life in a fantastical, yet familiar, future. I loved it, and I want more of it, and more from this studio - but I'm also very fond of Dear Esther, so bear that in mind. Cradle is more interactive than Dear Esther, but they share the same sort of sightseeing sensibility: You are here because you are here.
The one big stumble is the arcade sequences, which I'm assuming were wedged in to give Cradle some conventional "gameplay." But they're not particularly good, and woefully out of place; unless you're a determined cheevo hunter, I'd recommend skipping them entirely. (There's an option to do so.)
Beautiful soundtrack, too. If you're buying it, spring for the deluxe edition. The art book isn't much, but the soundtrack is more than worth the few extra bucks.

Cradle... quite intriguing, fun and impressive in the first hour or two.
Then it is a downward spiral of annoying "Tetris-like puzzle", nonsense story and with an abysmal ending. If you thought Mass Effect 3 ending was bad, you have a winner here with Cradle.
But not all is bad with this game. I feel like this is much more of a tech demo since the visuals are impressive (mostly). You get to walk around in this big open space but unfortunately, as big as that open world is, you only explore one big area (the Park) besides your yurt. Rest of the world feels very empty and there is nothing to find either. The voice acting is good and the selling point of this game would be it's soundtrack (good ambient music, very soothing too!).
Puzzles are quite bad in this game. Like I've mentionned earlier, to get some tech-device related to the story, you need to do some cube-base puzzle. At least, if you fail you can skip that boring thing (if only you could skip BEFORE starting that irritating puzzle). There was also some really unclear game objectives at times that made you look again and again everywhere to figure out what to do. In instance, you are tasked to find a "TV REMOTE". So logically, you look around the TV (can't find) then maybe near the bed? The couch? NO DICE! Went to Youtube and it was hidden under Ida's table! WHY?!%? Lots of misplaced objects in this game that only brought frustration then accomplishment.
Without spoiling too much about the ending but I can only say that the whole intrigue of the game doesn't get resolved in the ending. So you're left wondering WTF happened in that whole 5-6 hours of gameplay! Basically, you're barely informed at all in this game and left to wonder yourself about the events unfolding around you.
Even for a short game, I wish it was shorter for the whole amount of times I was annoyed by the gameplay!
Therefore, I cannot recommend this game.
Maybe worth it at 50% off though... but consider watching YouTube videos of this game to speed it up!
EDIT:
Game have 3440 x 1440p resolution and 21:9 ratio support! That is a plus but won't change my stance with the review.

I wouldn't classify Awesomenauts as being awesome, but it's mildly fun. Take a basic 2D platformer like Booster Trooper and turn it into a 3 vs 3 all out battle to destroy your opponents base, fighting through turrets along the way. I found the game content to be lacking in both character abilities and map selection--there are only 4 different maps, all identically laid out. All the characters have similar abilities which means they are all pretty evenly matched, but many of the abilities seem pretty useless. There are also unlockable abilities as you pursue the slow experience grind.
Matches last about 10-15 minutes and they are typically pretty lopsided, but occasionally you end up in an intense stalemate. The drop-in / drop-out support is excellent making it very quick and easy to find a game.
When they say "Saturday morning is back" they aren't kidding--it's very cartoony, giving it a nostalgic appeal for those who grew up in the 80s. All in all, it's kinda meh.

An interesting game. I quite like the sci-fi themes, with the robotic/cyborg sort of things going on. There graphics and design of the game is excellent.
I'd love to know more about this 'universe' and I'd love to play more stuff in it, explore more areas, go to the city etc. It's really enthralling and I've got an almost bittersweet feeling about it, because it feels like the game could have been bigger. I'm not knocking what we got; the game is superb. It just seems like it's part of a high-quality game and that we've only seen the first act or first few levels. This isn't really a fault, it just shows that they've got some wonderful worldbuilding. I'm hooked and would love to see it expanded further.
Anyway, some slight problems people may have:
Please note that there are a few parts to the game that involve a sort of 'minigame' where you need to collect boxes in a sort of computer arena. You'll see the screenshot here of the teal boxes, with a couple red and orange ones in. I quite enjoyed it, it was a different sort of twist in what's like a sci-fi puzzle/exploration game, but I can see how some other people wouldn't want that.
Minor spoiler (maybe, not really): it builds up a sort of mystery throughout the game, but it doesn't exactly explain itself when it comes to the end. You've got to read notes and stuff that's scattered about to try and get an idea about what has happened. It might just be be, but even then it wasn't exactly clear, but I did enjoy the sort of mystery. I think seeing little bits of information (like newspaper articles, or written notes) really helps to make the world seem bigger and I enjoyed it. It seemed quite natural and not forced (e.g. you didn't just get a big dump of information like you were reading a wiki article). However, some people may not like this and may prefer the game to be a bit more explicit with what's happening.
I would recommend this game.

- the music sometimes stops randomly
- it is often not really clear what to do. The Hint feature helps here a bit. However for the last puzzle there is no hint feature and it is absolutely not obvious what to do (My hint for you: Find a symmetric pattern).
- The game is really short. I finished it within 74 minutes. If the Main Character could run, I guess I would have been solving it in 45 minutes. If he could teleport, It would last about 20 minutes. So the game is really bad but the style is awsome.

You'll probably see this game referred to as the Grandaddy of a Digital Dungeons and Dragons style game - which is apt, to say the least.
Extremely enteraining to play solo; made exponentially so through Co-Op (Local or Online) shenanigans. From utilising the elements for devasting spell combinations (big numbers never felt so destructive) to pickpocketing every NPC in town, the deceptively large world is your oyster - so long as you remember to quicksave often, you never know when one enemy might suddenly become a dozen.
The main game is structured within three main acts:
Early game has superb pacing, both from a narrative perspective and for skill progression, with the 1st Act's boss fight testing how well you've built your character (and your team if you're playing offline). If you feel that you made a mistake in allocating that one attribute point or skill - fret not - you gain access to a free, re-usuable respec tool which allows you to finely tune your ongoing build (and for when you need to take points out of thievery and into persuasion for those occassional encounters).
In terms of story, the writing does a pretty good job of establishing the most important factor's to bear in mind when you first start the game. You are essentially a Force-User, only your powers bring forth demons, so the police force - the Magisters - have taken measures to stop this from happening. Only, those measures are a tad too far, and it's up to you, and possibly three others to secure your freedom. You can create a custom character, or start as one of six, pre-made origin stories. Aside from racial abilities, some dialogue choices and your character's personal quest, there is little consequence to not choosing said pre-made.
If you aren't sold on Divinity: Original Sin 2 yet, then you most likely won't enjoy playing it (fancy that). If your interest is piqued, then as a quick heads up, the average length of time to beat the game is 80-90~ hours. Playing with friends WILL shorten playtime since you don't have to worry about multiple character's gear, unlike singleplayer.
Bonus Features:(?) The game includes a built in DM style mode where you can create or import campaigns for your friends to join in and lollygag around in. Finally, the game does include a dedicated mode to PvP, however I have yet to test this myself, and so I cannot give details, other than it's like the regular game...but you'll be fighting players...duh.
Anyhow, it is important to note that this was an Early-Access game funded through Kickstarter. As such, you may want to up your expectancy in bugs, even for a PC game. It can be frustrating when you have five open quests that you either finished, or you can't complete because you skipped a step, but we're getting into First-World problems of the nth degree, and I personally did not come across anything game-breaking, though I'm sure you'll find numerous reports online of such cases.
In conclusion, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is an easy contender for my GOTY, joining the ranks of Breath of the Wild and Persona 5. A solid 9.9/10, because nothing is perfect.

Maybe the most unique one in my gaming history, and I am playing video games for 17 years already.
It is very hard to describe Get Even.
The combination is perfect thought, especially when you add well-written story and one of
And by in-game music I mean both soundtrack and narration with acting. In this regard, this game is as good as Bioshock Infinite, which for me is on the top.

The story is fluid and develops very quickly. In the end I caught myself playing like 5 or 6 hours straight just to see the ending... and it was suprising (in the positive way)! To make a final conclusion… If you love to discover new things about video games and you are into exploration games with some unique elements and strong psychological set-up, then this game is definitely for you. After playing 20 some hours of this game, I have to reccommend it. It is simply the best CRPG I have ever played hands down. Excellent graphics, story (So far), combat and choices, choices, choices! I plan on replaying this game right after I finish it once, simply just to experiment with different builds and quest line choices. Many games today present you with artificial choices where the end result is the same. This game has some Witcher 3 tier or maybe better branching quests. If you like RPGs or you like turn based combat this game is a must buy. $45 feels like a steal for such a dense game. If you are considering it, just buy it. You won't regret it!

Even as a free to play game it has kept up to a fairly high standard as there is very little in game you cannot get for free rather than through microtransactions (most of which is cosmetic and the remainder being so inefficient as to be impractical if one wishes to take the "pay to win" aproach).
All in all, Warframe is an incredible game and well worth at least a try, while it may be difficult to "get in to" for newer players due to lack of starter tutorials it has a very welcoming playerbase that is usually happy to answer most questions and it will keep you coming back for a long time.

The story is exceptional and utterly unique. It builds upon the sturdy framework set by DOS:1 and if you’re familiar with the first edition in the series I suspect you will be pretty pleased at the number of references littered throughout DOS:2.

Yay, the story itself is grand indeed. But it wouldn’t be half as grand without the guidance of DOS’s skilled writing team whose considerable talent and mastery over the written word is visibly displayed during each and every in-game interaction. What’s more? Each and every line of text in the game is voice acted! And voice acted well.
These voice actors can emote baby, and the manner in which they deliver each line will leave you stunned. Rest assured there will be moments during your playthrough that you will be so encapsulated by their delivery that you may, in fact, lose sight of reality altogether. It’s that good, or at least, THAT complimentary.
But all these details are almost surplus to demand in the face of what I firmly believe to be DOS:2’s most enjoyable feature – the combat. I love tactical combat. And this game nails it. It is truly, truly wonderful.
Admittedly there are a few chinks in the chain where combat is concerned, as others have already expressed, but I must once again emphasize that these issues are FEW in number and each was generally more amusing than irritating. And, I imagine most players will feel the same as me with the exception of those playing on the single save difficulty where even the slimmest amount of unpredictability can turn the tide of battle, but I digress.
For my part, my own playthrough was completed on tactician mode and so my comments are centered solely around that particular difficulty.
One of the major failings with DOS:1, for me, was that even on the hardest difficulty, during the latter half of the game enemies just started falling at your feet. You grew too strong, too fast. At least, relative to the enemies. But this issue is largely corrected in DOS:2 and for the most part the final encounters remain challenging/somewhat challenging – assuming you don’t cheese them.
One encounter of note which I found particularly thrilling:
The Doctor encounter in the final act; without cheese and without individually eliminating any participating enemies in advance, ergo, taking them all on at once - this encounter was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
God there’s so much more I’m forgetting!
TLDR: This game is banana’s – ♥♥♥♥ing banana’s, SO banana’s that I felt the overwhelming need to bring my appreciation to the forefront and actually write a review. Few games have roused that level of enthusiasm. Trust me, you want to play this game.

It's interesting how lands far away from your own experience their own chances and changes. In one game, you may notice a king's untimely death. His kingdom, now under the rule of his too young son, fractures due to internal and external threats. In another game, after dealing with your own enemies, you might glance across the continent and realize that kingdom, which had imploded last time, has become a domineering empire.
I'm not going to go through Crusader Kings II's strengths; obviously I've enjoyed the game. It's well worth buying the game and particular add-ons when they're on sale.
Nevertheless, there are flaws to take into account:
1. There are too few unique events given how quick it is to write and program them in. You'll often spend game years between encountering any, and you'll keep seeing some of the same ones over and over.
2. The RPG aspect needs work. The characters aren't as deep as they should be. Generally, what you do to one person, you can do to another, and the "whys" behind actions aren't taken into account. Relationships are based off arithmetic, and it's difficult to genuinely feel close to a friend, child, spouse, etc.
3. Computer-controlled rulers aren't very proactive or difficult to defeat. Want to wage war against the Holy Roman Empire, which controls ten times as many troops as your tiny kingdom does? No problem: bring in effective commanders, take advantage of terrain, and crush the enemy armies while they're still small and trying to group up. It's common to get rid of ten or tens of troops for every one you lose. Other nations aren't likely to try to conquer your own land, even if you're much weaker, creating passive games.
4. The game gets boring after you become the region's powerhouse. There's no point taking over the world, because by the time you have a respectable kingdom, nevermind an empire, you have no competitors. It just becomes a matter of time until you slowly conquer Eurasia, and your only difficulty becomes keeping your nation intact. After you get to this point, you might decide to start a new game in a different part of the world.
5. The biggest pain is efficiently delegating conquered territory to vassals; unless you let your steward do it for you, which brings its own problems, you'll have spent more time painstakingly distributing your land than gaining it.
It's an excellent game, and I'd like to see improvements to the aforementioned issues in future expansions or versions to make it a phenomenal game. But that's not going to happen, so these flaws will remain.

The saddest piece of this is that this was my first attempt at playing a hacker game (I have hacknet and uplink in my backlog, but because I was given this one by a friend, I tried this one first). During the whole time I was busy with this game, I wondered if tedious closing and opening programs and clicking on whatever buttons the developers made available (the shown programs have lots of buttons that doesn't do anything) while strictly following the one path tutorial was how "hacking" was perceived. But instead of opening up after getting to know a few tools, things must've bugged out somewhere. Not the best experience, especially since thus far this sounded a lot like my day job (which includes the "bugging out" part, unfortunately enough). Or rather: how I COULD go about things if I had no conscience or notion of proper grammar.
For reference sake, I opened up hacknet and was immediately greeted with the things I would think a hacker game would need: a sense of community, overall storyline (hack_me has a bunch of mini-missions), non-overlapping windows (you can't move windows around in this game, so you have to write things down on paper, close the program and then open the next one) and a command prompt with a hinting system. I'm not sure I can fault hack_me for not properly having all the symbols for an AZERTY-keyboard correctly, but as you can imagine, typing "D:\documents" isn't as fun if you have to check where they assigned : and \.
The thing is: I obviously can't code better. Projects like these are probably the best ways to learn to make a game, as graphical skills aren't needed (worse: the mr.Robot reference is almost cringeworthy, as the quality of the show is on a level so much higher that I feel sorry for those liking this game for the desktop background).

Cons

I have not had a great deal of experience with these ambient sort of games. Therefore, it should be understood that my experience is limited. I will, however, impart my review for those who are interested.
Cradle is ultimately a very unique and enjoyable game. I truly enjoyed many elements of the game:
The scenery is beautiful and fun to explore. But keep in mind that although the immediate area is seemingly immense, there are boundaries and very little interactive components.
The music is perhaps one of the most intriguing factors of the game. In this respect I'm glad that I purchased the soundtrack. The artwork that comes with the package is decent but nothing extraordinary.
The character design is also great although there are only a few characters. Ida is very compelling and I'm left wanting to know more about her. My gripe about the main character is his voice acting. I've read that his lack of intonation and inflexion was the director's intention. But it still comes across as flat and unauthentic which really took a while to get used to in the game (if I actually ever did).
So here is my final analysis:
The game was very enjoyable. I did enjoy the storyline, but unless you're prepared to read every scrap of paper you come across, and are willing to delve into a little deduction and theory, you may not enjoy the game. The storyline's denouement is not self-evident and rather cryptic.
The gripe that I do have about the storyline is that it ends just as it starts to become intriguing. I'm not so much opposed as to how the game ends as I am to when it ends. What actually seems like the beginning of a deeper storyline actually becomes the ending. The game had so much potential to be great by adding more content which would have inevitably provided a much richer storyline and experience for the player. I'm left wanting to play so much more knowing that it cannot happen.
For example (
):
I was also not so keen on the optional minigame which can be played a number of times as you advance through the game. I like challenges so I completed the minigame out of obligation. But I would've perfered that the developers spent more time extending the game rather than incorporating the minigame. But others may disagree with me on this point as it is relative to each person.
For the price the game is a good buy. I felt that I got my money's worth and really did enjoy the game. But it does have its issues which deprives Cradle from being phenomenal. Nevertheless, I recommned this game.

After two-three long years of Awesomenauts, I thought I might give you my full thoughts about this game, now that we are getting close to the end of the Starstorm DLC development and the new Matchmaking server.
First of all, my feelings toward this game are mostly positive. I love the general gameplay style, it's like Smash Bros meeting MOBAs like Dota and LoL, 2D and stuff.
Music, oh boy, Sonic Picnic has really given their best with the game's soundtrack.
Visuals, they're great, I love the 1980's cartoon style Ronimo has been going for, same goes for the characters and lore in general.
Ronimo keeps updating the game with more characters, visual and gameplay advancements, new features such as new bots you can play with, when not having players in game, new game modes in custom games, skins and announcers. It's the reason the game is still going on for it's 3rd year on Steam, has got PS4 release that is also updated from time to time, and Xbox One -version coming.
Community involvement is great thing with this game, as I myself have made some sort of "career" on YouTube somewhat because of Awesomenauts. We've walked the path of YouTube together for these +2 years. And I thank both this game and it's developers with cooperation :) Also, the community of players might sometimes feel childish etc, but there are a lot of smart people who strive to keep Awesomenauts, well, awesome. We have had some great tournaments and other events, our suggestion for character voice lines, skin and/or character ideas are passed down to the game in one form or another, and in example, Replays have given us options to make more different kinds of gameplay videos to YouTube.
Of course, this game has it's issues. Since Ronimo can't afford to rewrite the netcode for Awesomenauts to enable dedicated servers, players have to deal with P2P, which will cause problems if 1. Player/players have faulty connection and/or 2. players involved are from different countries. Of course you can limit the options your matchmaking queue goes for, but it's a bit flawed until Ronimo implements their new Matchmaking servers around the release of Overdrive expansion (which isn't required to use the matchmaking servers, mind you). Connection problems aren't fixed by that, but at least matchmaking will be more "fair" towards players of different skill levels and you are less likely to be put in a game against players from other side of the world.
Speaking of skill levels, new players might find problems to start the game if they skip beginner missions and jump right into the online games (which is not recommended). Skill level might vary even in the higher leagues of leaderboards, but there are cases that new players quit the game because they don't feel the need of commitment to learn the basics and advanced techniques of the game and it's characters.
Then there's character balance. Some characters are already pretty balanced in a sense, but then there are one's that are doomed to be bad or too good. But, balancing acharacter isn't a walk on a sunshine, it's like stacking a house of cards. One slip and the whole house of cards might collapse, of course, then you have to start over again, but once you get it right, man, it feels satisfying. Even though you're missing couple of cards, which in this game are incoming characters and maps.
But, my likes, which are plenty, clearly overpower the dislikes towards this game, and over 2000 hours in the game, I say that I love this game. I believe that Ronimo can and will strive to make this game stand out and stay alive for a long time, and I'm willing to stay with Ronimo until the day Awesomenauts has to move to a higher plane of existence.
For about 10 euros (and hefty amount of sales/giveaways you can get this game from) this game is worth your time for at least those 10 hours. DLCs are mostly skins and announcers, and the Starstorm Expansion, but even without those you can get some solid hours in to this game. It's also great with friends, be it normal games or Custom games. With the upcoming matchmaking servers, Overdrive Expansion with three new characters, not to mention free character Ix the Interloper from the 2nd Design-a-naut contest and Starstorm station map AND character art updates for older characters, this game gets the love it deserves from the company who made it, and it should get the love it deserves from you, too.
Buy it. Play it. NOW!

Submerged is a short little exploration game. While it isn't amazing in any one area, the overall experience is a nice way to spend a few hours, especially if you like climbing puzzles and collectible hunting.
The atmosphere of the game is probably its best aspect. The day/night cycle keeps things fresh, and being surrounded by a variety of wildlife is fun. The waves and the light play nicely with each other, creating good opportunities for nice looking screen grabs.
The story isn't anything particularly novel or noteworthy, but it's enough to justify your presence here and move things forward. It surprised me a little, which was pleasantly more than I was expecting.
For a game with no combat I had no trouble staying entertained and coming back across 4 or 5 sessions to drive my little boat around and complete everything. Submerged is a solid foundation to start from as a developer. I'm excited to see where they go from here.

First of all it has to be said that Cradle is stunningly beautiful and has some fantastic ideas going for it. The world feels unbeleivably fleshed out and detailed for such a short game, and it's practically certain that even the most dedicated completionist won't find all of those little details in a single play through. Normally that would be a good thing, but not so with Cradle. It was a serious disappointment for me.
The thing is, there's so much information crammed into the world that it becomes overwhelming, and when the ending comes, it comes suddenly and without explanation. The main path through the game reveals so little that it's entirely incomprehesible without a tremendous amount of tedious sifting through newspaper snippets, posters, letters and other bits and bobs. I get the feeling that there's a fantastic story hidden in there somewhere, but discovering it is a punishing experience. You'll want to know more for sure - but you're not going to enjoy trying to figure it out.
So what about the mechanics of this game? Well... There are two parts. One is searching for a multitude of hidden objects in a world full of clutter (find the TV remote simulator, anyone?) and the other is an oddly out of place mini game involving collecting cubes in a neon virtual reality world. It does tie into the storyline, in a tenuous way, but doesn't really add much to the whole.
Perhaps Cradle is meant for people who feel that working (really) hard for a story makes it all the more rewarding, but to me it felt more like a game which simply never came together properly. It's confusing, lacks polish in its mechanics and doesn't give itself enough time to go anywhere. That's a serious shame, because this is a world which deserves recognition for it's beauty, depth and originality.

This indie puzzle game is beautiful in both its visuals and music and the mechanic of its environments being an origami (folded paper) construction provides some engaging gameplay. The visuals are marvelous and how you can unfold areas of the map to expose new places and solve puzzles is well done. The transition between areas is done as if it is an actual pop-up book (the devs actually built some of these from what I've read) which makes the experience very authentic. The game does have some flaws though: some puzzles are obtuse and could lead to frustration (even with the hint system), there is currently an audio bug that suddenly stops the excellent music right in the middle (disabling and re-enabling music from the settings fixes that in many scenes but this still kills part of the enchantment of the vistas) and it is quite short. Still, an interesting, beautiful and unconventional game, worth buying.

2nd ed D&D terminology may be a bit confusing to someone newer though.
THAC0 (to hit armor class zero) - chance to hit with attacks basically, lower = better
-Effects with "+x to THAC0" will actually lower this value, which is good
AC - Armor class - how well armored you are, lower = better
-Effects with "+x to Armor Class" actually lower this value, which is good
Saving Throws - die roll you would need to save against a specific effect. lower =  better
-Effects with "+x to saving throws" actually lower this value, which is good

Tengami is an adventure game set in a Japanese inspired pop-up book where you control a nameless hero trying to restore life to a cherry tree.
Great art style and soundtrack are sadly paired with a gameplay too light to be truly interesting.
-amazing art, the 2d pop-up book style is truly well done and inspired
-great, relaxing soundtrack
-original concept
-the haikus between levels are quite nice
-has an hint system if you get stuck
-puzzles are either easy trial and error environment manipulations (where you pull/push part of the scenery as in a real pop-up book) or somewhat dull combination locks where you must scour the various pages for the proper solution: they're not very fun or engaging sadly
-no proper story, who are you? why are you doing all this? all of that is left to you
-slow walking speed makes navigating the various levels quite dull
-very short, can be completed in little more than an hour
It's sad that such a beautiful game squanders its potential by not providing an equally interesting adventure: the few puzzles aren't really that interesting or challenging so all that is left is admiring the scenery and enjoy the nice music.
If, like me, you can get it for a few cents in a bundle then you might find it worthwile to play it once to see what it has to offer, but for an higher price and as a game by itself Tengami is sadly lacking.

The gameplay is what I was most skeptical about, I like turn based games but I wasn't sure if a game like this would feel fluid enough to keep me entertained or remain constantly fun, Upon playing the game for the first intro hour I can say the combat is the most fluid I've ever played in a genre like this. The animations are smooth, turns don't take a long time, and theres A LOT of depth in what you can do and how skills and spells interact. The character progression is DEEP and OPEN easily allowing you to think of creative ideas that could potentially turn the tide of a fight. Nothings more satisfying in a tactical rpg than trying out a crazy strategy and seeing it work. Manipulating the enviornment, comboing skills, and progressing your characters around a team comp is a huge gameplay aspect for all you nerds out there, with difficulty modes that can help emphasize those features.
This game also features one other amazing feature which is Mutiplayer. This was simply didn't believe, I can play a modern baldurs gate like game WITH FRIENDS?! It sounded far too good to be true, and let me tell you it's not. My highest level character is in a mutiplayer playthrough with 2 of my friends and I must say the mutiplayer aspect feels extremely tuned. Your characters are hardly limited in where they can be in the world, for example your friend could be halfway across an island and the game won't care. Don't want to listen to some specific dialouge a friend is listening too? Don't listen go do whatever you want, features like this are just an example of the Quality of life changes this game brings to mutiplayer. You could technically have separate battles across the game at once, or disengage and help your friends(although I wouldn't advise splitting apart) the games so open on how you handle mutiple players. Divinity also has combat which feels amazing to play with and strategize with friends. For example my friend had a spell called bloodsucker which allows him to heal off blood, he was low so I used blood rain to rain blood  while also spreading eletricity from a lightning spell I cast soon after which stunned my enemies, the electric blood rain then gave my friend blood to heal with. This amount of depth in a game that has quality mutiplayer is rare and I highly recommend it.
Environment, World building and Npcs: 8/10
The Lore of divinity 2 is rich. From the start you're given some interesting lore to create a compelling story. This game does an excellent job of creating 2 ways to experience the story and lore, you could take it slow, ask questions, explore journals and notes, look at every detail to find something you could easily miss, or you could simply go about the barebones of the story getting just enough lore from the main story to still feel immeresed and entertained. It has enough dialouge and interest to be worthy of something similar to Baldurs gate.
The npcs that fill the world are great, Interesting and full of character, the depth of your typical npc isn't groundbreaking, but it's enough to feel as if they are real characters in a real world. Also a plus, most all of the games npcs have an attitude system and a trade system which makes even the most pointless begger npc someone potentially useful. What really makes this game good from a story aspect is the Custom and Party characters.
What I love most about party characters is the amount of backstory, and depth that goes into each one. As you progress along your journey learning about these characters and experiencing more of their personality as you go is something that I will never grow tired of in games like these. What sets divinity aside from the rest is your ability to play as one of these characters, experiencing the game with a premade motivation and unique insight in both events and dialouge you just wouldn't have from a custom character.
The environment of divinity 2 is amazing, and feels almost fully interactable. This game emphasizes exploring to unlock the secrets around you, and even the most unlikely place may hold a secret side quest or item or bit of lore that will keep you exploring every corner in the area. The beautiful graphics and changing environments will keep you immersed throughout your campaign.
Music 7/10
The music is great, and fitting for almost every area I've been to in the game. While nothing particulary amazing the soundtrack creates just the right feel for the right moment, an often overlooked but essential element of any game.
Overall 8.5/10
This game is amazing and is rising as my favorite game of 2017. I'd recommend it to anyone looking for something tactical or narrative heavy to play that allows for many hours of gameplay and replayability.
tldr: If you've ever enjoyed pillars of eternity or baldurs gate or want to play a deep tactical game with friends, and don't mind or like turn based combat then try out this game, it's sure to not disappoint.

Finally! This game scratches the RPG itch that I've had since vanilla WoW. 55 hours in and I only just finished the first starting area. I'll lay out the main points of this game, and if any of them sound like your cup of tea, then I strongly suggest you buy this game because you won't be disappointed.
- RPG/Customization - You create a main character and get to choose from a number of other companions (up to 3). All of the characters in your party share experience, loot, and full player control. You can get weapons and armor, as well as many other crafting materials and random loot in the game world. You choose what skills your characters have (Do I want a battle-mage, a tanky melee fighter, a healer who can turn enemies into chickens, etc.) and switch out each piece of armor depending on how you want to roll them. The game is highly forgiving of mistakes when specializing your characters, so you have plenty of chances to respec.
- Turn-Based Combat - This was my main worry in getting the game. I've never been big into hack-and-slash or CoD kind of games, but I was still concerned that the pace would be too slow. I found that the combat, while reasonably paced, holds so much interest in terms of what skills to use, how to interact with the environment, and where to place your players to gain the best advantages. So addicting. Strategizing could mean the difference between sending your players to a short and violent death, or a hilarious and satisfying win against the odds.
- Fully Voiced Characters - Not a selling point for me necessarily, but it makes the game so much more immersive.
- Very Challenging - I recommend starting with the "Tactician" game mode, which is the second hardest. It's a difficulty that will pit you against very smart AI enemies who will use every trick in the book to screw you over, and I love it.
- Beautiful and Interesting Game World - Really a pleasure to see each new area. There are so many hidden quests and items if you really take the time to search each area. Looting is really exciting because you never know what type of gear you'll get, and it's actually relevant to making your characters stronger. Sometimes the difference between winning and losing a fight relies on just a few updated pieces of armor.
- Choice - You decide what to do in this game for the most part. It's very much open-world, and the decisions that you make during conversations or in combat could have a real effect on your path.
- Funny - From talking animals (who are quite helpful) to skill-combo surprises, I really enjoy the humor.
If you made it this far, I recommend you buy the game and see for yourself. One of the best and most immersive games I've ever played.

As someone who is already very familiar with both HTML and CSS, I bought and played this game purely so I could review it, and possibly recommend it to friends who wanted to learn. I will not be doing the latter.
This game is honestly a really bad way to teach anyone HTML or CSS, due to both the way it tries to teach and the way it plays as a game.
The game doesn't attempt to explain anything regarding what tags do, and how they should be used. It simply tosses them on the screen and expects the player to arrange them properly. In a way this is fine if the player is someone who learns better by trying to figure things out for themselves, but further issues ruin that potential.
The player is never expected to type anything, instead all that they do is move blocks with words and tags around. This too would be fine, if it weren't for the fact that you can place blocks on top of each other in odd fashions that muddies the flow of the HTML so its difficult to understand what should be displayed. Furthermore, you can place the tags anywhere instead of the game encouraging any kind of neat arrangement.
This would result in a success even though all the tags are scattered about. This kind of arrangement is not a good thing to teach. To make it worse the game makes a point of saying it's trying to teach the proper way of doing things.
Now as to why it's a bad GAME aside from being an educational tool.
The UI and visuals are absolutely rubbish. The game should be displaying both the page preview and the goal at the same time, rather than the player needing to switch between the two. Additionally, the 'hints' should just be displayed all the time, as they're often information the player should know regardless of trying to work out the puzzle.
The gameplay is also tedious and irritating. You have to jump around the screen picking up and dropping the blocks, when simply dropping and dragging with a mouse would have been much more sensible and less pointlessly time consuming. Even worse, if you drop a block on top of another, it can become difficult to pick up unless you position the character correctly.
Overall, don't buy this. There are better ways to learn and teach HTML/CSS.

The story isn't anything particularly novel or noteworthy, but it's enough to justify your presence here and move things forward. It surprised me a little, which was pleasantly more than I was expecting.

Fantastic and breathtaking, if you're willing to deal with some slight unpolish.
Spoiler Free: This is a game best enjoyed slowly. Nothing about this game is fast paced. The story and exposition is delivered piecemeal, there is a fair bit of dialogue, a lot of reading, and even the run speed isn't particularly speedy. If you rush to the finish line you will not have a great time as I did. Which leads to the prime particuliarity of this game: the exposition is limited, the story will not hold your hand and it is largely up to the player to put everything together.
That isn't to say there aren't characters who will sit you down and explain things to you. That does happen. However whatever information you get from them is augmented by the dozens and dozens of notes, article clippings, phamplets and posters found in the Main Character's small home. Some of the keys you need to put the story together can only be found by combing through all the papers. The dialogue will only get you so far, and at one point the exposition stops. You will have everything you need if you're diligent (it isn't that hard, just reading) to add it all up, but the game isn't going to explain itself in the end. You'll only have theories. I feel pretty good that I'm right about mine which is enough to leave me satisfied, but that may not be everyone's cup of tea. Otherwise the world building and lore is top notch.
As for the actual gameplay, well. There are some mini games that are very platforming/jumping heavy and those aren't fantastic. There is a reason for those segments to exist story-wise, but they are the weakest parts of the game. They are thankfully slippable if you fail them once. I only managed to complete two, and they were not fun enough for me to want to retry the ones I failed. But that's OK, no penalties for failing and skipping. No combat, but there might be one or two instances where you need to throw sticks at things. You can keep some sticks in your inventory which is a tad clunky. The objects in the world will reset themselves after each storybeat/autosave and that was a blessing since I got a tad carried away with the physics and threw around everything.
There were occasional bugs, one of which required a fresh install to fix, and another to restart the game. Controller support technically exists but it's pretty poor.
The sounds and style are beautiful. I found myself honestly touched or upset at certain points in the story. The main character's voice acting is flat/monotone by design.
My recommendation is to play this game in a few chunks. I liked being able to chew on the story bits over night and let them ferment. It isn't a long game, and savoring the story and crafting theories helped build up the enjoyment. It gives you a compelling mystery, and I will play it again to experience it all from a new perspective. I still haven't found all the information and lore there is to find! Absolutely play this game (just know what you're getting into), it is one of my favourite scifi stories.

It's an okay game. While it is a Pay-to-Win game (you basically buy your Hull, Turret, Propulsion, Flag, Weapons, etc with the in-game currency G), you start off with a decent tank to fight. Within an hour, you should be able to make around 10+ G, allowing you change some stuff.
I would prefer playing Armored Core over this though. Overall, a very simplistic tank mod game but not something that would intrigue/excite me.
PROS
1. Modded Tanks
Pretty fun to try and mod your tanks, like Armored Core.
2. Wall climb
You have mods that allow you to wall climb while others can't
3. Swimming
It's odd, but you can't swim by default. You need a special form of Propulsion to stay afloat and that allows you to go around areas that others can't E.g. Under a bridge.
CONS
1. Pay to Win
You need a lot of G to unlock every single item.
2. Restrictive Slots
Even if you earn the items you still have to choose your best build. This is like bag slots in World of Warcraft, but paid with cash.
3. Clunky movement
WASD are for forward and backward movement with hull rotation while QE are your strafe. You can imagine the difficulty in a game where your hull rotates on its own when you hit an object.
4. No Right Click Zoom
No Zooming? Very troublesome
Notes : You can die if your tank drowns in the water or you dessert by running off the map.

At first glance this may seem like an artsy indie film house equivalent of an atmospheric adventure kind of game.

The art style is rather unique. I had only seen screenshots previous to playing so I only saw the paper cutout look. But in action every thing is a pop up book that folds and acts accordingly to how you'd expect, mind the water of course.
You play as a Japanese Samurai or it appears that way. I apologize, I'm not that well versed in the culture. Walking around inside of a pop up book. The goal, one can infer things but it seems more or less to bring the tree back to life by bringing back lotus petals. The puzzles are all fairly strait forward though there is a hint system that can be turned off should you choose. Near the end, I did have to retrieve some actual real pen and paper as one of the puzzles requires you to count symbols that are reflected in Kanji characters on a safe. The soundtrack is quite excellent. There was something about the character movement speed that made him feel detached from myself. Almost as if he himself had started listening to the music instead of focusing on the task at hand at the same time as me. Or maybe I'm crazy.
I was actually rather surprised to find out this was an iOS game first. This may sound weird but thats an actual platform for games now. Weird, experimental ones at that. The only issue I might mention is that this, being an atmospheric game, may be served better here on PC. Typically, PC games are consumed at home, perhaps isolated. Anyways, its real short but worth your time.

Not all of the individual parts of this game are noteworthy, but together they create a tremendously engrossing experience.
A brilliant story told through unusual means will allow you to play as Cole Black, a mercenary trying to remember how a rescue mission went horribly wrong. You'll find yourself inside an asylum run by a mysterious figure called Red, who wants you to explore his facility as well as your own memories, making choices along the way (choices that actually DO matter too).
As an FPS the gameplay is a little lacking, even with some neat gimmicks that include a gun that can look around corners. The puzzle sections are few and far between and aren't extremely challenging, but do keep the game feeling fresh as the story goes on. Expect to do a lot of document reading to fully understand your place within the asylum and what Red really wants of you.
What really stands out and what I would advise you get the game for is the story. Unfortunately though, I can't express my opinion on the story properly without spoiling things, so I'll just say you'll most likely be hooked with suspense.
The audio is also exceptional, perfectly blending the mood of the characters and action together in most sections.
The game will most likely last you 6-8 hours to complete, with another hour more to collect and visit everything you can.
Don't get this for the horror or the gunplay, but get it for the story and enjoy the action sequences along the way.

My gameplay hours trump most (despite being inflated by afking with game running) but i've stuck it out and tried to report as many bugs as possible. Simply put this is a great game potential mared by bugs everywhere (for a metric, patch 3 addressed over 100 features and bugs alone, many of which were known for months of early access). This makes the game, as it stands, very hard to enjoy as you don't know what is bugged and what is a feature. Moreover, quests, despite being completed correctly, still flag as incomplete (and thus the game treats you as having not done the stuff you did) and this alone is tire screeching for any RPG.
Features are generally much the same as D:OS1 but again they feel like beta or just bad in some areas, and splendid in others. Dialogue and Banter chat log feature has never once functioned to date. Some fights in game warrant explaination on wtf Larian was thinking (Dreamers Portal) and most of the status and features require trail and error to get a grasp of (Ring: 6 Vitality apparently means 'this ring gives you constant healing equal to the HP from 7 constitution (and each point of constitution give 7% vitality, which are your Hit Points). Personal preferences aside, quite a number of 'intended features' are either frustrating (not being able to mouse over enemy debuffs to read description) or simply are broken/never made it into the game. There is a good deal number of dialogues that are only partly voiced, meaning that its either more bugs (not playing voice script properly) or intended that way.
Another Example: The quest log (arguably important) is poorly implimented. Supposing you avoid the bugged logs, it doesn't fully complete for each zone. It also updates per interaction (so if you find a boss, then later find a note hinting where the boss is, the note will be the top update). This results in you not knowing if the quest if still in your current Act (and thus you will miss out if you leave) or if the quest is continued in the next act. We've run into a game breaking bug.  After all the patches we've been through, a game breaking bug shouldn't be present.
My wife and I both have the game.  Our inventories have become messed up we think.  The only indicators we have are five blank spots when we go to Crafting inventory.  We have even tracked down where they come from.
During Driftwood, you have a quest, Strange Cargo, to rescue a guy in a barrel.  The moment you tell him to come with you, he becomes part of your party.  In his inventory are five grenade items.  No matter what you do after that, you will have blank spaces in your Crafting inventory.  Whether you kill him on the spot, or lead him safely out of town.
You might wonder what a few missing spots would matter.  As did we.  But when you get ready to leave Act2 and go to Nameless Isle, you'll either get kicked back out to the main menu during the cutscene, or get Crash to Desktop.  If you get kicked back out, it gives Save Error 302.
We haven't been able to get any attention on the issue.  But I suspect more people may realize having the same problem as time goes on and people progress through the story.  And they'll probably lose three days worth of progress like we did, and really really not even want to finish the game anymore.  So until this is fixed, or maybe even if it does, there's gonna be at least two negative reviews on this game from us.

Having put in a little over 10 hours to reach the end I can say the story, and it's complex layers, is right up there in the works of 12 Monkeys and The Matrix.  I've been gaming for over 30 years now and I haven't seen a more complex story except for Bioshock Infinite.  My hats off to The Farm 51 for putting together such a diverse story.  I had a very difficult time understanding all the pieces but as you get to the end it all comes together with an amazing ending.  That being said, the gameplay is not without it's issues.
1.  There are times when baddies would get stuck in walls because you disturbed their walking patterns and they moved to new area and couldn't account for the movement changes.
2.  There are no knockout options so you are left with full on shooting (which is actually not encouraged in the game) or running around them until you could get to the next area where a door would close as a save point. I avoided killing many of the people but especially in the asylum the halls are so tight your non-lethal options were very difficult trying to avoid them.  As an example, near the end with the "Mad Hatter" there were pieces of clues in the room he was in and the area is so tight the only way to grab the clues is to shoot him or run into the room and quickly click them without reading them because there is no time, run away until the next door closes and then later go back to your drawboard room to read the notes later.  Another example of this was a guy with a crowbar who says "I See You" (I think) and comes at you.  You have to turn around, run through some rooms and down two flights of stairs to finally arrive in a corner room shaped like the letter "6" so that you can trick him into rushing in and running around him so you can make it back to the top without killing him.  Because of the "walls" issue I described above I had multiple times where the guy would not enter the room.  He would just stand there and taunt me as if he was hitting an invisible wall.  I had to push up against a side wall very close to him to trigger the guy to enter the room and dies multiple times because he was too close to me.  I did manage to get to done non lethally though.
3.  The other part I didn't like about finding clues was that there were multiple instances where there will be additional rooms to explore for clues.  If you choose the wrong room and this is a save point then the door automatically closes behind you and there is no way to go back because it just autosaved.  The only way to go back for these clues is to go back into the drawboard room and relive the memory which is tedious just to get that 1 or 2 missing clues.
I'd still recommend this game for the story alone and tell people going in that this game is a lot more stealth centric than anything else.

It's interesting how lands far away from your own experience their own chances and changes. In one game, you may notice a king's untimely death. His kingdom, now under the rule of his too young son, fractures due to internal and external threats. In another game, after dealing with your own enemies, you might glance across the continent and realize that kingdom, which had imploded last time, has become a domineering empire.
I'm not going to go through Crusader Kings II's strengths; obviously I've enjoyed the game. It's well worth buying the game and particular add-ons when they're on sale.
Nevertheless, there are flaws to take into account:
1. There are too few unique events given how quick it is to write and program them in. You'll often spend game years between encountering any, and you'll keep seeing some of the same ones over and over.
2. The RPG aspect needs work. The characters aren't as deep as they should be. Generally, what you do to one person, you can do to another, and the "whys" behind actions aren't taken into account. Relationships are based off arithmetic, and it's difficult to genuinely feel close to a friend, child, spouse, etc.
3. Computer-controlled rulers aren't very proactive or difficult to defeat. Want to wage war against the Holy Roman Empire, which controls ten times as many troops as your tiny kingdom does? No problem: bring in effective commanders, take advantage of terrain, and crush the enemy armies while they're still small and trying to group up. It's common to get rid of ten or tens of troops for every one you lose. Other nations aren't likely to try to conquer your own land, even if you're much weaker, creating passive games.
4. The game gets boring after you become the region's powerhouse. There's no point taking over the world, because by the time you have a respectable kingdom, nevermind an empire, you have no competitors. It just becomes a matter of time until you slowly conquer Eurasia, and your only difficulty becomes keeping your nation intact. After you get to this point, you might decide to start a new game in a different part of the world.
5. The biggest pain is efficiently delegating conquered territory to vassals; unless you let your steward do it for you, which brings its own problems, you'll have spent more time painstakingly distributing your land than gaining it.
It's an excellent game, and I'd like to see improvements to the aforementioned issues in future expansions or versions to make it a phenomenal game. But that's not going to happen, so these flaws will remain.

Basketball is a limited contact sport played on a rectangular court. While most often played as a team sport with five players on each side, three-on-three, two-on-two, and one-on-one competitions are also common. The objective is to shoot a ball through a hoop 18 inches (46 cm) in diameter and 10 feet (3.048 m) high that is mounted to a backboard at each end of the court. The game was invented in 1891 by Dr. James Naismith.
A team can score a field goal by shooting the ball through the basket being defended by the opposition team during regular play. A field goal scores three points for the shooting team if the player shoots from behind the three-point line, and two points if shot from in front of the line. A team can also score via free throws, which are worth one point, after the other team is assessed with certain fouls. The team with the most points at the end of the game wins, but additional time (overtime) is mandated when the score is tied at the end of regulation. The ball can be advanced on the court by passing it to a teammate, or by bouncing it while walking or running (dribbling). It is a violation to lift, or drag, one's pivot foot without dribbling the ball, to carry it, or to hold the ball with both hands then resume dribbling.
The game has many individual techniques for displaying skill—ball-handling, shooting, passing, dribbling, dunking, shot-blocking, and rebounding. Basketball teams generally have player positions, the tallest and strongest members of a team are called a center or power forward, while slightly shorter and more agile players are called small forward, and the shortest players or those who possess the best ball handling skills are called a point guard or shooting guard. The point guard directs the on court action of the team, implementing the coach's game plan, and managing the execution of offensive and defensive plays (player positioning).
Basketball is one of the world's most popular and widely viewed sports. The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the most popular and widely considered to be the highest level of professional basketball in the world and NBA players are the world's best paid athletes by average annual salary per player. Outside North America, the top clubs from national leagues qualify to continental championships such as the Euroleague and FIBA Americas League. The FIBA Basketball World Cup and Men's Olympic Basketball Tournament are the major international events of the sport and attract top national teams from around the world. Each continent hosts regional competitions for national teams, like EuroBasket and FIBA AmeriCup.
The FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup and Women's Olympic Basketball Tournament feature top national teams from continental championships. The main North American league is the WNBA (NCAA Women's Division I Basketball Championship is also popular), whereas strongest European clubs participate in the EuroLeague Women.

I don't have any actual experience with hacking and computer security myself, but from what I've read about it, it's a lot more action behind the scenes of the computer and very much less action than depicted in movies. I have a feeling the hacking in "hack_me" (using programs and applications) is probably closer to the reality of what happens.
But even if this game does happen to be more accurate, it's not necessarily more enjoyable. It's quite dry, the tasks are pretty repetitive, there's a very loose and basic story. I gather it was made for Russian audiences initially but the developer has Google Translated the script to English, and it shows.
You don't really end up solving any challenges, really just copying information into other boxes to reach an objective. Would have liked a challenge with the tasks, or maybe more choice around what tasks you could accomplish, or even an instructional booklet that allows you to read up on the task, rather than being hand-held to the objective.
Again, it might be hard to make an enjoyable yet authentic hacking game. However I did enjoy the parts where I typed and looked like I was writing a virus, a great trick for parties.

I'd first like to say that I absolutely love the original Rock Boshers. It is definitely one of my favorite Indie Games, if not my favorite. It captures all of the asethetics of ZX gaming to its fullest beauty, provides interesting and creative gameplay, a good chunk of difficulty (I still haven't beaten it after all of these years), and some light humor. I always assumed development of the game would go no where and it would fade into obscurity. Being remembered as merely a demake like Gang Garrison.
Man was I ever overjoyed when I discovered that DX existed! I haven't played it long yet, but it's definitely better than the original (which is a must-get already). Here's my breakdown...
-Graphics: Fantastic. It's difficult to work with such a minimal sprite resolution, but Dugan does it masterfully. I was worried that the graphics were updated when I saw the screenshots, but you can choose between Console Mode and Old Computer mode, so no worries. Very faithful to the ZX aesthetic.
-Sound: Just fine. Nothing repetitive or annoying.
-Music: The soundtrack is great. Though I'm personally pretty disappointed that the original old-school sounding soundtrack is not an option. It really added to the atmosphere.
Gameplay: I haven't gotten far yet, but the controls are tight, and I assume the difficulty will get as hard (if not harder) than the original. Which is really hard.
If you like old school, minimal, or just plain unique games; do yourself a favor and buy this.
Edit: Aw, what the hell? PS4 players get 4 Player Local Battle!? Why is that not included in the PC version? The game is an homage to old COMPUTER games and the developers leave out features for the COMPUTER release. How disappointing!

When I was young, the internet was something I still didn’t fully understand, and spending money was low, I used to invest in compilations of shareware games that lined the shelves of every PC gaming clearance rack. The games themselves were rarely any good, but given there were hundreds on each disc it provided at least a moderate distraction in a time when I wasn’t looking for much more.
Rock Boshers DX feels a lot like a game I would have found on one of those discs. It’s aesthetically nostalgic but in a way that feels less a product of a specific era in games, and more something that’s just attempting to pass itself off as one. It hasn’t any novel ideas of its own, nor does an adequate job establishing its very simple set of mechanics. It’s a game without a direction that’s perhaps a solid first step for a developer cutting their teeth on game design, but nothing I’d want to actually play.
I can’t exactly describe how Rock Boshers plays, because it tries to do so many different things that it can play dramatically different depending on which level you choose. One moment you might be exploring a ship in a sidescrolling perspective, the next shooting zombies from a top down view or running in circles collecting keys to open the door to the next level. This variety doesn’t come as an interesting compiling of mechanics though, but as a directionless buffet of equally distasteful parts.
The only context to be found to Rock Boshers inconsistency is a narrative that seems to think itself far more interesting than it actually is. Exposition sprouts everywhere and none of it has anything compelling to say. There’s a familiar plot of worker exploitation and experimentation somewhere here but it’s so clichéd that you could likely guess the entire storyline on that premise alone. Most often the narrative seems to exist for the purpose of contextualizing every poor design decision, taking the game in so many different directions that it comes out with no identity of its own.
Nothing in Rock Boshers ever feels like it exists for a purpose. Most levels are designed to send you running into every corner, tediously winding through tunnels and trying not to die as the difficulty ramps up rapidly. If Rock Boshers is dull at the start, it’s agonizing once the training wheels come off and it throws everything it has at you with no regard to whether you can realistically defend yourself or not.
It feels like a long time since I’ve yelled at my monitor in such extreme anger and frustration as I did attempting to finish Rock Boshers, each death feeling cheaper than the last. Your means of interacting with the game are so simplistic that you’re often left with only a very narrow means of completing a given level, yet what those means are is often a challenge in itself to comprehend, made worse when each level seems to introduce yet another half formed idea which you then need to learn on top of everything else.
For as commonplace as retro inspired games are now, Rock Boshers is one that feels far more reliant on nostalgia alone to sell itself than most. In that regard I can’t fault it for being a game I could have feasibly played two decades ago, but times have changed and even if it might have held my attention back then, I couldn’t wait to leave its soulless existence behind today. Rock Boshers is a game made for another time and place, it’s just a shame it’s one I never want to return to.
