STALKER is a great series in an interesting setting, and Call of Pripyat is a great addition to it. It has taken the good design elements from Clear Sky with things like quick travel and an upgrade system, and not included the terrible things about Clear Sky. Shadow of Chernobyl is the other great game in the series, and I think this surpasses it (although you should still play SoC if you like STALKER.)

When your focusing on using a hammer , every problem looks like a nail - unknown
First , this game is EA - So take that into account when reading reviews to mean - GAME FEATURES NOT FINISHED.
This is important , as EA is not just a config - balance state - thats BETA.  This game is EA so think Alpha.
There are some features that are in ... alot that are not ... and balance issues that are being addressed.
Second , Is this game in its current state worth buying?
To answer that lets look at the following.
1) Understanding that Conan Exiles is an EARLY ACCESS ( Not feature complete ) game , are you willing to pay
money to play non complete game?
If you are , continue reading. If not - this is not the game for you.
2) Still here eh? Ok so your willing in theory to support an indevelopment game. Good for you.
Now - What works so far in this game?
A: Building - learning how to build in this game is simple and retard proof easy. - I'm looking at you sir/madam.
Each structure you attempt to place after crafting it is represented by a GHOST ( see thru ) image of the structure you intend to place - and rotating crafting benches , stairs , foundations , walls , gates , door ways , doors , gateways etc is easy.
Walls / Gateways / Gates / Doorways / Doors etc all have the words " Outside facing " or words to that effect written across them and if you can see those words facing you - then the OUTSIDE facing side of that structure is going to be deployed facing you. Rotate it to make it face the opposing side. GREAT for when you want that fortified wall to face outside your base rather than inside.
B: Crafting ( which i probably should have touched first ) - simple and easy.
You unlock crafting options when you level up.   Select reciepes on your screen ... look at the item you want to learn
And it will display a level requirement - a required recipe requirement ( ie: u need X unlocked before you can grab Y ) - and a POINT COST -  with each level granting the player X amount of recipe points to spend - and YES you can save them till you want to use them.
Once you have unlocked your recipes - via the INVENTORY screen on the right hand side you can see your list of reciepes that the player can craft without a CRAFTING STATION.
At crafting stations - you will see a list of items you can craft assuming you have relevant recipes unlocked.
Each crafting option contains a list of ReSOURCES you need to have in the bench or on your character to complete the craft.
See - simples
C: Combat -  Ok ... this is honestly fairly basic.  It is NOT a game of finese fighting. More arcade hit , step to the side .. hit again .... and currently i do not see this being a PLAYER A is more skilled than PLAYER B ... and more of a PLAYER A has better gear and is high lever there for PLAYER B is #@#$'d.
Still - it is OK. But no one is writing positive glowing reviews about Conan Exiles COMBAT SYSTEM.
D:  Ok ... so how about Player leveling in general .. ?
Thats ok. It is fairly easy to level buy CRAFTING basic goods as a solo player until you can craft your first iron weapons or tier 2 structures.
In fact - Between 4 players of ours .. 2 going combat hunting NPC's , 1 resource gathering and 1 crafting base parts etc ... the guy crafting base parts leveled pretty close to the guys hunting NPCS at a HIGH TIER npc spawn area.  With the guy gathering resources leveling decent ... but no were near the other 3.
However - this game does allow for COMBAT leveling , RESOURCE leveling and CRAFTING leveling so ... what ever your play style - leveling up so not be an issue too much.
e: GODS?
Just no. Find a private server that does not allow them.
If there is one thing that would turn this review from a COME PLAY to a GO AWAY - its playing on a server with GODS.
They are broken in the state they exist currently. Just dont touch them.
--TLDR-- Can i sum this review up in 2 sentences?
Yes.
Buy it if you are willing to accept this as an EA title with bumps in the road. Some days are GREAT , some days you wont be able to play. That is just how it is.

**Update** 9/19/17
*Buy it* - the game's at a point where the base content is fun and interesting, you can easily put a lot of time into it. Beyond this, MODS. There are lots of mods - from levels, to campaigns, weapon additions, physics changes, new playable characters, etc etc etc. Here's a gameplay video of the first several levels:
(Note - they are still actively making changes to the campaign, so some of what's in the video is subject to change, but I think it's a pretty fair showcase of some of the base mechanics and feaatures that you can expect from the base game.)
**Update** 8/2/17
So, I think this game is probably now at a point where I could recommend spending money on it - there still isn't a whole lot of content, but the content that there is with the arenas has some replayability, and there are mods you can get from the workshop that enhance the experience. Seems at this point in the development process they're fast-tracking the primary campaign before adding any new content, so it seems it's up to the mod community to create more content between now and release. The arena mod content is fun in small doses, and I find myself playing a bit here and there to kill some time (and rabbits) or keep myself occupied.
**Update** 5/2/17
Game is now playable, with the campaign for Lugaru ported into it - the dialogue/cutscenes aren't great, in that it jumps around a lot and you miss most of it just trying to advance them, but.. there's gameplay! And it's generally pretty brutal. The tutorial also now exists, and while it doesn't really give you a great chance to practice many of the more complicated combat mechanics.... well, at you least it gives you an overview of it. The battle areas are now greatly improved and also enjoyable; you can't customize them or choose what kind of battles you want to do (it's completely random - sometimes one weapon or another, sometimes deathmatch or team deathmatch, etc), and because you can't set it up to practice certain setups or skills, you'll die a lot when it comes to weapon matches. (My pro tip so far....... anything but a knife, run around 'till everyone else dies, then huck your weapon at the opponent and hope they die too. If they block it... well... you were probably gonna die anyways. /shrug). Promising updates, and expecting a real campaign and solid arenas in the real future.
** Original review below** 12/28/15 Gonna be honest... I was really excited about this game back in 2009. I mean, really, when they announced they were making a sequel to Lugaru. That was kind of a while ago. If you like the idea of this game, go buy Lugaru, it's predecessor. It's a finished game, and there are a couple mods you can download that double the content of it. This game... I literally don't understand what's taking them so long to finish it. It updates pretty often. It isn't abandoned. They could slap some levels together in no time. It doesn't have a tutorial, even. I can't in good faith recommend anyone buy this until it has reasonable content. Makes me sad. So much potential here.

So, GSC is no more, and with GSC dies STALKER. It's sad, but then again, all good things come to an end, and an IP is easily traded or revived.

Most surprisingly, the game runs beautifully -- the bugs for which the STALKER franchise receives a great deal of criticism are almost entirely absent in Call of Pripyat, a welcome change for the series.
But this isn't a recommendation based on technical aspects. If you've never played a STALKER game, Call of Pripyat is the best one to start with. From the first moments, the gameplay draws you in, using that STALKER magic to conjure a world around you of mutants and anomalies, a cold world in a hellish landscape where your only friend is chambered in 5.45x39.
Get Call of Pripyat.

Get Even is some kind of first person detective sorta game that has a bit of gunplay, a few puzzles, a lot of reading and a lengthy story. There are some ups and downs but I'll tell you what I think.
First of all though I'll tell you the story in a spoilerish manner:
The story is quite good actually, its pretty long and has a few twists and turns, it definitely kept me interested the whole way through, it's not amazing but it's pretty high up there. The story is based in the UK so there's a lot of british voice actors doing their thing so if you want to experience a slice of the brits then this is the game for you.  The story has quite a few characters all with their own back stories and reasons for existing, all of the main characters connect to one another in some form. Can't say much else without spoilers. A solid 7.5 for the story though.
The gameplay isn't too bad, the main thing you'll be doing is walking around and picking up evidence to figure out the story stuff, you can do this with help from your trusty smartphone which has a UV light, a map, thermal vision and a scanner which is used to identify finger prints and blood and stuff. That's a pretty cool mechanic and is very useful most of the time. There is a bit of gunplay but the game itself encourages you not to shoot enemies for some reason. You can also stealth past enemies but they see you way too easily, the stealth in this game isn't great at all, you can be seen in pitch black darkness in a corner through a bush from 50m away. Yes that's how crap the stealth is. Ontop of that there isn't an option to jump. Yes you can't jump, bit annoying but not too bad I guess. There isn't much other gameplay aside from that however there are a few puzzles here and there which are a bit easy but pretty fun. There is a hub area in the game which you can replay levels and collect all the the things you missed which is quite good. You can also unlock a bunch of different weapons. I'd give gameplay a 7/10.
The graphics in the game are quite good, they're top level indie type graphics, they're nothing like todays triple a games though so don't expect anything amazing. The graphical options are pretty good too, lot of things you can turn up and down. I really do like the textures aswell. 7/10 for graphics there.
The music is quite good I have to admit, some of the music is actually a bit horrible sounding but a lot of it is good, especially the violin tracks which really remind me of Bioshock. The sound effects in the game are top notch and they don't sound like any crap sounds you can get for free so that's pretty solid. The voice acting is also pretty amazing, all types of emotions are projected very well and every voice personified each character perfectly. 9/10 for sounds.
The optimization of the game is good enough I guess, there are some small lag spikes here and there which is a bit disappointing since I have a high end pc but its barely noticeable so no worries. I got stuck on a rock at one point which was annoying and had to load a checkpoint, this is why the game should have had a jump button. There are only two difficulty modes which is odd so I just chose the easiest and even still one or two enemies can 1 shot you, not a big deal but a bit random. The game itself is quite linear and the only thing that gives it a bit of replay value is that you can make certain choices in the game, mainly to kill or not to kill certain characters. Probably not really worth playing more than once though. There does seem to be a couple or maybe a few endings but I haven't tried to get more than one yet so we'll see. This game is very different than the majority of games I've played and personally, it's one of the more unique games out there. At first you're probably wondering "What the @#$! am I playing?" but soon you get sucked into the mystery of the game that will have you confused until the very end (and even still confused if you don't complete enough, but it clicked for me and I understand most of it for it to make sense, still a little confused though).
While the combact is pretty difficult, it made complete sense: You don't have body armor or some fancy suit to protect you, so obviously a few hits can kill you (this ain't CoD or Battlefield ladies and gentleman, surprise!), so please people, understand this if you're just looking for another CoD type game, it's nothing like that.
There's a few choices that will leave you staring at your screen thinking "WTF did I just do?!". You thought that games like Mass Effect and Life Is Strange could prepare you for the choices of the game but it's totally true: You don't know you've made an important choice and you have no selection menu for dialogue to know if it really is an important choice or not.
The End, which I won't spoil, is where everything makes sense. Sound like I'm spoiling it? Nope. Even the Devs said exactly what I did, and I was still blown away and taken by surprise. Nothing can prepare you, not even those words.
I just wish they had more promotion on this game, I kept getting "What is that?" whenever I told people what I was playing when playing this.
Personally I would give this a 9.5/10 and I highly recommend this to anyone contemplating the purchase.
And here's some helpful info for anyone seeing the posts about bugs, general info that may help, or maybe checking here for a fix:
+For crashing, just relaunch the game. I didn't have an issue after that.
+For getting stuck, give it time, the Devs apparently put in a script to detect if you get stuck and will fix it for you. I got stuck several times in one area but it got fixed automatically every time
+The AI, as one review said, does know where you are if you alert one. If you do get this and encounter the AI in combat, it will all make sense when you think about it. Even the "bad guy" (don't know what else to call him) blatantly says something that makes it really obvious as to why the AI know where you are.

When I played this game a few years ago I found it a bit too repetitive and grindy, given it was after a 100 hours of playtime. Even after many updates some people may still feel this way, and if you are not keen on slow progression and want to own everything immediately without spending any money then you will most likely get annoyed after some time.
I would still recommend it even to people like this as they should enjoy it for at least a few dozen hours.
But if you are someone who enjoys working towards goals in games then you should give Warframe a go without a second thought. In some free-to-play games, even some paid ones these days, the progression is made in a way to trap someone into paying in order to enjoy the game. Warframe is not this kind of game as earning everything yourself is very rewarding, but if you want to spend money on it as I did, it is better to just buy cosmetics. Some things, like the aforementioned cosmetics, can be bought only with premium currency but do not worry,  you can easily earn it by selling parts you dropped while playing.
The devs and community are great. Even when there is something wrong with an update, the devs usually listen to the community and make changes. If you are a new player do not be afraid to ask for help if you see someone better than you because unlike many other games where people are toxic, it is the opposite most of the time in Warframe.
Even though this game is not PvP focused, it still gives countless hours of gameplay, especially with the updates. The amount of time I put into the game still leaves me with many things to experience and learn.
Tl;dr Give this game a go and you will either get some hours of fun or find yourself playing it non-stop.

Great game, it offers alot of freedom with how to finish quests and the flexibility you have in combat is unrivaled compared to any other game.
There's however some problems with the game that should be addressed, the bugged quests in particular.  The Fort Joy island seems to have no bugs or problems, most likely because it was thoroughly beta tested however when I got to Reaper's Coast, the second zone, the problems started to emerge. Here's the quests I personally have a problem with.
1. All in the Family - Tarquin the quest giver is at the boat and not at the graveyard where he should be, thus the quest can't be activated. This quest is heavily intertwined with the main quest later. This is however not a problem for everyone but it's still very common.
2. The Silent One - Not really a bug but it's just unfinished. Like the quest is made to be a two-parter but it misses the second part
3. Finder's Fee - Delivering the head doesn't give you a reward and keeps the quest unfinishable
4. Treated like Cattle - Quest doesn't end correctly unless you screw up on purpose(drink the potion instead of giving it to the cows)
5. The Three Altars - Also doesn't end correctly after praying at the 3 altars.
6. No Laughing Matter - Breaks and uncompletable if you kill Slumberjack before receiving the quest and talking to him.
7. A Man and his Dog - The dog mentions a statue that smells fishy but the statue is unfindable thus making the quest unfinishable
All these are just from the second zone, I haven't reached the 3rd zone yet.
Nevertheless it's a great game and the bugs are mostly pretty minor but it still makes the game unneccesarily tedious.

is quite the fun game.  It blends elements of tower defense, RPG, action-strategy, and bullet-dodging to form a short-and-sweet little game.  Personally, the game felt a lot like the “Protect the Queen” games I used to play on
custom maps.   There are no truly innovative mechanics to the game, but the way the pieces come together do manage to form a game that has a strong charm of novelty.
The game is short.  It took me just under 5 hours to earn all achievements.  That’s OK though, because it was a fun 5 hours and I didn’t really need any more.  If you find yourself wanting more you can compete on the leaderboards.

Also, the game is casual.  Even on the “insane” difficulty, the game becomes simple once you’ve bought enough upgrades.  As someone who enjoys casual games, I really felt the balance of difficulty in this game was very enjoyable.  You have to pay attention and play, but you won’t ever find yourself frustrated.  Having said that, people who like very difficult games may find themselves left wanting by
.
The gameplay itself is extremely simple.  You’ll have it all figured out in the first minute and it won’t change much after that.  There are new units and upgrades which you unlock that spice things up as you progress.  But I will admit, the content is rather limited.
The graphics are "cartoonish" and simple, but they fit the atmosphere.  The music is not bad by any means, but I felt it could have been a little more epic and various considering the game has strong musical undertones.   The controls are fluid and intuitive.  The game is stable; I experienced no glitches or crashing.
In summary, I would say
is very fun and worth playing.  It’s simple enough that almost anyone should be able to enjoy the gameplay.  If you are itching for something fresh and a little different you can probably get some fun out of this game.

This game is realistic and therefore very hard.  Perhaps too hard to be a video game.  On a small chance, the King dies leading his armies.  Well, your dynasty just fell apart, thanks for playing.  The game is unique and really, to play it well you need to think about your dynasty through the centuries.  There is a very steep learning curve.  The hardest part for me has been surviving the shakedown of the first 5 years of the game.  The different time periods start intentionally in a time of strife.  Translation: there's 90% chance something crazy will happen to screw you over.
I found the interface a little bit wanting.  There are many levels of organization and familial claims: empires (multiple kingdoms), kingdoms, duchies, counties.  Navigating this tree to figure out where the sneaky opportunities lie is nigh impossible.  At least, I have not figured out how to make it work.
If you are looking for a VERY HARD strategy game with political intrigue game mechanics, which you can't get anywhere else, this game is for you.  If hard to use interfaces without almost any intelligent searching help turns you off, go somewhere else.  As for me, if the interface were better, I could recommend it as a niche game, but I just can't get behind it.
UPDATE: I stuck with the game and learned its mechanics.   On the whole, the game is refreshing in that random events can completely change outcomes.  It makes for some fun stories epic fails, and loading save games.
In the end, I think the diplomacy lacks depth and therefore I won't be playing the game over for replay value.  You only have alliances with immediate family members and their spouses.  Perhaps that is realistic -- but what is not realistic is there is no negotiation as a part of joining a war, such as offering your ally land or other incentives.  It is stupid simple: how many families did you marry into?  This means that the computer players will attack you 3- or 4-on-one right after you have a succession to an heir (and lose all your alliances).  For me, it gets kind of annoying.
It is a testament to this game that you can do political maneuvering, and that I get frustrated because I can't execute some of the sneaky underhanded ideas I have.  In other words, I am inspired to scheme by this game captivating my imagination, but then also frustrated by not being able to execute it.  Sort of a love hate angle.
For example, I captured the (unmarried) French princess in battle.  I figured, hey I'll let her out of prison IF she marries my son.   Here is where advanced diplomacy trading could really shine, but is simply absent.

Cradle is an amalgam of different ideas that end up making the game less than the sum of its parts.
This game has some truly interesting thoughts on humanity's future and how people are valued, but these concepts are mixed in with a very ambiguous overall story that is conveyed almost entirely through notes and in-game art.  Even after analyzing most of those, the story is still very hard to make sense of.
The developers also went wrong in choosing to combine this confusing story with several cube/block based mini-games that you need to beat in order to advance the story.  They were frustrating and really hurt the pacing of the game; I wanted to keep exploring the story, not stopping to beat a level of frustrating gameplay every 30 minutes.
My advice to the developers: if you're going to make something story-based in a video game, you don't need to add in 'challenge' elements like a traditional game.  Make it more about experiencing the story, enjoying the art & environments, and connecting with the characters.
If you're looking for some great story-based gameplay that will leave you thinking about life instead of being frustrated and confused - go play SOMA or Firewatch.

Set somewhere in Mongolia, you play as Enebish (or so the game tells you..) the grandson of your late grandfather and parents. You wake up with amnesia not remembering anything of your previous life. The only connection you have to the past is a robot named Ida. Cradle is full of mystery and puzzles both strategy based and for the mind. It is a post apocalyptic game but it is a peaceful game that will keep you thinking and exploring for hours, even though it is a relativly short game. I still want to explore the surrounding area further now that I have finished the main storyline. This game is so detailed, you will lose items quickly!!! I lost so much important stuff in the yurt that I had to restart the game from my save point multiple times. Its one of those games that you have to play alone with headphones, it is so immersive that to get the whole experience you need to seclude yourself for a good 6 hours. Anyone who loves mysterious story emmersive puzzle games will love Cradle! You should definitaly give it a try!

Jet Set Radio just brings back good memories.
This classic was one of the first games to include cel-shaded rendering for a 3D game, but that doesn't do it enough justice. In Jet Set Radio, you take on the role of a group of rollerskaters in Japan, who are in this futuristic Tokyo where Jpop music and rollerskating are actually the cool thing. As part of the gameplay, you are tasked with going into neighborhoods and vandalizing them with your own Graffiti. As you start to spray onto windows and walls, the sinister police of the future will show up and try to beat you down, gas you and even shoot you. Thus, the game puts an emphasis on evading the violent cops, whilst fulfilling each level by spraying all graffiti on the walls before time runs out.
What makes this game so good? Well, it is very unique. The controls are simple and easy to become accustomed to, yet to master the game takes practice. It is thrilling because you can do stunts such as railgrinding, wallriding, etc while spraying. It is purely a sit down and have fun game, with a nice challenge. Unlike other skater games at its time, this one was less about crazy button mashing combos, and more about fluid movement. The quicker you finish, the higher the score you get. There are graffiti unlocks, and you even get to challenge other skaters to have them join your gang.
Another part of this game which is nice, is the iconic "JET SET RADIO!" station which plays real pop music from Japan and the US and even England; such as punk bands, Jpop music and so on. The artistic quality is very unique, sporting something along the lines of that early 2000's culture rush of "wacky and wild" sports games. In spite of being a game from the year 2000, 16 years later it still looks pretty good with its cel-shading, simply because cartoon graphics are not at all difficult to render. This game was a very daring release by Sega; and it definitely gave them some kind of competitive edge back in the day. Jet Set Radio Future was released on the Xbox, which gave it popularity as well.
The violence in the game is as cartoony as the game itself; and you will see funny behavior from the police when they fail to catch you "Damn!" while shaking their guns, etc. The attitude of the game is just so fun and exciting; it isn't dramatic or serious, just fun and enjoyable. One final piece of awesome: You can design your own graffiti! You can spray it freehand and even add letters, skew/reshape the way the appear as well. This makes you have more liberty in expressing yourself, as opposed to being restricted to the preset graffiti.
Pros:
+ Unique gameplay about Skating and graffiti.
+ Cartoon art style and graphics live well to this day.
+ Music selection makes me think I am in the late 90's, early 2000's.
+ Retrospective views on the future from this game are charming.
+ Challenging but fun, the faster you finish the better score.
+ Ability to make your own custom graffiti.
+ Widescreen + modern hardware support.
Cons:
- Sometimes, the control responsiveness can be odd. If you use a Steam Controller, you can fix this with some pad tweaks.
- No free roaming mode; but forgivable.
- Menu for save/load in the garage isn't really visible.
Conclusion:
I played this game long ago, and being invited back into it makes me so happy, especially on my PC with modern hardware support! I wish companies made games like this still, you know; challenging, fun, lacking in drama, lacking in DLC and horrid DRM... It is amazing to pick up an old game and review just how bad newer games can be in comparison.

Get Even has proven itself to be quite possibly the most difficult game to review that I've done. It's so tightly narrative focused that to talk about why I loved it is nigh impossible to do without spoilers, but I'll stay as free of them as I can.
Throughout my playthrough of Get Even, I was reminded over and over again of one game in particular, that being Frictional Games' SOMA. That game, much like Get Even, was, at its core, a rather mechanically derivative horror title held up by one of the most thought-provoking narratives I've experienced, one that's still turning in my head long after I'd finished it. Get Even is much the same way.
Mechanically, it's not the best game I've ever played. Various people who worked on the game claimed that “it's not a shooter, not a puzzle game, not a horror game, not a walking sim, nothing you've ever played.” While it's true that Get Even is difficult to classify, it's not exactly a never-before seen experience. The truth is, it includes all of these elements in the game, though combat is the one seen most often. It's also, thankfully, pretty enjoyable. While the enemy types are a bit boring, and the weapons nothing special, the Cornergun, which lets you aim around corners to avoid getting hit (you die extremely fast in this game,) is a wonderful idea I hope to see more games do. The other elements, puzzles, exploration, etc. are all pretty standard and nothing you haven't seen before, they're all in service to the game's story, instead of the other way around.
And this is most definitely a story worth experiencing. It's billed as a thriller about uncovering the truth  behind a tragic incident through an Inception-style exploration of memories, complete with themes of corporate espionage and betrayal, underneath all this is a heartbreaking and extremely personal story about love and loss. I can't go into much more without spoiling, but suffice to say it's one that I'll be thinking about for a very long time afterwards.
Visually, the game looks alright. It's use of photogammetry is nice, but the fact that it runs on the dated Unreal Engine 3 somewhat tanks the visual experience. The music, however, is wonderful, a beautiful mix of orchestral and electronic, and is easily one of the best scores in recent memory.
So, should you play Get Even? I'm sure you know I highly recommend it, but only if you want to experience one of the best stories gaming has to offer. If you're looking at it because you were a fan of The Farm 51's previous action-oriented games, this is most definitely not that. It's a much slower-paced game that plays a bit clunky at times, but if you were a fan of SOMA for the narrative, or want something very different than the usual crop of games out there, then give Get Even a go.

Let me get this right out of the way. This game is offensively bad and is definitely not worth the 30 dollar asking price. I beat the game in about 6 hours on the hardest difficulty and it lacks any replay value whatsoever. It's a simple linear, corridor, first person game with almost no redeeming qualities.
Pros:
+ Soundtrack
That's it for the pros. The only good thing I can say about this game is that it actually had a decent soundtrack. The rest game honestly does not deserve the soundtrack it got, because the OST is leagues above the rest of the game.
Cons:
- Graphics are horrendous, even for a 30 dollar game.
- Performance indoors is fine, but outside is a stuttering mess and the graphics don't justify the performance.
- Bugs. I ran into an annoying bug several times where I would just get stuck in walls for no reason and forced to restart.
- Gunplay is absolutely trash. It's the worst kind of generic gunplay. AI is beyond stupid and it feels like you're shooting targets, not people.
-Level design. The best levels in the game are in the asylum, where you focus on story, exploration, and puzzles. Unfortunately its not a very large part of the game and most of the time you will either spend outside in a generic lot or inside some office building shooting (or sneaking past) baddies.
- Story. The story is pretty boring and doesn't deserve the buildup to its several plot twists. None of the twists are particularly interesting, and the story goes into a poor direction near the end.
Like I said before. The game can't decide what it wants to be. It starts out playing like Condemend Criminal Origins (best parts IMO) but then with change into a generic FPS with garbage sneak elements. The Asylum is the best area of the game. This area is where you walk around and explore, using various software on your phone to unlock the mysterious of the Asylum. The phone basically get's thrown into the trash halfway through the game.
Don't bother with this trash unless you can get it for 5 to 10 dollars. This is one of the few games I can remember that I genuinely felt ripped off for buying.

Fun and challenging game. Fast paced roguelike hybrid.

As a concept, it's almost ok. The everything out of paper in a book idea... I suppose something can be done with that.
But the pacing is very slow, and there really isn't enough going on, visually, to make up for it. It's simple gradients and textures, and simple shapes, and you have a long time for things to sink in, because the dude walks pretty slowly. There is usually a full screen of space between elements you can interact with, and while I can appreciate this from an encapsulation perspective, the space between things plus the slow walking plus the simple art means that just moving around gets boring. Like, Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery also had you moving a person around at a pretty fixed walking speed, but the Scythian walks more quickly, and the environment is lush and alive. The soundtrack and the ambience are carefully developed, the bushes wiggle as little pixel squirrels run around: it's great, and Tengami has none of that. Halfassed sprite fire, halfassed sprite waterfalls, and halfassed polygon waves account for probably 90% of the animation you'll see that isn't your damn slow-walking dude.
The puzzles barely count as puzzles:
The hardest thing the puzzles make you do is occasionally backtrack, which is only hard because it's boring.
One extra sad moment: one puzzle involves counting a symbol that you can only see during the page transition, but it's in the game way after the page transition thing has lost its novelty, so instead of being the only point where the puzzles and concept interact meaningfully, it winds up being closer in effect to those parts in VGA point and click games where one of the things you had to click was really small and nondescript.
As for the music... it's like the mp3 collection of a Reiki practitioner. Very little of the music actually has a japanese song structure, or even melodic structure: it's western music in a vaguely Japanese scale on a synth Koto over soft breakbeats. Less "meditating samurai," more "ad for a zen retreat for retired white people."
The puzzles are there to slow down a story, in three acts, that involves a melancholy samurai wandering around abandoned places doing incoherent things in search of cherry blossoms. Your reward for each act is a 3-5-3 haiku in english, and getting to put a blossom onto a barren cherry tree, which triggers a transition (a fade through black) to that portion of the tree being in bloom. The finale is another haiku, which seems to want to suggest that this was maybe like a meditation on memory and aging and death and stuff. Or like, whatever. It has seasons, and cherry blossoms. That's pretty deep♥♥♥♥♥♥
Seriously, the written part of the story is maybe 55 syllables, if there was a haiku at the beginning. I don't remember, and it doesn't matter, because the point remains: there is effectively no story. You collect three cherry blossoms that, although they only blow away, are locked behind some pointlessly complicated yet easily defeatable barriers, and then apparently your life is over and you die or something. There are absolutely no other characters in the game, and no explanation for why this dude is alone for all of the incoherent stuff he does.
You saw the trailer video, and it showed a page turn. You already have everything this game has to offer.

Tengami, by Nyamyam, is a perfect example of the potential of the indie gaming scene, the ability to take a risk, not just on a new IP, but in gameplay, music, and even challenging what a videogame is and should be without the pretentious lack of meaning - do not mistake this for an interactive book.
Wolves sleeping
Beneath pale moonlight
Dreams unfold
Gameplay: 85/100 B
Tengami, like many #indie titles, love to revert back to simpler controls and concepts when it comes to gaming. With this game, however, we venture back to one of the oldest styles: point-and-click. Yes, I know to many, that phrase means "dull" and "boring" and I really can't say it isn't at times - there are a lot of boring point-and-clicks, but that doesn't mean they cannot be engaging, wonderful, and all around good, just look at The Secret of Monkey Island and the Myst series. On top of this, Tengami is also a puzzle game set in a pop up book, so two strikes already? Not quite. Another trademark of the indie scene is the ability to take a well established mechanic and adding a simple twist or two, either reinvigorating or reinventing said genre, and Tengami does this in a solid enough way to have it stand on its own.
For the most part, Tengami's gameplay is straightforward enough: click here, move this, solve that, continue on, and that is pretty much the whole of the game, but not to say it is bad in any way, just solid.
Audio: 93/100 A-
The music, sounds, and ambiance of this game is quite good when you get right down to it. Well crafted and fitting to the various settings within the game. The main issue I encountered was that the music would cut in between scenes or when I move from one page to another rather abruptly instead of transitioning. I don't know if this is a technical error on part of the game or something wrong with my sound hardware. Having said that, the music is one of those things I wouldn't mind having in my collection to listen to outside of the game, very classical Japanese music, things you could meditate to.

Visual: 90/100 A-
Visually, the game is very appealing and is most definitely pulling the "video games is art" card and there is nothing wrong with that, except in this case, the art style is the inspiration for the game. From the multilayered paper cutouts of the scenery, the moving set pieces, recalling the shadow puppets of the East, or even the simulated moving water, expressing in a repeating pattern flowing over and over again. Even your character moves around like a paper cutout, and disappearing for a fraction of a second when he turns, much like Paper Mario did. Aside from that aesthetic, the game isn't superior and won't cause your machine to chug and choke trying to run it. Tengami has an identity and style of its own, which is often times a hard thing to accomplish in an ever increasing video games market, indie or not.
Design: 83/100 B-
With a simple gameplay mechanic comes a simplicity in design, hints and actions are shown and highlighted with glowing rings either on objects or the sides of the screen, indicating a possible page turn. Paying close attention to when these appear will often point you in the right direction or show you the next thing you need to do, serving as a clue or hint on how to solve a particular puzzle. Speaking of the puzzles, they aren't anything mind bending or difficult in their presentation, but I also got the feeling that they weren't meant to be mind altering, life changing, puzzles. Much like the rest of the game, the puzzles serve the mechanics of the game, showing off the style and mechanics, allowing the player to move the plot along. There is also a "hints" button you can choose with no consequence, as far as I can tell, revealing things in one or two line suggestions.
Story: 75/100 C
Speaking of which, the story aspect of the game seems to be the weakest in that there really isn't one in a traditional sense. It's as open to one you make up in your head as the one that is already in place, much like Sonic the Hedgehog or Super Mario Bros. One nice thing that I do enjoy, isn't directly related to the story, per se, but at the end of each chapter, where a lovely haiku is presented:
A pristine waterfall
Cascading downwards
Crimson leaves
Content: 77/100 C+
Tengami, despite its beauty, is not that long of a game and can absolutely be completed in a single sitting. There is some satisfaction from solving the puzzles and is a game I would give to others to try out, but not just to my peers, but to those who are older than I, as well as those much younger than myself. I have always found that a puzzle game is successful, mechanic wise, when a child can explore, experiment, and still have fun with it. Portal, Monument Valley, and others are very much like this, but if you are looking for a game that offers more staying power or hours upon hours of replayability, you may want to look somewhere else. Just like its mechanics, Tengami works best when treated like a book, something you visit now and again between periods of time or shared with others.
Performance: 81/100 B-
Overall, the game ran fine on my PC. There are no real settings to fiddle with, but I did experience some sluggishness from time to time, only to discover I had another program running in the background. So I'm not positive whether or not it was the game's fault or my own.
Final Verdict: 83/100 B-

This is just one example of various I have available.  As for a serious review, my friends and I play this game when we need to get away from serious strategy games that require intellectual thought and planning as a way to "unwind" of sorts and be stupid, and the beauty about it is, after a relatively short amount of time, you're ready to play whatever game you were playing initially again.
For example, a group of friends and I were playing Men of War: Assault Squadron.  After getting steamrolled by the Germans for the third time in a row, we were basically fed up and needed time away from it.  It was looking like we were just going to call it a night and get off till a friend decided this would be a good idea, and bought me a copy while it was on sale.
What followed was about fifty minutes of utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and cancer.  It turned from a game about golfing with friends, to a breeding ground of divsion where the main goal was to sabotage the other player's efforts to win by sacrificing yourself and wasting your own time to knock them away.
After those fifty minutes, we were ready to go back to Men of War.  It should be noted, fifty minutes is a comparatively short time period, whereas otherwise we would have gotten off and the time would be measured in hours, rather than minutes.
If you're looking for a "filler" game to play in between gaming sessions where you and your friends can cool off and have fun (or lose your♥♥♥♥♥♥and ragequit), this is an excellent option.  Binge-play hours in a major title, take a thirty to sixty minute break in Golf With Your Friends, and you're easily ready to go back.
Or, simply play the game on your own, or, as the title suggests, with your friends.  The game is well off enough that it can stand independently and not as simple in-between filler.  The oftentimes challenging level design will encourage you to stay up, similar to a game of Civ, where you must get in that one, last turn to succeed.
It's well worth it, but prepare to lose your friends.

This game is realistic and therefore very hard.  Perhaps too hard to be a video game.  On a small chance, the King dies leading his armies.  Well, your dynasty just fell apart, thanks for playing.  The game is unique and really, to play it well you need to think about your dynasty through the centuries.  There is a very steep learning curve.  The hardest part for me has been surviving the shakedown of the first 5 years of the game.  The different time periods start intentionally in a time of strife.  Translation: there's 90% chance something crazy will happen to screw you over.
I found the interface a little bit wanting.  There are many levels of organization and familial claims: empires (multiple kingdoms), kingdoms, duchies, counties.  Navigating this tree to figure out where the sneaky opportunities lie is nigh impossible.  At least, I have not figured out how to make it work.
If you are looking for a VERY HARD strategy game with political intrigue game mechanics, which you can't get anywhere else, this game is for you.  If hard to use interfaces without almost any intelligent searching help turns you off, go somewhere else.  As for me, if the interface were better, I could recommend it as a niche game, but I just can't get behind it.
UPDATE: I stuck with the game and learned its mechanics.   On the whole, the game is refreshing in that random events can completely change outcomes.  It makes for some fun stories epic fails, and loading save games.
In the end, I think the diplomacy lacks depth and therefore I won't be playing the game over for replay value.  You only have alliances with immediate family members and their spouses.  Perhaps that is realistic -- but what is not realistic is there is no negotiation as a part of joining a war, such as offering your ally land or other incentives.  It is stupid simple: how many families did you marry into?  This means that the computer players will attack you 3- or 4-on-one right after you have a succession to an heir (and lose all your alliances).  For me, it gets kind of annoying.
It is a testament to this game that you can do political maneuvering, and that I get frustrated because I can't execute some of the sneaky underhanded ideas I have.  In other words, I am inspired to scheme by this game captivating my imagination, but then also frustrated by not being able to execute it.  Sort of a love hate angle.
For example, I captured the (unmarried) French princess in battle.  I figured, hey I'll let her out of prison IF she marries my son.   Here is where advanced diplomacy trading could really shine, but is simply absent.

I'd like to be clear from the start and state that my small review for Submerged is heavily influenced from the price of the game - without discounts, it costs a whopping 20€/$. Which is very very very very too much for a game like this, considering too that it's one of the first games ever made by Uppercut Games (and it's quite clear that it's somehow a "first game", judging to the general lack of depth and the easy/forced gameplay).
The story itself falls into that "atmospheric adventure" kind which is very slippery, one must have many right ideas at the right place in order to put together a game like this that focuses more on the plot and the general context rather than complex tactics or such.
The gameplay itself, as I said, is too simple and too forced, you can't do almost anything that one could expect from a 3D adventure with high expectations. Navigating with your boat gets quite annoying (and the controls are definitely not so great even with a controller) and after that you've got to climb palaces and structures following a somehow pre-ordered pattern. There isn't really space for exploration and more than this, there's nothing else than what the plot requires.
The beginning could be quite promising - a submerged unknown civilization, and your female protagonist that has to help step by step his little brother. There's no dialogue (so, ok, it's also translated into Italian but. there's no dialogue! not a lengthy work XD), there are no enemies, basically you can not die. And there's nothing really interesting and new besides this; the plot unfolds in a trivial way and the ending's not that satisfying at all. In a game without gameplay (and with bad control response) one should expect a great storyline, great graphics and great soundtracks but I've found none of them, apart something interesting in the water and in some parts of the music.
It seems really that every building is a copy of each other, and after you've done your first grab-and-come-back tasks you've already got all the game has to offer.
And all of this really - even if I hadn't spoilered at all the "story" - really does not deserve 20€.

I admit, I was unsure whether I wanted to give this a positive or negative review.  On balance, I recommend it but I want to make it clear from the outset - you do nothing except climb and sail.  There is no danger, no combat, you cannot die.  The secrets are not very secret and there are no real missions, just  find 10 quest items.
Having said that, the game is relaxing and fits a niche I like to keep in my games for when I am tired or not really feeling up to the focus requirement of most of my games.  The music is pleasant, as are the graphics.
The system requirements are not as high as it states - I am running this on an intel 4400 graphics card which should not be good enough, according to the stated requirements.  I did get this on 90% sale and would advise people to wait for another sale to get it, since there is not a lot of content.
The story itself is sorta touching.  You are trying to help your brother by obtaining supplies from partially-flooded buildings around your location, which you reach by your boat (which you can find propellor parts for) and climbing various ledges and vines.
I do wish more of the buildings were explorable and that you could dive underwater.  The game seems very open world until you realise that every place you can climb to contains a secret.  Some are just decoration.  So much more could have been done with this game, so while I did enjoy it mostly, I was a bit disappointed towards the end.

At first I was put off that Straima had multiplayer with up to four players and imagined that the game was built around that and would offer a subpar single-player experience; I was wrong.
Straima is an extremely difficult platformer set up with over 100 bite-sized stages. Each stage consists of a single, non-scrolling map that loops on each side. Focusing on a small space allows the level design to be very meaningful and not filled with fluff.  A few stages even offer nods to other games such as Tetris, Frogger, or VVVVV. The main goal for each stage is to squash every pink blob (pinkie) on the screen. There are also two side-goals for each stage; finish within a certain time and/or without dying. The game tracks your progress for the side-goals in the form of gold trophies next to the level on the menu and these goals can be met on separate runs. Most stages have a target time between 20-60 seconds. One might think that this is worrying for game length, but Straima offers excellent replayability.
The game can be rather addicting when it comes to completing a stage under the par time. There were many occasions where I was only a few seconds away from reaching it and couldn't walk away while thinking “I'll get it on the next try!”. Of course, the run I was looking for was sometimes a dozen or two attempts away. Though, there were times when I was stuck on certain levels (I'm looking at you, Pinball Wiz) and needed to move on to another. The great thing about Straima is that there are so many levels to choose from that this isn't an issue. As you play other stages, you will learn certain tricks that might allow you to shave off a few seconds from previous levels that the target time was just a hair out of reach. At times, Straima even felt like a puzzle game to me. I would sit here and map out my route, trying to finish the level in the quickest way possible. The time trials can be rather tight even if you don't die in a level which makes this planning very necessary. There are also stages that are designed to be a puzzle through use of mechanics such as levers to open and close passageways in a maze.
Each level is very unique compared to the rest and never once did I get the feeling that I played the same stage twice. This is rather impressive to me given the sheer number of levels put into the game. Straima achieves this through it's great variety of enemies, hazards, stage modifiers, and choice of power-ups. Utilizing the power-ups to the best of their ability is the key to completing each stage under the par time. When selecting a level, you are given the choice of picking one power-up out of a handful that pertain to the current stage being played. Sometimes, it is beneficial to use the slow-time power-up in order to dodge particularly difficult enemy fire; but is it worth using that over the ability to warp through the floor and potentially skip certain sections? I found these decisions to give a lot of weight to which power-up to choose when starting a stage. Through experimentation, you will learn the best application of each of these abilities.
There are two features that I didn't get around to using; a level editor and party play. The level editor offers the same tools that the developer used to create the core levels of the game. Created stages are able to be shared with others by downloading the file and placing it into their game folder. Unfortunately, it seems there is no community for this feature so right now even with a dedicated Steam sub-forum for user designs. As for the party play, it's local only and features a deathmatch mode for up to 4-players and a co-operative mode for 2-players. Most of the deathmatch stages are designed specifically for this mode whilst the co-operative mode shares stages with single-player.
Straima is definitely one of the better platformers that I've played in a long time. It's hard not to recommend a game that has such tight controls, varied level design, “one more” addictiveness, unique visuals, and great soundtrack. Keep in mind that even though it sounds like there is not a lot of content to be had with such short levels, it took me about 15 hours to achieve both trophies on all of the stages. If you're looking for a very challenging platforming experience, Straima is your game.

My final conclusion is to wait for a heavy discount and more patches to fix broken/bad content.
My gameplay hours trump most (despite being inflated by afking with game running) but i've stuck it out and tried to report as many bugs as possible. Simply put this is a great game potential mared by bugs everywhere (for a metric, patch 3 addressed over 100 features and bugs alone, many of which were known for months of early access). This makes the game, as it stands, very hard to enjoy as you don't know what is bugged and what is a feature. Moreover, quests, despite being completed correctly, still flag as incomplete (and thus the game treats you as having not done the stuff you did) and this alone is tire screeching for any RPG.
Features are generally much the same as D:OS1 but again they feel like beta or just bad in some areas, and splendid in others. Dialogue and Banter chat log feature has never once functioned to date. Some fights in game warrant explaination on wtf Larian was thinking (Dreamers Portal) and most of the status and features require trail and error to get a grasp of (Ring: 6 Vitality apparently means 'this ring gives you constant healing equal to the HP from 7 constitution (and each point of constitution give 7% vitality, which are your Hit Points). Personal preferences aside, quite a number of 'intended features' are either frustrating (not being able to mouse over enemy debuffs to read description) or simply are broken/never made it into the game. There is a good deal number of dialogues that are only partly voiced, meaning that its either more bugs (not playing voice script properly) or intended that way.
Another Example: The quest log (arguably important) is poorly implimented. Supposing you avoid the bugged logs, it doesn't fully complete for each zone. It also updates per interaction (so if you find a boss, then later find a note hinting where the boss is, the note will be the top update). This results in you not knowing if the quest if still in your current Act (and thus you will miss out if you leave) or if the quest is continued in the next act. Its guessing game or risk forum spoilers.
Comments always deleted (outside of genuine clarificationquestions), forums for discussion.

We've run into a game breaking bug.  After all the patches we've been through, a game breaking bug shouldn't be present.
My wife and I both have the game.  Our inventories have become messed up we think.  The only indicators we have are five blank spots when we go to Crafting inventory.  We have even tracked down where they come from.
During Driftwood, you have a quest, Strange Cargo, to rescue a guy in a barrel.  The moment you tell him to come with you, he becomes part of your party.  In his inventory are five grenade items.  No matter what you do after that, you will have blank spaces in your Crafting inventory.  Whether you kill him on the spot, or lead him safely out of town.
You might wonder what a few missing spots would matter.  As did we.  But when you get ready to leave Act2 and go to Nameless Isle, you'll either get kicked back out to the main menu during the cutscene, or get Crash to Desktop.  If you get kicked back out, it gives Save Error 302.
We haven't been able to get any attention on the issue.  But I suspect more people may realize having the same problem as time goes on and people progress through the story.  And they'll probably lose three days worth of progress like we did, and really really not even want to finish the game anymore.  So until this is fixed, or maybe even if it does, there's gonna be at least two negative reviews on this game from us.

Brad the Barbarian has grown tired of the XP grind, but he can't stop the need to have to farm gold.
Bardbarian is a clever twist of taking elements from RPGs and Tower Defense into an action game where you are protecting your town's crystal from monsters, except that YOU are not. Brad decided he doesn't want to be a fighter, but a musician. So now he plays rock music. He summons warriors, temporarily boosts their stats, and stuns enemies with his music. The power of music eh?
There is a Campaign, Survival mode, and Endless (running as far as you can) mode. The last two are both challenges where you can compare your skill against your friends and the rest of the world, and also sources where you can earn gold to upgrade for the campaign. The campaign is pretty tough. Mainly because it will require a combination of skill, and the right upgrades from the countless times of playing.
You'll definitely get your money's worth buying this game, if this is the kind of thing you are into. If you like Tower Defense, and you don't mind working the hours needed to earn that "in-game" money, you'll probably dig this game.

There are only two things you need to know about Divinity: Original Sin 2.
First, within one week of launch it became the highest-rated games of all time on Metacritic (it currently has a metascore of 95).
Second, all of that critical acclaim is completely deserved.
You see, a very long time ago there was a game called Baldur's Gate 2. It was incredible. An enormous CRPG with engaging combat, compelling characters, and an intriguiing narrative. It demonstrated just how good a roleplaying game could be, and established a standard of quality that would cast a shadow over every subsequent CRPG for decades. For a very long time, we convinved ourselves that Baldur's Gate 2 was an outlier. An abberation. That we would never see another game of similar scope, scale or quality again. And that we were wrong to expect such grand ambitions from even our most beloved of developers.
But we were wrong.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is the game we have been waiting for. It is a spectacular, transcendental experience. Compex, challenging gameplay married to a well-written and extraordinarily dynamic narrative; gorgeous visuals and skilled voice acting; a phenomenal soundtrack and an overall design that grants players an unprecedented level of freedom.
But you know all of this already. Original Sin 2 has already thoroughly enmeshed itself into the zeitgeist. That metascore did not happen by accident, and you know it. The 10,000+ user reviews that are almost exclusively positive are likewise no accident.
This is it. The game that was promised. The game we never thought would come. Divinity Original Sin 2 is, finally, the true successor to Baldur's gate, not because it has a similar style of gameplay, or a similar tone or narrative style, but because of what it represents: a new standard for the genre.  Truly, it is one CRPG fit to rule them all.

I bought this game on a whim, based on my love for Japanese art and culture,  and I'm very glad I did. Tengami is a unique experience, it's like a playable work of art. I've never before seen a game utilize the mechanics of a pop-up book before, which made it that much more exciting. Every chapter unfolds slowly and gracefully, showcasing beautiful landscapes and thought-provoking puzzles to solve. You pull, push, and slide tabs, revealing hidden secrets and routes in order to guide your character on his path.
The colors are rich and vibrant, and the style evokes the gorgeous art of the Edo Period. I love the feel of it, like wandering through a painting or a dream. The puzzles are challenging but intuitive enough for you to figure them out without much frustration. The serene music adds to overall experience. I also very much enjoyed the use of haiku, which was really the only narrative in the game at all. It's minimalistic as far as plot goes but it's a powerful one, about the cycle of life and death. Your character does not speak, nor is there any intrusive messages telling you where to go or what to do. It's incredibly relaxing.  If you wish, though, you can choose to view hints for the various puzzles in the pause menu.
My only complaint, isn't much of one at all. I noticed there was no way to make your character move any faster, and yes, travelling from one place to the next and back again can be a very slow and lengthy enterprise.  But then I came to realize this was also part of the game. They don't want you to run or rush through things, it would only ruin the experience. You must play the game with an open and thoughtful mind to truly appreciate it.

The game length is short but plenty long enough to get the concept across.  I look forward to more in-depth work from this crew in the future.

This is a very short but highly thought-provoking game.  It doesn't hold your hand the way most modern games do (thankfully), but it's not very challenging either.  Most of its puzzles are logical and/or intuitive and generally fairly forgiving.  The virtual minigames were the worst part only because they were tedious.  The art is a little scattered:  the interior of the yurt (where you live) is done very realistically, but the landscape outside (particularly the sky) looks like a fantasy painting, which is a little jarring.  It was like the artists couldn't decide whether they wanted to be realistic or fantastical.  People with OCD might also have difficulties with the fact that if you pick something up, in many cases it's nearly impossible to put it neatly back where it was (eventually, it will fix itself, though).
What I really liked about this game, though, were its story, setting, and characters.  You're dropped into this world with no memory of who you are or where you are, so it's very easy to get into the role of the character you're playing, because it allows you to ask basic questions you need to ask to understand things without it being out of character.  If you want just the general gist of things, you'll have to ask lots of questions as you move through the story.  To
understand what's going on, though, you have to take your time and read even seemingly inconsequential things left lying around.  If you don't, when you get to the end, you'll probably just be confused and/or feeling like the ending was abrupt.  On the other hand, if you've paid attention and put enough clues together as you go along, the ending is both absolutely amazing and poetic.

There is a lot here to recommend Cradle.  The visuals, for the most part, are beautiful.  About half of the voice acting is  quality work.  The concepts and characters are compelling and can be generally identified with fairly readily.
However,
Cradle falls short.  It is so good in certain ways but...  It's like a beautiful woman who is wearing heels too tall for her.  It looks beautiful, it seems like it might even have something interesting to say, and then it takes a misstep and falls on its face.
The subgames, though explained halfway through, feel jarringly out of place until that point.  Walking through the beautiful landscape generates a certain feeling that does not mesh well with the subgames, feeling like a hacking puzzle in an FPS, a contrived challenge that is just there to act as a weak barrier for you to mill through, separating chapters, making you backtrack, and not even being unique among themselves.  I feel like the game could have easily been better without them.
The story, though a bit confusing at times, is very well told for the most part.  The little snippets of information provided by the readings and the conversations point to a fascinating world with fascinating possibilities and a future like you've never quite imagined.
And then you go back into the subgame, completely disengaging you from the storyline and presenting you with hoops you don't even have to jump through.  (I'll spoil this with no guilt.  If you fail a subgame, you can just skip it and still get the achievement.)  When you finish it and get back into the storyline, it gets even more interesting and tantalizing, a bit more of the story is revealed.  And then it goes back to the subgame.
Worst of all is the ending.  It seems like it's really building to something.  It seems like it's getting ready for the big reveal, answers for your questions.  But it isn't.  It's going to give you a halfhearted hand waved in the vague direction of the answers to your questions and then ENDS WITH A DAMNED MUSIC VIDEO.  I'm not saying everything has to be handed to the player but there basically is no third act.  It jumps clear past it to a climax without epilogue, like watching the first two LotR movies and then skipping to the big final battle from the third movie and ending once the battle is won with no more explanation.
I will say this though.  The soundtrack is beautiful.  I am still torn as to whether it's worth buying but it's definitely beautiful.
It was so good, except when it wasn't.  It could have been so much better, but it wasn't.  I'm not sorry I played it but no, I cannot recommend it.

Typically I only review games which I feel very passionate about, meaning that pretty much all of my reviews are positive. However considering just how bad I found this game to be, combined with the asking price of 20 Euro, I felt the need to write a review just to give a heads up to any of my friends that might be considering this purchase.
I bought Submerged on sale for 2 Euro, and while I didn't have the highest of expectations I did think that at the very least it would provide for a relaxing experience. However, after actually playing the game it made me question if it was even worth the 2 Euro I had spent, let alone the normal asking price.
To clarify, I am saying this all as someone who has a love for many games which are short, simple, and cost around the same price as Submerged. By no means does short or simple mean a game is boring or cannot be a wonderful experience. However the difference is that those games actually offer things which make them a worthwhile experience in one way or another, while I really didn't find anything about Submerged redeeeming and struggle to call it an experience at all.
To sum up my reasoning I'll simply list it as such:
• The gameplay consists of nothing more than driving your boat around to various buildings and then climbing said buildings to find supplies. Once you have scaled one building you've pretty much scaled them all, there really isn't much (if any) variety in these structures or how you explore them. You can't even enter any of these buildings, you simply climb up one after another, each pretty much a clone of the previous one.
• To add to this, the mechanics are extremely clunky. Basically the only two things you do in the entire game are drive your boat around and climb buildings, and the mechanics for both of these things reeks of a complete and total lack of polish. I tried playing both with my keyboard and mouse and my controller, and while I found the controller to be the best option it still didn't take away from just how awkward these controls are.
• You can't die or even take any injury. This isn't necessarily a bad thing of course, but considering just how boring the game is already, this makes for a complete and total lack of any kind of suspense and really just made everything feel all that more bland.
• The best part of the entire game for me is the wildlife, as you will sometimes see a whale, dolphin, or a select few other creatures. Provided there are very few, but it is at least something that helps the world not feel completely dead. However this quickly lost its charm for me when I accidentally ran into a whale, only to find that I bounced right off of it as though I was driving a bumper car. For a game such as this that is pretty much relying on the environment, this really doesn't do any favors for the feeling of immersion.
• For a brief period of time I was actually interested in the storyline and it was pretty much the only thing that kept me from quitting and requesting a refund. However the ending of the story is very much like the actual gameplay- extremely underwhelming.
• I've seen some positive reviews which call the game beautiful or even gorgeous. Of course this is subjective, but I really didn't find anything about the way the world is crafted to be nearly impressive enough to describe it in nearly such enthusiastic terms. At first glance it is pretty at best, but after just a short amount of exploration I found that the scenery is very repetitive. Save for a few landmarks (which are really nothing special), everything really looks the same.
I can appreciate what Submerged was going for, and feel that the focus might have been intended to be on the world rather than the actual gameplay, something that can be great when done right. However with Submerged it ultimately falls flat, and between an underwhelming world and the underwhelming gameplay what you're left with is a game that feels much too empty to even be appreciated for being relaxing. Overall, more simplistic games such as this can be a very rewarding experience if done well, but sadly I really can't say there's anything that Submerged gets right. Of course you might feel differently than me, but I urge you to at the very least wait until a sale, because this is absolutely not worth the 20 Euro price tag.

American Truck Simulator is basically 18 Wheels of Steel with updated resolution, controls and textures. I own the CD-rom original of that game and I enjoyed it the same way I am enjoying this. It is not perfect by any means.
It is fun and I do like it but this is a simulator the same way Half Life 2 is a firearms simulator. Sure, thats how some guns operate but everything else is not very realistic.
The creators have no idea how American traffic works. The traffic laws are not very accurate (ie no right turn on reds to enter an on ramp in this game, but no sign indicating no turn on red)  The traffic AI is not very good either.
The devs spent 90% of the time detailing the trucks and working on creating a great "truck driving" experience by focusing on the realism of driving and controlling the trucks. The other 10% of the time was spent copy and pasting textures across the map.
I would have loved to see more work done on map realism. It looks OK. It is not good. There is a lot left out in feels like in terms of making this a good "simulator". Its fun to sit back and get a quick job, drive from one end of the map to other, cash in and do it again.
The controls are very good. all things considered. I am not buying a racing wheel ,stick and pedals, although that would add to this I am sure. The XBOX 360 controller AND my Thrustmaster HOTAS Flight Stick (no really) work VERY well.
For what it is and getting on sale ($ 13.99 is the max I would pay) it IS very good. It is NOT perfect and really just feels like the maps are a bit lack luster. I would like to see more towns, more detail and more unique textures and environment. Nevada and California and New Mexico all look the same. Even if they just added a few unique landmarks along the way in each state, something to break up the monotony of seeing the exact same scenery 300x.
Gameplay- 4/5. Controls are easy to figure out. Has a WIDE variety of control configurations and options. Driving a truck was never more fun. The quick jobs are a fun easy way to start leveling up and the entire XP system, while a bit basic, is fun to progress to add on to the experience.
Sound- 4/5. It sounds really good. Not much else to say honestly
Graphics- 3/5. The trucks look good. Inside and out. Everything else is VERY basic and minimalistic. Aliasing all over the place on the roads, scenery other cars, regardless of settings. HD but texture details are very limited. Could have been better
Overall- 4/5. For what it is and what you can pay to own it, it is very good. Buy it on sale. If you are a hardcore trucker sim enthusiast you might enjoy it more than I , a casual gamer. I really like playing it but feel there are things that could be MUCH better to call it a proper sim. Fixes need to be made to the traffic AI. Fixes should be made to adjust for traffic laws in the US.
Otherwise a fun game

The updates recently are small and unimpressive. 3 new arenas in arena mode as well as some bug fixing was the most recent as of writing. First let me say I played Divinity Original Sin through twice. I loved that game. So naturally I was looking forward to DOS2. Admittedly both games have alot in common but not everything. The big exception seems to be play balance. The play balance in the classic mode of DOS was nearly perfect and I played the entire gamne through in that mode. Classic mode wasn't so easy it would be boring and just difficult enough so you had to be careful about your strategy or suffer death. Not so with DOS2.
I started playing in classic mode at Fort Joy and found it challanging but not impossible. However after heading to Reapers Cove it became impossible to beat any mob unless there was some trick to it that permitted me to beat them without fighting. Each mob was at least two levels above me and they always got to attack first. Worse each member of the mob would have three or four moves even before I was able to attack. So with an mob of 4 guys they would make up to 12- 16 moves BEFORE I could even attack. Bythat time each of my guys would be low on armor, frozen, diseased, poisoned outflanked etc. That automatically put me in a defensive mode to heal armor and/or health points which meant I wasn't hitting back. When I was able to hit back my attacks did far less damage to them than they did to me. This doesn't include them using spells on me that weren't available for purchase or too expensive to buy.
So I figured I try playing in story mode which is so easy I could probably take on a voidwoken with a toothbrush and win.
I don't know what the developers did to screw up the game balance but it's not longer fun to play in either story or classic mode. I don't want to give it a thumbs down becasue I'm  going to play in story mode to gain a few levels to even things out and then go back to classic mode to see if there's a difference. But I can't give it a thumbs up either because things might end up just as unbalanced when I switch back to classic mode. Since I have to choose one or the other I have to give it a thumbs down based on my experience so far. Hopefully all will be well if I level a couple of times but I'm not keeping my fingers crossed.
Ok, heres a second take on DOS II. The game is buggy, and not in a minor way. For example the pipe puzzle quest doesn't work. Nothing flows into the pipe channels when I press the control tiles. I was able to get around it somewhat by standing at the right or left corner of the control panel and placing a transport pyramid on the other side of the barrier (I'm sure that's a bug too). Then I transported down to where the three valves are and manually turned them. That got the holy elements flowing into the channels.  Unfortunately they don't flow in the correct direction when I move the control tiles. I hate this. This is a game stopper inasmuch to the best of my knowledge I need to finish this in order to continue the main quest.  IMO there's no excuse for this. When the smaller quests are bugged it's irritating but I can get around them. But now I can't advance in a game I shelled out $40 for.  What a joke.
