Me writing a review for Warframe is long over due. (I mean I played more than 2k hours of it by now, but I guess I get an achievement for it now so I might as well get on it.)
First of all the game is extremely fun and rewarding to play. While the grind or just the sheer bulk of content of warframe might seem overwhelming at first but if given the chance you will be drawn into the thrilling gameplay completely within a few hours. The variations in gameplay styles the game offers are seemingly endless.(over 400 weapons and counting same goes for the about 40 frames we have including primes.) In it's crisp gun-, and swordplay extremely refined and honestly unique movement system what stands out the most is how the titular Warframes differentiate themselves from other similair concepts coming from various other games (not namedropping any here tho) and manage to make the player feel like and actual "robot-mini-evangelion-space-ninja-wizard" (or something like that). The word that comes to mind here is not only "fun" or "rewarding" but it's gameplay has a truly "empowering" aspect to it.
Now Warframe is free to play in the truest sense that you can literally buy anything, even the "premium" items presented in the market, by just playing the game (and it doesn't even take that long just farm some prime parts, you're good to go). However I wouldn't be surprised to see anyone actually paying for microtransactions in Warframe. (I know I did....nearly 1$ per hour °D ....my only regret is not finding the game early enough to buy a founders package, I was like 3 months too late or something.) This is all due to the games design philosophy and model, in short Warframe might be the only game that gets free to play completely right at this point in time.
All of this is only possible to because of the extremely talanted people at DE (Digital Extremes), (Seriously thank you guys for making such a great game.) who not only put tons of effort into the actual game but also keep in touch with their community like no other company and who keep doing so even though Warframe is way past being considered indie anymore or any such thing.(They have like 200 people or so working on it now but we still get Devstreams every second week? Most other devs either can't or won't put in as much effort as tweeting regularly) Go watch the Devstreams, watch the community managers Livestream like 3 times a week or even in their free time, visit the forums, watch Steve on periscope, these people truly love what they are doing and the game they created and it shows in the product.
So in short Warframe might be the best game out here and at the same time also the game with the most potential. I highly recommend anyone to play Warframe and follow it actively, you won't be wasting your time. For anyone who ever aspires to make games of their own this applies especially for I believe DE to be the studio that "gets it most" even beyond the making of the game but also the the community interaction parts, which is so rare in todays gameindustry that I didn't even believe I'd ever see anything similair to the effort DE puts in.

Cradle, A first person walking, exploration game, focused entirely on the story itself, you begin your small yet surprisingly lore filled journey in a matter of seconds upon the beginning of the game. A relatively small team worked on this game, and you feel a lot of effort had been made for this creation, struggles were raised, as well solutions arising. Such is the nature of this game, or any game I imagine, well lets have a look at what we have here?
You’ll find yourself in a small Mongolian yurt, (which is a hut to anyone who does’ant know!) upon which you’ll find a note addressed to you from your grandfather, or father? im not so sure, the note will tell you to begin fixing, finding, and preparing a meal for someone who is on their way to your home. Upon completing the task an eagle shows up, turns out that’s who your were preparing and cooking the meal for. Discovering that I immediately knew from then on that this game is really good at hiding what it does’t want to show you, don’t misunderstand, there are plenty of key items you can discover in the house, and if your someone that likes to guess stories, you might hit the sweet spot, but if your someone who enjoys a story head on like me, your in for at treat!
The Story itself focuses on human kind discovering and inventing new technology that allows people to transfer, essentially there conscious as well memories to a new body, that is a machine representation of , but It will be you. Through exploring the game, you’ll come across fake articles that describe everything that is happening with that technology, how even a lot of old people don’t really want to use it, but change there mind’s when death is truly coming around that corner. In all honestly there are multiple arch’s you’ll discover when playing this game, I won’t say what they are, but I find this game’s whole story to be just amazing, the world feel’s organic, the characters you meet convey there own personalities, which help’s with every character feeling individual in the story. Probity is a word I’d use to describe every character in the game, always honest, if always reluctant...
So the games does end in manner that leaves you with implication’s as to what’s happening all around you, no actual answers are really given to you, only thoughts and pictures is all you can really imply, I can imagine that this will disappoint some players, I personally love this kind of loosely translated story, makes you scratch your head.
The game play itself hold’s pretty well if your good with old point and clicks, this might be a run for your money, but overall it’s mostly trivial objectives that you will be given, there are some problem solving mini games that you will come across, however if you fail these games, you can opt to skip them, which is what I did! That’s really about it for the game play, there’s a sprint button, a small inventory, as well a hold in hand option, and a throw item button once the item is in your hand. I recommend exploring the grounds around your yurt, may end up helping you more than you think. Also I should mention there is a black cloud, or you’ll find these little black clouds when progressing further into the game, all they do is knock you out for a second, no real cause for alarm, height can be a factor for knocking you out as well. Don’t worry, When you wake up for any of these moments your pretty much standing in the same spot you fell down on.
Final say, the music is amazing, there’s controller support, mouse and keyboard work great, im not sure how well of a computer you’ll need for this, The voice acting is wonderful I think, some odd moments, all in all I paid twenty dollars for this, giving me around six hours before completing this game. I missed some collectable’s, I would like to find them in the future. I think this is personally fine for anyone to play, I highly recommend this gem!

This game is honestly one of my favorite games of all time. Keep in mind the fact that I like history more than the average person, and I love this kind of game. If you like constant action, it might not be the best choice. But the amazing thing about this game is that it has the ability to make you amazing with some of the best traits, then you have a daughter that is an imbecile, ugly, club-footed, and has a hunchback. It is capable of keeping you interested and constantly interacting with one or more features in the game. For example, one play through I started as a count in Ireland, which in the game is probably the easiest spot to start for beginners (Not much happens so you have time to adjust things and learn the game to a point where you are comfortable). As this count in Ireland, I expanded my one county into a duchy, which is an even greater title and provided me with a lot of happiness and wealth. But then, my half-brother decided to call a revolt, saying he should be in control of the duchy. I went to war and lost, and he ended up throwing me in the darkest deepest dungeon possible (I still kept one county, which I was suprised about, seeing as he wanted to kill me) When in this dungeon, I contracted typhoid fever, and my brother decided to put me on house arrest. My youngest son randomly broke me out, and I went back to my county. I had married off my daughters, and at the time my allies couldn't help with the revolt my brother called on me. So I decided enough was enough, and declared war. Scotland, Mercia, and Wessex came down with their armies (Which to me at the time was a very huge amount of men) And we decimated my brother. I regained my throne, and began raising troops. I took my army to war against the rest of the single counties, seeing as I had lost a large amount of my life to the dungeon. I took enough land (80% of the Kingdom of Ireland) to create the kingdom. As soon as I made it, I passed away. My oldest son took over the majority of my kingdom, while the duchy went to my youngest (Still in the same country). Being a new character (My oldest son) I decided it was time to expand the kingdom I had made. I fought until I reached scotland, killed my sister to end the alliance, and then declared war and took it. I had so much power, that I wanted to make the Empire of Britannia to match how I felt. I did exactly that, and became the Emperor. However, after some time of ruling the Empire, a foreign country wanted my land, so we went to war. I had over half the amount of troops he had (At least I thought I did) and I felt extremely confident I was going to prevail. Little did I know that the Emperor of the HRE didn't like me. I didn't know the reason, until I saw that he was the previous king of Scotland, and his father was the Emperor of the HRE before me. So now I was facing a 10k+ army included with the 4k coming from another country. They killed my army instantly, all of my land was sieged and burnt, and my children and siblings were all arrested and died from disease. I had nothing after so long that I actually felt a real anger building. It was the first time in a long time a game had brought emotion so real into my heart. That is when I realized how good this game was. It is so amazing, it is able to upset you, but at the same time bring happiness and satisfaction when you destroy your enemies. You can call Jihads as the Caliph of Islam, you can join crusades for the holy sites in the world, you can rule or be ruled. So many opportunities in this game, and all of them bring good or bad feelings. Oh, and about my story, my character ended up being excommunicated by the pope, and I was assassinated.

The term "walking simulator" doesn't have to be derogatory. Some of them can be quite good - hell, The Stanley Parable was a decent game. But for a walking simulator to be good, it really needs to have an interesting world to explore, and the story needs to be well-written enough that we care enough to look around and try to figure out what's going on. Cradle is a beautiful game, but it is otherwise unbearable. The exploration is slow and humdrum, there are constant fetch quests, and the writing is incredibly bad. Not only that, but the game is dreadful on a technical level, with inexplicably jerky, slow movement, a frame rate which drops to about 15 fps unless a controller is plugged in, even when playing with the keyboard, and when trying to play with a controller, turning around causes your character to keep slow spinning in the same direction, as if all movement takes place on ice. Stay away from this one.

(Note: my steam playtime does not show my playtime with Nexon's standalone launcher from during the beta, actual playtime is around 80 hours)
With regards to the PvE content, it contains the standard MMO tropes of leveling: experience points and stat based gear progression.
The dungeons are fun, the monsters are neat, and the storyline is alright.
The varied enemy types actually do different attacks and have slightly different A.I., even between palatte swaps.  If it looks different, it behaves differently.
The cut scenes are entertaining i suppose, but its really all about combat.
Leveling does eventually slow down dramatcially, once you run out of the standard "go kill everything in this dungeon" quests, requiring you to re-play dungeons and boss rooms, over and over, just to level up.
With regards to the actual overall character progression, its mainly about upgrading your weapons (and armor too of course).
This is where the Pay to Win comes in, but ill get to that in a minute.
If you want to upgrade an item, you can minimally improve it up until level eight (the weapons level, not the character).
Every time you upgrade an item, you spend the materials to perform the upgrade.
Occasionally, the upgrade fails, meaning you lose the mats but keep the item.
After level eight, you risk several random outcomes:
breaking the weapon (or armor) entirely,
downgrading the weapon by 3 levels,
merely losing your mats with no change in stats,
or actually upgrading the item by one level.
The potential to completely lose your item is very real, and is especially painful, making you go back to previously played content to get a replacement, which you would then need to upgrade again.
So, you can lose your item on a bad "roll" of the upgrade luck dice (metaphorical).
What can be done about this?
You can pay real money to buy "seals", which protect your item from breaking. (but not from the other potentially bad outcomes, such as deleveling the item.)
The pay to win ethos permeates the rest of the game as well, with visual changes not actually being tied to the majority of the gear you can get through gameplay.
Its sort of like if TF2 only let you buy hats, no crafting, no drops; they can only be bought with real money.
The other problem with these "costume" items, is that they also give your character stats, such as "permenant run speed increase of X %", or "+ str, + int" etc.
Now, on to the PvP stuff!  This is where DN shines.
The PvP combat is epic, there are juggles, and tons of fun to use skills on timers (much like WoW).  DN combat is more about positional awareness, but it still relies on knowing what cooldowns are not active for your enemies.
However, since there are juggles, if your "get out of a juggle" cooldowns are cooling down, then you're just hosed and can take a significant amount of damage while not being able to do anything about it, much like playing Marvel vs Capcom.
This issue is even more present, since you're fighting more than one enemy at a time.
Also, since DN is so focused on what gear you have and how upgraded it is, you are forced to play the PvE to level up, to get good gear, and to get the mats to improve your gear.  Additionally this means that PvP is more of a side thought, than a legitimate alternate way to level up or progress.
Overall i had tons of fun with DN, but once you understand the upgrade system, why it is Pay to Win, and how PvE recycles content, id say its a worthy way to spend some time, but ultimately i felt cheated by its Cash Shop.
Beware, Nexon may only be the distributor, but all of their games are notorious for abusing the Cash Shop mechanic, just like Dragon Nest does.

Cradle is riddled with a number of bugs that can make it nearly unplayable unless you happen to have the perfect set of circumstances for it.
Major Bug #1: You must plug an official Playstation or Xbox brand controller into your computer before starting up the game. Otherwise the frame rate drops to an jerky, unplayable mess. I am not the only one who has complained about this. I easily found comments on the forums complaining about this bug since the beginning of November and not a thing has been done to correct it.
Major Bug #2: If you have an official Playstation or Xbox brand controller plugged into your system when you try to play the game, you will find yourself locked into Crouch mode. You will find yourself staring at the undersides of tables and having to jump just to read the first note or interact with nearly anything. Again, the developers seem to be doing nothing to fix this problem besides saying that they are working on it.
So these two bugs combined to make my first few minutes of the game frustrating and absolutely intollerable for a game relying solely on environment immersement. Coupled that with the fact that the last patch to the game came in Early October, I had to return it. I do not expect the issues to be fixed any time soon and that truely saddens me. I wanted to like this game so much, but the bugs make it unplayable.

Negatives: There are numerous spelling errors in the captions and some slight bugs in the programming that cut out audio and speech sometimes, and the game is rather short and doesn't have the greatest depth when it comes to puzzles.
To improve the game I would recommend a proofread of the speech captions and a once-over for the bug-fixes, checking that all audio and animaton cues are in the right place. It's polish like that that would push this game into great status whereas it's resting comfortably in the 'good' category.
As a sidenote, what would make this game go above and beyond and make it excellent would be to involve more emotional themes, the main character doesn't feel like they have any stakes in the story precisely thus far beyond curiosity and a general feeling of helpfulness.

American Truck Simulator is basically 18 Wheels of Steel with updated resolution, controls and textures. I own the CD-rom original of that game and I enjoyed it the same way I am enjoying this. It is not perfect by any means.
It is fun and I do like it but this is a simulator the same way Half Life 2 is a firearms simulator. Sure, thats how some guns operate but everything else is not very realistic.
The creators have no idea how American traffic works. The traffic laws are not very accurate (ie no right turn on reds to enter an on ramp in this game, but no sign indicating no turn on red)  The traffic AI is not very good either.
The devs spent 90% of the time detailing the trucks and working on creating a great "truck driving" experience by focusing on the realism of driving and controlling the trucks. The other 10% of the time was spent copy and pasting textures across the map.
I would have loved to see more work done on map realism. It looks OK. It is not good. There is a lot left out in feels like in terms of making this a good "simulator". Its fun to sit back and get a quick job, drive from one end of the map to other, cash in and do it again.
The controls are very good. all things considered. I am not buying a racing wheel ,stick and pedals, although that would add to this I am sure. The XBOX 360 controller AND my Thrustmaster HOTAS Flight Stick (no really) work VERY well.
For what it is and getting on sale ($ 13.99 is the max I would pay) it IS very good. It is NOT perfect and really just feels like the maps are a bit lack luster. I would like to see more towns, more detail and more unique textures and environment. Nevada and California and New Mexico all look the same. Even if they just added a few unique landmarks along the way in each state, something to break up the monotony of seeing the exact same scenery 300x.
Gameplay- 4/5. Controls are easy to figure out. Has a WIDE variety of control configurations and options. Driving a truck was never more fun. The quick jobs are a fun easy way to start leveling up and the entire XP system, while a bit basic, is fun to progress to add on to the experience.
Sound- 4/5. It sounds really good. Not much else to say honestly
Graphics- 3/5. The trucks look good. Inside and out. Everything else is VERY basic and minimalistic. Aliasing all over the place on the roads, scenery other cars, regardless of settings. HD but texture details are very limited. Could have been better
Overall- 4/5. For what it is and what you can pay to own it, it is very good. Buy it on sale. If you are a hardcore trucker sim enthusiast you might enjoy it more than I , a casual gamer. I really like playing it but feel there are things that could be MUCH better to call it a proper sim. Fixes need to be made to the traffic AI. Fixes should be made to adjust for traffic laws in the US.

Between the time when the oceans drank gaming, and the rise of the sons of freemium, there was an age undreamed of. And unto this, Conan Exiles, destined to wear the jeweled crown of Early Access games upon a troubled brow. It is I, his chronicler, who alone can tell thee of his saga. Let me tell you of the days of high adventure!
The game has a lot of potential and in it's current state with typical early access bugs is still a good game. The Pvp is fun and so is the base building.
For anyone who has followed Funcom, the developers have a point to prove, their goal for Conan Exiles is for it to be the gold standard for early access games. I think they are a company made for early access, whether that is bad or good is up to your opinion of early access.
Their previous MMO was Age of Conan (2008), while it had initial problems at launch which caused it to never reach it's full potential. They worked hard and fixed the majority of the bugs after launch and added new content for the game until 2014. While it is disapointing the game never reached it's full potential you can't accuse the developers of giving up on the game. It is still playable on steam today through a free to play/subscription model.
With that context, the Funcom team seem to have a vision for what the 'complete' Conan Exiles will be. For instance dealing with end game content which is arguably the biggest fault of the early access survival genre. They have been communicating some MMO style end game content such as dungeons, raids, city building and a purge system where armies of NPCs will roam across the battlefield attacking player's bases.
I think this game will only be recognised as good game by the wider community after the full release which is currently scheduled for Q1 2018. Until then it is just an above average early access survival game that i recommend if you have any desire to know the riddle of steel and not to be cast out of Valhalla and laughed at by Crom!!

Fantastic game! Oblivion is one of those games that only comes from time to time, just imagine how much the developers put into this game, time, ideas , money. Thank you Bethesda! I confess it was the first game in the Elder Scrolls series I played, so I can not compare to Morrowind, and Skyrim I barely played, then I'll make a review based solely on impressions of the game.
It took a while until I get to continue on a character and finish the main quest, the game requires dedication, Cyrodill world is vast , the possibilities in a TES game well, you need to explore,  learn about, otherwise you will getting lost as I did several times and so I abandoned the progress with other characters.

The graphics are outdated and mechanics are strange at first sight, especially the combat and movement, and the animation of NPCs give the impression that they do not have emotions. Despite this the game is still very good, the graphics can be improved with mods, you get used to the mechanics and also the sound effects are well done. The community is huge and active, there are thousands of fan-made mods that help solve problems, improve gameplay, graphics and add content that make it practically a new game.
I highly recommend it, but as said, you need to devote to it, it takes a while to get a feel and learn how the gameplay works, how the skill system and leveling for example. But there are wikis for it with everything you can know about TES: Oblivion, I recommend consulting to aid, but being careful with spoilers, of course.

Unlike Plants vs Zombies, you are free to move about; not bound to setting up your towers/plants.
You are Brad, a barbarian who has rigged his axe into a lute. Monsters are attacking the village. You use your axe/lute (so "axe") to call companions; you've further solo's to buff yourself and those followers. A dynamic conga-line, you weave between enemies' projectiles, enabling your companions to return fire. You collect Gold (you can buy a Ratcoon to collect the loot for you) to purchase upgrades.
Very addicting.
***There are two other game modes in addition to the Campaign:
--Endless plants you into the thick of it; you only have your three Buff solo's at your disposal. Companions/Health randomly drop. The challenge is to recruit those Companions and not have them die THE SECOND they start following you. The game claims that this is a good mode for farming gold. Too bad your Ratcoon is absent; So sad that Companions (your only means of dispatching enemies) survive for mere seconds. Totally unfair, in my opinion.
--Escape has you running from a wall of darkness. No companions to worry about, no strategy in using solo's; strictly a runner mode - one hit kills you. It's much more fun than Endless, though hardly related to the main game.

At first glance Conan Exiles looks to be a great game.   Hidden behind the amazing graphics of the game are clunky combat controls, an even worse building mechanic, extremely bad animations such as the death animation, and problems scattered about in what is actually a hacked together proof of concept more than a playable game.
In a true sandbox game the enviornment is the players play thing, modling and shapping it as they see fit.  In Conan however the terrain will laugh at you as you try to place basic structure pieces.  This results in very uneven floors/walls and not in a good way.  The static structures you are given to work with are brilliantly made to work like a jigsaw piece that fits together no matter how times you place it.  However, with the terrain unforgiving about where you can and can't place objects this results in a great piece of programing/art not being noticable at all.  Most times you may get four floor pieces in line together for your builds before you are forced by the layout of the terrain to place your next few floor pieces either higher or lower than the previous one.  With the walls being forced to connect to floor pieces this results in uneven builds with holes all around your builds.  Bye far the worst building mechanics I've seen a sandbox so far.
I'm not even sure what they were trying to do with the combat system in this garbage.  It's extremely basic and very unfullfilling hacking away at your targets.  But oh wait I have a dodge ability, WHY?!?!?!  The combat in this game isn't fast enough or good enough to even warrent the idea of being able to dodge an attack.  Not only that but most animations aren't timed at all with when you actually take damage.  I'm mean seriously what gives?  It's almost as if they knew the combat was terrible and thought giving you a dodge ability would make it better... nope, it doesn't.  The combat in this is extremely terrible.  Range combat is more my thing in most games but this one is by far the worst at range combat I've ever seen.  The arch of the arrows doesn't make any sense as they suddenly go to the ground after five feet. Increasing the arch of your shots increases your range by centimeters.  I mean what in the hell??? I know it's Early Access as they work on it but man do they have a long way to go.  This isn't Alpha or Beta stage, like I said earlier this is more Proof of Concept stages.
I'm really confused as to the high level of texture detial on most everything, bad animations or no animations in game, teleporting enemies (no they aren't supposed to teleport) that just pop into existense as you run away, Static NPCs which confused the hell out of me because all the creatures move around a little including walking through terrain but the human ones... stand in one spot till you get close enough... and then float towards you... wait what?  I know these guys run I've watched people play on Twitch... so why are they floating towards me instead of running?  The also have basic fighting animations so basic in fact that it would fit into Minecraft.  I mean I was expecting a combat system and visuals that rivaled Skyrim instead of feeling like I'm playing something from the time frame of jumping to full 3D games.  Also why is there a sneak key in this game?  Far as I could tell it doesn't work or has little to no effect.  While we are on the controls you can't set any of them to toggle on/off.
The graphics are nice in most cases... The models look good but after a while you'll start noticing inconsistances with them.  Blood splatters are generic and have a classic texture fade.  PC Death animation is sloppy and you will see it a bunch... three times per death it's about a second long is on a loop as the game lets you know hey you died... oh and whatever killed you keeps attacking your corpse till you respawn.  For a game based on Conan I was expecting a lot more with the death of your character or something extremely different such as wild animals eating your corpse.  Nope, nothing a short little loop of you grabbing your neck and then you kill over.  The model for you corpse also needs some work as it tends to get distorted depending on which one of the three corpse models you get and how you ended up.  Oh yeah no ragdoll pyhsics here either  s be prepared for pre rendered dead bodies.
Now the nuditiy option in this game is pointless.  There doesn't really seem to be any reason at all for you to be naked or clothed at all.  Frankly it adds nothing to the game play at all other than making you see someone's bare♥♥♥♥♥run around on screen.  The nudity also isn't true full nudity, what I mean by this is that for some reason they didn't render or texture the female characters ♥♥♥♥♥♥, odd they did her breast and a males♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but did nothing for the female genitals???  So I ask... what was the point of including this useless feature and then not do any detail on the female crotch.
In most Sandbox games or more correctly ANY GAME TODAY if you save your progress in any way it stays where you saved or placed an item that will cause you to respawn there if you die.  Well that's true in Conan as well with the most basic bed you can make, however, that's where this starts to kick you in balls for buying it.  The basic bed breaks after each death meaning that you'll respawn at the static starting area till you place another  one... oh joy.  It doesn't help that most enemies that will aggro at you will kill you in only a few hits untill you get some armor.  Armor you may never see as the game continues to road block you.  EVERY ITEM IN THE GAME REQUIRES YOU TO BE LEVEL "X" TO UNLOCK THE ABILITY TO MAKE IT!!!  As near as I could tell this means that you must be atleast level 20 to make... fur armor.  WHAT?!?!?!?!?! most games out there making or buying that fur armor is normally simple and quick as it's the lowest level of armor you can get... maybe levels 1-5  and it doesn't take much to make it.  Not so with Conan, first you got to get to around level 15 in order to unlock the tanning rack so you make the necessary itmes for the armor... then you got to unlock EACH PIECE of the armor in order to make it.
Now this game also runs on an RPG Point based leveling system... ugh I hate these.  This is where each level you get so many points to put into Health, Stamina, etc...  omg no.   I only made it to level 8 before I decided to write my review and realize that this game is not worth the time and effort to put into it.  I couldn't even really explore the playable area without one of 5 basic enemies killing me... most notably the crocdiles... if you get the game avoid them like they are a plague because you won't kill them early on in the game without dying atleast twice to ONE.
I really can't recommend this one.  It seems like a great concept and that's about it.  Major overhuals on the Combat system are needed for this to even be playable.  The static enviroment needs to be replaced with one worthy of the sandbox genre.  Being over encombered in a sandbox game to me just needs to be removed, in others this takes on the form of having a full inventory to which you can't pick up any new items.  It would be fine in a more action based game such as Skyrim but doesn't fit into a world where you are supposed to be able to build whatever you want.  Now this and the leveling system can be adjust in the world creation screen but is something I didn't mess with because I wanted to play as the developer intended... big mistake that was.  Frankly this game is so early I'm surprised I had to pay for it to test it out versus being payed to test it out.

Edit: Okay, finally, time for an actual (really quick) review.
Dragon Nest is an Action-MMO (Aka, not your typical tab-target, spam F1-F5 MAX DPS ROTATION GOOOO WoW clone) with a fairly deep story, and decently done in game cinematics.
Its a dungeon based 3d-beat-em-up meets MMO essentially. There are 6 characters, each with 2 subclasses, and then 2 more subclasses branching from those, and a 7th character (The Assassin) somewhere down the line coming.
Controls are pretty tight, and the game looks great. Each class has a large amount of varied skills, and you have the freedom to build the characters how you want (though, there are obviously prereqs for skills you may have to meet).
NPCs are actually fun to talk to, and there's quite a large amount of dungeons in game.
Those things being said, there are a few downsides, and I highly suggest you take them into consideration before you sink time (and money) into the game:
1. While leveling, you'll find yourself making very long trips into town to talk to a bunch of really spread out npcs for questing reasons. Its tolerable in Lotus Marsh and the starter towns since they're pretty small, but its utterly atrocious in Saint's Haven, as its such a big place, and entering the castle counts as a map change. It drags the pace of the game down considerably at times.
2. Its hosted by Nexon. For those of us familiar with them, I need not say more. For those who aren't, Nexon is a VERY greedy company, known for charging their players out the (insert word for butt here) for many things. While the game is free to play, you'll find yourself wanting avatars (armor that provides slight stat bonuses, but mainly exists for cosmetic reasons), and other things from their in-game shop. The prices in the shop for said avatars are misleading, as those are the prices for the shortest duration non-permanent version of the item. Instead, if you wish to keep things forever, you'll find yourself paying about 5 bucks per piece, which well, is a lot. Which is further compounded by the fact that NX items are not tradeable, so you can't just buy them off other people with in-game money outside of specific circumstances.
Those two probems aside (pace-breaking quest gathering sequences that take up to 20 minutes sometimes), and overpriced cash shop items, its an extremely fun game gameplay-wise, and I'd suggest checking it out if you're looking for an actual game when you think of MMOs.

This is a point-n-click adventure game. It's just the first chapter and is quite short. Most of the game time is spent waiting for your character to walk from one place to another to either examine an object, talk to someone, use something or pick up stuff.
Children should like the premise - you're a kid monster investigating a mysterious occurrence with the help of your friends. The dialogue, content and general presentation are all very "kiddy": colourful, big characters; childish conversations; simple adventure obstacles. Adults (like myself) may find it far too juvenile to be enjoyable.
The game needs better language editing: spelling and grammar errors are prevalent. If I were a parent, I'd be concerned about my child picking up the wrong thing.
And there are a few off-putting gameplay issues:
- Game requires MS .NET framework. On first run, it took a very long time to install, and crashed immediately after download.
- When changing scenes the game takes ages to load. In fact the first time it showed "Loading...", I thought the game had hung because I had to wait so long.
- Very often, the game just "misses" right-clicks (e.g. when you want to fast forward text, you sometimes need to right-click 2-3 times before it'll register).
- Text doesn't match voice. I noticed on at least 10 different occasions that the written dialogue and what the voice actor said were not the same.
- On-screen exits are not apparent. Because the game screen "overflows" (i.e. the scene isn't contained on 1 screen), you have to walk left/right to see if there's any way to exit the scene there. Which wouldn't be so bad if your character walked faster. Then again I suppose kids (who are the obvious target audience) have all the time in the world.
I can see the appeal in this title for kids aged 3-10, but the game needs to be polished somewhat first, bearing in mind what I've highlighted above, especially with regards to the linguistic errors. And given that this is only the 1st chapter you're paying for, it's not worth the asking price at all.

The game has an amazing world and a pretty neat premise. Unfortunately, for me, it failed to live up to the possibilities it sets out. While the world looks really expansive and cool, the entirety of the game takes place at 2 locations (the yurt and the gardens). There's some "exploration", but it's mostly looking for the right marker/object in a very small setting. I was really hoping to have a chance to explore more of the world, but that never happens.
The story is... contentious, I guess. It seems like there's a cool story in there somewhere, but as someone who read as many of the "ancillary" documents (newspapers, letters, etc.) as I could find, I still couldn't really figure out what was going on with the story. You can find lots of fan theories on the Steam discussion boards, but frankly, I'm at an age where I don't want to have to go onto forums to figure out the story of the game I played. Again, the ideas seem cool, with cloning, time-travel, telepathy, epdiemics, etc. But there are just too many moving parts and, at least for me, they didn't come together at all.
The puzzles are not very inspired, to say the least. IMO, the best puzzle is probably at the start of the game, when you have to look at various notes to figure out which container contains salt. Other puzzles are really frustrating. The "cube" minigames feel out of place and are made difficult primarily because the controls are not great and it's difficult to know what exactly is going on around you. Similarly, the flower finding puzzle suffers from poor controls and graphical issues (it's easy to drop the magnifying glass and lose it, forcing you to restart). I think the main issue with the puzzles is that they are frequently hampered by the game's physics. It's easy to know what you have to do, but difficult to actually do it (not the sort of thing I enjoy in a puzzle game).
Overall, it's a game with a really cool world and a neat concept that, for me, failed to deliver.

This game is honestly one of my favorite games of all time. Keep in mind the fact that I like history more than the average person, and I love this kind of game. If you like constant action, it might not be the best choice. But the amazing thing about this game is that it has the ability to make you amazing with some of the best traits, then you have a daughter that is an imbecile, ugly, club-footed, and has a hunchback. It is capable of keeping you interested and constantly interacting with one or more features in the game. For example, one play through I started as a count in Ireland, which in the game is probably the easiest spot to start for beginners (Not much happens so you have time to adjust things and learn the game to a point where you are comfortable). As this count in Ireland, I expanded my one county into a duchy, which is an even greater title and provided me with a lot of happiness and wealth. But then, my half-brother decided to call a revolt, saying he should be in control of the duchy. I went to war and lost, and he ended up throwing me in the darkest deepest dungeon possible (I still kept one county, which I was suprised about, seeing as he wanted to kill me) When in this dungeon, I contracted typhoid fever, and my brother decided to put me on house arrest. My youngest son randomly broke me out, and I went back to my county. I had married off my daughters, and at the time my allies couldn't help with the revolt my brother called on me. So I decided enough was enough, and declared war. Scotland, Mercia, and Wessex came down with their armies (Which to me at the time was a very huge amount of men) And we decimated my brother. I regained my throne, and began raising troops. I took my army to war against the rest of the single counties, seeing as I had lost a large amount of my life to the dungeon. I took enough land (80% of the Kingdom of Ireland) to create the kingdom. As soon as I made it, I passed away. My oldest son took over the majority of my kingdom, while the duchy went to my youngest (Still in the same country). Being a new character (My oldest son) I decided it was time to expand the kingdom I had made. I fought until I reached scotland, killed my sister to end the alliance, and then declared war and took it. I had so much power, that I wanted to make the Empire of Britannia to match how I felt. I did exactly that, and became the Emperor. However, after some time of ruling the Empire, a foreign country wanted my land, so we went to war. I had over half the amount of troops he had (At least I thought I did) and I felt extremely confident I was going to prevail. Little did I know that the Emperor of the HRE didn't like me. I didn't know the reason, until I saw that he was the previous king of Scotland, and his father was the Emperor of the HRE before me. So now I was facing a 10k+ army included with the 4k coming from another country. They killed my army instantly, all of my land was sieged and burnt, and my children and siblings were all arrested and died from disease. I had nothing after so long that I actually felt a real anger building. It was the first time in a long time a game had brought emotion so real into my heart. That is when I realized how good this game was. It is so amazing, it is able to upset you, but at the same time bring happiness and satisfaction when you destroy your enemies. You can call Jihads as the Caliph of Islam, you can join crusades for the holy sites in the world, you can rule or be ruled. So many opportunities in this game, and all of them bring good or bad feelings. Oh, and about my story, my character ended up being excommunicated by the pope, and I was assassinated.

The MOBA genre isn't one I'm used to; case in point, I played League of Legends for about four days because a friend tried to get me into it, then haven't touched it since, and I found it slightly confusing.
Then enter Awesomenauts.
The game as a MOBA genre game is very easily accessible for newer players, and one of those games that is quick to learn but much longer to master. The teams of 3-vs-3 are simpler, and the items/upgrades are more character-centric, rather than League of Legends throwing whole item shops in your face and letting you figure it all out for yourself.
That doesn't mean it doesn't have the capability to be loved by those who love MOBAs however. Although easier to learn and play, you still get plenty of action.
With strong support from its creators, the game has ongoing DLC options as well as new characters and patches rolled out regularly; plus, they seem to listen to their audience.
MOBA lover or not, I highly recommend this game.

My earlier review of this game was way out of date. Since that review there was another state added, a revamp in the entire map to make it bigger, some new stuff all around including a Multiplayer mod, so it's time to revamp this review!
American Truck Simulator is great, especially with the new state and the map revamp. The states are wonderfully designed and look like real live cities, the trucks look and sound great and there's a fairamount of differing loads and places to pick up and drop off at. But lets get into some finer points.
Pros:
- Great detailed cities. As stated above, these cities look great. Going through Las Vegas seems like real las vegas with the bright lights and such. San Fran is hilly and they just seem... real.
- Map Revamp. The map has been revamped to be bigger which is great. Now to get from one city in the bottom of California to the top of Nevada is around 12 hours I believe. Doesn't sound great right away but dream to the day when you're running from California to New York...
- Great truck sounds and looks. The trucks look fantastic and sound great too. There's a fair bit of customization with them as well, adjusting aux lights, paints, bull bars, steps and door handles!
There's so much more but there's also some bad...
- For one, there's only 3 states... and they are mostly all desert which leads to a lot of boring drives as you pass by desert... and sand... and cacti... and desert... and sand... and oh look! A tree! and desert... And from rumors, sounds like they're sticking with that desert state thing...
- While the trucks look great and sound great... there's only a few. There's 2 truck brands, Peterbilt and Kensworth. That's it, and they each have maybe 3 or 4 trucks each... that gets boring after a short while once you get the truck you want, my case the Kensworth W900 and get it too look the way you want only 15 hours into the game...
- The company managment is still weak. You buy a truck, hire a driver and that's it. You can tell them what to specialize in... or just leave it balanced and after a few hours of playing they will be maxed...
- Ai is kinda dumb. They'll cut you off or pull really close to you when trying to make a turn and damage you or your truck...
- Runs badly sometimes. I don't have a beefy computer, just a laptop but I can run ETS2 at average of 50 fps, while ATS is average of 20... don't know why but it just does...
Overall this game is fantastic in some aspects but light in others. If you want a truck simulator game with lots of content and stuff to do, please go to Euro Truck Simulator 2 which as more cities, more trucks, and more content in gernal.
However... this hasn't covered the Multiplayer mod TruckersMP. This is a mod that allows you to play online with other people. It's a great mod, works great and allos you to convey with friends. Most people on there aren't too dumb and don't cut you off or anything. Servers are good too. Just... it doesn't have AI so sometimes it feels very lonely.

At first I thought that maybe judging this as  game was the wrong way to go and it turned out after playing all the way through it, that yes, I was going about this the wrong way. To call it a game is  kind of a misnomer, games typically have failure states and while a few of the puzzles can be kind of annoying, they are not failure states in themseves(wolves don't eat you for failing them and such).
I think the customer should know what theya re getting into. This isn't a game, so much as a visual novel with game like elements in it. That said, it does have some problems.  Firstly, the options are limited, while the game really doesn't need AA or shadow effects or anything else ina big video menu, it does lack a resolution option and maybe an audio slider. Keybindings are not an issue since the game is essentially point, click and drag for all of the puzzles you will encounter.
The second issue I have is this visual novel of sorts is  very short. For someone thats good at puzzles they can probably go through it in about an hour, 2 hours for those that don't play puzzle games often and maybe 3 hours tops for those that don't play puzzle games at all.
Lastly, the price point; is 1-2 hours of entertainment/zen calm worth 7.49 USD or 10$ if you are buying this after its special? For some maybe not, other probably so. That part all depends on your personal income and expendable cash.
However, should you pick this visual novel up during a steam sale?
Absolutely.
This experience is something you typically do not get out of games. The entire thing is riddled with puzzles, references to the cycles of life and other deep philosiphy things that I will not ruin here. It is also very relaxing with its music, sound and visuals. It is also a game that is entirely child friendly, even young children.
It may not be 'game of the year' or a triple A blockbuster, but for what it was worth it was something entirely different and unexpected. A rare feat to pull off nowadays.

Baldur's Gate II rates as my favorite game of all time, which might make this review a little tough to swallow so I'll try to be as unbiased as possible when I say this: This is absolutely a great game...it's just not for everyone.
What made the original a classic: the characters, story and dialogue are all here and as good as they ever were, but a clumsy interface and non-obvious mechanics bog down the actual gameplay to a crawl (the manual the original game came with is 263 pages long). If you've never played a CRPG from the 'good old days' you might find BGII incredibly tough to comprehend and a slog to play, but put some effort into trying and you'll be rewarded with a sprawling adventure with space hamsters, rotten nobles and insane sorcerers.
The enhanced edition comes with the expansion which ties the whole story up, adds some new party members and new content to play through, which makes this the version to get.
Looking for an RPG to sink some time into, then you might want to check Baldurs Gate II out, just know what you're getting into.

Why, oh why do I always do this to myself?
Firstly, because being the unquestioned sovereign of a hive is actually a pretty interesting idea for a game. The world of ants is sufficiently gritty and subject to sufficient questions of tactics, strategy and logisitics that you could certainly make a pretty good game out of it - the concept is juicy enough that I almost invariably buy every one of these games that I see - everything from Sim Ant on up.
I bought this game. I really have buyers remorse.
It's hard for me to write a detailed report on what's wrong with the game - but the short version is 'everything you thought might be wrong with it when you decided to check out some reviews before you purchased it yourself.' The graphics are so simple as to be childish, but set in a realistic design that prevents them from being cute. Colony management mechanics are not hard-edged enough to make you feel in control, instead you make vague decisions that conflate with other vague factors to lead to a vague sort of direction towards either success or failure.
Increasingly, however, you'll be confronted with a definite sense that the game is simply not good enough. The design of the gameplay mechanics wasn't good enough, the graphics aren't good enough, the sound is equally lack lustre - and so it goes.
I wandered off in vague disquiet roughly 20 minutes into my first play and now find myself wishing I wandered back and made the hard call on this game sooner. A week ago, I might have had a pretty decent chance of getting a refund - now, I'm not so sure.
I'm still going to try.

I'm gonna say it. Look I know you're probably going to shoot me for it, but after hitting about the half way mark for the game I just feel like I need to say it. It needs to be let out in a written form, and when I do say it please take into consideration the time gap, and how that plays into it for sure (modernization and all).
Here goes....this game is better than BALDUR'S GATE II as far as greatest RPG I've personally ever played.
Now look I played BGI when it came out, and BG II when it came out, so I did experience (and have the emotions) of what those games gave me when they were initially released. BG II's story is so far better in my opinion than DOS2, BUT All the other RPG elements of DOS2 and the way they revolutionize turn based combat that relies on the environment so much is just so incredibly well done that from an emotional perspective I've been enjoying DOS2 more than I enjoyed my first playthrough of BGII. Oh and there's the fact that DOS2 has so many different ways that the game can go.
Look I know it's crazy, I seriously thought nothing could beat BG II. However, everything Feels in DOS2. If you do something a certain way then hey you just missed out on that side quest, or perhaps you evolved that side quest to come to a different ending than if you had completed a different way.
It's just so darn good, there's really very few absolutely useless NPCs. They almost all have some form of purpose (even if it's just a good conversation).
If you don't like turn based combat, don't get this game. However if enjoy turned based combat in the slightest then get this game. I mean my goodness perhaps you DON'T enjoy that style of combat, but enjoy a good story then get this game and set the difficulty to exploration mode.
I myself prefer tactician, because once you get a good build going classic becomes too easy.
You just won't find a better game than this, and yes that's my personal opinion. It should be noted though that I'm Not the type of person to Ever say a game is truly the greatest of it's genre, but I am unashamedly stating that now, because for me it's just so stinking true.

Cradle is a fantastic game with only a few minor control issues.  The story is very involved and deep, intriguing and original.  The game creators have done a great job with providing backstory content scattered throughout the "world."  It's a complicated story, but one that is adequately (and realistically) explained.  I say realistically because, were this the real world and you just woke up to it, there wouldn’t be a book lying next to you that had an answer to your every question.  You would have to piece things together from bits of information - which is exactly what the game makes you do.  It results in a very realistic and believable world.  So if you don't like reading or can't be bothered to read, then give this game a miss as you will not really understand what is happening, why it's happening, and certainly will not get the full enjoyment that you otherwise might.
The music is exceptional and the art is very well done.  The ending is just about perfect in my opinion.  Some say it was too abrupt or confusing - but I disagree.  If you actually take the time to explore the environment, read everything, and actually think about and process what you read, then the ending is just about as good as it gets - very well executed.
My only complaint is a minor one, and that is I feel the controls are a bit fuzzy (as in not precise - certainly doesn't have the precision of position/movement that a FPS might).  I don't know if this is intentional or just how the control implementation ended up.  For 99% of the game this is a non-issue.  For me, the 1 time precision was needed was a nightmare.  I ended up dying around 35 times.  In a row.  I felt it was quite unnecessary to the story - at no other point is that level of precision required in the game.  If you play the game and have no idea what I am talking about, consider yourself lucky.
At any rate, apart from the weird control responsiveness/behavior, the game is highly enjoyable and very satisfying from a storytelling perspective, and I recommend you giving it a play.  Just be prepared to read ;)

What I liked:
- The graphics are beautiful
- The music is great
- The unusual setting: this is the first game I ever came across that puts you in the middle of the Mongolian steppe
What I didn't like:
- The game is way too short, you'll beat it in 6 - 7 hours
- The ridiculous cube puzzle games that not only are not fun at all but also stick out like a sore thumb compared to the rest of the game - and they will make up a significant amount of your game time
- The background and storyline are incomplete. You'll end the game with more questions than you started with
- Some of the turns this game takes and decisions you make just make no sense
- The voice acting is monotonous and passionless
Cradle starts out on a very positive note, putting you in some yurt in the middle of the steppe with very beautifully designed interior and lots of objects to interact with. Bits of background information are scattered in the form of newspaper pieces, overall the place looks very "lived in" rather than like an artificial stage. The gynoid you probably know from the trailer is there too and can be partially taken apart but is not functioning yet. For your first puzzle you need to do some detective work and interact with several different objects. So far so good.
Once you get to the point where the gynoid is switched on however, the game suddenly turns very linear and any more background information is not earned by looking for clues any more but one-sidedly handed out to you. It turns into a chase for robot body parts one after another where for each one you need to do a cube puzzle mini game which are tedious, frustrating and feel so much out of place that they basically scream in your face the developers' lack of better ideas. Afterwards, the robot just breaks down and you do one last task for which you get absolutely no explanation why you're doing it and somehow you end up sending a text message consisting of a single four digit number back in time to save the world... wonder how and why a number will save the world? Too bad, no answers. All this is located in a vast steppe which is beautiful but apart from just two locations completely and utterly empty. The dialogues are voiced but the actors are at best mediocre, delivering their lines with little to no emotion behind them.
Bottom line: without the time-filler puzzles the game boils down to only a few hours of entertainment, while the parts of the story that exist show promise it is half-cooked with as many holes as a Swiss cheese and leaves you sitting with all your questions still unanswered and the turns make little sense. It seems the developers just ran out of good ideas, money, time or all of the above, though that's just speculation. While for the first hour the impression is good, it runs out of steam almost immediately after that and turns out to be one of the emptiest and most stunted games I ever played. I'm sorry to have to advise anyone who reads this not to fall for the inital good impression the advertisement makes and stay away from this game - you'll save yourself a huge disappointment.

Tengami is based on a smart and elegant premise: browsing a japanese pop-up book to go through a game.
Tengami  even develops this concept in a tasteful, thoughtful direction: a contemplative series of puzzles linked by a sibylline narrative.
However, Tengami falls short of being a memorable experience because none of its components ever reach their apex potential and neither do they mesh into a coherent, meaningful experience.
On the visual side, there are some stunning set pieces (mostly in the third segment), but the character representation and the overall rendering miss that extra-polish, that extra expert craftmanship that would make them feel organic and mastered. As is, it feels very 'computery' and artificial, with no warmth or tactile feel to it. The UI, destination indicator and main menu are completely sub-par; as if afterthoughts.
In a similar way, though the puzzles manage to establish a coherent and inspiring grammar in a fairly efficient and transparent manner; they remain mostly pedestrian and except for one sign-chasing puzzle at the end, I never wondered over or was drawn in by their use of the pop-up book aspect.
Finally, the storytelling is either too obscure for me to comprehend or too divorced from the gameplay for me to grasp its relevance: the puzzle remain very abstract and are seldom informed. The poetry at the end of each segment shows an intent of conveying a certain flavor of contemplation, but without it showing in the rest of the game, it feels like a cope out.
Overall, Tengami feels more like a thorough proof of concept than the fully explored experience its starting points should have led to; and  it's a testament to the quality of the indie scene - most notably in the puzzle genre - that this doesn't feel  good enough.
This is where I wish Steam had more than 'Recommend' and 'Do not Recommend': Tengami is unique enough that it warrants to be played, but it is pales in comparison of other narrative, puzzle based or contemplative experiences.
Still, I'm looking forward to what Nyamyam will do in the future: I hope they'll have the means and focus to explore their concepts more boldly, with greater attention to details and with an increased emphasis on the experience as a whole.

A vast improvement compared to the first (DOS:EE) installment of the modern series.
- In-depth turn based combat system
- Beautiful visuals, both in and out of combat
- Deep lore in relation to the world that you explore and the characters that inhabit it
- Multiple ways to go about accomplishing a central objective
- Origin characters with a rich backstory exist along custom player-made characters
- Replayability is present for 2 or 3 playthroughs in total as long as you don't get bored of the main story
- Infinite respeccing options allowing you to completely change each of your characters on the fly with no penalty
whatsoever
- Magnificent soundtrack and audio work
- Although an improvement compared to DOS:EE, the game at times is still fairly unintuitive (looking at you, Arx)
- Some minor bugs pose an equally minor annoyance (some characters keep infinitely looping dialogue, audio bugs)
- Very lackluster ending
- Unable to go back to previous areas after having moved on to the next act / area
- Unable to free roam and tie off any loose ends after completeing the game
DOS:2 is a very fun game that I find was worth the money that I've invested into it. I bought it the moment it came out of early access and have sunk a total of 64 hours into it. You can definitely sink more time into this (around 75 or 80 hours total maybe) if you go around and finish every side quest and origin character questline. As I've already mentioned it's a shame that we can't go back and freeroam all of the areas once we finish the game. This was an issue in DOS:EE as well and it's sad to see that the same problem persists here. Either way I must give credit to Larian for a near flawless second installment. If you're on the fence about buying this game I would advise you to wait for the winter sale and see if it drops in price, and if it doesn't, then buy it anyway. The price will not change from $45.

The reason the first games that pulled many of us older  RPG fans from pnp to video games permanantly was final fantasy 2 and 3 was because of the story, party recruiting, and how each party member got legit, emotional back/side stories. Read the journal, go to the area, click stuff till you find.  we didn't have game wikis if we got stuck back then!  Shoot, I had dialup until 2002!  If you like apgs, crpgs, or played da-o and liked pause and play, try this!  Its like party based diablo with way less loot and way more story!!  I plan on playing thru bg 1, 2 and then tob all at once.  I have some time coming up now that I decided I will NOT be buying Elder Scrolls Online!  MMORPGS are designed to keep you subscribed, not to throw game content at you!  Time Sink with little reward!  I'd rather experience limited static content across multiple games then raid the same dungeons over and over with people I barely like!

For the very few people who actually read this review, I’m going to start off with everything bad that it does.
1)	The community feels as dead as all the enemies I had to kill to complete one objective
2)	The game does nothing new, it is very generic and copy-paste of other games in the genre.
The purpose of a game like this is to do what similar games of its genre did and build on those ideas and make them better. Not fabricate what already exists and slap a “done” sticker on the front. I want something new, with a quirk or unique feature, not a copy paste.
3)	There is very little explanation about how skills, items and game mechanics work, only basic key mapping like moving, turning and combat.
4)	The story is fairly mild at best
5)	Melee combat is dull and unsatisfying
6)	Quests have a tendency to “bug out” or have confusing objectives, one situation was where I needed to go to a point on the map, let an NPC follow me and walk back to the start point. Apart from I failed the quest somehow on the first try, the game never explained how or why.
When I went back there the NPC that was meant to follow me no longer appears, and as such I have no idea how to complete the quest.
Other situations like questing disappearing from my menu also happen frequently, meaning quests I was halfway through needed to be picked up again from a guy quite literally 3 miles away and completed in one go.
7)	Menus are very clunky, from the start I was bombarded by a bunch of skills I didn’t know (and still don’t know) the effects or uses of.
8)	The crafting system does nothing new, by which I mean it's all dull bashing objects togeather to make something out of thin air.
It's also crafted in real time, which can sometimes be up to half an hour for some items. Maybe more.
9)	How skills work is never explained, you have to figure it out via tooltips.
10)	For me this game took over 50 minutes to download, unpack and patch before I could play. This was on a 100 mbp/s connection with no bottlenecks and commonly downloads big budget triple A games in under 30 mins.
11)	I have no idea how they got the screenshots on the store page, I push everything to max and it still looks like something a commodore 64 would play.
12)   Fallen Earth tries way to hard to be funny. Often forcing vulgar 12 year old humour at every turn.
Well for a start the skills menu and the depth of control you have is refreshing. You don’t get your hand held and from the start you can wander in any direction you please.

Tucked away within the confines of a treasured pop-up book featuring a vivid far eastern landscape and natural entities of the surrounding wildlife; Tengami is a casual but moving journey with very few, if any, words yet still a majestic story told merely through imagery.
The experience is described by the developers as something they envisioned being played "in bed before going to sleep or in the afternoon on the sofa with a hot beverage", and I felt that description was very apt. As I played from my shabby studio apartment on a cold and rainy day with some hot tea completing each relaxing chapter I felt a particular sense of warmth, a certain kind of satisfying radiance. I almost forgot about the cold, grey city surrounding me that I call home.
As you move through each beautifully vibrant page of an old Japanese pop-up book that act as chapters to the story, you are faced with earthly obstacles that stand in your path. Finding the solution to uncovering the brighter path ahead of your wintery beginnings involves puzzle-solving of a very organic kind, puzzles that feel less like interacting with a game and more like interacting with nature itself.
All around you rivers, temples and old wooden bridges pull out from tabs in pop-up book fashion, revealing the beaten path ahead which beckons our unknown hero on his mysterious adventure. In a snowy forest a wild pack of wolves howls in unison to the sound of wind chimes you control in a game of 'Simon Says', a strange and ancient bell changes the seasons at your will altering the land to reveal new key items to collect, and an old broken wooden boat must be reconstructed with broken pieces pulled from the ocean waters among swimming fish.
The wonderfully natural atmosphere of the game is complimented by the twanging of Shamisen or Koto and calming sounds of wooden flute, all drawing you into a zen-like state of deep calmness. The usage of colors makes everything incredibly pleasing to look at and each visual theme is very evocative of its respective season.
Spring environments have a lush green with blue flowing rivers, and Fall stands out with its vibrant pinkish-orange hues much like a sunset, with Winter bearing a harsh mixture of white and greys with frozen rivers that no longer flow. The settings all glow with a distinct array of colors that evoke the same shifting of emotions our real-world seasons stir in us.
Tengami exists outside of the boundaries of any particular demographic, being something that is just as enjoyable to the youngest audiences as it is to the oldest. If you aren't too caught up on games needing to be difficult or long, or "hardcore', then this is by far the most memorable and comforting trip into a Far Eastern world of mystique.
Come and witness nature and the changing of seasons conveyed through a colorful world of picture book pages, flip through the dusty old pages of Tengami!

When I first saw this game on Steam I thought it would be something like the old school Ant War game I used to play as a kid, so I decided to give it a try. I completed the game about halfway and was very disappointed with it.
The game consists of about 15 scripted missions for you to complete. There is no sandbox mode. As you complete missions, more and more units get unlocked for you to breed. Units have different roles that they take on to help you run your colony. Nurser ants feed the Ant Queen and help the larvae develop into ants. Worker ants collect food from outside the colony and bring it back. Digger ants dig new tunnels and chambers in your colony and deposit the dirt outside. Soldier ants fight against other insects and protect your colony. There is also the Queen Ant, who produces larvae. Her health bar drains every time she produces a larave and every few seconds depending on how many ants are in your colony. The health bar can regenerate by eating food. Each above mentioned unit (besides the Queen) has several different versions, which have more specialized stats.
The missions themselves are very straightforward. Some will require you to collect enough food, some will require you to survive against insect invasions for a set time limit, and some will require you to expand your colony by digging new tunnels (which are predeterminated, you do not get to pick and choose how to build your colony.)
Units are not directly controlled. Instead, you either turn on or turn off specific tasks for your workers to complete. These tasks include collecting food, developing larvae, digging tunnels, patrolling above ground, or fighting enemies. The AI seems to spend most of its time blindly walking around instead of actually completing these tasks however. Digger ants especially are useless for half the game, as there is no digging for them to do other than in specific missions. This means they drain your Queen's health without contributing anything to the well-being of the colony.
This game is simply awful, and asking for $17.99 for it is a joke. There were no reviews when I bought game so I took a chance on it. I don't want anyone else to make the same mistake I did. Spend the $2.99 for Ant War: Domination instead if you want something significantly better.

A marvelous adventure with Belgian detective Hercule Poirot in a traditional point & click scheme and following a case where appearences can deceive.
Hercule Poirot sided by his friend Arthur Hastings are being challenged by a mysterious murderer that announced his future murders with letters. The most incredible aspect of this murderer is that he's always signing himself as A.B.C. and his murders will progress in alphabetical order, where both the city and the victim's name start with the same letter. The case is very complicated and Poirot will have a hard time to collect all the necessary clues to ake him to the right conclusion.
It is worth pointing out that this story is faithfully taken from the original book, so if you read it already there won't be much of a surprise. Otherwise prepare for a great case!
The game has been developed in Unity and has a cartoonish style with some light cel shading and simple yet effective graphic style. You will visit different locations both outside and inside, detail level is not the highest ever seen but it has been built with various decorations and a proper quantity of items to analyze and look at
I personally love the main theme and some tracks are a pleasure to listen while playing, too bad that the main one is the only outstanding and there is a small variety of songs as well. In other words a good work, but small as well.
Besides the story gameplay is one of the brightest sides. As a classic point & click adventure there are the classic features, you move and act with your mouse, you speak with other characters and so on. You must analyze clues around, solve riddles and puzzles (getting more difficult towards the end of course) and to proceed with the investigations you must analyze and associate concept and ideas by giving the correct answers to questions as soon as you have all the clues from the scene. This last part in particular is the most interesting and ambiguous one. If it's challenging to actually reason with all clues sometimes can get frustrating finding the correct group of answers or concepts because some of them are almost the same. Luckily it's pretty simple as you can make your selection and see immediatly if it's correct or not. You could bluntly just find the correct combination without reading, but later on it gets more difficult as more clues and more concepts come together.
Another compelling part is the crime reconstruction where you visualize the scene the moment the crime is being perpetrated, you follow the murderer and moment by moment select the correct action seeing and recreating the murder. Very dark but very good idea as well.
Nothing serious, this is a good and entertaining product but there are a few things that could have done better. More details with the construction of ambiences, more music and a bit more polished riddles/puzzles interface could hve made this game a superior product. Not to mention the fact that the story and the case follows the book and will never surprise in any way someone that already read the book.

I hesitate to say that this game is... you know, "good" in any real identifiable way. The backgrounds and settings are nice, but the puzzles vary from sort of fine to tedious to repetitive, the voice acting is stilted, and the interrogation sequences don't really seem to have any stakes (I don't actually think it's possible to fail them outright?). The game reuses voice clips every chance it gets, and watching Hercule Poirot sloooowly saunter from one end of the screen to the other can get old pretty quick.
Still, I somehow feel like it was still worth the 8 and a half hours or so I spent with The ABC Murders. I found myself getting kind of sucked into its slow pacing and awkward charm. By the end, I didn't even mind having to hear Poirot's "let us try and get our brain cells to work!" soundbite for the eight millionth time.
I tentatively recommend it, only because it was an oddly cozy and relaxing game to settle in with for a couple evenings. It is by far the most chill murder mystery I've ever experienced.

My earlier review of this game was way out of date. Since that review there was another state added, a revamp in the entire map to make it bigger, some new stuff all around including a Multiplayer mod, so it's time to revamp this review!
American Truck Simulator is great, especially with the new state and the map revamp. The states are wonderfully designed and look like real live cities, the trucks look and sound great and there's a fairamount of differing loads and places to pick up and drop off at. But lets get into some finer points.
Pros:
- Great detailed cities. As stated above, these cities look great. Going through Las Vegas seems like real las vegas with the bright lights and such. San Fran is hilly and they just seem... real.
- Map Revamp. The map has been revamped to be bigger which is great. Now to get from one city in the bottom of California to the top of Nevada is around 12 hours I believe. Doesn't sound great right away but dream to the day when you're running from California to New York...
- Great truck sounds and looks. The trucks look fantastic and sound great too. There's a fair bit of customization with them as well, adjusting aux lights, paints, bull bars, steps and door handles!
There's so much more but there's also some bad...
- For one, there's only 3 states... and they are mostly all desert which leads to a lot of boring drives as you pass by desert... and sand... and cacti... and desert... and sand... and oh look! A tree! and desert... And from rumors, sounds like they're sticking with that desert state thing...
- While the trucks look great and sound great... there's only a few. There's 2 truck brands, Peterbilt and Kensworth. That's it, and they each have maybe 3 or 4 trucks each... that gets boring after a short while once you get the truck you want, my case the Kensworth W900 and get it too look the way you want only 15 hours into the game...
- The company managment is still weak. You buy a truck, hire a driver and that's it. You can tell them what to specialize in... or just leave it balanced and after a few hours of playing they will be maxed...
- Ai is kinda dumb. They'll cut you off or pull really close to you when trying to make a turn and damage you or your truck...
- Runs badly sometimes. I don't have a beefy computer, just a laptop but I can run ETS2 at average of 50 fps, while ATS is average of 20... don't know why but it just does...
Overall this game is fantastic in some aspects but light in others. If you want a truck simulator game with lots of content and stuff to do, please go to Euro Truck Simulator 2 which as more cities, more trucks, and more content in gernal.
However... this hasn't covered the Multiplayer mod TruckersMP. This is a mod that allows you to play online with other people. It's a great mod, works great and allos you to convey with friends. Most people on there aren't too dumb and don't cut you off or anything. Servers are good too. Just... it doesn't have AI so sometimes it feels very lonely.
