Fun, but bugged beyond all belief. The "Enhanced" version is actually WORSE than the original -- and that simply should not be! EG: 1) At least one of the "rez" spells DOESN'T -- it merely harms the caster and leaves the dead character dead. 2) The pathing of the characters, whether controlled by the player or the AI, is almost offensively nonsensical, resulting in members of the party wandering off in the OPPOSITE direction of where they are supposed to be heading or taking the most circuitous and perilous path to a space mere feet away. The AI will often halt a character mid-path and just leave them there, meaning you may find yourself missing a member of your party during an important battle. 3) The voices cut in and out, sometimes not even finishing sentences or words. 4) The "triggered" dialogue will sometimes skip ahead several steps, ruining some potential romances and preventing the player from making their own choices. 5) The AI-controlled party members will often disengage or cease attacking enemies, and casters will often stop casting spells or just freeze mid-spell. What is more, many characters will freeze in the middle of drinking a potion, meaning they receive no benefit from the potion but also cannot/will not fight back when attacked. 6) Many NPCs will simply stand in place, refusing to move, which can be game-breaking if they are blocking the only doorway or path to a game-crucial location. 7) Characters can have the wrong abilities for their class and/or race.
It's so bad, it's virtually unplayable at points. Sometimes you have to start the entire game over again and hope that an issue won't occur again. I've literally seen people in the official forums advising new players to just uninstall this and get the original, older version because it (ironically) has LESS bugs than this new "Enhanced" edition. A tragic wasted opportunity to revive a classic rpg.

I thoroughly enjoyed Cradle.  For me, it's pros outweigh its quirky cons.  I bought the game because I tend to like science fiction and games that address cybernetics, artificial intelligence, singularity and transhumanist type concepts.  However, this story turned out to be very surreal and deals mostly with some really imaginative metaphyscis.  It feels like a myth transpiring against a sci-fi backdrop, which is really very charming.
The game pulled me in, with the very first room.  You start out in this wonderful little yurt, and it's obvious that the designers lovingly crafted the whole interior.  There is so much detail the place could be real.  The protagonist has no idea what is happening, which leaves you sifting through the contents of the dwelling, to try to make sense of things.  From there, you encounter several point and click adventure style puzzles and a few arcade mini-game sequences.  As you progress, the dialog helps make more sense of things.  But, if you want the ending to make sense, you have to thoroughly explore and read everything.  It's completely possible to finish the game without having any idea what the ending sequence is about, because all the reading that clears it up is completely optional.
The graphics are great, and really contribute to the immersive feel of the game.  The sound track is sparse, but beautiful in my opinion.  The voice acting is pretty solid, with 2 out of 3 primary speaking parts delivered quite well. Controls are simple and well suited to the genre.
The cons.  Running on Ubuntu 15, on a laptop with i7 and Windows Iris, I've had a few stability issues.  This has been the main drawback to the game. Also, the arcade mini games feel a bit clunky and agravating at times and the point and click style puzzles can be a bit on the easy side.  As wonderful and immsersive as the yurt is, it turns out there isn't really much more.  While practically every square inch of the place is interactive, there are few other locations, and everything else is very sparsely populated with interactive elements. Basically, the setting is just so immersive and interesting, that it leaves you wishing there was more.

Developed by a small indie studio with a limited budget, Cradle nonetheless successfully features both a huge world of the future and meditative, contemplative gameplay focused on exploration of a small but rich to details fragment of it. With its rich narrative and details this game resembles a good sci-fi book; however, Cradle never tries to put the all answers in front of you, so you'll have to do some research and exploration to uncover every detail!
Unlike other story-based quests, Cradle also features some platformer/puzzle mini-games. Many people are complaining about them, and actually I was surprised to see these complaints. The mini-games are actually well-designed, fun to play and also they fit the story.  Only if you're playing only slow-paced quests and never played platformers or puzzle games like Portal, they will probably appear tricky or boring to you.
This game isn't perfect to everyone, but it is certainly unique and beautiful. It has its own atmosphere, incredible story, stunning graphics and contemplative experience - that's why I recommend it.

This game is simply fantastic. The whole world is very filled up, to the point where you an just spend hours going dungeon to dungeon getting new loot. The towns all have enough variation to make them all feel different from each other and have their own feel. The combat has a pretty strategic feel to it; the game gives you different effects which each melee power attack as you progress, allowing for some pretty engaging fights. Unfortunately, the ranged combat types don't have quite as much detail as the melee, but they make up for this in sheer effectiveness. The magic is very fun to use, as you can create your own spells later in the game, which give you some advantages in both combat and passive situations. But wait, there's more!
The absolute BEST part of this game is the modding community. It's really, REALLY big. You can change how your combat works, get armor retextures, even change the game to have an XP system. You won't really run out of stuff to do; quest mods are there too (Some of them are pretty fantastic, I recommend Knights of the Nine: Revelation). All in all, the game is fantastic, and you should pick it up if you don't already have it.

It is very relaxing, since there is no failure state. You can't die, you can't fall when climbing, there is no enemy, no combat and no dead end. The key element is trying to find everything you want to find and enjoying the view as you do it, because the game is really beautiful. It almost feels like a tech demo since the game has so much more eye candy than deep gameplay elements.
The only thing I could criticize is the full price. I got it discounted and I think it is worth less than 5€. I wouldn't pay 20€ for it. Getting all content in the game took me 4.5h. After that it has practically zero replayability.

Let me start off by saying that this game gets infrequent updates and will probably get a full release after Half Life 3. Now that my only major negative point is out of the way, let me say that this game, in my opinion, has the best combat in any game that I have played so far. Instead of a health system, like most games have, the combat is based on a bone structure system, enemies' bodies will react realistically to being hit, and a single fight with one opponent can take quite a while, which might not be good for everyone, but it's something I really enjoy. You can perform various moves that you can figure out yourself, for example a jump kick, that allows you to bounce off enemies and sometimes land head-first on the ground and snap your neck. There are a few levels already in the game, along with some challenges and an arena, but there is a vast selection of custom maps for you to enjoy, all made with the in-game editor. The parkour, while hard to learn, is VERY satisfying once you are able to even perform some basic actions. This game is definitely not without its problems, but shows a lot of promise, especially considering that it's this fun while it's in alpha.

I've been playing this game for a very long time now, longer than what my Steam hours say. I can honestly say that this game is not perfect, but worth spending a half an hour\hour to. ) I've spent a lot longer than that, though. ) This is my very first review, but I'll try to break it down.
Pros: Amazing combat system, so detailed and at times, brutal. A mix of offense and defense is essential for victory.
Physics are pretty spot on.
Animations are superb. Very well done.
RAGDOLL! This can make for some very badass and hilarious moments. It's happened with me. :O
There are many weapons in the game and they work wonderfully. Daggers are somewhat OP, however.
Mod support! There are many mods for the game out there, ranging from maps, to characters, to weapons. It helps in adding replayability and for more content to do.
Very well done parkour system. The gore is also quite good, though somewhat lacking, but much more detailed than most games.
Cons: Incredibly slow development. The game has been in development since 2008, if I recall correctly.
Not much to do. Even with mods and maps, all there really is to do is either do a parkour map, or just do a map where you fight through a bunch of enemies until you get to the "boss". Or a mix betwixt the two.
Devs don't communicate much with fans.
Despite its incredibly slow update releases, this game is still worth checking out at the very least. It's got a LOT of attention to detail put into it and in about a few more years, I can really see this game becoming one of the best PC games out there. And to address the slow update subject, the dev team used to be 3. Then they took a long hiatus to hire more people. Now the team is 18 members and are attempting to release updates every 1-2 weeks. As a tech demo, it is outstanding. There's an excellent sense of movement and weight to your character as they move, which makes the freerunning mechanics of game really shine. The combat is brutal, unforgiving and very fun. It's a simple left-click to attack and right-click to block, but add in the quick movement, sound and fantastic animation the combat is bliss. In it's current state there's also an arena mode that to allow you to only fight. It's very barebones, but it demonstrates the games excellent capabilities. The concept of ninja bunnies and other creatures like cats and dogs is great and I do look forward to how this idea will play out. The game is also easy to mod and has a solid creator tool for making your own environments and arenas. Did I mention the game has the best blood physics of any game I've ever seen?
From what I know Overgrowth has been in development for seven years and I've been playing it for two of those years. In all that time the game has changed very little. Since I got it in 2013, there have been a few new, but small features, new models, new items and a bevy of bug fixes. None of these however really changed the games experience or made it feel improved all that much. I understand some games take time to develop, but this is just silly given how much money you have to pay for the game. There's no campaign (yet) and there's very little voice acting aside from the occasional grunt and yell. The game also crashes, a lot. There's also a good deal of bugs, some even gamebreaking.
It hurts to see such a good idea and base game stagnate. It's a lot of fun, but paying that price for something with such a lack of things to do, I just can't condone buying it right now. I can condone waiting for it to improve, but we've been waiting a very long time already so don't get your hopes up. If you really like freerunning ninja bunnies who beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of each other and you're willing to pay the price, you'll have plenty of fun for a while. If you're like me, someone who expected more for what they payed, add it to your wishlist and wait until a sale or until the game reaches a more complete state.

TL;DR - The ABC Murders is an average point-and-click adventure game with its fair share of annoyances and gameplay issues. For casual gamers into these types of things, it should tick enough boxes to be enjoyable for a few hours, but for the rest of us, I'd give it a pass.
At it's heart, Agatha Christie - The ABC Murders is a simple point-and-click adventure game. From what I can gather, as somebody with no prior knowledge of Christie's work, the game follows the novel's plot line closely enough. For somebody like me, who had never read The ABC Murders, this is fine, given that it is a mystery after all, but I can't imagine there's much here for anybody familiar with the work. I suspect a hardcore Hercule Poirot fan might get some enjoyment seeing a favorite character, but then again, I also suspect they would be much more satisfied with a new mystery to solve.
But, down to what really matters - how the game plays. For starters, I was surprised to find that the resolution seemed locked to a 4:3 aspect ratio. If there does exist a way to change this to 16:9, I couldn't find it. In fact, I couldn't find many things I would expect to find in a PC game launched in 2016. Audio and video options are confined to a small handful of basic sliders, with only the bare minumum effort it seems being put into the menu design. Artefact Studios seems to be a relatively small developer, however, so I can give this a pass, mostly.
What I can't be so forgiving with, however, is the sometimes awkward and difficult way the game controls. Poirot moves wherever you click on screen, but often times in order to interact with certain objects near the edge of a room, you need near pixel-perfect precision in your movements, else Poirot merely stands there, with his arms near his chest, observing the room yet being unable to notice the one thing you want him to see.
The character models are servicable, with a sort of cell shaded look that, I'm assuming, is meant to emulate the look of graphic novels, and not Borderlands. Facial animations are, again, servicable, with enough detail to get the idea across that this character is in fact talking, though some desync does happen. The voice acotrs themselves get the job done, but the dialog can be clunky an frankly uninspired at times. The subtitles that are on by default can sometimes have descrepencies with what the voice actors are saying. Perhaps the biggest and most noticeable times when an issue like this happens is when Poirot makes a comment about his "brain cells," while the subtitles refer to them as "little grey cells." Yes, it's a small issue, but it persisted from the first time they're mentioned straight until the end credits roll. At times, animations can be laggy or just plain broken, but this was rare on my playthrough.
The game itself lasts about 6 hours, though I imagine you could spend more time trying to unlock every achievement, if you were so inclined. The primary game mechanic is in making observations, which is a sort of hidden object style minigame - only here there are maybe five objects in a mostly barren area, and your cursor creates a vignette whenever you mouse over an object you're trying to find. In addition to this is the occasional puzzle, wherein Piorot attempts tp physically manipulate some object (usually a locked box or cabinet) with a very specific orer of steps which need to be completed. There are also the aforementioned "little grey cells" minigames, which are essentially word association puzzles. You are presented with a question (eg "How did the murderer enter the tobacco shop") and must drag the corresponding answer to a little circle. If it fits, it turns green and you continue, if not, nothing happens. I hated most of these, as they tend to be fairly arbitray in nature.
Most of the time, the puzzles are engaging enough, but don't take very much time, but on occassion are almost too easy, or, especially near the end of the game, insanely difficult. I was wholly unable to actually solve one of the final grey cells puzzles in the game, despite being able to glide through most of the others without much difficulty. Which brings me to the biggest flaw with the puzzles in the game. Nearly every one can be fairly easily be brute forced with only margianally more effort than solving the puzzle "correctly" if need be.
Overall, I think The ABC Murders is a decent enough casual mystery game. At 15 USD, I can't fully fault it for many of it's issues, but I still have to awknowlege they exist. If you particularly enjoy point-and-click, hidden object type games, sure it might be worth a buy, especially on sale, but for the more "hardcore" gamers, I don't think you'll find much to love. It's no Myst or Day of the Tentacle, after all. Reccommended, but only just.

Compared to it's successor, this game can easily hold it's own. The only thing lacking is the local co-op concepts they've added to JSRF.
It's about living the life in Tokyo-to, tagging the streets, listening to the underground pirate radio and dancing even when someone is talking to you. There really is no other game I've seen similar to this. Roller skates are used by each character all the time and cannot be taken off to walk around. This isn't much of an issue as moving about is relatively simple and easy. It gets a bit complicated at certain points when you want to stop as it does take time to come to a full stop from full speed. None the less the game tries it's best to go over the top with what they gave you. Grinding (on rails) is another big aspect to the game. I remember it being a lot easier in JSRF than it is in JSR. In JSRF, you could be near the rail and have a bit of leeway if you missed your mark. In JSR, you have to be pretty precise in your movements to land on top of the area you want to grind. In JSRF, you were allowed to walk into a grind whereas here, you'll need to press jump ("A") before you get going. Once you get how the game mechanics work, it'll all slowly fall into place. There are times you may find yourself randomly falling off grind rails. This may be due in part that you are actually colliding with something that you should be jumping over. There were certain parts in the game where for the life of me, I couldn't figure out why my characters would suddenly just stop, drop and free fall from a grind. I later noticed that indeed, you do need to jump over or avoid certain obstacles. This is most notable with power poles. Either than that, the grinding is actually pretty smooth and some pretty sick combos/jumps can be made rail to rail.
Imagine grinding on a rail, then riding a billboard, jumping onto a truck and grinding that, then jumping on power lines then finally, grinding on roofs to reach a "tag point" (where you need to graffiti). This is just one of the many possible combos available. Unlike JSRF, you cannot do moves as you are grinding on a rail. Meaning in the newer game, you were able to press x if you were grinding for a while to do a technique on the rail. Here, you are only able to do moves when you are jumping. Moves can be strung together by timing your next jump right. By keeping the timing right, this also let's you keep your momentum and speed. Tagging is a lot more inclusive in this one than JSRF. They will ask you to rotate the stick in all sorts of directions to complete your graffiti art. Bigger murals will take more time, technique and paint. Besides having the basic movements of jumping and tagging, the player may also hit the sprint button ("RT") for a little extra umph while the right stick allows you to move the camera.
For future Jet Set games, I would recommend adding more actions (such as shouldering people as your moving through an area) or something along those lines. More controls means more action. The story itself is pretty cool and characters are nothing short of creative. It starts out as small time gangs beefing in which it starts to turn into all out war with a certain group of unknowns. When you initially start tagging the streets, police will show up and try to take you down. The first guy is not too bad, but pretty soon you'll have riot police with tear gas, tanks, helicopters and even pyromaniacs chasing you down. Although this adds great excitement to the game, there is one great flaw that the other game had that this one didn't : you cannot retaliate! You can't hit back or even tag your enemies to knock them down. If you run into a cop full speed, you'll be taking the brunt of the damage. If you run into another character, they will sort of stumble but your character will feel all the force (especially your health bar). This is the one little thing I couldn't get over as I want to fight back! I know it ain't easy going against tanks but hey, if a little spray paint gets into their engines, I'm sure their check engine lights will go on. You may retaliate to certain extents. There is a level where helicopters will be hovering by power cables in which you can tag them as you pass along (leading to their extermination). The levels try their best to stay diverse and to challenge the player differently. There will be surprise levels where someone will ask to join your squad. You may have to race these people to a tag spot or battle it out with them by tagging their backs. Cops won't always chase you if you manage to reach a safe zone.
Levels at first may seem a bit small, but they've done a hell of a job putting everything together. You will start off small in one area which eventually will allow you to travel to other areas as you progress through the game. You will have to be attentive though as you may have tagged everything in this area, but there is still another area within the city to tag! It's not always super obvious that you are going to the next area. Sometimes it is a bit hard to tell which graphics are simply background graphics and which graphics can lead you to another area. None the less, I think it is great that they decided to make levels interconnected to make them feel bigger. In JSRF, going from place to place is a lot easier than JSR. Red arrows will indicate areas that are needed to be tagged in order to beat the level while green arrows will indicate optional tags (for more points)! An addition this game had that JSRF didn't have was the ability to ride on the back of cars! Don't want to go up a big hill? Catch a ride!
My biggest issue deciding whether or not to purchase this game was it's graphics. This game was released in 2000 which is extremely hard to believe and it would be harder to play because I already played the newer version. Nonetheless, the graphics did not bother me at all. The ABC Murders is a mixture of good and bad, but in the end it's just not fun.
The puzzles are easy and the game shoves hints down your throat constantly, so you won't get stuck. There are a few puzzles that require leaps of logic, but even when the solution isn't fed to you, it can be brute-forced, and there's a (weak) hint system to help you do that.
The story as a whole is sufficiently interesting, as is to be expected, but the storytelling is boring because Poirot is meandering, most puzzles are contrived, and the puzzle-box segments in particular infuriatingly tank the framerate. Occasional cuts to the murderer going about his day are just baffling.
The voice acting is not engaging, quite the opposite. Some game mechanics do work in a Poirot story, such as the deduction minigame that lets Poirot explicate on the case, but others like the constant preening and rummaging do not. There is an interrogation minigame that is actually possible to fail in, and could be used to greater effect in briging Poirot's personality to the game, but sadly there are only a few instances of it.
The game has a massive 50 achievements, 90% of which you get for merely progressing with the story. That means you are constantly spammed with achievement notices - and what's worse, the achievements are extremely boring and have but the remotest relation to what they are awarded for. There's also a timeline section where you can go review the story while you're playing - though I didn't find any need to.
If the puzzle-box puzzles were removed, I might recommend this game as a participatory story. With them present, it's just a bad attempt at gamefication: more boring than intriguing, and more annoying than puzzling.

Fun, but bugged beyond all belief. The "Enhanced" version is actually WORSE than the original -- and that simply should not be! EG: 1) At least one of the "rez" spells DOESN'T -- it merely harms the caster and leaves the dead character dead. 2) The pathing of the characters, whether controlled by the player or the AI, is almost offensively nonsensical, resulting in members of the party wandering off in the OPPOSITE direction of where they are supposed to be heading or taking the most circuitous and perilous path to a space mere feet away. The AI will often halt a character mid-path and just leave them there, meaning you may find yourself missing a member of your party during an important battle. 3) The voices cut in and out, sometimes not even finishing sentences or words. 4) The "triggered" dialogue will sometimes skip ahead several steps, ruining some potential romances and preventing the player from making their own choices. 5) The AI-controlled party members will often disengage or cease attacking enemies, and casters will often stop casting spells or just freeze mid-spell. What is more, many characters will freeze in the middle of drinking a potion, meaning they receive no benefit from the potion but also cannot/will not fight back when attacked. 6) Many NPCs will simply stand in place, refusing to move, which can be game-breaking if they are blocking the only doorway or path to a game-crucial location. 7) Characters can have the wrong abilities for their class and/or race.
It's so bad, it's virtually unplayable at points. Sometimes you have to start the entire game over again and hope that an issue won't occur again. I've literally seen people in the official forums advising new players to just uninstall this and get the original, older version because it (ironically) has LESS bugs than this new "Enhanced" edition. A tragic wasted opportunity to revive a classic rpg.

PLEASE NOTE:  There may be some spoilers in here.  Maybe not? But just in case, I'm going to mention a few things that might make you like "Ooh, there's a cyborg vase!? Darn, I wish I could have figured that out all on my own...."  Well, not really, but you get the point. Read at your own risk.  Most of you are probably reading this after making the purchase anyway.  For those of you who want to be surprised, go ahead and buy the game, especially if it's on-sale!
First off, I enjoyed a lot of things about this game:
1) The "open world" (which is pretty much just two locations, some frustrating virtual reality mini-games, and a secret horse a few miles away) feels really nice.  Someone obviously took a lot of time to design the world, and its inhabitants.
2) I enjoyed talking to the sexy cyborg vase.  It was fun interacting with her in the various ways afforded. I'm being vague because I want to avoid spoilers here.  She's one of the best parts of the game, and I wish they'd spent more time expanding her role.
3) The cool Golden Eagle.  It's awesome!  It makes cool sounds, and looks really eagle-y!  I do wish, again, they'd expanded its role in the world.
4) When you take the time to explore, you find a lot of text hidden all over the place.  Scattered - sometimes annoyingly - in the oddest of places.  Some of the text is short, teasing, while others are a little longer, with additional information.  If you take the time to read all of the text in the game, you'll know a heck of a lot more about the world, which I think is a good thing.
5) The story!  I have to say the story is excellent, and it unfolds at just the right pace IF...the mini-games weren't slam-jammed right in the middle of the story.  Which, unfortunately, they are.
Let's talk about why I clicked that I do not recommend this game.  Why I -sadly- do not recommend this game. I wish more people would play it, but I think they'd just get frustrated with the stuff I'm going to write below.  Make your own decision, of course, but be forewarned:
1) The mini-games are too-challenging and don't fit the pace of (what I hope and believe to be) the central core of this wonderful game: its story and the world.  Yes, you can say that the mini-games serve a role in both the game itself, and the mythos of the world and story, but really, all of the mini-games are basically just a single, really tough, TIMED (OMGOMGOMG), 3D platforming thing that gave me a headache.  True, the mini-games change a bit - a color here, a bad-guy-response there - but at the mini-games' core, they're just annoying and ruin the game/story for me, and apparently a lot of other people too.
2) Had the developers realized that the mini-games were a terrible idea, they might have taken the time spent developing these mini-games and focused that time, attention, money on the rest of the game - filling out the "open world" which feels essentially empty aside from the two main locations.  The mini-games are not really a location - they're just a claustrophobic panic attack waiting to happen for some people.  But yes, I would have preferred all of that energy applied to revealing more of the back-story and present-day situation.  You can figure out some of it, but there are some gaping holes in the way the world/plot/story was revealed, leaving a lot of folks feeling unsatisfied and confused at the end of the game.  I hope someday there's a sequel within this same universe that explains a little more, but I fear there won't be, or it will simply be like reading bad Harry Potter fan fiction or, worse, Twilight slash story. This leads to the second bad thing: the best part of the game is WAY too short.  It should be longer.  We should see more. We don't, and that's sad.
3) Based on the two items above, I have to say that the game is overpriced.  It's worth, like, $4.99 or maybe $9.99 but anything over $10 and I just feel ripped off.  True, I did buy the Deluxe Edition, so I paid a little more, but it still feels like I overpaid. I'm sure there's some "magic number" for what a game like this costs to develop, and how much it needs to sell for in order for the game to make a profit, but if you look at the maddening mini-games as half the experience, I feel like I deserve half a refund for this game.
Anyway....  I'd like to see more people play this game, and say "Oh, no, the mini-games aren't so bad. You just have to do this, or that...." But frankly, I don't have time to master a 3D platforming game, when I bought into a 3D Walking Simulator.
I think the only way I would begrudgingly give this a "Recommended" is if they A) reduced the price of the game to below $9.99 and B) either eliminated the mini-games altogether, or made them easier.  The mini-game pacing is frenetic and being forced to play through them - even with the option to "skip" them after failing - heart-sinkingly annoying.  Maybe remove the monsters, or allow for a "difficulty level" that makes the games so easy, a child could play it.  Or rather, so easy an adult can play it.  When I heard "mini-game" I thought something simple, like an in-game puzzle game, or whatever.  But no, there's this whole 3D virtual world that I have to QUICKLY interact with, avoid the lava, and oh no, there's a monster that's going to ruin my day in super annoying ways.  Skipping the games feels empty, but the alternative (actually playing them) is worse – much, much worse.
Having said all that, I hope this company makes more games, better games, and takes the time to listen to the customers' consensus and...tweak things a little for the next round.  I'm sure the next one could be awesome.  But please, re-think this mini-game format.

Bardbarian is a somewhat fun game that mixes elements of bullet-hell and tower defense.  The gameplay feels interesting, at first, but lacks more than a few hours of gameplay.  I beat the game on Insane difficulty in about 3 hours.  I have basically everything unlocked and maxed except for a few units (which would require grinding for another hour or so).  Even on Insane difficulty, I found myself standing at the front gate killing enemies before they could even get a single shot off.  Eventually you'd hit a wave / boss that's a brick wall and would require you to die and upgrade (sometimes a few times) before you could pass it.  If the developer could smooth out this progression, it would feel much more exciting to play.
Besides all of the cons I've listed above, the game is some sort of Flash port.  I have a gaming PC, and I get about 3 frames per second on the main title in windowed mode.  In fullscreen mode, the main screen doesn't even load and the game crashes.  I spent the first few hours after purchasing this game trying to solve this problem.  The game is littered with other bugs as well.
I would avoid this game, personally, but if you like grindy games, I suppose I could recommend it at $1 or in a bundle somewhere.

WHAT DO THE MINI-GAMES IN CRADLE FEEL LIKE? ...SEE END OF REVIEW.
NOTE: This is actually a "Not Recommended" review despite the "thumbs up".
PRO: Looks great. Interesting story. Amazing music, beginning to end.
CONS: Mini-games, Unskippable mini-games, Lengthy unskippable mini-games, Repetitive lengthy unskippable mini-games. Incongruous repetitive lengthy unskippable mini-games.  Extremely incongruous repetitive lengthy unskippable mini-games.  Also, mini-games.
PERSONAL GRIPES: Game struggled on a system that flew through Mad Max, Batman: Arkham Whatever, etc., Important items obfuscated/difficult to identify.  Prefer text only for dialogue, no need for voiceover/dialogue/actors, that way I can choose to continue at my own pace... as it stands, even if i've already read the paragraph, i still feel obligated to let the actor finish, Once the setting gets toward dusk, the painted sky looks completely cartoony in art style compared to the rest of the game and the other times of day (which look amazing, especially the constellations at night - actually gave me goosebumps)

However, in reality, the mini-games are such a poor choice that they really do take a 5/5 game and drop it straight down to a "not recommended" but since, as mentioned, I would like to see more from this developer about this universe, that I changed my rec to thumbs up (while still vehemently protesting against the mini-games).  Please note that I am not exaggerating when I describe how deplorable these mini-games are.  Imagine playing Myst for the very first time... you get about 20 mins in and you cannot believe how amazing everything looks and sounds and the pacing is awesome and you are trying to just wrap your head around everything and right then, right when you are about to have some epiphany, someone SMASHES the keyboard on your desk and SHOVES a nintendo controller in your face and says HEY YOU!!! DRIVE ! DRIVE!!!!!.... (18 laps later, 12 laps to go!)... DRIVE !!! DRIVE !!! !DRIVE! !!  ! ! DRIVE !!! (8 laps later, 4 laps still left!) DRIVE!!! DRIVE !!! DRIVE !!!!! Cradle is a tough one. It's one of those types of games that can be quite immersive, but unfortunately is plagued by several shortcomings.
It is generally a good looking game, but the FOV is bad for many.* And while the performance is good for a low-action game, the engine often feels poorly optimized.
The keys can't be rebound, and the arrow keys do not dupe the WSAD keys. Lefty hate again.*
The "Key Features" descriptions  are a little over-enthusiastic, especially about the mini-GAME (as in there's only one). It's repeated a couple times too many, varying only slightly each time (at least one of its modes is easier to beat).
The story and lore is absolutely fantastic, but the presentation feels disjointed. It would have been so much nicer if there was an in-game journal that collected everything you read, so you can go back and read it any time you want to understand things better. And the way the game ends makes it feel like chapter 1 of a series, but apparently the story is self-contained and resolved.
All in all, Cradle is still a recommended experience for those who love this type of game.

Ever played Assassin's Creed? Remember how the loading screens are little animus-voids where you can just run around in circles for a bit while the game loads properly? That's basically what this game feels like.
It's the exciting tale of a man walking into a restaurant and then walking out 90 minutes later with a slightly bigger belly, and I almost feel compelled to put down a spoiler warning there because it's practically a perfect metaphor for the plot, as much as you can say that there is a plot.
Credit where credit is due, the world building is very nicely done, the city feels alive with all the wildlife and looks impressive under the various weathers the game cycles through. The city itself is definitely the most interesting character, it's just a shame that they put all this effort into crafting such a beautiful setting but then they forgot to put anything to do in it.
There's no gameplay here, unless holding W counts as gameplay now. You sail to a building then climb the building to reach a crate at the top that contains a permission slip to go and climb another building. Repeat 8 times and the game is over.
I know the focus isn't meant to be on the gameplay here, but it's quite obvious the developers misunderstood that once you remove the need for gameplay, you need to up your game everywhere else. They did great on the world building, but I get the impression they did the storyboarding during a bring your daughter to work day, because it feels like it was written by an 8 year old. I won't go into details for obvious spoiler warnings, but the restaurant analogy really is apt for this one.
You'd also be forgiven for thinking that a game with no gameplay would be well polished in other departments, but it's really not. Textures look good from afar but when staring them down during one of the lengthy building climbs they just devolve into a horribly pallid brown mess, and for a game that gets mileage out of its visuals it sure does detract from the overall beauty of the setting. Not to mention the stoic animations that make the characters feel like androids.
I feel sorry for anyone who had to spend £15 on this, even at £1.50 I felt a little ripped off. If for some reason you're actually interested in buying this, do yourself a favour and just read the plot synopsis online, and keep that money for a Mars bar or something

I'm really not sure whether to recommend this or not... I've played Jet Set Radio Future before, which was great, and on the surface this seems just as good – it's got the charming cel-shaded graphics, cool levels and a great soundtrack. But the gameplay is just really frustrating. First off, it's really difficult to control your character, you can never seem to get where you'd want to. Secondly, it feels like you never have enough speed to do anything – you constantly bump into something, which kills your momentum, and you can forget grinding upwards; just get used to slowly walking the stairs. That wastes a lot of time, and of course there's a time limit. The spray cans seem pretty scarce, too, and the graffiti prompt doesn't seem to pop up very easily.
With a bit of practice though, you can get a feel for the controls, and the game does have some fun moments when you manage to complete missions. But the missions get pretty hard fast, and it becomes more frustrating than fun.
So overall, I have mixed feelings... It would be a great game if it wasn't so difficult and clumsy. But maybe I'm just bad at it, maybe others have more patience to play it. I guess I'll recommend it with caution.

I Might Need Rehabilitation
...when this game is released.
The mechanics of the fighting in this game are VERY in depth for the few number of actual button inputs given. Q, Space, Shift, WADS, Right click, Left click. Besides options/load/menu/creation keys, this is all you need and Q is only used for items (only weapons right now?). But the number of actions you can perform is very deep. You can jump, flip, jump off walls, FLIP off walls, roll, duck, low kick, punch, straight kick, roundhouse kick, passive block, active block (just guard), throw, escape throw, hit them while they’re down, FLYING JUMP KICK, attack with weapons, THROW WEAPONS, climb walls, save fall, roll from fall, sneak grab choke hold, move bodies, roll to pick up weapons faster, catch weapons in mid air after they’ve been thrown at you..I may have missed some actions...but these things combined, with so few buttons, creates a VERY intense skill cap. Multiplayer, which has already started implementation in the form of a special 1 screen game mode (with split screen option even), will be very fierce and competitive right out of the gate. The fighting mechanics take about an hour to get used to. The hand to hand mechanics, after 8+ hours of gameplay, I still haven’t mastered. The weapons mechanics are an enigma to me. The AI actually fights intelligently and will give you a consistent challenge. I could sit here and train for hours, which I have...if the game wasn’t crashing every 30 or so minutes.
It IS after all just in alpha, so this is to be expected. Surprisingly few crashes with that in mind. But they will have to be smoothed out before release.
This game is so shiny, I need sunglasses.
I’ve mentioned this multiple times, it’s in alpha, but it LOOKS and FEELS like a full scale production game, but it’s only worked on by 4 people, bug reporters notwithstanding. However if you ever watch a video, you can see a character’s torso move around… you may think “oh that’s cool it bobs and weaves”. What you are actually seeing is a direct reflection (with very little latency) of the WADS keys being pressed. The feet are simply following along with what the body is wanting to do. And while this is not exactly proportional to real physics, it is very good to have in a game where you need to be exactly where you want to be as soon as possible, and that is what determines how close you ACTUALLY are to your opponent/wall/objective.
The ragdolls are absolutely adorable to watch. Dying is actually fun because of that. Hitting someone at just the right time before they kick the bucket can result in them being sent reeling across the fighting area. It’s rather comical, yet heartwarming at the same time. The game is an absolute gem of quality workmanship and the people working on it deserve a very special recognition for that. KUDOS and BRAVO to them. The game FEELS alive, it LOOKS alive, I mentioned the blood in the addiction factor section. It’s such a well made game, even though, ONCE AGAIN, it crashes frequently.
If this game were a human, it would be a woman. That’s how complex it is.
I don’t even need to go into detail about the complexity of the game as it had to be mentioned in the addiction section due to the high skill cap bringing back for more.
There is also a scripting and level editing mode. Scripting is done through .xml files and level editing is done right in the game itself, including placing actors/objects.
However, it’s only downfall in this topic right now would be...you guessed it...it’s lack of content. The game itself is great, but it’s not a game yet, but I can’t wait to see it when it’s done. I will be following this game for the next few years to come and you should too.
Summary
Overgrowth is a fun game. The alpha costs money, but even so, it’s worth it. You will get hours of entertainment out of this game and the single system multiplayer is great in itself.
Buy this game if you love developing your skills, violence and parkour.

Agatha Christie really was the queen of crime, and I've enjoyed the PC games fashioned after her novels over the years.
While it doesn't hold a candle to the older 'And Then there were None', I enjoyed the interactive mystery and being behind the working grey cells of the infamous Hercule Poirot.
Graphics are decently impressive and of course remind of an English style golden-age mystery.
Point and click becomes second nature, although I did get tired of observing people.
Clever puzzles are clever puzzles but sometimes they go from ridiculously hard (like the turntable) to short and easy.
I adored the fact that they put in the amusing bald joke regarding Hastings from the novel, although seeing big-game hunter photos wasn't especially endearing.
While I enjoyed the interactive aspects, doing tedious things like walking to the car to leave instead of the game just loading into the next inevitable scene was a chore rather than a charm.
The mystery is clever - I knew it from the book - and it follows it closely.
Agatha Christie fans should get this one for sure, although it's not the best of the lot. I wish they would bring the other Agatha Christie games back, and make news ones while they're at it. The score of the game suits the storyline perfectly. I love you have so many achievements to earn, but was irritated I was still missing ten after finishing the full game.

All in all, it would be nice to see a sequel.

Tengami combines the gameplay of a point-and-click adventure with the visuals of a pop-up book together into one neat, small little package. The keyword here is ‘pop-up book’; does it have the depth of a real pop-up book or does it actually tell a deeper story? Hop on to the next paragraph and read along.

The game starts off almost immediately. You choose New Game (or Continue if you’ve already played, of course) and off you go. You’re first shown a small ‘cinematic’ that shows - not tells - a part of the story and after that you can immediately play and eventually finish the game without almost any interruptions.  And yes, you read that right. The game doesn’t use any speech and just a few lines of text to tell parts of its story, and these lines even feel a bit cryptic.

You only have to control the mouse to control your character. You just click on the ground and your character will walk towards the place you just clicked. If you can interact with an area small, pulsating circles can be seen where you can grab with the mouse and then you can slide it towards a specific direction to show more of the book, or to initiate a puzzle.

The puzzles in general are fairly simple. There were maybe 1 or 2 puzzles that required a bit of attention but other than that these can easily be solved by pretty much anyone.  Especially if you’ve played point-and-click adventures in the past you’ll probably breeze through it all. You can definitely tell that these are aimed at a casual audience. I personally didn’t mind, because the game has a relaxing vibe and it allows you to take your time to do whatever you want. The problem is that there just isn’t enough to do. Except for solving puzzles and traveling through one amazingly, gorgeous looking world there are no side activities or collectibles whatsoever (or anything else for that matter). And since the puzzles don’t offer any real depth and the game is very short this a bit disappointing I have to say. I do admire the developers for focusing purely on the story here, but once you’ve played through this that’s it; you’re done. There’s no incentive to replay this, not even once. On the other side, I know of very little (point-and-click) adventure games that offer any other activities besides solving puzzles and unfolding a story so I can’t really blame it. Therefore, it is excused.
In any case, the puzzles mostly consist of moving pieces of the environment around so that you can pass to the other side or by moving certain objects. It all feels natural and the controls are extremely tight, as is the pathfinding of the character. Bravo for this.
Now, if you’re too lazy to complete a puzzle, or you just need some help because you really can’t figure it out, the game offers a hint system that helps you on your way. Whenever you arrive at an ‘important’ puzzle you can bring up the menu to let the game offer you a hint. It won’t really be necessary for most people, but it’s still good that it’s there and it can still be helpful for the younger players out there.
All in all it’s a very simplistic point-and-click adventure.

This is where Tengami really shines. With beautiful high res art this game looks nothing short of amazing. I have one small nitpick, though and that is that I wish the camera would zoom in a bit more often because the close up intro ‘cinematic’ and the ending look terrific with the brilliant use of colors and the sharp art. Yes, even the colors are sublime. As you can see I can’t praise the graphics enough. Think of Paper Mario with more realistic environments and characters and you have an idea what it looks like.
The audio is very minimalist and has a Japanese vibe to it. It blends in perfectly with the rest of the game and you’ll enjoy it and not get distracted by it. Again, nothing but praise here.

This is the department where the game fails a bit. I managed to finish the game in roughly 90 minutes but I can’t imagine anyone taking over 2 hours to complete it. And let’s face it, that’s short. Sure, it doesn’t overstay its welcome, but it’s a good and cool experience that I wish would last just a tad longer. I’m not necessarily talking content here, but the puzzles could’ve been harder and maybe some more (story related) cinematics to extend it all a bit.

Tengami is a fine little game that’s a fun, but short experience for casual and experienced point-and-click gamers alike. For me personally the quality of the puzzles dragged the game down a bit but it certainly compensated this by providing a more than terrific audiovisual experience. As far as the story is concerned; I don’t think it will blow anyone away, but overall it’s a charming adventure that you should absolutely give a try if you have the money and/or time for it.

Pros:
+ Gorgeous visuals
+ Audio blends in very well with the rest of the game
+ Tight point-and-click adventure gameplay (controls wise)

Mixed:
+/- Casual puzzles are great for beginners/casual players, but not so much for experienced players

Cons:
- On the short side (less than 2 hours)

Before Divinity, RPGs were assumed to have crappy combat.
It was kinda of a given that if you were a sprawling epic adventure, something would have to suffer.  Time and time again combat would draw the short straw.  Even in some of the most beloved RPGs ever made (Baldur's Gate,  Planescape Torment), it's tough to point to the combat as a high point.  At best, it was serviceable.
Divinity's combat is nothing short of incredible.  At its heart is the concept of combining elements to produce effects that are greater than the sum of their parts.  Shooting a character with a lightning bolt might not do much damage, but zapping a pudlde of water could electrify an entire group of powerful enemies, effectively disabling them.  Shooting an arrow at an enemy isn't especially powerful, but placing your character in a tower above the battleground gives massive bonuses to both the range and damage of their arrows.  Divinity gives you a mind boggling number of tactical options, and demands that you use as many of them as possible.  The difficulty is nothing short of punishing.  This is one game where playing on "normal" translates to "hard" and playing on "hard" (tactician mode) translates to "nearly impossible".  And yet, if you take the time to combine spell effects correctly and plan each fight out before it starts you will find yourself victorious more times than not.  Divinity wants you to THINK when you fight.  If you're looking for a mindless dungeon crawler where you can steamroll enemy hordes as soon as you find a +1 weapon, this isn't it.  Gear helps, but it's never enough on its own.  Tactics are king here.
Having said all that, Divinity is more than just great tactical combat.
It also immerses you in its world with a deep narrative, and interesting characters.  The writing is top notch and has a uniquely dark and sarcastic humor.  I can't think of many games that let you have conversations with demonic chickens, or play as a face stealing skeletal mage.
It's a large game, too!  I've sunk about 40 hours into it so far and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface of the world. The amount of exploration that can be done is almost mind boggling, with secrets stuffed in every corner of the map to reward patient and methodical players who (literally) leave no stone unturned. (No, really, you often have to move rocks to find secrets underneath!)
So if all this sounds like I'm gushing,  It's because the game is *that* good.  I will repeat my previous caveat though.  Divinity is HARD.  And I don't mean,  "gee, that was kind of a challenge" hard, I mean Dark Souls "How the ♥♥♥♥ could I possibly win this?" hard.   If you're someone who wants a nice casual stroll through a fantasy world,  this may not be the game for you.

This game has no microtransactions.
Stats-wise, there is absolutely no difference between unpaid and paid players. Every part can be unlocked by unpaid players. Making a one-time purchase(!) for Basic makes them unlock faster and Premium unlocks them all. The paid versions also allow you to save vehicle loadouts.
The mechanics of the game are very impressive. The trade-offs between mobility, defense, speed, stability, and offense seem very well thought-out, although I wish they were better communicated in the buying menu.
Strategy and driving skill play a huge part in this game. Lighter, nimbler vehicles can literally drive circles around heavier opponents, such that the heavy turrets won't rotate quickly enough to keep up, and projectile travel time means that dodging enemy fire is entirely possible at long range. Powerups can quickly tip the scales in favor of players that remember to grab them, and using cover effectively, especially with weapons that have slow rates of fire, can make a world of difference in terms of survivability.
In short, this is a fun, ten-minute vehicle brawler with lots of depth and none of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that plagues many F2P titles. Recommended.

Play this more for its story and puzzle aspects than anything else. Sure, sometimes you wander around for a while looking for items you need because there are no hints as to where stuff is, and the world is kinda small meaning you'll visit the same two places the whole game, but the world is pretty and the visuals are uniquely beautiful.
The story deals with the concept of Neuro-copies and a plague that forces most of mankind into "M-bodies" (embody, get it?). You work to revive your flowerpot android and then the two of you will uncover both of your pasts as well as the history of nearby Gerbera Garden. This game is very story-driven with a LOT of dialogue and text to pay attention to.
Secondary to the story is solving puzzles as well as a platforming "mini" game where you collect blocks. If you're even slightly familiar with Minecraft you'll understand the essence of the mini-games. As for the puzzles, they aren't terribly straightforward but also not ridiculously abstract. Finding items you'll need can take time, but given that your character has amnesia I suppose it makes sense to not really know where things are. For instance, I spent the better part of half an hour looking for roots to grind up to put in my bird soup only to find them right outside the front door.
Lastly, there are some flaws with how some story stuff doesn't appear to tie together at the end. Keep in mind it is entirely possible that I forgot some stuff because playing games on Ambien causes me to forget a LOT. Anyways, I imagine that the pieces I missed are probably actually there in the form of text items I missed. In fact, there is a LOT of flavor text. There is a bit of a problem discerning which pieces of text are "flavor" and which are "main ingredients" at times though.
Anyways, if you want something with a good story, is fairly short (Maybe 4-6 hours including stumbling around looking for roots which are right outside the front door), has a nice puzzle aspect, and doesn't like quite like anything else I've ever seen; get this game. Just keep in mind there are a few flaws, some of which will get annoying (Like not knowing the roots are actually super close-by). At the very least, get this game on sale, but for the most part it's worth its price

This game really requires you to dive in and invest in exploring and learning about the world itself. If you're not ready for that, you'll get a quick game filled with annoying time wasting puzzles (learned after the fact they could be skipped, but didn't mind them too much).

The additional content is definitely worth the extra $5.

Full disclosure here, I'm really involved with Awesomenauts. I've met the developers, Ronimo, in person more than twice and have been contracted to do work for them. I've cast tournament events in a professional capacity, wrote and recorded an in-game announcer, earned a "Golden Duck" (the Ronimo community award), and attribute any real success of my YouTube channel to Awesomenauts and the community that surrounds it. Awesomenauts is my single most played game of all time, sitting at 2800+ hours at the time of this writing, and has been a core part of my life for over 5 years. I've bought the game and the old expansions for myself and several friends, and contributed to their Starstorm Kickstarter for $162, and have bought most of the cosmetic skins available. With that said, let's continue.
Awesomenauts is what happens when you take the guts of a 2D platformer, put them inside a MOBA framework, and present it with all the energy and enthusiasm and 80's Saturday morning cartoon can muster. Awesomenauts is fast, frenetic, and easy to pick up while being deep enough to warrant hundreds of hours of gameplay.
Awesomenauts controls like a 2D action platformer.  You jump and shoot, though every character, or Awesomenaut, is a unique expression of the genre. Most walk, but some have multiple jumps, flutter, and others outright fly to name just a couple of mobility options. All of their attacks and abilities differ as well, and the cast features everything from cowboy blasters and oversized rocket launchers to time vortexes, nuclear explosions, and black holes. Every single character of the 30+ roster is a unique experience in its own right, and offers a huge amount of variety to players looking for longterm investment in the game. This is especially true when you can combine different abilities and attacks to create devastating combinations and effective strategies.
The goal of the game is to destroy the enemy team's core. Doing this means fighting your way through base defenses, waves of drones, and the enemy Awesomenauts themselves. This last one is where the game's 2D platforming mechanics really shine. Certain characters are stellar chasers capable of quick, responsive platforming, while others are slow and have lousy jumps. Chasing and being chased around a level in Awesomenauts is a thrilling experience.
During a match, players earn 2 resources: solar and experience. Solar is the individual means of improving your character. Killing enemies and destroying turrets earns solar for every team member. Solar can also be picked up off the ground from collecting coloured cubes that dot the landscape or from dead drones. Solar can be spent on upgrades back at your base, which can increase everything from the damage dealt by an ability or the health of the player to more unique effects such as reflecting projectiles or creating exploding cocoons.
Experience is gained as a team, like in Heroes of the Storm. Every point you collect by completing objectives goes towards the team's level, where higher levels passively increase the team's damage dealt and health bar. This system conditions players to stay out in the field longer, which leads to them helping team mates and pushing out enemy drone waves: excellent habits to have. Team experience doesn't fix the "bad player♥♥♥♥♥♥game" symptom of MOBAs, but good teams can boost a weaker player into a position where that player can be effective and participate while also dampening the effect of a player who's very skilled comparatively. This results in more even games for most.
Awesomenauts, now being free to play, features a typical meta-game progression that is very similar to how Heroes of the Storm's system works, including a meta currency, account levels, character levels, and so on. None of this is particularly new, but it's worth mentioning that Awesomenauts' tutorial system grants enough meta-currency that players can acquire at least 1 character once they're done the tutorial quests. They don’t have to choose blindly either; the armory gives players the chance to try a character before buying. If players want access to all the characters, Awesomenauts borrows a page from SMITE's book and allows consumers to buy the "All-Nauts pack," which grants access to all the Awesomenauts available now and in the future.
Cosmetics are difficult to come by. Aside from account portraits and drop pod skins, Awesomepoints can only buy new characters. The majority of character skins and announcers are only acquirable through real money purchases. Even though skins and announcers purely cosmetic, the Awesomenauts experience is definitely less without them; reason being, the cosmetics are fantastic. The announcers are full of character and inject each game with a completely different feel. Some are laugh out loud hilarious, while others offer a more serious approach. The skins are even more interesting; basic skins simply reskin a character, but the legendary skins replace art, voice work, and even character themes entirely without sacrificing their identity.
Still, the base game experience is a treat for the eyes and ears. The characters are well animated and fun to listen to. Characters even have their own unique theme music and killing spree, which helps convey their personalities better than any skin available in the store. The levels you blast your way through are hand drawn, meticulously put together, and have plenty of little touches that add life to the worlds you fight over.
Still, Awesomenauts isn’t perfect. For instance, the presentation of menus is not the best. Unintuitive interfaces and burried menu options are not clearly explained or shown, meaning that players will likely get lost trying to find the options they're looking for. Nothing shows this more than the muting and reporting system. Muting a player shouldn't take more than 1 click to do and should be dead simple. This is not the case; It takes at least 3 clicks and one drop-down menu to mute and report someone, which is 2 clicks too long when I'm rushed, angry, or otherwise upset and want to get rid of the problem quickly.
Awesomenauts is also online-only. There's no way to play the game without an internet connection, even if all you want to do is play against bots. This is not a design decision Ronimo will turn back on, unfortunately, even if it makes sense considering the difficulty of making an effective free to play game that is offline able. It's mostly disappointing because Awesomenauts used to have an offline mode before it went free to play, which I found useful on occasion in the past when I'd be traveling or out someplace remote.
For those looking for more from Awesomenauts, the game has two additional features that expand on the game immensely; custom games and a level editor. The level editor is incredibly powerful and allows players to make all kinds of maps and game types, including platform racing, tower defense maps, and small character campaigns. These maps can be played in custom games, which offer a huge amount of control to players. A huge number of settings can be tweaked, including solar gain, respawn times, creep spawn rates, or spawning a solar boss anytime a player dies. Since all of these work within the Steam Workshop, it's an easy matter to subscribe to new maps and modes you can use whenever you like.
All in all, Awesomenauts has 3 things I absolutely love; the 2D mechanics are fun and well designed, they add a still unique take on a MOBA (which is a genre I love), and the game presentation is without compare. Despite the issues present within any multiplayer game, unfortunate offline incompatibility, and some unintuitive interface issues, Awesomenauts has been my go to game for 5 years. It does a better job of making MOBAs accessible than any other MOBA on the market, triple A or otherwise, while still providing a deeply engaging game for committed players.

It took nine years to make the tools for creating a great game, but this "game" was made in less than six months.
Even though this game is a HUGE disappointment, there are some aspects that I can't help but admire:
+The game looks great.
+The game's controls are tight and responsive.
+Whenever you fight and you know what the ♥♥♥♥ you are doing, (and you don't abuse the jump kick)
the combat is quite fluid, engaging, and spectacular for the most part.
+The art assets genuinely had a great amount of passion and love put into them.
+The procedural animations featured in this game are awesome and they are a significant techinical feat at least for me.
+The sound design is rather unappreciated, as every bone cracking and blood gushing sound effect felt very chilling.
+The soundtrack was very pleasant and complemented the art style and tone of the game beautifully.
Every part of this game except for the game itself are all crafted beautifully.
HOWEVER, the levels are pathetic.
-The levels feel like they were designed by an artist, and not a level designer. (That's really the case though. :P)
-The campaign is WAY too short obviously. I literally finished the game in one sitting in about four hours.
-The Lugaru campaign is only a FRACTION of the Overgrowth campaign. I finished it in about 35 minutes on my first try without ever even playing the original Lugaru.
-The game is still somewhat buggy and crashy. Allegedly, many other people are suffering bugs that prevent the game from starting.
-You can literally kill the last boss in the game with one single air kick. Sometimes, he can even jump out a window and kill himself!
-The entire narrative feels very amateurish to me, almost as if a middle schooler wrote it. The story went by way too quickly for me to have any emotional attachment to any character in the game.
-Many of the platform sections in this game are essentially trial and error. Particularly in the ice cliff platforming segment, I was lost throughout the latter half and I died many times as a result. That was very frustrating to say the least.
I have MANY more gripes that I don't even begin to feel like typing.
This game had way too much potential to end up the way it does now. I feel like that if the game had just sat in the Early Access oven for at the very least another year, I feel that this game could have been something very special.
That is a damn shame, because when the game wasn't being bogged down by an overwhelmingly lackluster campaign, I was having a blast.

Baldur's Gate - A 16 year old game stands up to the test of time, and it's co-op!
So during the steam summer sale, a friend of mine bought me Baldur's Gate 1(Enhanced Edition) so we could play together(the 4 pack was 20 bucks). 6 months later, we had never played together once so I finally decided that I wanted to play, so I played it solo.
Now there's a few things you should know about Baldur's Gate. The game was originally released in 1998. I played it while I was in high school my senior year. It introduced a LOT of new people to Dungeons & Dragons. It's a 3rd person isometric RPG in which you control all members of your party. It's paused based(instead of turn based), which means that when combat starts, you pause, issue commands, unpause, wait for something to happen, pause again, issue commands, etc, etc. There are lots of games with that type of system now, but as far as I know, BG was the first.
So the way you're -supposed- to play it solo is to create one character and go along recruiting AI NPCs to join your party of up to six. Well you can get around all that by playing in multiplayer mode by yourself. Multiplayer mode lets you create all six party members and tweak them to your desire. You can also export/import different characters at any time. You can easily get away with this from an RP(roleplaying) perspective by saving your game in an inn and swapping party members in and out saying "Oh I met this guy at this inn". So to start with, I created my own party of 3: Human Fighter(me), Paladin, and Cleric, then I pick up NPCs along the way. Not completely satisfied with the NPCs in game, I finished the game with 5/6 party members self generated, and only one in-game NPC(Yeslick the Dwarven Fighter/Cleric). If you enjoy character creation and tweaking things and micromanaging party members, gear, stats, and other RPG elements, this game is definately for you.
Lets talk about the story. This is where the game really drew a lot of people in. For those of you that have already played, you know what I'm talking about. I'm not going to spoil it for anyone that may play the game in the future(even if it IS 16 years old), but it's a great, great story that lets you choose your own path. Of course my path is that of the good soldier fighting for... well... good. But if you enjoy the darker side of things, it's always allowed, which a lot of games give you trouble doing. You can lie, cheat, steal, and murder and still complete the game.
Oftentimes now that I'm in my 3rd decade of life, I've gone back and tried to play games from my childhood that I remember really enjoying, and graphically none of them have stood up to the test of time(X-Com, Doom, etc). Since all of the assets in BG are more or less hand drawn and the enhanced edition lets you play at your native resolution, the game still looks pretty damn good, especially amidst the recent indy dev 8 bit gaming boom. So graphically, it passes the test. The environments are pretty freakin cool too. A whole lot of unique, hand drawn areas that I had forgotten about since I first played a long time ago that made me say "huh, cool" when I came across them recently.
And now let's talk difficulty. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this game hard. It's been so long since I've played a game that didn't just blatantly hold my hand and coddle me the whole way through I'd forgotten what it's like to play a game that punishes you. AD&D 2.0 core rules are a huge ♥♥♥♥♥ and completely unforgiving. There are 5 difficulty levels in the game:
-Easy - Everything does half damage, all hit point gains per level are maximized, and characters can't permanently die.
- Normal - Everything does 75% damage, all hit point gains per level are maximized, and characters can't permanently die.
- Core Rules - Everything does 100% damage, hit point gains are randomized(so you can get as little as 1 hp/level on your badass front-line fighter that needs ~10 hp/level), and characters can permanently die.
- Hard - Everything does 150% damage
- Insane - Everything does 200% damage and you are a satan worshipping masochist
I may have added that last little part on the insane bit.
So being the badass gaming veteran I am, I of course choose Core Rules. I understand what THAC0 is, I know what the different classes are, I know how to D&D. I'm good.
Or so I thought.
I'm actually not as good as I had thought. I had to do a LOT of fights multiple times because Jesus Christ, this game can be hard. Mostly with the crowd control abilities the enemies get(note - If you fight against a group that has a mage, KEEP YOUR PARTY SPREAD OUT just like in ArmA). A lot of times I'd get hit with an AoE fear or confuse or stun, etc, etc, etc. It could be infuriating, but I kept re-loading and going at the fights in different manners from different angles, and analyzing my party and their abilities and switching things around until finally, at the end of the game, I had SOME sort of idea of what I was doing... I thought... until the final battle.
Let's just say that the final battle in Baldur's Gate had me curled up in a fetal position in the corner of my room praying to Torm asking him what I had done so poorly to have been punished so badly.
So somewhere between 20 and 50 attempts later, I managed to defeat the final boss and win the game. I even had to google strategies for the final boss. I actually felt a sense of accomplishment like I haven't felt in a game in a long, long time. The funny part is, 17 year old me beat the game in 1998 without the internet for guidance. I have NO CLUE how I managed that feat.
So I immediately went to steam and bought Baldur's Gate 2 enhanced edition, even though it's not on sale, and started a new game. This time, however, I'm playing on normal mode. It seems to be a much better balance of playability vs difficulty. I've still lost some fights, but I've learned a whole damn lot and built my party around the strengths needed.
I have a Cavalier paladin because he: 1. Can't be feared, charmed, mind controller, or poisoned; and 2. He can make the entire party immune to fear pretty much all the time. He's also a badass tank alongside my main character which is a frontline fully maximized fighter with sword and shield. I also have a pure Dwarven Cleric, Fighter/Thief, Fighter/Mage, and Dragon Disciple Sorcerer. I dual classed the Thief and Mage with Fighter bases so they could use longbows for good DPS instead of being relegated to a shortbow and a sling. The nice side to that is that they get fighter HP for their first 7 levels so they're pretty beefy on top of it all.
I just pretend(roleplay) that my entire group is a squad of trained military soldiers that have been sent on a mission, so they almost all have that base fighter class from their military training.
So I have 2 tanks(FIghter/Cavalier Paladin), a pure healing Cleric, and 3 pure DPS(Thief/Mage/Sorcerer). But don't be fooled, that fighter and paladin can put out some melee hurt too. The cleric is really the only non-dps class. Oh... Make sure you -always- have a thief in your party with the script that makes him passively detect traps. Trust me on this. You don't necessarily need a thief/rogue that can stealth, but you damn sure need one that can detect/disarm traps and pick locks.
And on that note, there are pre-set scripts that you can use for each character. There are about 20 for all the different classes in the game to mess around with. I pretty much have my whole group on the standard "I see an enemy and attack with my equipped weapon", except for my rogue, who is set to always passively detect traps when not in combat, and my cleric who is set to dynamically run around and heal. I micromanage everything else(mage spells mostly).

Baldur's Gate 2 EE is frequently (but not always) given the crown for best of the classic isometric Forgotten Realms RPGs, and that reputation is well deserved. With a dark and provacative main story arc, the ability to play as both good and evil with alignment-appropriate companions, side quests with enough content to rival main quests in other games, compelling companions with deep stories, and a RTwP (real time w/ pause) combat system that manages to make combat both chaotic and strategic - BG2EE should be a slam-dunk recommend. Unfortunately the game does have flaws, and I'll use this review to detail these weaknesses so that users on the fence can make an informed decision before buying.

BG2EE owes much of its incredible story to the environment in which its set. The Dungeons and Dragons universe is rich with both lore and mechanics. While the game unarguably benefits from the rich lore, the same cannot be said of the mechanics. The AD&D ruleset, cumbersome and obtuse even in its time during pen and paper play, is a harsh ruleset for a PC RPG.
New players will need to spend a substantial amount of time learning about AC, THAC0, weapon proficiences, Ability Score modifiers, weapon enchantment levels, combat protection spells, spell protection spells, various dispels, and so much more. Diving into the game without a basic understanding of these rules will almost certainly lead to a 'gimped' charachter and near-guaranteed slaughter by certain encounters.
The need for an intimate understanding of the rulesets is made worse by the choices the developers made in crafting companions. Your companions, while having emotionally compelling stories that draw you deeply into the game, will join your party with weapon profeciencies and leveling decisions that are questionable (at best). My recommendation on this is to download EEKeeper and use it to tweak your companions' weapon proficiencies. Problem solved, so long as you have the dicipline to not break the game by boosting instead of tweaking.
You'll find another flaw with BG2EE when you examine how the story is balanced. Completionists (as I imagine most hardcore RPG players looking at this title are) will want to complete all available sidequests before advancing to the next main story chapter. In BG1EE, this worked fine. Every chapter unlocked additional sidequests in a relatively steady flow. Not so in BG2EE. You'll step out of the introductory dungeon with the vast majority of the game's sidequests front loaded. Literally dozens of hours of deep, rich content that will you keep you enthralled for days before you even touch the main quest.
Normally this wouldn't be an issue, and most would consider it a good thing, except the main story arc's hook is to remove from play one of your best (imo) companion choices. This made party selection more difficult than it needed to be, at least for me.
To wrap this review up, which has now become my longest review to date, I'll say this:
If you're willing to play the prequel and immerse yourself in the story and willing to take the time to learn the mechanics, plan out your party choices, and use EEKeeper to  tweak those companions - Baldur's Gate 2 EE will be guaranteed to be one of your most unforgetable gaming experiences. If not, you're still likely to have a great time, but the experience may be tainted by frustration and confusion.

Cradle is an interesting game along the lines of Gone Home or Dear Esther - you are unfolding a story as you progress. You will solve some not overly complicated puzzles to advance the story.
The atmosphere in the game world is hauntingly beautiful.  The lighting, music, dialogue - everything is perfectly honed to create a sense of eerie sadness and mystery.  I personally loved the slower pace of the game, it was fun for me to try to uncover information as to what has happened in this world.
The mini games were ok, a little tedious and you can skip them if you fail with no repercussions on the storyline.

Keen Stalker fans will recognize some similar themes here, experiments on conciousness and contaminated zones, you can see the loose influence the Stalker franchise has had here, having some ex-Stalker devs working on it.
The ending may seem abrupt but if you pay attention to the dialogue throughout, and the clues scattered around your home, it makes more sense than if you skip through a lot of the details.
