Cradle is terrible. I mean, it's honestly great, but the terrible parts are so bad that it ruins the entire experience. Read on...
The base game - that is to say the stuff you spend 90% of your time actually doing - is fantastic. It takes place in the Mongolian Steppe, a location pretty much otherwise unknown in videogames. It's beautiful and quiet, sort of mysterious and sad. There's this strange plot line you need to unravel and it's kind of like a weird eastern European Myst. It's amazing.
Then.... Then you get to the minigame "puzzles" you must solve to move the plot forward. Simply put, these are some of the worst puzzles ever designed for a videogame. Ever. They're extremely difficult, totally outside the graphical / aesthetic design sensibilites of the rest of the game and they feel tacked more tacked on than the boss fights in Deus Ex. The designers of the game know, in fact, that you most likely won't be able to finish these puzzles -- they're that unfair. After you lose, you have an option to skip them entirely. But losing takes, like, 5-10 minutes each time. And there are probably 6-7 of these "puzzles".
That's the thing about Cradle. It's like a perfectly designed meal, with beautiful and intriguing flavors and textures, except every ten minutes someone comes out and throws up all over your food. That would ruin the meal and, similarly, it ruins this game.

You're going to hear the same people, but they won't be saying the same things in the same way, and that personality helps to bring the world to life in ways that aren't simply technological. Oblivion may be less handsome than its successor, Skyrim, but it excels by giving you a more colorful, interesting swath of country to explore. Spring for the Deluxe Edition, too. Bardbarian is a casual action game with hints of tower defense. I wasn't a huge fan of the game's cartoonish look, but tower defense is my favorite casual genre of game, and I go out of my way to try any game of the genre, whether it claims to add something new or not.
Bardbarian is fun in doses, but it quickly wears out its welcome. It adds something new to the tower defense genre, which is the fact that your "towers" are various characters that you can upgrade and you can influence their actions using music. You also have no stationary units (other than a full upgrade later on in the game where you can have units defend from on top of two buildings), and you are in charge of moving to the enemies and killing them off before they get close to your town center. While this is a new take on the genre, I didn't find that it added much enjoyment gameplay-wise, and in many cases, it turned out to be frustrating. You essentially have three entrances where enemies spawn, and the screen isn't large enough to cover the entire "field", so it's easy to be focusing on defeating enemies on one side of the screen and completely miss enemies coming through on the other side, because they are not visible on screen but only on the mini-map.
One of my favorite things about the tower defense genre is conquering maps and moving onto new challenging maps, and figuring out the best strategies for handling the routes enemies would take. Unfortunately, Bardbarian has one map, and one map only. It's understandable, in a way, because your towers are not stationary, so therefore new maps wouldn't be necessary. However, the game quickly becomes dull and repetitive because your surroundings are never changing. To add insult to injury, this game is one of the biggest grindfests I've ever played. Reading other reviews that state it was developed for phones now that I've played the game makes total sense, because this game sure does play like a phone game. Expect to play the same levels and waves of enemies over and over and over and over in order to save enough gold to buy even some of the most basic upgrades. Also, there are 20 waves of enemies, total, in the game. 20 waves TOTAL, which is equal to about one or two maps in most other tower defense games. The game only saves your level progress at every five levels, so if you don't beat the boss at the ends of levels 5, 10, 15, and 20, don't expect to start back on the level you died on. You have to go all the way back to the beginning of that "section" to try again.
Another issue I find with the game is the fact that your units are so easily killed, even when fully upgraded. Playing through a grindfest of a game to save enough for certain upgrades can be somewhat justified if those upgrades make the player feel as if it was worth it, but upgrading anything--anything, from the Barbarian's own health to his units or the town itself--feels ultimately underwhelming.
The game also sports a survival mode (with one map to choose from) and an escape mode (one map). Both are ways to post high scores, add small value to the game, and potentially make a little extra gold. Survival mode is fun for a few tries, but escape wasn't really my cup of tea.
In summary, I began this review with the intention on giving the game a "recommended, but only on sale for $2.00 or less," but the more I thought about the game to write this, the more I realized I couldn't justify recommending it. In the end, it's up to you to decide, but I implore those fellow tower defense fans out there to find a different game of the genre to try. Bardbarian removes more enjoyment from the genre than it adds, and to be completely honest, it's possible that tagging this game as tower defense does it an injustice, because I went into this game wanting something that I ultimately did not get. Bardbarian can be fun, but it plays like an action casual phone or online Flash game. If you are willing to pay to purchase it with that in mind, you probably won't be disappointed. Otherwise, I'm sorry, but I cannot recommend this.

This review is from a perspective of of someone who did not read the book and only watched a few episodes of Agatha Christie's Poirot television series. At the time this review was written I have finished the game once.
Agatha Christie - The ABC Murders is a criminal investigation point and click adventure game. It is based on the book and the television series. The game feels very much like you're watching one of the episodes so you may want this game if you're a fan of Poirot. Other than that it's a easy small point and click adventure with an interesting story. Perhaps too easy and short for some but sometimes you don't really want a difficult game.
+ Feels like a television episode
+ The puzzles are not too hard to understand
+ There are many guides so you don't get stuck
- There are a few repeated tasks
- The character slow pace is somewhat annoying
- Perhaps too easy for some people
- Somewhat short
- No easy way to clear all achievements
When you start this game you will immediately notice that it is very similar to the television show. The characters look the same and the voice actors are identical. You control Hercule Poirot, a fairly conventional but very efficient detective with many peculiarities. You are investigating the case of a killer who leaves A.B.C. railway guide as it's signature.
This game is basically a point and click adventure. You will be looking for clues, solving puzzles and making questions to other people. It is an easy game. You never really lose and there are lots of tips on what you have to do next. You have a counter of how many clues are left for you to check, a list of missions objectives, main menu "I give up" tips and so on. The puzzles are also fairly easy and include opening complex boxes or completing a clue graph. Sometimes you even have to think as brute force often solves some puzzles. Some people like this formula while others not so much.
The main attraction of this game is perhaps the atmosphere and this game in my opinion does it very well. The characters although in cartoon style look, act and sound very similar to the television show. The backgrounds are visually appealing and the music helps get you into the game. It's a very polished game in that regard.
There are some small issues. Poirot is somewhat annoyingly slow but since the maps are small it's not a big deal. There are some funny bugs like being able to move Poirot while checking clues or infinite spin when leaving a clue. The game is also small and I haven't found much of a reason to replay the game. There's no real easy way to complete all achievements.
I like the game even it's small and easy especially due to the story and atmosphere. Of course your mileage may vary and there's really only one way to find out.

I have been following Gear Up since I first saw it on Greenlight.  It actually caught my eye because it looked like a fun, generic tank game.  So I signed up for alpha, and months later the developers handed out keys for Premium to existing testers.  That's how I ended up with a paid copy of early access to a generic tank game, and have in the process found it to be substantially more.
To be honest, there's really only so much you can expect from this type of game.  It's not going to have photo-realistic graphics, or perfect part-balancing; especially in its early stages.  But for what it is, it really is quite fun.  Even though it has a leveling/ranking system, I don't really need incentive of any kind to keep playing it.  You just sit down with your favorite build and blow things up.
While that would be reason enough to give this game a simple thumbs up, I feel that I should say something about the maps.  Maybe it's just me, but the maps are really something else.  I get so excited whenever I see that the developers have put another map in, because the maps are a blast to explore.  You can tell that they put a lot of work into each one; and I'm glad that they did, because for all of the FPS-ish games I've played (which isn't many, admittedly), none had maps that had as much character to them as these.  Whenever I join a game and we cycle through each round, I find myself saying, "Oh, I love this map!" ...for every single map.
Speaking of the developers, though, they've been rather active in the... err, development of the game.  I still see changelogs pop up in my activity feed from time to time, which although relatively infrequent do tend to boast a lot of changes with each new update.  And it's fun to see them playing the game so much.  In fact, I almost feel like I have a rivalry with Jesper.  My speed jets and shotgun will blast his silly little hovercraft to the junk pile over and over again.
But yeah.  Fun game.  The developers have been working hard on it for a long time, and their work deserves a thumbs up.

An excellent example of a free to play game. It's got a bit of a learning curve, but if you stick with it and you like a game with a grind, this might be for you. I repeat... this game is a grind and you'll be doing many of the same things over and over.
As of this review, I'm 96 hours into the game and haven't even reached the end game content. Not even close. Considering how long this game has been out, it's nice to see the devs still adding content so often. It seems Digital Extremes really care about their game as well as the game's community.
So what actually is Warframe? I think it's best described as a 3rd person space ninja action RPG simulator. I think that description is borderline a meme at this point, but it's accurate. You'll go through various missions with different space ninjas collecting components, experience, and killing many things. If you like the combat of the game, you'll probably stick with it. It's very good at making you feel like a powerful, fast badass as you mow down your enemies.
So in conclusion, give this game a try if you like action games or games with some RPG elements. After all it is free and try not to be too intimidated when you first start. There's a lot to take in, but the community is very helpful.

I can't decide if this game is my number 1 favorite game of all time, or just 2nd place. There are so many positive things to say almost no bad.
If you like D&D and/or tactical RPG's, you'll love it. It's basically 2nd edition D&D placed into a video game. The quests are fun and interesting, the tactical combat is satisfying and engaging, and the characters feel real. The plot of the main storyline is very smooth, well-paced, and highly immersive. Not to mention really cool.
I could go on all day about it, but you could easily read anything I would say on a review of the original game. Instead, I'm going to adress the differences between this Enhanced Edition and the original.
1. Praise to lord you can actually play the game again. The original had a nasty habit of not working with newer computers. You had to be a computer expert to get it to work, and even then it was unlikely. Until this came out, I feared I would never play it again.
2. The graphics are highly improved. You can run it in double the resoloution of the original. No more blurry combat and squinting hard at the screen through a grainy and pixelated mess.
3. There is a lot new content for this game. There are 4 new party members, and each has their own quest associated with them. And that goes for both SoA and ToB, so that is 8 new missions and 4 new party members.
4. While still a little bit buggy, it's much less buggy than the original. And it's nothing you can't fix with the console commands.
Some people don't think it's worth 25 dollars. I say thats a bargain. You get to play a game that hasn't been working for a decade and is also vastly improved, indulge your nostalgia, and play new content.

Take leadership of one of the many houses of medieval Europe in this powerhouse of real time strategy from Paradox!
Have you ever wanted to see what would happen if you were head of a powerful (or not so powerful) family at any point across 700 years of European history? If so then this si the game for you!
When coupled with the vast array of additional content this game becomes simply the most in depth and immersive gaming experience for any strategy game fan. Take for instance my own recent game starting at the Petty King of Cornwall, going on to become the King of Wales and Ireland, only to lose the lot in a brutal and bloody civil war started by an aggrieved half-brother.
Not only that but with the “Way of Life” add-on you can direct your current ruler down personal paths that can result in Great Hunts for mythical white stags or go only holy pilgrimage with the “Son of Abraham” pack. Whilst many people criticise Paradox for the incredible amount of post release additional content that must be purchased, I believe that this small games developer is taking care of its customers by continuously updating a game that is loved by many. The real question is would you rather have a game that was never updated or a game that is continually improved at a small fee, after all game developing requires skill and investment that many small companies cannot afford.
It isn’t all sunshine and roses, Crusader Kings 2 has issues just like any game, for instance the early game for a small less powerful family can be a little tedious, and events in the game can become a little repetitive. Total War fans out there may find issue with the lack of controllable combat, numbers of a screen changing to show the state of a battle is not the most exciting thing in the world. Finally the lack of a story driven campaign could be an issue for some, however tat is the fun, the campaign is your families story, you create the excitement from day one the story is down to you, to aid with the game keep excellent track of the events and sagas that occur in your family whether that is in the form of Peasants in Devon seeing a dragon or the brutal could blooded assassination of your wife at the age of 83. It is up to you to remember the grudges and seek vengeance.
So, where next for the Kings of South West England? Step aside Byzantium, the Cornish are coming!
8/10
On a side note,  watch out for this great game in steam sales as it is often available for 75% less than the RRP!

This game is so badass. However It does not last long. It gets really dull pretty fast. It's not very
fun playing it in one long sitting. It's a fun free mod to play once in a while.
Your mission? You're placed into an areana with either aliens from HL2 or Combine Soldiers from HL2. You must kill everyone. You're given a couple weapons on start, and you must search the area for additional weapons (which I will get into soon). The game might sound very simple but it has some great features in it.
The game has a really cool feature; Slow-mo. It is (in my opinion) one of the best inventions to put into a video game. The guns from Half-Life 2 are still around, but given some different features like sound, looks and the mechanics. There's also a couple extra weapons like the Desert Eagle, which is my favorite weapon from just how powerful it is in this game. All the weapons are unique in their own way. You can 360 no scope everyone in slow motion while jumping off a ledge. It's amazing. The gore in this game makes it all just satisfying. Also... did I mention you can kick? Yes, there is kicking in this game and it's also amazing. It really reminds me of F.E.A.R. You wouldn't really use it as much, cause it's not as effective as shooting, but it's handy. You do still have Gordon Freemans armour, you can 'find' higher quality armor around the map, but they're not hard to find, so that sorta ruins the point.
Is the game hard? I hear you ask. No. not if you know what you're doing you're doing. You're constantly on the move. You get NO breaks. It's annoying, but this is the game you chose. I really hate it when games don't give you time to catch a breath. It get's boring quick if you don't get time to better appreciate the actual fights. I'm not excaclty sure on how to make a part of the game where you don't fight enemies for a while, but my closest bet is to make waves of enemies. Not constantly respawning. Kill everything and you get rewarded with time to search the map for weapons, ammunition, armor and gear.
I might have to mention the enemies. Nothing new, nothing bad. There's a few new combine guys, like the Assassin from beta HL2 that has dual pistols. They jump around athletically and they are so difficult to kill. That's probably the most unique combine carracter from this game.
Movement in this game is like a Quake game. You can B-hop around the map so quickly and It is fun.
I must mention the maps! They are nothing great. They're just taken from HL2:DM and HL2 but just modified a little. They are small for this game. And the original maps for this game also seem to look like a small map from
. They are also too small and cluttered! One of the biggest problems in this game is that there are places where enemies can't get you! Vents, high places, props etc. So that would mean you would have to force yourself to fight the enemy, because of how boring it would be to not have enemies to fight.
I do recommend this game, however It gets pretty old really quick. There is no campaign, obviously, and there probably wont ever be. There are archievements in this for steam so if you're an archievement person, dig in. It's free and totally worth it.

If you are looking for an unforgettable exploration/adventure game oozing with atmosphere and fascinating dark sci-fi concepts – you need to experience Cradle.
Cradle builds a superbly unique and colorful vision of the future. There's a drastic contrast between the rolling hills and meandering rivers of the steppe and the stark ruins of the “amusement park”, retro- futuristic mongolian yurt and hover train rings. There's something desolate, yet peaceful about the environment. The sweeping vistas are beautifully realized and the world feels lived in; by the end I was dying to see more.
The soundtrack is perfect for the setting and varies in flavor from relaxing eastern melodies to driving synth tracks amidst the more dramatic sequences.
I personally enjoyed the narrative but it seems the ending is one of the highly debated topics on the community forums. If you get confused, many plot elements are clarified via clues densely scattered around the environment so a thorough playthrough is definitely rewarded. There is also a continually evolving community discussion on plot line theories and meaning for reference after completing the game.
The only real complaint I have is that some of the mechanics can be slightly frustrating and repetitive, although, to the devs credit, they give an option to skip these sequences.
In the end, Cradle is one of those games that draws you in and before you know it, it's two in the morning. If you are a sci-fi or adventure game fan - it's well worth the cost just to experience Cradle's unique dystopian vision of the future. You won't regret it.

This is a hard gme to write a review for with out spoiling. Its a first person, exploration scfi story. One of the best stories I have seen. Very entertaining. Slightly diappointing in length, but i think that was because I was really enjoying it. Beautiful graphics. Really nice. The backwards and forwards nature of the game becomes clear quite soon. Basically, there are 3 places you will visit during the game, and all of them are with a couple mins walking distance of each other. The game world looks huge, and you can watch things disappear in to the distance. A lot of space, only to have you run around in a couple of hundred square metre space. S you have a conversation. Go to a place. Complete a puzzle. Get rewarded with a plot item. Return home. Have another conversation. Go back to the same place and complete the same puzzle and get another plot item. This becaomes transparent quite early on, but the astonishing story kept me going. I just wanted to find out what happens next. Then, just as you start to find out who you are, it ends. The game just ends. I have never played a game that ends so abruptly. I don't get it. Its awul, and it marred the overall experience. If there is more to come, at least put 'To Be Continued...' but it just ends, and goes in to weird FMV sequence, with some awful music. if you would like to see the game, i have a start to finish playlist (the end will be published on 11th sept) so you can either just enjoy the story, or use it as a walkthrough. i will include a link at the end.
my overall impressions of this game were good. its a great story, well told, but marred by a large map with lots of wasted space, and a very abrupt and inconclusive ending. recommended.

Bardbarian is fun, but it's the sort of simple and short-lived fun that makes it difficult to forget that it's a smartphone game at heart. All of the indie game tie-in characters add a flash of whimsy to this casual hybrid of Real Time Strategy and Tower Defense, but it's hard to gloss over the fact that you'll have experienced much of what the game has to offer in about 30 seconds of play. To its credit, the game packs in a lot of things to do in the form of different modes, minigames, and achievements. Unfortunately, the strategy aspect of Bardbarian is very shallow, and you can steamroll through about 98% of this game just by leveling any three units enough. Still, the action is instantly gratifying and the prospect of leveling your abilities to get just that little bit further makes the game addictive for the limited amount of time you'll spend on it. While I'd hardly call this game essential to your library, at the end of the day, I had $5 worth of fun and a good time getting all of the achievements.

is a free-to-play game that is a hybrid between a third-person shooter and a high-action brawler game. There are no cover mechanics here; it's extremely fast-paced. Players sprint, sneak, and parkour through procedurally-generated cooperative missions with a variety of objectives ranging from the simple "exterminate" to the stealthy "spy" and the mechanically-varied "sabotage" missions. There are also difficult boss encounters, as well as richly detailed story missions that unlock new mechanics and equipment.
Besides the cooperative missions, there are also flying missions called "Archwing" as well as competitive modes including the deathmatch-like Conclave and the "Lunaro" cyber-ball-sport. Recently, the game got an update that added large, open-world gameplay to the mix as well.
Players take on the role of "Tenno", the pilots of the eponymous "Warframes", which are sort of like (but not actually) armored combat suits with mystical powers. Each Warframe has four or more unique powers as well as individualized characteristics such as health, shielding, armor, and movement capabilities.
Along with their Warframe, players can equip primary (rifle, shotgun, sniper, bow, launcher) and secondary (pistol, shotgun, SMG, throwing knives) ranged weapons, as well as as melee weapons, companions (in the form of auto-turret-like Sentinels or AI-controlled animal companions), and consumable gear items. The range of weapons and equipment is extremely vast; there are already over 350 unique weapons in the game and more are being added all the time.
The shooter gameplay feels a lot like a modernized version of classic shooter games like Quake. While it does have features only found in more modern shooter games like reloading, iron-sighting, and headshots, player movement is incredibly fast and fluid and there is a good mix of projectile-based and hitscan weaponry. Many of the ranged weapons defy expectations given their category; there are lightweight and fast-handling primary weapons as well as secondary weapons that are launchers, cannons, and other oddities.
Meanwhile, the melee combat is similar to (albeit much simpler than) complex 3D brawler games like Bayonetta or Nier Automata. There are a wide variety of weapon types to choose from, including swords, staves, spears, hammers, axes, polearms, whips, nunchaku, sword-whips, stun batons, and two-handed versions of most of the above. The iconic "glaive" weapon from Digital Extremes' last title "Dark Sector" (inspired by the classic sci-fantasy movie Krull) makes an appearance in several forms here as well.
—the depth and breadth of this game are
suited for casual players. At this time I have like 1900 hours on Steam and I have another 1200 hours in this game outside of Steam. I'm still playing it to this day because there's still content I haven't unlocked. This game has so much content available for free that it makes other games just look bad. In the face of the recent SWBF2 lootbox controversy, the fact that progression in Warframe has relatively little RNG required makes me smile.

I play this not so much for the combat itself (although sniping a controller from a carefully selected position produces a nice amount of satisfaction) but more for the feeling of exploring in the Zone and that constant uncertainty of what I'm going to run into during my travels.

Whilst not as open world as the original and the DRM infested shed-fest of unoptimisation (Nevermind constant weapon jams to the point of hilarity) that was Clear Sky, Call of Pripyat is what the previous two outings to a degree should have been.
Many of the weapons work best here, and the user interface has been overhauled and to a degree slightly slightly streamlined whilst containing at the core what Stalker is.
Artifiact hunting is not as dull as it was in Clear Sky, and the open world does leave for a lot of random moments that you would not find in other FPS'es.
Sure not all the bugs are ironed out. It wouldn't be a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game if it was perfect. However, the flaws within the game environment are another part of Call of Pripyat's charm.
Sick of being a Space Marine but don't want to wander around being a poxy gnome or  cutesy mage? Well I said come in, don't just stand there! Possibly the greatest Singleplayer FPS I have ever played.
Now, get out of here Stalker!

Before Divinity, RPGs were assumed to have crappy combat.
It was kinda of a given that if you were a sprawling epic adventure, something would have to suffer.  Time and time again combat would draw the short straw.  Even in some of the most beloved RPGs ever made (Baldur's Gate,  Planescape Torment), it's tough to point to the combat as a high point.  At best, it was serviceable.
Divinity's combat is nothing short of incredible.  At its heart is the concept of combining elements to produce effects that are greater than the sum of their parts.  Shooting a character with a lightning bolt might not do much damage, but zapping a pudlde of water could electrify an entire group of powerful enemies, effectively disabling them.  Shooting an arrow at an enemy isn't especially powerful, but placing your character in a tower above the battleground gives massive bonuses to both the range and damage of their arrows.  Divinity gives you a mind boggling number of tactical options, and demands that you use as many of them as possible.  The difficulty is nothing short of punishing.  This is one game where playing on "normal" translates to "hard" and playing on "hard" (tactician mode) translates to "nearly impossible".  And yet, if you take the time to combine spell effects correctly and plan each fight out before it starts you will find yourself victorious more times than not.  Divinity wants you to THINK when you fight.  If you're looking for a mindless dungeon crawler where you can steamroll enemy hordes as soon as you find a +1 weapon, this isn't it.  Gear helps, but it's never enough on its own.  Tactics are king here.
Having said all that, Divinity is more than just great tactical combat.
It also immerses you in its world with a deep narrative, and interesting characters.  The writing is top notch and has a uniquely dark and sarcastic humor.  I can't think of many games that let you have conversations with demonic chickens, or play as a face stealing skeletal mage.
It's a large game, too!  I've sunk about 40 hours into it so far and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface of the world. The amount of exploration that can be done is almost mind boggling, with secrets stuffed in every corner of the map to reward patient and methodical players who (literally) leave no stone unturned. (No, really, you often have to move rocks to find secrets underneath!)
So if all this sounds like I'm gushing,  It's because the game is *that* good.  I will repeat my previous caveat though.  Divinity is HARD.  And I don't mean,  "gee, that was kind of a challenge" hard, I mean Dark Souls "How the ♥♥♥♥ could I possibly win this?" hard.   If you're someone who wants a nice casual stroll through a fantasy world,  this may not be the game for you.

SpeedRunners is one of the games that can be proud that it broke the early access curse and was fully released not too long ago.
SpeedRunners at least in my eyes is one of the most fun games I've played in recent memory. The thrill of being in first and the feeling that you can't be stopped by your opponents is just purely amazing and I think everyone needs to experience it.
In the story mode of SpeedRunners you play as Speedrunner and you try to become the best by overthrowing the other speedrunners.
But enough about the story, let's get into the gameplay:
The entire game is based on speed. You try to outrun all your opponents and the last one alive wins, win three times and you win the game.
Anything goes, you can use weapons,grapling hooks, explosives and all sorts of stuff. Some stuff can backfire on you so be careful on how you use the power ups.
The Graphics are awesome and I love the art style. Everything from animations, backgrounds and characters, everything looks amazing.
The soundtrack at first, I liked, but it get's tiresome really fast and I just really prefer to either mute the game and put on something else or just don't wear headphones.
The main campaign took me 1 hour to finish, and there is some replay value. You can go through the campaign more than a few times and unlock more stuff like maps and characters.

I didn't encounter any issues while running this game and I highly doubt anyone will too, so you are good to go.
Overall I don't have anything bad to say about SpeedRunners. It's an amazing game and I highly suggest you check it out and you will get sucked into it.

Cradle is an interesting idea, with great art direction, and an interesting story, all wrapped in a coating of absolute garbage.
Its essentially a point and click first person puzzle game. Which would be perfect, because thats a genre that desperately needs some love, if it wasnt for the fact that all the puzzling is interspersed with some of the absolute worst attempts at "gameplay" ive come across in years in the form of Cradles Block puzzle rooms. Yes, these rooms are skippable, thankfully, but you still have to spend time actually trying to fail the block puzzles in order to skip them.
Playing Cradle is essentially like playing a really obtuse puzzle game, where the puzzles are weird enough to be kinda irritating, but the overall story and world is interesting enough that you want to see it through, but then the game throws a godawful first person platforming block puzzle at you just to really test the limits of your patience. Also, there are literally only maybe 3 locations in the entire game. Your tent, the amusement park, and the flying train thing. If youve seen screenshots of this game, youve probably seen every single thing there is to see.
If the devs ever patch in a button to auto skip the block puzzle rooms, i would recommend it as a curiosity worth taking a look at, until then, avoid. At full price, i absolutely cannot recommend this game. Wait for a sale if you must.

The game has beautiful visuals and nice atmosphere.  It feels unique, and that's a rare quality.  The concepts in the story are interesting and make nice twists on stanard cyberpunk ideas.
Unfortunately,  the 3d platforming minigames necessary to advance the plot, while justified by the story, are repetitive.  Once you've done one, you've done them all, but you've no choice to keep doing them.  Additionally, the ultimate resolution to the story is a cheap deus-ex-machina that is only a step or two above "and then you wake up and it was all a dream."    It resoluves the plot on a macro level, but not the characters that we care about.
Still, Cradle deserves credit for its uniqueness and for its attempt to tell a complex story full of imaginative scientific and metaphysical musings, even if the ultimate payoff for the story is anticlimactic.

Cradle has a lot of really good an really bad components. The atmosphere is the best part of the game, and it could probably succeed on it alone. While the explorable area is rather small, the enchanting environment of the Mongolian stepp is exceptionally captivating. The first impression it creates really made me want to like the rest of the game, but it clearly falls flat in a few areas.
The gameplay is partly point-click puzzling, which really prompts you to dig deep into the environment, however small. The other part is in strange cube-based block building/throwing minigames (of which I dreaded after the second time). Both of these become somewhat repetitive over time.
The story is woven from an amnesia-based "I forgot everything about who I am" perspective, allowing you to learn about the world through documents and a couple of characters in the game, who's presences are reserved and limited, contributing to the serenity of the atmosphere. The story that's built up is very intriguing, but ends like the game stopped telling the story, instead of concluding it.
I don't know anything about the developer, but I would greatly appreciate a concise, free expansion/DLC to really conclude the game from them.
The largest plot-hole at the end and repetitive gameplay still don't completely outweigh the incredible atmosphere and environment, so I would still recommend this game, though waiting for a price drop or sale seems like a better idea. The soundtrack is also worth it, in my opinion.

Cradle is a SciFi story. Go into it expecting to be the character you're playing. After completing the first play-through, I believe there is a major view that the player should prepare to take, that is, the view of life/culture-shock. If you can empathize with people in a coma, who wake up after being asleep for even just 10 years, and see the confusion they're in, then I believe you'll be able to welcome this game (and it's concept) with open arms.
Now onto the game itself.
Story: Phenomenal, I've read a lot of SciFi and this story feels extremely original and compelling. You can tell almost immediately that the devs focused heavily on building this entire world to be a possible alternate future, filled with cultural, medical, and societal changes. If anything I hope they use the success of Cradle to create a series of games built from this world (it's that compelling).
Gameplay: A little rough. The game controls very simply, but asks you to find and do some rather specific things that sometimes are just a tad frustrating. It feels as though the devs didn't get many chances to playtest the game to beta-testers.
Sound: Very good, though somewhat forceful at times. The music walks the fine line between 'forcing emotion' and 'boosting emotion'. As in, there's many moments in the game where a rush of powerful music doesn't push me to feel something, but rather, allows me to be overwhelmed with that feeling. Just now I'm realizing that whole situation may play purposefully in tandem with the game's core themes.
Value: For $12, absolutely worth. It's like going to the movies and watching Interstellar with popcorn and soda. Only you can be at home and actually move at your own pace through the story (and have much cheaper popcorn and soda).
So ya, that's my takeaway. For those put-off by the ending (I'll be honest, I was pretty confused as well), please checkout the 'Ending' thread in the community hub, a lot of users there have already started piecing together the rather vague elements of the story.

I really hope Conan can rejoice because his namesake game has crushed me. Driven me away. And he can now hear my lamentations!
After about 15 to 16 hours I really began to feel like a barbarian, at least that bloodfrenzy part was there. I died. A lot. Because of stupidity? Maybe. But mostly I died because I was new and alone.
And this is what really makes me angry. I played other survival games (hundreds of hours of 7 Days to Die - which is way better) and maybe Conan is just different, or at least tries to be. But there's nothing new apart from naked people *scream!* ....  Let me tell you about my high adventure!
Key Problems as a beginner (single player)
1) Thirst and Hunger go up way fast... you almost need to sprint towards the pool at the end of the road. Even worse if you overlook the almost empty water skin near your start or don't look at the writings on the some wall to your far right to get a hint... Dying clueless. Great start!
2) You have a few recipes and the need A TON of Material, especially considering that you have to repair them after EVERY fight (needs up to the same amount of crafting it in the first place)
3) The fights: Good thing - your first fights are really quick; bad thing - you die and have to walk miles (see below). Fighting is basically far less tactical than promoted. The one with the higher stamina/ higher damage output wins. The strikes are about as accurate as .... well, they're not. It's more a strike in a "gender direction" and hoping to catch a pixel of the monster. Old games like "Daggerfall" were infinitely more precise than that.
Oh and really nice: The first kind of monster scan already stun you and one hit you. Fun!
4) Save Points: After scrounge away on the few scrubs you can find, TADA!, your bedroll! Save haven of respawn and replenishment! at least ONCE. Seriously, you have to build a new one every time you die. AND you have to make sure to save yourself to it, otherwise it's useless. For the life of
5) My first Base: After avoiding some fights and finally building the first walls, which took AGES (see below), I was still running after food and drink, I realized: Respawn. The monsters and "nudist bandits" simply respawn and attack you again and again. No real feeling of progress there.
6) ENCUMBRANCE: That might have been the tipping point. I had to spend every single newly gained attribute point from level ups into my "attribute" encumbrance (no not strength, that would be silly!) to be able to carry one crushed boulder and a few logs.....  It saves some weight to build walls etc. from it on the spot (because those are far less heay in your inventory...right). But overall: I PAID FOR A GAME! Not wasting time by doing the same trips for hours without seeing quite some progress because someone thought up "encumbrance" and assumed - probably in a drug haze or riding a sadistic vibe - that that would be fun for players. Who knows.
So, to be clear and end my lamentations: I am not a hardcore gamer. I work. I have about two hours to relax a day and I like playing computer games. And I felt the need to write this down to deal with my frustration and maybe give other casual gamers a glimpse into what to expect.  Purely my personal point of view (which others might still not get.)
Hopefully it will all be fixed but for now the game is shelved and I will have to dry me tears and carry on.
Thanks for reading and ignoring my spelling (not a native speaker).

I dont usually write reviews but felt like i had to give this game credit where it's due.
A lot of poeple are calling this pay to win, this is not the case. yes you can pay to unlock ALL the items but you can unlock them without paying for them. You're probably thinking now that im a moron and that it takes months of game play to unlock them all... Not at all. Lets say for example that there is the best combination of items (turret, body, transport, gun etc) you could unlock all of those within 30 to 90 minutes of game play (depending on your skill). The restriction on the free players is that you can not have ALL the parts at the same time, you have a limited parts slots. This is a little restrictive at the beginning but as you level up you get more parts slots. I currently have 12 slots and considering a vehicle takes about 5 parts (With some combinations you can fit more) that's room for a good amount of variation. I have also earnt more than enough of the currency to sell things i dont want and swap them out if really needed. I believe at some point i have bought all the guns at least once.
As for the game play, its quick and fluid with plenty of variation. It's true there's not many players but i have rarely had trouble finding a game and even with 2-4 people connected it's still fun.

Crusader Kings II wasn't my first foray into Paradox's grand strategy games, but it's definitely the one that got me actually into them. The game is very intricate with many nuances, yet manages to be reasonably accessible to a new player without spending hours upon hours learning the very basics. And once you've scratched the service the game is totally addicting. It's very rare to be able to genuinely say it, but no two games of Crusader Kings II are alike.
My first attempt at Paradox's games was Hearts of Iron III. It was the most appealing time era for me and one of the more recent ones at the time. But it was quite an experience for a newcomer. I played the tutorial all the way through as recommended and got a rudimentary idea of how it worked. Even after 15 hours I felt like I had no idea what was going on though. There were no graphics, there were too many units, too much going on all at once. Even if the AI could be turned on to handle details of the game you didn't care about, just one section felt like a monumentous task on its own. Everything was just a number, it was totally detached even if it was interesting. Compare that to this game, where you are just one guy. One guy. Maybe you own one county, maybe you own an empire. But in the end, the game is about your character and his family. There are plenty of decisions to be made still, but they're more top level - "What do I want to do and how do I want to do it", not three tiers down. You spend more time on the plan than the actual execution of the plan, which is what I would expect from a game that bills itelf "Grand Strategy". You're the king of the castle, the executive of the company. Knowing the intricacies of your empire works to your advantage most certainly. But it is only an aide, not a necessity to execute your plan if that shines any light into the accessibility.
But that's not the only draw. The game also has character, something incredibly difficult to do with regard to faceless nations. You are your king. You live life. Good things happen. Bad things happen. You never know exactly how things will turn out. Sometimes your king will live till 50. Sometimes it'll be 70. Maybe he'll get murdered or sick. Maybe he'll abandon having an heir for a life of celibacy. Or maybe he'll go completely insane. Your king, his family, and the relationships with his vassals is a very pivotal part of the game. Bribe, manipulate, persuade, it feels just like a political position when you're in charge of a large empire. It adds a layer of immersivity that maps of Europe simply don't have. The uncertainty of life is very real in this game.
If you are someone who had been turned off from Paradox's other grand strategy games I would highly recommend picking this up. There are so many different things to do and unique ways to play in the intricate simulated world of Crusader Kings II. I'm utterly hooked on this game and can see myself putting 1000 hours in it with all the DLC.

Alright. After finishing both campaigns, I think it's high-time to give this a proper review.
It's a solid... Meh out of Eh.
I had high hopes for this game. Honestly. I remained faithful that the Devs after 9 years would be able to work wonders. They kind of did, I suppose. The combat is challenging albeit frustrating at times, the controls are tight and responsive, the parkour is... Mesmerizing.
All the mechanics that they showed off so proudly all those many years ago have been polished until they almost shined.
That will be a running theme to this review:
I pre-ordered this game back in late 2014-Early 2015. It was priced for Thirty USD, and after it's release it has kept that pricetag. Now, the big question is: Is this game worth a damn?
Answer: Eh, kinda.
The
campaign has been completely ported into this game, so you're getting two games in one with this now. I never played the original Lugaru so all I know of it is.. Well this.
The Lugaru campaign itself is a solid... 5.5/10?
It's definitely the weaker of the two campaigns, pretty.. Dumb and confusing at times. It's really dumb, actually.
I won't go into spoiler details but this definitely doesn't show off it's good witty writing or solid character development.
But it does show that the universe this story takes place in sucks serious wolf dong.
So all in all, the gameplay is.. Meh, and the story for Lugaru is really iffy.
But that's not the shining star of this, no no no no.
That belongs to the
campaign.
It's..
6.5 or a 7/10.
It is not that much better but to be frank, it's leagues funnier than Lugaru's was. Sometimes unintentionally. I personally was invested in the story a lot more than I think most players will be because I followed the comic to it's end(Which, by the way, hasn't been updated since I pre-ordered all those years ago. It's also never directly referenced apart from maybe you making a connection to it that isn't there), so I paid attention to more details than most.
There's certainly more humor to this, there's more reason for things to be happening(Leave your disbelief at the door or you'll have a bad time), and although it has a rough start, the middle is certainly very.. Interesting?
The ending is absolute dog♥♥♥♥♥♥♥though I must say.
It ends more abruptly than the Lugaru campaign and it feels very rushed.
It was almost an 8/10 if the last quarter of the game had been better polished, and didn't feel like a custom level younger me created before I understood things like level design, navigation paths, or.. anything.
That also brings me to a BIG issue the entire game has: Level design.
One problem seems to be exclusively for the Lugaru side of things, where levels will last less than 1 minute and have a loading time of 2-3. You will not be exploring the levels in either campaign as there is no point. It is actually detrimental if you choose to do so.
Only one level near the very end of the Overgrowth campaign even hints that you can do that, but even then it still narrows down to a one-way-in-one-way-out deal.
In the 'parkour-exclusive' segments you will find yourself constantly frustrated at the sheer amount of luck that is required to make it to a ledge. Whether it being the wall jump doesn't key in, you juuust manage to fall short on a vault, or you just.. Backflip off a wall.
Yeah that happens more often than you think.
So, overall, I'd say that.. Well. It's not worth $30. Not at all. If you ordered it ages ago then, sure, by all means it is a better game.

This game is a wonderful enigma. There are questions that will never be answered. The world is strange, unnatural and begs exploration. You will look through dozens of small clues to get a big clue to get access to a bigger puzzle. That said none of this is part of the game. You will be doing this on your own OUTSIDE of the actual game.
The actual game is composed of a linear go here, solve basic puzzle structure of missions with timed events that will not trigger, unlock or be completable until you have solved the previous puzzle. It is the strictest of railroads we are speaking here. Should you find a piece of a puzzle three objectives down the line you shant be allowed to solve it on pain of the game forcing you to reload because you screwed up. On top of this are several minigames where you collect cubes, one stage of which I would like to punch whoever designed it.
The real game is a weird question. What the hell is going on? One which remains completely utterly unanswered. No matter of searching, no matter of thinking and no matter how far you roam you won't find the clues required to get an actual answer. The best you will do is some vague idea of what happened and a little sprinkle of magic. The why, for what reason or how won't really be answered.
That is why I can and both can't recommend this game.
If you enjoy thinking about a game long after it's done, going back and rereading certain messages and documents to make a bit more sense of it all, knowing you will never get an actual answer this is a game for you. The athmosphere is perfectly unsettling. The world so strange you will want to know more about it.
However be warned that the game really is nothing more than a few dozen one quite obvious solution puzzles intersperced with a few block collecting minigames, that don't change except for a completely ridiculous difficulty spike on the third minigame. You will NOT get a satisfying conclusion to this story as even the meaning of what you did cannot be answered despite you sort of being able to puzzle together what you did. Having just finished this game I feel incredibly compelled to write a review about it. This is largely due to what all the contents of the game have amounted in.
There's really not much to do in the game. While exploring the environment is fun for a little while you find yourself running between the same to places and completing the same challenge over and over. This challenge is really just a cube gathering minigame that feels amazingly out of place with the rest of the game.
There's also the fact that the voice acting brings nothing to the game. With a flat tone, even in dramatic parts of the game, it feels like there's no personality behind the characters. This detracts from the story greatly and makes me care more about the world I'm in than the characters I interact with.
The biggest shortcoming of the game is its ending. It feels rushed and really makes little sense.  In what could easily have been a halfway point for the game where everything gets turned around and all the questions get answered you instead get a 30 second blurry clip with some indie rock over it. The clip explains nothing and leaves you wondering about all the other things that had happened in the game and what they mean.
In the end the game is a fun distraction for a bit but its repetitiveness, lack of character development, and unfortunate ending all culminate into a game that could have been. It may have an interesting story but it fails to present it in an engaging way. It would be far better as a short story than a $13 game. For these reasons I can not honestly recommend this game to someone.

Mini-Review for Oblivion, requested by an user.
The question I've received: With skyrim having a great modding community, is there any reason to still pick up Oblivion?
Well, Yes. But allow me to explain.
Skyrim has the better graphics, better soundtrack, better combat, better ai, yada yada. All the stuff expected from having a better engine.
While vanilla oblivion in itself can offer you a lot:
A main quest that's of a grander scale as the one in Skyrim.
Far, far more side quests.
A plethora of explorable areas.
Actually more in-depth factions, reputations and guilds.
Better item distribution and item quality dispersion(when do you get this/that type).
Enfin, the real question is: All that vanilla stuff is great, but it can be modded into skyrim as well!
Well... Oblivion's mod-database is still far greater than the one skyrim has to offer as of now.
Graphics and Music can be easily improved, especially in the realm of character textures.
I'd personally also recommend many of the city overhauls and terrain improvements.
However, the real treats are in the more complex mods. Oblivion has had a far larger amount of time to develop it's mod pool and thus has far more complex mods for whatever tickles your fancies.
In short: If you're in love with modding your Bethesda games, Oblivion is certainly worth picking up and is easily moddable to your heart's content.
Even if you're not into modding the game itself holds its own unique charm and well worth experiencing, especially if it happens to go on sale!
So, hereby answering the request: Oblivion is a must have if you're fan of the TES series, well worth considering if you love modding games, worth a try if you started at skyrim and wondered what events lead to it, and if you're new to Bethesda's TES series a fair point to start.

Let me start by saying Jet Set Radio is the predecessor to one of my favorite games of all time. So I'll admit I'm a bit biased when talking about the series. Jet Set Radio (or Jet Grind radio) is originally a Dreamcast game published by SEGA that came out in 2000. And is basically the game that started cel-shaded graphics. The game takes place in the fictional city Tokyo-to where skater youth gangs tag the streets on their futuristic as ♥♥♥♥ roller blades. The gameplay consists of Skating, Grinding and spray painting, this is all rather enjoyable when you're not battling the controls which is where the game shows it's age a little. I won't lie there's a certain amount of precision required here that most skate games don't share, this can lead to frustration at times but after prolonged exposure and a better understanding of the movement system this becomes less of an issue. This does add a certain level of challenge that can feel very rewarding when you nail a particularly difficult stunt. Besides that I think the game holds up rather well, in my opinion it has all the qualities of most timeless classics. The game is just fun to play, it's cheerful and loud nature just sucks you into the incredible stylistic world. Typically graphics in these older games are a non-factor but this is what I would call a special case, there's something about the aesthetic of this game that is just so infectious. There's nothing better then having one of your favorite songs come on while you grind off telephone wires and bounce in between neon signs on buildings, even picking a character you like to play the most or customizing you gangs graffiti I felt continually invested. And man does this game have style, one of the most important elements in Jet Set radio is the phenomenal soundtrack that is just so fitting and contagious. This coupled with the vibrant in your face cel-shaded art style creates a very memorable experience. So ya I would highly recommend playing Jet Set Radio, you should buy it. Also can someone tell ♥♥♥♥ing SEGA to get off their♥♥♥♥♥and make a HD JSRF already. Seriously wtf are they waiting for.

I'd been looking forward to this for a long time since I first saw some of the development videos with the eagle and mechanical girl. On the plus side, it's beautiful to look at, and the soundtrack is very good too (and worth getting), and there's a lot of setting detail to explore.
Unfortunately though, while the final product is a valiant attempt, it's somewhat flawed:
For example - the background setting is pretty interesting, but it's somewhat incoherent. Concepts are introduced and then nothing is done with them. There's a lot of it scattered around the yurt that is your 'home base' but you don't really know which bits are important for the story and which aren't.
The four cube-puzzle mini-games also seem out of place and yanked me out of the atmosphere of the rest of the game somewhat. While they have an explanation in the plot, they're not really necessary to progress through the game (and fortunately you can skip them once you've played them once - but it would have been nicer to be able to skip them completely). Plus it gets a bit repetitive to have to keep going back to the Garden just to get more bits for Ida to continue the plot. Also, I thought the last game was pretty difficult to get to and particularly frustrating to play, which was really annoying.
The biggest problem though is the story itself. It just doesn't really hang together, and first time you see the ending I think there's a very good chance that you'll be saying "What?! WTF just happened here?". There are clues whose locations in the yurt are revealed in the final video, but you don't have a chance to look at them at that point and I was just left baffled by what I saw in the final sequence (and I didn't even know those specific clues were relevant beforehand anyway). I think that's pretty poor storytelling - they could have got Ida to do some more exposition about those clues during the game instead to make them stick in your memory more. And really, only three or four clues are relevant to the resolution of the story anyway. The other problem is that a big mystery of the game is who you actually are and what happened to you... and that's not revealed at all. That left me feeling very unsatisfied at the end, along with the failure of the ending to make any sense.
Having seen the ending and gone back to look at the clues and read some of the ideas on the forums about it afterwards, it kinda makes more sense now, but the flaws remain - the way it was put together just didn't work, and critical things are left totally unexplained. Don't get me wrong, I like endings that aren't handed to you on a plate, but I don't think we're given enough material to figure it out for ourselves the first time around.
So... it's an interesting setting (which in the end doesn't have all that much to do with the story being told here), but the key parts aren't really explained that well so it left me feeling very unsatisfied at the end. Would I recommend it though? Yes... despite its flaws I think I actually would, but wait a while and get it for cheap in a steam sale. The soundtrack is definitely worth getting though.

Crusader Kings II wasn't my first foray into Paradox's grand strategy games, but it's definitely the one that got me actually into them. The game is very intricate with many nuances, yet manages to be reasonably accessible to a new player without spending hours upon hours learning the very basics. And once you've scratched the service the game is totally addicting. It's very rare to be able to genuinely say it, but no two games of Crusader Kings II are alike.
My first attempt at Paradox's games was Hearts of Iron III. It was the most appealing time era for me and one of the more recent ones at the time. But it was quite an experience for a newcomer. I played the tutorial all the way through as recommended and got a rudimentary idea of how it worked. Even after 15 hours I felt like I had no idea what was going on though. There were no graphics, there were too many units, too much going on all at once. Even if the AI could be turned on to handle details of the game you didn't care about, just one section felt like a monumentous task on its own. Everything was just a number, it was totally detached even if it was interesting. Compare that to this game, where you are just one guy. One guy. Maybe you own one county, maybe you own an empire. But in the end, the game is about your character and his family. There are plenty of decisions to be made still, but they're more top level - "What do I want to do and how do I want to do it", not three tiers down. You spend more time on the plan than the actual execution of the plan, which is what I would expect from a game that bills itelf "Grand Strategy". You're the king of the castle, the executive of the company. Knowing the intricacies of your empire works to your advantage most certainly. But it is only an aide, not a necessity to execute your plan if that shines any light into the accessibility.
But that's not the only draw. The game also has character, something incredibly difficult to do with regard to faceless nations. You are your king. You live life. Good things happen. Bad things happen. You never know exactly how things will turn out. Sometimes your king will live till 50. Sometimes it'll be 70. Maybe he'll get murdered or sick. Maybe he'll abandon having an heir for a life of celibacy. Or maybe he'll go completely insane. Your king, his family, and the relationships with his vassals is a very pivotal part of the game. Bribe, manipulate, persuade, it feels just like a political position when you're in charge of a large empire. It adds a layer of immersivity that maps of Europe simply don't have. The uncertainty of life is very real in this game.
If you are someone who had been turned off from Paradox's other grand strategy games I would highly recommend picking this up. There are so many different things to do and unique ways to play in the intricate simulated world of Crusader Kings II. I'm utterly hooked on this game and can see myself putting 1000 hours in it with all the DLC.

I'm torn. What gameplay we do have is brilliant; everything controls with fluidity and weight (albeit a relatively light weight which is by no means a bad thing) and beams with an artistic genius. However, updates are few and far between with little comparable content. The devs seem to focus updates on animation, controls, and other components they have already fine-tuned to a more than playable state, in doing so neglecting content. You have your arena for gladiator-esque hosted fights, a few maps with some enemies and a level editor but no signs of a campaign mode, npc interaction outside of combat, or anything else that many players are looking for.
If you write a novel you are prompted to finish as fast as possible, forgiving yourself for any errors, irregularities and the total lack of polish because a first draft is a first draft - it's your alpha. Overgrowth is what happens when you fix the errors, irregularities and polish a product anally... with the product barely being there in the first place. The quality over quantity approach is overlooked, but I've lost track of the years this has sat in my library.
I'd recommend the game. Perhaps something you can pass down to your grandkids. Who knows, maybe their grandkids will play version 1.0.

I thought I should use a controller for this type of game, which is fully supported, but immediately noticed some goofy things. Walking forward (especially slowly) gives you that kind of 2003 era third person adventure shuffle slide walk animation, as well as the lack of a "step up" animation so the girl just kind of teleports about a foot upwards on top of the ledge. The funny thing about that is, for 90% of the locations it's completely flat ground, but they centralize you on an area with an angled roof where you basically have to do it any time you leave. Just kind of a goofy choice, and again, a bit of a lack of polish.
On the subject of animations, they're pretty harsh. Nothing is smooth and fluid with the girl except for her typical light and breezy scarf/sash thing. You'd kind of expect when all the jump distances are the same, and you only have three types of movement (Walking, shimmying on a ledge, and hanging) that they would be much smoother. Instead it's almost like they pulled something off the Unreal marketplace and just made it "work." It's pretty evident in the videos, the girl starts a jump, the animation ends abruptly, then she reaches the ledge and the grabbing animation plays abruptly. Every single ledge in the game is exactly the same height, I don't honestly understand how this could look so goofy and unpolished other than using premade assets and slapping them in place.
The exception to this rule is the 8 forms of wildlife scattered around the world, although I suppose fish aren't that hard to animate.
The art style is decent, but the actual graphics tend to leave me unimpressed. There's very few very often repeating low quality textures, and of course assets like plants, rubble, etc... along with what appears the dark depths of either the black lagoon or hell itself as the water is a deep blue and has no translucency at all. I don't necessarily need/want a 150 foot deep view of the city streets below the water, but watching whales, dolphins, fish, buildings, floating garbage just instantly disappear under this mysterious void is a little disconcerting.
I could easily get over the vegetation and other repeating assets, but the low quality textures and poor water (being ~80% of the graphics) really reduces the "WOW! This looks amazing!" factor.
Again, there's exceptions to this, as the game (inexplicably really) has rather nice day/night and weather cycles which constantly change the lighting schemes and gives off those nice beautiful colors to reflect off the... crappy textures and actually not very reflective water.
I (as mentioned) haven't collected all the story pages, but they're just very simple drawings wherein you try to infer as to what's happening in them. To it's credit, most of them are actually fairly easy to understand. The only I know for certain *spoilers I guess* is that there seems to be some type of algae sickness that's spread to all the animals, people, and the girl, of which turns the humans into gross green algae mutants. I've also seen a dead robot on top of the altar of the main hub which piqued my interst more than anything.
The big problem in doing hidden story pages throughout the world is that it's just easier to Google them up rather than taking your slow sweet♥♥♥♥♥time gathering them, and you don't miss out on anything.
The biggest plus to this game is the audio, which has its own minus. The sound mixing is actually surprisingly great, and works with full 5.1, with the lovely (and also rather bassy) piano medley music, wherein lies the rub.
After a while of puttering about in your boat the music ends and... that's it. Doesn't repeat, doesn't play another song, just ends. So it's just you and the sounds of wind and the stupidly large amount of whales and dolphins jumping around, though cruising along with dolphins around you is kinda neat.
And that's really all I have to say about this game. Nice sound design.

This game is set somewhere in Mongolia year 2076. You wake up in a hut, or Yurt, and have no memory of who you are or where you are.
The game doesn't hold your hand in the way of storytelling, you have to figure out the story all by yourself, if you have time you can find a ton of reading material in the hut about what has happened, but the main story comes from the android woman on your desk which you have to repair. The game does however hold your hand through all the tasks you are given and tells you exactly how to solve everything, though you can choose not to read these hints if you want to, so it's not so bad.
Back to the woman on your desk, the story progresses when you repair/replace a part in her and new information is revealed to you through her, because as she gains new components she remembers more things about her past. There is also another person/android which I think is an old friend, I'm not quite sure, but he reveals more information about the past in exchange for flowers (you will get it if you play it).
Now, the way you collect these new parts is quite dull, you have to play one minigame for each part, which doesn't sound bad at first until you get to the second minigame and realize it's the same one, just altered a tiny bit. The whole thing becomes tedious after a while and you find yourself trying to rush through it so you can unlock more storytelling and not play stupid minigames involving cubes. The story reveals why these minigames exists and why you get parts after completing them, and also why they are so dull, but this could easily have been changed so they all are completely different from each other and not all consisting of cubes and still fit it into the story. This is one of the two things I didn't like about the game.
The second thing is that it states that it is open world, which it is, but you only go between two places all the time, you even find a thing so you can travel between these places quicker, and they are only like 500m apart. Sure you can go explore but there is nothing to be found, it's just a big steppe or whatever it's called. I think there are some collectibles laying around but I didn't find a single one.
Where this game really shines is in its story, they have created a really good backstory and an explanation to almost everything, there is a certain
I have not found the explanation to yet, hopefully it is buried somewhere in all the readable things laying around, and yes, everything is readable, every little scrap of paper laying on the floor to long news articles, and everything is relevant in one way or another. You really get the sense that this guy is living out here all by himself, making his own electricity, food, water and selling flowers to his friend which comes by once in a while with supplies in exchange.
The graphics are what to be expected from a game in 2014. They have created an almost Borderlands type of filter, so it looks a bit cartooney or like it's drawn by hand. The skybox is a bit lacking in my opinion, the clouds do not fit in with the rest of the game so well, but I see where they are going with it, they just made it a bit too much 'hand drawn on paper'. But overall it's almost stunning how good they set the mood with the graphics alone.
The soundtrack of this game is also amazing, it really fits in with the story and setting. I never buy soundtracks for games but for this I am considering buying it, maybe.
If you buy this game for the story, not the gameplay, you will have a great experience and a huge "aha" moment at the end. It's even fun to play through a second time when you know all the lore and understand everything that is being said. I played through it in a day, so it's not so long. It's 3€ too expensive in my opinion but still worth the money. I'm hoping for some sort of sequel, or even a prequel because the story is so rich and it would be interesting to see how other people live, and what the cities look like.

This game is amazing for a number of reasons. Here are a few of my favorite aspects of the game:
1 It's gorgeous. The attention to detail on the scenery and the characters is top notch.
2 It's intuitive. The controls are smooth and the designers used color, light, and other clever cues to make your basic options obvious without spoiling the realism.
3 The story is subtle, but epic. There is far more to the story than just "sister saves brother" (though that part of the story is very compellingly told). I don't want to spoil anything here, but even just the basic campaign content has some interesting twists, though they are very understated (a bit like Shadow of the Colossus). But if you delve into the secrets to learn the story of the city, and decipher the script, there is even more interesting things going on in this world. Very good stuff.
4 The music is perfect for the mood of the game. Relaxing, but somber.
5 The exploration mechanics are great. As some negative reviews have mentioned, this isn't the kind of Tomb Raider experience where you have lots of heart-pounding action avoid monsters and traps, or have lots of puzzles to solve. But that doesn't diminish the game at all. This is an exploration game. The challenge is figuring out "How do I get there from here?" and I think that is a very satisfying mechanic.
I think this game is a masterpiece.

I'm decent friends with one of the developers, so when he mentioned a game he was working on with his studio, I was excited. He gave me an alpha build of the game, so I catagorized my impressions. However, after around an hour, I could give it a positive review because besides a few glitches, it's a fairly solid game with satisfying controls. Stretching across the galaxy might take awhile, but you feel like you're actually doing something either way, and the space combat is satisfying, feeling almost like a multiplayer version of Asteroid! While there are a few problems, like how the lazer based ships feel like pointing a lazer pointer at the enemy, it's a competent game, and is only going to get better as it is only in Alpha. I would pick it up, but don't play too much of it until the Beta, because then it will really start to shine!

Sure, there are still some bugs and it has a ways to go, but every Alpha game does, and I see a bright future for this one.  For those who have been playing and finding bugs, I highly recommend letting the creators know, as I've gotten some really good feedback on the bugs I've reported that were not previously known by them.  Instead of bashing the game for being new, why not report them and help the developers make the game even better for those who are yet to play?
Overall, I really enjoy this game so far and will recommend it to my other friends on here.  I also think it would be really helpful if those who reviewed the game early on would go back to ensure that their reviews are still up to date with what the game is like, especially since this game is undergoing a lot of bug fixes still.

Even as a skeptic of early access games, I have thoroughly enjoyed the time I have played single player and multiplayer. I considered other sandbox games, yet because of the familiarity of Conan, I decided it was likely more worthwhile for me to play. That being said, while the game lacks environmental editing to dig tunnels, the sandbox itself is filled with opulent oasis flora and desert ruins. I am looking forward to what develops as it is balanced by playing, and think it is a good chance for community involvement to actually make a game better - instead of just grinding it into oblivion. It is discouraging to see so much critique based on mechanics shared by other games, especially when most examples given to contrast Conan Exiles are similarly made in the survival style made popular by Minecraft. Common sense should dictate that realistic tools have realistic purposes. As someone who wanted a mature sandbox I find building can be frustrating still at times with tile placement such as wedges and triangles. However, I was surprised by the realism of the combat. It is reminiscent of Chivalry in first person, and hearkens back to days of Bushido Blade when one or two well-placed strikes can easily prove fatal in combat. When so many games involve ridiculous amounts of hitpoints with no-sold animations simply dropping HP, even animals in Conan Exiles won't hesitate to throw you on your hind end and deliver a fatal blow. I suggest using spears to deal with gators.

To elaborate more...
The original Shadow of Chernobyl was an incredible game in many ways, offering players an opportunity to explore an exceptionally realized, radiation-blasted setting seeded with horror and entertainment. Yet it was also lacking in a few areas, one being polish, and another being a solid character progression infrastructure. With Call of Pripyat, GSC Game World delivers its most stable and playable version of the Zone yet. Though it's not quite as surprising as the original, it's still a standout game that deserves to be given a chance by anyone that reads this. There aren't many titles able to offer up such an affecting atmosphere mixed with enjoyable mechanics, and even if some bits of the game remain uneven, it's an experience that will stick with you long after it's over.
PROS:
+Standard story but consisting an interesting tale.
+Powerful atmosphere throughout to keep you hooked.
+Far more polished product than previous Stalker games, namely Shadow of Chernobyl, that had many gamebreaking bugs at release.
+Improved graphics.
+Haunting landscapes.
+Tense soundtrack, just like previous STALKER games.
+Weapon and creature sound effects are impressive.
+Gameplay is solid! The shooting mechanics and the new upgrade options make for entertaining battles and a satisfying sense of progression without forgetting the inventory management.
CONS:
-Some weak voice acting .
-Weak and tacked on multiplayer. Multiplayer suite might be built in CoP, but honestly, discovering new quests and locations in the single-player game are the main draw and lasting appeal of Call of Pripyat.
OVERALL:
If you have ever played any other STALKER games before, give CoP a shot right away! I'd say it is the best of the franchise since it added a lot more to the series than previous games. To new comers of STALKER, imagine playing a Fallout game in a more mature setting but with better FPS gunplay.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!
