I'm gonna say it. Look I know you're probably going to shoot me for it, but after hitting about the half way mark for the game I just feel like I need to say it. It needs to be let out in a written form, and when I do say it please take into consideration the time gap, and how that plays into it for sure (modernization and all).
Here goes....this game is better than BALDUR'S GATE II as far as greatest RPG I've personally ever played.
Now look I played BGI when it came out, and BG II when it came out, so I did experience (and have the emotions) of what those games gave me when they were initially released. BG II's story is so far better in my opinion than DOS2, BUT All the other RPG elements of DOS2 and the way they revolutionize turn based combat that relies on the environment so much is just so incredibly well done that from an emotional perspective I've been enjoying DOS2 more than I enjoyed my first playthrough of BGII. Oh and there's the fact that DOS2 has so many different ways that the game can go.
Look I know it's crazy, I seriously thought nothing could beat BG II. However, everything Feels in DOS2. If you do something a certain way then hey you just missed out on that side quest, or perhaps you evolved that side quest to come to a different ending than if you had completed a different way.
It's just so darn good, there's really very few absolutely useless NPCs. They almost all have some form of purpose (even if it's just a good conversation).
If you don't like turn based combat, don't get this game. However if enjoy turned based combat in the slightest then get this game. I mean my goodness perhaps you DON'T enjoy that style of combat, but enjoy a good story then get this game and set the difficulty to exploration mode.
I myself prefer tactician, because once you get a good build going classic becomes too easy.
You just won't find a better game than this, and yes that's my personal opinion. It should be noted though that I'm Not the type of person to Ever say a game is truly the greatest of it's genre, but I am unashamedly stating that now, because for me it's just so stinking true.

BEST GAME EVER
My favorite games create an atmosphere that acts as a world of the game.  When I play Call of Pripyat, or the original S.T.A.L.K.E.R. I feel as though I am truly in "The Zone".   It's not all that welcoming of an environment but in the STALKER series I feel like I'm actually stepping into another world.  Think of it as the Russian equivalent of the recent additions to the Fallout Series, with no hand holding.  There are missions but don't expect much in the way of an in-game interface when it comes to ongoing quests.  You'll get a marker on your map and that's about it.
Weapons in the game feel realistic, don't expect to take out an enemy in one shot.  Ammo is scarce and weapons degrade overtime.
STALKER: Call of Pripyat was the first game to use DirectX 11, and although I still find the graphics to be just fine, several mods exist that completely overhaul the games looks.  STALKER Complete has long been the best and most well known but a newer mod called MISERY completely retools everything; the graphics, the difficulty(as if the game was not challenging enough already), the weapons, weather, everything.   If you are on the fence at all about buying this game check out the MISERY mod.   But do yourself a favor and play through the game once in vanilla before you go shaking things up with MISERY.

And do not judge my recorded playtime.  I have played this game for well over 100 hours while offline, which Steam does not record.   Do yourself a favor and pick this game up the instant it goes on sale (the developers have long since disbanded - some went on to make the METRO 2033 series) or trade for it or do whatever you have to do to add this game to your library.  If I had to pick 5 games to keep on my Steam account, after CSGO and TF2, STALKER would be my number one choice of games that I would keep.  (I would also keep Tales of Maj'Eyal and number 5 would be a toss-up).
Even with a dev that is no longer in business STALKER has a thriving mod community and continues to be improved upon.  So just as I feel that I am entering another world when I play it, "The Zone" continues to be a living breathing and ever changing world.

Before you buy this game, please read the  reviews thoroughly and know what you are buying.  I hoped Cradle would be similar to Sunless Sea, a narrative style game I paid the same amount for, played for 95 hours, and enjoyed thoroughly.  It didn't turn out that way.  The favorable reviews will tell you what's right with the game, but I had three major problems with it.
First, Cradle had massive lag between control inputs and responses.  I had to turn all the quality settings to minimum,
, in order to make the game playable.  As a result, the graphics were not pretty at all.  My computer meets the listed hardware requirements and is capable of better than this.
Second, I see now that none of the reviewers have logged more than seven hours of play time.  The game is short, and that's disappointing.  Seven hours isn't even enough time for the keyboard controls to feel natural to me, so I never got past that awkwardness to feel immersed in the game.
Third, the cubes.  I had read about this controversial minigame, so I lowered my expectations.  But I found it jarringly out of place in Cradle and it further broke the game's immersion for me.  You can skip the minigame, but only after you've actually failed it.  I tried just walking away from the computer for a while during the cubes thing, but that didn't cause me to lose the round - you have to actively play badly in order to lose and get through the section.  Worst of all, you have to play the minigame not once but four times.  When I learned that, I was actually angry.
The devs have somehow got me to pay good money and spend my precious time playing some kind of Cube Crush Saga game like the ones my mother-in-law is constantly inviting me to play on FB.
As I write this, I'm three quarters of the way through the game and having trouble motivating myself to lose the fourth round of Cubes With Friends so I can, you know, read the ending.  Especially because other people seem pretty lukewarm about that ending.  I agree with other reviewers who have said this should have been a book, not a game.

Submerged Review
Beautifully simple and simply beautiful.
There is a lot to love about this game.  There’s actually not a lot to this game but what it does it does well.
The first thing to strike me is how visually absorbing the world is.  There are an array of structures, and enough variety to convince you that this was a real city now submerged beneath a vast sea.  There is little in the way of duplication.  It just kept drawing me in.
The story, gameplay and mechanics essentially are quite simple but nicely executed.  It is basically a puzzle, platformer within a 3D world.  The in game map is invaluable and easy to read.   The boat is really fun to use and withstands all the abuse you want to throw at it.  Level design was really good and provided the right amount of challenge, not too easy, not too hard.  At no point was I throwing the controller at the monitor in frustration.
The atmospheric game engine just adds to the authenticity of the world.  You have a day/night cycle that passes about once every 30 minutes.  Weather conditions cycle too on a regular basis.  Small details haven’t been overlooked.  For example, when the girl looks up she hears the wind howling but when she looks down this changes to the sound of the waves.
The sound is well designed.  Overall, it has a sombre, melancholic tone to it.  This complements the story which itself has a sadness.  However, I felt that the world environment created its own soundscape which created a nice balance.
The biggest letdown for me was the cut scenes which occur at the end of each progressive level.  There are 10 levels each of which is completed once certain supplies are found.  For the most part these scenes were quite repetitive and ambiguous.  This side of the game felt like it had been rushed.  Some better, more varied cut scenes maybe depicting events leading up to the current world condition would’ve helped in this regard.
The game designers opted for achievement style story cards instead of voice acting to progress the narrative.  The story cards in turn are supposed to complement the animated cutscenes.  It sort of works but the art chosen on the story cards is like the style of prehistoric cave paintings.  It is up to you to interpret them correctly and make of them what you will.  Overall, they were understandable.  There were just a few that didn’t seem to make sense or fit with the rest of the story.
On the whole, I loved exploring this world and collecting the trinkets, secrets and supplies.  I wish there had been more to find as I could easily have spent another 10 hours bombing around in that boat.  This world deserved a bigger and better back story.  It’s definitely one to recommend and has replay value when you get fed up of all the heavy, oppressive storylines out there.

Couple of guys working in a basement brought about this lovechild of "A Bard's Tale" and "Plants vs. Zombies".
Simple theme:
A warrior who's tired of killing vows never to swing his axe again and makes a lute of out it.  A few seconds later goblins start attacking.  You build up notes (form of currency) over time, and use them to hire different troops and buy 10 second buffs.  The goblins are trying to run up your yard and destroy the Town Crystal (a building at the other end of the yard) but will attack you if you get close.  There are several different types of goblins and monsters and after about 5 rounds, a boss of some sort, then you move straight on to the next level.
You can play a Day Campaign (the levels Morning, Noon, Evening and Night), start from a previously-reached level, Survival Mode or Escape Mode (dodging scroller variant w/ no fighting).
Killing enemies also generates gold which can be used to upgrade just about everything multiple times.
Epic music, simple controls, fast gratification, and easy on the harddrive makes this good for a gamer's quicky.
As they say,
Go play some notes and kick some scroats.

TL;DR 6/10, would not recommend purchasing at full price.
Pros: 
+ Great plot
+ Lovely stylized graphics
+ Excellent voice acting for Poirot
+ Engaging investigative process
Cons:
+ Bug ridden (explained below)
+ Awkward mechanics/pathing
+ Inconsistent voice acting
+ Way too many “trophies” (nitpicky, I know)
I really wanted to love this game, but in the end the bugs and tedious gameplay frustrated me to no end. My GF however, really enjoyed this game, so we decided to meet in the middle and give it a 6/10.
Several of the “puzzles” (figuring out how to manipulate a box or cabinet so that it can be opened) in this game were very unpleasant for us. Not necessarily because they were obscure or difficult, primarily because there are so many bugs that make it not possible to change the POV so that you can click on the item you need. We had to use the hint feature in the pause menu to bypass these bugs, which took a while to reload, causing us to spend a fair amount of time just waiting.
The style and graphics for the game are excellent. The backgrounds are nicely detailed and the shading is very well done. We particularly thought the section in Bexhill was lovely.
The plot is fantastic. We kept guessing “whodunit” and didn’t get it right for a little while, which is great. The small details you gather and piece together really envelope you in the world of investigation, which is really fun.
The voice acting was very hit and miss. The voice actor for Poirot was absolutely brilliant, whereas a few other characters were acceptable, and one was just downright awful.
The “trophies” for this game were really annoying to me. Not a big deal, or even really a concern for most, but you get a different achievement/trophy for almost every action which I found obnoxious.
All in all, I would definitely not recommend purchasing this at full price given the bugs, awkward pathing mechanics, linear progression, and relative short playtime. I would recommend this game for $5 or less for the fantastic plot and great graphic aesthetics.
Happy gaming!

Commandos: Beyond the Call of Duty is a stand-alone expansion pack for the critically acclaimed classic isometric strategy/stealth game, Behind Enemy Lines.
Like the base game, it features a group of commandos in eight scenarios, who must complete a set of objectives– mostly sabotage– deep inside enemy territory. Although all missions are loosely based on historical events, there is no actual plot, only short briefings.
BtCoD is notorious even among old Commandos fans for its difficulty. The levels are not only gigantic– larger than the biggest one in BEL– but they are also full of enemies placed in the most nefarious ways possible.
To combat this, all commandos received new abilities. Some are unique, some are universal: for example, anyone can now distract soldiers by throwing rocks, or lure them with cigarette packs.
There is also a non-lethal way to deal with enemies now, letting you take hostages to use as distractions. On some levels it’s almost impossible to progress without using these “puppets”.
The imbalance between characters wasn’t really addressed, since you still need to use the Green Beret or the Spy to silently kill or knock out, and to carry enemies. Therefore, the role of the others is mostly reduced to hostage controllers.
Still, this difficulty is what made BtCoD more memorable, and probably even more loved than the original, which will seem way too easy and short in comparison. So, if you ever want to experience some difficult game that is not just another indie platformer, you can always rely on Pyro Studio’s classic.

Even as a skeptic of early access games, I have thoroughly enjoyed the time I have played single player and multiplayer. I considered other sandbox games, yet because of the familiarity of Conan, I decided it was likely more worthwhile for me to play. That being said, while the game lacks environmental editing to dig tunnels, the sandbox itself is filled with opulent oasis flora and desert ruins. I am looking forward to what develops as it is balanced by playing, and think it is a good chance for community involvement to actually make a game better - instead of just grinding it into oblivion. It is discouraging to see so much critique based on mechanics shared by other games, especially when most examples given to contrast Conan Exiles are similarly made in the survival style made popular by Minecraft. Common sense should dictate that realistic tools have realistic purposes. As someone who wanted a mature sandbox I find building can be frustrating still at times with tile placement such as wedges and triangles. However, I was surprised by the realism of the combat. It is reminiscent of Chivalry in first person, and hearkens back to days of Bushido Blade when one or two well-placed strikes can easily prove fatal in combat. When so many games involve ridiculous amounts of hitpoints with no-sold animations simply dropping HP, even animals in Conan Exiles won't hesitate to throw you on your hind end and deliver a fatal blow. I suggest using spears to deal with gators.

Take leadership of one of the many houses of medieval Europe in this powerhouse of real time strategy from Paradox!
Have you ever wanted to see what would happen if you were head of a powerful (or not so powerful) family at any point across 700 years of European history? If so then this si the game for you!
When coupled with the vast array of additional content this game becomes simply the most in depth and immersive gaming experience for any strategy game fan. Take for instance my own recent game starting at the Petty King of Cornwall, going on to become the King of Wales and Ireland, only to lose the lot in a brutal and bloody civil war started by an aggrieved half-brother.
Not only that but with the “Way of Life” add-on you can direct your current ruler down personal paths that can result in Great Hunts for mythical white stags or go only holy pilgrimage with the “Son of Abraham” pack. Whilst many people criticise Paradox for the incredible amount of post release additional content that must be purchased, I believe that this small games developer is taking care of its customers by continuously updating a game that is loved by many. The real question is would you rather have a game that was never updated or a game that is continually improved at a small fee, after all game developing requires skill and investment that many small companies cannot afford.
It isn’t all sunshine and roses, Crusader Kings 2 has issues just like any game, for instance the early game for a small less powerful family can be a little tedious, and events in the game can become a little repetitive. Total War fans out there may find issue with the lack of controllable combat, numbers of a screen changing to show the state of a battle is not the most exciting thing in the world. Finally the lack of a story driven campaign could be an issue for some, however tat is the fun, the campaign is your families story, you create the excitement from day one the story is down to you, to aid with the game keep excellent track of the events and sagas that occur in your family whether that is in the form of Peasants in Devon seeing a dragon or the brutal could blooded assassination of your wife at the age of 83. It is up to you to remember the grudges and seek vengeance.
So, where next for the Kings of South West England? Step aside Byzantium, the Cornish are coming!

It's a great concept and fairly fun as well as super easy to jump into. I'm giving it a thumbs up but mainly because it's free. In it's current form I couldn't see paying money for this - there are a lot of bugs and kinks that need to worked out.
On the plus side:
- Super easy to jump into and pretty fun
- Getting in game currency to buy more parts isn't so bad after the first hour or so and you actually have a viable robot
- Addicting as games are only about 10 minutes and the next part or upgrade is always, 'just one more game' away
- Really cool old school level designs
- Building robot tank guys is fun
On the negative side
---(about the beta factor of the game)---
- The menus are clunky. It took me forever to figure out how to sell a part and where even half my parts were (scroll to the right)
- Controls are effy. Some vehicles have the ability to strafe.This begs for a FPS control scheme which is not currently possible and leaves controlling vehicles awkward and frustrating.
- No testing or demonstration of parts which you haven't yet bought. For example, I finally saved up enough points to buy a hull I wanted only to find out with the current control scheme, it was nearly unusable. Sell back is for less than half value so it was like 30-40 minutes of m y time wasted which is frustrating.
---(about the actual game play and concept)---
- Suffers from moment issues. There's not enough active servers so everyone is mixed together. What this means is, players who are higher levels with better gear rip through players just starting off, often in one or two hits. As such, they are the board leaders and get more points so they can get better gear... New players have to either be lucky enough to be on a server with other new players, hope to skitter around and pick off people left damaged after a fight, or just suffer through constant 10 minute matches to get 1 point (the cheapest items are 4 points).
Overall the game is still fairly fun and a good casual time killer. I'm interested to see how it develops.

If you're desperate for a Half-Life fix, then Firefight Reloaded is just what you need. It's a free HL2 mod focused on survival/firefight/horde mode mechanics with a fast-paced, arcade-style twist to its gameplay - you'll be bunny hopping across the map, blasting enemies from both HL1 and HL2, with a variety of unique weapons from several Valve games, buying and acquiring upgrades, perks and more, as you go. It also has bullet time, so there's that.
There's a lot of content in here; and a lot of really great customizability (game modes, game variables), along with Steam Workshop support and legacy builds for tinkerers and enthusiasts (and the mod is actually open-source, too). Future updates are set to add even more content to the game, which sounds great.There's even multiplayer co-op - but it's in a work-in-progress state for the time being.
The spawning system could use some work, though, and hopefully more maps are on the way soon. Overall, I really do recommend this mod - and did I mention it's totally free!?

I have to say I am absolutely stunned by how great this game. It is extremely refreshing to finally have an original combat system that is actually enjoyable. In fact it's so enjoyable that the only disappointment I have about this game is the lack of opportunity to experience it. Having played through to the end of the campaign I felt sort of slapped in the face at the end. You mean to say I made all of this progress just to be thrown into a small area with a couple of npcs that repeat the same dialogue? Now don't get me wrong, the experience was definitely worth what I paid. However, I was expecting at least some sort of system where I could enjoy randomized dungeons and build on to all of that progress. If you are like me and enjoy gameplay over dialogues you will be gravely disappointed by this game's replayablity factor. No one finds it exciting to replay encounters on a higher difficulty consisting of the same enemies slapped with higher resistances and damage capabilities. Now sure if you're a sucker for the story and want to see what the other three follower's have to offer then you'll likely have another enjoyable playthrough. That is as long as you don't change the difficulty and become frustrated with encounters that used to last ten minutes or so now lasting about a half of an hour. I think this feels really forced and isn't the kind of "difficulty" we are looking for.
The only other complaint I have regards the party customization. You mean I can't join a friend's game and create my own character to play how I like? Was it supposed to be fun to play as one of their undergeared side characters that recieved little attention in regard to how their skills were allocated? As if that wasn't enough, you are only able to make one completely customized character for your party throughout the entire playthrough. Why put these limits on such a beautiful game with great character customization?
Overall this was a great game that just deserves a little more thought in terms of replayability. Don't let these things sway you against buying the game. You likely won't be bothered by any of these issues until you've spent about 100 hours travelling about Rivellon or until you finish exploring all it has to offer. If you're a fan of RPGs, get it. DOS 2 is likely the best release of it's genre in the last decade

I'm having a hard time deciding what to think of this one. I want to like it, but at the same time there are a lot of negative points that are making me uncertain.
Cradle isn't a god-awful game, but it's not great either. It is a first-person exploration game set in a unique science-fiction world, with plenty working with and against it:
THE GOOD:
First off, the game, it's graphics and animations are absolutely gorgeous. The environments are beautifully rendered with small caring touches of artistic liberties to give it more of a unique appearance, such as sky formations, texture patterns and plant life. I absolutely love the designs taken, they're subtle but far from invisible and are lovely to look at. Animations are also very well done, especially with the NPC's who look, act and generally feel very lifelike, made even more believable with the outstanding use of emotion-display technology with the eyes, using real "actor eyes" to make the interactions that much more enjoyable.
Second: The soundtrack. My god it's wonderful. Fits with the situation and sets up the atmosphere while being easy to listen to.
Third: The game's world, lore and story. The storyline is immersive and gives depth to the world that is visibly crafted with extra care by the developers, making the world feel immensely larger than the game and creates an opening to what I feel could easily become a unique sci-fi franchise.
(
)
Taking place in future Mongolia, the player also witnesses a pretty convincing union between technological innovations and cultural traditions in the environment. The world feels like a real place where real people live and work with the developers effort being obvious.
THE BAD:
First and foremost, one of Cradle's main selling points is "the story being built around the relations of the protagonist and a mechanical girl". Both the protagonist and the supporting NPC are pretty boring, their relationship hardly goes beyond story exposition and Q&A, and the voice acting for both of them is detached and uninvested. The two always speak in a disinterested monotone (but she's a robot, so it's partially forgivable), and often the interaction ends when the girl suddenly says "whoops lol I'm broken again fix me pls".
Which leads me to my next point: The game is repetitive. After talking to the girl for a bit and having her spew story exposition and lore like a fountain of uninterested monotone, you have to set out to a nearby park to collect a new part to keep her operational and repeat the process. To collect these parts you play some minigames, and my god they are so bland. There are only two variants of minigames that you're forced to play several times over the course of the game, and both of them are in essence pretty much the same. The objective is collect 30 colored blocks, work around a hazard and try not to notice the recycled concept. This is made even worse by Cradle's control scheme which isn't suited to this kind of gameplay. The controls are stiff, slow, blocky, sticky and awkward. Making a minigame that is supposed to be simple in it's design become more frustrating than it's worth.
Finally, the open world is in essence restricted to 3 areas worth seeing. Everything else is barren, uninteresting and not worth the time or effort to sort through. Making the open world mechanic entirely pointless.
So with all things considered, do I recommend this game? It's tough to say, I'm feeling pretty neutral leaning slightly towards the positive side. The effort put into the world is obvious, but it falls short with boring characters. The map looks beautiful, but is dragged down by the lack of anything worth exploring to see. The storyline is great, and I mean really, really great, but the gameplay is so slow and feels bogged down.
So my recommendation? Take it for what it's worth, a possible entry into a great game world filled with a lot of possibilities. I would love to see a franchise grow from this, because it would be a waste of potential if it ended here.

Call of Pripyat is the much awaited sequel of Shadow of Chernobyl, the first STALKER game. As soon as I completed SoC I sought this game out. Needless to say it took a few hours inorder to get really into it.
The game starts out rather slow, though arguably all the STALKER games do. Once you get into the gameplay and fully immersed into the game world, you truly enjoy it. Pripyat is far more stable and less buggy then Shadow of Chernobyl was. Which is a major upside to the frequent crashing and freezing that game had. The gameplay feels a lot more streamlined with closer ties to sandbox games like Grand Theft Auto then RPGs.
Really Call of Pripyat is well worth the price of admission. It lacks the heavy plot and character presence that Shadow of Chernobyl had, but makes up for it greatly in gameplay.

the world:
-abandoned city, partially under water
-water, vines and algeas everywhere
mechanics:
-no enemies
-no combat
-no damage or dying
-just driving a boat, climbing and objects to gather
story:
-mainly driven by cutscenes (after using supply drops) and pictures found in abandoned structures
-linear and short
setting:
-weather variety (has no gameplay effect, just visuals): normal, sunny, rainy, storm
-day / night cycles (again just visuals)
-the game is somewhat between scary at night due to the huge whales coming your way and all the abandoned structures and beautiful if the sun comes into play with the reflections on structures and water
I think the game is best described as explorative adventure: You're either using your boat to explore, to get somewhere or you'll be climbing structures.
Your only real choice is where you go, so you're free to explore and aren't forced to do anything in any specific order. That's not an issue as in this game there's neither combat nor falling nor death nor are there enemies.
The controls work pretty well for climbing, no complicated inputs required, are very simple. The boat is a little wonky but well controlable.
On water you can find other boats to scavenge them and upgrade your boat's engine, which prolongs it's turbo boost a little.
On any of the abandoned structures you'll find 2 things:
-paintings, telling the story of what happened
-supply goods (better loot those only after you're done looting the place)
Finding all the supplies is the goal of the whole game. Each time one supply drop is looted you're brought back to your starting area and the story continues, adding new tasks after that.
The game has a lot of good design decisions for it's simplicity. The spyglass allows marking spotted objects on the map and even points an arrow towards objects not yet on your screen for you to focus and mark them. You don't even need to zoom in, it's a good and useful feature, especially if used from high positions. The camera, which in other games is often an issue, actually helps spotting objects you might have missed otherwise and is freely turnable, even while climbing. Objects to interact with always highlight the "use" button above them when being close enough, so that it's always clear what can and can't be interacted with. Such objects also emit a "shine" effect from time to time from a distance, making it easier to find them when driving by with the boat. The controls are simple and respond well. Neither climbing nor using the boat causes any trouble and no special input is required at any time. It's just simple and it works.
The downsides: The game is short, linear and much of the same. The replay value is zero, except if you're in the mood for the game again, as each new game will be exactly the same, as the only difference you can make is by your choice where you go.
I'd recommend this game to you if you
-like exploring places
-are okay with the fact that you'll spend quite some time with boat driving and climbing
-want to spend some time in a stress-free environment
-care about a game's story and it's setting
The more of these points don't match the less I'd recommend this game to you. This one won't ever be a super-awesome must recommend game because it's too repetitive, with too little content and it's not randomized a bit BUT it's well made with what's in it. Good for one playthrough.

I dont typically write long reviews, people dont read them anyways, but I feel the necessity to say something with this game.  It surprisingly blew me away.
Ill just do the pros/cons list and after than some tips with no story spoilers but with gameplay tips that will help your enjoyment if you get this game.
Pros:
- The graphics are well done. Day and night sequences and weather effects all seem realistic and draw you into the atmosphere of the city. The water, which is prevalent in the game, is one of the most realistic renderings I have ever seen.
- Im not a huge fan of 3rd person control, but with no fighting, its very easily managed.
- The story: I finished the game without collecting everything because I felt compelled. I wanted to do so (saying why would be a spoiler).  But you can continue to collect the secrets after the end of the story, so no problem.
- When obtaining story mode items, the paths are long, but the game cutscenes and doesnt make you backtrack.
- The game explains the tools which are available to you, but Ill still give some tips.
Cons:
- For anyone who likes action, this is not your game.  You cant die (although for me thats almost a pro).
- It is rather short.  Would be a fairer price for the length of the game at 10. Try to get it on sale.
Gameplay tips which are helpful to know, even though you would figure them out eventually:
- Get a bunch (you dont need that many though) of boat parts to help you zip around the city quicker.
- Use your telescope early and often.  Its the easiest way to find items in the city and the game would be impossible without it.  Every time you climb to a new level of any building, use it in all directions you can.  Some items are not visible from lower levels, whilst some may not be visible from higher levels.
- Lose yourself in the story and pay attention to the secrets.  The story pictures are vague enough to let you interpret the story in your on way.

Graphics

Gameplay

I have played Oblivion for about 80+ hours, completed The Shivering Isles and the main questline. I still haven't gotten around to completing EVERY quest in the game, but I got most of it.
In Oblivion, you start out in a prison cell after a small monologue and character creator. An NPC mocks your choice of race and then the emporer himself comes to your cell. The Septim line is being attacked by an unknown force, and he is escaping the city to survive. Destiny destiny destiny, tutorial, class picking, bla bla bla... and then you finally are put into the world. When you first step out, you'll either say one of two things: "Wow! This is amazing!" Or: "Wow! These graphics suck!" Oblivion is a dated classic, and doesn't look as good as games do now. But, if you can look past that, you can really find a gem.
Like many RPGs, they either leave much to be desired or a years worth of adventure. The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is full of places to go and things to do. But, this is where some problems arise. With so much to do leaves a lot to be desired, and some quests end up being your typical dungeon crawler. But the idea of having an open world to explore and do whatever you want is overwhelming and terrific. Every 1 in 3 quests though did have a great amount of originality to it, from stealing a prized gem in the imperial castle itself or going to another dimension to stop a man from destroying the world. It really is amazing if you can look past the typical dungeon quests that get boring after a while.
Finally, the gameplay; the meat of the review. Oblivion's leveling is complicated at best and very hard to do sometimes. It tends to be stressful, and quite honestly, dull. Skyrim had done it much better. Swordplay tends to be just slashing around a sword hoping to hit. Magic is cool, though, as if you can get into the mages college, you can customize your spells. Archery takes precision and is pretty fun to try out. The difficulty slider in the options menu is literally just "How many times do you want to hit this guy until he goes down?" There is no reason whatsoever to put it up, just keep it 1/4 up to make it better. Fighting is fun in general, TL:DR.
In the end, Oblivion is fun. It's really hard to critique this without coming across as a fan. But, I am a big fan of RPGs and you should take this review in the eyes of one. I can't see a huge FPS fan getting this and having as much fun as I did. This is really only a game for people who are not new to RPGs in general and like the idea of them. This game is a great game though, and I do fully recommend it from the eyes of an RPG fan.

Let me tell you a story:
It was a Saturday night, I had just gotten back from a party and I wanted, no needed to play some games. I chose Chivalry because I hadn't played it for weeks. I had been oddly thinking about Batman for some reason. And then it hit me. I will become the Dark knight himself by punching and kicking my way through the forces of evil. Yes, In a world full of Messercopters and Poptart shields, I will become the hero Chivalry has, but probably doesn't need. I joined a server. The map was Dining hall, and people where dying left, right, and center. Men armed with abnormally large hammers could be seen terrorizing the populace. I sheathed my sword, and out came my trusty fists. I'd seen a man's head get squashed right before my eyes. Taken aback by such cruelty, I chased after the murderer and hit him in the back of his thick golden helmet. He appeared a bit disoriented as he groggily swung his hammer. It hit me in the stomach, knocking me out for the count. The referee had just gotten to 10 as he too fell to the men with hammers. It hurt to much to get up for the judge's final decision, as my assailant taunted over my unconscious body. I woke up an hour later. My guantlets had been bloodied. I had slain 9 crooks, and everyone else had died. Seeing that I had obviously emerged victorious, I leaped out the window. I never really did learn how to fly, and the plated armor I had been wearing didn't appear to have a cape attached to it. Damn you Alfred. I hit the ground with a loud thud. I got up and walked off. Chivalry still hadn't been purified of the evil that I set out to destroy. But the day was mine and that's all that mattered.

This is a very fun mod, and I really enjoy the arcade-esque feel and new weapons. I also like the kicking ability, and I feel like this really appeals to fans of SMOD. I also love the tons of options to customize your game, although I feel there are some areas that need some more customization options. While I genuinely enjoy this game, I have a few complaints and suggestions. First, the complaints. Whenever I play combine firefight, about five minutes in the game crashes. This is very frustrating for me because it is my favorite gamemode. I also feel like there are too few maps. It gets boring playing on the same map over and over again.
Now for the suggestions: I feel like there are too few maps, and I know that these are Half life 2 Deathmatch maps, but I would enjoy some more custom maps for the game. This would allow many more hours of gameplay for me, because playing on the same maps gets boring quickly.
Another suggestion I have is the statistics of enemies. I believe that it would be a really cool feature to be able to customize the types of weapons that certain enemies use, the amount of health for enemies, and the ability to change how common certain enemies are. I would really enjoy this, as I feel like it would allow you to make the game easier or harder for players. Another reason for wanting to be able to customize enemies health and weapons is a smaller complaint, but a complaint nonetheless. When I have played Combine Firefight, I have found it very frustrating that it seems like almost every enemy spawns with a shotgun. I feel like this is rather annoying, because I will have an abundance of shotgun ammo and no ammo of any other type. I would like it if either enemies spawned only with class specific weaponry, like Combine soldiers will only spawn with AR2's or Smg1's, and shotgunners will spawn with only shotguns, or if the game allows players to determine what weapons specific enemies spawned with.
Overall, I really enjoy this game and I can't wait for it to achieve a more polished and professional state.

A somewhat fresh and unique take on a horrific robot future that I personally can't wait for in real life.
But back to the game. This is another one of those slightly ambiguous get as much out of the story as you put into it kinda of narrative experiences. So saying anything specific is full on spoiler territory and honestly one of the best features about this game is the way its told. The way the world feels real and actually lived in.
Let me start by saying I absolutely hate reading things in games. Not in real life but in games it always feels contrived, forced as if they could think of no other way of communicating the idea. It does not feel that way in Cradle.
In Cradle, there are newspaper articles that are stuck to the insides of cabinets, buried under clothes or old cooking utensils. And you can read all of them. The strange part was, I actually wanted to. It gives you just enough information each time that you want to click on everything to try to piece together one more string or on going theory as to the nature of the world as it is.
Your character has amnesia.. this is never really explained which is slightly disappointing not only because its cliche and a narrative explanation would be great but because everything else in the world is explained. The only reason I could come up with for the character to have amnesia is a conceit for why he needs to ask and explore so many things. A story telling mechanic. Now at this point you're probably aware you speak to robots in the game. I won't reveal the nature of them in game but their eyes are actual video of a real humans. AND to top it off this is actually explained narratively within the games lore and it totally fits. Not only does it add incredible interesting visuals to the world its actually there for a reason.
Now for the parts I didn't care for, There is a mini game in which you collect blocks and throw them into a tube of light to collect them. Its fine. You do this multiple times however and one of them is a little much. Its more frustrating than not. However I did find through this you can skip the mini games. I only skipped the one but some part of me is sad I didn't rise to the occasion and prevail. I thought about it later and realized that's not what I came here for anyways and not being frustrated was much more of a desired outcome. I wanted to know more about the world. As I stated previously this mini games existence is not just fodder for your fingers to increase play through time. It is also explained within the lore.
I will state however the ending does not give all the answers and leaves you to interpret details and is arguably better for leaving those details for you to ponder afterward.

I love the story of this game, but there are enough other problems with it that I simply can't recommend it.
The first and most egregious  problem is the 'block game' that you play to progress the story several times.  It isn't fun, and is tied to the story of the game only through symbolism that the game never bothers to explain.  It's first person platforming, which barely works at the best of times, while the environment is changed by red enemies that modify the level around you while you aren't looking.  No, no thank you.  I want more story and absolutely zero of that.
The other problem is that the story simply isn't in the game.  I've read some theories put together by people that make the story of the game make more sense, but the game doesn't get you there.  It simply implies greater things...that's not enough.  If you're going to tell a story, tell it.  Don't make us put together the symbolism to show off how clever your story is.  Once again, no thank you.
I want more games like this, I want more games in this universe, even.  I want to know about the story of this game, but the game can't be bothered to tell its own story, and the gameplay it uses to gate it's story is no fun at all.  No, there's a glimmer of something brilliant here, but this impementation isn't something you want.

Agatha Christie - The ABC Murders
Not often I do game reviews, but thought I’d give my two cents after finishing this one.
Before playing this game I’d never heard of Hercule Poirot, and was pleasantly surprised to look further into him and Agatha Christie’s portfolio.
I’m a fan of Frogware’s Sherlock Holmes games and thought I’d give this one a try. Surprisingly, this game’s developer Artefacts Studios is not the studio I would have expected to make this game looking at their past works. But those games were most likely to finance making this game, which all right.
The game is a point & click mystery game following Hercule Poirot as he tries to discover the identity of the ABC murder. For a first-time game in this genre, it’s a rather good first entry from the developer. Although one might initially think of Poirot as a Sherlock Holmes rip-off, he’s a noticeably different character. He doesn’t rely on deductive reasoning nearly as much as Holmes, he’s vainer, and is a Belgium who uses Belgian and French words in his talk. One of the unique (and very amusing) elements of the game was how you can collect “Ego points” for acting like Poirot. One fun way of doing this is by clicking on mirrors so he can examine and manicure his moustache. XD I enjoyed the setting, story, characters, and locations in the game. The puzzles were a little difficult, providing unique and interesting challenges, and not being as hard as other puzzle games like in the Sherlock ones.
It could use a bit more polishing, but that’s to be expected with further installments. Frogware’s Sherlock games didn’t start out all that great, but they progressed with each installment. Some elements in this game that I think needed improvement are: having a mouse sensitivity and other control options. Most of the voice acting was good but some actors could have tried a bit harder. Also, the trophies constantly popping up in game, many for just progressing through the story were getting a bit emersion breaking. I mean I liked all the funny names for them, but there were a lot, many for just doing basic progressing of the story.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game, it was fun and brought me into pre-WWII England with these characters. The game takes care to acknowledge Poirot’s past and his interactions with characters from the books. Artefacts Studios did a great job adapting the characters and feel (from what I can tell, I’ll admit I haven’t read the books, just overviews) of the Poirot series. I hope they continue to do more of Agatha Christie’s stories. Very recommended. :)

Agatha Christie - The ABC Murders makes valiant attempt to turn a wonderful mystery novel into a game. While the production value and voice acting are for the most part on point, game design seems a bit forced and over all fails to do the novel justice.
Let me start off by saying I played the game first and then listened to the audio book for comparison. There were some differences in the story details. But Microid mostly made changes where Hercule Poirot was simply not involved in the case.  However, there were some changes that were a bit odd. The novel makes it a point to keep the number of suspects open. But very quickly the game drops the suspect count down to two.  Now, this is done so that you could get a sense progress in the game but it makes the ending a forgone conclusion. Moreover, they outright cut out the last murder due to the fact the Hercule Poirot was not involved in its direct investigation. This, and some other altered scenes, actually robs the criminal of some vital planning they had done. I wouldn’t say any change was a deal breaker, but some may consider the changes a bad interpretation of the story.
The game, however, does well enough with visuals and voice acting. It use a cell shaded style that’s not to taxing on GPUs. Voice acting is nice and clear and doesn’t leave you wanting. The failure is in game design. Gameplay is compartmentalized into about 4 styles. First, is good old fashion Point and Click evidence searching, where you look around a crime scene for items you might need. Can’t say it was a fun part of the game though, there was more pixel hunting than I cared for. Next, there was an Interview type game element, not unlike L.A. Noirs interviews, where you first examine a person to determine their state then you get a choice of questions to ask. Depending on what you ask you could get the interviewee to cooperate well or to cooperate not so well.  Beyond getting some points, it really was just dialog. The Third game play style came in the form of a quiz.  You would take what you know to answer questions about the case, sometimes the answers where straight forward, other required a bit of a leap. The last gameplay style was “Room”-esque puzzle solving. Everyone seems to have a locked object that requires a complicated means of opening it. This definitely felt out of place, but it’s the main driving force of game play. None of the 4 styles of gameplay really meshed well with each other.
So with weak gameplay, it begs the question. Why not just make this a visual novel? Really, if you’re interested in Agatha Christie or mysteries in general you may enjoy the game.  While the gameplay did nothing genre defining or captivating, the story was interesting enough to push me forward. So if you are going to get this game, get it for the story.

Ah.  Baldur's gate.
I cant even tell you how many times i've played this game through to the end.  The world is massive, the NPCs feel human,  the quests are exciting, and the combat system is deep and nuanced.
And then there's the 'Enhanced Edition'.
It's difficult for me to recommend the enhancements 'overhaul games' added to baldur's gate simply because there aren't very many of them.  Almost all of the issues which existed in 2001 are present in the enhanced edition.   This includes (but is not limited to) :
- Cheating the combat system by initiating dialogue with a neutral NPC and then attacking them while they are stuck in the 'i want to talk to you' animation.
- Casting a spell in an area covered by fog of war and having your spellcaster get stuck in an endless casting loop which never results in the spell actually being cast.
- Pathfinding bugs
- Awkward looting of certain objects which requires that your character be in a specific spot to interact with the object.
I could go on.
In Overhaul's defense, they did add a few new NPCs to the mix, all of whom seem interesting and useful in their own right.  But it feels like they did this to try and distract from the underlying issue -  which is that they are adding icing on top of an old, rotting, cake.
I love baldur's gate and i'm enjoying the enhanced edition, but Bioware / Black Isle deserve the credit for that,  not Overhaul.  Only get this if you are a rabid fan of anything Baldur's Gate (like me) and just want to have one last spin around Faerun.  Everyone else should probably just buy the original version from
.  You'll save money, and you're getting almost exactly the same experience.

I personally liked the game. It's a nifty time-killer. You sail around a sunken city, climb dilapadated buildings and find stuff. That's about it. There are no enemies, there is no time limit. My dying brother survived for days without water and medicine while I was messing around, so you're in no hurry or anything. It's impossible to die in the game. The controlls are fine. The graphics are all right, it took some time to get used to them, but they do a nice job of setting the atmoshpere. The weather changes, time changes, it's nice. The music is okay. "Submereged" is a nice way to relax.
Basically, this game reminded me of "Shadow of the Colossus", only without the Colussuses, and, of course, of "Journey" and "Abzu". It's a climbing simulator, and the only danger is getting lost or bored. If this is your jam, sure, go ahead, buy the game. I had fun. I got my money's worth for about 10 bucks. If it were 20 bucks - not so much. Unless you want to support the developers, which is a good cause, I guess.
The trick to enjoying it is not to expect any challenge. Well, there are climbing puzzles, if you're interested in finding all of the secrets, and sailing around looking for animals, boat parts and scenery pieces, but that's about it. All in all, a relaxing experience. Maybe it could've been something more, but it's okay for what it is. A solid "B".
Now, the negatives.
- I understand how some people might find it boring. But it's my kind of boring, so I don't mind it that much. But it does get repetative. So if messing around with nothing much to do for a few hours isn't your idea of fun, you might want to skip this game. Even I had at one point or another wished for some element of excitement or, I don't know, urgency. Still, it felt fine, all in all.
- I found the speed of the character somewhat strange. She runs rather slowly, but climbs like a monkey. Just messed a bit with the pace, I guess.
- There is a minor possibility of getting stuck between a palm tree, a bush and a wall, but that happened to me only once, so, well, there's that. Just avoid tight spaces, and you'll be fine.
- Aaaand the big one. The game crashed twice. On the second-to-last cutscene, and on the very last cutscene. I had to see the ending on youtube. Well, at the very least it picked up after restart with the loot already in my posession, so I didn't have to climb all the way back for it again. But yeah, that was disappointing.
Still, I'd say "Yeah, sure, go ahead, I recomend it. Just make sure you know what you're getting into."

In full disclosure: 1) I haven't played a TON of early access games. 2) I don't typically enjoy sandbox games. 3) I'm a software developer so my perspective may be skewed.
This was a great experience from day one, I created a small local private server for myself and friends to play on and we had a blast for hours on end.
The game itself is being worked on constantly, the developers have patched issues as fast as can be expected for an early access game.
The game has a lot of features already, crafting and building is very functional with a decent amount of craftables, three tiers of building material options and a small handlful of offensive equipment that is currently heavily weighted to melee players.
I can't speak for the games entertainment value on a public server or in a PvP setting, I imagine it's fileld with the same level of grief that any game like this does and makes it unplayable.  In a personal/private setting you have the opportunity to explore a very unique world and build to your hearts content.
For early access there's a good 30 hours of content with base server settings before you'll start capping out on that "growth" feeling but there's plenty of caves/dungeons and a whole handful of world bosses scattered around to tackle as well as a lot of land to cover.
I haven't had a whole lot of technical issues that haven't been easily resolved; it's a fairly simple process to customize the settings of a server to make the game feel completely different.  I've never lost anything to updates and bugs and overall it's been a great experience.

Whilst the team porting this have done a superb job fixing the speed and saves, if you still have issues with it freezing / crashing - Try setting the conman_mp.exe file to run in Windows 95 compatibility mode (it's located in the game files) - Whilst you annoyingly have to validate this each time you want to play (it asks if you're ok with it making changes) this has given me 100% stability on this great game again

You can knock enemies unconscious (to gain control to distract other guards), divert with stones or lure with cigarettes (a particular favourite). Fortunately this doesn't detract from the ruthless difficulty that this game has thankfully retained. You're still left carefully studying enemy movements and scratching your head as you try to figure out the best approach - all without raising the dreaded alarm... that is, of course, until you get to blow the hell out of the place - Which still continues to be a satisfying sight
Quite frankly, if you loved the first one then you'll have no reason not to like this one

This game is an absolute classic of the RPG genre, and the gaming community as a whole. Oblivion had a certain spark to it that really set itself apart from any other RPG or Elder Scrolls game in the series. Though a bit dated now, I will recommend this game to any RPG fanatic come 20 years from now.
Now for the technical crap: The combat is a tad clunky, but not so much as to pull you out of the immersion. For its time the graphics were stunning, and it is still an amazingly beautiful game to this day. The main quest held what was undoubtedly one of the best storylines out of all the Elder Scroll games thus far, with hundreds of engaging side-quests that didn't feel like complete rubbish. Aside from the main quest, each side-quest had you feeling like you were actually helping or doing something resourceful in some way, much unlike Skyrim.
Now, all opinion aside, this game really did have quite a fantastic set of DLC. Knights of the Nine is a fantastic DLC that adds a hundred more hours into the game- what a fantastic DLC. If you are contemplating buying this game, or already have it, buy the game with all the DLC for a heightened Oblivion experience.
The only complaint I had with this game is the character creation/character models. They just look flat out stupid. If you mess around with the customization you can get your character to look halfway decent, but even for its time the facial textures on the character models were just plain weird looking. Though its not a game breaker by any means, not really THAT noticeable either, it is something to note.

The king of kings in the fantasy gaming community. This game series defined what a fantasy world should be like and is the foundation of any good fantasy RPG. Though it seems old to many young gamers, this game is a must have for any gamer that loves fantasy settings.
Each race in Oblivion has its own strengths and weaknesses, greatly defining each race and seperating them from everyone else. For instance, Bretons (A race in Oblivion) can wield powerful magics and start off with more magical energies than other races, though they are weaker than most. Khajit can sneak around more easily and can use their claws as weapons to hurt their foes.
There are many different classes in this game, each one serving a certain role. Do you want a warrior who also uses magic? Or would you rather prefer and rouge that uses illusions to hide his tracks as he steals jewels? If you don't like any of the classes, there is an option where you can create your own class, tailoring it to your own needs and wants. Combining a magic wielding class with a race that specilizes in certain classes of magics will allow you to become the greatest mage in the world or creating a two handed wielding orc to become the most feared barbarian in the lands.
And the fun doesn't stop there, each adventure is more interesting than the last. One play through may have you encounter a door to Oblivion where you must close the door before more demons pour through. Another play through may have you collect a strange weed with mystical powers. No play through is ever the same.
If you haven't played Oblivion and you are interested in Fantasy Settings, then Oblivion is a must have in your library.

Crusader Kings is a truly phenomonal Grand Strategy game and opened me up to what a true Grand Strategy is. My previous experience with the genre consisted of the Total War franchise, this game goes so much deeper than they did. Intrigue, War, Assassanation and Diplomacy all play integral parts in a game of Crusader Kings and allow such a great level of freedom that you'll be able to sink hundreds of hours into it. The DLC adds even more depth to an already great game, extending the time periods that are playable and adding in more nations, more religions and more mechanics.
My primary criticism of the game lies with something i've been praising previously: The DLC. Although some of the packs are great and add in a whole host of new features that truly expand the game, many are not, many are song packs, portrait packs and other such minor things. Although they are 'optional', I still feel their existence does taint the game a bit, especially when some of them include features that should have been in the game as a base (portraits for each major ethnic group). Another minor niggling is the visuals, the map is passable and the faces are medicore at best but honestly, its only a minor fault because that isnt really what I look for in a grand strategy.
Despite those criticisms, I would still wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in grand strategy, just be warned, its a difficult game to get to grips with. But it is worth it when you do.

It doesn't have quite the oppressive, loner atmosphere that characterized the first game, but mods (in particular, Misery) easily fill in that void. This game has three very large open areas to explore and a great deal of handcrafted, well-scripted quests as opposed to the endlessly generated "go here, fetch that" quests that were the daily fare of the previous two games.
The overall plot arc isn't as interesting as its predecessors, but it does reference them well. It also has several endings, Fallout slideshow style, based upon your involvement throughout the game, which lends towards a satisfying conclusion and encourages replayability. Call of Pripyat is the culmination of the systems introduced in the previous two games - setting, gameplay mechanics, and introduces an extra layer of attention to detail and care that pushes it above its predecessors.\
I'd call it the most complete S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience. If you play only one of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, pick this one.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is an extremely fun game with interesting mechanics that give it a great longevity. It is very fun to play.
For about 9 hours(ish).
Chivalry unfortunately is a game that doesn't get better with age. Rather, it ages like milk. After 9 hours of brutal slaughter and decapitations you will begin to enter the game's seamy underbelly.
This is due to their two different server types: Beginner and Advanced.
Beginner is where you will spend the first 9 or so hours in Chivalry, playing with those under level 15. Matches in these servers are incredibly fun to play, with everyone at an even level allows for fun, fair - albeit gratuitous- fights.
This part of the game I loved, playing nearly daily to get my fill of medieval mediation.
But then we level up, become a big boy, and the gates to beginner servers close.
Due to this you have no choice but to play in the advanced servers, but this seems fair right? I mean, isn't it good that there is a separation in skill levels?
True, but as you begin your first tentative steps into advanced matches, you'll notice that the game you loved so much is just a little bit different. That fiery girl you fell in love with turned out to be no girl at all; in fact, as she undresses before your eyes you realise, she's a tumour.
And a pretty bad tumour at that, poor thing.
What I mean to say, through poor analogies, that the advanced section of the game is unmoderated garbage.
Hey, did you enjoy intricate duels where you used the mechanics to simulate a real fight?
Not any more, now it's a lot easier: majority of players seem to instead  prefer exploiting the game's mechanics by switching to third-person and violently moving there mouse in various directions to break the physics and strike with moves that are near-impossible to defend from.
And if you love that notion, then I'm sure that knowing that (at least in my personal experience) about 1 in every 3 players has some kind of cheats or hacks enabled will come as an absolute treat.
This wouldn't be a huge issue, if the devs did anything about it, such as enforcing better anti-cheat policies, or even setting up moderated servers specifically for those who want actual battles.
But in the meantime we just have to make do with a cancerous community and a broken game.
So yeah, with the state that Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is in, I just can't reccommend it.
Which sucks, because under that pile of broken garbage lies a genuinely fun game.
I could semi-reccommmend picking it up in a sale, just so you can play the early servers; or just create another steam account once you reach level 15, whatever helps you sleep at night.
Alternatively you could sit pretty until the devs decide to change some things up.
But to be honest, I kind of doubt that much - if anything - will change in the game, I doubt the devs are gonna put much more time into it.
But hey, could be wrong, hopefully I am.
So pick Chivalry up if you want some limited fun, or if you're into broken games.
Or save your money for a rainy day, or Mafia III, or whatever.

The interesting thing for me about Knightmare Tower is that it was one of the few games I played first on the Ouya.  However, despite being on the not-so-great Ouya, it played well and was a ton of fun.  So much so that I bought it again on Steam, even with it being the same game.  That’s not something I believe I’ve done very often when you exclude remasters.
Knightmare Tower is a simple game, one I believe first came out on Android and subsequently migrated to every platform that would have it.  The Steam version of course allows mouse control that I think feels a little more responsive than using a controller.  The game itself has you launching yourself up a tower and attacking/jumping off enemies that pop up from below to keep yourself propelled upward as lava (for some reason) chases you from below. You gain gold and rescue princesses that you use to upgrade yourself to go faster, do more damage, and accomplish more in general.  The end goal is getting to the top and fighting a simply designed yet challenging boss.
It sounds very basic, and to some degree it is, but it’s a well-polished experience that is still challenging and felt like a much deeper game than it actually was.  It just makes me wish that Juicy Beast would bring more games to Steam given that they are still actively developing them.  If you think you’d be interested in Knightmare Tower but don’t want to shell out the $4 (or whatever the sale price is), there is a Flash version of the game out there – assuming Flash hasn’t fully died by the time you read this review.  So you can use that to gauge whether you want a more complete version with all the progress that comes with an installation and saves.  Either way, Knightmare Tower is a definite recommendation from me, and I hope the developer has another game planned for Steam sometime in the near future… maybe Burrito Bison: Launcha Libre (pls)?

The good:
- true successor to dungeon keeper with same gameplay mechanics (unlike Dungeons)
- variety of new content and abilities
- irreplaceable old mentor brings amazing voice acting
The bad:
- campaign is just to short  and rushed to properly utilize all new gameplay features
- some missions introduce bunch of new abilities and aspects that you will never have time to test properly
- there is a feeling that you are being rushed out at every step, even by the mentor
- "mentor" seems to be the boss, with you just being his tool
- limited building space in many missions (apparently addressed in Heart of gold expansion?)
- creature management is much more automatic leaving you to just build rooms and place rally flags
- bad engine optimization causing framerate to drop from 200 to 30 as you dungeon grows
- the wall tiles are perfect squares without charming variation in shape and elevation as seen in DK2
- less memorable creatures with less interesting designs than originals
Conclusion:
Do I recommend it?
- Yes, definitely if you are Dungeon Keeper fan. There is just no other alternative.
Is it good as original Dungeon Keeper 1/2?
- Not even close, unfortunately
But it has a good development team that worked hard and passed through a lot of trouble to make it the way it is and their effort should be saluted.

Before I launch into the meat of my review: you're not going to get Dungeon Keeper 3... ever. It's been 20 years. Go back and play DK2 and you'll see a lot of great ideas, but really poor execution. I bought this game in Early Access because it was one of several attempts to recapture the "magic." I later picked up DK and DK2 through another service; and, even in Early Access, this game was surperior.
I'm finally posting a review because I thought WftO was robbed for the "Labor of Love" trophy during the '17 Winter Sale. I played this through Early Access and beat it upon release. Picking the game up now, I see that it has been polished to a high-sheen... and, I hope that the developers make a sequel that takes us to the Overworld.
In the meantime, the Dungeons franchise by Kalypso picked up the torch and did an admirable job of making a sequel. I won't compare the two, except to say that the dungeon-building and combat in WftO is much tighter and well-balanced. That's what you get when you try to pull a Molyneux, mix genres, and pack too much into one game.
This has been a labor of love for the developers, and really should stand (on its own) as the pinnacle-example of the dungeon-building genre.

So, Jet Set Radio, despite how much older it is, is still a great game. This re-release however, helps cements it's place. Though I think Jet Set Radio Future is better (even though they haven't ported it yet), JSR is still a good game.
Pros:
-The controls feel nice, as it is a game that helped shape Sports Platforming games (yep, that's what Tony Hawk Pro Skater is too)
-The pretty cell-shaded textures, which kind of help it age better than most games.
-The unlockable characters, graffiti, and bonus tracks (which are optional, but make the game better.)
-The excellent soundtrack that fits the game.
-The real graffiti that you can use in the game to tag walls in missions.
-The story isn't bad, and helps keep the pace of the game up.
-The voice actors did a well job, making the chase scenes much more memorable.
-The game works with almost any gamepad.
-Option to make your own grafitti
-Has a good points system, allowing you to have a fair way of getting points.
-The ability to use your gained characters after you beat the game (sort of like a Start+ sorta deal)
-The "rival" challenges to gain the extra characters in-game are pretty fun on their own.
Cons:
-Has a difficultly spike for inexperienced players, some levels even requiring me to play over 10 times...
-Tutorial is harder than the actual game, but the game is playable without it nonetheless.
-Unless you have a gamepad, this game is hard as balls.
-The controls are not as responsive when you are in the air, sometimes making you miss a platform/railing.
-The story feels rushed sometimes, but you aren't playing this game for story, are you?
-No restart button... In a sports/platform game... So back to the map and selecting it if you fail.
-Some characters are almost impossible to play normal missions with (exspecially Combo or Pots if you unlock them)
-Boss battle is a let down compaired to the previous missions, but still hard.
-The camera can mess you up sometimes, so be prepaired to press the camera reset alot.
-I beat it once in around 12 hours, but you might want a longer game.
-Only single-player, so unless you and your friend like waiting...
Personal score: 7.75
A good game, and stands up through time, but isn't as great as it used to be I guess. It's still a game I recommend.
Hopefully, it's sequel JSRF will get a port, but for now buy this. I promise you won't be sorry... except when you fail a mission... then you can be sorry for missing that jump on the railing to get over the waterway... besides, the only way for JSRF to be here is if enough of this game is sold, and they realize we want JSRF.

This game is an amazing love letter to Dungeon Keeper. Seriously, if you have ever played Dungeon Keeper, and loved it as much as I do, then do yourself a favor and buy this game!
There are many Dungeon Keeper clones on the market, but War for the Overworld is the one that stays closest to the original. Honestly, it feels more like the true sequel we never got, rather than a spiritual successor.
For those of you who never played Dungeon Keeper, allow me to endarken you:
You play as the antagonist. You are the bad guy, and you are here to oversee your own personal underground dungeon. You do this from an isometric perspective. You control your minions to build and gather resources for you, while training monsters to hunt down and slaughter pesky adventurers and heroes trying to raid your dungeon. In some instances you can even directly possess anyone of your creatures and take to the fight directly through the first-person perspective.
The game is incredibly deep when you realize that different monsters level up and unlock new abilities which can help out tremendously in your battle to defend and expand your dungeon.
Toss in some dark humor and you have yourself an amazing treasure of a game.
This one of those games that you can focus and be directly involved in every skirmish,
or sit back and let your minions do the heavy lifting, if you're watching YouTube and Netflix.
It is a fantastic game to unwind and explore with. Each dungeon you design will feel like a masterpiece once you discover how to efficently cater to your playstyle.
Do create a baracks and train goblins to be your main fighting force?
Or do you take enemy heroes prisoner, and convert them to your side through torture and interrogation in the torture chamber?
Hell, maybe you prefer an army of beast creatures instead. Or spellcasters. Or any combination. Will your dungeon rely on traps and barricades to keep out invaders, or will you focus on massing monsters to combat any threat?
The pet dungeon is the place to experiment and play the game at your own pace. No pressure, unless you want to add enemy heroes to invade in waves. Or even pick and choose which heroes you want to attack and from where. The pet dungeon is the best sandbox base builder you'll ever find.
Fair warning, you may lose track of time playing this gem!

Bardbarian is way, way cool.  It's a remarkably-good mashup of tower-defence, overhead-view arena shmup, and console-RPG, with a couple of extra modes that not only add to replay value, but help advance the main game, too.
There's a lot of tongue-in-cheek humor going on here.  The gameplay is really solid -- I've never felt that I've been defeated unfairly -- it always feels to me as though I've screwed up something simple to get myself given out.
This game has a whole lot of "just one more go" in it... and the nice bit is that almost every go, no matter how poor it turns out, will help advance Brad, his entourage, and the town, just a bit further towards surviving the onslaught of evil.
In short, you will get a helluva lot of fun for your $5 (or less, on sale).  The artwork oozes character and style, and so does the writing (which is mostly descriptions of units and items, but still.. the humor and thoughtfulness shine even there).  It's a totally charming game and a great bending of the tower-defence genre.   I love that it plays very much like a bullet-hell arena shooter, though maybe not quite as hellish as real BH shmups.

Bardbarian is one of these games I went into "just to try", and find myself returning to now quite regularly. It has quite an original concept, being a tower defense with more than a twist. There is a central point to defend, and there are enemies coming in to attack, ever more, ever more strong. So far, so good.
But. The towers to defend your stronghold are not static, but are attached as party-members to the Bard you can steer around the battlefield, destroying enemies "on the fly" as it were. You do not attack yourself, but one can enhance the attacks of your party-members by playing short guitar-riffs, played free by collecting notes. Extra attack, speed, defence and a short freeze of the enemies come in handy as the waves of enemies get stronger. As usual, units and your Bard himself can be upgraded, for this one needs the coins the enemies drop in abundance.
In order to succeed, fast reactions and speedy thinking are necesarry. I found it difficult at first to keep an overview of the battlefield, as several issues need attention: where are the enemies coming in at thier strongest, which buffs are needed, did any of my units die so I have to summon a new one, is my stronghold still going strong, .... But after a while I got used to it and enjoyed running all over the place, with my little but brave party. Playing it with an Xbox 360-controller certainly helps and feels most natural.
Enemies get quite strong before halfway in the game, and so sustaining the 20 waves is no easy task. Every 5 levels there is a boss, but for the most part enemies do not change that much during the game. Still, with an extra "free run" mode (try to get as far as you can dodging the enemies) and with a "survival mode", one can come back to this game again and again. As can be expected nowadays, there are Steam trading cards and some inviting achievements, which really help to appreciate the game to the full. No classic, but still very enjoyable. Don't hesitate to buy this, especially when it's on sale or in a bundle.
Gameplay: 20/30

Technical & stability: 9/10
Personal rating: 7/10
Overall: 71/100

As an Agatha Christie fan, there are a lot of things I like about this game. It feels like a proper Poirot story: no big action scenes or rushing in half-cocked, that just isn't his style. You figure out the clues bit by bit by examining your surroundings and asking the right questions of your suspects.
The game is well-made and the graphics and music fit the style well. Unfortunately, it glitched and lagged a bit on my computer. Not enough to make it unplayable, but it was a mild annoyance and caused me to miss a few observations that I needed for one of the achievements. (As a personal gripe, I did not think the voice actor for Poirot was a very good choice, but there we are.)
All in all I enjoyed the game, and it gave me a meaty story to sink my teeth into (~10 hours to finish). I just hope that they will smooth out the rough edges a bit more with the next Poirot title: that would make for a game -really- worth playing.
