I wake up in what seems like a strange hut. It’s adorned with all sorts of decorations that feel Central Asian. At first glance, it’s filled with familiar items you would expect to see in this setting such as a firewood stove, but on closer inspection, I see things straight out of the future. Strange contraptions, digitized flowers, and most peculiar of all, a mechanical woman is sitting on the table. Her upper body seems normal, but she’s been altered from the waist down to act as some sort of vase for the digitized flowers. She is deactivated. The big red button beckons me to press it. She starts to twitch randomly, then settles down for a brief moment and looks straight at me before she slouches over and shuts down once again. There’s a calendar by the door. It’s the year 2076 and I’m in Mongolia. This isn’t a hut, it’s a yurt. I open the door and step outside. At first I see a small fenced yard beyond which the horizon stretches out to uncover rolling hills among the steppes. I get the feeling that this is going to be one hell of a journey of discovery.
Cradle is a first-person adventure game by Ukrainian developer Flying Cafe for Semianimals. It weaves a fascinating, intriguing and wholly original science fiction story set in a world in which a cataclysmic event has made people unable to reproduce. In a desperate attempt to preserve humanity until a permanent solution is found, people transfer their souls and consciousness into mechanical bodies. You will discover many details about this complex, layered story as you freely inspect and interact with pretty much any item you find in the world such as magazines, journals, pictures and so on. You will also be able to interact with a couple of characters who will provide information and tasks which will move the story along. The writing is strong throughout and while it provides plenty of exposition regarding the world and what has been happening on a global scale, it failed to provide a meaningful emotional and personal connection between the two main characters. The fact that the voice acting for the playable character is rather stiff and detached created an even wider gulf in their relationship. However, I have to point out that the voice acting for the two non-playable characters is very convincing.
The true star of the game is its game world. While it is structured as an open world, it’s relatively small and mostly takes place in and around the yurt and a nearby deteriorated entertainment park. I didn’t found this to be a negative at all, I felt this focus created a true bond between the player and the surroundings. This strong sense of place is further heightened by the magnificent art style. There aren’t a whole lot of landmarks in the game, but each one is superbly detailed and everything just feels cohesive which is odd considering that it is a mixture of Central Asian, Eastern European (visible in the tram design, for example) and cyberpunk influences. I deeply appreciated the fact that the developers were able to create a world in which the old Mongolian tradition of eagle hunting mixes with cutting edge concepts such as transferring consciousness onto artificial carriers in a way that makes perfect sense. The subdued yet poignant soundtrack also added to the atmosphere immensely. I simply cannot overstate the impact of the game world on the enjoyment of the game.
Regarding the gameplay, Cradle will mostly task you to find certain objects and use them in the appropriate way. For example, in the very beginning, the player is tasked to make breakfast. That means you’ll have to light the firewood stove, put the pot on it and then find and use all the necessary ingredients. Even though the game is a bit too obtuse at times (at one point, I spent around 15 minutes looking for a TV remote in the yurt which I found to be completely unnecessary and flat-out bad design), it is mostly rather generous with its hints and most items are where it makes sense for them to be. You have limited inventory slots at your disposal which is fine because you don’t need to collect and carry around everything you see and find. The puzzles are situational and you will only need certain items at specific points in time. Another big gameplay element are the mini-games you’ll have to do in the run-down entertainment park. These are arguably the weakest parts of the game. Basically, each time you’re placed a large room filled with cubes and you have to throw cubes of a certain color into some sort of digital stream in the center of the room. Your progress is impeded by digital enemies which will destroy cubes and/or block access to the stream. The whole ordeal feels tedious and laborious and it feels as if it was thrown in there just to provide some gameplay. Happily, you have the option to skip these segments if you happen to fail them, but you still have to endure the whole thing until you either succeed or fail.
My biggest and most serious complaint comes from the purely technical side. It’s not the game’s performance, it runs pretty well even on more modest systems, it’s the limited options and lack of key remapping. Just like a lot of warm-blooded PC gamers, the first thing I do when I start up a game is go to the settings menu. When I clicked on Cradle’s settings menu, it opened a single window with rather limited graphics options. There’s the V-sync, AA, texture and just a few other options including a 1-10 quality slider. Needless to say, it’s not really clear at all what this slider affects. However, while having limited graphics options is certainly not great, it’s not really such a big deal. On the other hand, I was appalled once I realized I cannot remap input controls in any way. The game uses a WASD control scheme which I’m sure a lot of people use and they’re fine with it, but the fact of the matter is that a lot of people do not use that scheme and it is simply inexcusable to release a PC game without the ability to remap keys. Cradle also does not have gamepad support, so the developers are quite literally saying that it’s their way or the highway. Being forced to play the game with a control scheme I do not prefer definitely had an impact on my overall enjoyment of the game and was the direct cause of frustration in certain segments of the game.
Cradle is a remarkable yet flawed game and I cannot escape the feeling that it could have been truly exceptional. It is held back by certain design and storytelling issues as well as an ending that is far too ambiguous for its own good, and it fails to provide all the necessary options for the player, but it shines due to its beautiful game world, intriguing theme and characters, and strong atmosphere. Despite its flaws, it is a game that should definitely be experienced by anyone who enjoys exploring fantastic worlds woven with a fresh science fiction story.

They are both definitely worth getting as they are the definite modern way to experience these fantastic classic games that offer a tremendous amount of content, quests, great dialogue and a huge sense of freedom. Visually there have been few improvements, and a shocking lack of options is disturbing, but if you can set aside these problems and have the patience to learn these obviously outdated gameplay mechanics then both Baldur's Gate 1: Enhanced Edition and Baldur's Gate 2: Enhanced Edition are absolutely worth it.

First of all: I sank some 80+ hours into this game, over two playthroughs, but most of those hours are counted on Origin rather than Steam, since claiming the bonus content in the Deluxe Edition forces you to download and use Origin. Bothered me big time at first, now I just tolerate it as typical EA behaviour.
The game itself is, simply put, stellar. ME2 continues the first game's magnificence, expanding upon the finely-crafted setting and introducing much-needed gameplay improvements. The new cast members are also intriguing, each of them with a distinct, layered personality that just invites you to talk to them after every mission (protip: do it. Some of the game's most hilarious, most heartwarming, most excellent dialogue happens in these intimate chats with your crew). The exquisite cinematography returns, sidequests now have varying maps, and the endgame is thrilling to the core.
On the downside, the weapons customisation is completely taken out, leaving only a few basic weapons to choose from. And while they removed the hair-tearing Mako rides, they added planet scanning, which is either extremely tedious or thoughtlessly calming, YMMV. Also, thermal clips. Just, why?
tl;dr: A solid sequel, its main strength lies in its colourful cast of crewmates and characterisation, once more immersing you into the role and setting perfectly. Cons include a weird weapon system and less solid main plot. 8.5/10

I was losing a war badly and needed money to pay for a mercenary army to defend my lands. I borrowed money from the jews but did not want to pay them back, so I chose to expel them from my kingdom, allowing me to confiscate a ton of cash. I used this to hire my armies and win my war. A few months later I would begin to lose technology points in events, because the jews were heavily involved intelectuals. This set me back quite a bit in bonuses to my units and building.
Choices like this define your game and build your own personal story. Many times you'll find yourself pausing for a few minutes, unable to decide between two terrible choices, plotting on the best way to get yourself out of a nearly impossible problem.
This game takes patience and a willingness to create your own idea of what "Winning and Losing" are.
As a whole I can't recomend this game enough, especially for those that love history.

So, Jet Set Radio, despite how much older it is, is still a great game. This re-release however, helps cements it's place. Though I think Jet Set Radio Future is better (even though they haven't ported it yet), JSR is still a good game.
Pros:
-The controls feel nice, as it is a game that helped shape Sports Platforming games (yep, that's what Tony Hawk Pro Skater is too)
-The pretty cell-shaded textures, which kind of help it age better than most games.
-The unlockable characters, graffiti, and bonus tracks (which are optional, but make the game better.)
-The excellent soundtrack that fits the game.
-The real graffiti that you can use in the game to tag walls in missions.
-The story isn't bad, and helps keep the pace of the game up.
-The voice actors did a well job, making the chase scenes much more memorable.
-The game works with almost any gamepad.
-Option to make your own grafitti
-Has a good points system, allowing you to have a fair way of getting points.
-The ability to use your gained characters after you beat the game (sort of like a Start+ sorta deal)
-The "rival" challenges to gain the extra characters in-game are pretty fun on their own.
Cons:
-Has a difficultly spike for inexperienced players, some levels even requiring me to play over 10 times...
-Tutorial is harder than the actual game, but the game is playable without it nonetheless.
-Unless you have a gamepad, this game is hard as balls.
-The controls are not as responsive when you are in the air, sometimes making you miss a platform/railing.
-The story feels rushed sometimes, but you aren't playing this game for story, are you?
-No restart button... In a sports/platform game... So back to the map and selecting it if you fail.
-Some characters are almost impossible to play normal missions with (exspecially Combo or Pots if you unlock them)
-Boss battle is a let down compaired to the previous missions, but still hard.
-The camera can mess you up sometimes, so be prepaired to press the camera reset alot.
-I beat it once in around 12 hours, but you might want a longer game.
-Only single-player, so unless you and your friend like waiting...
Personal score: 7.75
A good game, and stands up through time, but isn't as great as it used to be I guess. It's still a game I recommend.
Hopefully, it's sequel JSRF will get a port, but for now buy this. I promise you won't be sorry... except when you fail a mission... then you can be sorry for missing that jump on the railing to get over the waterway... besides, the only way for JSRF to be here is if enough of this game is sold, and they realize we want JSRF.

I first played this game on Android a couple of years ago and instantly fell in love with it. It's a casual game that does not disappoint. It will consume hours of your spare time. When I got an iPhone, I also bought it on the App Store.
Today, I was playing Knightmare Tower on my tablet and I wondered "I have a Steam and PS4 controller. They both have gyro. That's one big reason they (the devs) would port this awesome game to the PC." The only reason that made me wonder if it had a PC version on Steam is because of how the controls are handled in a mobile device- with a gyroscope. So i decided to check it on Steam since most successful casual games on mobile either come FROM PC or port the mobile game TO PC. To my surprise, this game was originally a web game, and it's available on Steam! So i get this bad boy and rush to my PC to purchas and install this game. Waited for a few seconds and there it is, waiting to be played. I turned on my Steam Controller and pushed the Steam button once the game started up and checked to see if there's an action set on the gyro, but sadly there isn't. At that point I pretty much knew the PC game didn't FULLY support any controller with a gyro, Steam or PS4 controllers. But hey, that's the beauty of Steam, you could configure an action to the gyro. So I tried hooking up the horizontal movement of the left joystick to the always-on gyro, played it a few minutes and admitted defeat. The movement wasn't as smooth and controlled with the mobile versions. I really wanted to get used to it but controlling with a joystick is FAR better than using the gyro. I hope the devs could add full gyro support in the PC version. Otherwise, it's still a great game with or without gyro.
I recommend also getting it on a mobile device (especially a tablet) for extra challenge. The gyro will add a little bit of difficulty especially when fighting the boss.
[TL;DR]
1. Game controls use joystick instead of gyro (if you've first encountered this game on mobile)
2. No difference in mobile game (again, except for the controls)
3. Controllers with gyro not fully supported in this game. (however you can us the gyro as movement through Steam if you want to.)

The ABC Murders follows the original book rather faithfully, which may work against it if you already know the story. It is only a mild disadvantage though, as it captures Poirot’s character and the observation-based mechanics of the investigation well enough to recommend it to any adventure game or Agatha Christie fan.
‘The ABC Murders’ is one of the most famous Agatha Christie novels, thanks to its carefully-crafted cat-and-mouse nature of showing Poirot going against a mysterious serial killer.
This fame also means many players will already know the important bits of the story, but the developers expected this, since they tried to shake things up a little (like adding an entire new scenario in Churston or mostly skipping Doncaster).
Instead of playing as the original narrator, Hastings, we control Poirot directly. Unlike his portrayal in the novels, here he doesn’t rely solely on conversations, psychological profiling, and drawing logical conclusions, but puts a large emphasis on material evidence as well. In gameplay, this mostly translates to a series of almost individual logic-based minigames—including a few mechanical puzzle boxes—that somehow have to form some coherent whole.
The result is a bit of a strange mix. The story deviances will probably upset some purists, but they are not enough to add in any actual surprises. The dual nature of point ‘n’ click mechanics mixed with semi-independent minigames tends to fragment the gameplay flow. The difficulty is highly mobile game oriented, meaning it is impossible to get stuck as the game holds the player’s hands, but some achievements are incredibly cryptic and hard to get.
Still, if you can live with all of these, then you will likely enjoy what this adaptation of The ABC Murders can offer to you.

You can use powerups and a stun attack to affect the battle but most the time your dodging projectiles and trying to get within the proper range of an enemy. The controller support is flawed, often you wont be able to preform the stun move and you have to restart the game for it to work again (at least on 360 controllers). Also, the soundtrack and sound effects are annoying and repetitive. I could see how this would be a better IOS game if you just wanted to mindlessly kill a few minutes but I wouldn't suggest buying it on Steam.  On the plus side it does have nice art and the Steam exclusive characters are pretty cool.

I liked it, but thumbs down because I have mixed feelings and cannot recommend it just to anybody. This will hopefully make it easier for people to see what might at least be questionable about the game.
It's a game with an interesting world and interesting characters, but for the better or worse the story can be confusing and leaves room for interpretation and there is rather little gameplay at the core of this game even with the advertised exploration or by some Steam users falsely tagged "open-world" parts not necessarily filling just what you would expect of that. This is a relatively straightforward explorative adventure that has you fiddle around with one or another physics objects in the world, talk with people as well as play some minigames (each of them is skippable if failed once).
Essentially there are three places for you to go in this game: Your yurt/tent with the female, immobilized android "Ida" inside, the train station and the "amusement park" near it. Sometimes you'll be lead a little astray into the Mongolian steppe but not too far. Straying off on your own will never really yield anything interesting to speak of but only make you realize that you better stay on course to save you the travel time (that's how I at least felt after a few attempts of searching the steppe on my own).
This leads to the game have you do backtracking. You visit the three beforementioned essential places pretty much constantly in that order back and forth without ever really given any reason to wander elsewhere on your own accord. You are accompanied by some nice ambiant sounds and music or by Ida - if not talking to her in person - giving you more background info via what could've been some sort of radio connection on the park, her person or the events and procedures that surrounded it (without her it would be a pretty damn lonely game, really). But it's still a constant back and forth. At one point I was wondering why my character wouldn't just decide to do all the minigames in the dome in one run rather than go fetching one thing after another from there for Ida again and again. In this dome - even as highly detailed and immersively as it is designed just like the other essential places - you do the pretty much same kind of minigames all the time rather than some genuine exploration, puzzling or adventuring. These minigames fit with what the park is said to be about, but it's still "just" minigames that some may see as an unwelcome distraction. After you've seen the first you basically have seen them all. I found them okay, they were neither too interesting nor hard, but I could have lived without them as well.
What redeemed the game for me is the interesting Mongolian steppe setting, the quite nice art/visuals and the good amount of details the essential places have (the steppe itself is rather boring). And, even as few as there are, the characters. You are "Enebish", a native Mongolian who used to live with his late grandfather in the yurt having your big semi-mechanical eagle "Ongots" hunt for hare and yourself "baking"/"digitizing" flowers from the park's vincinity into "phytocopies" and selling them to other folk for their "beautiful" DNA via the merchant "Tabaha" who is travelling the hovering-magnetic "Sky Ring" train line that cuts through the steppe and alongside your yurt.
Ida has been in your yurt for a longer while going back to your late grandfather; after using a peculiar machine in it you lose your own memories and set out to get those back as well as help Ida find hers. Eventually you find connections between each other that run deeper than expected and hope to fix some things that have happened. You two form something of a bond, at least I liked and felt for Ida. I did care about her and her past and wanted to know more about her and the world around me, even if the time with her is rather short because the game is just that if you cut the minigames, the back and forth and the possible occasional desperate searches inside your yurt for items that are at best vaguely described in your brief "goal" log and at worst hidden by design or by you tossing them around carelessly in dark corners even the sharpest eyes may miss (I looked up video walkthroughs a few times). I liked to listen to Ida's explanations and voice actress and felt the pain she suffered in her android body, while Enebish is voiced in a monotonous and highly uninteresting manner (which apparently was intended by the devs, there are possible explanations to this story-wise but that's speculative and I can't go deeper without spoiling too much).
There are some very interesting things about the world, there are quite a lot of scientific details and hiccups to like or be irritated about depending on your own stance to this kind of sci-fi "fanservice"/mumble jumble. Through parts of it the actual struggles and pain of a post-apocalyptic society and their people are shining through, even to someone like you who has been living isolated from the rest of the world for as long as he can think. For the better or worse some important details are delivered only through tiny, unremarkable bits of paper scattered messily throughout your yurt that even at better graphical settings are rather low-res and can easily be missed because they are usually not modeled by themselves but part of the  textures of the other assets albeit differently colored. Similarly there are "magical" or "esoteric" elements that surround yourself and the events in the steppe and apparently some Buddhistic symbolism one will have, or can try to, wrap his own mind around, perhaps with the help of the relatively engaged discussions here on Steam. These can help to understand the ending as well, which can feel abrupt and depending on the amount of research you did in your yurt confusing as well.
So, even with the little gameplay value Cradle has: You can think, wonder and discuss quite a lot about it and some people apparently have already done multiple playthroughs (and read on Buddhistic fables/tales even) in an attempt to understand things better. The way some information you need to scrape out of your yurt and in some apparently hidden parts of the steppe I haven't found myself yet like the literal needle in the haystack has spawned some negative feedback by other players but I'm rather indecisive about it at the moment. The ending felt abrupt to me, I understood the gist of it I think, but I can see how someone who doesn't pay as much attention to all the details around the yurt and to the subtle implications by Ida or Enebish can feel heavily confused or "lost" after seeing the game's staff role. I would have loved to spend more time with Ida, maybe just do my own cosy thing in the steppe with her and Ongots, but this isn't the Cozyiness Simulator 2015 so I suppose it was right to end it as it did. But, that being said, I wouldn't mind to see other games that have me roam/experience unusal settings/places/cultures/ways of life like Cradle did.

I really want to like this game, but judging by the pace the development is going, I think my grandchildren are still never going to see the finished game. Ever since I backed the project (what has been maybe a year or two ago) I've seen NO visible changes in the game. Sure, every couple months there's the occasional bug fix, but these usually deal with some animation issue or a minor tweak to combat that you never noticed anyway. The larger bugs, such as the constant crashes or failing to load, the developers have steered clear of and have not attempted to fix in any way.
However, there is one pro to the game - it has, what I consider, the absolute BEST combat in any game out there. It feels like you're really in the action, allowing you to control exactly how you hit while keeping the game very quick paced (and it manages to do this without the "mash X to kill" technique many games use - if you haven't looked up the controls, go do it, I think you'll be pleasantly surprised). As such, if you find you enjoy sitting in the arena and fighting a couple rounds every once in a while, then I would wholeheartedly recommend this game. However, you shouldn't expect any more progress to be made on it - not now, not ever - because it simply isn't coming.

I hate puzzle games; my aptience for any of the mini-games and having to try every possible combination of every stupid little thing in a game jsut drives me nuts. However, when you have an interesting story line - a gripping narrative will help you put aside your gripes for various game mechanics.
Thats what Cradle does. The story draws you in while the world around you leaves you puzzled, curious, and your inner dialogue screams at you to learn everything that you can about this world you find yourself stuck in. Mayn games try to force you into a sense of a desperate need to understand your scenario. But they usually lack imagination and they can hardly ever really hook and reel you in.
Ive read the forums and people are complaining that the game is too short or they disparagingly call it a "walking simulator"; a crude attempt and transparent attempt at being facetious that immediately falls flat. Some people just play a lot of puzzle and narrative-driven games. They tend to make short work of them. Thats their own fault. Since I dont play a lot of puzzle games it takes me a while to figure some things out. And because my journey is more challenging it also tends to be more rewarding. I have a good amount of time into the game already. And the save system shows the chapters. Im about halfway through. So the $13 price point is spot on. Any more and it wouldve felt overpriced. Any less and it wouldve seemed like they were under-rating the value to try and dump copies on everyone, including people that only bought it because it was cheap.
If youre only going to play a few puzzle. story driven, simulation style games, then you have to own this one.

I've never played the original version of this game before, but I can definitely say this is one of the best Western RPGs ever crafted. The story picks up directly after Baldur's Gate 1, so I would say its definitely necessary to play that game before this one and for the fact that it gives a much better pacing in the actual gameplay because in BG1; You start off as a lowly level 1 and can slowly learn all the ins and outs of the DND 3.5 system and fight smaller challenges because in BG2, you start off at a much higher level with advanced skills and greater challenges to face and might possibly have some difficulty especially if you choose a hard area to go to first.

If you're looking for a review you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.﻿

To start things off, I copied a quote from the ‘About this Game’ blurb from Steam:
‘A serene and relaxing game experience; take your time to enjoy the sunrise and beautiful vistas, listen to the sound of the ocean, or observe the playfulness of the creatures that inhabit this place. There is only one pace in this game and that’s your own.’
The above statement pretty much sums up this game ‘Submerged’ from Uppercut Games Pty Ltd. It took away all the obligatory kill everything that glances your way, enemies and even death. Yes, you cannot die in this game, no matter what. Then again, some adventure games you cannot die too however that’s another story. So, if you took away all of these elements that conceivably makes video games fun then what has Submerged then have to offer with regards to the ‘fun’ factor? Again, it comes back to the above statement as its sole purpose is to make the player having a relaxing time exploring the world whilst doing a bit of searching for collectables along the way.
And now here comes the contradiction – the storyline. Yes, there is a story to this game however it really feels like as an afterthought; like Uppercut Games had this brilliant idea of exploring the world in your own pace without the fear of death yet need to string a story to make some sort of purpose build into it. The plot, in the most simplistic form, revolves around the main character (i.e. what you control) named Miku, and her brother Taku both arrived via a small fishing boat to the submerged city of unknown origins. The catch is her brother is dying and it’s up to you (Miku) to save him by finding supplies that’s hidden throughout this once bustling city.
Now here’s the contradiction – the game tells you to admire the scenery and soak up in the atmosphere; basically, take your sweet time doing what needs to be done to save your dying brother (?). I found this concept a little difficult to swallow as, and remarkably so, I felt a connection for the two characters even though Miku is almost a mute. However, as the saying goes ‘A picture is worth a thousand words’ and this game Submerged is like viewing a silent movie where this time you control the pace (as opposed to a movie where it dictates the course of action). So, you have this sense of urgency build in (a.k.a. dying brother) yet the main character cannot die period. Crazy stuff.
As the game encourages exploration, it can extend the life of this product. For me, it took around 8 hours to complete however I really explored every nook and cranny to locate every single item (for which I did – yet it will be great to have a little fan fair about this however it wasn’t the case). However, it’s not unheard of that others can finish this under 3 hours. The map is quite small considering however it was developed by an indie developer made in Australia – and being Australian myself, the Australian gaming industry is miniscule with little government support.
Yet to those achievement hunters, there are ten to collect and they are all achievable on your first run. Yet there’s a bug where the progression count for the collectables are not recorded in steam yet it does unlock when locating them all. According to the developers, they mentioned it has to do with the game engine itself (Unreal 4). I have no idea whether this is true though. Also, there are five collectable cards and they are all nice looking (and not some copy / paste garbage from other games that I won’t mention here). All five are concept arts from the game so that’s a nice touch.
With the asking price of $20 and an additional $10 for the soundtrack (for which I highly recommend as it’s composed by Jeff Van Dyck - Total War / Need for Speed series), I cannot recommend this game for that price. Honestly, it’s a really hurts for me to say this as I really enjoyed this game as it did suck me in until the end. I love the characters, love the idea of exploration and taking my sweet time doing so, love just sitting there soaking up the scenery however, because of the storyline involves a dying boy, it did add a sense of urgency. That’s not to say that’s a bad thing however it does contradict to the overall pitch for the game. Yet I even adore the storytelling montage and the uniqueness that brought it into the game. Also, I’m aware the lack of support of the gaming industry in Australia has that may have an effect of driving prices up. If the price was $20 that should include the soundtrack and not as a DLC.
Thankfully this game does go on sale from time to time and I even seen it at 75% off – that’s a total steal in my eyes. Also, because the game has a lot of evidence of love poured into it making this game wonderful, for this reason I can lean towards recommending it. So, you have on one hand a short, contradicting pitch (dying boy vs admire the scenery), missing mini map (that will enhance the gameplay), lack of zoom function (to view multiple paths instead of backtracking) and high purchasing price vs likable characters, dare to be different, beautiful scenery and decent backstory that plays upon real life scenarios (instead of you are the chosen one). I’m opting the latter thus giving my overall recommendation.
But take heed what I have stated.
6 / 10 (lots of love poured into this game however it does need some serious overhaul to the entire game).

I'm not voting this down because I didn't like the 'game' but because this is really one of those reviews where you wish there was a 'meh' option and because the currently score is probably misleadingly high.
I was hoping this would have classic Tomb Raider style platforming but it doesn't really.  It's extremely linear without any puzzles or logic involved (the towers that is, the city is open).  In fact this really isn't describable as a game as there is no gameplay.   It's a walking simulator except you're boating/climbing more than walking.
Pros:
Lovely unique and interesting setting
Relaxing
Short (that's a pro in my books since my time is so limited, those are the only games I end up finishing)
Cons:
Story - This was really the biggest failing since there's no gameplay it's up to the story to really sell the experience.  The story starts out interestingly enough but by about half-way through you realize the kids story is really trite and basic, and that the world's story just isn't all that interesting that it's worth the bother to collect all the 'story' bits littering the place to learn more about it.  Worse is the wrap-up is too clean and basically both leaves too much unanswered and takes away any potential meaning/depth the story might have provided.  You're left with 'That's it?'
Graphics - okay but look dated and textures are reused so much that it give every building a very 'samey' quality to them.
Level design - Towers are linear.  You go the only (and obvious) way you can.   You might miss some extra collectables not looking for alternative paths but... meh.  Boating is open but aside from collecting stuff (that gradually loses any point of collecting) there's little to do aside from finding the next tower to climb.
Upgrades - You can upgrade your boat by finding other boats lying around.  However the only upgrade appears to be to make your engine last a little longer and really by the sixth or so upgrade (out of 26 I believe) you're good.  You're not rocketting across the entire map at any point so the upgrades become increasing meaningless as you can boost for periods continuously longer than you're ever likely too.
Short - Which for full price isn't worth it.  I got it in a humble bundle (glad I did) but okay if you're buying on sale.
In conclusion - it's okay.  It held my interest up to the disappointing end.  Ignore my time played, I tend to start games and leave them running until I can get around to finishing them  (so only maybe 4 hours were actual play time).  You might enjoy it, you might not.  There are a lot of better games (that have actual gameplay - Papa & Yo comes to mind - excellent puzzles and story) but if you're still interested and it's cheap, you'll probably get enough enjoyment out of it to make it worth your while.

One of the deepest strategy games I've ever had the pleasure of experincing. The terms and mechanics can get some taking used to. I don't suggest playing Ironman mode for your first couple tries (This allows you only one save slot, game has auto save so it doesn't allow you to reload wherever you want)
You'll find yourself doing a lot of things that will screw over your dynasty if you're not careful in the begining. There are so many things to consider when making even the most basic decesion, things that seem small can come back to bite you,

I was losing a war badly and needed money to pay for a mercenary army to defend my lands. Upfront: played with a Controller over Steam Link.  This is a difficult game to review.  On the one hand, it looks very nice and the music and sound design are solid.  On the other hand, this title has a lot more in common with a walking simulator than an adventure game or even an exploration game.  Now, I like walking sims generally--but when I purchased this title, I honestly expected more gameplay and story elements than are present.
Despite any videos that show your character hopping on ledges, etc., you should know that there is no consequence to any of that.  You cannot fall, you cannot die.  This game is not a platformer in the least--you really cannot deviate from very narrow paths and you cannot suffer any consequence for any action.  The "gameplay" is very simplistic and VERY repetitive.  You use a telescope and it will automatically note any structure that contains supplies, etc.  You then take a boat to those spots (using the automatically annotated map) and pick up the supplies and then you are automagically transported back to your "home."  Repeat this mechanic 15 times.  Whatever "exploration" is involved is superficial at best.  You cannot enter buildings--you merely boat to a limited number of pre-determined structures, press a button/key and begin to climb.  You can't fall and you can't really explore (e.g. you cannot explore the vast majority of structures since they don't have supplies.  Getting to the top of the buildings might take a minute to figure out, but there is generally one path to each goal.  You can't even go inside the buildings--it's all just basically clmbing ledges from which you cannot fall.  Yes, there are some runes also scattered in these buildings that help tell the "story" but oddly, the game not only allows you to proceed if you miss them, it actually causes you to not get them by immediately transporting you back as soon as you pick up the supplies.  This is a baffling design choice.  It would have been preferable to allow the player to choose when they are finished looking around.
While playing Submerged, I was reminded of the game Brothers-A Tale of 2 Sons.  That game includes actual puzzle features that must be figured out to progress--this does not.  Brothers has real gameplay elements--this one only offers the illusion of gameplay.  Like I mentioned previously, Submerged has a lot more in common with a walking sim than an adventure game--there are no consequences for mistakes, you follow a fairly linear, limited path, and the payoff has more to do with mood .  That said, you might be tempted to compare this to a title like Abzu, which relies heavily on style.  The difference though is that Abzu contains zero "gameplay" elements--i.e. it doesn't pretend to be something it's not (like Submerged).  Abzu is 100% an experiential game that rewards the player with stunning graphics, music, and sense of exploration.  It is a far superior game than Submerged because it has no artifice of gameplay and actually is able to tell a story with visuals that really make you contemplate things.
Finally, I'd note that despite the often beautiful graphics on display, the mechanics of the game can be highly frustrating.  Specifically, being a 3rd person title, the camera will often be positioned incorrectly obscuring your vision (especially common whilst on buildings near foliage).  Jumping/climbing ledges similarly was frustrating (with a controller) because the slightest tap can have you jumping up on a ledge as opposed to climbing left/right.  Again, there's zero consequence so it's just time consuming and frustrating.
I wanted to like this title--I really did.  I can only recommend it while it is on sale, and only then if you don't mind very repetitive "gameplay."  I hate to say it, but this title really is all style and no substance.  It has loads of style--beautiful style.  There is an idea of a story, but the tedious, meaningless and highly repetitive pseudo-gameplay elements begin to really detract.  Play it in very small doses and you won't be as disappointed.

Tour America the American way, on your chair/couch in front of your TV/Computer.
BUT!!! There is more to the game than "ooh I get to drive a truck"
The driving controls are good. So, it's a good driving game. There is a lot of detail in the driving, such as turn signals, different kinds of breaks and complex car thingies, and loads of controller support. Your trailer also moves in a way that adds challenge (gets stuck when you turn -_-). Then, there's the business management side. You start off by doing small jobs for companies, but eventually make enough money so you can maybe buy a truck. Or you can get a loan. As you level up, you can get longer routes, higher value cargo, or stress-inducing timed deliveries. Once you can afford your truck, you start making your empire big, and somehow the game isn't repetitive/boring. Finally, there's the maps. The maps are really good, even if you take the highway most of the time. Once you get your own truck, you can free-drive across America, and truly admire the amount of DETAIL they put into the game.
tl;dr: Good driving game, good business management game, lots of detail

For those who are unfamiliar with the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, it is one of the most atmospheric open world games ever to be developed. It's nailbitingly difficult and oppressively grim, and completely unlike any game you have ever played before. I highly recommend it! Call of Pripyat is the final game in the trilogy.
Call of Pripyat is certainly not as atmospheric as Shadow of Chernobyl, but it maintains some of the challenge, presenting it in a more accessible way. It is much more "open" than the other two games, and of the "vanilla" unmodded experiences, this one is the strongest, with few glitches and little need for modding. However, there are still tons of mods to improve the base game.
I recommend completing Shadow of Chernobyl first, with Complete Mod or Zone Reclaimation Project installed to improve the base experience. Complete mod is much easier to find and install, but ZRP stays closer to the true S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience (but may be intimmidating and difficult to install for non-technical users).
After completing Shadow of Chernobyl, finish Call of Pripyat vanilla. After you've finished Call of Pripyat, if you're craving more S.T.A.L.K.E.R., I highly recommend the Call of Chernobyl Mod. This mod bridges all three games into one super game where you can visit all areas, collect all items, and revisit familiar characters. Call of Chernobyl Mod feels like the truest S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience, but it's not for new players.
You can probably skip Clear Sky, but I think it's worth playing.

This is a game for fans of Agatha Christie and especially Poirot.  The game is full of fanservice moments like Poirot preening himself in front of the mirror and being pompous.
Gameplay is mostly adventure game pixel hunts along with some puzzle boxes and logic puzzles.  Additionally, there is a roleplay component where you earn "Ego" by responding in an appropriately Poirot manner at all times.  Ego doesn't seem to do anything, but it's still fun to get that little prize for keeping in charcter.  Finally, there is a "little grey cell" minigame where you combine clues to make deductions about the case.
There was only one puzzle in the game that I found unfairly confusing, but it is reasonably solveable with random flips so it's not a huge problem.  The only real problem is the translation is a bit uneven in places, and some of the little grey cell minigames end up requiring a lot of guesswork simply because the objective was incorrectly translated.  This mostly happens near the end of the game, early on it works fairly well.
There are a handful of further minor nits to pick like reusing the typewriter comparison minigame and the frustratingly leisurely pace Poirot has, but that's also part of the fanservice.
The difficulty level is not very high, so even if you aren't a "gamer" this is still accessable.  There's no "adventure game logic" in here, most everything you do make sense and conclusions are drawn from sensible places.  I've never read the novel this game is based off of, but I suspect that faithfulness to the source material helps keep the natural adventure game dev tendencies in check.  Only the weird prolifieration of intricite mechanical puzzle boxes reminds you that you're playing a game.
I had zero crashes or data corruption as far as I can tell.
All in all this is a must buy if you're a fan of Poirot and have not read the novel yet.  It's a really novel experience.  If you are just into adventure games it's still a good buy.  If you like action then pass, it's slow and talky.  I enjoyed it a lot.

This is a review of a game that has been in development for many years.  Since the game isn't complete, I'm going to give my impressions of the current state of gameplay.
What it is:  A game of exploration and combat with anthropomorphic animals.  Exploration is done by using physics based "parkour" on objects in the environment.  Combat is also physics based using punches, kicks, blocks, jumps, rolls, and melee weapons (which can be thrown and even caught).  It's probably better to view one of the many videos out there than try to comprehend my explanation of it here.  Don't worry, there are no spoilers yet, since there is no main game campaign as of the time I write this.
The initial Steam install contains some basic maps in which one can experience the gameplay.  There is a combat map where two people can fight matches on the same computer using keyboard/mouse and a controller.  While the mouse has an invert look option in the setup menu, the controller does not.  Another level is a simple arena where one can fight endless battles against the AI.  The AI doesn't currently have all the move sets possible to the player, but it's still quite capable of killing me!  It's probably the best single player experience available for the game so far.  The remaining maps are basic environments, sometimes with a few enemies to be defeated.
In addition to the basic installation, there are mods created by the community that are available for download and automatic installation via the Wolfire website and the SUMLauncher application, which is currently required for managing your game install.  Overgrowth can be launched directly from SUMLauncher or by Steam, but only launching through Steam allows access to the overlay and hours spent playing the game.
The community mods are a mixed bag.  Some haven't been updated with the game and will likely crash.  Most of the others suffer from poor level design and bad optimization.  Still, despite my personal criticisms, I have to say that the game seems wide open for modders to express their creativity and hone their skills.  It's a tinkerer's paradise, to be sure!
Should you buy it?  If you want a polished and finished gaming experience, NO.  If you don't mind supporting a small developer who has built a framework for what could be a great adventure game in the future, then yes.  The potential is certainly there, and you could do worse.  As with any Early Access game, only buy it if you are willing to take the risk that what you buy is all you'll ever get.  Recommended, but with strong caution that you know what you're getting into.

Background:
Purchased as part of a bundle from Bundle Stars. I played the first two games in the series to death back when they came out.
Impressions:
The game stands up today much as it did when it came out. It's a damn fine strategy game that's a blast to play and highly rewarding. However unlike it's predecessor this game is more of an expansion pack, with only 8 missions they instead ramped the difficulty to near frustrating levels.
While still fun and rewarding for the most part I really started to detest the 'mansion kidnap', 'rail yard' and final mission for the sheer bloody minded difficulty of sections those missions where trail and error started to get irritating.
There are some missteps for sure with elements that are seemingly only solvable in a single method and theres one right in the first mission that can leave you stranded just as you thought you were done and you have to go back a few saves or even start again.
Fixes:
As with Behind enemy lines there are a number of serious issues with the game on a modern PC that make it almost unplayable.
See the page on the 'Commandos Wikia' for 'Commandos: Beyond the call of Duty Fixes' for a collection of bug fixes to stabilise the game and make it playable.
The Good:
*A classic formula that stands up today for it's simplicity and functions.
*Missions can be tackled many ways.
*The settings have a historical context and introduced as such.
*Missions are huge and diverse.
*Fast save/load system makes experimentation less frustrating than you'd think.
*Huge sense of triumph from executing a plan that takes out even a single awkward guard.
*Looks pretty good considering it's age.
*New mechanics, some of which are interesting and alter your tactics.
The Bad:
*Installs ok on Steam but multi-core affinity issues requires some manual tweaking.
*Many missions have sections where there is only one practical solution.
*The difficulty level is a massive leap up upward over the original game.
*A new character only appears in a single mission.
*Cigarette packs effectively give everyone a Decoy box, messing with the balance.
*Shorter tougher campaign.
Recommended for: War, Action and isometric strategy fans and fans of the original.
Conclusion.
7/10. Once the stability issue is fixed it's a reasonable follow up to the original.

The armored Cataphract regiments from the Komnenian household guard led my Anatolian armies in the east while a smaller force of Varangians led a simultaneous invasion of muslim-held Sicily in the west. Infidel armies were crushed underfoot, provinces fell one by one, and the petty emir's begged for peace as the Byzantine Restoration swept to all shores of the Mediterranean. "Good!," I said, "this was getting too easy!" when the Sunni's finally declared a jihad. My forces took the initiative and several large mercenary companies and 20,000 Byzantines landed near the Nile before the first infidel armies even reached my borders. Small muslim armies were swatted away as they attempted to repel my invasion, but they were no match for my men as we ravaged the Egyptian delta.
The Shiites declared their own jihad against the recently "liberated" sicilian holdings a few months after we landed in Egypt. "Whatever," I chuckled, "the mighty sons of Rome do not fear a these desert men!" I recruited more mercenaries and landed in Sicily just as the first Shiite armies began to trickle in by boat. Each month brought a fresh wave of infidels and we crushed each attack and pressed on with the sieges.
But months turned in to years, and the trickle of muslim armies became a steady stream of larger and larger enemy armies. My fleets began to frantically criss-cross the Mediterranean, ferrying whatever regiments I could spare from theatre to theatre to counter each wave. My men were winning every battle, but we were losing soldiers faster than they could be replaced. I watched in disbelief as my army and Varangian core in Sicily was overrun, trapped, and annihilated, and the Shiites crossed the strait to capture my holdings in Italy. Then my armies holding eastern Anatolia were forced to pull back to a defensive line near the Bosphorus as large muslim hosts pressed towards my capital. My Egyptian invasion force had been significantly weakened by endless waves of Sunni's, and the desert sun was killing even more. I evacuated Egypt and pulled back the remaining armies to regroup in Greece.
My war chest was also running out, which forced me to disband the remaining mercenary companies to keep them from rebelling, and scrapped large portions of my fleet. My disbelief turned to horror as the Shiites landed in Greece and the Sunni's crossed the Bosporus and laid siege to Constantinople. I gathered what remained of my fragmented forces, nearly 20k men, around Athens and won a close battle over a large Shiite force that had crossed into western Greece, and finally convinced the desert men to agree to peace in exchange for the Sicilian duchy I had won years earlier. My men then charged north, defeating a small muslim host that surrounded Constantinople and relieving the city for a few months. But another Sunni host of some 50k crossed the strait soon after, forcing my army to retreat and threatening to destroy my last hopes for the Restoration. The situation had gone from dire to impossible.
And that is when they appeared- A force of 50k imperials arrived on a fleet outside my capital, led by the Kaiser himself. A few years into the war, I had arranged for my son to marry the daughter of the Holy Roman Emperor in the west, and although he had officially joined the war in my defense, up to this point, I had only seen a few small inneffective armies in Italy. I marched the last sons of Rome north-east, and joined battle just as the Kaiser landed at the head of his great army. Together we overpowered and crushed the muslim forces, and the Kaiser's fleet prevented a muslim escape into Anatolia. The infidels were completely destroyed. Soon after, the Sunni's finally agreed to a white peace that left my Eastern empire intact. I never forgot that the true sons of Rome had been saved by the pretenders in the west, and our alliance lasted for generations until the new Roman Empire and the title of Augustus was finally restored.
For those of you wondering, this did actually happen during my play through way back in 2013 and it was the reason I became hooked on CKII until I eventually graduated to Europa Universalis 4. Got this game as part of a Humble Bundle. Try as I might, I just didn't like it.
The premise is sound and the graphics are lovely for an indie game. I was delighted by the random animals that popped out of the ocean as you boated by.
But where it drops the ball is its most critical component: the gameplay. Climb buildings. Collect stuff. That's all you do. the only progression is you get a snippet of what brought the main character here after you collect each major item. There's no increase in difficulty from building to building; you can do any one at any time. There's no way to fail, no skill to master. The buildings are glorified vertical labyrinths, where you just choose a direction and hope that's the right way to the quest item at the top and backtrack if not.
There are lots of random "collectibles" but they don't really add anything to the game for me. Even the ones that are supposed to give you some history of the city. Furthermore, they're not fun to find; just annoying.
It feels like someone's valiant first attempt at a game, but I can't recommend it.

Tour America the American way, on your chair/couch in front of your TV/Computer.
BUT!!! There is more to the game than "ooh I get to drive a truck"
The driving controls are good. So, it's a good driving game. There is a lot of detail in the driving, such as turn signals, different kinds of breaks and complex car thingies, and loads of controller support. Your trailer also moves in a way that adds challenge (gets stuck when you turn -_-). Then, there's the business management side. You start off by doing small jobs for companies, but eventually make enough money so you can maybe buy a truck. Or you can get a loan. As you level up, you can get longer routes, higher value cargo, or stress-inducing timed deliveries. Once you can afford your truck, you start making your empire big, and somehow the game isn't repetitive/boring. Finally, there's the maps. The maps are really good, even if you take the highway most of the time. Once you get your own truck, you can free-drive across America, and truly admire the amount of DETAIL they put into the game.
tl;dr: Good driving game, good business management game, lots of detail

For those who are unfamiliar with the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, it is one of the most atmospheric open world games ever to be developed. It's nailbitingly difficult and oppressively grim, and completely unlike any game you have ever played before. I highly recommend it! Call of Pripyat is the final game in the trilogy.
Call of Pripyat is certainly not as atmospheric as Shadow of Chernobyl, but it maintains some of the challenge, presenting it in a more accessible way. It is much more "open" than the other two games, and of the "vanilla" unmodded experiences, this one is the strongest, with few glitches and little need for modding. However, there are still tons of mods to improve the base game.
I recommend completing Shadow of Chernobyl first, with Complete Mod or Zone Reclaimation Project installed to improve the base experience. Complete mod is much easier to find and install, but ZRP stays closer to the true S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience (but may be intimmidating and difficult to install for non-technical users).
After completing Shadow of Chernobyl, finish Call of Pripyat vanilla. After you've finished Call of Pripyat, if you're craving more S.T.A.L.K.E.R., I highly recommend the Call of Chernobyl Mod. This mod bridges all three games into one super game where you can visit all areas, collect all items, and revisit familiar characters. Call of Chernobyl Mod feels like the truest S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience, but it's not for new players.
You can probably skip Clear Sky, but I think it's worth playing.

The gameplay is simple, yet addicting like hell - Especially if you want to 100% this game.
You move your knight from left to right, enganging enemies in a never-ending fight.
Well nearly never-ending. You "level up"/"gear up" your knight in the shop with money earned and picked up during gameplay, which helps make the game more compelling.
However, it's pretty simplistic but in a way that suits the game decently.
Since there's only one type of weapon and all enemy attacks (those who have it) deal the same amount of damage, there is no reason for a more "complex gearing/leveling system".
Which brings me to the pricetag. I only bought it because I was looking at some brief fun but most importantly: I had a 66% off coupon.
I would NEVER consider a game like this (without trading cards) with a pricetag like this when you're done with it after ~5 hours.
It may sound harsh, but the reality is I'm not sure if I'm ever going to play the game again after completing it.
Atleast the developer put in a "Start new game" feature which might help in replay-ability.
Which again brings me to my next point.. as others have already stated, you're not able to rebind the controls.
You'll quickly learn them however, and I only found it frustrating once I broke "zeh purhfect g4m3".
You're able to pause the game with Esc - However, if you want to resume, you have to press space.
If you press esc it restarts, and if you press enter you'll enter the shop (or vice versa - Sue me, I can't remember haha).
Overall the game did its trick - I ultimately had fun with it.
If you like casual games, with simplistic gameplay and "level up system" this might rock your boat.
The graphics and animations, in my opinion, are great.
The sound/music is also awesome, however there's a slight audio glitch with the final potion making overlap noises if you stack them.
The game doesn't crash or anything, it just sounds weird when the second potion is about to wear out).

Well I don't really know how to start this off so I suppose I will dive right into it. This game is unfortunately a shotty shell of what it seemingly was meant to be. I didn't even play for very long before I got tired of it.
What I don't like:
Non-Intuitive Controls - Seriously, the controls in this game don't make much sense at all. This game is an MMO style game. Most MMO games use the same basic control system for things like interacting with the environment, and looting. This is fixed by spending about 5 minutes remapping the keys to what they SHOULD be for an MMO. It is almost as if the Devs had never played an MMO before to understand what the keyboard layout is. Why are Q and E mapped to "rotate the character left and right?" What game even has those as keys? Q should be a hotkey ability and E should access looting, same with a right click.
Clunky First Person Mode - Here is the thing about making an MMO with the ability to play in first person. Either polish it to the point where it is remotely functional, or DONT HAVE A FIRST PERSON MODE.
In short, don't waste your time with this game unless the devs decide to make the UI acceptable.

I will admit that I am not familiar with the source material.  I have heard of Agatha Christie, but have never read any of her books, so I was going into this game fresh.  The player character is Hercule Poirot, a French(?) detective.  He has a sidekick named Hastings, who reminds me of Watson.  In fact, not to throw shade at Mrs Christie, but man does this entire concept seem like a straight rip-off of Sherlock Holmes.  They even make a joke about it during the game.  Plagiarism aside, I did have a good time playing it.  The game starts with Poirot and Hastings receiving a letter from a serial killer, challenging the detective to a game and detailing the location of the first murder.  Apparently Poirot has a reputation of being a great detective, so the killer wants him to prove it.
The gameplay, like the recent Sherlock Holmes games, consists of light puzzle solving and basic deduction logic puzzles where you gather clues and then use them to come to conclusions.  There are also Telltale-esque conversation choices you can make that affect a witness/interviewee’s responses, though to be honest the game seems very linear so I am not sure if there is really any right or wrong answer.  The choices you make can earn you some “ego” points, but I haven’t seen that there is any way to fail an interview.  A few times I seemed to have angered someone and the conversation ended abruptly, but I never had a point in which I didn’t have enough clues to move forward in the story.  There were also occasions where I had angered someone clearly, but because I didn’t pick the “correct” option, Poirot immediately asked the right question in order to get the clue I needed.  So I am assuming that the “ego” points are simply a way to encourage multiple play-throughs in order to get all 400.  The art is well done, and despite some slight hiccups while loading cutscenes, there weren’t many bugs or any game crashes.
Overall, if you are a fan of the genre I think you would enjoy this game.  The puzzles don’t make any sense in the context of the story (why does a tobacco selling 50 year old woman have a complex puzzle box?) but they are decently challenging, if not a bit too far in-between.

I have to say I am absolutely stunned by how great this game. It is extremely refreshing to finally have an original combat system that is actually enjoyable. In fact it's so enjoyable that the only disappointment I have about this game is the lack of opportunity to experience it. Having played through to the end of the campaign I felt sort of slapped in the face at the end. You mean to say I made all of this progress just to be thrown into a small area with a couple of npcs that repeat the same dialogue? Now don't get me wrong, the experience was definitely worth what I paid. However, I was expecting at least some sort of system where I could enjoy randomized dungeons and build on to all of that progress. If you are like me and enjoy gameplay over dialogues you will be gravely disappointed by this game's replayablity factor. No one finds it exciting to replay encounters on a higher difficulty consisting of the same enemies slapped with higher resistances and damage capabilities. Now sure if you're a sucker for the story and want to see what the other three follower's have to offer then you'll likely have another enjoyable playthrough. That is as long as you don't change the difficulty and become frustrated with encounters that used to last ten minutes or so now lasting about a half of an hour. I think this feels really forced and isn't the kind of "difficulty" we are looking for.
The only other complaint I have regards the party customization. You mean I can't join a friend's game and create my own character to play how I like? Was it supposed to be fun to play as one of their undergeared side characters that recieved little attention in regard to how their skills were allocated? As if that wasn't enough, you are only able to make one completely customized character for your party throughout the entire playthrough. Why put these limits on such a beautiful game with great character customization?
Overall this was a great game that just deserves a little more thought in terms of replayability. Don't let these things sway you against buying the game. You likely won't be bothered by any of these issues until you've spent about 100 hours travelling about Rivellon or until you finish exploring all it has to offer. If you're a fan of RPGs, get it. I have 146 hours in Conan Exiles so far. I was drawn in by the Conan theme which Funcom has a lot of experience with and do very well. Rather than trying to “sanitize” the Conan world, they have really tried to embrace all its themes including the brutality and horror. They didn’t shy away from themes of slavery, human sacrifice, etc. Stylistically they have made some very bold choices, and really appear to be trying to stay true the Conan universe.
You start off as a naked outcast without even two rocks to rub together, and gradually are supposed to work your way up to be King. (one of the final items you can craft is a throne). There are “blitz” servers that wipe every month, and start fresh, beginning again the race to see who get to the top  the fastest.
It is my first survival game, and just to stay alive for the first few hours was really challenging as I struggled to learn all the things you need to do to not die. Once you get the hang of it, it’s gets easier and you can move on to bigger challenges at your own pace. (keep in mind, sandstorms don’t do damage yet, in the future that will be very dangerous to new players who haven’t built a shelter  yet.) Nighttime is difficult, you can venture outwith a torch but its easy to get lost. The monsters don’t change between night and day, which I think is a missed opportunity. There should be some nocturnal beasts that prowl at night.
I had a blast my first few days. However it becomes apparent this game is still very unfinished. There are caves/dungeons filled with beasts and sometimes a “boss”, but most of them don’t have any treasure or special items in them. There is only a cursory smatter of lore (which makes it very special when you do find a new clue). I suspect they will be adding a lot more to the dungeons and caves, but for now they are a bit bland.
The creatures spawn very fast, especially in caves, which is difficult for solo players. (It appears the game is more balanced for clan/tribal play but since I am a solo player this review will be from the solo perspective.)
Building is fun, and you can start building within the first few hours of play (unlike some RPGs where crafting a castle is relegated to the end-game). However, it can be very discouraging when your base gets raided and you lose all the crafting stations and supplies that you spent many hours getting. For this reason, as a solo player, I try to find a “hidden”, out of the way spot, and tend to keep my base as a small as possible so it won’t be noticed. It’s not that hard to build a very large sandstone castle, but its also easy for any steel-tier player to bash it down. If you prefer, you can also find PVE and Casual-PVP servers that do not allow player structures to be destroyed.
There is currently no “fog” on the map, so you can see the whole world and people on reddit and youtube have mapped out everything, showing where to find every special thrall/priest/dungeon/etc. I think you are only cheating yourself and your own fun if you use those guides. I like learning the map myself through my own exploration. It’s a great landscape with lots of hidden surprises and interesting habitats around every corner. I look forward to them adding more biomes and monsters.
Unlike some games, The potions you can craft  do not instantly heal all wounds, they just give you a slight boost over a period of time. This feels more realistic than many RPGs where you stop and eat a muffin in the middle of a battle to instantly heal yourself.
At character creation you can chose 1 of 3 religions ( 4 if you count Crom, but Crom doesn’t do anything in the game -- It seems to be the  “atheists” option). But whatever you choose, once in the game you can learn all 3 religions and build temples for all 3 gods. To compete against other players, its best to learn all 3 and build all 3 temples as they offer different weapons, special foods and healing drinks. But the game doesn’t even let you build temples close to each other. This may be okay as a “game mechanic” but it really kills the immersion roleplay/realism. It seems very artificial, why cant you build temples close to each other if the gods don’t care about you worshipping all the gods? I think if people want to learn a new religion, they should lose their old one and no longer be able to get items from that temple. There should also be a Grand Temple somewhere on the map for each god where any worshipper of that religion can go and craft a special item.
Also on religion, all 3 gods require “human sacrifice” to craft the special foods/drinks. This seems a bit lazy on the part of the devs. I can see Yog and maybe Set requiring human sacrifice. But Mitra should use a different mechanic and could be the god-of-choice for people who don’t want to do human sacrifices. Instead of butchering the corpse, Mitra followers could bless it, sprinkle holy water, cremate it, or purify it some way, and receive a purified essence  in that way.
The thrall system is a great concept. Hunting and capturing thralls is one of my favourite things to do in the game.  It would be great if they had more thralls able to craft special items, even if the items they make are just decorative, for example, Dafari windchimes.
The weapon progression is very unbalanced at the moment. It’s shockingly bad. Example: You can get a broadsword at level 12 that does 72 DPS. Then at lvl 20 you can get a khopesh that does 69 DPS (less than the broadsword) then at lvl 26 you can get a falcatte that does 69 dps (still worse than the lvl 12 sword)  then at lvl 28 you can get a cutlass than does 72 dps, (same as the lvl 12 sword) , then finally at lvl 30 you can get a longsword that does 96 dps.  It’s terrible and nonsensical.
The game advances from stone weapons, to iron and then steel. I would like to see more tiers in the weapons, and a longer progression from starter weapons to top tier, with upgrades available every 5 levels or so. Right now its very flat. You get a good sword at level 12, and a better one at level 30, with nothing decent in between. (And this game only goes up to level 50).  They could improve  this by adding a “bronze age” when you need to gather “tin” to craft bronze, before you can later advance to get to iron. Or they could put something even better than steel, like some kind of Atlantean Adamantine, that is very rare (perhaps only found in the monster caves?).
Two-handed weapons handi-cap you by not allowing you to carry a shield, torch (so they are useless at night) or a capture leash, but they don’t offer more damage to balance those drawbacks. I would suggest two-handed weapons should generally do more damage those similar-tier one-handed weapons (this would improve balance and realism).
There are only 8 quickbar slots for all your gear, which is really not enough. Every minute I am in my inventory swapping quickbar items.
Combat is very limited and spammy at the moment. A sword can only slash. A spear can only jab. Shields block well, but are slow to bring up unless you anticipate the attack. I think they need to add, at a minimum, a simplified-Chivalry style combat system. Every weapon should have a slash, stab, and overhead. I think Funcom is aware they need to spice up combat. However it’s really up in the air how exactly they will fix it. Everything else can be fixed by “adding more content” and “fixing bugs/balance” but I think how they deal with the combat system will be the issue that will really “make or break” this game.

Take for example the following exchange of dialogue between you and a former squad member in one of the game's DLCs , Lair of the Shadow Broker (keep in mind that while there is a lot of DLC, one can attain them all for free with a few google searches)
The exchange in question occurs during a car chase.
You: "What kind of guns does this thing have?"
Teammate: "It's a taxi, it has a fare meter!"
It was these small moments that made the game so much more realistic, and the characters so much more lifelike.
Like I said, this is an absolute gem of a game. If you're going to play it, I recommend a few things:
- Play ME1 (that way you can import your character into this game, and then into 3)
- Install whatever mods you wish (The main one I'd recommend is ALOT, it changes heaps of the game's textures to look more crisp)
- Get all squadmates loyal and buy all upgrades for the Normandy. Play the game and you'll find out why.
