The popular flash game now has a full release on Steam. Knightmare Tower is a simple concept that is executed with little flaw. It's a game that boasts accessibility, but can still be challenging to experienced gamers. So brandish your blade and fuel up the rocket, we don't want anyone falling down the tower.
Knightmare starts with a simple story; ten princesses have been kidnapped and need rescuing from a tower. The tower is in control of... let's just call him Boss, and his monsters and minions will do anything to keep you from reaching the damsels.
The gameplay however is quite unique; You are launched from a rocket and propelled into the air. Monsters approach from beneath to attack you, to which you can perform a downward slash with your sword. Slashing enemies propels you further into the air, with the idea of gaining higher speeds and maintaining momentum. Without hitting enemies you will eventually lose momentum and fall in to the quicly approaching lava, causing your run to end. Monsters can also end your run by attacking you and depleting your health. Forcing you to attack monsters as soon as they appear, as opposed to letting them act first. This adds a madness to runs as there can be tens of monsters chasing you up the tower at once. Bouncing off their heads becomes very satisfying and fun.
Knightmare Tower is a roguetype, meaning its broken into runs and after each run you have the chance to spend your loot on upgrades. Such as: better armor that increase your health bar, a better sword that deals more damage to difficult enemies, and potions that can be found during your runs and improve your character in some way for a short  time. This means many runs are needed before having the necessary equipment to take on the boss. There are also quests that can be completed on each run. You have multiple attempts at the same three quests, adding more challenge for players who want it. After each quest is completed, you are rewarded with gold, and a new quest takes it's place. There are dozens of quests in the game to complete, but none feel out of the reach of experienced players.
Reaching certain points in a run, will let you break a ceiling, and pass through to the next section of the tower. Higher sections of the castle have slightly more difficult enemies than the lower sections, but become much easier with upgraded tools. Additionaly each ceiling you brake through rescues another princess; who has a special power attached to her. These powers show up in bubbles during runs. When attacked these powers activate and can have varying effects. Some just deal massive damage to enemies on screen, while others summon mini bosses. This changes up the gameplay and helps it feel fresh, even after a few hours in.
The main game isn't very long, but you would be leaving a lot behind to stop after rescuing the princesses and defeating the boss. You probably won't have all of the gear upgrades, and a survival mode is unlocked after beating the story, with all new quests. There is easily another couple of hours after the main story of things to complete, and many of the Steam achievments demand more playtime. The replayability of this game adequite, and the games design is fun enough that completing a story is somewhat in the back of the gamer's head anyway. This game is just fun to throw on and play.
Knightmare Tower has tight controls, a fluent artstyle, and an addictive gameplay. For under five dollars this is a no brainer game for anyones library. You will be hacking a slashing monster for hours without slashing your bank account. If you played the flash version, or are new to the franchise, you will not be disapointed.

As always I'm slightly on the edge should I recommend this. I loved the world, the writing. the aesthetics and the athmosphere. I actually enjoyed the openness of the ending witch seems to be complaint for many. But it's slightly on the short side and I see how this could have been one of the definitive gaming experience of my adult life but it just falls slightly flat... If there just had been some side quests to let us settle more into the world, maybe even third place to visit beside the yurt and dome. Maybe more interaction between the girl and our main character not directly involving the main storyline.
Other gripe I've got is the decition to have player character have a voice. That feels a bit uncanny in a first person game, especially as the english voice actor was slightly on the stiff side. This tought I could overcome as the writing of the dialog is solid, as is the case with all the other writing done for this game. I also got a weird vegetanion sprite missalligment where leaves didn't touch the trunks of trees and the flowers didn't connect to any of the traws coming from the ground. Also the lack of FOV-slider and key-rebinding in the options menu, is to be mention. Altought it didn't bother me as I don't get motion sick and play with WASD.
Then on to the positive side as aesthetics and graphics of this game are amazing. The world seems vibrant, but slighly washed out giving a feeling of mixture of reality and aquarelle painting. The visual desing of the android bodies is just something that will blow you away altought there's just two of them. They really look like something real humans have transferred their consciousness to. Something they live in and have personalised. The video eyes gives them amazing character and liveliness altought no other part of their face moves. The world feel lived in and seems to well match the slowly progressing disaster that is revealed have happen to humanity.
Continuing with the positives music and the sound desing are also solid. You feel like you are on the mongolian steppe as the wind blows trought the trees and birds shirp in the air. Music is just spot on and is eary in the right way. Even in the pavillions the slightly cheerier music gives this overall wibe of something beeing slightly off.
After those positives I've got one more gripe. There actually feels to be a slight pacing issue in the game. The main mechanic around exploring is not in any way timed or rushed. As for the opposition narrative driven in conversations with the girl drives a sense of urgency fairly early on (for spoiler reasons I will not reveal). I think this could have been fixed with more 'casual' conversations with the girl and the third character, and so giving the main conversational narrative a space to breathe same way the exploration has. Othervice the story and writing as mentioned is great. All the clippings are well written, characters make sense and even the lameish amnesia startingpoint is made to work trought what you find in the world and how you want to interpret them.
At the end I'd recommend this, but with a disclaimer. This game is mostly about the aesthetics, world, story and the athmosphere. It is somewhat lacking in the mechanics department having very limited and scripted interactions with the world. I would even compare it to 'Dear Esther' as a virtual installation altought with lots more interaction. In both narrative is given to you in pieces for you to interpret and the ending gives similar feeling of who or what was our pov-character in the end and what actually happenned.
Despite there is lack of replay value with my other gripes, this game will most likely end up there with the rare games that I will revisit from time to time for that 'reading that familiar book wibe' and if I could find new angle on interpreting it.

Instead this is a point and click adventure centered around the idea of waking up inside a tent with amneisa next to a non-functional android and being required to piece together your memories and her body by solving puzzles, riddles and mini-games. Whether or not you like this game will depend strongly on whether or not you can appreciate story driven "investigating" and first-person puzzle games, I personally was able to get into both and really enjoyed this game.
The story is really where this game shines, I love cyberpunk, psychological mystery type stuff and this story really covers a lot of ground.
The only downside I find is that the ending feels .. unfinished. Yea, its one of "those" .. where its supposed to have you come up with the answers yourself but instead looks like they ran out of time and had to ship the game without an ending.
However, the journey, the story and the adventuring and the puzzling were all enjoyable for me and I recommend this game to anyone who likes point-and-click adventure games. Just make sure you really know what this game is about before trying it.

After about 70 hours in this game i was able to finish the game on classic mode.
Turns out there were a few notable things:
- If you rush the game like I did, you miss great parts of the game like lore, quests, areas etc. (Yup, I "rushed" the game in 70 hours, turns out i missed about 40% of the game)
- The game itself isn't hard at all, once you start to question yourself about some decisions (Especially once I started thinking "Can I fight?" or "Where do I want to fight?", the game became far easier and also more interesting). Before that I was sometimes somewhat maddened by some fights, even considering them unfair, even though they sure were not (especially Alexander, Radeka, Doctor, Braccus)
- Don't kill NPC's you aren't sure about you won't need them anymore (like Migo or Stingtail for example). If you want the XP, do the quests first, you can always kill them afterwards
Pros:
- Incredibly rewarding feelings when you figure out how to achieve your goals, since you have so many ways for problem solution in this game (well, most of the time)
- Good synchro / story (I usually play all my games in english so I don't actually care about localization)
- Reworked AP / SP system makes your choices more meaningful
- Reworked armor types and status protection causes you to think in a more strategic way (even in lower difficulty)
- Graphics and atmosphere is just awesome
- More races than in D.OS 1
- Skill crafting lets you combine your favourite spells to even better ones
- Definitly my personal game of the year 2017
Cons:
- There sure are some bugs in this game, but nothing to major (e.g. I had some random teleporting back to earlier positions / Re-Equipping stuff I wanted to mark as wares / Annoyingly slow item pickup when using the ALT key)
- Autocamera keeps screwing up some places in the game, especially when there are some huge high differences (Mainly on the Nameless Isle)
- The AI sometimes behaves somewhat irratic (e.g. Doing basically nothing in a turn / Attacking their own guys with massive AOE just to scratch my tank / Too dumb to dispell invisibility)
Conclusion:
I'm about 10 hours in the next playthrough (Lone Wolf / Honour Mode), making up for all the stuff I missed before. I still think this game was/is worth every penny I spent.
Also there still is multiplayer and gamemaster mode (gosh, there is still so much waiting for me).
Already looking forward to D:OS 3 ;)
Edit for the interested:
- Wiped my savegame on the Burning Witch (Screw your "Shining Lights")
- Wiped it a second time in arx due to some deathfog (...)
- Other than that, basically easier than normal difficulty (Somewhat strange that you can kill the Doctor and Braccus in a single turn lol)

Submerged is a short exploration game that I feel just barely missed the mark for being an exceptional game and left me wishing there was more to it.
Visually the game is beautifully realized, if a bit repetitive. The city is large, haunting and begs to be explored. There's a lot of sights to be seen, and a treat for people who like abandoned or post-apocalyptic cityscapes. I think this is where I feel most disappointed in the game though, because I felt that it had so much more to offer with the environment it gives you to explore. A vast majority of the city is just window dressing, and is strictly look-but-don't-touch. I would have loved to actually been able to scale any of the buildings, and being able to go inside them an take a look around would have been heaven. As it is, there's actually very little to do in a world that looks like there would be a ton of stuff to do. It feels like a missed opportunity.
Gameplay basically boils down to exploring the city on your boat, with some of the taller buildings acting as islands that you can scale. The climbing portion is the main aspect of Submerged, and I feel that it would have been better suited as a platformer. Video and pictures may give the impression of a platformer, but your actions are performed automatically for you, and so there's no skills required to play this game. Lacking the need for timing, spacing or precision that a platformer needs, this is essentially a maze-based exploration game: you simply pick a path and follow it through. I understand that Submerged isn't meant to be a platformer, but again, it just feels like it should have been something more.
I recommended the game, but with some big reservations. First, at full price it's really difficult to justify what you'll get. There are other exploration, narrative focused games that offer a similar, if not better, experience for less money. At about 5 hours worth of gameplay, I'd put the value of this game at about $10 USD, anymore than that is pushing it. Secondly, there's very little actual gameplay. Your skills won't be tested, there's no progression, and you can't fail in anyway. This game is more about uncovering the mistery of the city, your character's story, seeing the sights the world has to offer. If you can enjoy that and don't mind a repetitive but beautiful world, then get the game.

After the first hour of playing this game, I wasn't sure I wanted to continue. It's rather pretty on the whole, but the textures are bland, the movement animation of the player character is the stiffest I've seen in many years, and the movement of the boat seems unnatural. Also, the only real action in the game--climbing buildings, à la Ubisoft towers--is not at all challenging or even clever for the most part. (To be fair, it isn't challenging in Ubisoft games, either; but those games offer other challenges, which this game does not.)
But then I found myself coming back the next day to play some more. In part this was because of the interesting way the story unfolds via pictograms. There are two stories, one about the main characters, a brother and sister (you play the sister), and the other about how the world came to be "submerged." The city story is the longer of the two and I found it a bit hard to parse, but I appreciated the unique way the story was told was told. The pictograms are unlocked by finding collectibles, which gives you a reason to explore the world beyond finding the ten supply crates needed to nurse your injured little brother back to health, which is the primary motivation of the game.
I was also struck by the natural beauty. Though the boat handles rather awkwardly, there are impressive moments as you zip along and a pod of dolphins comes to swim alongside your boat, or a ray soars over your head, or a giant whale breaches the water in front of you, backlit by a lovely sunset. There is no combat and you can't die. The game is just a charming palate cleanser, which is exactly what I needed after almost 45 brutal hours of Mafia 3.

I swear I had reviewed this game months ago but well, no. There are no traces of a review of mine here so well, I don't know, I played it really a lot in order to get all the achievements (which are all secret, but fortunately the developers themselves published an official walkthrough XD) 'cos for some reasons I couldn't manage to get some endings but we'll be back to this in a short time.
I studied Japanese during my first academical degree, well that's Katakana in the title and reads Buruumuun (I always loved to double the vocals, like instead of ō I didn't write ō itself or "ou" like you often find but always "oo" and so on; in Japanese it's very common to find those double vowels both in hiragana katakana or kanji scripts!).. which being Katakana of course renders in Japanese the English Blue (buruu) and Moon (muun).
I don't precisely know why they chose to write such a strange bilingual title but anyways here it is, Star Sky - Blue Moon.
It's a minimalistic game with lost of endings, and it unfolds during a night journey. What you see in my screenshots or in the game's store page and such is what you'll get - you're a shadow, a man, and you'll encounter some triggers: a girl, a flower, a sign, a house, a hill. Each one of them can change your future and your ending: you can stop besides the flower, take it and give it to the girl (another shadow of course, it's night XD) or you can make it rain by doing another action by the signpost and so on.
The game mechanics works like this, but bear in mind that you can't go back so you have to pay attention to everything in the background.
And many things will amaze you - the artwork in this game is simply astonishing and full of atmosphere. The night sky and the whole scenario makes you literally jump into the game like it was reality itself.
It's true what other reviewers noted: the game itself is quite short, and if you refer to guides can be even shorter (even though it took me some hours to unlock and watch everything), and since it takes place in the very same pathway it doesn't offer much replayability. But it's an original idea, it's been amazingly programmed and it's 100% worth to be played from the start to the beginning of every (short) route/ending.
Not to talk, of course, about the audio; graphics are the most emotional aspect, but also the sounds of the night are fundamental to enjoy as a whole the game experience. Well, more than a game it's an animated novel. You can't die, lose or such, you just have to walk and take decisions that will change the destiny of yourself and of the whole atmosphere around you, from rainy and starry skies to rainbows.
It's very relaxing and touching, and I obviously will recommend this game to everyone.
One should not though expect a true "game" as I said, it's not a platformer and not even a minimalistic arcade game. It's a visual and audio experience, but it will take lots of thinking to get all the possible endings and well, if you're into these kinds of games trust me, it will be an awesome afternoon :)
There's only one downside: the price. 4€, in my currency, is way too much. But it's too good to be left out in my opinion, so don't waste 4 full euros (or dollars, now we're like 1 to 1,1 eur-usd xD) but instead place it in your wishlist. When it will come out for just 0,4€ or such, like I did last summer, buy it as soon as possible.. you won't be disappointed for sure. I fully understand many points noted by players that rated this game down, but to me it's been a pleasure to play for hours and I'm sure it will be the same for everyone who's into these experiences :)

This is a very involved and complex game. When you hit the turn button, be prepared to wait a bit until it is your turn again. It takes time to generate the turns for the other nations. This doesn't bother me, but some players don't care for it. I usually keep my mobile phone handy and surf the web while I wait. When your turn comes round again, you get a list at the bottom of the screen you can scroll through that alerts you to what other nations have done as well as what your nation traded and took in via taxation.
In a nutshell, you might think of this as a vastly superior version of Imperialism. Imperialism was a game from the 1990s that featured industry, trade, diplomacy, national resource development and a military component.
You have military units, some with leaders. Your military requires you keep up supply lines for them. There are a lot of units. I have played Japan thus far and have found available what one would expect from an army of the 1850s in Japan but with some surprises like signals units, balloon observation and medical units. Players also have naval units available.
Trade is pretty straightforward, as is the colonial aspect and the diplomacy. Research seems to be carried out without player intervention for the most part.
There is a political component. Under the regional census tab, you can attempt to enact social reforms and laws. Under trade and commerce, you can enact trade policies which will effect inflation and wealth along with domestic contentment. You can also adjust taxation as it is broken down into income taxes, tarriffs, etc.
The number of things that you can build in this game is amazing. From farms of all differing types of agriculture, to manufacturing, military and naval buildings, you can do quite a bit. Hovering over the structure, or improvement, tells you the number of days to build and components you need to do it. A turn is 15 days, so some structures take a while to come online. An area that will allow you to build a particular item lights up green, which makes thing move a bit faster.
I would certainly recommend this game. There is a learning curve and the game features several tutorial modules that are very helpful. I recommend playing those. After the tutorial, I chose the nation of Japan to play because it is a smaller nation and I thought it would be easier to learn with versus trying to play Britain or France. There are also several scenarios included with the game and the developers have created others to go with it. The update tab on the starting screen takes you to the developer's website where you can purchase the other scenarios.

An extremely addicting arcade game made by Juicy Beast Studios, one of the best (in my opinion) indie game developers out there.
The first thing that caught my eye was the art style, which itself has a slick, smooth, cartoon-y look to it that reminds me of games such as Castle Crashers, the art in which I also find amazing. All the monsters in the game slowly evolve depending on how far up the tower you go, and their models gradually become more sinister but also more detailed.
The gameplay is very much reminiscent of Burrito Bison (another game I enjoyed a lot but unfortunately is a flash game and not on Steam at the moment), mainly because it was also made by Juicy Beast. It shares similar game mechanics, where you make your way from a point A to point B while defeating enemies and collecting money. You then use this money to upgrade your equipment and thus can get further in the game, and collect more money and repeat. The main twist on this formula however is that in this game you travel up instead of to the right.
The amount of content in this game is very surprising, as it is a decent price and does not look like much. However, the wealth of interesting upgrades and unique quests will occupy you for hours. The enemies progressively get harder and more plentiful, the death lava at the bottom of the screen rises faster, and the game generally keeps you on edge and stays challenging. There is even a boss fight included in the game.
You will feel very satisfied when you finally purchase that last upgrade or get to a floor you've been struggling to get to for a while. In the end, in order to 100% complete the game and get all achievements, you will have to master the Survival mode, which is infinite and will test your skill immensely.
Overall, a refreshing and unique take on this area of arcade games and I am definitely looking forward to more games from Juicy Beast, and maybe even Burrito Bison on Steam? :D

A decent game with some unfortunate design decisions.
The cube minigames are optional, but you have to play them through to continue.  If you fail, you have the choice of continuing anyhow, apparently.  When I failed the first one, I just quit the game before I was given this option.  I found out about the option from the forums here on Steam.  And then I beat all 4 of them without failing again, making it a moot point.  I don't find the cube games fun at all, just a time-waster.
The rest of the game is more like a sparsely-population hidden object game than a point-and-click adventure.  There are quite a few things to look at and move that are useless, and a few things here and there, usually hidden or halfway hidden, that are actually useful.  Unfortunately, if you find something early, you can't do any better than just remembering where it is.
Your inventory is limited, and if you quit and load your game, everything is back where it was originally, unless it has to do with something that was changed permanently in a previous quest.
It's also possible to lose important items, forcing you to quit and load a game in order to be able to find them again.
Finally, the story is...  illogical.  A lot of it makes no sense at all, and if you're a technical person you could very well rage against the tings they try to pass off as logical.
In the end, though, I enjoyed the game overall, so I'm recommending it.  I've focused on the bad points here, but the game is beautiful, the voice acting is pretty good, and it's fun to explore and solve even simple puzzles in such an environment.
Steam says I spent 5.4 hrs playing the game at this point, but I'll probably go back and try to find some of the hidden texts that the achievements reference, so I'm guessing my hours will be higher later.  My wife might want to play it through as well.

--------------------
- Intro
--------------------
In this game you are put in control of Brad the local Hero. One day monsters attack Brad's village but when the local townspeople call upon his help Brad does not really feel in the mood for fighting.
So he picks up his custom guitar to play some tunes instead. With his massive tunes Brad can summon forth units of all sorts and sizes to protect him and fight in his place.
Will Brad be able to protect the towns Crystal and will he be able to fend of waves of foes come to destroy it?
--------------------
- About the Game
--------------------
To control Brad you can use either, keyboard or controller. Though a controller is highly recommended to get the best fun out of this game.
While standing still Brad plays his instrument which only then generates musical notes that can be used, like currency, to summon forth several units.
Those units will follow Brad around and do the attacking instead. The units are anything from close to long range combat, each with unique attacks, strength and weaknesses.
At the beginning your maximum party size can only contain 3 summoned units, though this can be increased through upgrades you can purchase with gold coins that drop from enemies.
Musical notes are also used to allow the purchase of temporary buffs, such as increased speed, strength or raised defence.
Brad also has a special Stun skill that charges with each kill and is your out of Jail skill when things get hairy.
The game is progressing through waves of enemies which will try and destroy the town's Crystal. If the Crystal or you die the game ends and you will have to start from scratch again.
Though after several waves a Boss is encountered and upon defeating the boss you unlock a save point you can choose to continue from after you die.
Between deaths, you can use collected gold coins to upgrade the town, Brad himself, your units or purchase general perks.
Upgrades can be anything from stronger units to higher health, bigger party sizes (allowing more units to be summoned at any one time), increased musical note generation and much much more.
During each wave of enemies you must run around to get close to the enemies so your units can attack them. Be careful though as your units as well as yourself can get damaged and die.
If you die the game ends, if your units die you can re-summon another unit at the cost of Musical Notes which are not endless as they only generate when Brad stands still.
Sometimes musical notes are also dropped by enemies or can be given to you by supporting town folks you can purchase as perks in the upgrade store.
--------------------
- Summary
--------------------
The game is a lot of fun and the upgrade store has a lot to offer to make the game more interesting as you continue to play it adding great replay value. Death is expected in this game as it gives you then a chance to spend your hard-earned gold coins on upgrades and perks to support you to blast through more waves than before.
I definitely would recommend this game.
--------------------
- Known Bugs
--------------------
Brads special Stun skill is most of the time bugged and cannot be executed by keyboard or by controller.
The game is still fun and even without that skill very playable, just a little more challenging.
I don't know if it effects all users or only users with controllers or certain combination of things but either way the developers have replied in
that they are aware of it, had even released a fix in July but it still is bugged. (For me anyway).
I assume/hope another update is soon to follow.

Bardbarian "is a mixture of Tower Defense, RPG & RTS with some 'Shmup and Snake elements". I have no clue where the RTS element is.
It's essentially a game about defending your town crystal from incoming waves of enemies. How do you defend it? You summon party members with different abilities, and you run around dodging bullets and buffing your party (you do not control your attacks, that's all done automatically).
When I saw this game, I thought it looked interesting enough to give it a go. The reviews were surprisingly positive, so... why not?
I'll just say that I was extremely disappointed with this game, and the reviews are unbelievable. I honestly don't know why people think this is a good game of PC! Here's a more lengthy analysis.
First off,
.
The
look a bit average to me, but they're fine. What you see is what you get (from the screenshots). One problem with it, is that it's highly repetitive, even visually, since you have only one map for the campaign. And it doesn't really change its look. Other modes have different maps, but nothing beautiful or interesting.
They're
. That's all I can say about it.
The
was actually not bad. It's almost neo-classical metal, instrumental only. Unfortunately, there's only one song on the campaign. The song loops the entire time, which can (and does) get repetitive after listening to it hours on end. The song loops pretty seemlessly, so that's good (from what I could tell). It was just background music, didn't really add to the experience.
There were no volume sliders either. Only music/sound-effects on/off.
overall. A bit more effort and it could have been much more enjoyable, but playing the same track over and over and over... not good.
The
was fine. The mouse support works fine on the menus. I played the game with a Gamepad and it worked well as well, so good job on that. Unfortunately, the concept of an Options Meny seems to be very foreign to the developer. There's barely anything, which is really annoying. But hey, at least it had rebindable keys!
It's.. again, fine. Nothing noteworthy here, it's missing a bunch of options, but it didn't really prove to be a problem, in my experience.
So, how's
?
Well, it's a grindfest. Almost a waiting game...
As I said, you don't actually attack. So, your whole job is to summon party members, and run around the map, getting close enough for your party to attack. You can also boost the party with +Attack, +Speed, +Defense, or a special Stun ability. If your party member dies, you'll have to summon them again, at a cost. If you Bard dies, or your Crystal is destroyed, you lose. Simple enough.
To summon units and use buffs, you'll need to gather "Notes". You gain a few over time, and you get some more from enemy drops, sometimes.
And that's pretty much it, as gameplay.
Enemy variety was pretty good. They'll shoot at you, with some of them being faster, some firing multiple shots, in multiple directions, etc. It felt inspired by The Binding of Isaac (in a good way). That's not to say that the enemy variety is even remotely closer. Not at all. There are about 10 different enemies, and some of them are fairly similar.
So, all you have to do is literally run around, for the most part. And it gets very old, very fast. It's clearly designed as an iOS game... And a lazy one.
It does have some bullet hell elements. And those could have saved the game! But, there's a huge problem with that. As I mentioned, you have units. These run around you. Which means that your hitbox is huge, and very inconsistent. You simply can't do those awesome dodges you would in a bullet hell. There's no way.
There's an upgrade on the shop for the party to stick closer together, but it barely helps... Everytime you move, they'll stay a bit behind, which would be fine, but it provides nothing of worth! It simply inutilizes most of the dodging. Which means that you'll always play safe, run around, not feeling like a badass.
That's all the gameplay is. Running around.
The Boss fights were significantly better, but still not very good. A few simple patterns, but they at least felt more refreshing.
The second part of this game, is the upgrading system. The game is structured with 4 times of the day, each with 5 levels (a Boss Fight in the 5th). Once you beat a Boss, you can't start from that point after you die, or you can go back to the beginning. This could have been fine, but it isn't.
The upgrades are absolutely necessary. It's literally impossible to make any progress without upgrading everything. And that's usually how games go, but this is different. Your progress is 95% affected by your upgrades. There's no skill involved. It's a question of either having enough damage, or not having it. Even if you're a good player, you'll simply be overun by enemies that will rush you crystal. Once you die, there you go upgrade some more, and then beat it easily. And that's the whole game. The upgrades aren't at all interesting.
This makes for a very, very stale game. You're always doing the same thing! Running around, collecting gold so that you can buy more upgrades, until you reach the end. There are no deep mechanics to learn or master, no strategy, no anything.
The only glimpse of strategy, is choosing your units. You'll unlock different units throughout the game, with different abilities. There's a huge problem with it, though. First off, some of them are pretty much useless. They're not helpful at all, so there's no point in even existing. The other problem, is unit upgrades.
You can upgrade them too (see it as levels, basically. higher level=better version of the unit, simply that). BUT, if you want to test a unit, and see if they're any good, you'll have to upgrade them to the same level that your other units are. Otherwise, you can't compare them very well, can you? But, to upgrade them, you'll waste gold, that you only want to use in a unit that you know will be useful. And this is where the system falls apart.
To try the unit, you'll have to waste gold already, otherwise, there's no point, as they'll be incredibly underpowered. This makes it a waste of gold (which equals to a waste of time, as your play time is simply to collect enough gold to make progress!).
. This leads to a very limited cast of characters. I stuck around with most of the initial ones because of it. And I've done fine. Different characters could interact differently, but when the gameplay is literally just running around, it makes almost no difference! You don't play with the characters, they play themselves.
To its credit, there are 2 other game modes. One is just survival, in which you get a random unit spawn that you must collect, and sometimes food (healing). There are bosses, from time to time, and the enemies will try to kill you (no crystal this time).
The other one is an infinite runner mode, you a few stationary enemies (pretty much towers), and randomly spawned obstacles. Both of these modes unlock 2 cross-over characters, so you are encouraged to try them out.
The achievements were... meh. Barely anything to encourage you different (and interesting) character combinations, which is a really big miss. They're mostly for beating each Boss, unlocking characters, upgrades, etc. Nothing interesting. And that's unfortunate.

This is one of my favorite games that I have played in a few years.  The past 2 or 3 years I have begun playing many games halfway through then stopping to play another as they just don't hold my attention very well as they all seem to be lacking one or more things in favor of something else.  This game probably isn't for everyone so here are the major reasons that I enjoyed this game so much were:
1) The way tasks worked like many older games there aren't arrows pointing to all of your objectives on the top of your screen or on a minimap.
2) The backstory and plot were done in a way that makes sense, and you have to piece it all together from what you read, find in the enviroment, and learn from dialogue so it keeps the player more engaged rather than spoon feeding all of the story to them as they mash random buttons to victory.  This makes people like me who enjoy reading everything they can find in a game feel more rewarded.
3) The game is all about exploration there really isn't any combat (though there sort of can be if you find the laser sword).
4) The art style of the game is very well done everything in it all looks like it belongs nothing feels out of place, and there are a lot of small details that are very easy to miss.
5) Most objects in the enviroment can be interacted with in a way similar to games such as Amnesia.
The game isn't perfect but I had a lot of fun with it and would say that it was easily worth the price.  If you decide to get this game my one piece of advice would be to read everything you find, and pay attention to it even if it doesn't seem important at the time there are notes hidden all over, and they will help you make sense of the story.

I really enjoyed this game, it was a change of pace from spamming my assault rifle in Fallout 4 or any number of other games.  No one shoots at you, you can't die, you can't fall.  This is not a survival or FPS game; it is an exploration game with climbing puzzles.  The reason it is different, is how it tells tales without words in a rather elegant way.
Technical & Game Play:
The game loads quickly and I played through without a single technical problem.  The controls are all wasd and mouse to view in any direction even while moving. something I applaud is there is no separate control set for running the boat. When driving the boat it reacts pretty much as you would expect a boat to.  The spy-glass is a cool feature that lets you spot items of interest (boat parts, lore books, or emergency supplies your brother needs).
Story:
As I mentioned, the game tells tales without words. The most obvious is the story of saving your brother's life, and provide the only words you get in the game to tell you the player what the current goal is.  These are along the lines of: “I need X to fix my brother's problem.” after a cut-scene of you caring for him in some way.  You will need to explore and climb to find emergency supplies on building tops.
As you return to your brother after gathering needed supplies you get a cut-scene of you caring for his injury.  As you rest afterward you get another set of pictographs that represent your family's past, how and why your brother was wounded, your journey, and so on.  This is a linear story told with pictographs as you complete the various stages.  Also hidden aspects of your exploration start to become apparent.
If you explore around you can gather all the various bits of pictographic lore.  These pictographs tell the tale of the city and to some degree the world as a whole.  Since you don't pick these up in order it allows you to slowly start piecing together the story of the city. This serves as an incentive to poke about and have fun
Things I Didn't Like (or thought could be improved):
Beware, once you open the chest with the emergency supplies you automatically return to your brother's side for another cut-scene, so be certain you have thoroughly explored the building or you may need to revisit it to gather lore.  This was likely to keep players to not need to climb down after picking up the supplies but I would have liked a choice to either “cut to camp” or “stay and explore”.
In a game called 'Submerged' I would have liked to be able to swim and gaining entrance to at least one set of supplies via swimming would have been cool.
Some of the terrain puzzles have you go a good deal out of your way to cross a broken roof by using wobbly board or more wall scaling when you could cross a single 1'-2' gap with a simple jump.  This is less about not having the ability to jump and more about the terrain puzzle logic.
Last Thoughts:
This is a great game for relaxing with whales to watch, dolphins to race, and sights to see.  Even better is the stories told hint at the larger picture and world just enough to spark one's imagination.
History has a exciting and morbit charme. Play this game and you will understand the actions of our ancestors by being thrown into they're shoes.

First of all the game has great assets. The music is stellar, some of the best video game music I have ever heard. The graphics are very upbeat and quite good for when the game came out, and because of their cartoony style they stand the test of time rather well.
The gameplay itself is quite entertaining. The game is by no means easy, and the game seems to have a lot of emergent depth, especially when it comes to finding creative tricks. There are a lot of interesting paths through levels and secrets to discover. It's also just a sheer blast to skate through the streets and paint things.
Unfortunately the controls aren't really intuitive. It will take a level or two to become comfortable with them. The first time I beat the game I was on M/K so I can confirm it is possible and fun, but gamepad works much better.
In terms of replay value, the game has two options: there are highscore systems oriented around clear time and points, and there is the ability to replay the game again with all characters unlocked. I haven't looked much into the highscore setups, but I am guessing that the game is not very deep in that area since there are a number of "infinite loops" which are difficult to spot and maybe not intended to be in the game but which can be used to get very high scores pretty easily. I haven't played much of the time-attack type modes, maybe they are more interesting.
As for replaying the game, it becomes much easier to clear the levels, in fact trivially so, after developing the skills needed to go through the game once. But there is a ranking system to each level, and getting an S rank on levels is very difficult. So the game gets a lot of replay value by virtue of this challenge.
Overall a pretty super game, I definitely recommend it.

Pride of nations is conceptually very good and for the right people I can give it a solid recommendation. However I will start this review with the bad and some of the cons are quite big.
-Graphics look like they are from 1995.  Not a huge problem, but honestly I expect even basic graphics to at least maintain the resolution of my screen and have writing not pixel out on counters.
-Learning to play is terribly difficult. Interface is confusion and not self explanitory. Introduction tutotrial gives an overview of the buttons but none of the specifics, such as loading troops onto ships. It consists of a few text pages and some arrows which point to the wrong parts of the screen.  Game features a rule BOOK and you are better off reading that.
-Turn times are long. Too long. The game is complex so there is a lot to be done. To further the problem there are parts of the game which the player will turn through quickly because there is nothing going on. I can get a lot done in the time it takes for a turn to go by
-Poor player feedback. This goes back to the interface. But often it is not easy to get the information you need. For example if someone is offering you an alliance that requires attention. The notification is hidden in an event list filled with transactions. Or inorder to figure out the unemployment (important if creating new jobs) in an area you need to find the population then find and subtract workers from each local jobsite.  Often it is difficult to understand the implications of your actions without consulting the full details of the rules. And good luck if its diplomact which the manual gives no explaination on how the AI thinks.
-Private capital is spent by the government or private projects. This kind breaks the emmusion a little because this is not how nations nfluence their economy.
Now to the good.
This is the single most detailed all inclusive game about the age of imperialism.  Every aspect of the 19th century is put into this game.  It is not clear or well explained but it all it there. I am a big board gamer and this sorta reminds me of one of my favorits Pax Brittanica. Therefore there is not way I cannot recommmend this to anyone who is interested in a deep strategy game.  The game is not too micromanagy once the poor interface is figured out.

Ok where do I start with this one... Jet Set Radio was easily one of the best games that the dreamcast had to offer. I hadn't played the game but I knew from word of mouth that it was great and had some great graphics for its time. Ok I bought this version on sale cause I thought why the ♥♥♥♥ not? Little to my knowledge did I know that this game had horrible controls. This is my first complaint, the keyboard conrtols were so damn awful. It was hard to be precise when trying to board a rail at max speed. This was unbearable. I also had a problem in which the A and D keys were turning the camera left and right aswell as turning the character. These controls were so frustrating. My second issue was that the game kept crashing. Whether it tabbing out to check stuff or completing a mission, the game would always crash back to my desktop. This was a major problem that just turned me off from continuing this game.

I have never seen any game do this before and it was an absolute nightmare trying to get around.
The graphics and sound were nice. The cell shading works well making this classic look as good today as it did back then on the dreamcast. The voice acting is some of the best I've seen in a dreamcast game. Especially better than a certain horrible mess of a game people praise for some reason. The soundtrack is also good. The music really suits what's going on in each stage and is pretty chilled out.
Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-graphics
-voice acting
-music
cons:
-horrible keyboard controls
-terrible launcher navigation
-many crashes

A mystery game where you follow a detective's investigations through a single case. It's more of a narrative game where you follow the detective's actions and logic than one where you do things for yourself. Visuals and music are good enough although sometimes the animations are a little off. Story is fine, apparently based off a book and movie. For me, the story was the strong part while the interactive part of the game was just something to do while I awaited the next breakthrough in the story (similar to other narrative games like this). The interactive parts are kept pretty straightforward so it's not too frustrating or contrived.
Maybe a few leaps of logic but nothing impossible. There's only so many interactions to do so you can get through some parts with guesswork. I had some trouble with a few puzzles but steam forums helped me through them. I think there's a hint button in the escape menu but I didn't try it.
It's very useful if you have a game mindset when investigating things.
It has multiple profiles but doesn't allow you to manually save and load. It would be nice to have multiple save file slots so you can choose different options and see what happens without repeating a full playthrough. They probably didn't want it to prevent 'easy' achievements but the story doesn't really branch out from choices (so instead they want to to replay everything to see different choices). However, if you're so inclined you can do save scumming per the achievement guide.
Other thoughts:
Worth a try if you're in the mood for a decent detective story where you are guided through things (so more of a passive experience).

First impressions:
As you can see (at the time of writing), I haven't played the game much, as such I can only write about first impressions.
Loading the game initially through steam, account setup is pretty basic (log in, verify e-mail, get to playing) except for one tiny detail... you can't choose your user name. The software generates a hash code for your name (around 20 characters in length including upper/lower case letters, numbers, and hyphens ( - ) ) and I have to say... the support team is *FAR* less than helpful (their response : we can't change unique user names)...
Okay, let me rant a moment... so what they're saying is their programmers can't use SQL? Can't use PHP? Can't... um... access their OWN databases? I think not... I think someone is too lazy to correct their mistake. Log in with an e-mail because "that's the username"... but tried logging in with my e-mail and it says "invalid username" but using the hash... all hunky dory.
There, that's out of the way, let's get to the game itself and not the customer service.
The game is old-school. The graphics sit somewhere between Fallout 2 and Fallout 3. The NPCs and "Monsters" are all standing around in one place, tethered to a spot (where they will chase after you for a predetermined distance before giving up and returning to their spawn) ~ a lot like EverQuest 1. The world itself is a little on the empty side, but I cannot honestly say if it remains this way (the internal zones and buildings are pretty cool, and for a game that is set in a wasted world, it's as desolate as it should be).
The story-line is thoughtful and creative, even if it's a little flat and tired. It is interesting, it is engaging, it's just that it's a bit 'old.'
The GMs are super helpful, and I've seen them online every time I've logged in. The help channel is busy, and responsive (I can't even begin to say how refreshing that is)! That said... they have the typical censored chat system that is pretty much par for the course... but don't bother censoring your own words (like: aw s*** that sucks) because a GM will threaten to mute you for language (a redundancy which borders on zealous). Hardly anything to complain about... keep it clean (and PG so you don't offend the super-innocent teenagers playing this game - note sarcasm).
Movement is a bit cumbersome and unweildly ~ but once you're used to it it isn't too bad (such as hitting tab or the middle mouse button to turn on targeting, and therefore a locked mouselook instead of free-look). It's pretty hard to get the camera around front of your character (but it's entirely possible I've just overlooked something).
Skills, stats, levelling, trades... a detailed system. A wonderfully detailed system. APs (which I may mistakenly believe to mean "action points") are granted frequently in small doses for everything from quest completion to simply levelling up your trade skills. Mousing over anything will give you a clear and detailed description of what that thing is for and what it does and what it effects - I've long desired that games did this, some do, but FE starts with this right out of the gate... they do NOT leave you in the dark (as long as you can read at a Junior High level, it's sweet).
Questing is a bit weird to get used to - the map (okay, the map... WOW... if you like detailed maps that don't hold your hand, but make some pretty obvious markers... then this map system is for you - detail, detail, detail... easily one of the most beautiful map systems I've seen in a game in a LONG time)... anyway, the map... shows a little red X on your radar that when you mouse-over it will show you the name of the quest it's for. There are no indications of distance on the radar or for quests, and some quests are a bit ambiguous (really, they just don't hold your hand there - read it... then figure it out ya lazy bums)!
Will I continue playing? You bet. What is the not free to play? Buying keys for dropped lockboxes. Unlocking your entire wardrobe. Paying for premium content (usually access to skills, timers, clothing, zones, etc) in three different monthly plans (from about $12 to $30), not so bad - but pretty steep considering you can get a great deal more out of a game like LotRO (Lord of the Rings Online) for about $15/month, with far better quality and content. Still, not too bad, save that it's comfortably on the expensive side (especially for what it is and offers).
Do I recommend it? Yes. Get past the opening stuff. Put some points into Intelligence and Perception (both of those increase your maximums for tradeskills), and READ THE QUESTS.
If you don't like reading, or actively engaging a game... this isn't for you. I, however, love reading the content in a game (I want to see what other writers and creative teams are doing with their work) and I enjoy a challenge. As such, I really enjoy this.
In short, a rocky start, some negative experience with the customer service and GMs, a bit unweildly and old-school, and expensive beyond the F2P... but a game that grows on you quickly and really eats up time (that's a mark of a good game right there).
Test it out. If you liked Fallout 2 and 3, then you'll probably enjoy this. I don't think it's a "long term" game (as far as playability) in my books, but that's simply my own opinion and nothing more. Plenty of players are really enjoying this game, and that speaks volumes about the overall content and quality.

If you are into bullet-hell, mouse-manipulation, defense, and/or snake-style games, you should really enjoy this game.
I had played a similar style of game on the IOS, and it was super responsive because it was all through the touch screen. The app was very fleshed out.
This game is just as fleshed out, and I have enjoyed playing it thus far.
You play as a bard, so your player character does not actually attack. Instead, you summon support units (ex: archer, fighter, mage; party limit is initially 3 max) who follow you around, snake-style, and attack the closest enemies. In the beginning, you will notice that the party is a little spread out, and this is fixed by upgrading "body spray" in the store. The game is very charming and comical, the art and music is very good.
Enemies spawn on the right side of the map and make their way toward your town gem on the left. Over time, you slowly gain "notes" that you use to summon units (you can select 3 from you unit pool to take along with you into the levels) and also to trigger buffs like enchanced damage, speed, or defense.
The upgrading is pretty well fleshed out, as you can upgrade your units, your hero, and the town. For your units, it is basic overall upgrades like health and damage. There are also unlockable characters like Octodad and Super Meat Boy, which is a cute addition. Your hero can upgrade health, party size, party closeness (body spray), and other things. It is critical to upgrade the bard, as once he is dead, your round is over.
Upgrading the town is crucial as well, as you can unlock things like a town pet who grabs gold for you (allowing you to effectively dodge more enemy projectiles and not worry about disappearing loot), a town drunk who periodically vomits, slowing any enemies that enter the bile radius. Later, you may unlock a high level barracks or college, which generates extra free units to help you in defense of the town.
The game is really, really fun if you like this style of gameplay, and you can easily spend time playing this if you enjoy upgrading to completion.
The controls are very responsive, you can easily play with just the mouse, but I recommend you either use the keyboard (WASD) to move + mouse to trigger skills, or to use the mouse to move and the keyboard hotkeys to summon units and trigger skills. The tutorial is short, skippable, and very helpful. Learning curve is minimal, however, the game is suprisingly difficult in thr beginning - I had thought I was fighting the boss, but it was only the "pre-boss" (indicated by a skull on the minimap. The real bosses come when you move onto a red (vs. blue) square on the minimap.
Needless to say, I got served very hard.
Give it a try, definitely recommend.

One of Christie's more famous novels, you can't really complain about the quality of the story, its a classic Poirot novel.
Not to everyone's taste, I quite like the cell shaded graphics
All 5 points go to the music which suits the game without excelling, the voice acting is absolutely horrific, ranging from an AWFUL Poirot to a robotic lifeless side cast.
Sigh, this is disappointing, because it has good ideas but it's littered with bad ones.
Its worth playing without excelling, which is a shame because the story deserves so much more.
The story is brilliant, a classic Detective Vs Killer mystery in which a killer is leaving an "ABC" book of train times at each murder. However before the killings, he challenges Poirot by sending a letter(signed A.B.C) telling him when and were the killings will take place. I have no qualms with the story at all, if you like classic detectives or the best selling crime writer of all time, you will like the story. It needs little to no introduction or explanation.
The Graphics I loved, it would be easy for them to take a gritty realism option like they have done with Sherlock Holmes. However Poirot isn't so much like that, he is a more colorful character. I really didn't enjoy the way that they animated the walking of Poirot or any of the characters, it looked really weird. I had no frame rate problems or crashes/freezes, apart from the animation looking weird and the fact that I realise cel shading isn't to everyone's liking, I would have given it more than a 7/10.
The Sound was God Awful and made the game borderline unplayable at times, maybe I'm used to hearing David Suchet play Poirot but the voicing was terrible. The accent was strained and barely passable. There was some half decent performances of a few witnesses, however the main cast was frankly unacceptable. The detective was wooden, Poirot was laughable and most the questioned suspects sounded like they were reading a script on the day with no emotion. It's a slight shame because the actual music used in the game is fitting without excelling, I quite enjoyed it. There was even a musical case(kind of) and a jukebox playing appropriate music.
The gameplay is what lets the game down more than most. They copied parts of Sherlock Holmes Crime and Punishment with the observation part which I liked and was used much better in fact than Crimes and Punishment used it. They also stole/borrowed the "decuctions" part of Crime and Punishment which was very good again. They used Poirots OCD to good effect allowing him to fiddle with his moustaches in mirrors and re-arrange messy things.
However, they also, which totally ruined the game, placed totally obtuse puzzles in the way of progressing through the game. They were needlessly difficult and felt totally out of place in a Poirot game, he did not solve intense jigsaw puzzles or false passage bookcase puzzles. He wasn't part of the mystery machine with Scooby Doo. It detracted massively from the game, without it the gameplay gets around a 6/7 out of 10. It copied the good parts of other games, which isnt bad but isnt breaking any new ground. The puzzles ruined it.
Overall, its worth playing because the story is excellent and its fun being Poirot. However use a guide for the puzzles or just take frequent breaks so you dont have to force yourself through them

Cradle is a mixed bag that provides a unique and interesting world and story that strings you along until the ending suddenly throws you into a wall.
In terms of puzzles:
It's not great. Something I've seen mentioned in many positive reviews is people praising how you can interact with so many items, but I find this claim disingenuous at best. There are plenty of items that you can pick up, carry around, and drop. Aside from that there's barely any interactivity in the game, and every item with an actual use has one use and one use only, at one point in the game, in one specific way. There's no freedom here, and most of the puzzles amount to "find X, pick up X, find Y, use X on Y". The other puzzles amount to searching for the next location you need to reach based on sometimes cryptic and not particularly specific clues (to find the X located there, naturally), so it doesn't exactly have much going for it in the gameplay department, other than walking back and forth, which you'll be doing a lot of, as the game repeatedly requires you to make the needlessly long trip between the yurt and the dome thanks to...
The minigames:
Four times in the game you're sent off to do a simulation game where you have to find coloured blocks and throw them into an "elevator" until the game ends. While doing this you're hounded by an enemy that destroys blocks at regular intervals, and if you fall to the bottom of the game's arena, you lose blocks from your total. These are frustrating, tedious, boring, awkward, take too long, and really offer nothing to the game experience other than padding it out. They fit in the context of the game world, but they don't fit in the context of the gameplay. It's a poorly integrated distraction from the real appeal of the game, which is...
The story:
As an amnesiac protagonist, you wake up in a yurt with little idea of what's going on, and you spend the game trying to figure out who you are and what the story is of the robot girl Ida, who is immobilised there. If you think that "show, don't tell" are words to live by, this is not the game for you, because absolutely everything about the story is "tell, don't show". You read notes in the yurt to be told about the world's history. You listen to Ida tell you about her past, and the past of the game's area. You listen to Tabaha not really say much worth listening to at all, really. All this talking isn't helped by the player character's absolutely atrocious and monotonous voice acting putting a damper on every emotional scene, either. Then as you've been told enough for the story to hook you in, it ends.
Since the story is the main draw, the abrupt and unsatisfying ending is not in its favour. You can figure out what's going on by scrawling through all the notes strewn about the game's world, and putting it together piece by piece, but this is a matter of grasping at straws and picking up on offhand mentions of crucial elements of the story hidden among page after page of less relevant world building.
It's not a satisfying way to deliver the story. It's not a satisfying story in the end either because even after piecing it together it still leaves much of it very vague, with the events boiling down to "well, it happened because it happened."
All in all, Cradle isn't a satisfying experience. It doesn't deliver satisfying puzzles. It doesn't deliver satisfying gameplay. It doesn't deliver satisfying exploration. And most of all, it doesn't deliver a satisfying story.

You drift into a city in that is in a post-apocalyptic state, half submerged. You are the older sister to a brother who needs medical attention. Using your boat and a telescope you explore this desolate, overgrown place to find what you need to help your brother. Along the way, you learn the city's story and your own, told without words but in the form of cards. As you progress you learn more and more.
Each building you explore has ledges and ridges you use to climb and descend. Underway you discover creatures, landmarks and upgrade your boat and of course magnificent vistas. There are no enemies to fight.

The story is pretty simple, you gather a crew and start expanding your turf through your graffiti.
Other crews want to take over your turf and kidnap your dog, while trying to get your dog back you see a black car drop a disc piece, this leads to you collecting the other pieces. Turs out a guy named Goji thinks the disc is something demonic and wants to get it so he can make a pact with a demon. He wants to take down all the graffiti and make it so there are no more skaters/graffiti artists.
He puts Golden Rhino posters all over the graffiti you need to spray graffiti on all of them and show him you aren't scared. After all that it's time to take him on!
You beat him in a final battle and the credits start to roll.
The graphics have aged well in my opinion, the game is colorful and the art style really catches your eye.
Some of the effects are pretty well done too.
The gameplay is exactly what you would expect from this game. You are rolling around at the speed of sound while tagging graffiti and collecting spray cans so you can tag even more.
The red spray cans refill your health, the yellow spray cans give you 1 spray can and the blue spray cans give you a couple of spray cans. Like it's original name ,,Jet Grind Radio" the main focus is grinding and tagging.
You perform cooler tricks the faster you are moving, for example if you are really slow and press the jump button you just do a simple jump but if you are going fast and press the jump button your character performs a trick.
You can clear stages in a simple casual way or you can be the speed runner and just breeze through the level.
You unlock new spray art by finding them around the map. You can customize you tag with letters of your choice or the ones you have unlocked.
+Nice soundtrack
+Catchy graphics
+Freedom in stages
+Multiple playable characters.
+Good controls (if you are used to them)
+Characters MEW and GUM (rule 34) ;]
-Shows XBOX 360 controls instead of keyboard keys.
-Freedom in stages (under a time limit). there is plenty of time on the other hand.
-Controls may feel clunky if you are not used to them. (You will get used pretty fast, after failing once or twice).

Knightmare Tower has the distinct honour of being the last free online flash game I played before I was consumed by the behemoth that is Steam. With it now on Steam, I feel like I've practically come full circle.
Juicy Beast Studio primarily develop free flash games, with a few ported to mobile devices. Knightmare Tower represents their first title on Steam. Now, before I continue, let me just link you to a post where Juicy Beast explain the differences between the flash version and the Steam version:
.
Much like the flash version, this one was relatively short to complete. I managed to complete the main game in...I forget...maybe a few hours? It shouldn't take too long to upgrade everything and challenge the boss. Following that, survival mode proved to be a fun, and slightly harder, distraction. Alas, it did feel a bit too short and I finished the main Steam achievements very quickly. I do wish there was more content added to the game.

Not unlike other AGEOD games I've played in the past, the game mechanics for Pride of Nations look like they've got a lot of potential to be really good.  However, also not unlike other AGEOD games, the user interface of the game is not up to the task of the mechanics.  Lists of nations that you have to click to scroll down one at a time, clunky and variable scrolling speeds for a map (and you'll spend a lot of time scrolling across the map), a painfully limited messaging system (you have a new turn, here's 157 new messages....!  There's no filter, no way of focussing things).  It's playable, but it's the kind of game that you would literally need to have a notepad and paper next to you to play properly, because the game doesn't convey enough of the required information itself (or have a built-in system of reminders/overlays that is effective).  The diplomatic UI is particularly obtuse, for a game where (unlike many other AGEOD games) diplomacy is very important.
The in-game tutorials are also very limited, and nowhere near up to scratch for a game of this type.  They repeatedly refer players back to the manual, but for a game that as far as I know was only released digitally, relying on a manual is a bit silly.  At the very least, make the manual text available in-game, and far more preferably available contextually in-game.
If you can look past the UI to the game mechanics, it really does like like there's a potential gem here.  I haven't played enough of it to be able to rate the AI, but AGEOD games tend to be fairly strong on this front.  The mechanics look great, the attention to detail in set-up situations and a decent number (4-5) of extra scenarios as well as the grand campaign mean there's a substantial amount of game here, but the tools given to play the game are not up to scratch, and you'll have to persevere through them to get to the gameplay underneath.

Sega's responsibility when developing this game was to just get it working, and after many an hour lost in game due to corrupt savegames, I have to say that they failed.
Though the issue is now fixed, it took far too long and I feel that the amount I payed for little more than what an emulator can offer was not worth it. Furthermore, those with a keyboard may find gameplay difficult, with some controls available on controller not functioning properly or feeling compatible with a keyboard. The camera which, on controller, is the right thumb stick is on keyboard the arrow keys, and the comfort of changing the camera with the thumbstick is no longer there on the keyboard, with it serving as a chore, so the player is stuck with the camera following them behind.
If you have the power, then you'd probably feel that you'd inputted the same amount of effort into running it through an emu (not that I am suggesting such a thing, as that may be illegal). Sega dissapoints in the development of this game, with it being a buggy rereleased which has been patched numerous times but the error remaining.
In regards to the gameplay, it's an enjoyable, albeit difficult game which I feel like putting my time into, something I don't always do, and I leave with the beautiful soundtrack stuck in my head hoping for more.
To summarise, the game is great, this port is not. Players with a controller will find the controls to be of ease, while those without may find a different experience.

I really wanted to enjoy this title but I can't get into it. The new armor system is a let down. You can't even taunt targets without stripping them of all their armor points first. Magic is extremely difficult to use without risking friendly fire. Some of the fights are extremely poorly designed (ship fight between Acts 1 and 2, I'm looking at you) and the devs love to 'gotcha' by introducing enemies and elements into combat you couldn't have known about before starting the engagement (much save / reload and trial / error required).

The illusion of choice is also especially bad. Basically you have the way the developers want you to solve the problem and then all the wrong ways. Feel free to select the wrong way if you want things to be more difficult. On top of those things I found the story to be an extremely typical 'you are the chosen one and only you can save the universe' tale. Some very eye rolling fondling over your character really turned me off of the plot. The individual character stories are more interesting but only make up a tiny percentage of what you'll spend your time doing - which is mostly wandering around large environments looting barrels and managing your inventory.

Some final notes. Crafting is a chore but at least it's completely ignorable. There's a ton of things to read but most of that is also easily ignored. You will likely feel compelled to play one of the 'origin' characters instead of making a custom character because you miss out on content if you don't. Graphics and sounds are fine but nothing really stands out as outstanding. The entire game is voice acted which is great, although that voice acting is just serviceable. Lastly this is an incredibly long game, which I suppose means good value to some but to me means bloat and poor pacing. Divinity lost me in Act 2, which is about half way through, and I can't see myself playing another 40-50 hours of this.

The game reminds me of Dear Esther, or The Old City. Or even to some extent, a game like FNAF. What I mean is that the game is interesting and mysterious, but to really understand what's going on you have to be prepared to read into the game a lot. Read and listen to every piece of article, text and conversation. Treat everything as important, even if it doesn't seem to have significance. You have a lot of opportunity to skip over the lore in this game (some conversation with Ida is optional, and you're not obligated to read any of the loose papers and articles around the hut), and unfortanately it can make the game's ending very confusing.
If you're the kind of person who needs everything narrated and explained to you, and you're not one to care for reading and discovering all these things on your own or trying to build the timeline from what pieces you're given, you're probably going to have a bad time with this game from a narrative perspective.
You'll probably find a lot of people giving reviews here saying that the game ends confusingly and abruptly. It kind of does I suppose, but don't think that it ends on a cliff hanger or leaves you without closure. If you weren't paying close attention to the conversations with Ida or the whole talk about certain sensations and certain characters, I can see how the ending would make absolutely no sense if you're lacking some context.
Not that there isn't a bunch of little stuff to speculate about-- there's certainly plenty of gaps for players to fill in, much the same way you see people filling in the timeline from a game like FNAF. I certainly wouldn't mind seeing a Game Theory video on this game, actually. :)

- Some few FPS drops out of the blue, but not for long and not too annoying.

It is a pity that this potentially good game is disappointing, for one major reason in my opinion.
First the positives: Fun game with easy-to-control tanks and some nice maps. Easy to understand upgrade tree and relatively fair in game currency system. There is no annoying chat with aggressive players like in World of Tanks, which for me is a big positive.  It could be a nice, light-weight alternative for WoT.
Why would I not recommend this game then? After some 60 hours of playing I noticed that the real "tanks" in the game with tank-like cannon turrets and relatively heavy armour are far too disadvantaged against the faster "vehicles", which move more like cars than tanks. And then there are the annoying and unrealistic weapons like freeze, flamethrower and plasma guns which are usually fitted to these fast vehicles. That's where the fun is gone for me. I like blowing up stuff with cannons and get blown up myself, that is fun. In this game, especially in the small maps, the same people with these very fast vehicles come towards you again and again after re-spawning, just  in a couple of seconds. You can not respond properly if you get frozen or burned by some extremely fast vehicle revolving around you faster than your turret can turn.
Science fiction vehicles and weapons can be fun, like in Gear Up which I also play. But that's not what I expect in a tank game. If you are looking for some classical tank fun (but fed up with World of Tanks  like me) unfortunately this is not the right game.

First of all, this review is from the perspective of an avid FPS, RTS gamer that also likes racing games. I look for games that can give me about $0.50 or less per hour of entertainment. At $13, I was hoping to get maybe 20-25 hours or so out of it but I don't think I can last that long.
I was looking for a casual relaxing adventure game and Cradle caught my eye. After watching some game play on YouTube I decided to buy it. Fours hours in and I'm disappointed. It seems to get you into a grind, or misbehaves completely causing you to restart the game from a game defined save point.
Pros:
Great atmospherics, rich unique story line and really great music. This game has tremendous potential.
Cons:
The cube game. Tiring and doesn't enrich the overall story (that I could determine). I usually walk away and come back later to “skip” the game because I've lost and I get the game item anyhow.
Bad or inconsistent game physics. Picking things up and dropping/throwing them at times is tedious or difficult. I placed an item on the bed so I wouldn't have to look around on the floor for it. Wrong move. I could never pick up the item because the bed is selectable, all I could do was “sleep” when I tried to select the item on the bed. I had to restart the game and do a bunch of tedious things all over again.
Inventory. I believe an item was added to my inventory without my knowledge, but I can't be certain. Also, there is no callout on items, so you can pick up some technical thing and have no idea what it is. OK, maybe that's part of the game, but can add to the overall frustration.
Conclusion. Wonderful wonderful imagery, story line and music, and figuring out what to do in this “open world” is really fun. However basic game rules are inconsistent. Maybe this needs some really good QA. Not sure if this was early access with user feedback, if not, it should have been. Maybe this IS early access?
Finally: Watch some YouTube game play and if you don't mind some grind and rule bending by the game machine, you might really enjoy this.

In my last review I mentioned that the game was not P2P. Well within a day they changed that. They added premium accounts that give buyers advantages in most ways possible.
Looking back at the game's path, it started out great but has slowly declined. Every update that should have improved the game has also brought a feature that pulled it down.
Here are the reasons I would not recommend this game:
- The matchmaking is terrible. You will often be put in a battle that your team is already losing.
- The only way to increase ranking is for your team to win. They seem to think that you are the one that is at fault when your team loses.
- The game makers have turned the balanced original game where you fought players with the same level tank as you to a game where you fight people based on how equal you are in your ranking. This means they can have vastly better stuff then you.
- You cannot choose what map you want to play on. You're stuck with whatever the game chooses.
- There is no goal to work towards. The only use of ranking up your modules is to keep yourself from losing. It get fairly annoying. Adding some benefit to ranking up would be a great step forward.
- While not a huge deal, there are several obvious grammar errors in the game that make me cring.
