is an indie adventure/walking simulator with a (skipable) puzzle minigame. Your entire playthrough of ~6-10  hours is limited to a relatively small, specific environment, so I'll try to keep these impressions to a minimum and as spoiler-free as possible.
The graphics, art style and environment are gorgeous, but given the limited region the game takes place in, the visuals probably aren't the reason to buy unless you're a die-hard sci-fi junkie. Likewise, from a mechanics standpoint, there's nothing particularly interesting about the game unless you really enjoy the first-person platforming puzzle minigame (which is okay, but nothing special imo). Enemies do exist in the game (barely), you can jump, your character does have a (small) inventory, but all of that hides the fact that this is mostly a walking simulator or the modern day equivalent of the ole fetch quest point-and-click games. So what's the fuss about then? The story, and it's a good one with the caveat that the developers make a lot of it optional.  o_O
You will chat with other characters, so this isn't a hands-off interactive novella like Gone Home. However, the developers buried a lot of the story in text that players are entirely free to ignore which is... odd. Put another way, if you simply go through the game doing the fetch quests and ignoring all the optional newspapers, clippings, photos etc, then the ending of the game will likely feel abrupt and make very little sense (tip: in conversations, click the bottom choice when multiple dialogue options appear to get the extended details).  Maybe this was laziness on the dev's part, or a deliberate design decision from the off, but it is what it is. When I played through the game, before I did
else including the first quest, I ravenously devoured all the tidbits of text and I'd recommend anyone interested in the story do something similar early on, if not right at the start.  The whole game will make a lot more sense if you do.
Screenies:
Mixed in with the high detail artwork found on the ground are the unusual skyscapes evoking cell shaded games like Zelda Wind Walker or the oil painting motif from Dishonored
Much of the story (including major plot details) is hidden away in this stuff on the ground, on shelves, framed on walls, etc.
The game isn't open-world, and most of the terrain isn't worth exploring, but the player can still cover huge distances if so inclined. In fact, doing so can net you a DAMN SPIFFY toy. Clicking this
. Probably best to wait till you've completed the game and are achievement hunting.

-- Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore— While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping, As of some one gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door. “’Tis some visitor,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door—Only this and nothing more.” --
The Raven by Edgar Allen Poe is one of the most famous poems in classical english literature for the simple fact that it establishes all of its content and atmosphere in very simple ways. But when you read between the lines and take a step back to look what the poem is about, there is actually a great deal of depth there which is never directly referenced throughout the poem. The loss of a loved one, the grief of the main character and the way the poem builds tension in the mind of the reader. Why is this relevant to this review? Because Submerged is a visual poem. Short, but filled with emotion and atmosphere.
Although not as clever or subtle as The Raven it tells the story of a world following a disaster, how people survived and the tale of how this young brother and sister came to be here. If you are expecting this to be a platformer then you'll be mistaken as it has more in common with walking simulators. Although it is very short, this works to the game's advantage as the environment is only interesting for a couple hours of exploration but nevertheless you really do get a great deal of atmosphere and some fantastic scenary to look at as the developer has spent a great deal of time polishing this one large environment. It's post-apocalyptic in a way you rarely see in games or movies. No deserts or char-filled ruins but rather a city that has been reclaimed by nature. There is the potential to explore the flooded city and find all of the secrets which reveal pictorial clues to the tale of this desolate place but once you've collected about half of them you can figure out what happened from the images. The tale of the siblings is certainly bitter-sweet and is not long to win any awards for originality but the animations and music convay the young girls personality very well despite the fact that she hardly utters a word. On the subject of animations however, although they did a fine job in most areas, the girl's running animation feels far too 'floaty' and may distract players from enjoying the game. Thankfully much of the game is spent in the boat or climbing and the animations here look fantastic.
The downside to this game is that it may not be appealing for some players who are expecting an adventure. This is a game to relax to and not one to challenge you at all. Which is partly why it is good that you can see it through from start to end in a few hours. However, when you consider the price tag for doing this I would say that it isn't good value for money unless it is on sale for under £5. I picked this up during the winter sale and frankly it feels like money well spent as the experience was enjoyable from start to finish. But saddly there is absolutely zero replay value.
It's great to see games that aren't about killing people or fighting in general. I'd love to see this developer do more games like this.

Submerged is an atmospheric game at its simpliest : you play as Miku, a young girl who needs to take care of her wounded and sick little brother. You explore a submerged city, looking for different items to improve the well-being of your brother.
The game use a foreign dialect, like Ico. But it is pretty easy to understand what the characters are thinking. There are no enemies in this game and you cannot die. You just explore until you find a package containing medecine, food, water, etc. You accomplish this by climbing buildings, but don't expect Uncharted : the mechanics are really simple, although clunky a bit. Miku also moves slowly.
The game is pretty, and the water effects are nicely done. The soundtrack is magnificent, although there are not a lot of different songs. There are also many secrets to be found, that explain what happened to the world. Miku has a lense that helps her spots hidden secrets.
I recommend it because it is pretty different than your average game : no combat, no death, just a girl and her boat exploring a sunken city. If you want something different, you should give this game a shot.

This is a short mini action-adventure game with simple controls and beautiful aesthetics.
You play as Miku, a young woman taking care of her younger brother.  As the game continues the story unravels and you discover the history of not only the siblings but the city they find themselves in as well.
The game is short - four hours maximum to complete, with the same again to catch all the achievements.  The best part for me was not having to kill anyone.  Yes, that's right - there's no combat.  As an over 40 year-old with arthritis in the hands, FPS are not a genre for me, so this game was perfect.
Some other reviews have termed this a walking simulator, which I agree with - I actually spent about one hour just sailing around in the boat, enjoying the rise and fall of the waves and watching the beautiful day/night cycle spin round.  Add a simple yet beautiful soundtrack and the experience is really quite relaxing.
In summary:
Combat:      None
Visuals:       Stunning
Gameplay:  Basic (walking, sailing and climbing)
Story:          Limited, revealed through pictograms
Length:       < 4 hours (basic game)
Music:         Very relaxing and beautiful
Price:          Overpriced at $19.99 - wait for a Steam sale to buy

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is an absolutely great title and is one of, if not, the best titles in the Elder Scrolls series. Oblivion was my very first introduction to the Elder Scrolls and I enjoyed the game so very much from start to finish. The sense of immersion along with the well balanced gameplay and epic storyline was quite enjoyable for a roleplaying enthusiast like me. This title is so chock full of adventure and combat that it will keep you busy for hour upon hour which will eventually compile into weeks and months before you realize it. Graphically, you have to remember that this title was released quite a few years ago, it pales in comparison to some of todays RPG's but even so I found the basic game to be quite beautiful with a uniqueness of it own that completely fits the fantasy world and story that it places you in. I said that graphically "it pales in comparison to some of todays titles" but I think this game still looks as good if not better than alot of the current roleplaying games available...this title was ahead of it's time and the work that the developers put into it definitely shows. Of course, as with many of Bethesdas RPG's, after you finish the basic game the first time you have the ability to modify the game to your liking for many more playthroughs by way of the Oblivion Nexus. You can mod the game from the start but I as well as others agree that playing through the base untouched game the first time is a wise thing to do. This title is simply fantastic and is highly recommended!!!

A rockin' rollin' brightly-coloured platform/skate adventure through little parts of a super-styled tokyo.
Jet Set Radio's name may precede it, but it's all with good cause. Encouraging players to express their will for freedom against an oppressive regime through the use of simple acrobatic skating moves on electric/magnetic rollerblades (it's from the early noughties, they're blades, not skates, "dude") and graffiti (a small minigame of matching movements when painting makes the challenge different every time).
Simple single-stick controls with triggers for paint control your character as they stick to any railed surface and grind it, and collect paint. Occasionally, like with all Dreamcast games (and games of that era) the camera can be a little moody, but it's forgivable.
Throughout the game, colourful characters join, support or oppose your gang, leaving you needing to paint their backs, outskate them etc.
So, the music. Most people will mention this first - as it's a character in its own right. Featurring trip-hop and street beats, funked and drummed up to a hyperactive party level (without being pretentious), I challenge you not to love it.
As for the game as a whole? I love the remake, and will always want more. Get it. Now. Seriously. I'll pay if I have to :P

I make no secret of the fact that I don't like difficult games so after an hour and a half of trying and failing to simply complete the tutorial, this wasn't looking good. The developers didn't seem to understand the concept of a tutorial, if someone needs to write a walkthrough to explain how to complete the tutorial it is not really fulfilling the remit of a tutorial. Even once you have found out how to complete the tutorial it is massively infuriating and only the most devoted 5.3% of people who play this on Steam have managed to complete the tutorial. After abandoning the tutorial I started the actual game which ironically starts with what is effectively a tutorial level. I managed to grind (in both senses of the word) through the first chapter before I got too annoyed and gave up.
I bought this game thinking it would be like a more cartoony version of the Tony Hawk games and that is probably why I found this game so difficult. Despite it being a few years since I last played a Tony Hawk game this game was similar enough to trigger certain reflex button combinations which were all wrong for this game. The different jumping mechanic took a lot of getting used to then there are the grinding mechanics. In the Tony Hawk's games you hold down the jump button then release to jump here you press jump to jump and hold it down to jump further. That took a little getting used to but the thing I never got used to was the angle of jumping out of a grind. The speed you are travelling seems to affect the angle you jump out of a grind but not in a way that felt natural or predictable to me. Also this game seems a lot more pernickety about what you can grind on, With Tony Hawk's games you press the grind button when you are near a rail and you are fine but here you have to line up your jump correctly. These control issues make getting around a lot less fluid and more aggravating. Also the way the levels work with the police coming after you means you really have to complete the graffiti in the correct order, so you can't just explore the level and complete the graffiti as you find it you have to attempt each level a number times just to work out the correct order to complete it.
I suspect if you were a fan of this game on the Dreamcast and you are used to the controls then you will probably love to play this game again but if you are not coming from that background it looks cool but the controls are going to make it more frustrating than fun. If you are coming to this as a fan of Tony Hawk's games then you are going to be doubly frustrated.

Although many would claim there is a steep learning curve, and a select few would claim it takes too long to learn the game mechanics, I would have to disagree with both of these statements. Personally, it only took me maybe 8 hours to learn just about all of the game mechanics in the core game. Given I've only put in a couple hundred hours since I first got this game, it feels to me that there are not enough features within the game to make it as playable as one would like it to be.
For my third time playing as Leon (My other save games were lost with my old computer) 6 months later from the last time I touched this game, I was able to take all of the provinces of Hispania within my second generation playing as the House of Jimena, within 50 years of in-game time, with enough of an army to still rush Jeruselum in the First and the Second Crusade (and take the Kingdom of Jeruselum single-handedly both times (Giving the actual province of Jerusalum to the papal states), while playing in Ironman mode for the first time. Because of this, I feel that this game is not challenging enough for someone such as myself who can accomplish such a feat with little to no effort.
But why do I still recommend this game if it seems so pointless and unchallenging? Well, military expansionism is only one small part of the game. All of the internal politics that come with running a kingdom/empire can and will try to bend you over for a chance to usurp everything you've ever worked for. All of your actions define whether or not you will see everything you worked for become a waste of time and effort.
You will see that after becoming Emperor of Hispania, that when you assassinate the current pope to put your anti-pope into succession, you will anger the Holy Roman Empire (the only rival that can utterly ruin your life) while angering enough of your vassals to the point where your wife and all of your heirs are assassinated, leading you to try and assassinate your half-brother (whose father is unfortunately the Kaiser) who is behind those plots as well as the leader of an active plot to assassinate you in order to usurp your entire empire and annex it into the Holy Roman Empire. The same half-brother that has 3/4 of your own entire empire backing him up to support his claim. This resulting in a war that last for 26 years where while this is going on you manage to take a new wife (since your original one was also assassinated) from the House of Capet (which annexed all of England in a war that you help them win), who helps you beat back the HRE into utter submission within the last 4 years of the war, leaving you with a legitimized heir within the last month you live, dying from your battle wounds at the ripe age of 96.
Oh and since this new heir is a girl, you have that to worry about for the next 16 years :/
10/10 would assassinate the pope again to put all of europe into war leading to the annexation of the HRE 100 years afterwards.

I also really like that there are PVP areas and the entire game is not a free for all. That is what usually steers me away from FPS games, the thought of walking up to a vendor and someone just taking me out and running off. I've experienced this and it is annoying.
The other feature I really like is the real time crafting system. You can craft while doing other things as well so you aren't stuck in one place waiting for an item to finish. In all honesty, it feels like a game that is more enjoyable with friends, which is the only reason I don't have it now but it can be good for some solo play. It's one of the good games in the free to play category, I'd definitely recommend it as I have a few times now. In fact, I am grabbing it again as I type this right now. I give Fallen Earth 10/10

=Long Review Incoming(With Spoilers)=
While this game is great, I find it difficult to give this game an 8 or 9 out of 10. A 7/10 would be my score. I would like to remind players that my opinions should not affect yours while playing the game, keep an open mind while playing it. For all you know, you might be surprised at what you get.
Graphics: The graphics of the game was not too much of a bother for me, in fact, it reminds me more of a comic book or Telltale games. It wasn't bad.
Gameplay: This game plays similarly to the Sherlock Holmes franchise which I very much prefer, however, there are gameplay aspects that were really well done, like the reconstruction of the murders. There are many things that the Sherlock Holmes franchise does better but this game does it simpler and easier. I played this game with a controller and it was frustrating at times. Similarly, one thing that brought it down was the laughable animations, I laughed at many instances of animations. One gameplay aspect that was a tad bit frustrating was the Ego Points which does nothing other than letting you know that that is how Hercule Poirot would speak. I ended up with 444/600 Ego Points and I was like "huh, not bad."
Story: I admit that I have yet to read any Agatha Christie novels but this one was fairly interesting, the player, as Hercule Poirot, is taunted by the ABC murderer and is required to solve 3 cases which are linked. It started off quite interesting then it got a little less interesting during the second case but it improved. The murderer seemed obvious and was very convincing but the "twist" at the end was predictable as well. I predicted the real murderer when interrogating ABC and was very hopeful to have the choice of picking the murderer out of all the suspects, however it did not happen, as it was part of the story and it was the one thing that I find very lacking from a detective game, the ability of choice
Characters: The characters that Agatha Christie created are oddly similar to the characters Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created. I found this very unsettling and was unsatisfied, however I wouldn't go as far as to call them out as copies of Sherlock Holmes, John Watson and Inspector Lestrade. They were still okay characters though! Although Poirot's default stance bothers me a lot. The voice acting was decent, it annoyed me every bloody time Poirot went "NOW LET US TRY AND GET OUR BRAIN CELLS TO WORK." LIKE JESUS CHRIST, STOP SAYING THAT!
Puzzles: The puzzles are fairly easy, some more difficult than others but still easy.
Overall, I enjoyed this game as a detective fan, it was simple, it wasn't too hard, in fact it was fairly easy, and most importantly, it was fun! Honestly, I was expecting it to be more challenging but I was disappointed in that aspect. However, I spent 6 hours or less(I left it on while cooking dinner and showering) in this game and those 6 hours were worth it.
TL;DR: 7/10, Recommended for detective fans.

War for the Overworld wasn't released as a great game, and it's got it's problems even now. Some are endearing, some are annoying. Some are from people that wanted Dungeon Keeper 3, but didn't get it.
Nonetheless, it's obviously well loved by the people that made it, and it's still got a following from the community that loves the game. I love the game. The Devs are nice, the people following it are nice. It's got good graphics, the DLC are all reasonably priced, and it's had one heck of a roller coaster ride.
A lot of Indie studios might have given up after the reception it first received, or might have given up when they didn't get everything right in the immediate base game upon release. Not these guys. These guys got to work, listened to the feedback they received, fixed bugs, worked on expansions and cosmetic DLC (called "Charity" at the time because it was to support them), and trudged along because they loved this game and wanted it to succeed. If any game deserves the Labour of Love award, it's this one.

Two people with scrambled memories try to piece together the particulars of a transhumanist tragedy in the secluded steppes of Mongolia.
The completely realised world, from the Mongolian aesthetic to the unsettling interactions with Ida to the sci-fi realism to the immersive world elements.
people who find transhumanism gripping, or who like spending as much time thinking about the ending as they do experiencing the story.
's world is unique, and that's not a word you get to use often when dealing with near-future sci-fi.  The game is set on the Mongolian steppes, and you're living in what a yurt would look like if it were 2086.  The incredible attention to detail makes this feel like a real residence, not a pastiche of orientalism; there's a mix of Mongolian and English writing, of futuretech and steppe tradition.  There's an incredibly unusual modernisation of the hunter-gatherer lifestyle, where the central character's life is occupied by scanning local flowers for genetic purity and then packaging them as art to be sold in the city.
shows the way globalisation sits alongside tradition in this near-future world.
The art style is just perfect.  You're neighbours with the Gerbera Centre, a sort of abandoned theme park, which itself is set up like a steel and future-tech tent, with visual elements drawn from the flags, banners and ribbons of Mongolian aesthetics.  There's a real attention to tiny detail in the way this game is drawn, from the subtle light arcs in the night sky to the faded, decayed tiles of the flower gardens.  This game manages a deep, colourful palette without taking away from the faded, eroded, washed-out and almost lifeless scene it's painting.  The world has both a sense of immense scale and a feeling of emptiness at the same time.
The interactions with Ida, the android who is central to the narrative, are ... unsettling to say the least.  Elements of her personal story and her situation give a poignancy to the broad transhumanist arc being played out in the articles you read strewn about the yurt.  This is capped off by the uncanny valley decision to use FMV eyes on the digital art body.  To see real human eyes blinking and flicking about while you are walking around the room is deeply uncomfortable, and really drives home that feeling that something is wrong.
Because, like a lot of sci-fi in this area, something is deeply wrong, and the game does a great job of communicating that even before you get the details of what happened in this world.  Your room is a mess, technology is fritzing, the world is washed out, and everything feels wrong.  That feeling doesn't go away until the final video sequence that ends the game.
Some people found the ending abrupt or unsatisfying, which is totally valid, but I thought the final exchange with Ida was beautiful and perfectly paced, and the concluding video gorgeous and uplifting.  The broad strokes of the ending are definite; you'll spend some time piecing together info gathered in-game to explain the little details, but that's an appropriate ending for a story like this.
Criticisms, I do have a couple.  The Unreal 4 engine is not great at handling object interactions; very clever steps are taken to mitigate this, but there's an immersion-breaking issue here when you have to stand two metres away from a piece of fruit lying on the floor under a table in order to turn it into soup.  And the cube minigame ...  opinions are divided.  I think it's more frustrating than fun.
That said,
's been in development for four or five years, and it shows.  It is incredibly polished, beautifully, gorgeously detailed, perfectly paced.  If transhumanism is your thing, play Cradle.  If you want an almost
-feeling immersive world, play Cradle.  If you enjoy analysing little details and interpreting the ending of games, definitely play Cradle - it is a game which rewards the player who is inquisitive.  Putting aside a couple of minor issues
stands as one of the best games I've played this year.

This is even worse if they have a shield on their back, because that lowers the area in which they can be hit for damage. If you're even a tiny bit in the swing radius of an attack it does full damage. This game doesn't account for momentum or anything like that. So imagine you're standing next to an enemy who's facing away from you, if you're even barely inside his swing radius on the right side, his sword will teleport inside you and do full damage, killing you. You can turn 180 degrees instantly, meaning that you'd never suspect the guy you're about to stab in the back is going to magically be facing you now and block your attack an inch from when it hit him.
The blocking feature is terrible. Oh you have a tiny hatchet designed for chopping small logs? Well clearly that can block a two-handed long-sword swung at full strength while the enemy was lunging at you, there's no way that could fail. The enemy is sitting in front of you spamming the dodge button? Oh it doesn't matter that you're swinging your sword straight through their body over and over and over again, they're pressing the dodge button so that means they dodge swords going inside their body.
And although the archery in this game does take skill, it's way over-powered. I mean what's the point of having 4 different classes if a skilled archer can one shot any of them, it's no wonder the game caps how many archers can be on one team. But instead of making arrow damage a bit more realistic, just limit each team to 4 archers, thats fine.

Set in the Mongolian steppes about 60 years in the future, Cradle is a first-person adventure game with a rather unique premise. You wake up in a wonderfully detailed yurt that looks convincingly lived-in. Most of the worldbuilding in the game is concentrated in this tiny space, with dozens of newspaper clippings and foreign objects outlining a fascinating transhumanist future which has partially, but not completely, also arrived to this tent in the middle of nowhere.
Outside on the vast plains, a hovertram line stretches out to the horizon with precious few other landmarks besides a huge, abandoned dome of some sorts. It's up to you to puzzle out the story and the big picture by reading and observing things, but mostly by gathering parts to an old android in your possession.
Getting that thing to talk for the first time is a revelation in a game which had been very silent and tranquil up to that point. Unfortunately, at that time you will already have passed the best portions of the game. The first few hours of Cradle are as good as anything I've played, with a truly engaging world and lots of fresh ideas. Sure, you do run up against a rather jarring piece of videogame logic right in the first puzzle, but I was willing to forgive the game for that. However, it got much worse.
It's like the writers and designers eventually had no idea what to do with their creation. The story gets progressively less interesting when more and more details about it are revealed. The puzzles wither down to simple "find the switch" challenges that can get truly frustrating if you get stuck. The game isn't really willing to give you much pointers at all, which I can appreciate, but it is a bummer to run in circles for an hour just because you've missed a switch.
Eventually, the game settles into you just hiking between two points on continuous errands and forcing you to repeatedly play a ridiculous minigame that feels unbelieveably out of place with everything else and is absolutely not fun in the slightest. The minigame feels like an attempt to add more gameplay to decidedly a pretty walking-simulator-ish experience, but it just doesn't work at all. I feel like the entire sections could be stripped completely and the game would only be better for it.
Better or, well, as good it could be with the rest of the story continuing the sabotage the experience the futher you get. The story ends up being such a letdown, a mishmash of different scifi cliches slapped together to form a jumbled mess of disappointment.
After the first few hours, I really thought Cradle would be one of my games of the year. After completing it, it's nowhere even close. It has an extremely engaging atmosphere and impressive graphics, but the story just twists upon itself way too many times and you end up feeling like chasing your own tail for half of the game. Such a shame! Huge wasted potential.

Submerged is a game that survives primarily on design and atmosphere.  The deserted, withered, plant-covered city lends itself to an isolated yet peaceful feeling as you sail around and through it.  The fact that it changes from day to night, the landmarks you come across, the view from the tops of buildings, it's a treat.  The creatures you come across are also kind of interesting in design, albeit a little too simple, and they add a serene calm to the game.  It's especially fun seeing one of them behave differently as you watch, and I won't spoil what the creature is, but I will say it's worth sailing around.  Exploring the area and taking in the sights is easily the most engaging thing about this game.  Sadly, however, the gameplay and the story kind of work against the game as a whole.  The gameplay largely consists of point A to point B then climbing point B; while it lets you take in the scenery, it’s not exactly thrilling or challenging.  And that really does drag this game down considering…well, that this is a game.  The story, meanwhile, is incredibly simple, and that does work to the advantage of the atmosphere, but without giving anything away, the ending makes no sense.  Additionally, the concept of the plot has been done before in better games.  There is also a backstory given to both your character and the world itself, told through cave painting-like images, and it’s admittedly a little creative.  But while the character’s backstory is easy enough to follow (excluding the very last pieces), the world’s backstory requires thorough exploration for which there really is little reward outside of achievement hunting.  This is very much an atmospheric game alone, but it is enjoyable in that respect.  If you want a game you can take in and relax with, I do honestly recommend it getting it on sale like I did.  Just don’t expect to fall in love with it.

One of the things I love most about a new Far Cry game is the exploration; getting to poke around a rich, vivid, exotic and imaginative play area. My first goal is always to climb all of the radio towers on the map, just for the joy of finding new places.
This isn't Far Cry. It does, however, let you roam at will around a vivid play area and find climbing routes up buildings from where you can find new places to explore. Best of all, you're not getting shot at all the time by people who clearly don't like tourists. Submerged should, in other words, be perfect for me.
And yet.
And yet I feel oddly underwhelmed, even after completing it.
There's no combat, and about bloody time someone was brave enough to do a game like that. Top marks. There's enough of a story, told through basic but nicely done pictograms, to give you a reason to explore if you need one. It's clearly made to be pretty, even going as far as building in a "Postcard" feature, and the visual impact can sometimes be stunning. The soundtrack is beautiful, and fits the atmosphere of the game perfectly. Controls are trivial to learn, in a good way.
I'm a bit less sure about the level of challenge. Basically there isn't any. That's not necessarily a bad thing; I loved Abzu and Burly Men at Sea and neither of those have any real danger or challenge. The difference is that they both left you to explore - the hidden items and places were actually hidden, hard to find, whereas Submerged leaves absolutely everything clearly marked. If you can climb on something you'll see that it's climbable from some distance away, and it even goes as far as using fixed camera angles in some places to show you a "secret". In a game where the fun is purely in exploration, taking the satisfaction of finding things away leaves... well, nothing.
It's also a very short game. Again, not necessarily a problem; Abzu was short. Portal was short. Both were stunning, in completely different ways. Just be aware. I'm a fairly casual gamer and completed it in 3 hours, including quite a lot of OCD-driven map completion.
And finally on to the bad. Submerged uses Unreal Engine 4, which is capable of doing some remarkable things. Professional reviews tend to comment on how stunning Submerged looks and, in static screenshots, it does.
Saying this makes me feel like I'm kicking kittens, but for me Submerged just doesn't hold up visually. It comes across as a Playstation 2 or Voodoo 3 era game. It's a game that's betting on being haunting and beautiful but the rough edges just murder any sense of immersion.
The subtle lighting effects from the day/night cycle are great - but there's a wide halo around buildings and other moving objects where you can see that the post-processing lighting filter isn't being applied. There's a gorgeous red sunset reflecting on the water, but the buildings and the main character have a bright blue water halo. A building will have hundreds of windows, all of which are broken in an identical way because they use exactly the same texture. Cloth flaps in the wind, but it's clearly a pre-drawn cloth texture on top of a pre-animated square with polygons that both float free of, and clip straight through, other nearby objects. The main character's hands and feet clip through buildings, as does the boat you get around in. Seagulls perched on ledges bob up and down as if they were on water, and only flap their wings once every couple of seconds when they're flying. Butterflies are clearly one painted square per wing with two frames of animation. Clouds of bees are made up of a load of static sprites which look like a divide sign, just a line with two dots. Trees sprout out of perfectly flat concrete with no roots and clip through railings. Objects pop into view about 20 feet away, and merge visibly between quite different models as the distance changes. Leaves on trees are low-polygon shapes with palm-tree textures painted on. Depth of field stops abruptly, changing from thick vaseline to crystal clear within a tiny space. All of the models, including the main character, are very, very low polygon and so look visibly angular.
And so on.
In fact, it's so thorougly 10-15 years out of date that I almost convinced myself that it was done deliberately as an art style, maybe to evoke nostalgia. Almost.
More than anything else, this reminds me of some of the climbing levels of Tomb Raider. Not the recent ones, I mean maybe Tomb Raider 1 or 2. All of the many, many graphical shortfalls would have been forgivable in the late 90s (and yes, I do clearly remember buying a Voodoo 1 to play the original Tomb Raider on) but at the end of 2016 in a game which is selling itself on it's beauty are just crippling. For reference, this is with a GTX 1080 and all the settings maxed out.
Does the exploration save it, then? Well, again, it's a nice-try-but-no-cigar result for me. I love exploration in open-world games, way more so than the combat which just gets in the way of finding cool new places, so a peaceful roam around a submerged city should be perfect. The trouble is that there's really only four things to look for; red flowers mean you can climb a wall, a wide ledge can be walked on, a broken ledge can be grappled along, and pipes can be used to move up and down. That's it, apart from occasional ladders, which do the same as the pipes. Neither items or paths are ever hidden, which means there's no satsifaction to be had in getting to hard-to-reach places. The teenage girl you control can effortlessly leap 6 feet straight up while hanging from her fingertips, but can't step over a knee-high wall. In fact the only times I managed to go somewhere that wasn't clearly marked as a path was then I fell through or got stuck inside the terrain. Three times in three hours. Luckily, restarting puts you back in a sensible place.
I don't regret buying this. Nor do I regret the time I spent playing it; it was a few hours of badly needed tranquility and a reminder that people can do things which are meant to give joy rather than hails of bullets. I'd like to encourage the developers to keep going and do something else like this in the future. What I really do regret that is that it could so easily have been vastly better, just by applying a little more variation and challenge, and an entire bucketful of polish, to what is actually there.

As the developer makes very clear, Star Sky is not a game for everyone.
In Star Sky you take control of a nameless man taking a walk through the countryside late at night. You walk from left to right, and your only controls are to walk, run, or stop; there is no way to go back. If you feel so inclined, you can simply run all the way through the game world in a couple of minutes flat, but that defeats the purpose of Star Sky entirely, which the developer states is to see everything there is to see -- to experience all of the game's events, in other words.
Each of these events is either available every time you play the game, or is unlocked by past events, either in your current or a past play through. You can't see all of the events in a single play; I played through at least a dozen times before unlocking everything.
But the point is not to rush, or at least, that's what I took out of it. Instead, you should just walk along, enjoying the atmospheric sound effects and eye-soothing art, and letting the game guide you to each event. Try different combinations of events, and take hints from the names of the events, which you will see at the end of your first play through.
The sound, as already mentioned, is lovely. The graphics are very pretty, with everything shown in silhouette against the night sky, although I must say I wasn't too impressed with the character animations (apart from the woman when she runs, which seemed to me to be quite good).
Overall, I enjoyed Star Sky as a unique experience, to relax and just think about things for a couple of hours in an evening. In my opinion it's not great value at full price, given the length of the game, but I'm still happy to recommend it to anyone wanting a mellow experience that's different to pretty much everything else on Steam.

It's one of those minimalistic games that makes it difficult for me to write about again.. *sighs and cracks knuckles* Let us get stuck into this.
A man takes a midnight stroll to find out what surprising adventures he can find in the night. There are a handful of different endings and a few different events that can happen within one nights play-through or many.
The one thing this game has to offer, if nothing else, is how pretty it is. It's so simplistically gorgeous and really sets a bar for how it should feel; atmospheric, magical and mysterious.
There isn't really much of one either. It's just the 'magical sound' that plays when you are close to a trigger event spot and honestly, it's trying a tad too hard to be whimsical and deep when it lacks a lot of content to be such.
It's a tad bit pretentious with its 'I'm Adele kind of deep' take on itself, because in reality, it would need a lot of work and a lot added to it to in fact.. Be deep. It's pretty, and has good ideas, but doesn't execute them in such a way that feels meaningful - It just leaves you in awe of a pretty thing for a minute or so.
Trigger spots aren't distinct enough for them to stick within your memory - This is annoying simply because you can't step backwards, this means that even if you misstep once just outside of the trigger-zone, you have the replay the entire walk to find that spot/sequence of events to trigger and ending or scene. This would be fine to do if the environment changed substantially, or the events changed and it was just all random, but it isn't. It's the same thing over and over again that you have to reply to ~see all there is to offer~
I understand the idea of what the game is trying to achieve in the "You can only move forwards" insinuation, as well as the making you patiently wait for your desired result, but even with those stretches it doesn't justify not being able to correct errors you may make a long the way. While you cannot erase them, you can fix them - the inability to walk backwards completely role-blocks that.
At the end of the day you really take what you want from it.
It is a pretty looking game, it won't cost you much to experience it, and despite all I have complained about, I'd still suggest you go play it for yourself.

As Space Cowboy said below "IMHO, this is one of the best and underrated MMOs I've player on my entire gaming life (20 years of gaming so far).
Why, you might ask me? I'll tell ya.
STORY:
The background story is amazing and it mixes Fallout series, Mad Max movies and also A Boy and His Dog references (if you ever saw this movie, you, sir, consider yourself lucky). The game has an unique atmosphere aswell. Not only a futurist set, but a post-apocalyptic one, finely made.
MAP:
The map is HUGE, I mean, HUGE (already tell ya that ♥♥♥♥ is huge?!). You could spent like 8-10 hours to cross the sectors on foot, if you make it alive.
CRAFTING:
Forget everything else about other's game crafting. This is THE ♥♥♥♥.
You can craft your own vehicles or train your own animals! Ride a mutant chicken or a horse (you can have many, many different kind of horses) or go in a bad ♥♥♥ mode on a bike.
You can craft almost everything, even tents, campsites and stuff like that to get temporary area buffs.
Craft armors, firearms, melee weapon, explosives, medicine, steroids, recipes, foods, drinks, mutagenics... the list is so big that probably I'd spend all the reviews talking about it.
Also, you need to craft ammunition for your weapons and gas, diesel or biodiesel for your vehicles, besides ration for your animals and repair kits for heal equipment damage from fights.
After all, even if it bothers some people, I must say that I LOVE the time required to crafting. Everything you make by crafting need proper time to get done, from just a few secs to hours or even weeks. A single tire for a car requires 8-12 hours.
COMBAT:
It's a partial FPS where you need to land your blows and aim to shot manually. No auto-target, which is great for PvP. Headshots cause a lot of extra fatal damage, rewarding you for your skill player.
The game have a lot of customization, meaning your character can max various skills to fulfill different roles on a party or even solo. You could be a mutant DPS or a healer, a gunslinger, a rifleman, sniper, fight with a big axe, two tires, be a sneaking rogue, a buffer/debuffer leader or pretty much anything.
PVP:
Awesome.
The game is partial-PvP. I mean, it's not a full PvP map, but, instead, we have PvP zones. On these zones, players need to fight over rare resources like petroleum! People can build settlements and siege-like stuff aswell.
The game has 6 factions which the player can join. Each one has it's owns charateristics, RP-related and PvP gear. These factions are at war/alliance relationships with each other.
The game also have a lot of player's guilds and alliances and people Pvping over resource nodes and PvP zones.
MORE PROS (MORE AWESOME IN YOUR AWESOMENESS):
- Not just more of the same. It really brings something NEW and FRESH to MMO players looking for something special.
- F2P (doesn't matter to me, but it's nice to try for free if you're not sure about it).
- Buy, craft and dye clothes and use them over your regular armor on cosmetic slots. You can even paint and customize your car, bike, etc.
- Active, nice and helpful GMs; 24/7 on chat.
- A LOT OF DANCE MOVES, including MJ and the awesome Carlton Banks dance (Alfonso to his close friends).
- A LOT of creative skills that you don't see everyday.
- Welcoming and active community (don't let the Steam numbers fool you, cause the most people playing it are using the non-Steam client).
- Deep and beautiful scenarios.
- Scary voiceover (turn it off, man).
- You have a flashlight.
- Immersion feel on every step you take.
- Level up takes a long long time, giving you some sense of importance in the world.
- Awesome PvP.
- You can fight while riding or driving! Man, EVERY SINGLE MMO should have this. Drive fast while unloading a submachinegun clip on a pursuit, why not? Not a Fast & Furious type? You can do the cowboy Texas style aswell and shoot you Colt Anaconda on the horseback.
- You can have a dog! (anyone remember Dogmeat from Fallout 2?)
- Different paces of walking/driving/riding. You can walk, jog or run and drive/ride at speed as you like. Not so fast, no so slow, the way you want.
CONS:
- One thing I dislike in this game is it's name. Should be called Awesome Earth.
- Performance issues on some PCs.
- "Dated" graphics (I've player UO for 11 years, ask me if I give a dame for graphics?!)
- "Hardcore", even not having a full loot system like Darkfall, Ultima Online and Mortal Online (love them all). What makes this game "hardcore" for some users is the fact that you need build and plan your character very carefully or it could be useless or disapointing at some point.
- Unfriendly interface and learning curve."

I really wanted to enjoy this title but I can't get into it. The new armor system is a let down. You can't even taunt targets without stripping them of all their armor points first. Magic is extremely difficult to use without risking friendly fire. Some of the fights are extremely poorly designed (ship fight between Acts 1 and 2, I'm looking at you) and the devs love to 'gotcha' by introducing enemies and elements into combat you couldn't have known about before starting the engagement (much save / reload and trial / error required).

The illusion of choice is also especially bad. Basically you have the way the developers want you to solve the problem and then all the wrong ways. Feel free to select the wrong way if you want things to be more difficult. On top of those things I found the story to be an extremely typical 'you are the chosen one and only you can save the universe' tale. Some very eye rolling fondling over your character really turned me off of the plot. The individual character stories are more interesting but only make up a tiny percentage of what you'll spend your time doing - which is mostly wandering around large environments looting barrels and managing your inventory.

Some final notes. Crafting is a chore but at least it's completely ignorable. There's a ton of things to read but most of that is also easily ignored. You will likely feel compelled to play one of the 'origin' characters instead of making a custom character because you miss out on content if you don't. Graphics and sounds are fine but nothing really stands out as outstanding. The entire game is voice acted which is great, although that voice acting is just serviceable. Lastly this is an incredibly long game, which I suppose means good value to some but to me means bloat and poor pacing. Divinity lost me in Act 2, which is about half way through, and I can't see myself playing another 40-50 hours of this.

When I first heard about this project I was rather second-guessing the idea: 1. I have already read the book and seen a couple of movie adaptations of this story. What new could the game provide? The answer is Experience.
Agathe Christie - The ABC Murders is one of those point-and-click experiences you just have to try.
The visual style is the one thing that makes this project unique. With the cartoony animation and art, this game is a new take on the genre, bringing more of a Tale Tales feeling and less a reminder of previous projects such as Murder on the Orient Express.
It will seem a bit awkward if you are not used to this style, but once you get this out of the way, there is no stopping you.
I finished the game with just a couple of hardships,  mostly due to the fact that I didn't pay enough attention to dialogues.
The gameplay is easy and mostly intuitive. You operate with the mouse and go around the world without much ado. Most puzzles are fairly easy if you know what you're doing, but there is a small case of a repeating puzzle. Still in the gameplay department, the puzzles did have a couple of bugs when I played the game such as the game denying me the right to click a specific part of one e.g. It was not a game-breaking experience.
The story is represented quite well, not doing any harm to the original novel (which I'm not such a big fan of anyway). Keep in mind that the game of nor 100% copied from the book nor is it totally unrelated. The team obviously *tried* to provide new experience even for the ones who read the story.
You have lacks in character development in the sense that most end up being exactly the way they seem to be in the first place, but that's also valid for the book.
In short, the experience of worth some of the full price. Definitely pleasurable and worth it when you have the current p'n'c *diversity*

Sadly, Cradle is a disappointing game that I can't recommend. It's got a fascinating world but is lacking in content - there's not much to explore once you leave the yurt. I love the premise and I wish I could recommend this game but it has a couple serious problems:
First and foremost is the story. The story actually starts out great. You wake up in a Mongolian yurt with no memory. You're forced to piece together the world around you using different bits of context provided by all of the items in the yurt. After you piece together a robot friend you discover that she too has amnesia and you both begin a quest to discover your identities.
Unfortunately the story ends without actually resolving this conflict. Just as it feels like you're turning a corner and discovering who you are and what's going on, the game just ends - out of nowhere. Ida the robot gives a cryptic line out of nowhere about
and then shuts off. After a quick jolt of electricity to Ida and an even quicker conversation with her (seriously, it's maybe 10 lines total), the last line of the game is
which is followed immediately by the credits and an even more confusing video playing behind them.
It felt like there was an entire chunk of the story missing or just not explained. If it was presented in a piece of paper on the floor or something similar I'm not sure where that piece of paper could have been. I tried to be pretty thorough when I was looking around inside the yurt and at the nearby complex. I couldn't find anything that mentioned
.
Second is the cube-collecting minigame. The developers were "smart" not to feature much of this gameplay in the trailer because, frankly, I found it offputting. It's not necessarily bad, it's just really out of place in a game specifically advertised to focus on exploration.
The basic premise is that you're placed in a virtual world made of cubes and you have to collect 30 cubes of one specific color. You also have to enemies that blow up and destroy the ground underneath you and try not to fall to the bottom of the level. If you fall to the bottom you lose some of the cubes you've already collected.
Unfortunately there are quite a few of these puzzles and there's a stretch of the game where you'll play the minigame, talk to Ida back at the yurt, and then go play a slight variation of the same minigame you JUST played with no real puzzle solving or exploration in between.
4 years in and it still just getting better.

Thoughts after my first playthrough:
First off, this is a
short campaign. The story itself takes place between three locations within very close proximity. All told, if you play it straight through it'll take only three or four hours at most.
But that's only if you do nothing but the quests while ignoring everything else, of which there is lots.
If you want to get the most out of the game, be prepared for a
of reading. Every scrap of paper down to the newspaper that lines kitchen drawers holds bits of plot. Fortunately, it's very engaging text! While reading these is not technically necessary to finish the game, you are going to be
confused if you don't.
That said, what gameplay there is maintained my interest and left me wanting more up until the credits rolled.
Speaking of the ending: If you are someone who needs your endings to neatly wrap up the plot threads in a a nice neat package, this game is probably not for you. Or if you do play it, definitely seek out every bit of reading material you possibly can and, to lead into my final point...
...EXPLORE. EVERYTHING.
There is a vast desert out there! Once you get the mechanics down, walk away from the plot for a while and go exploring. There are things out there that you will never even get the chance to notice if you strictly follow the plot.
All in all, it's exactly what I hoped it would be: A fascinating story with interesting game mechanics wrapped in an expansive world that you can get lost in for as long as you want.
Plus it's only $16 for the deluxe edition with the kickarse soundtrack!

In regards to the ending; many reviews are complaining about it but I personally liked it a lot. When I got to the ending it seemed a little bit confusing but after going back to read all the newspaper clippings in the yurt everything fell into place and left me quite satisfied.
My one and only complaint would be the use of a checkpoint save system but luckily Cradle's checkpoint saves work well and work logically unlike Ethan Carter.

Here are some things I would add or change about this game:
* The cops seem way too Barney Fife about giving you tickets. They give you speeding tickets for going just a few mph's over the limit. They show no tolerance for the "9 over rule." They also gave me a "red light violation" for stopping at a red light. Wat? Maybe I was too far out in the intersection? I really don't think so. It would also be cool if instead of magically handing you your ticket while your driving if they actually pulled you over and you had to stop; costing you time and delaying your shipment as well as a fine.

* More driver focused interactions and let the driver get out of the truck and free roam. This is a simulator, so what about all the unthought of things that a truck driver has to deal with? Like eating and going to the bathroom? Where are the waffle houses? It would be so cool to be able to jump out of the truck and stretch your legs, walk into a gas station and buy some coffee or energy drinks to keep awake for the final stretch of highway. And things like flat tires, you would have to get out and change your tire.
* I want to see more states! I want to drive from coast to coast! If not, at least Colorado, I love driving through mountains!
* User-made routes players can share in the workshop.
* Small truck deliveries, like "PostEd."
* Bus driving. It's more or less a truck.... You can transport people from city to city. Just something extra to do to earn some cash and keep the game a little fresh.
* Wildlife and livestock. Deer and such running across the road you need to avoid hitting.
* The trains need to be longer than just a locomotive.
That's it for now. I'll edit as things change.

Basically Highlander, but with invisible minigolf clubs instead of swords and no Sean Connery. Please know that while any friendship that goes into this game together will not survive to the 18th hole, infinitely more is at stake here.
Buying this game will force you to make a choice -- will you alone emerge victorious against up to 7 others in a climactic final battle set into motion aeons ago by a cruel and laughing god? Or will you be savagely obliterated and reduced to nothing but mere ash, cast into the howling winds of eternity?

Submerged is a game created by Uppercut Games Pty Ltd, three gamers who set it upon themselves to make fun games for most if not every platform currently out there. In fact check out their website to find out all about the trio and support them, if you want:
.
Enough about the developers though. Submerged is a game without combat or death or voices for that matter. Every moment of the game is framed by music from award winning composer Jeff van Dyck, who some might know produced the music for Alien: Isolation, several Total War titles and, one game I myself enjoy, Hand of Fate. The soundtrack that plays throughout the game is beautifully calm and brings about a sense of wonder as you travel and explore the sunken city. The city itself is wonderfully detailed, with vines climbing the sides of the submerged skyscrapers and landmarks, and various creatures swimming beneath the water. There is a sense of mystery about the city and a constant question that you will ask every time you travel out on you small boat; “What happened here?”. As you progress you can find boxes and notes dotted about the city that will give a brief hint about the goings on before you came to the city. Collect every note and you will uncover the truth.
Mechanically the game flows fairly smoothly. There aren’t all that many complex or difficult things to get your head around, which is great seeing as the game is more or less purely focused on exploration. You, as Miku, can climb the various structures in the sunken city and travel to the very tops of skyscrapers, and take in the beautiful view. You travel around in a small, but stable, wooden boat which  make you almost feel like your playing The Legend of Zelda: Windwaker. As you speed through the waves you’ll come across various creatures that have been changed by the strange aura that seems to surround the city. Huge, moss covered whales will swim past you, launching jets of water into the air and green and blue dolphins will leap out of the water whilst chittering and squeaking. Everything feels natural and calm, along with the music it’s a great atmosphere.
Story-wise, the game, doesn’t really have a huge in-depth plot line. Apart from gathering resources to save your ill younger brother, there isn’t really all that much to it. Granted the cities story is a fascinating mystery to uncover, making you almost want to play until you unfold the entire tale.
To conclude, I’d say Uppercut Games have created a beautiful and original exploration game. With wonderfully detailed graphics, a huge sunken city to explore and a fantastic soundtrack there’s little to not love about Submerged. Good Day!

I am fond of independent games, as well as I am fond of different takes on videogames, specially those that cast a different perspectiva and experience to the player. However, it seems fo me that some developers are going too far in their attempt to create "artistic" games and are actually creating products that are entirely devoid of any significant experiencie to the player. Star Sky fits unfortunately in this category. It can barelly be called a game at all since the only playable aspect of the game is to move the character forward (he doesn't go other way), while standind still at some points of the screen which enables certain effects (as rain, for instance), and the different combinations of what you do produce differente effects that, in the end, unlocks achievements, but have very little inner significance to the player. Star Sky relies almost entirely on the interest of the player to unlock achievements since the "rewards" to the player's actions in the game are irrelevant. The interface the game presents could be potentially used to tell an interesting and engaging story, but Star Sky is not.

Let me start off by saying first that Star Sky has a nice concept, but the content is not here. The attempt is there, it's a unique concept, but a far too expensive one with far too little content available.
My first impression from reading the description of the game was that there would be multiple roads to walk down, and it's ultimately left up to the player which roads to take. This is not the case. What you do is hold the right arrow key, continuously walk right, and stop whenever you hear music playing so that you can trigger events.
There are multiple ways to trigger events, and there are a total of 18 events to trigger; each one with their own achievement. However, in a mere 22 minutes I unlocked 14 of the 18 events. This game isn't very long at all, in 50 minutes I unlocked all of the events, and at an asking price of nearly $5.00 CAD it's just not worth it.
I could defend the value of the game if the graphics were more than 'stylish' silhouettes with backgrounds that would've taken a couple hours tops to make in Photoshop. The fact that Star Sky has the same look and feel to it that any browser based Flash game does really doesn't help to push this game at its selling price, either.

Short review :
Simplistic and bugged all to hell.
In Detail :
Took a reinstall and several restarts to progress from the first crime scene to Poirot's apartment which is where I encountered another game breaking bug - the game just hangs there, not actually "frozen", since hitting escape opens the menu and the game is still actually running, but there's no way to progress, no cursor, no options etc.  The discussion forum  suggests having Windows 10 might be a solution - yeah, no thanks, that's like curing a patient by killing him, his family, his pets, and setting fire to his baseball card collection.
From what I've been able to actually see of the gameplay, the "investigative" side of things is incredibly simplistic, you just mouse around until the cursor changes to something, you take a closer look to use Poirot's famous observational skills to gather clues, but it's impossible to miss anything since the cursor changes to let you know to hover it there.  They should have made this far less obvious to give players a challenge and make them use THEIR brains instead of Poirot's.  That said, the few puzzles where you have to manipulate objects I encountered at the first crime scene were fairly well done.
Along the same simplistic lines are using your little grey cells to put clues together.  As far as I can tell there's no way to fail this, you put between 2 and 3 clues into a chain thing and if it turns green it auto-completes and success is yours.  Woo...
TLDR : Not recommended unless you're able to actually get it to run and you're buying it for a kid or a diehard Poirot fan (Who will probably be disappointed it isn't David Suchet voicing the titular role)

Ah, you know, I can see that a lot of people didn't like the game and thought it was boring, but I really enjoyed it.
To look at people's major complaints, I didn't think that Poirot walked too slowly, and he sped up if you double-clicked. Furthermore, there really wasn't all that much walking to be done. The vast majority of the time he was in small rooms. As an avid point and click gamer, I can tell you that needless walking is present in many games, but this really isn't one of them.
Another complaint is that the puzzles repeated themselves, but there is only one puzzle that does that. This is, in fact, a head scratcher, but the puzzle that repeats is so easy it barely counts as a puzzle and can be completed in well under a minute.
To me, the most important things in a modern P&C game are puzzles, story, interface and voice acting (when it's available), and all four of these are done well.
Puzzles: The puzzles are as logical as you get in P&C games. Most of them are fairly easy, but I found a few fairly challenging. There were no unnecessary puzzles like you get in a lot of older games where you have to run errands for people, etc.  I'd basically put the puzzles into 2 categories. One type was strictly logic-based where you are trying to connect clues for the case. The other type reminded me of the game The Room, where you are trying to open objects to get to the clues inside.  I found both types to be fun and rewarding.
Story: The story is ripped straight from an excellent novel. If you like detective stories and mysteries, then you will like the story. Also, if you play Poirot as the a-hole that he is in the books, there's a decent amount of comedy to be had.
Interface: The interface was simple and inobtrusive. Very easily worked. Also, if you get stuck, there is a "Clue" function you can use to get you headed in the right direction. I used this a couple of times when I was being thick and found that it worked really well.
Voice Acting: I'd say it was above average. The person who portrayed Poirot did an excellent job. All the other characters were at least servicable.
Anyway, if you like P&C games and detective stories, I'd say you will enjoy this. If you've already read the book, you might still enjoy it for its puzzles and humorous dialogue.

It's a pretty good game and worth the money compared to many others, but if you can get in on sale even better.

Main cons:
- It seems like one woman did all the female voice acting, and one man did all of the male voice acting. Most of the characters sound like they don't give a toss, and there's very little emotion in the tone. Not very convincing.
- Puzzles can be repetitive. Many of them are original, but you have to do one three times when it's bleedin' obvious that the letter was written on the same typewriter! It was fun the first time, but .... seriously?
- No fail state; there's no downside to failing to make a good observation. All there is in this regard is "ego points", where you have to try and act like Poirot - you can maximise these, but there's no failure. There's little benefit to getting more ego points, anyway.
- Some parts of the story are quite obvious, but take a long time to pan out. There isn't much of a climax, and you can spot the plot twist immediately.
- The puzzles usually keep people's posessions safe, but it's absolutely absurd. It'd take twenty minutes to turn on a gramophone if this were reality! (Of course, take this with a pinch of salt - a major element of the game is the puzzles. They have to put in puzzles where they can.)
Pros:
+ Decent music
+ Good loading times (on an SSD)
+ Mostly obvious what to do (this could be a con though). Sometimes it's really hard to know what to do, though - but there's a "clue" feature that helps you in these times
+ Easy to play. Simple controls.

A fairly nicely done 3d graphic adventure, vaguely feeling like Grim Fandango. Attractive graphics and some innovative ideas around using one's "little grey cells" to make deductions. However, the game is let down by user experience issues; there are a number of occasions when it's clear what needs to be done but not clear how to make the game actually do it, or worse that you can do it but the game doesn't register you as having done it.
The game also suffers from ambiguity in making deductions: one is presented with a question ("Was this chap present at the murder scene?") and then a list of discovered "facts" or statements, and one chooses the statements that lead to an answer for the question. But the choice of which "facts" lead to this conclusion is sometimes very arbitrary: given (as a made up example) "the chap was seen at the scene", "he has mud on his boots from the scene", and "he said he was there" as "facts" one has to pick two, and only the "correct" two as chosen by the game developers will work. So what this leads to is trying all possible combinations, because the puzzle stops becoming "work out what the answer is" and instead becomes "work out which arbitrary selection the game developers
the answer is.
There's also the problem of derailment, common to detective-type games. If you're interrogating a subject and you need to ask them the "right" question to get the clue you need, what should the game do if you get it wrong? Actual detectives, if they don't ask the right question, don't get the clue and don't solve the case, but that's fairly unacceptable in a video game. So, on quite a few occasions, the game merely throws up a vaguely-in-context "wrong!" statement ("the subject shakes their head angrily") and then proceeds as if you'd chosen the correct question to begin with. In some places this is handled well -- reconstructions are nicely done, and errors cause you to replay, but in a way that makes sense -- but in others this can make the game feel like just watching a film where you have to press mouse buttons every ten seconds to make it keep playing. Not very interactive, in other words.
There's also quite a bit of suspension of disbelief required around how everyone in the game keeps their valuables in some sort of complicated puzzle box rather than, e.g., a safe like normal people. This does make the game feel like The 7th Guest in places; the plot needs working out a bit more.
Spoilers for the plot:
Despite all this, and despite the rather clumsy language and dubbing at times -- the game is by a French developer team, and this shows at times in the English version -- the game's enjoyable to play if not very mentally taxing, and it does look good. The built-in hint system is excellent for situations where you know what you want to do but can't work out how to tell the game to do it -- choosing a hint will make Poirot do the next action for you, and then the hint "recharges" so you have to wait before using it again. If you're happy with a few hours of mildly challenging puzzle boxes and Poirot-speak, and you can find it on sale (because otherwise it's a bit expensive), consider this recommended.

I'm not really sure what to think about this one. While I do enjoy the combat, and the level editor is as deep and accessible as that of Farcry 2, there really isn't enough content to justify the price tag. Depth is fine, but even the "levels" made for expressly showcasing said depth are plagued by errors that contradict their intended purpose. There are faulty checkpoints, glitched movement in some areas, crashes, and AI that doesn't know what to do with itself. Modders have done a much better job creating good-looking levels that fully use the power of the game.
Visually, the game is great, except when I start hitting hiccups associated wih either bad hardware optimization and missing files. (I found the "checker skybox" to be particularly amusing.) Once these glitches start, they don't stop.
I could forgive all of this, except for one fact. Before playing it again for this review, I last sat down with it at least half a year ago. I was impressed, but I remember thinking, "I bet this is going to have more content later." Present day, I played again, and was confused at how little had been added.
Such a wait is minimal, from what I've heard. Apparently, this game has been in development limbo for almost seven years. During the time this game has been in its alpha stages, I've seen members of my family be born and later attend first grade, and this game still isn't finished. I understand that not many people are working on it, but charging $30 for a product that has taken this long, that is this devoid of longevity, and that still has not been completed... ah...
It's like paying for a car that's over half a decade old, and missing pieces, under the promise that one day, I will be able to drive it around and have fun.
Until then, this game is little more than a glorified level editor for ninja animals.

3rd person explorer ONLY game, no combat.  Worth ~$10, goes on sale for $5, and you'll get 8-12 hours out of it depending on how astute you are at uncovering the map and using your telescope.  Fairly simple 100% achi, though it'll take a few hours.
8.5/10 for its genre, and I would buy again.
-game IS exactly what it's billed as, and the trailers give a good idea of what you will find
-simple controls (I used kb+m; controller is also supported)
-straightforward mission/directives
-acceptable progress measure (map icons dull/pale after pickup of objectives)
-
graphics on ultra settings, but there isn't too much 'fluff' to obscure points of interest
-easy (automatic!) return to home base upon objective collection (see CON related to this point)
-mysterious aspect to certain ingame plot devices (cutscenes tell a story of their own)
-inspired blend of endearing & exciting, without being too cutesy or nagging
-aspect of how exploration games used to be, long ago, before items were marked or outlined, or glowing, or... obvious; once you're on top of them (or use spyglass to find them) they're easy to see, but until then, you are in fact
-cards, for those who like them
-
no bugs.  I got stuck on a tree twice, but when I quit out and then continued the same game, it sent me back to the area where I first entered that level of the building (assume under 60 seconds lost time in all cases).  Other than that, it's smooth and pretty.
-forgiving environment; if you're a parent or busy with something else, you can walk away at any time without concern of losing progress or items or time.
-
Worthy of metion because exploring buildings that have only a single, small, or partly obscured path to an objective sometimes must be traveresed more than once.  The scenery is beautiful, but after a while the slow-run can become tedious.
-No hint button.  You're very strictly on your own, which isn't a problem per se, but a few of the buildings have convoluted routes.  Again, enjoy the scenery.
-Regarding auto-return to base upon picking up a crate: you do NOT have a choice.  In other words, if you don't have all the objectives in a building when you take the crate, you'll be retruning to the building to find parts of the story.  Not horrible, but worth mentioning.
-$20 price tag.  Too much for this game, despite how much I liked it on every level.  I'd pay $10 or $12 for sure, and when it goes on sale for $5 it's a fantastic bargain.  As a rule, I do not agree with a game that does not have a dollar-per-hour return on the price.  As stated, you'll get about 8-12 hours out of this game, thus, this observation.  (Of my ~19 hours played, about 5-6 of that was idle time).
All in all, at the $5 price I paid, I'm very satisfied, and I'll be looking for more from Uppercut Games in the future - great job guys!

What a sparkling little gem this game is!  A true visual treat.
A girl arrives at a submerged city with her sick little brother.  She has to search all corners of the map for supplies to get him well, scaling deserted buildings and roaming the creature-filled waters in a small boat.  Finding all the secrets scattered around the city slowly reveals the past: the siblings' story as well as the events that befell the city.
Submerged is beautiful all around, from the characters and the story to the colourful world with its creatures, blue sea, sunrises and sunsets (day and night cycle).
The keyboard and mouse controls for the game are very simple.  No complicated moves or combinations of keys to master, which leaves the player free to explore and enjoy the scenery.  And the calming piano and orchestra music leaves one in absolutely no real hurry to find all the supplies, secrets and boat upgrades.  In fact, you may well be tempted to spend some time observing and following the whales, the dolphins, the manta rays ...  Our heroine can't die and she can't fall from buildings or high places, although figuring out what ledges to follow and where certain items are located on buildings may provide some small puzzles.
Submerged is a game of exploration: finding items and finding the past.  It is about saving your little brother's life but at the same time it is about relaxing and taking in the beautiful surroundings.  It is a welcome retreat from the chaos of fast-paced action games.  It is about enjoyment, a respect for life, being inspired.  The developers took great care to create a visually attractive and endearing game.  I would recommend this game any day.

What can I say that hasn't been said over 8,000 times? This game gives you complete control over what your character does and says. And I don't mean in the sense of "Oh, I can walk over here and I have dialogue options." I mean that if you don't like one of those Main Quest essential NPCs, you can attack and kill them. Few games take this risk, but Divinity: Original Sin 2 does and does it beautifully. It gives you options upon options on ways to accomplish your goals and completing quests. I have 25 hours in the game, all of them spent inside Fort Joy, re-loading, restarting and trying to make sure I didn't screw quests up. One quest has you find a dog's lost mate (if you have Pet Pal that is) and you eventually find her in the dungeons. Little did I know, if you escape the fort and then come back, every Magister and Source Hound will attack you on site. So I loaded back to make sure I could talk to the dog and complete the quest without killing his ex-mate.The game feels like a true virtualization of a DnD campaign. Where you choose your actions, the narrator narrates what happens and the world and people react. I've never played a game like this because I was always turned off to turn based combat in video games. But this game does it beautifully, incorporating strategy into the placement of every character and making the environment interactable with different elements and being able to use the landscape your advantage. The enemies can also do this, and will do it more as you turn up the difficulty. I had an enemy cast rain and, before my next turn, one of her cronies shocked my entire party. The rain and standing water caused by it allowing the spell to travel through the party. It's unbelievable what they were able to achieve with this game and I honestly can't wait to see what happens next
