Speedrunners is a amazingly fun competitive game that's easy to pick up and hard to master. Offering great fun on a couch with friends as well as a intense competitive experience.
Full Video Review:
Textual summary:
The summary can never compare to the full video, so i always recommend watching that for the best possible impression of the title.
First things first: The game is a TON of fun, which is as always, the most important part of a game. The fast paced and hectic nature coupled with the various items that throw a curve ball at the players means that it's unpredictable and a great way to spend time with friends.
On the competitive side the various leagues are set up quite well and while the lower leagues might have some issues with smurfs, I've found them to be less of an issue than they appear. As with all competitive games, knowing the tracks and timing are often the most important part of a game and provide a barrier to entry to those new.
Thankfully, the game offers a variety of ways to practice from Bot and Solo runs as well as non-ranked mode quick matches. All in all the game provides quite a few tools outside of the ranked play to both learn as well as enjoy the game.
One criticism i have for the title is that it REALLY doesn't like you fiddling with alt-tab and options. while recording the review i experienced several crashes. Theses never occur during normal play, but it's still worth noting.
Other than that i have nothing but the greatest of recommendations for this title. It's quick, easy to pick up and understand and a absolute BLAST to play.

Reading many other reviews, I often found statements like "the game has great potential" from guys who spent only a few hours in the game. I felt I had to respond to those claims. Steam doesn t seem to allow a second review in another language. Thats why I added this english part to my german review (down below)
In my opinion, without fundamental changes, Conan Exiles has NO POTENTIAL at all.
And here is why..:
The Game-Design behind this game is not working.  Low level players are prey for high level players and offline-raiding is basically the way to win. There is no protection. Your char can be killed and your base can be destroyed while you are offline. That itself isn t bad, there are other games where offline raiding is possible.
BUT one of the big differences to similiar games is, that in Conan Exiles the buildings are containers for items which ONLY the owner can access. This means, if you want to loot your enemies base you basically HAVE to destroy all the buildings while in other games you can loot and leave the buildings standing - giving your enemy the chance to recover (after all its a game we are playing together).
The next difference to similar games is the claim-system. For example, in compareable games you build ONE special building and claim the land around it. The Game-Design of Conan Exiles uses a different approach.
In this game you build foundations to claim your territory. The foundations make it impossible for other players to build nearby and also block the respawn of NPCs. The problem is, that you can build an infinite number of foundations and spam those all over the map. There are players doing so, intentionally blocking good spots to settle down or intentionally blocking the respawn of NPCs (for example the religion teachers). To destroy all those spammed foundations is almost impossible (you would need hundreds of hours and alot of steel and bombs; some foundations are out of reach, build several meters high above the ground). There is no decay-system - meaning those spammed foundations will stay there for eternity, making huge parts of the map impossible to settle down.
To find a good spot to build a base gets even harder considering building on the ground is basically a death sentence (on pvp-servers you are guranteed to get (offline-) raided and if someone uses a god your base will be gone in an instant - no matter what level your walls are). There are also many abandoned bases from players who left the server/game blocking even more parts of the map. And to make things worse, High level players have several bases spread over the map.
The next problem with the game-design is the respawn itself.  If you get the aggro of NPCs and go out off their reach (running away or dying) the system kills/despawns all NPCs who had aggro. This means, if someone ran through the city and pulled all those mobs with him, the next player coming around might be standing in an empty city and has to wait for respawn.
Those are big issues in the Game-Design which have quit an impact on the gameplay - and early access is no excuse for that.
The building/claiming-feature is THE KEY-FEATURE of this Game, and it IS NOT WORKING in its current form.
What else has the game to offer ?
PVE ? -> respawn problems, bad balancing
PVP ? -> High lvl hunting low lvl, offline-raiding wins, instant death by gods
What this game has is alot of BUGS and many problems (just to name some: no /stuck command, 3-4 times server down a day ( + the regular server restart without warning), instant death after relogging (NPCs hit you while you still have the loading screen), buggy dismantle-option, exploits, the weight (arrows weigh more than logs) and cost of arrows making bows ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons, stacking poison (spiders), stacking root (several hyenas), overlapping UI, language changes not being saved, durability of tools and weapons (its quit annoying how often you have to repair and how much resources you need to do that, doing that like a hundred times you get the feeling you farm resources just to repair ur stuff), immortal NPCs, potions not working.... and the list goes on and on)
So... WHAT YOU SHOULD ASK YOURSELF is: does this game, ignoring all the bugs and problems, just considering the current Game-Design, really has potential ? and is it worth 30 Euros ?

Probleme:
- gute Siedlungsplätze zu finden. Auf dem Boden zu Bauen bedeutet auf PvP-Servern einen garantierten (Offline-) Raid und Instant-death wenn jemand einen Gott beschwört. Nur Felsen sind halbwegs sicher.
Siedlungsplätze werden durch Steinfundamente geclaimt. Diese Fundamente blockieren in einem bestimmten Umkreis die Siedlungsgründung durch andere Spieler und den respawn von NPCs. Fundamente kann man in unendlicher Anzahl bauen - was dazu führt dass diese Fundamente von manchen Spielern intentionell auf der ganzen Karte gespammt werden um zu verhindern, dass dort wer siedelt (quasi alle guten Siedlungspots auf Felsen sind schnell geblockt) oder NPCs respawnen (z.B. die NPCs die Religionen lehren). All diese Fundamente zu beseitigen ist quasi unmöglich (Stichwort Stahlwaffen oder Bomben bzw. Fundamente in unerreichbaren Höhen). Hören Spieler auf zu zocken (sind einige) oder ziehen auf der map um hinterlassen sie ihre leeren Gebäude die zusätzlich Siedlungsplätze blockieren. So werden mit der Zeit ganze Teile der Map nicht besiedelbar.  Ein Decay-System für Fundamente gibt es nicht.
- Server-Downs: 3-4 mal am Tag, ohne Vorwarnung. Beim erneuten Einloggen ins Game erlebt man häufig einen instant death da NPCs auf den Char einkloppen noch während man den Ladebildschirm sieht (wegrennen oder kämpfen also unmöglich), ebenfalls ist ertrinken möglich wenn du vor dem server down im wasser warst. Du respawnst noch dem Tod komplett nackt und darfst dann versuchen so zu der Leiche des Chars zu sprinten, evtl. kilometer entfernt, bevor diese mitsamt all deinen Items despawnt. Stirbst du unterwegs, wird der vorherige Leichnam ebenfalls gelöscht und durch einen neuen ersetzt. Bist du vor dem Server-down gestorben wird die Leiche automatisch beim Serverneustart gelöscht.
- Es gibt kein /stuck Befehl. Hängst du irgendwo fest, bleibt nur der Suizid. Alle deine Items sind idR verloren da der Leichnam nicht erreichbar ist.
- Gebäudeteile abreißen. Es kann scheinbar passieren, dass Gebäude hinter dem abzureißenden Objekt einfach mit zerstört werden und die dort gelagerten Items alle verloren gehen.
- Wenn du aggro von NPCs ziehst werden die NPCs, sobald du außer Reichweite bist (also stirbst oder wegrennst,) alle vom System getötet/gelöscht. Das bedeutet, dass wenn ein Spieler vor dir durch die NPC Stadt rennt und aggro zieht kann es passieren, dass du in einer leeren Stadt stehst und auf den respawn warten muss.
- Das  Balancing ist ziemlicher Mist. Gift ist nervtötend da es gestackt wird. Wenn du nicht zufällig hunderte Flaschen Gegengift dabei hast (was wohl kaum einer hat) ist dein Char schnell fällig. Pfeile wiegen mehr als Baumstämme (du musst also mittels Attribut-Punkten dein Inventar vergößern)) und sind aufwendig zu produzieren - das macht Fernkampf zu kostspielig.
- Bugs (z.B. Tränke gehen oft nicht), Exploits, UI-Überlagerungen, Spracheinstellungen werden nicht gespeichert.... usw. Die Liste ist endlos.
Das Spiel mag Early-Access sein, aber meiner Meinung nach ist das keine Entschuldigung dafür, dass die Basics des Spiels nicht funktionieren (Stichwort claimen mittels Fundamenten, (Offline-) Raiding-System). Das ist einfach schlechtes Game-Design - das zu einem total überteuerten Preis versucht wird den Leuten unterzujubeln.

SpeedRunners is a simple and fun multiplayer game that presents itself with frustrating matchmaking, but incredibly fun mechanics and well-designed maps!
SpeedRunners’ main hook is it’s emphasis on competitive skill. It emphasizes map memorization, a good understanding of the game’s momentum, and effectively using/dodging items in order to win. It stays as a comfortable party game while also being something that those seeking high-level play can pick up.
And this is what really makes SpeedRunners a really fun game to play. It’s mechanics are all well-built, with it being meticulously designed to be easy to pick-up but hard to master. Items can be used to get yourself an edge if you use it right, and the maps are designed so the multiple paths don’t always favor towards players picking the shortcut. The level design, while simple, is incredibly effective. And there’s a lot of these high-quality, well-designed maps in the game. It’s the case where Quantity = Quality.
The game’s mainly built on its multiplayer, which is definitely good fun. When playing with friends locally, it was a blast, and almost no issues were had with the game’s overall performance. Online Play is a bit unstable, but still playable. For some reason, getting matched up with players your own skill is incredibly difficult, and this is when you’re not being matched with players two leagues above you and literally playing from the other half of the continent. Unfortunately, the game’s matchmaking is quite problematic, although it’s nothing that they can’t fix over-time.
Another problem I have with the game’s Ranked Play is it’s ranking system. It has the old Rocket League points system that I really hate where you’re almost eternally stuck to the bottom rank due to ranking up requiring such a high number of points.
The game’s single-player content is sorta just there. There’s a story mode that’s really uninteresting unless you want to unlock in-game comics, but the bots are fairly well-designed for single-player and you’ll be able to practice alone if you wish. It’s a OK offering for a mainly multiplayer-only experience.
The Custom Level Editor/Trail Editor are nice additions, and certainly help bring another side of the community together. For the most part, the tools presented are already good enough for players who want to design levels or make cosmetic trails, and this is apparent due to a lot of the Workshop maps being well-designed.
The game’s presentation is relatively decent. The art-style is nice, but the UI is a bit messy. The game’s soundtrack is repetitive due to it being only a handful of in-game tracks, but it’s definitely well-composed and invokes the excitement that comes to the game’s matches.
It can run alright on lower-end hardware too, so you don’t have to break the bank to get it to work. However, I noticed considerable framedips on my lower-end laptop when playing it, and when the game got anywhere below 50 FPS, it was practically unplayable.
For the most part despite the technical issues I’ve had with SpeedRunners, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. There’s some real potential for a brand new competitive e-sport, but on it’s own, it’s fantastic fun with friends. If only the Online Multiplayer wasn’t quite the mess.

Playing this without ANY prior knowledge of the Agatha Christie novel it is adapted from, The ABC murders proved to still be a satisfying experience with unique puzzle mechanics with quirky characters,  however, it is not without its faults.
The ABC Murders indulges the player with bits of commentary on everything that you can pick up or examine, the story is interesting, the puzzles aren't too easy nor challenging and the characters are vibrant yet bizzare. The rich dialogue and 1930's setting help the player become more immersed into what I would term a 'light-hearted' mystery. Being able to make choices within conversations adds to the fun and slightly changes the course of the conversation. For instance, a female character was absolutely appalled at my advice to ask for a divorce when a characters husband was abusive. She insisted that she has morals and women have no right to take back vows to a man like that!  Oh the 1930's!
Now for the not so good:
The mouse mechanics are very irritating ESPECIALLY during the puzzle solving process. Clicking on one area may send you to an entirely different area. Trying to pin-point the clue that you need to find to progress in a large room can be very tedious as once again, if two clues are close in proximity to each other, it is quite difficult to select it without accidently selecting the other clue which you have already observed.
Trying to deduce the clues into a logical explanation is most of the time - illogical. For example, 'What do we know about *insert character name* and then you as the player must pick from various select clues to match the statement, except, the statement is so very vague that almost everything could be applied to it. Trial and error I guess?
Overall, The ABC Murders is a fun little detective experience of finding clues and then linking them all together to catch  the culprit. Its bizzare characters with strong, seemingly out of place accents to match boost the games light hearted take on what would otherwise be a very serious serial murder case
The ABC Murders relies very heavily on dialogue, as to be expected with the detective/mystery genre but if you don't enjoy reading vast amounts of text and listening to conversations and get the urge to skip them - then this game isn't for you.

Fallen Earth, at its time of release, was actually a pretty fun romp. The world and landscape was vast and full of nice locations, as well as keeping an excellent post apocalyptic tone to everything. There was a lot to do, many places to explore, mutants and enemy factions to hunt down and kill, and hundreds of items to craft. In fact over 90% of all in game items where craft-able at the time. It was a ambitious game that didn't quite hit the mark on a lot of things.
While it was a pretty game and offered a lot of options as far as what you could do and where you could go, the big headaches of the game ended up dragging it down. For starters it used a skill system that was pretty open ended. Normally i would say "Ah hell yeah, i can really be what i want to be!" Unfortunately that is not the case. It was pretty easy to bork a character and you really had to specialize if you wanted to be remotely effective in anything. The skills you could learn and acquire throughout the game where nothing amazing, there just wasn't any wow factor. It also implemented a quasi magic system, which acted more like a enhancement to a weapon style vs a more caster role. A pure caster is possible, but in game it just wasn't all that effective.
Combat itself was about as boring as it could get. Weapons where just a bore to use. The game offered multiple firearm classes to specialize in as well as melee. The animations and sounds where nothing short of drab. Weapons felt like peashooters, even if it was a higher tier rifle or machine gun, all guns just "felt" like you where shooting a BB gun. Melee was even worse, as the animations and damage indication was sloppy. On top of that, mobs sit around, waiting to be engaged. I'm a little over early MMO troupes, how about you?
However, even though i may be a little harsh on its short coming, with a group of friends, this game can be a blast. There are a ton of areas to explore, side missions to cash in on and a mid/late game faction based pvp zone. This is where it can really get interesting. All players have the option of joining a faction, and each faction has some special skills and perks associated with them. Fighting over control towns and resource fields are really fun with the right gang of people.
Fallen Earth will not be for everyone. If you can get past the poor combat system and dated MMO style of quests and combat, it is a pretty big game to explore and get sucked into. Its even F2P, so if you like Post Apoc settings and are up for something different and new, give it a shot. It might surprise the hell out of you.

It's a short game - took me about 6 and a half hours. If you wanted to rush through you can probably finish it in much less than half that; But you'd probably entirely miss what it was really about. If you want clear direction, and the thought of searching through and discovering things for youself (opening cupboards, reading newspaper scraps etc) sounds unappealling then you probably won't enjoy this game. If you like the idea of discovering things for yourself, and finding enough fragments to paint a picture of a truely alien world, then this game will definitely be the ticket.
To define it in terms of mechanics: It's essentially a point and click adventure game, where you discover clues and also progress along a story. It's also first person, so a lot of discovery involves exploring the world yourself, and picking up and moving around objects (and a simple inventory system). The actual gameplay side of the story is fairly short, but the lore side is wonderfully wide, as long as you the player choose to search it out.
The game is fairly graphically intensive (probably best played with a gtx 760 min or equiv.) and doesn't really come with many graphical settings - just a quality slider, and the ability to choose resolution and antialiasing.
There's no input configuration controls, so if you can't play with wsad you're out of luck.
All that being said I found the story pretty amazing. It definitely left me with a strong feeling.
it does not spell things out for you entirely. If you don't like piecing parts of the story together (the pieces
all there, you just to find them, and piece them together yourself) you will probably be left confused.  But if you
then you'll love this game too.

First a warning, then my reason for liking the game:
Warning:
The game is short - about 6 hours on your first playthrough if you don't rush.
While it advertizes itself as open world, and you can indeed walk around freely inside the world, the world has only 3-5 distinct locations which are all within short walking distance from each other. There is not much to explore in this game - but the locations that are there are very rich and detailed.
The ending is sudden, but thought provoking. Chances are you'll about the story and the ending long after you've finished the game and you'll likely want to play a second time to better understand the story.
Why I liked it anyway:
The setting is fresh and mysterious - you don't know what to expect and gradually descovering pieces of information about the world in this game is stimulating for your imagination.
This coupled with the great soundtrack and decent voice acting makes for an immersive experience.
Aside from the main puzzles, the game gives you many snippets of information about the game world, it's history and the protagonst - but for the most part this is entirely optional - the game doesn't go out of it's way to reveal it's story in an foolproof way - you'll have solve the puzzle on your own if you want to make sense of what you've experienced.
For me this game was a unique experience that I liked.
I expected a bit more content, so the price might be a bit high for what you get, but I can't say I feel ripped off.
If you watch the trailer and it really clicks with you, you may want to buy it and will probably enjoy it.

I've got severely mixed feelings about this game. Heck, given the option, I'd give it a neutral recommendation. But we don't have that, we need to pick either a thumbs up icon, or a thumbs down icon, and as much as it pains me to do so, I went with the one pointing downward.
Allow me to explain why.
First, I was really excited about it - the premise looked solid - this is what sold me on the game in the first place. "Androids" with eyes displayed for emotions? Awesome! A futuristic yet retro tram? Yes please!
And you know what? That premise IS in fact in the game. It's a great combination of new and old, wrapped in very pretty visuals (even if there are a few technical hiccups, but these can overlooked). The story starts off on the confusing side, then gets interesting, and then...
Well, then comes the kicker.
It then ends. I've played, and finished, the game in 5 hours - and that's including that at one point I think I left the game on to get myself some tea and chat with my girlfriend.
Don't get me wrong - I don't mind short games when they offer a complete experience. Like, say, Thomas Was Alone. But Cradle just kind of ends - it feels like it ends right in the middle of something far greater. What's even more frustrating is that it ends with the words "I'll explain everything" and then does the exact opposite (a short video during the credits places even more questions). If the answers are buried in the piles of randomly discarded newspaper clippings in the game world, then that's not a fun way to tell a story. :/
All in all, I enjoyed the journey, but the sudden end left me angry and dissapointed and with that, I sadly cannot recommend the game. Perhaps if it were a lot cheaper*?
*- No, I don't mean free! ~50% off, and while I would still dislike the sudden ending, I wouldn't feel as cheated on the length.

Submerged is an explorative story based game. If you're looking for your regular shooters this isn't for you.
But this is for me, and probably many other people out there.
There are basically three storylines within this game;
1. the main story follows a brother and sister - you're playing as the sister and exploring this sumberged city to help your brother
2. the story you uncover of why you're there once you collect each supply crate
3. the story of the city as you collect each secret (these aren't given in order so you'll have to read it at the end once you've got all 60)
I really enjoyed this game as it felt like a breath of fresh air amongst the other games I'm currently playing and on top of good story telling the game itself is beautiful. I loved the design of the city, the animals within in it, and the Remnants.
Other positives about this game are its open world (though not huge), theres a day/night cycle, and weather changes (including a thunder storm) which all adds up to a nice atmosphere.
Keep in mind that the main story isn't super long and will be completed quicker if you don't stop to explore other buildings/gather secrets on the way. Climbing the buildings allows for good lookout spots to enjoy the scenery and take in the beautiful design of the world created.
Don't waste your money on this. Play Rust.

This review will be mostly negative but stick through it, I'll sing this game's praises soon enough. First off I'd like to say what a disappointment this port is on a technical level. Stuttering textures and cut off sound bites are all throughout the game, and though the last time I play JSR was 10 years ago, I think I can safely say I don't remember these issues on the Dreamcast version. There's also a bug where your game might not be able to save, but will indicate that it has, which is only fixable by editing the hex values of the game's executable (where it turns out one instance of the word SAVE should be lowercase).
Despite the incompetence of whoever allowed these bugs to blight such a colorful weave in the tapestry of gaming history, JSR still fares okay. The art style is vibrant and colorful, there's excellent music that fits the tone perfectly, and the world it presents is interesting and lively. In fact, the game's flair is essentially it's only selling point, as the gameplay is stiff and feels alien to control, like your actions have a hard time corresponding to your key presses, messing up the energetic flow that every other part of the experience is trying to create.
You'll be cruising down Benten-Cho with Miller Ball Breakers thumping rhythmically; you're getting all pumped and ready to do some nice tricks, but you get snagged on wayward geometry or land one micrometer away from the rail you were trying to stick because despite the cartoony art style and space physics, JSR can require almost real-life skating precision sometimes. It's frustrating and it takes way too long to recover from bailing, which wouldn't be so bad were it not for the missions being timed and often involving chases. The controls are so jerky it's actually somehow preferable to play on a keyboard, which I didn't think was possible with a skating game.
It's a game of missed potential, but is still worth a buy just to get entrenched in the youthful, rebellious atmo, and get a handle on what the Dreamcast brought to the table as a launch title, so there's a historic glimmer to it that way.

SpeedRunners is a simple and fun multiplayer game that presents itself with frustrating matchmaking, but incredibly fun mechanics and well-designed maps!
SpeedRunners’ main hook is it’s emphasis on competitive skill. It emphasizes map memorization, a good understanding of the game’s momentum, and effectively using/dodging items in order to win. It stays as a comfortable party game while also being something that those seeking high-level play can pick up.
And this is what really makes SpeedRunners a really fun game to play. It’s mechanics are all well-built, with it being meticulously designed to be easy to pick-up but hard to master. Items can be used to get yourself an edge if you use it right, and the maps are designed so the multiple paths don’t always favor towards players picking the shortcut. The level design, while simple, is incredibly effective. And there’s a lot of these high-quality, well-designed maps in the game. It’s the case where Quantity = Quality.
The game’s mainly built on its multiplayer, which is definitely good fun. When playing with friends locally, it was a blast, and almost no issues were had with the game’s overall performance. Online Play is a bit unstable, but still playable. For some reason, getting matched up with players your own skill is incredibly difficult, and this is when you’re not being matched with players two leagues above you and literally playing from the other half of the continent. Unfortunately, the game’s matchmaking is quite problematic, although it’s nothing that they can’t fix over-time.
Another problem I have with the game’s Ranked Play is it’s ranking system. It has the old Rocket League points system that I really hate where you’re almost eternally stuck to the bottom rank due to ranking up requiring such a high number of points.
The game’s single-player content is sorta just there. There’s a story mode that’s really uninteresting unless you want to unlock in-game comics, but the bots are fairly well-designed for single-player and you’ll be able to practice alone if you wish. It’s a OK offering for a mainly multiplayer-only experience.
The Custom Level Editor/Trail Editor are nice additions, and certainly help bring another side of the community together. For the most part, the tools presented are already good enough for players who want to design levels or make cosmetic trails, and this is apparent due to a lot of the Workshop maps being well-designed.
The game’s presentation is relatively decent. The art-style is nice, but the UI is a bit messy. The game’s soundtrack is repetitive due to it being only a handful of in-game tracks, but it’s definitely well-composed and invokes the excitement that comes to the game’s matches.
It can run alright on lower-end hardware too, so you don’t have to break the bank to get it to work. However, I noticed considerable framedips on my lower-end laptop when playing it, and when the game got anywhere below 50 FPS, it was practically unplayable.
For the most part despite the technical issues I’ve had with SpeedRunners, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. There’s some real potential for a brand new competitive e-sport, but on it’s own, it’s fantastic fun with friends. If only the Online Multiplayer wasn’t quite the mess.

I mainly play strategy or RPGs, but enjoy the occasional casual game. I like adventure games and am happy they're making a come-back. I like mystery games. I've played HO games based on Agathe Christie (not nearly as much fun as an adventure game) and enjoyed them.
I did not enjoy ABC Murders, mainly because of the repetitive nature of puxzles and poorly thought-out gameplay.
PROS:
* No one tells a mystery the way Agathe Christie does.
* One of my favorite Christie stories
* Intricate mystery. Hard to judge this one as a game since I already knew the story.
* Funny ways to earn "ego points" that have nothing to do with the mystery
* Poirot was very much Poirot
* Voice acting good for the most part
* Some of the puzzles were intricate and took a lot of time to solve, but I'm not sure I'd call them "good" puzzles. People might like their complexity, so into the pro column this goes.
CONS:
*  Poirot ambles. That makes sense. He's not the sort of character who hurries. However, this can be maddening when you watch him amble across the screen, amble back, and basically force the player to sit around and wait. Better to have them go off-screen and appear at their next destination. Do we really need to watch them amble about just to tell a taxi to take them somewhere?
* Repetitive puzzles. The puzzles for the most part were well-thought out, but there was one that you need to do about 4 times where you compare items and look for differences and simularities. The logical thing would be to place the two items side-by-side on the screen so you can swiftly click all the areas. But, no. You need to first select the item, then zoom in on it, then click on one difference, hear the voice-over describe *in the same exact words as he does each time* the oddity. Then zoom back out to where you see both items, select the second item, zoom in on it, find the same bit you want to compare.
I wasn't expecting this to be as fun as it was. its a bit of tower defense meets shooter.  If you like incremental progression and easy relaxation games, then I recommend it.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 by developer Larian Studios is a role-playing adventure game where you are a Sorcerer, those of which are to be imprisoned on an island named Fort Joy. You’ll explore the game with a character you create with the tremendous amount of customization provided, not only for your character’s appearance, but also for their overall skillset and abilities. The game will immerse you with its rich and extensive storyline as you discover characters and locations that provide more lore and backstory.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 gives you the option to choose the game’s difficulty based on what kind of player you are, whether that’s explorer, classic, tactician, or honor mode. Each mode provides either handicaps to make the game more difficult or boosts in stats to experience the game in easier conditions.
The customization allowed for the player is very immense. You can customize the character’s origin, appearance, attributes, skills, abilities, talents, and tags. The range of options given is so wide, allowing the player to create their character and experience the game however they want, which adds a lot in terms of the game’s replay value.
The storyline is one of Divinity: Original Sin 2’s strongest points. The amount of content packed into the game is so extensive because just about everything has a backstory to it. Every character you meet will have their own story and it helps to connect with them if they join your team. Not only that, but the side quests have a much more significant feeling to them because you’re more immersed, where in other games it just feels like a chore to complete them. Each character’s personality also changes how you choose to address them, based on what you know about them and how you think they’ll react. Also, the voice acting is top notch which adds to each character’s personality as well.
The overall control provided within the combat is also an excellent feature. An Action Point (AP) system is implemented into the game and it adds a lot more compared to standard turn-based games, where you only have one move and you’re done. It allows you to be able to plan strategies that are centered around your team composition rather than just straightforward fighting. Movement during combat is also a lot better than most turn-based games, because it’s a lot less limited than isometric or hexagon type fields, allowing a lot more control over your characters.
Most of the flaws in Divinity: Original Sin 2 revolve around their exploration controls. To move around you click anywhere on the terrain, and because of the multitude of items and interactions, you may accidentally click on objects you didn’t mean to, and even worse, accidentally steal them. This can have the negative consequence of affecting the attitude others have toward your character. Also, the mini map seems like a good option for pathfinding, but clicking on it won’t do anything. You must click in-game to be able to move, which sometimes means moving the camera around to be able to find your destination, which can be a bit tedious and annoying.
Additionally, there’s no quest screen provided within the game. There is, however, a journal which keeps track of various events and updates if any new findings are discovered. There are also flags that serve as hints on how to progress, but it is mainly up to the player to explore and continue the story.
Overall, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a great role-playing adventure game. The storyline is amazing with the amount of backstory added to all the characters that add to the overall game feel. The combat is done excellently and values strategy immensely. The control given over characters on your team is executed very well in both movement and dialogue options. Character customization for skills, abilities, and talents allows the player to replay the game and enjoy it all over again.
Rating: 9/10

The puzzles, which are the core of detective games, are too basic, the clues for them are within the puzzles themselves (or, even better, there's no need for any clues at all), and not to mention that it's really repetitive. Moving Poirot around is mostly annoying, and using a controller is out of question (even though it says it has "Full controller support"). Art is horrible, the character design is bad, voice acting isn't that special either. The game is too easy, there's absolutely no challenge,
There's really no good point by which I could recommend the game.
It's no wonder the price went down from $30 at launch to $15.

There are many things this game did wonderfully, such as the fantastic voice acting, the art style, and how the interviews adapt depending on what you chose to say. I really appreciate the achievements as it could have been realy easy for the developers to put in achievements based on ego points the game awards, but instead have them based on the story or investigating people, places, and objects.
While the puzzles do seem easy, I found that the game does seem to weigh it based on which part of the game it is located in, such as in chapter one you have puzzles you can easily figure out (as a way to introduce looking around for clues) and the last puzzles you do (in chapter three) involve investigating outside of the puzzle.
However, there are some things that more or less annoyed me personally or did not exactly make sense:
-The Eagle Eye achievement
I found this achievement very confusing as the clue given is "Poirot excels in observing human nature! You are receiving this trophy for having penetrated all the people's thoughts with a simple look". It just seems you only have to investigate people, but in reality you have to investigate everything. I'm not sure if it was only me that thought this, but nonetheless it is very confusing as most of the time, the game will not let you leave an area without investigating key items anyway (or clues that will be used later on).
-Investigating items in inventory
The game tells you early on that you should look at items just in case you can interact with them, which is indicated by a hand on the side. I think this would hav worked better if this was either taken out and let the player figure it out or the game tells you when it uses it. This aspect does not come into play till the last chapter. A way I can see this being introduced better (or lack of): As the few objects you can investigate are used in puzzles, and the player already knows you can use items in inventory for puzzles, the player can figure out that these objects are involved, and in turn, see that they can interact with them (as the hand has already been associated with interacting already).
-The signet ring
On the topic of items, one item got me: the signet ring. While first getting the ring, the game tells you the number on it, but not when you go to investigate it for a puzzle. WHen investigating it, it tells you that numbers are written on it and that's it. In both playthroughs I had, I couldn't find the numbers on the ring. I'm not sure if this was the case for everyone though.
-Option the investigate the same items
I found this weird, especially when Pariot says the same thing as he said when you investigated earlier. And with the Eagle Eye achievement, this can be annoying by thinking you would not have to investigate it again when in reality, you will have to get it again. I feel like these items should not have reset (in a sense where it recounts it) , but instead have an option to investigate it again.
-Investigating the letters
I found myself groaning at this part of the gameplay after the second time. Pariot says the same thing each time despite after seeing how the letters are from the same typewriter and already deducting facts about the murderer. I found this pointless considering it really was the same thing except with different letters.
-Just some small things
Obvious investigations: Some deductions are very obvious to the point where Pariot should not have needed the player to deduce it themselves. Along with this, at one point Pariot does ignore an obvious item is missing and act obvilious later on(which did not make sense considering Pariot is supposed to notice these things).
Most puzzles involve the owner hiding items, but these are usually not reset except for a few. You would think the owners would freak out and question why Pariot gone through them without permission (especially in a certain section) and could have made an interesting part in the game if the characters did notice (the game could just fast forward through solving the puzzle again to take away having the player redo it).
Either way, I do recommend this game. As I wish some of the repetitive aspects were not as annoying (and Pariot's talking did not halt the player) this is a great experience.

This game has been criticized for being a flash game, originaly avaiable for free. While it's true that there is a free of charge flash version, the one avaiable on steam has been completely rebuilt on the Unity engine. Now, moving on to the acttual review.
Knightmare Tower is an arcade style game. You play a night going up the tower to save 10 princesses and ultimately deffeat the boss at the top of the tower. Seem's pretty bland, right? It would be, if not for the way you ascend the tower is by hitting your enemies with your sword. You basicly fly around at the top of the screen, slowly falling dow until you hit an enemy or dashing straight at them so that you can get up again. It's the type of arcade game where you're gonna keep failing until you purchase the right upgrades.
Speaking of upgrades. While ascending the tower, you will keep finding stuff that'll aid you in you journey. Bombs that'll deliver a hit to each enemy curently on the screen, horn that will spawn odd, non hostile creatures you can wack down to go up higher and gain some gold and, well, bags of gold. The last one is obviously used to purchase the previously mentioned upgrades. Those are chategorized as: Equipment, Upgrades and potions. Upgrading your equipment will make your rocket go higher, make you able to withstand more damage or deliver it or just make your movement more fluid. Upgrades are less noticeble, but they still help you a great deal! Potions are another item you can find, and upgrading it in the store will keep adding effects to it like speed or damage boost.
The game features a variety of different foes. From the harmless demons you use as fodder for your sword, to weird, centipede-like things that you can only hit in the head. Some ill shoot at you, others will blow fire, some others will just use spikes to protect themselves. You've gotta be carefull and time your dashes just right to nog get hit. Also, it's important to note that if you dash and hit no enemys you will fall of the tower. A rocket will quickly get you back up, but you will lose a great deal of your speed, wich will leave you vulnerable to the biggest foe of them all. Lava. Lava will start following you if you don't ascend the tower fast enough. It doesn't mess around. If you fall into it, game over, no matter how much damage you can withsand.
So you've gone up the tower, saved all the princesses and and defeated the final boss. What now, you might ask. Well now, you unlock a survival mode. The tower is infinite in height and the monsters more fierce than ever! This is where the "endgame" begins. If you want to squeeze a bit more out of this game, you'll have a lot of fun trying to get into the leaderboards! Now, the monsters in this tower are always the same, and the only thing that changes is their health, spawn rates and the speed of the lava, as you go up the tower. Make no mistake, though, this get's real hard, real quick!
As for achievements, the game only has 6 of them, wich will propably turn off anyone who look's to bump up their achievement count, but if you're looking for a challenge, you're gonna find it here. Sure, finishing the game and getting everything there is to get in the shop aren't hard achievements, but getting up to 100.00 meters in survival mode? Good luck.
Honestly, I cannot reccomend this game enough. I am having tons of fun with it, and I bet most of you will too. Happy gaming!

7.1/10 – It’s Really Awesome at The Price of $5! No More.
This game does an amazing job hooking you from the store; it just has that majestic city look that makes you want to dive right in! At first glance the world is breathtaking, giving me exactly what I want. The campaign was minimalistic, no words are exchanged, but still an interesting story evolves. You piece together the history of the former city while working to save your brother who is dwindling. The campaign is progressed by finding the (10) supplies needed to save your brother’s life; of course these are always atop the highest points!
Unfortunately, my high hopes were soon deflated. I was able to traverse the entire map in about 10 minutes. So although it's an open world it proves to be quite small. The campaign was completed for me in about 3.5 hours and that's with exploring the whole map and just cruising around. The world is beautiful but quite repetitive, for how small the world is I would have liked to see some more dynamic buildings.
The game does have some good stuff going on especially with the boating and climbing which the game revolves around.  The climbing mechanics is exactly like Assassins Creed where you must dangle and navigate up a perilous building to reach the objective. The boating is pretty awesome; you command a small vessel that is greatly impacted by the hostility of the waves.
Overall, $20 is crazy expensive for this! Based on the content and experience I'd look to grab this for $5 or so!

Submerged
Intro:
This is a pretty special game and I would completely agree if one says that it is pretty difficult to rate it either with a thumbs up or down.
Yet there is a saying that perfectly fits to describe Submerged in a very few words – no risk, no fun!
Very recently completed this game and actually it is the first game that I considered for completion of achievements as there aren't many to get.
I've bought Submerged solely because I liked the artwork of the game and most of all I hoped for great music done by Jeff van Dyck (Total War Rome 1 OST and other).
But at the end of the day I was rather disappointed by the game.
Submerged is ok for people that seek a smaller distraction from the daily life but the repetitiveness throughout the game makes one (at least me) sick.
Not only the soundtrack - well-crafted as expected - brings too less variation into the game, also the graphics and the options what you are going to do in this game are pretty limited.
Actually this game is forcing you to do very few things - good enough to taught a child some focus and patience. But it is seriously not so enjoyable for an older grown up like me.
So what is this game about?
You are landing in an abandoned mostly sunken city with many buildings and references to our human culture so it is not completely fictional at all. There is just you and your seriously wounded brother. Your mission is to give up your own in sake of restoring your brother’s health.
Pro's and cons:
And thats pretty much it. This story may have provided some good stuff for a real drama, but this game is far from being one.
In the first place one might think Lara Croft could get jealous - as this girl is able to climb up and jump climb up and jump and climb down and actually able to climb either ladders, rain water downpipes or 2 variants of red brushwood. But actually there is a big difference to Lara in the end.
This climbing action quite all action you can have in the game to interact with the complete and big environment of Submerged. And this makes this game soooo boring. You cannot hurt yourself, you cannot make a wrong step and fall down from a high building as well. You are getting ill over time but don't have to supply yourself in any way. It is all about the brother.
Everything seems perfectly peaceful. The music does contribute to this very much but gets repetitive as well soon enough.
The most interesting thing this game has to offer are actually the very beautiful visuals because weather, day and night changes. The Buildings look impressive and seem to have many variants in the first place, but soon enough you notice they are just dead blocks of stone, assembled with some plants to let them look wild and exploreable. They are the only objects that a player can actually interact within the game (and a boat) - and so your options are extremely limited.
This game would have been much more enjoyable to me if there were more real secrets to find, if I could have explored the majestic monuments, doing a skydive from the highest point in the map - simply having more immersion in any way.
Jeff van Dyck has done a good job on the music but there is also too less music to give this game enough live and most of all tension.
And most of all there only one aspect of tension in the game and that's about some golems and the urgent question how this all would come to an end. If your brother will make it through or not.
This sadness cannot be compensated by some animals striving around in the water (only), while the buildings are completely abandoned.
Conclusion and rating:
Submerged is a pretty special game - it is on the edge of my liking and I'd rate it with a thumbs up for the original idea and music, but not for the gameplay that is too shallow.
I rate submerged with a fair 5/10. Where the most points are spent for the pure nostalgia of listening to some new tunes of Jeff van Dyck and the basically interesting idea of the game.

I don't have as many hours as some on this game, but I'd like to provide a review of my experience thus far.
As is explicitly stated by Funcom, this game is in Early Access. There are going to be bugs, exploits, and all manner of problems from the moment you first login to a server - whether it be an official server or not.
That being said, Funcom has managed to create the foundation of what I believe to be a great gaming experience. Survival sandbox games have been on the rise where we now have versions that put us in a zombie apocalypse (Day Z), a Dinosaur island (ARK), or various others I'm sure are out there.
Conan Exiles gives us a fresh new theme, Hyboria, a gritty and dangerous high fantasy setting that is as satisfying as it is unforgiving. Survival has always been an underlying theme within the Conan lore, and thriving thereafter. Conan Exiles gives you the ability to forge a story much like Conan the Barbarian's, in a manner however you see fit.
While not nearly as feature rich as more polished survival games out today, one must bear in mind that even those games had humble beginnings. With enough patience and community driven feedback and constructive criticism, Conan Exiles stands to be an incredible game.

Having played only a few levels, the first game that immediately popped into my mind was Fez. In The Shadows is thick with atmosphere and tells a story, that you unlock by finding more secrets. The puzzles in the game have an appropriate range of difficulty, although some levels are rather short. And at times I wasn't sure if I solved the riddle or just happened to find a workaround. But I suppose that's also part of the charm in puzzle games.
At two points in the game I stumbled upon a bug, but you can always restart the levels, and since the levels are short - the bugs are by no means game breaking.
The game itself took me about 5 hours to complete, having found all the stars in all but one level. That's a bit too short for my taste at the current price, but if you're a fan of puzzle games - it's no excuse to miss out on this experience.

The mechanics are also faulty; at a couple of places the game got held up trying to figure out how to use a simple object, while also having to listen to Poirot name the object each time you click on it ("A bottle of solvent" heard more than ten times in a couple of minutes is something no paying customer should have to endure). At another crucial junction my interface mysteriously vanished altogether, requiring a restart. And, of course, like all detective games, the replay value is just about zero, unless you enjoy collecting achievements you've missed or hearing every dialogue option.

Overall, In The Shadows is an enjoyable puzzle game with some platforming parts. Having followed the devlog and after backing ITS on Kickstarter, it was good to finally play it. It took about four hours to complete, plus I spent some extra time on trying to collect all the stars with many rooms yet to be completed. However, there are a few things that could've made it even better. Pros: -Beautiful visuals. My guess is that most people assume that the game uses pixel graphics but actually it's using That's why casting shadows with lights looks so good. Check out the Cubicle Constructor link in the description. -Puzzles. Having played lots of games over the decades, I still found many of the light/shadow mechanic puzzles interesting. Collect all the stars on every level for extra challenge. -Great soundtrack. Both for the game and also for stand-alone listening. -After completing a level, that level can be easily accessed. So if you've already found all the stars on some levels then you can skip those if you wish to find all the stars on every level. Cons: -Puzzle variety. Having followed the devlog, the developer's signature picture has 11 shadow creatures. I assumed that all of those would be in the game, but ... I think you know where I'm going with this. -Story. There are certain things (memory sequences) that give the game a certain framework, but there are two things that would've been better. 1) The beginning. Having seen/read/heard many stories and being a puzzle fan, I guessed early on what the events were about. That actually didn't bother me much. Rather, it was the beginning where I felt that the intro cutscene could've explained a bit more. Without that, you just have a sence that "something is wrong" and you're going on some kind of journey but not sure why. Adding a few more details regarding what the situation is about would've given more connection to the character and could've helped with motivation. 2) I thought that there would be more to -There is one achivement called I remember it all. Perhaps if you collect all the stars and watch the memory scenes, then some of issues mentioned above might be resolved. However, it would've been nice to have a full closure after a normal play through without an NG+ or "achievemnt-wall". -Sound effects. The "pixel game" sounds. I don't mind those for actual pixel games but the visuals of this game are much more detailed and I would prefer the sound effects to be "high resolution". Especially, since the music isn't "pixel style" either. Due to visuals and overall atmosphere, I'll play it again and try to find all the stars or sometimes a nice "mini-vacation". :)

I've given up on this game. I first played during a free play weekend and was thrilled! So much fun! Then I got it in a Humble Bundle and the fun was already fading away.
Even in the Entry League, players are very good and you have to know the levels very well to have a good chance. I made it twice into Beginner League, only to be demoted very soon after that. In almost every lobby there is someone who should be at least two leagues higher and wins the match with 3 wins and all others having zero. Balanced lobbies are very rare, I'd say one in twenty.
And now that I started to know my way around the official levels, everyone is selecting workshop levels and the "fun" is starting all over again. The levels are so much harder and pure frustration for the "Beginner" I seem to be in this game.
This is my biggest problem with this game: The difficulty curve is so steep, you can barely get better. If you get matched with better players, which is very likely when you start playing this game, you have almost no chance to get to know the level. And if you don't want to spend multiple hours per day to learn the levels in private lobbies, you're lost.
When I play 10 games per day, only one or two are fun. The rest is frustration either due to much better players in my lobby that don't leave me any chance or workshop levels that are so much more difficult than the already difficult official levels that I spend most of the time waiting for the next round.
It is a shame, because I really started to like this game. But it has changed so much that it became a source of frustration and anger, rather than enjoyment.
P.S.: The community is basically the same. You do meet very nice people, helping you, explaining moves, levels, etc. But more often then that, you meet elitists that don't give a damn about you being a beginner and struggeling with the game.

I LOVE THIS GAME! I felt like I was playing FEZ again for the first time!
The developer's use of light and shadows in the game is amazing compared to other pixel-art platformers and is very refreshing!
So far I have played the first 10 levels or so, and I have got to say that the game is very reminiscent of FEZ on how the character's movement is paced. You don't run around like in other platformers e.g. meatboy. It's more of a fast-walking or jogging speed.
That being said the controls are fine and play into the core game really well. The only issue I have is there are a few clipping issues on some of the platforms, but honestly nothing I found to be game breaking or repetetively annoying.
Some segments are more challenging than others early on however you can always skip them and head straight for the door if you're feeling overwhelmed. The caveat to this is in later stages the door becomes harder and harder to reach and more obstacles get in your way. This isn't always the case but for certain stages it is.
Story wise, there isn't necessarily a ton of content there, however, the atmosphere the minor amount of story builds up is perfect for what the game offers. It's not exactly what you would call "Story driven". Like I said, again, it is very atmospheric.
Music isn't half bad either and I didn't find the background music to be repetetive, just fitting for the mood.
The enemies in the game consist of various shadow creatures that turn into utility objects when exposed to light. It's definitely something different, because in some circumstances you will have to avoid touching them but also quickly turn on a light to turn them into a usable object and it can get somewhat tense. The caveat to this is for some reason dying does not reset the level, it just places you on a nearby platform you recently were standing on. It removes some of the threat from the enemies in my opinion.
Overall the game is great, I'd give it a solid 8/10 and would recommend it if you're interested in the platformer genre. It has controller support so there's that as well.

I do not like to give negative reviews but I would not recommend this game to any adventure games fan. Neither I would to any fan of the previous installments of the Agatha Chrstie gaming franchise. The game has some good ideas combined with many horrible and repetitive mechanics.
I have played for five hours and I think I will not finish the game. Puzzles are useless and seem extremely out of context. It seems like the game throws you puzzle after puzzle just fo fill content and hours of game. Then the observation mini puzzles are way too repetitive. A few of them -to identify characteristics of suspects/victims- could be fine, but you end up doing this process with almost everything.
There are almost no items to collect, up to now there were no combination of items, there were not any components of a classic adventure.
Some good ideas brought from modern adventures are pretty bad implemented. While conducting interrogations, it seems it does not matter the choice you make. The suspects / witnesses will always give you the answer you are looking for. If you make a mistake, Poirot will make the correct question later. Maybe this changes later in the game, but I feel it will not.
Then the "little grey cells" mini games are pretty straightforward. And then if you fail nothing happens. Poirot will not make any wrong assumption, it will just wait until you make the correct choice, like a triall and error minigame. It is absurd.
The story is not bad. After all it is picked from a novel by Agatha Christie. But is the only good thing.
To summarise, do not buy it. If you want a classic adventure game, this is not your choice. If you want a modern adventure game, then play something like Life is Strange. If you want to play an Agatha Christie game, pick Evil Under The Sun or some other installment (Murder on the Orient Express or even Ten Little Indians -And Then There Were None-). But not this one.

Play time can vary depending on how many achievements you want to pick up, but you can spend as little as five minutes on this game and still have a great time. Survival mode is challenging to even the most hardened player and the Escape style mode is a great way to earn yourself some extra gold while actually testing your reflexes and mental sharpness.
I wholly recommend this game to everyone and anyone, but especially those that enjoy the format of summoning or tower defence games. You may come away with finger cramp, but you won't regret it.

There are a few annoyances in Cradle that you should be aware of: The FOV is quite low and not configurable, mouse input has a weird smoothing applied to it and the first hour of the game is spent in a cramped indoor environment. If you get motion sickness easily from games, the first hour of gameplay will be pretty bad for you. Not as bad as Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but still noticeably bad. After you leave the indoor environment, it becomes a lot easier to deal with.
This game is about 4 hours long, but it has a satisfying ending and doesn't drag out any longer than it should. I'd say it's worth every penny.

NOTE: Fritz is not for casual chess players.  You should at least be a Class B or Class A player. If you are below Class B, you will not be able to use this program effectively.   I am writing this review from the perspective of a Class A player.
Fritz is not your normal chess game against the AI (if you want to play casual chess against computers, there are many free programs out there for that purpose). You are paying for the strength of the engine and it's ability to analyze lines quickly and powerfully.
For those looking to play against the AI, the Fritz Engine, which is what this AI uses, is much stronger than the engines the free programs use.
For those looking to analyze their games or lines, the Fritz Engine is strong enough to compete with Stockfish. Fritz also offers multi-core threading, allowing you to analyze lines deeply and quickly.
For those looking to expand their opening reportire, Fritz's UI can be unintuitive, but the strength of the engine allows detailed analysis of each viable move, allowing you to study the openings you want to use.
For those looking to work on their middlegame tactics, unfortunately Fritz's 'training' program simply links you to a 3rd party website. Do not buy this game for this purpose.
For those looking to analyze endgame positions, Fritz Engine is unbelievably strong at analyzing all kinds of positions.
If you use Stockfish, you can add the Stockfish engine to Fritz.

In spite of the blurb, Fritz 15 isn’t best at chess playing.  Sure, one can goof around with playing chess against the engine, and the supplied one is unquestionably super-GM strength.  On this point, the included “rated game mode” can adjust the engine to a level us mortals can appreciate.  It will even attempt to assess a game with an Elo number (as opposed to the typical loss in centi-pawns).  Mileage will vary with this.  But with that said, chess playing is not Fritz 15’s purpose.
Think of Fritz 15 as an introduction to the wonders of computer chess categorization and organisation.  Games can be stored and their quality assessed by a chess engine.  The supplied engine/s are totally fine, but there are somewhat stronger ones available at a price between free and $USD50 or so.  Games also can be analysed on screen, with variations easily recorded, and the potential is there to dive into the parent ChessBase software (at further expense) to compare your games with a master database.  Once committed there is no turning back.
In my opinion, chess game collections and the included Playchess subscription are the meat here.  This version of Fritz added around 500K chess games (80K at GM level) to my chess games database.  A Playchess sub can increase further access to chess games, and what’s more I have lost myself in the chess videos therein that probably haven’t done much for my game (ditto with the abovementioned database features) but are a heck of a lot of fun in rendering a complicated game easier.  I am surprised this access doesn’t seem to be the key hook in buying the latest Fritz license.
To be sure there are expense/s here: this Fritz license and probably ChessBase and an ongoing Playchess subscription are typical.  But once those up-front costs are met, there is in here an all-consuming hobby like little else.
I have been asked as a frequent Fritz user whether the latest version is worth a price premium.  My answer is probably not.  Fritz 15 still has a couple of quirks around organizing databases, but certainly looks cleaner.  The “rated game mode” is a great way to guarantee a slow chess game, but the engine isn’t all that human-like and the calculated Elo grade must be taken with a grain of salt.  However, the six months Playchess subscription included is worth something (it retails for around €25-€30) and indeed would be enough to draw out an upgrade.

I'm happy I could buy this on sale. Mind that, its not a casual chess program just to have fun. It's an educational program to help improve your playing strenght if you take chess seriously. It's not about having the best engine for your money, you have many other options, free ones and paid ones. It's not about to have nice 3d chess-sets in the game.  It's about the options in the GUI for training, analyzing, marking tactical opportunities and errors in your game, and next time you check your match the program gives you the puzzle ("you missed a good move, try to play the best move") etc, creating, managing your own databases, practicing your own opening lines that you analyzed, etc. You also get a 2million games database, which is okay, ofc you can get more from other sources aswell, and you can use them altogether. "Friend mode" option is quite good. Ofcouse at first, Fritz need to evaluate your playing strengh, it might be too easy, or hard at the beggining, but the more games you play against it (it is modifying your rating), the more balanced will it become. I realy like the little green light under the board in friend mode. When the computer makes tactical mistakes (coz it has to play as suck as you do :D ) the little green light start flashing, warning you, that you have a good move. If you don't play the good move, the game still continoues, but it will give it as a tactical puzzle after the game, and if you cant solve it, ofcourse it will tell you the solution. Need a little time to get used to the menus, the options, etc, I used SCID for years, and it wasnt any easier at the first time. I liked SCID, but comparing to this, it was way slower, buggy at times, its still a
nice alternative if you don't want to pay money, because its still free, but I realy think fritz 15 is a step up. Program runs without any problem with my win7 64 bit system. You don't need steam after you installed the game, it can run without it. That's why it says i have only 41 mins playtime, but I spent endless hours of last night to experience the good features Fritz provides. Make sure you install the game properly, activate your steam serial key when the program asks for it, + once more in the playchess.account, and you get what they promised in the descriptions. You have to invest time and energy to get the maximum out of this program, for example I'm creating my own database, and my own endgame training from a good old book, so later I can get to practice the positions way faster, than searching them from the dusty pages. :D. The help system in the program not the best, I have to admit that, but once you find out what is what, I belive it can make your chess improve significantly.

Submerged
Intro:
This is a pretty special game and I would completely agree if one says that it is pretty difficult to rate it either with a thumbs up or down.
Yet there is a saying that perfectly fits to describe Submerged in a very few words – no risk, no fun!
Very recently completed this game and actually it is the first game that I considered for completion of achievements as there aren't many to get.
I've bought Submerged solely because I liked the artwork of the game and most of all I hoped for great music done by Jeff van Dyck (Total War Rome 1 OST and other).
But at the end of the day I was rather disappointed by the game.
Submerged is ok for people that seek a smaller distraction from the daily life but the repetitiveness throughout the game makes one (at least me) sick.
Not only the soundtrack - well-crafted as expected - brings too less variation into the game, also the graphics and the options what you are going to do in this game are pretty limited.
Actually this game is forcing you to do very few things - good enough to taught a child some focus and patience. But it is seriously not so enjoyable for an older grown up like me.
So what is this game about?
You are landing in an abandoned mostly sunken city with many buildings and references to our human culture so it is not completely fictional at all. There is just you and your seriously wounded brother. Your mission is to give up your own in sake of restoring your brother’s health.
Pro's and cons:
And thats pretty much it. This story may have provided some good stuff for a real drama, but this game is far from being one.
In the first place one might think Lara Croft could get jealous - as this girl is able to climb up and jump climb up and jump and climb down and actually able to climb either ladders, rain water downpipes or 2 variants of red brushwood. But actually there is a big difference to Lara in the end.
This climbing action quite all action you can have in the game to interact with the complete and big environment of Submerged. And this makes this game soooo boring. You cannot hurt yourself, you cannot make a wrong step and fall down from a high building as well. You are getting ill over time but don't have to supply yourself in any way. It is all about the brother.
Everything seems perfectly peaceful. The music does contribute to this very much but gets repetitive as well soon enough.
The most interesting thing this game has to offer are actually the very beautiful visuals because weather, day and night changes. The Buildings look impressive and seem to have many variants in the first place, but soon enough you notice they are just dead blocks of stone, assembled with some plants to let them look wild and exploreable. They are the only objects that a player can actually interact within the game (and a boat) - and so your options are extremely limited.
This game would have been much more enjoyable to me if there were more real secrets to find, if I could have explored the majestic monuments, doing a skydive from the highest point in the map - simply having more immersion in any way.
Jeff van Dyck has done a good job on the music but there is also too less music to give this game enough live and most of all tension.
And most of all there only one aspect of tension in the game and that's about some golems and the urgent question how this all would come to an end. If your brother will make it through or not.
This sadness cannot be compensated by some animals striving around in the water (only), while the buildings are completely abandoned.
Conclusion and rating:
Submerged is a pretty special game - it is on the edge of my liking and I'd rate it with a thumbs up for the original idea and music, but not for the gameplay that is too shallow.
I rate submerged with a fair 5/10. Where the most points are spent for the pure nostalgia of listening to some new tunes of Jeff van Dyck and the basically interesting idea of the game.

I am completely charmed by "Submerged"! It is a simple yet elegant exploration game with beautiful graphics and a soothing soundtrack.  The objective strategy is simple: use a motor-driven boat to find secrets in the environment, which is a partially submerged city, abandoned after some apocalyptic event.  Despite the title, all the exploration occurs above the water line.  It requires navigating the boat to open up the map and clambering up set paths across ledges and vines on the protruding buildings.  You cannot fall.  There is no diving to see what is below.
The specific goals are to find the following items:
1. Essential supplies to save the life of the protagonist's little brother; finding all of these completes the story.
2. Entries for the journal that tell the back story in pictorial form of the protagonist and the city
3. Discover specific species of fauna of the city
4. Pick up parts for the  motorboat.  (These did not seem to help or hinder the capability to explore, including distance or speed.)
The story of the girl and her brother is poignant in a larger tragedy, although the mood of the world is neutral to upbeat due to the focused objectives, soothing sound track and gorgeous setting. I loved this setting and graphics style: buildings, gigantic statues, cranes, and bridges, reclaimed by flowers, palm tees, and vines and surrounded by an ocean alive with whales, manta rays, diving birds, and dolphins that trail you as you explore.  The whale animations are wonderful.  You can view them at water level or from up in the buildings. The color palette is rich and changes as night and day cycle.  Reflections on the water dazzle the eye with colors like a find pastel painting.
The climbing is vaguely reminiscent of Tombraider without the jumping, leaping, and gymnastics.  No traps or dangers of any kind, however.
A handy shortcut that is built in: after you complete a particularly complex climb up and around a building to claim the main objective atop or inside, you are immediately transported back to the main camp, so you don't have to retrace your steps down the building to your boat.
Also, there is a spyglass tool that will affix secret locations to your map, making navigating to them easier. You don't have to use it, however.
If you finish the main game objective, the "Resume" link of the menu changes to "Explore," and you can continue to retrieve the remaining secrets.  Incidentally, the story line is linear; exploration is not.
The graphics, setting, and story are so pleasing that they easily outweigh any negatives of the game.  Still, here are mine:
Cons:
* Only specific buildings can be climbed
* The world is small.  I would love a larger world based on this story and environment.
* If you have not claimed all the secrets of a building, before you claim the primary objective there, you must come back because of the automatic return.  It's a small world, though, so going back is not a terrible hardship.
* There are only 8 species to find!  They are so well done; there should be more.
This game was definitely worthwhile for me, as I love to wile away time in beautiful environments. It was just the right length for a pleasant interlude.

DEVELOPERS! I say now, despite my posting, that I do not recommend this game only because of it's currently unfinished state and I wish to reach the Developers minds, for I will most likely still play this game despite all that I say below.
I hope that you all will read through this for I want the time I have spent in this game to have value and not be in vain. Honestly, after around 100 hours of singleplayer and more of the multiplayer combined, I have come to the conclusion that this game is the kind you have to dedicate a portion of your life to and willingly be open minded to the idea that it may or may not of been worth your time in the end of it all. It takes A RIDICULOUS amount of time to gain levels via building and killing, and establish a camp or in long term a castle, crafting certain items takes a considerable amount of time and even dramatically longer if trying to make something that requires that item such as iron and then for tools or weapons. Not to mention that you have a limited amount of investable points to learn recipes for crafting items and objects, ergo, you cannot unlock everything. Harvesting does not yield very much in materials with the exception of wood due to a clause that not much wood is required for crafting except for workbenches and alike, and for using it a fuel for melting iron and alike. The creatures are relentless and overkill at low level. Once people have built to near a camp of npcs the npcs no longer spawn. People build intentionally to block off or shut down areas of the game that are either important or hot spots, I have yet to see a priest in a multiplayer server, as well as dancers (characters that assist in the progression of the game). The Beginner area is filled with building making it difficult to get started. Maintenance of your tools and weapons is constant, the durability is not very good even for higher grade tools and weapons. Enemies can be easily vanquished if positioned on high ground properly or within a structure as enemies can clip through your walls. As far as the storyline it lacks direction, and by that I mean where to go to find the next story piece, not to mention living through the challenges. Though the game is vast the terrain is repetitive and predictable except for only a few places that present a difference in theme and style. I believe the images do not capture the trueness of the game. I have not explored and seen all of it, no have I played the PVP version of the game but from all that I hear in game PVE, PVP is terrible, can you imagine between admins cheating and people constantly battling and destroying your structures, considering if you're offline? It would be a constant 24/7 involvement that most of the community can't abide by and enjoy the game, what little there is to enjoy, which is only if you play by the default and level up or craft a new level set of tools or weapons but because of the server settings that are available, all you have to do is create your own server and change the multipliers, but then, to me, that feels like cheating. So in short, great graphics, great Theme work, good map design, unique craftables, extensive building capabilities, story needs improvement, direction needs improvement, leveling needs improvement, and the default harvesting, damage tables, enemies needs improvement.
As the core default goes, it is truly challenging and I do not recommend it for beginners, or even people who have patience, for the reward feels little and the time requiring it is more than long, at bare minimum in default settings, to have the game be faster paced, you would at least need 4 people to compartmentalize the level up and recipe system, BUT, if you're looking for fun and don't care about the "cheating" that I previously stated then there are more than enough servers with modified multipliers that make the game more fun.
