I would love to say that this game is finally a long-awaited continuation to the Dungeon Keeper series which fullfills the fan's nees... I woul dreally do.
BUT I CAN'T
This game is just a simple copy of the core elements without any creativity and improvements. It seems to me that the developers simply copied the DK2, but didn't know what to do with all of it and just thew it all together repalcing the models and puring a huge amount of random stuff.
You open the game and it looks and plays just like DK2, so for a couple of minutes you are happy. Than comes the disappointment.
1.Progression. It's a mess. DK had a wellthought-through progression that was pretty srtaight-forward but left some space for creativity and random fun stuff. Each room gave you some benifits like new spells from library or new traps from the foundry. Here all of it is put in one pile that you can gradually open up through "sin points" that come from library. And everything is there: rooms, traps, doors, spells. (And the spells are now divided in three groups: spells, potions and rituals. And each needs a separate room not to research but to be able to use them. Whats the point of that? No point it was just to "add more content").
I can see the idea to give player some choice about his game style. Being the classic dungeon keeper, a necromancer or unleash a horde of mindless beasts. But all of it is jumpled in one pile! So in the end it doesnt matter you will get all of it and the outsome is the same. Again, what's the point? DK had all of those themes nicely blended together in one system and it played much better.
2. The Atmosphere. Again at first it seems like it's there. The cool narrator helps a lot. But 15 min into the game you can see it's nowhere near where it should be. The humour is only present in the beginning and later you will see nothing funny or interesting. In DK creatures had some kind of individuality to them, They would often go out of the room assosiated with them and do some random stuff. Some would exlpore the caves, others woul djust stick to training all the time. Mistresses on the other side would often abandon training to go and torture themselves or each other. Warlocks would occasionally test their spells on imps that disturb them in their library. In original dungeon keeper they had a great system where some types of creatures would hate each other and start fights. Not to mention the Grim Reaper who hated everybody. It all gave a sense of a living society.
Here they are just doing the same things in their rooms. Like automatons they will simply perform the same tasks assigned to them. That leaves you with basically nothing to do in between fighting and building.
AND THE MAIN FLAW in my opiniion. A crap-pickle on a turd-sandwich as AVGN would say:
3. The CREATURES. DK series had 3 main creatures associated with the series and acting as their mascots: Bile Demon, Horned Reaper and Mistress.
It is perfectly understandable that due to copyright issues they couldn't use these beloved-by-many minions of evil. But they coul've come up with some creative replacements. How hard can it be? You have a typical toilet-humor  character, a badass demon and a kinky sexualized female. Apparenly it is very hard  becaus they failed all three.
The Bile demon replacement was created by a simple scheme "they had the one that farted, lets make the one that barfs". How bloody creative. And the design of the creature is as plain as it can be: simply a green bean with limbs and a and ugly hammer-hat. It looks like nothing. Bile demon was disgusting but it also was powerfull and looked like and actual demon. It even had strong resemblance to the Horned Reaper. the Chunders are just pathetic and not funny. They look like the were  quickly put together in 3dsmax in 5 min befoe release.
The Horned Reaper is the easiest. Just replace him with some badass demon  or better yet some Grim Reaper character and it's ok. But there is none in the game. There are a couple of boring special summoned cratures that again are very unimaginative. And the awesome summoning thing where you had to summo some speciic pwerfull creatures to the dark gods in order to get the Reaper was moved to a vampire.
And here is the main sin of the developers - the Mistress. She was the most adored creature of all (for obvious reasons). Not only because she was a bimbo, but because Bullfrog managed to give them a strong personality.  Again How hard could it be to create something similar just with different model.
THEY FAILED.
They took the obvious route of replacing the creature with a Succubus (pretty fine, the lore fits perfectly), but they  gave them nothing of the Mistress'  vibe. No love for the torture chamber when it's empty, no kinky battle sounds, no phrases or jokes.
AND THE MODEL IS HIDEOUS!!!
It has no sex appeal of the original at all. Instead it looks like it's covered in some kind of bone plating, which ruins the shape completely.
BUT IT GETS WORSE!
The colors of the model are all very similar tones of biege, so it all blends together and the creature looks like some fungus-covered human. Couldn't they at least make the colors somwhat contrast? Like the plating could be dark-coloured with some kind of fiery red  highlight or something like that. Anything but this vomit-color.
And they gave the rest of the creatures some "creative names". The obvious goblin whish is almost identical to the DK ones is called Gnarling. The warlock is called the Cultist. Whats up with that? Did they really thing it would make them look original? No it makes them look like wannabe smartasses. We can see it's a goblin, call it a goblin for Evil's sake!
Ordinary it is wrong to judge the game by the scale if similarity to the other game. But in this case that was the sole purpose of this porduct. To be a replacement of the outdated DK2 and improve it's ideas and mechanics while prserving them. And it failed.
I'm sad.

The trailers made this game look like a Poirot-themed redux of the incredible Crimes and Punishments game that Frogware put out, but in truth it is somewhat less than that. There is no allowance in the plot for your wrong answers; there are no what-if scenarios where you (and thus, Poirot) ♥♥♥♥ up the investigation and send the wrong man to jail; and there's not a lot of freedom in how you approach things. Despite how it looks, ABC Murders is pretty oldschool-adventure in a lot of ways. Or, to be more accurate, it's pretty oldschool-Frogwares -- Poirot's investigation here has some things in common with how Sherlock investigated Jack the Ripper or looked into whatever the ♥♥♥♥ Testament was about. You get to build a timeline, you get to stick clues together to supplement Poirot's ideas about the case, and you get to solve inane inventory puzzles and open puzzle boxes because apparently half of London shops at the Mondo Puzzlebox Outlet and they put damn near everything in them. There is a goddamn puzzlebox built inside a cash register, which is the kind of asinine nonsense that only could happen inside of an adventure game. It doesn't even contain anything that would justify such a confusing security scheme, because surely if someone has broken into your shop and robbed you they can break into the back room as well and also our puzzle-minded shopkeeper decided to write the code on the register anyway, it's all nonsense, who cares, Poirot is a cool guy and he solve a crime, 9 moustaches/10

All jokes aside, chivalry is a great game. I remember my first time playing, hardly getting 4 kills but being happy at the end of the match just because of the pure enjoyment and rush of battle.
This game really needs some more population, at least for the central United States area. Most servers that are populated now days are east coast servers that I'll do good to get ping around 80 or so, instead of the 30 and below mark. Ping is crucial to enjoying this game. Lag kills the fun. Everyone knows that.
I have a few words of wisdom to all players considering buying the game or players who are just new to the game. Chivalry is a fairly straight forward game, though there is a very steep learning curve if you so choose to progress in the game. a good 85 - 90% of the people you run into will be seasoned and have many tricks up their sleeve, thus making it extremely difficult for the newer guys to have fun and stick with the game. I've seen it many times. Example, a level 17 going against a horde of level 35's who have been trained by vets or are on alternate accounts. Usually the 17 will just quit out of frustration and never play again because they literally stand no chance. That was their experience of the game. Some will argue that "That's what the level 0 - 15 servers are for..." But, what good does that do if you have the people making alternate accounts to exploit the low level servers? On top of that, from level 0 - 15, in an environment made strictly of those levels, you will NOT learn how to efficiently protect yourself from the higher level and more experienced players. as soon as you hit 16, you're thrown out with the sharks. The point of all this being to practice, ask questions to the higher level players, look up videos, and observe.
My overall review would be to recommend you purchase the game. But do it knowing what you're getting yourself into. Hope the review helps you gain an understanding of what this game consists of nowdays. Good luck my friends.

is a single player exploration/adventure game set in a partially submerged city, the remnants of an undisclosed apocalyptic event. You play as a nameless older sister trying to save the life of your younger brother who has suffered a grievous wound that has caused him to slip into a coma. What happens in this submerged city will decide the fate of both you and your brother.
The story in Submerged is quite interesting in its presentation. Rather than relying on dialogue, notes, or anything coming close to resembling that, it relies solely on actual exploration which triggers events and unlocks hieroglyphic frames that in turn unveil a riveting and yet somewhat indistinct tale.
For this reason, while the main story revolving around your attempt to heal and bring your brother out of his coma are clear, the events preceding this and the way in which the world found itself submerged, post-apocalyptic state are completely a matter of personal interpretation.
I found the subjective interpretation of the story in Submerged to be particularly enjoyable. Based on everything I witnessed and interacted within the game, I have drawn this tale for myself (feel free to reach your own conclusions though):
The world isnt completely covered in water. This is suggested through the hieroglyphs you unlock via completing story goals. The sister and brother fled their home on the boat which you, the sister, use throughout the game due to the events which caused the brother’s severe injuries. The apocalypse seems to have included radiation somehow, as the water and all the creatures have a peculiar coloration and glow to them. The apocalypse also seems to have happened far back in the past as the buildings that remain have been overtaken by plant life and people seem to have regressed to tribalism.
Anyway, those are just some of my thoughts on the story. I found myself thoroughly engaged throughout my playthrough, coming up with theories regarding the world presented while taking in the story arc focus of the siblings themselves. The story in Submerged receives an 8.5 out of 10.
The gameplay in Submerged was quite intuitive. I never found myself having any issues with the controls and experienced no bugs whatsoever.
There are a couple actual gameplay aspects to this game. Your main mode of transportation will be your boat. Simple steering via L/R sticks, acceleration/brakes with your R1/L1, and speed boost with L2. You will find the wreckage of other boats in the city, and these allow you to upgrade your speed boost, which gives it a longer duration. The only real practical use for this is simply to get around the city faster, as there are no enemies to worry about and no hazards to face.
Climbing is the other important aspect to Submerged. You will be seeking out old supply drops, presumably dating back to before or just after whatever apocalyptic events that changed the world actually occurred. The supply drops are found on the top of some of the taller buildings you must climb. The routes upward are rarely straightforward, and each of these buildings also features “secrets”, which take the form of books that reveal a little bit more about the world. The supply drops themselves essentially represent the chapters in Submerged, with each one found triggering the next part of the story as you work towards healing your brother and bringing him out of his coma.
You have a telescope which you can use to get a better view of things. However, a more practical use of the telescope is its help in identifying the location of overturned boats, collectibles and supply drops. There is also a map which I found to be quite useful in finding areas I had missed and remembering where supply drops I had spied previously were actually located relative to my position on the map.
Other things of note in Submerged are the aquatic wildlife which you will observe and in their totality unlock an achievement in the game. There are also a number of landmarks to be found. Each one is named and one of them is required to unlock two more achievements.
The gameplay was fairly well seamless. It deserves a 9 out of 10
Submerged is one of the more beautiful games you will ever encounter. Not only is the desolation, mystery, vibrancy and vigor of this mostly drowned city brought to life in full effect, but the detail involved in every frame was both stunning and awe-inspiring. There actually is a postcard mode in game to help show off the graphics but really, they dont need any help. Submerged is a gorgeous game through and through.
This is an easy 10 out of 10. Few games are as beautiful to behold. You will spend a lot of your play time simply taking in the amazing vistas.
The audio in Submerged was somewhat dynamic, shifting based on mood, time of day, progression through the story and so on. However, in my opinion it was also the weakest part of this game. Though well done, you will have heard every track pretty quickly during your playthrough and then for the rest of the game after that. The saving grace for this is that the music never gets annoying and really just serves as a backdrop to the story and scenery in Submerged anyway. Unobtrusive despite its repetitiveness.
7.5 hits the mark for this category.
Ultimately, Submerged is a game that truly shines in both conveying a sense of desolation and mystery while still offering serenity and a compelling, if subjective story. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game and hope to see more adventure/walking simulator style games offer similarly deep experiences in the future.
One further note for achievement hunters. There is a free roam option after you finish the story so as to find any missing collectibles and ship parts.

So, you know I joined TO in 2013, right? So obviously I am an old TO player. I first accessed this game in like the 27th of April 2016 as far as I can remember. From the start, Tanki X's graphics had amazed me. The Tanki X developers have made so many significant changes to this game. So, first off, let's start with the
of the game:
+Obviously the game has decent graphics.
+Great optimization. As a non-browser online tank game, this never crashes.
+Unique turrets: Freeze, Isida, Ricochet, every turret is unique in their own ways.
+TX skins look nice, compared to TO's skins, particularly XTs.
Now, here are the
:
- The game's balance has always been very unsatisfactory since the beginning. Ricochet is dead as ♥♥♥♥. I'm okey with its range, but its rate of fire is poor and its projectile speed is ridiculously slow. This makes Ricochet the most useless and least common turret in the game; that's pathetic. Twins may have better rate of fire, but that doesn't mean I'm not disappointed with its balance; I am. I can almost never use this turret in Tanki X. Even worse, Arms Race killed the game's balance in terms of gameplay.  I've experienced early battle endings, because it's like the enemy team doesn't exist. Either that or you just feel like you're the only one fighting against them.
- The aspects of some old modules have changed in a bad way, and some new modules are unnecessary. For example, The mine and the spider mine used to disappear once the owner gets desroyed; it was perfectly fine that way. Now, they still exist regardless of the owner being destroyed. And not to mention that you can drop a maximum of two mines in the battle. I discover that the battles are polluted with mines and spider mines, which comes to the point where camping is becoming a big problem in Tanki X. You just have to drug your♥♥♥♥♥off to get to the flag. Also speed boost and increased damage are no use unless you pick 'em up in battles. Also, let's talk about one of the unnecessary new modules,
Rage. Rage is an example of a mistake made with Arms Race in terms of balance. It is the type of module that would encourage
. All you have to do is finish off enemies to reduce the cooldowns of your modules. The more you kill, the sooner your modules recover. In other words, you would definitely recommend your friends use a long-range weapon, like Railgun and Thunder, if they wanna use this module.
- The Tier-3 modules are
pay2win. In order to obtain those modules as a Bronze League member or under, you
purchase x-crystals with real money, purchase blueprints with x-crystals, like purchase as much blueprints as you can to activate the Tier-3 modules.
. Oh, and you can even buy blueprints to upgrade modules to make your tank stronger. So basically you are ♥♥♥♥ed if you don't have real money or don't wanna buy♥♥♥♥♥♥ because you can face opponents who are 10x stronger than you and they have better god damn modules.

- The red cross-hair makes long-range weapons easier to use than they should. Say you're using Smoky or Thunder; you can fire instantly and never miss once you see the cross-hair, especially if you're far from the enemy tank. Thus, the aiming requires no skill.

Submerged is a fairly short game that centers on exploring a flooded world.  The story is told without speech, using pictures and some text.  The narrative is effective and interesting.  The exploration is done in two different parts, in a boat and climbing buildings.  The climbing is straight forward and easy to control.  The main character has the grip strength of Ezio Auditore da Firenze.  the larger buildings are small puzzles of a sort.
The visuals are very nice.  The world itself is a character.  Much effort clearly went into the design.  The music is sweet, but melancholy.  It fits the game perfectly.
As I said above, it is short.  I finished it completely in about 5 hours.  That said, the length feels right for this game.  Any longer and it may have felt overwrought.
If you like relaxing games that tell an interesting story (in a novel way), then give this a try.

It looks like a nice and atmospheric adventure game but there honestly isn't anything else to this game than holding down W, controlling your camera with your mouse and occasionally using a telescope to search for the next dull building to climb. There is no combat (which in my opinion isn't necessarily a bad thing), and there isn't anything else to this game either. You can't fail any of the climbs, you don't have to do any jumps, you don't even have to balance when you walk on narrow beams, there are no time limits (even though your brother is dying), there is no dialogue, the "atmospheric soundtrack" is a couple of dull and repetitive piano tracks and the so-called background story is just scribbled pictures which I felt like were the result of lack of imagination / interest / skill from the developer rather than a fresh idea. The world is ridiculously small and collecting the journal "entries" (again, scribbled pictures) feels like a waste of time considering how little they have to say.
Except for the lack of dialogue, it feels like a visual novel that is completed by holding down one button. I've played 90 minutes and I've completed most of the main "story", but I am not going to finish it since I'm refunding after writing this review.
Overall it's just your average indie game; an overpriced, expected disappointment that somehow manages to get a ton positive reviews in steam.

As much as I love the idea of a Dungeon Keeper revival/tribute, this particular attempt doesn't do much more than appeal to nostalgia. As a game, it fails on too many fronts to recommend.
Pros:
- the art style is very well done, clearly inspired by the original DK games, but with enough unique flourishes of its own
- the narrator is back
Cons:
- lots of redundancy in spells, potions (spells that require gold investment), rituals (spells that need a long time to prepare), defenses, constructs, and even monsters
- too much happening at once to really have a sense of control
- barely any need to pay attention to your economy (gold is so abundant you never need to use the spells/potions/rituals that create money)
- barely any need to cleverly construct a dungeon: layout doesn't really matter, only a handful of rooms are actually needed most of the time; I never had to build a dungeon I was proud of, just plonk down a few basic rooms before bum rushing the AI
- combat tactics boil down to dropping rally flags and spamming a bit of healing,
- AI mostly incompetent
- poor performance across the board, lots of fps drops, occasional crashes
- the narrator won't shut up
In short: WftO is a superficial tribute to the original DK games, that confuses quantity with quality and frustrates rather than challenges. The developer should have stuck to way fewer additional features and focused on game balance and optimization instead.

I played Bardbarian for about 2 hours, and I find it to be an entertaining, tower defense type of casual game.  I've never played it on android phone before, so this review is strictly from the perspective of a PC game.   I tried playing both via keyboard and a xbox 360 controller, and I recommend playing this with the controller.
At a glance, the main game is deceptively simple.  Your tower is on the left side of the map, and creatures approach from the right side of the map.  The hordes of monsters will continuously come at you (first) and the tower (second).  Your Brad the Bardbarian can't do any attacks on his own.  He needs to drum up some tunes on his axe-lute to call up the cavalry--troops who follow your character and fire at the mobs.  You will die sooner or later, but your goal is to last long enough to accumulate gold to buy upgrades for your troops, your hero character, and your town.  These upgrades DO carry over.  The challenge continually increases as monsters appear in greater numbers, and more powerful to boot.  And it becomes apparent that you need upgrades in order to advance further in the story mode.
The game also comes with a survival mode, and a distance mode.  The survival mode consists of a timer to see how long you last while trying to get troops and dodging enemy fire.  Distance mode involves your character moving from left to right while dodging environmental obstacles and enemy fire.  Both allow you to accumlate gold and possibly unlock new troop units.
I purchased this game for $5.24 on sale at Steam, and to me it's money well spent.

Gear Up is a fun little tank combat simulator that plays more like a shooter on wheels. You get to build your engine of chaos and destruction from the ground up with a variety of chassis, turrets, weapons, and even a selection of treads, wheels, hoverfans, or even legs. And you can color each part individually.
And despite there being an unlock system with a slight power curve, the whole thing feels nicely balanced, even just jumping in the first time in the free version. Victory is more about picking tactics for your design than raw power. (though building a tank with two turrets and a stack of missle pods -is- admittedly quite effective)
All in all an excellent little diversion, expecially at the price of FREE.
Or even, you know, ten bucks. There's a whole pile of extra parts behind that little premium tag.
Update: This is not to say there are not issues to be ironed out. Like the fact that as of this writing, the game will kick you out of matches if it doesn't think your framerate is high enough, or issues getting it to start at all. Still a fun little diversion when it works, though.

Im not going to give you a list of Pros and Cons for this game, only Major Cons. The reason is because i think this is a really good game "For its time" which means everything i dont mention in my Cons list is working to a satisfactory level even to this day, keeping in mind this game came out in 2005, I want to make that clear.
Melee combat: is a chore to learn and seems undoubtedly inferior to the two ranged characters that completely cheese the game if you compare the two, i dont see how you would choose melee over ranged at any point in the game other that fighting shield mini bosses early game.
Camera: is pretty anoying at times especially when exploring areas where there is more than one floor and you need to use ladders or steep stairways. After fights the camera will spin around when switching from combat to free roam view which can lead you to walking out the wrong area, causing you to redo the area fight again, which brings me to my next point.
Combat Zones: The games mainly linear free roam is broken up into what i call Combat Zones, as soon as you walk into these zones (Usually indicated by interactable gates or doors) the gate or door will close and you will have to defeat all spawed enemies to proceed or leave the area, 90% of the time you HAVE to fight a group of enemies that are designated to that part of the map with a small chance that they arent the exact same enemies you just fought in the last combat zone, this just makes the game become boring faster and makes traveling a chore at times.
Loading: This sounds like a not so important Con but its really bad in this game, which is what you'd expect from a 2005 RPG game as big as this. There are so many doors in this game especially in the main city and minor cities you visit.
Difficulty: This game is hard, im not just complaining here, you dont passive heal in this game as you must use potions which are hard to find when not buying them from a vendor (Which by the way is expensive as hell). Mana for Ailish is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to maintain when using her spells later in the game and melee is hard to master as previously mentioned, if you are struggling badly in this game i reccomend playing as Elco, the gunslinging inventor whenever possible.
This review is for those who dont want to nitpick every little thing and just play and see for themselves, these are just things to look out for before playing.

After 650 hours over three years, this game has hit my number one spot on my personal "best games ever list".  I've been thinking about writing a small review for it for a while but damn there is just way too much to say.  I own all the DLC, each one bought on day one - that is how good this game is.  Sadly, the DLC makes the game so if you're on a budget, wait for it to go on sale and be sure to pick up the Old Gods, Legacy of Rome, Sword of Islam, The Republic, Rajas of India and Horse Lords DLCs, as this will grant you access to most if not all characters in the game.
As for the gameplay, I have never known a better story telling game, role playing game, or strategy game all rolled into one package.  CKII players are always swapping stories about what their characters and their character's families have been going through.  One player on the sub reddit saw his whole Muslim Kingdom become a Western Spanish Jewish Kingdom, another's child turned out to be Satan incarnate, causing witches to flock to his lands and bolster his armies and yet another died of an infected wound a day into the game and got kicked from the server.  It is different each time you play, and I am still adding at least an hour to five hours a week into this game.  Even if no more DLC was to be released, I could see myself playing this game for another 600+ hours.
My own personal story happened when I was playing my first campaign.  I had created my character with the Ruler Designer DLC, and played a single county Count under the newly crowned King William the Conqueror.  My character outlived the King, and grabbed the Kingdom of England for himself.  From the age of 50 to 78, my character solidified his new power and placed his sons on the thrones of the multiple Duchies of the Kingdom until, at the age of 78, he died in battle against rebels in York.
Immediately after his death, his sons took to civil war to fight over their dead father's crown.  I, now playing as the eldest son and new King, found myself fighting all five of my brothers when a divine act of mercy took place.  My mother was a Jimena, daughter of the King of Castille in Northern Spain and I inherited the Kingdom.  The war in England was lost anyway, so when the fifth and final brother demanded he be crowned King of England, I said "Sure buddy, have fun!" and fled to my new Spanish Kingdom.
Fast forward a hundred years and I am now the Emperor of Hispania, having converted all the Spanish penisula into English Catholics, I marry my cousin, the Queen of England, and inherit the Kingdom on my next character.  The rightful King of England had returned, and I soon added Aquitaine and France to my Empire, forming a mighty Western Empire the likes of which had never been seen.  All on my first run.
Then Paradox released a new patch and broke my save.  That doesn't happen so much anymore, but I've yet to have a more enjoyable run.  Do yourself a favour and get this game.

It took until the final boss fight before I could decide whether to give this game a thumbs up or thumbs down.
But the final boss fight made me rage.  Not with the actual boss mechanics - they seem mostly fine.  I've worked out his moves and what I have to do.  What makes me shout at the screen, and why this game gets a thumbs down, is the cumulative effect of a bunch of crappy parts of the battle mechanics and UI.
There are a lot of things to like about this game, and a lot of minor and major negatives.  There is a surprisingly large amount of story and gameplay - it seemed at first that it was going to be a fairly slight game, along the lines of Fable - and the visual styling is a lot like Fable in many ways.  Gameplay-wise it's kind of a cross between Final Fantasy and Fable.
The story itself, and the dialog, are passable.  Fairly typical; nothing too awful, nothing great either.  The actual mythical scenario is quite intriguing, and well introduced (with a Tom Baker voiceover no less - bonus points in the game's favour there).
The RPG elements are ok - putting points into skills and getting better gear and upgrading with augmentations is all ok - nothing particularly deep, but it's there.
The enemies are generally fine - visually distinctive and fairly well animated (particularly for a 2004 game), enough variety to keep fights from all feeling the same.  The encounter mechanism (apart from the stuff directly tied into the main story) is a bit unfortunate - there are effectively marked areas where you are likely to be forced into a fight - not 100% of the time, but most of the time, and there is some randomness in what types of monsters may pop up at any given time.  But every time you enter these areas you are most likely going to have to have pretty much the same fight.  Any time you go exploring and step in one of these areas you can expect to fight, even if you literally just took one step outside the area and realised you needed to go the other way ... fight again!  Hurrah.  It gets old fairly quickly.  Combined with the camera swinging around for no good reason when the fight finishes and it's easy to get disoriented and head the wrong way after a fight ... only to be punished by having to redo the fights to get back on track.
The main character models I found unappealing for a variety of reasons - the boys are just ugly models and the girls are clearly dressed in a way to appeal to 13 year old boys, which is not my cup of tea.  And the ladder climbing animation for the girls - no one in the history of humans climbing ladders has ever climbed a ladder like that.  But meh, it's not a big deal.
What is a big deal is the camera.  This camera is the absolute worst.  It literally prevented me from seeing important parts of the terrain - I could not get it to look where I needed to look (and where the characters could clearly see if only the frickin' camera wasn't being entirely useless).  And the other times when it would swing wildly both disorienting me and completely screwing with movement controls at the same time.  This camera suuuuuuuucks.
The UI is pretty awful in general.  Clunky, slow, menus that are a pain to navigate.  Navigating the clunky menus for certain purposes (using items that are not in your quick access slots eg) does not pause the game - it slows the game down, but you still have to try to find the right item while things are still going on around you, and finding the right item from the crappy lists is just annoying.
Then we get to the characters you control.  The makeup of the group changed throughout the story Final Fantasy style so it mixed up which characters you had access to.  I kind of liked that you could choose which of the gang you wanted to control and let the others mostly just do their own thing.  If you preferred one of the melee characters you could mostly stick with them, or alternatively stick with ranged damage dealers.  I did the latter because I just couldn't get used to the melee battle - it was always a chore.  And sadly at times you are forced into using particular melee characters and it felt clumsy.  The controls always felt clunky - frequent times in combat where there was an enforced delay before you could do something combined with the combo system just made me feel useless - the combos rely on timing, and yet it never felt like the character was in a position to do the attack I wanted them to do at the time I wanted them to do it.  And the blocking/rolling ... grrr ... it was always touch and go whether it would register that you were holding the button to go defensive, and (using a controller) overloading this state to do defensive rolls if you push a direction button was very poorly implemented.
All of that unhappiness with the melee combat resulted in the thumbs down at the final boss fight - you can only use a particular melee character at the end, and it's obviously meant to be a tough challenging fight.  The fact I went basically the entire game avoiding using the melee characters meant it was quite unfamiliar to me anyway, and all the reasons why I had avoided using them came to a glorious symphonic crescendo of hate.  Ugh.
If the final boss fight had not been such a combined mess I would probably have recommended this - barely, given the camera and the crappy UI etc, but still it was engaging enough in its own way.  I do feel I should be forgiving of what is now a fairly old game, but still.  Maybe if you respond better to the melee controls than I did you might enjoy the whole experience that much more.

Holy cow is this game addicting. It's really minimalistic in its controls, but the way it's executed makes it an intense game of skill with a little bit of luck.
Here's a quick look video if you want to see gameplay with my impressions of it. If you'd rather read, just continue below for generally the same thing.

Now before I begin, I'll say you can play this game for free online with pretty much all of the same content. But since it's good to support the devs, you can play it on steam with a better resolution, smoother gameplay, and a controller, which is very much worth it. It also serves as a good demo to see if you'd like the game. Now with that sorted, let's continue this review.
So what is this game? It's about a knight flying up a tower off a rocket and his enemies' face. Why does he do it? Because he wants a harem of princess like any good chap.
Okay, maybe the concept is silly. I get that. But great feeling of progression this game gives is fantastic. Every time you fly up the tower, you amass gold for when you die (and you will die) for the next round when you upgrade your stuff. You can upgrade your sword, health, rocket, potions, luck, and plenty more to give you an edge to make your way up the tower just a little bit farther. Every so often as you scale higher up the tower, you'll reach a princess who will give you a bonus powerup/enemy that'll make your life easier in the next runs. And you'll keep this system up as you fly farther than ever before, encountering harder and more challenging enemies the higher you go.
And that's pretty much it. But while it's so simple, it's a ton of fun with great replayability. It's doesn't even grindy at all since the game has no problem awarding you with gold so you can get that next powerup. There's even achievements and quests that give you side objectives for even more gold. It's really a great system.
If I had anything to ding this game for, it's just how short it is. You'll probably beat the main quest after 2-3 hours. But it does give you a survival mode, so you'll have something to do after that.
But all in all, this is a solid $4 game. Worth every penny. It's mindless fun and a joy to play.

Sudeki is an older game, and I'll admit to having some bias because of nostalgia.  But, as long as you use a gamepad or controller, the port is pretty solid.  My one real complaint is that the game just kind of ends...  You put a lot of hours into growing your characters, and getting to know the world.  And then it's just over. This is essentially a puzzle game, set in a graphically rich, ancient flooded city. You have no weapons, there is no opposition to fight, and you can't die. You must travel from ruined building to ruined building climbing up and around and through every building, finding the supplies and useful items to aid you in your search. As a complete break from any sort of game where you do have a weapon of any sort for offence or defence, I found this a gorgeous water playground, cruising through the very realistic looking deep ocean swells, then clambouring up some very tall buildings working out how to get down, up, around to find everything. Not a particularly long game but a relaxing break from playing the shooters and with some lovely eye candy tossed in as well. If they made a bigger map and added a few extra types of items/buildings... I'd be in like Flynn to buy that too :)

I got so excited when I saw this for $4.99 on Steam. I loved this game as a kid even though I sucked at it. Now I get a chance to play through it all again properly levelling up!
I was worried at first if the port would work on PC, as I had read reviews for Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee being a very poor port worth the same amount on Steam. I saw that Sudeki had received patches and took a leap of faith, was NOT disappointed!
I've clocked 5 hours of gameplay so far and there's no crashing, no glitching or frame drops of any kind. The cutscenes are very blocky (to be fair, it is a super old OG Xbox game) but in-game it looks smooth as silk. I did notice a slight amount of rocky camera movement while running ahead in places but overall that's the only flaw I found. Of course this is mostly a review for the port performance, which I am very pleased and impressed with. The game itself is a fun RPG, charmingly cheesy, terrible voice acting (again, old game), but also gorgeous graphics for its time.
Overall, I'm very happy with how the port for this game turned out. I would definitely recommend it!

An underrated title I am lucky to have played when it was originally released. I don't know many people who have played it but I would recommend it to anyone I know.
While it doesn't seem much different that many other action/adventure titles of it's time this game is unique in almost every way.
The game is a semi open world adventure where you can explore a beautifully designed and colorful world. There are sections of this world that essentially serve as arenas where you have to defeat various enemies before you can move on. The combat in these areas is a combination of either combo based melee or first person shooting and special moves that serve various functions. Each of the four playable characters has different combat abilities that allow them to fit into different roles while all still being balanced and fun characters on their own.
The story is fairly straight forward but still unique and makes the journey through the world very interesting and pushes you forward. The music in the game is also amazing in my opinion and captures the feel of each area very well.
Personally this will always be one of my favorite games of all time, just wish there were more like it.

Just so you know, yes this game has been in production since 2005 when it was named Luguru 2 (which by definition even in Alpha state i believe it surpasses the first Luguru game). Within 2008 it was renamed to Overgrowth, and in 2011 released on steam. Yes....that's a long time to develop a game....but....note this. This IS NOT a AAA title nor is it made by professional developers. Wolfire is comprised of only 4 devs, and that's why updates come slowly and its still in early access. Also They are now moving to a new engine due to the crashes that is being complained about....Now this definately will take a while with only 4 devs. Now lets get back to talking about a triple A game....which is comprised of not just a single team...but multiple teams of Devs up to over hundreds of developers.....How do you think its capable for a CoD game to come out yearly? Plus in games like those they reuse mechanics and code to make  development easier. And NO this game is not abandoned.

I should also point out there, that they plan on taking the campaign/story from Luguru and implementing it within this since......so far it doesn't have any....so that's something to look forward too after the engine transfer (Unreal Engine 4)

As a solo player, I'm of the opinion that this game has tremendous potential. I struggled getting into games like Rust because multiplayer is so unforgiving and I'm so lacking in skill, and I had problems with similar survival games that claimed to have robust single player because either they were barren without other players, they limted my options, or they were so absurdly difficult right from the start that I could never get off the ground.
I'm happy to say Conan Exiles feels like none of these. The early curve is challenging but absolutely surmountable, and there are enough NPCs even out in the wasteland I started out in to make me feel like I'm not the only being in the world. I haven't even gotten to civilization yet and it already feels more populated than single player competitors' games.
For the record, I have pretty much zero familiarity with the Conan lore, but I've still found myself settling in comfortably rather quickly. In fact, at the rate it's going, it may introduce me to a new mythos I end up really enjoying.
Strong recommendation. If the game is this fun this early in development, I can only imagine how engaging it'll be down the road. (Side note: If you're like me and you lack a hardcore gaming rig, you're in luck: Conan Exiles has very scalable graphics and still looks "pretty enough" on low settings that my GT 730 runs it perfectly acceptably.)

I decided to give it a chance anyway, and I'm glad I did.
It's not what I was looking to play, but I actually really like it, at least as far as the campaign is concerned. You can't pause to issue orders, which is disappointing, but you can slow the action down and play at a pace that works for you. Unit sorting is complicated, but I never really feel like I need it, I just plop down a war banner at the center of the action and keep my units healed with magic. I can't really tell if I'm winning because I'm doing well, or because the campaign is just easy, but it's still an RTS that I can actually enjoy, and has made me decide to try more games in the genre, so in my book that's a pretty big accomplishment.

Not quite as challenging as Morrowind or as epic as Skyrim, but still a great game for RPG fans (even if you don't buy any DLC) and this installment is what made the Elder Scrolls series known to a lot of people including myself.
The magic combat has the right amount of variety (Skyrim had too few spell effects and Morrowind had too many) and you can make your own spells and enchantments reasonably early on in the game (Join the Mage's Guild).
Close range combat can be a bit tedious after a while; swipe left, swipe right and hope the enemy is dead before too long (and a lot of spinning when you do power attacks).
The most fun I had from the combat system was with bows. I always had fun testing what extreme distances you can kill someone from.
There's a lot of room for actual roleplaying as well. I've heard of players dressing up as guards and patroling towns, ones that WALK between towns instead of running all the way and so on. Sounds pretty wierd to me but it's just not my cup of tea.
The only downside is there doesn't seem to be a Steam version that comes with ALL the DLC (Wizard's Tower, The Orrery, Thieve's Den ect.); just the main two for now.
9/10, wholly recommended and all my time spent playing was worth it.

If you were around for the Dreamcast's brief lifespan, you'll remember some of the stylized, imaginative, and just plain "they would never approve this as a full budget disc release today" games that marked the system's legacy, shortly before it flamed out amongst the likes of the Playstation 2 and the XBox. Jet Grind Radio, as we knew it in North America, was a big deal at the time, thanks in no small part to the cel-shaded graphics ("it looks like a cartoon!") and its absurd premise of street ruffians with magnetic inline skates tagging their turf with graffiti while evading an escalating police onslaught tantamount to the Five-O's response in a Grand Theft Auto game. Apparently urban vandalism is an offense so severe as to warrant an "execute on sight" approach by the logic of JSR's universe, and yet tagging is the only thing that can stop an evil corporate overlord with a giant turntable on top of a skyscraper from using a forbidden vinyl record to summon the devil. Look, if you weren't already drawn in by the aesthetic, the plot isn't going to make converts of anyone.
I'll be the first to admit more than a little bit of bias due to the affection that I and others from my gaming generation have for the Dreamcast. Without making a wholesale "you kind of had to be there" qualifier in my endorsement of Jet Set Radio, the fact is that some of its gameplay aspects haven't held up very well. The controls never felt quite right while trying to stick a rail and initiate a grind, a skill that is crucial to master if you're going to get a handle for traversing the game's maps to make all your tagging goals within the time limit. Sometimes it feels like the geometry could have been a little more forgiving, other times it's the camera that causes you to fumble around in empty space before plummeting past your intended rail, and even after hours of play it's hard to get a feel positioning your character for grinds. Tricks were never supposed to be the game's selling point, but every time a half pipe shows up, the weird space-time dilation of your skater's momentum that occurs combined with the camera's abrupt low swoop gives me a sense of mild vertigo. I usually end up just skating up the side of the pipe and coming to a stop so I can scoot my way forward to the tagging point I'm supposed to hit. Fun.
The PC port supplements the basic Dreamcast controls by adding camera control with the right analog stick, which while not an unwelcome addition, doesn't add much benefit while trying to navigate levels that were never designed to be these massive sprawling cityscapes. The result is that panning the camera around makes the environment seem a little more claustrophobic. JSR's graphical aesthetic still holds up pretty well, although as a game originally intended for 480i televisions, some of the seams start to show on a modern high resolution monitor. The primitive models for bystanders stand out much more in comparison to your articulate skater, and some of the textures are just butt ugly.
Still, time hasn't done much to dilute Jet Set Radio's charm, and I can't rightly call it a bad game despite its more frustrating gameplay moments (there's that bias showing again, whither goest thou, objectivity?). Some will undoubtedly be less tolerant of the clunky controls than I was during my revisit of it, and had it been framed as a regular inline skating game with less heart and a celebrity endorsement and Offspring songs, I probably wouldn't have given it much of my time either. If you want to briefly reconnect with the good feels that JSR gave you back in the day, this port will scratch that itch. But if you still have a (functioning) Dreamcast sitting in the attic, you might as well dust that off and fire up some of the other classics from that era.

Actually I am sitting on the fence a bit with this new Spellforce game. I've clocked a number of hours but haven't got a long way through as yet. But I'll give it a thumbs up merely because I think it will end up ok - vastly different to the number of thumbs down reviews here from people who have spent little time in the game and their issues sound more like technical or other problems rather then an actual "review" of the game itself.
Sure, it's got a few bugs, but I haven't seen a game release in ages that didn't have bugs first up - sometimes badly affecting even being able to play. It does have some other developer issues like the stealth mission in the Stepping Stones "My god what were they thinking!". This kind of mission doesn't suit this type of top down rpg/rts at all. And there are bugs where if you skip missions, do things in the wrong order or something, some weird things show up. But like all other games, the dev's do hear about these issues and I'm sure there's patches coming.
The game itself, well if you have ever played the other Spellforce games, it will be instantly recognisable. it's much the same gameplay. What they are doing here is finishing up the story of the entire series. Considering the series started a long time ago, I've forgotten most of the story anyway... but, certain things do spark a memory flash in my brain at times.
The game is reasonably priced, it's not an "A" title, so don't expect the latest graphics and latest engine, it's running on the old Spellforce 2 engine. So far it's reasonably enjoyable, although sometimes a little frustrating. Mainly because the game so far is pretty linear in format. Even though they have lots of side quests (so they say) they are really nothing and get swallowed up by the main quest ie: if you complete a section of the main quest line then bang! Those side quests you had are now irrelevant or unplayable because you moved on - literally - it shifts you to a different area in the game world.
I guess Spellforce has always been a bit like this - just wasn't expecting for it to hit me so hard in the face with it, like when it transports you off to the Stepping Stones and you are sitting there going "No, I need to level up and I wanted to visit the merchants and that side quest I was doing...oh...bugger".
But as I said, it's not an "A" title and it's price means it's most probably worth it, so give it a shot - whether you've played Spellforce before or not.

Spellforce 2: Demons Of The Past is an RPG and strategy game by Hungarian developer Mind Over Matter, under the command Nordic Games, who also published Faith in Destiny, the second SpellForce 2 expansion.
With a new single player campaign offering 25+ hours of gameplay, Spellforce 2: Demons of the past provides the cherry on Spellforce 2’s cake. In a game where nearly all Races are playable — Pact, Shaikan and even the Undead, Demons Of The Past provides a rounding-off experience of the series. The standalone expansion also features the popular free multiplayer game mode, where the events of the single player campaign can be experienced with friends and adversaries alike. Further than the multiplayer aspect, a new survival mode has been created with distinctive objectives and gameplay.
In one word: let-down. One of the issues that strikes me with Demons Of The Past is the apparant lack of effort that went into the game. Whilst the storyline carries on in applaud-able fashion, with the threat of seemingly endless armies of The Nameless Evil, with the expected appearances from dragons and formidable unearthly forces, the quality and initial ease of play is enough to make playing the game nothing short of painful. The storyline carries the game well, with some frankly beautiful digital artwork in the cut scenes, but it is impossible to ignore the dummy-like mouth movements of the characters in conversation, who stop talking even though the audio of their voices carries on warning of war and treachery. All this and more interruptions occur whilst you try and build defences from skeleton warriors, and lament for the lack of simplicity in some of the gameplay aspects.

Although Faith in Destiny, the previous (also chronologically) installment of Spellforce series, was slightly disappointing, Demons of the Past is an amazing game, especially for the fans of the Spellforce series.
Gameplay - RTS and RPG mix still exists. Although I always liked Spellforce 1 (platinum edition on Steam)'s RPG system (skill building, etc.) more, the RPG side of Demons of the Past is pretty great still. Many side quests and main quests give you many details about the story, making it long, good and rich. RTS, on the other hand, is really good - challenging, yet easy to do still. The system also makes it easier to use some of the skills, spells and other special abilities. Army often can even do it on their own. It may be a bit hard for the newcomers at the start, but not too hard.
Soundtrack - as always, soundtrack to this new part of the series is pretty good.
Voice acting - it has certainly improved from previous titles.
Bugs - there may be a couple, but nothing too big. They haven't really bothered me.
I haven't played multiplayer with DotP much yet, but previous titles were already a lot of fun. You can even play the campaign with someone cooperatively.
Overall - 4 out of 5. It brings a good end to Spellforce 2, similar to Dragon Storm, and perhaps equally dark to Shadow of the Phoenix. Although the engine is old, it was improved. It may have some bugs and/or a downside or two here and there, but it has been a very enjoyable game with a very good story and also a good to Spellforce 2.

Submerged is a 3d exploration game set in the overgrown ruins of a partly flooded city. You navigate your boat through the ruins until you find natural mooring places - at these, you can leave the boat and climb the respective building. The goal of the game is to save your injured brother by finding 10 supply crates, which are scattered across the city. Optionally, you can also search for 60 "secrets" that will tell you more about the city's history. While the game progresses, you will also learn more about your own past.
The stories about your past (and that of the city) are told by showing simple images, which look like child drawings and form story sequences. I found them touching in their melancholy, even though they remained quite simple.
The climbing mechanics, which form the main part of the gameplay, are very simple as well. You cannot fail or fall, invisible walls rein you in. Surprisingly for a game that focuses so much on exploration, there is actually not much freedom for doing so. Many buildings are just decoration, some just consist of two ledges that lead to a "secret" - less than a dozen buildings actually provide areas to explore. Even on those, you can only climb along very few pre-defined linear paths, with occasional branches. Your character cannot jump, so even a knee-high step poses an insurmountable obstacle.
The graphics are amazingly beautiful, though a bit repetitive. There are lots of copy-pasted plants and walls, but you'll also keep finding the occasional new structure while exploring. Excellent, calm music enhances the relaxing gameplay and the melancholic atmosphere.
The game seems very polished, as it provides many of the convenience features that often get forgotten:
Personally I liked the game for its beauty, its emotional (if simple) story, and its relaxing atmosphere. I was disappointed by the very limited freedom of movement while exploring the ruins, but still enjoyed the experience. In the end this is a short and rather simplistic game that does not try to offer a lot of things, but does quite well on most of the aspects that it
offer. I feel, however, that the current price tag (20€ SRP, down to 6.79€ on sales) is too high for the game's limited content. At this price, I'll recommend to wait. At half that price, I'd recommend to buy it, if the game's strong points cover things that you like.

If you’ve ever become totally immersed in a game, then you know what it is to experience the world of Submerged. With an unarmed young female protagonist possessing nothing but a small boat, you wander a silent, lonely apocalyptic city that is submerged in a futuristic fantasy oceanic world. Nature has reclaimed what appears to be a formerly advanced civilization. Statues and monuments half protrude majestically from the water. And with the loss of civilization, you witness the death of words.

The graphics and audio are unbelievably fresh and real. I can feel the water. I smell the salt in the air! The aged grandeur of the archeology and architecture remind me of Enslaved: Odyssey to the West. But, the similarity stops there. A more accurate comparison would be to the Uncharted series which is on the PlayStation platform only. In the unparalleled world of Uncharted, you have a 4 way combination of platforming, combat, puzzle solving, and treasure hunting that has something for everyone embedded in exotic locales. Submerged takes the two areas of platforming and treasure hunting apart from the heavier elements of risk and submerges you in an environment of total safety to allow you to focus on treasure hunting and uncovering a wordless story. The experience is, in a word, surreal and the music is a haunting melody.
The mystery is unhampered by this non-violent approach. Without providing any spoilers, you remain focused on solving the mysteries of your world, this partially submerged city, and your own family by searching for pieces of the story high and low on the buildings, while you search for medicine and supplies for your little brother who is unconscious. You use your map, compass, and telescope to search for treasures and clues to solve the mystery. There are no maluses, and no damage is taken from any actions in the game. But, watching the young girl climb on the buildings certainly brings back memories of childhood spent climbing trees and exploring the mountains.
The search is conducted from your boat, which is great fun to drive. As you find pieces from other abandoned boats, you are able to upgrade the speed of your own boat. This makes it possible to speed across to hidden parts of the map in search of missing clues. Basically, it also forces you to take the early game slower to allow you to experience the silent world that might be missed by flying through too quickly.
You could possibly play through in just a few hours, though I spent a dozen on the first play-through. It took a few more to collect the remaining clues. Not only is the game worth the price I paid, but I will definitely be buying it on PlayStation IV, just because I want to play it again on that platform. It really is a great game.
The story is presented entirely in the visuals of the architecture, the statues, the people, and the rebus story pieces, which have a post-modern feel of having slipped back into a prehistoric world without speech. Hieroglyphic letters are seen with the images, but you can’t decipher them. The girl speaks, but it’s an unknown dialect/language of only a few syllables. When you encounter new locations and objects the names appear on screen.
The names of the statues reveal story themselves. As an example, a grand horse appears that is named only, ‘The Obdurate Creature.’
This name points to more of the mystery which I will not spoil.

The game is, unfortunately, marred by many flaws.
The primary one, for a game of this type, is that the art quality simply isn't up to the standards of modern Triple-A game that's going to be seen at 1080p resolution. The art itself is well done, and the engine seems to do a reasonable job of rendering what's there, but tripling the artist-hours put in to this game and allowing for 10 GB rather than 2.5 GB of textures would have made a huge difference. That said, this is forgivable for an indie project where a huge artist budget simply isn't there; perhaps it's better to think of this as a demo of what the developers could really do, and a demo well worth playing.
The other major flaw is in certain areas of game design that simply, it appears, did not get enough time, testing and reworking. For example, a fair amount of clambering and climbing is required to reach a supply chest, which is the major item of progression in the game. Upon opening it you are immediately transported back to your home base, even if there are secrets yet to uncover nearby. When you go back (through the same complex route), there is no longer any quick way out; you must reverse what you did to come in. (Remember, it's impossible to die in this game; you can't fall off a ledge.)
The rest of the much more minor flaws are mentioned extensively in other reviews: the short playtime (which didn't bother me--my backlog is long enough already!), the repetition, and so on. They don't really affect the core of the game; they affect only how much you should pay for it.
And that's where we come to the price: $20 is probably a little too rich for most people who would otherwise like this game. Possibly this is simply part of a "frequent sales" marketing strategy, which is fair enough, though, especially on Steam. I paid $5 for this game myself, and I'd rate it at worth $5-$10. If ten bucks isn't a big deal to you, buy it at that price or even more; if $5-$7 is an amount you think about before spending, wait for that price, and you'll get your money's worth.
Before ending the review, I must mention the brilliant "Postcard Mode": this pauses the game and lets you move the camera around to set up a screenshot. This is a brilliant feature that I wish all games had, and is also a great learning tool for budding in-game photographers.

Not quite as challenging as Morrowind or as epic as Skyrim, but still a great game for RPG fans (even if you don't buy any DLC) and this installment is what made the Elder Scrolls series known to a lot of people including myself.
The magic combat has the right amount of variety (Skyrim had too few spell effects and Morrowind had too many) and you can make your own spells and enchantments reasonably early on in the game (Join the Mage's Guild).
Close range combat can be a bit tedious after a while; swipe left, swipe right and hope the enemy is dead before too long (and a lot of spinning when you do power attacks).
The most fun I had from the combat system was with bows. I always had fun testing what extreme distances you can kill someone from.
There's a lot of room for actual roleplaying as well. I've heard of players dressing up as guards and patroling towns, ones that WALK between towns instead of running all the way and so on. Sounds pretty wierd to me but it's just not my cup of tea.
The only downside is there doesn't seem to be a Steam version that comes with ALL the DLC (Wizard's Tower, The Orrery, Thieve's Den ect.); just the main two for now.
9/10, wholly recommended and all my time spent playing was worth it.

This game... It's hard for me to describe. It's incredibly interesting, fun, but brain smashingly deep and slow paced. I'm just going to be frank with you. This game, isn't for everyone. In fact, it's not for a lot of people. Even HUGE fans of video games who have been playing for decades and love seeing new things are going to be put off by it. So why am I rating it as a must buy? Because if those problems don't bother you and you're willing to give this game a shot it's really rewarding.
First things first: You must, and I can't stress this enough you MUST play through the entire tutorial. The tutorial alone will probably take you an hour or two and by the time you're finished you're still going to be unbelievably horrid at the game. But that's the price you have to pay to get started in this title. Once you've finished the tutorials it's time to head into the game itself.
Second: Choose a smaller nation to start, I'd suggest Denmark. Don't do what I did and go straight to England. Because 10 seconds into the start of the game you're going to be invaded by William the Conqueror, and he's going to smash everything you have and, well, conquer the entire island. (Hence the title, you don't earn a title like that from being a nice "live and let live" kind of a guy) From Denmark you'll have a chance to really test your hand at the game and expand your influence slowly. Play that nation for a hundred years or so to get a feel for things and then move on to something more interesting and start over with a larger nation and more issues. I'd suggest France, big armies, lots of influence, and no invading Normans (though you'll lose a lot of your Nothern lands because of William. You can take them back later)
Third: Try playing as France for a while. If you're anything like me, you still don't know exactly what your doing and♥♥♥♥♥♥off the nobles so much that the kingdom splits into 4 different smaller kingdoms in a state of perpetual civil war. Time to start over again.
Fourth: Start again as France. This time, do what you need to do to keep your nobles happy and in line. Maybe take some time off of politics and declare holy war on the Muslims living in Spain. (Pro tip, if you can get away with it send the armies of the nobles who don't like you so much there to conquer everything. Their men will die and if they rebel you can crush them that much easier)
Fifth: Now that you've spent about 13 hours learning how to play the dang game it's time to try to build a lasting legacy. Welcome to Crusader Kings 2!
Pros:
-Holy information dump Batman! I'm not kidding when I say this, but you are going to learn a TON while playing this game if you have the mind to. From wikipedia articles detailing the histories of the nobility to tems like casus belli you will walk away smarter for having played. (I told you video games would make me smarter mom!)
-The characters in the game, as they are, actually act according to their stats and traits (perish the thought)
-Moral dilemmas all over the place. Do you punish that rival duke by taking his lands and making everyone else hate you for it, or do you just throw him in prison. What do you do with your only son who is an imbecile and your current king doesn't have much time left to live. etc.
Cons:
-There is soooo much to remember and keep track of that the barrier to entry of this game is huge. Imagine attacking a castle wall that is: on fire, covered in poisoned chainsaws, and patrolled by every single boss from the Dark/Demon Souls franchise armed only with a copy of this months Cosmopolitan and a tube sock. This game's barrier to entry is worse than that!
-Art style is very basic. It still looks good, but if you don't enjoy staring at old maps for a long time this isn't the game for you.
All in all, you need to give this game serious and careful consideration before you put down one penny on it. For some people (maybe, 15-20% tops of the gaming crowd) they are going to have a great time with this game. For everyone else, move on, nothing to see here.

Sudeki begins by setting out the theme of duality using shadow puppets, and this theme is largely carried through its story as you fight against the darkness for the light. The story, though clearly cartoony, is decently solid within the game's theme and trappings. Its a shame the shadow puppets aren't used more though.
Mechanically, the Sudeki is linear with character building elements from RPGs. In combat it plays as a hack and slash or FPS depending on teh character you are using, while the other characters serve as distractions. You can cycle through different characters during battle though, enabling you to maximize use of special abilities. This was certainly novel at the time of the game's creation and its not poorly implemented.
What is poorly implemented is the camera. Sometimes you have complete control over it. Sometimes you have none. Sometimes it turns the opposite way that you want it. Of course, when the camera shifts, so does the direct you are moving your toon, sometimes even causing your character to go the opposite direction, locking you into constantly occilating camera angles. This caused the game to crash once.
On the whole, although Sudeki shows its age, it was fun and worth the sale price.

Oh boy. Not even an hour of play and I already have a review ready. And as you can tell, no, I can't recommend the game at this stage.
Tanki X is, quite obviously, a third-person tank shooter. At the time of writing it has been in Early Access for about 3 months. While it shows some faint glimmer of promise, it's buried beneath a complete lack of thought behind pretty much all of the mechanics, as I'll detail below.
So first, in its favor, the game looks pretty great, and is fairly well optimized. Rock-solid 60fps on an i5-6600, 8GB DDR4 2133, and a 1050Ti, at what the game claims was 4k, but was actually quite obviously 1080p because it didn't supersample correctly.
So to start things off, you're given a menu where you can quickly jump into a game or visit the garage in which you customize your tank. Starting off you have literally no customization options available to you, so into a match you go.
So your starting tank is pretty much a jack-of-all trades. Medium armor, range, and firepower set you up nicely to do fairly well. But in your first match you will immediately see a problem. Namely that the gameplay is stupidly simplistic, to the point that your ability to succeed depends wholly on either your ability to gank other players, or your ability to flank because literally every other player is as dumb as a sack of bricks. I'm not kidding. I have literally sat to the right side of five other players who were focused on something way down range, and killed three of them before anyone noticed something was wrong. There's also powerups from the looks of it, but I can't figure out how to actually pick them up, or even if I can, so I can't comment on those.
Now what I said about the gameplay is very easily explained. You see, you don't really have any ability to aim at all. You point your camera in the general vicinity of an enemy tank, a red lock-on symbol appears, and then you can fire freely and will literally never miss. The shell travel times are so stupidly fast that no matter how fast a tank moves you cannot avoid shots through mobility. It's so bad at first I thought it was hitscan. While there are some vague attempts to add more depth, these just serve to provide more overt advantages with no counters. For example, if you take higher ground, you'll have longer range and tanks lower to the ground will have a harder time targeting you. Due to this, the obvious solution would be to move up to more even footing with the enemy... except most high ground is stupidly defensible, and you can kill pretty much anyone before they can reach you unless there's three or four all after you at once. And with these variations removed all things do is turn into a contest to see who can withstand more hits before blowing up. Or who has better range, on larger maps.
So while the basic gameplay is plainly lacking, maybe the tank customization will make it better and add more variety and strategy? Well no. Not at all. You see, you have two things you can alter: The turret and the main body. There are a myriad of different turret types, and the game does a good job of making each one feel unique. But it doesn't matter in the slightest because the style of gameplay is such that you have no reason to pick anything but the longest-range weapon you can, or if you're in really close quarters, something with a good mix of range and power. You encounter the same problem when choosing a main body. While there's a bunch of variety, there's no reason to pick anything but the slowest, most durable body you can, because it's impossible to move fast enough for shells to not hit you 100% of the time. So you may as well just increase your survivability.
While I have some other, more minor complaints relating to the graphics options, ultimately those are a matter of personal preference and as such will not be covered here.
TL;DR: While I can applaud the idea of trying to make a tank game far less complex than the competition, this game takes that idea to its worst extreme to create an extremely bland title that promotes only one style of gameplay.
While some may argue that due to its early access status this may easily change, I have to say that this game should never have been put into early access in the first place. The entire point of early access is to give players access to raise money for further development, but if there's nothing to keep someone playing, then there's no reason for someone to actually buy anything in-game.

The game isn't long, about 5-10 hours to complete the game (grab all the secrets and collectibles, and achieve every achievement); but what a wonderful 5-10 hours you'll have if you enjoy atmospheric games.
Exploration is fun and gives the illusion of freedom well enough to keep you immersed, even if the building climbing is a set path(s). It can be annoying if you missed a secret, but even that isn't too awful.
The world itself is beautiful and the character design is well done and matches the world design, especially as you get into the story. And the backstory is interesting as you must interpret a series of pictures (world backstory is gained from finding secrets and character backstory is discovered from story progression) that explain how things came to be.
It's also a "safe" game: the only way to fail is to quit and give up. However, that doesn't mean there aren't a couple of more tense moments.
And the music, while not the pinnacle of anything, is beautiful; and I'm not upset at the extra money the soundtrack cost.
I purchased it on sale and recommend that anyone interested grab it for that; but don't be afraid to pay full price if you can spare the extra money and like the idea of a no-rush, safe, atmospheric game when you want a break from the normal.

If you you're like me, you stumbled upon this in search of spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper 1\2...
You've found it.
The narration is on point. The mechanics are everything you remember, and what's been added doesn't feel out of place. As a matter of fact, I picked up DKII after making it through the campaign, and (with a degree of guilt) I have to say this truly surpasses it.
The campaign, admittedly, leans towards the short side. You'll still put a decent amount of time into it (I can't recall how long it took me tbh), but it leaves you wanting a bit more. You would put in some effort, but I never really felt tested (others may disagree, for different reasons, but that was how I was left feeling about it). Nonetheless, it was great. It satisfied exactly what I needed, and actually improved upon the DK experience. Familiar but refreshing I guess.
When the campaign finished, I played the My Pet Dungeon level that was included (it's a little bit different than MPD in DKII, but in the best ways). The My Pet Dungeon level, I was happy to find had actual objectives. You can play at your own pace, like a sandbox, but you have motivation that keeps it going. This was refreshing to me, as objectiveless play, especially for something like this, just gets old. There were actually some points that I found myself more challenged than in the campaign (odd, but a pleasant surprise). The My Pet Dungeon levels were a great addition... but then I made it through those as well, and why not keep a good thing going...
So, I went ahead and got the Heart of Gold Expansion... Again, thoroughly enjoyed ALMOST every bit of it... The ONLY thing I didn't care for, and I mean the ONLY thing, was that you would start off each level with pretty much everything unlocked... I prefer a bit of a paced struggle to the top, but right away, all the spells and everything were available to me... Oh well, can't win 'em all. Regardless, I highly recommend it. Adds some new fun toys, and provides a new campaign to burn through (though, it's half of the original campaign's length... so if that's a deal-breaker for you, there you have it...).
Now, a big thing for me that I've recently started playing around with, is the Skirmish mode... Never dabbled with it in DK (that I remember), but it's actually quite a bit of fun. I've been turning that into my new campaign, map by map... It's been a fun new challenge, and provides objective based replay. I actually played with the map editor for the first time last night. I spent an hour-hour and half messing with it, and it actually turned out great. I plan on making a series of maps as I get more comfortable with it. The only real gripe I have, is there aren't really any terrain brushes (ie. Size, Randomization, etc.), and there isn't (that I've found, only messed with it once, so apologies if I'm mistaken!) an event editor... So scenarios you create have to be crafted by the map. No triggering invasions, this, that, or the other at the moment.
I have a bad habit of getting games, putting a few hours in, and moving on. I've only had this game for prly 2 months, and have put 100+ hours in. For me to put that much time into video games in general is a lot. I'm really hoping they publish a few more campaign expansions, but even if they don't I've gotten more than my moneys worth, and will continue to.
Overall   9.5/10
